en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Discourse on the Summary of the Abhidhamma:

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, upon the yellow sandalwood stone slab. There, the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Abhidhamma to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
1. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī Matrix:
The Threefold Matrix Wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states. States associated with pleasant feeling...
Phenomena associated with painful feeling; phenomena associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Resultant phenomena; phenomena that are of the nature to result; phenomena that are neither resultant nor of the nature to result.

Phenomena that are appropriated and subject to clinging; phenomena that are not appropriated but subject to clinging; phenomena that are neither appropriated nor subject to clinging. Defiled and subject to defilement.
States that are not defiled but subject to defilement; states that are neither defiled nor subject to defilement. States with applied thought and sustained thought;
states without applied thought and with sustained thought only; states without applied thought and without sustained thought. States accompanied by rapture; states accompanied by pleasure;
states accompanied by equanimity. States to be abandoned by vision; [states to be abandoned] by cultivation...
States to be abandoned; states not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation. States whose roots are to be abandoned by vision;
states whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation; states whose roots are not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
States leading to accumulation; states leading to dispersal; states leading neither to accumulation nor to dispersal.
States of those in training (sekha), states of those beyond training (asekha), and states that are neither of those in training nor beyond training.
Limited states, exalted states, and immeasurable states. States with limited objects, states with exalted objects, and states with immeasurable objects.
Inferior states, intermediate states, and superior states. States fixed in falsehood, and states fixed in rightness.
Dhammas; indeterminate dhammas. Dhammas having the Path as their object, dhammas caused by the Path, dhammas dominated by the Path.
Arisen dhammas, unarisen dhammas, dhammas liable to arise. Past dhammas, future dhammas, present dhammas.
Dhammas having the past as their object, dhammas having the future as their object, dhammas having the present as their object.
Phenomena (dhammas). Internal phenomena, external phenomena, internal-external phenomena.
Phenomena with internal objects, phenomena with external objects, phenomena with internal-external objects.
Phenomena that are visible and impinging, phenomena that are invisible but impinging, phenomena that are invisible and non-impinging.
The Twenty-Twofold Set.
The Twofold Matrix.
The Group on Causes.
States that are roots; states that are not roots. States accompanied by roots; states without roots.
States associated with roots; states dissociated from roots. States that are both roots and accompanied by roots; states that are accompanied by roots but are not roots.
States that are both roots and associated with roots; states that are associated with roots but are not roots. States that are not roots.
Furthermore, phenomena (dhammas) are both with cause and without cause. This is the Group on Causes (Hetugocchaka).
The Minor Intermediate Dyad:
phenomena with conditions and phenomena without conditions; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; visible phenomena...
Phenomena; non-demonstrable phenomena. Phenomena with resistance; phenomena without resistance. Material phenomena;
immaterial phenomena. Mundane phenomena; supramundane phenomena. Phenomena cognizable by something; phenomena not cognizable by anything.
This is the Minor Intermediate Dyads.
The Group on Taints (Āsavagocchaka):
States that are taints; states that are not taints. States associated with taints;
states dissociated from taints. States that are both taints and associated with taints; states that are associated with taints but are not taints.
States that are both taints and associated with taints; states that are associated with taints but are not themselves taints;
and states that are dissociated from taints, which may be either with taints or without taints.
This is the group on taints. The group on fetters.
States that are fetters; states that are not fetters. States that are conducive to fetters; states that are not conducive to fetters.
States associated with fetters; states dissociated from fetters. States that are both fetters and conducive to fetters;
states that are conducive to fetters but are not fetters. States that are both fetters and associated with fetters; states associated with fetters...

And there are states that are not fetters. Furthermore, states dissociated from the fetters are both subject to fettering and not subject to fettering. This is the group of fetters (*saññojana-gocchaka*).
The group of ties (*gantha-gocchaka*):
states that are ties, states that are not ties; states subject to tying, states not subject to tying; states associated with ties...
Phenomena; phenomena dissociated from the ties. Phenomena that are both ties and subject to the ties; phenomena that are subject to the ties but are not themselves ties.
Phenomena that are both ties and associated with the ties; phenomena that are associated with the ties but are not themselves ties.
Furthermore, phenomena dissociated from the ties may be either subject to the ties or not subject to the ties. This concludes the group on the ties (*gantha*).

The Group on Floods: states that are floods; states that are not floods. States that are subject to floods; states that are not subject to floods. States associated with floods; states dissociated from floods.
States that are both floods and subject to floods; states that are subject to floods but are not floods.
There are states that are both floods and associated with floods; there are states that are associated with floods but are not floods.
Furthermore, states dissociated from floods are both subject to floods and not subject to floods. This is the group on floods.
The group on bonds.
States that are yokes; states that are not yokes. States that lead to the yokes; states that do not lead to the yokes. States associated with the yokes; states dissociated from the yokes.
States that are both yokes and lead to the yokes; states that lead to the yokes but are not yokes.
States that are both yokes and associated with the yokes; states that are associated with the yokes but are not yokes. States dissociated from the yokes.
Furthermore, phenomena are both conducive to bondage (*yoganiya*) and not conducive to bondage (*ayoganiya*). This is the group on bondage (*yogagocchaka*).
The group on hindrances (*nīvaraṇagocchaka*):

phenomena that are hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), phenomena that are not hindrances; phenomena conducive to hindrances (*nīvaraṇiya*), phenomena not conducive to hindrances; [phenomena] associated with hindrances (*nīvaraṇasampayutta*).

States; states dissociated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). There are states that are both hindrances and subject to hindrance (*nīvaraṇiya*); there are states that are subject to hindrance but are not themselves hindrances.
There are states that are both hindrances and associated with hindrances; there are states that are associated with hindrances but are not themselves hindrances.
Furthermore, states dissociated from the hindrances may be either subject to hindrance or not subject to hindrance. This concludes the group on the hindrances.
The Group on Misapprehension: states that are misapprehensions; states that are not misapprehensions. States that are misapprehended; states that are not misapprehended.
States associated with misapprehension; states dissociated from misapprehension. States that are both misapprehensions and misapprehended; states that are misapprehended but are not misapprehensions.
Dhammas that are not graspings. Furthermore, dhammas dissociated from grasping are both grasped and not grasped. The Group on Grasping. The Great Intermediate Dyads:
Dhammas with an object; dhammas without an object. Dhammas that are consciousness; dhammas that are not consciousness. Dhammas that are mental factors.

Mental factors (acetasika dhammā). Phenomena associated with consciousness (cittasampayutta dhammā), phenomena dissociated from consciousness (cittavippayutta dhammā). Phenomena conjoined with consciousness (cittasaṃsaṭṭha dhammā), phenomena not conjoined with consciousness (cittavisaṃsaṭṭha dhammā).
Phenomena originated by consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhāna dhammā), phenomena not originated by consciousness (no cittasamuṭṭhāna dhammā).

Phenomena co-existent with consciousness (cittasahabhū dhammā), phenomena not co-existent with consciousness (no cittasahabhū dhammā). Phenomena that follow consciousness (cittānuparivatti dhammā), phenomena that do not follow consciousness (no cittānuparivatti dhammā).
Phenomena. Phenomena conjoined with and produced by mind; phenomena not conjoined with and produced by mind. Phenomena conjoined with, produced by, and co-existent with mind;
phenomena not conjoined with, produced by, and co-existent with mind. Phenomena that follow upon what is conjoined with and produced by mind;
phenomena that do not follow upon what is conjoined with and produced by mind. Internal phenomena; external phenomena.
Phenomena. Phenomena that are clinging, phenomena that are not clinging. Phenomena that are grasped, phenomena that are not grasped.
The Great Pair. The Group on Clinging:
phenomena that are clinging, phenomena that are not clinging; phenomena that are objects of clinging, phenomena that are not objects of clinging; phenomena associated with clinging.
States; states dissociated from clinging. States that are both clinging and objects of clinging; states that are objects of clinging but are not clinging.
States that are both clinging and associated with clinging; states that are associated with clinging but are not clinging.
Furthermore, states dissociated from clinging may be either objects of clinging or not objects of clinging. This is the Group on Clinging (*upādāna-gocchaka*).
The Group on Defilements: phenomena that are defilements; phenomena that are not defilements. Phenomena that are subject to defilement; phenomena that are not subject to defilement.
Phenomena that are defiled; phenomena that are not defiled. Phenomena associated with defilement; phenomena dissociated from defilement. Defilements.
There are phenomena that are both defiling and defilements; there are phenomena that are defiling but are not defilements.
There are phenomena that are both defilements and defiled; there are phenomena that are defiled but are not defilements. There are phenomena that are both defilements and associated with defilements;
there are phenomena that are associated with defilements but are not defilements. Furthermore, phenomena dissociated from defilements may also be defiling.
Also those that are non-defiled. The Group on Defilements.
The Subsequent Pair:
states to be abandoned by vision, states not to be abandoned by vision; states to be abandoned by cultivation.
States not to be abandoned by cultivation; states whose roots are to be abandoned by vision, states whose roots are not to be abandoned by vision;
states whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation, states whose roots are not to be abandoned by cultivation;
states with applied thought, states without applied thought; states with sustained thought, states without sustained thought; states accompanied by rapture, states without rapture.
Phenomena. Phenomena accompanied by rapture, phenomena not accompanied by rapture. Phenomena accompanied by pleasure, phenomena not accompanied by pleasure.
Phenomena accompanied by equanimity, phenomena not accompanied by equanimity. Phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, phenomena not belonging to the sense sphere.
Phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere, phenomena not belonging to the fine-material sphere. Phenomena belonging to the immaterial sphere, phenomena not [belonging to the immaterial sphere].
States belonging to the formless realm. States that are included, states that are not included. States that lead out, states that do not lead out.
States that are fixed, states that are unfixed. States that have something higher, states that have nothing higher.
States with conflict, states without conflict. This is the "Backward Pair."
The Abhidhamma Duka Matrix.
The Sutta Duka Matrix:
states pertaining to clear knowledge, states not pertaining to clear knowledge; states comparable to lightning, states comparable to a thunderbolt; fools...
Dhammas; wise dhammas. Dark dhammas, bright dhammas. Dhammas that lead to remorse, dhammas that do not lead to remorse.
Designations, the pathways of designation. Language, the pathways of language. Descriptions, the pathways of description.
Name and form. Ignorance and craving for existence. The view of existence.
And the view of non-existence and the view of existence; the view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism; the view of finitude and the view of infinity;
the view regarding the past and the view regarding the future; moral shamelessness and lack of dread of wrongdoing; moral shame and dread of wrongdoing;
being difficult to speak to and having evil friends; and being easy to speak to and having virtuous friends.
Skillfulness regarding offenses and skillfulness regarding emergence from offenses; skillfulness regarding meditative attainments and skillfulness regarding emergence from meditative attainments;
skillfulness regarding the elements and skillfulness regarding attention; skillfulness regarding the sense bases and skillfulness regarding dependent origination;
skillfulness regarding the possible and skillfulness regarding the impossible; uprightness and gentleness; patience and amiability.
Kindness and hospitality; lack of restraint of the sense faculties and lack of moderation in eating;
restraint of the sense faculties and moderation in eating; forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension;
mindfulness and clear comprehension; the power of reflection and the power of cultivation; serenity and insight.
And: the sign of serenity and the sign of exertion; exertion and non-distraction;
failure in virtue and failure in view; perfection in virtue and perfection in view; purification of virtue and purification of view;
and, moreover, the striving of one who has seen according to the view, as well as spiritual urgency regarding things that inspire urgency.
The eight bases, and for one who is stirred by spiritual urgency, wise exertion; lack of contentment with wholesome qualities, and non-reversal in exertion;
true knowledge and liberation; the knowledge of destruction, and the knowledge of non-arising.
This is the Matrix of Pairs from the Discourses.
The Schedule of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* is finished.
2. The Schedule of the *Vibhaṅga*:
The Analysis of the Aggregates (*Khandhavibhaṅga*).

The five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. This is the Analysis of the Aggregates.
The Analysis of the Bases:
The twelve bases—the eye base, the form base, the ear base, the sound base, the nose base, the odor base... [and so forth].
The base of odors, the base of tongue, the base of tastes, the base of body, the base of tangibles, the base of mind, and the base of mental phenomena.
This is the Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga). Now, the Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga):
The eighteen elements: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-object element.
The mind-consciousness element. The Analysis of Elements.
The Analysis of Truths:

The Four Noble Truths—noble truth of suffering, noble truth of the origin of suffering, noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The Analysis of Truths.
The Analysis of the Faculties: There are twenty-two faculties— the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty,
the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, and the joy faculty.

The faculty of mental displeasure, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known. This is the Analysis of the Faculties.
Next, the Analysis of Dependent Origination.

With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging and death arise.
Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise; such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
The Analysis of Dependent Origination. The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness.
The four foundations of mindfulness: here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally,
he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally— ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful,
having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating mind in mind internally; he dwells contemplating mind in mind externally; he dwells contemplating mind in mind both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena, he dwells contemplating phenomena in external phenomena,
and he dwells contemplating phenomena in both internal and external phenomena— ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This is the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*).
The Analysis of the Right Exertions:
There are four right exertions. Herein, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen. This is the Analysis of the Right Strivings (*sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga*).
The Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power:
There are four bases of psychic power. Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving;

he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving.

He develops the basis for spiritual power; he develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with the volitional formations of striving and concentration through investigation. The Analysis of the Bases for Spiritual Power (*Iddhipādavibhaṅga*).

The Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (*Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga*): There are seven factors of enlightenment—the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. The Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment.
The Analysis of the Factors of the Path:

The Noble Eightfold Path. That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This concludes the Analysis of the Factors of the Path.
The Analysis of the Meditative Absorptions (Jhāna).
Here, a bhikkhu dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults;

he trains himself, having undertaken the rules of training; he guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, with constant mindfulness and discernment regarding the states conducive to enlightenment.
He is devoted to the practice of meditation.
He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl.
He acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in discharging excrement and urine;
he acts with clear comprehension in walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
He frequents secluded lodgings: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, or a heap of straw.
A forest retreat, an open space, a heap of straw— quiet, with little noise, free from the breath of men,
secluded from people, and suitable for seclusion.
Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise...
Having set his body erect and established mindfulness before him, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness for the world, having abandoned covetousness;

he purifies his mind of covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate and kind toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. [He abandons] sloth and torpor...
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from perplexity regarding wholesome states.
...he purifies his mind of doubt regarding phenomena.
Having abandoned these five hindrances— defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— and being secluded from sensual pleasures,
secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Having attained and dwelling therein, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal tranquility and singleness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness;
and with the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body.
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous.
With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, [perceiving] "space is infinite.
With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, [perceiving] "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. With the complete...
Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness;
having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This concludes the Analysis of Jhāna (Jhānavibhaṅga).
Next is the Analysis of the Illimitables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga).
The four immeasurables: here a bhikkhu dwells, having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.
Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity.
He dwells pervading with a mind imbued with non-affliction.
He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.
Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.
Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.
Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. The Analysis of the Immeasurables.
The Analysis of the Training Precepts:
The five training precepts—the training precept of abstaining from taking life, the training precept of abstaining from taking what is not given...

The training rule of abstaining from sexual misconduct; the training rule of abstaining from false speech; the training rule of abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence. The Analysis of the Training Rules.
The Analysis of the Discriminations.

The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā): the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). This concludes the Analysis of Analytical Knowledge (Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga).
Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇa-vibhaṅga):

Under the category of the singlefold basis for knowledge: the five types of sensory consciousness are not roots (na hetū), are rootless (ahetukā), are dissociated from roots (hetu-vippayuttā), and are conditioned (sappaccayā).
Conditioned, immaterial, mundane, subject to cankers, subject to fetters, subject to ties, subject to floods, subject to yokes, subject to hindrances, adhered to, subject to clinging,
defiled, indeterminate, with an object, non-mental factors, resultants, acquired and subject to clinging, neither defiled nor defiling,
neither with applied thought and sustained thought, nor without applied thought and with only sustained thought, but without applied thought and without sustained thought.
They are not accompanied by joy; they are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation; they do not have roots that are to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation;
they lead neither to accumulation nor to diminution; they are neither for those in training nor for those beyond training; they are limited;

they belong to the sense sphere, not the fine-material sphere, nor the immaterial sphere; they are included within the mundane, not excluded from it; they are undetermined and do not lead to liberation.
Having arisen bases, having arisen objects; having pre-arisen bases, having pre-arisen objects;
having internal bases, having external objects; having unmixed bases, having unmixed objects; having various bases, having various objects;
they do not experience each other’s domain and range; they do not arise without attention; they do not arise without mental engagement.
They arise not in succession, they do not arise one after another, they do not arise neither before nor after, and they do not arise immediately following one another.
The five consciousnesses are effortless; by means of the five consciousnesses, one does not discern any phenomenon, except for...
At the mere moment of impact, even immediately after the five types of consciousness, one does not discern any mental state;
by means of the five types of consciousness, one does not assume any posture; even immediately after the five types of consciousness, one does not assume any posture;
and by means of the five types of consciousness, one does not initiate any bodily or verbal action.
Immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not initiate bodily action or verbal action;

by means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states; immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states;
and by means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one neither enters nor emerges from meditative absorption.
Immediately following the five types of consciousness, one neither enters nor emerges from meditative attainment;
by means of the five types of consciousness, one does not pass away nor is one reborn; immediately following the five types of consciousness, one does not pass away nor is one reborn;
by means of the five types of consciousness, one does not sleep, nor does one wake up, nor does one see a dream. Of the five types of consciousness...
Immediately thereafter, one neither sleeps, nor wakes, nor sees dreams; this is wisdom as the manifestation of things as they truly are.
Thus is the basis of knowledge in its singlefold division.
The basis of knowledge in its twofold division: mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom. Wisdom that is cognizable by some, and [wisdom] by others...
Wisdom is not to be cognized [as an object]. Wisdom is with taints; wisdom is without taints. Wisdom dissociated from the taints is with taints; wisdom dissociated from the taints is without taints.
Wisdom is subject to fetters; wisdom is not subject to fetters. Wisdom dissociated from the fetters is subject to fetters;
wisdom dissociated from the fetters is not subject to fetters. Wisdom is subject to the ties; wisdom is not subject to the ties.
Wisdom dissociated from the ties but subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the ties and not subject to them.
Wisdom subject to the floods; wisdom not subject to the floods. Wisdom dissociated from the floods but subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the floods and not subject to them.
Wisdom subject to the yokes; wisdom not subject to the yokes. Wisdom dissociated from the yokes but subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the yokes...

Wisdom that leads to the unwholesome; wisdom that is subject to the hindrances, and wisdom that is not subject to the hindrances. Wisdom that is associated with the hindrances though dissociated from them;
wisdom that is dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to them. Wisdom that is adhered to, and wisdom that is not adhered to.
Wisdom that is associated with clinging though dissociated from it; wisdom that is dissociated from clinging and not adhered to. Wisdom that is grasped...

Wisdom that is not grasped; wisdom that is subject to grasping and wisdom that is not subject to grasping; wisdom that is dissociated from grasping yet subject to grasping, and wisdom that is dissociated from grasping and not subject to grasping;
wisdom that is defiled and wisdom that is undefiled; wisdom that is dissociated from the defilements yet defiled, and wisdom that is dissociated from the defilements...
Wisdom that is undefiled. Wisdom with applied thought, wisdom without applied thought. Wisdom with sustained thought, wisdom without sustained thought.
Wisdom accompanied by rapture, wisdom unaccompanied by rapture. Wisdom associated with rapture, wisdom not associated with rapture.

Relying on this power, the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.

liberations, concentrations, and attainments. That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments— this too is a power of the Tathāgata.
Relying upon which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel;
furthermore, the Tathāgata understands the recollection of past lives as it really is—this, too, is a power of the Tathāgata... [and so on].
He understands the recollection of past lives as it really is; this too is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata.
Relying on which power, the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the passing away and rebirth of beings;
that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the passing away and rebirth of beings—this too is a power of the Tathāgata.
Relying on this power, the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, and roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.

The Discourse on the Person.
The Positive-Negative Analysis of the Pure Real Aspect:
"Is a person apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense? — "Yes. "Does that person exist as a real entity in the ultimate sense from that very same real aspect which is the ultimate sense?
— "One should not say so. Understand this refutation: If indeed a person is apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense, then by that very fact...
It should be said: "That person is apprehended as a real, ultimate fact from that which is a real, ultimate fact.

As for what you said there—"It should indeed be said that 'the person is apprehended as a real, ultimate fact,' but it should not be said that 'that person is apprehended as a real, ultimate fact from that which is a real, ultimate fact'"—that is incorrect.
But if it cannot be said that "the person is apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense from that which is a real entity in the ultimate sense," then indeed,
sir, you must not say that "the person is apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense.
As for what you said there— "it can be said that 'the person is apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense,' but it cannot be said..."
‘That person is apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense from that which is a real entity in the ultimate sense,’ this is false.

This is the fivefold series of conformable propositions. [Question: “The person is not apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense”? [Answer: Yes. [Question: “From that which is a real entity in the ultimate sense, that person is not apprehended as a real entity in the ultimate sense”? One should not say so.
Understand the counter-argument: If indeed a person is not apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, then, O sir, you must surely say:
"Insofar as there is a real and ultimate fact, from that perspective a person is not apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact.
As for what you said there—"One must say that 'a person is not apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact'—but not..."
And if it must be said: "In that which is the true state, the ultimate reality, that person is not found by way of the true state, the ultimate reality," that is false.

But if it cannot be said that "in that which is the true state, the ultimate reality, that person is not found by way of the true state, the ultimate reality," then indeed, sir, you must not say that "the person is found by way of the true state, the ultimate reality. As for that which therein...

You say: "It should indeed be said that 'the person is not apprehended as a real and ultimate fact,' yet it should not be said that 'the person is not apprehended as a real and ultimate fact from that which is a real and ultimate fact,'" which is false.
This concludes the tetrad on counter-arguments.

But if you think: "One may indeed say, 'A person is not apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact,' yet one cannot say, 'That person is not apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact from which [the person] derives its reality,'" then, since you have made that admission as your reason for that position, you should be refuted in this manner when you maintain such a claim. And then, that...

The Section on Designations:
There are three formations—bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation. In-breathing and out-breathing are bodily formation;
applied thought and sustained thought are verbal formation; perception and feeling are mental formation, excluding applied and sustained thought.
All phenomena associated with consciousness are also formations of consciousness (*cittasaṅkhāra*).
This concludes the section on the purification of terms in the forward order (*anuloma*).

The Section on the Distinction of Time for Arising and Cessation

For whomsoever the consciousness arises but does not cease, for that person the consciousness will cease but will not arise. Or rather, for whomsoever the consciousness will cease but will not arise, for that person the consciousness arises but does not cease.

For whomsoever the consciousness does not arise but ceases, for that person the consciousness will not cease but will arise. Or rather, for whomsoever the consciousness will not cease but will arise, for that person the consciousness does not arise but ceases.
2. The Section on Arising and Aroused.
For whomsoever consciousness arises, for him consciousness has arisen. Or else, for whomsoever consciousness has arisen, for him consciousness arises.
For whomsoever consciousness does not arise, for him consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever consciousness has not arisen, for him consciousness does not arise.

For whomsoever consciousness ceases, for that one consciousness has arisen. Or else, for whomsoever consciousness has arisen, for that one consciousness ceases.
For whomsoever consciousness does not cease, for that one consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever consciousness has not arisen, for that one consciousness does not cease.

For whomsoever the consciousness is not arising, for that one the consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever the consciousness has not arisen, for that one the consciousness is not arising.

For whomsoever the consciousness is ceasing, for that one the consciousness has arisen. Or else, for whomsoever the consciousness has arisen, for that one the consciousness is ceasing.

For whomsoever the consciousness is not ceasing, for that one the consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever the consciousness has not arisen, for that one the consciousness is not ceasing.
10. The Chapter on the Arisen and the Arising.
For whomsoever consciousness has arisen, for that person consciousness had arisen. Or else, for whomsoever consciousness had arisen, for that person consciousness has arisen.
For whomsoever consciousness has not arisen, for that person consciousness had not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever consciousness had not arisen, for that person consciousness has not arisen.

For whom the consciousness has not arisen, for that one the consciousness will not arise. Or else, for whom the consciousness will not arise, for that one the consciousness has not arisen.
11. Section on the Past and Future:

For whom the consciousness had arisen, but for that one the consciousness has not [currently] arisen, for that one the consciousness will arise. Or else, for whom the consciousness will arise, but for that one the consciousness has not [currently] arisen, for that one the consciousness had arisen.
For whomsoever the mind had not arisen, and for whom it is not the case that the mind has not arisen, for him the mind will not arise.
Or else, for whomsoever the mind will not arise, and for whom it is not the case that the mind has not arisen, for him the mind had not arisen.
12. The Chapter on the Aroused and the Arousing.
The arisen and that which is arising; that which is arising and the arisen.
Not the arisen and not that which is arising; not that which is arising and not the arisen.
13. The Section on the Ceased and That Which Is Ceasing.
Ceased is ceasing; ceasing is ceased. Not ceased is not ceasing; not ceasing is not ceased.
14. The Section on the Transcended Time.
For whomsoever the mind, while arising, transcends moment after moment and has passed beyond time;
and for whomsoever the mind, while ceasing, transcends moment after moment and has passed beyond time—that is his mind.
Or rather, for whomsoever the mind, while ceasing, transcends moment after moment and has passed beyond time, [and] while arising, transcends moment after moment...
His mind has transcended its time.
His mind is one that, while arising, does not transcend moment after moment, thus transcending its time;
his mind is one that, while ceasing, does not transcend moment after moment, thus transcending its time. Or alternatively, his mind is one that, while ceasing...
Moment by moment, his mind has transcended and passed beyond the arising moment; it has transcended and passed beyond the time [of that arising].
This is the commonality of pure consciousness.

Section on the Distinction of Arising, Cessation, and Time.

Whatever consciousness arises and does not cease, that consciousness will cease and will not arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will cease and will not arise, that consciousness arises and does not cease.
That consciousness which does not arise and does not cease will not cease and will arise. Or rather, that consciousness which will not cease and will arise does not arise and does not cease.
2. The Chapter on Arising and Arisen:
That consciousness which arises has arisen. Or rather, that consciousness which has arisen arises.
Whatever consciousness does not arise, that consciousness has not arisen. Or else, whatever consciousness has not arisen, that consciousness does not arise.
3. Section on Cessation and Arising:
Whatever consciousness ceases, that consciousness has arisen. Or else, whatever consciousness has arisen, that consciousness ceases.
That consciousness which does not cease has not arisen; or else, that consciousness which has not arisen does not cease.
4. The Section on Arising:
That consciousness which arises has already arisen; or else, that consciousness which has already arisen is arising.
Whatever consciousness does not arise, that consciousness did not arise. Or else, whatever consciousness did not arise, that consciousness does not arise.
Whatever consciousness arises, that consciousness will arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will arise, that consciousness arises.
Whatever consciousness does not arise, that consciousness will not arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will not arise, that consciousness does not arise.
Whatever consciousness has arisen, that consciousness will arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will arise, that consciousness has arisen.
Whatever consciousness has not arisen, that consciousness will not arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will not arise, that consciousness has not arisen.
5. Section on Cessation.
Whatever consciousness ceases, that consciousness has ceased. Or else, whatever consciousness has ceased, that consciousness ceases.
Whatever consciousness does not cease, that consciousness has not ceased. Or else, whatever consciousness has not ceased, that consciousness does not cease.
Whatever consciousness ceases, that consciousness will cease. Or else, whatever consciousness will cease, that consciousness ceases.
Whatever consciousness does not cease, that consciousness will not cease. Or else, whatever consciousness will not cease, that consciousness does not cease.
Whatever consciousness has ceased, that consciousness will cease. Or else, whatever consciousness will cease, that consciousness has ceased.
Whatever consciousness has not ceased, that consciousness will not cease. Or else, whatever consciousness will not cease, that consciousness has not ceased.
6. Section on Arising and Cessation Whatever consciousness arises, that consciousness has ceased. Or else, whatever consciousness has ceased, that consciousness arises.
Whatever consciousness does not arise, that consciousness has not ceased. Or else, whatever consciousness has not ceased, that consciousness does not arise.
Whatever consciousness arises, that consciousness will cease. Or rather, whatever consciousness will cease, that consciousness arises.
Whatever consciousness does not arise, that consciousness will not cease. Or rather, whatever consciousness will not cease, that consciousness does not arise.
Whatever consciousness has arisen, that consciousness will cease. Or rather, whatever consciousness will cease, that consciousness has arisen.
Whatever consciousness has not arisen, that consciousness will not cease. Or else, whatever consciousness will not cease, that consciousness has not arisen.
7. The Section on Arising and Ceasing:
Whatever consciousness is arising, that consciousness does not cease. Or else, whatever consciousness does not cease, that consciousness is arising.
Whatever consciousness does not arise, that consciousness ceases. Or else, whatever consciousness ceases, that consciousness does not arise.
8. Section on Arising and Aroused:
Whatever consciousness is arising, that consciousness is aroused. Or else, whatever consciousness is aroused, that consciousness is arising.
That consciousness which is not arising is that consciousness which has not arisen. Or else, that consciousness which has not arisen is that consciousness which is not arising.
9. The Section on the Ceasing and the Arousing:
That consciousness which is ceasing is that consciousness which has arisen. Or else, that consciousness which has arisen is that consciousness which is ceasing.
That consciousness which is not ceasing is not arisen; or rather, that consciousness which is not arisen is not ceasing.
10. The Section on the Arisen and the Arising:
That consciousness which has arisen has already arisen; or rather, that consciousness which has already arisen has arisen.
Whatever consciousness has not arisen, that consciousness has not arisen in the past. Or else, whatever consciousness has not arisen in the past, that consciousness has not arisen [now].
Whatever consciousness has arisen, that consciousness will arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will arise, that consciousness has arisen.
Whatever consciousness has not arisen, that consciousness will not arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will not arise, that consciousness has not arisen.

11. Chapter on the Past and Future Whatever consciousness has arisen, that consciousness has not [just] arisen; that consciousness will arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will arise, that consciousness has not [just] arisen; that consciousness has arisen. Whatever consciousness has not arisen, that consciousness has not [just] arisen;
that consciousness will not arise. Or else, whatever consciousness will not arise, that consciousness has not [just] arisen; that consciousness has not arisen.
12. Chapter on the Arisen and the Arising:
That which has arisen is arising; that which is arising has arisen.
That which has not arisen is not arising; that which is not arising has not arisen.
13. Section on the Ceased and the Ceasing:
That which has ceased is ceasing; that which is ceasing has ceased.
That which has not ceased is not ceasing; that which is not ceasing has not ceased.
14. The Section on Transcending Time:
That consciousness which, while arising, transcends moment after moment and thus transcends time;
and that consciousness which, while ceasing, transcends moment after moment and thus transcends time—that is consciousness. Or else, that consciousness which, while ceasing, transcends the moment...
That consciousness which has transcended the moment of arising, having passed beyond that time;
that consciousness which has not transcended the moment of arising, having not passed beyond that time;
and that consciousness which has not transcended the moment of ceasing, having not passed beyond that time. Or rather, that consciousness which is not ceasing...
Moment by moment, it transcends and passes beyond the moment; that consciousness does not arise as the moment by moment that is transcended and passed beyond.
This is the commonality of pure consciousness.
Section on Persons and Phenomena:
Chapter 1. The Section on the Distinction of Arising, Cessation, and Time.
For whichever person a certain consciousness arises and does not cease, for that person that consciousness will cease and will not arise.
Or again, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will cease but will not arise, for him that consciousness arises but does not cease.
For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise but ceases, for him that consciousness will not cease but will arise.
Or again, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not cease but will arise, for him that consciousness does not arise but ceases.

2. Section on Arising and Having Arisen For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises, for that person that consciousness has arisen. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for that person that consciousness arises.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise, for that person that consciousness has not arisen. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for that person that consciousness does not arise.

3. The Chapter on Cessation and Arising For whomsoever a certain consciousness ceases, for that person that consciousness has arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for that person that consciousness ceases.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not cease, for that person that consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for that person that consciousness does not cease.

4. The Section on Arising (Uppādavāra) For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises, for that person that consciousness had arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness had arisen, for that person that consciousness arises.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise, for that person that consciousness had not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness had not arisen, for that person that consciousness does not arise.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises, for that person that consciousness will arise. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will arise, for that person that consciousness is arising.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise, for that person that consciousness will not arise. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not arise, for that person that consciousness is not arising.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for that person that consciousness will arise. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will arise, for that person that consciousness has arisen.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for that person that consciousness will not arise. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not arise, for that person that consciousness had not arisen.

5. The Section on Cessation (Nirodhavāra) For whomsoever a certain consciousness ceases, for that person that consciousness had ceased. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness had ceased, for that person that consciousness ceases.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not cease, for that person that consciousness has not ceased. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has not ceased, for that person that consciousness does not cease.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness ceases, for that person that consciousness will cease. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will cease, for that person that consciousness ceases.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not cease, for that person that consciousness will not cease. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not cease, for that person that consciousness does not cease.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has ceased, for that person that consciousness will cease. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will cease, for that person that consciousness has ceased.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has not ceased, for that person that consciousness will not cease. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not cease, for that person that consciousness has not ceased.
6. The Section on Arising and Cessation:
For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises, for that person that consciousness has ceased. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has ceased, for that person that consciousness arises.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise, for that person that consciousness has not ceased. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has not ceased, for that person that consciousness does not arise.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises, for that person that consciousness will cease. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will cease, for that person that consciousness arises.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise, for that person that consciousness will not cease. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not cease, for that person that consciousness did not arise.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for that person that consciousness will cease. Or conversely, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will cease, for that person that consciousness had arisen.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for him that consciousness will not cease. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not cease, for him that consciousness had not arisen.

7. The Section on Arising and Ceasing For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises, for him that consciousness does not cease. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness does not cease, for him that consciousness arises.
For whomsoever a certain consciousness does not arise, for him that consciousness ceases. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness ceases, for him that consciousness does not arise.
8. The Section on Arising and Present:
For whomsoever a certain consciousness is arising, for him that consciousness is present. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness is present, for him that consciousness is arising.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness is not arising, for that person that consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for that person that consciousness is not arising.
9. The Section on the Ceasing and the Arising [of Consciousness]:

For whomsoever a certain consciousness is ceasing, for that person that consciousness has arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for that person that consciousness is ceasing.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness is not ceasing, for that person that consciousness has not arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for that person that consciousness is not ceasing.
10. The Section on the Arisen and the Arousing:

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for that person that consciousness had already arisen. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness had already arisen, for that person that consciousness has arisen.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for him that consciousness had not arisen. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness had not arisen, for him that consciousness has not arisen.
For whomsoever a certain consciousness has arisen, for him that consciousness will arise. Or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will arise, for him that consciousness has arisen.

For whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, for him that consciousness will not arise; or rather, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not arise, for him that consciousness has not arisen.
11. Section on the Past and Future:
For whatever mind has arisen for someone, but that mind has not [yet] arisen [at that moment], that mind will arise for him.
Or else, for whatever mind will arise for someone, but that mind has not [yet] arisen [at that moment], that mind has arisen for him.
For whomsoever a certain consciousness has not arisen, and yet that consciousness has not [now] ceased to have arisen,
for him that consciousness will not arise. Or else, for whomsoever a certain consciousness will not arise,
and yet that consciousness has not [now] ceased to have arisen, for him that consciousness had not arisen.
12. Section on the Arisen and the Arising The arisen is the arising; the arising is the arisen.
That which is neither arisen nor arising is neither arising nor arisen.
13. Section on the Ceased and the Ceasing:
That which has ceased is ceasing; that which is ceasing has ceased.
That which has not ceased is not ceasing; that which is not ceasing has not ceased.
14. The Section on Transcending Time:
For whatever consciousness, when arising, transcends moment after moment and thus transcends time;
and for whatever consciousness, when ceasing, transcends moment after moment and thus transcends time—that is that consciousness. Or alternatively, for whatever consciousness...

That consciousness of his has transcended and passed beyond each moment of its ceasing, having transcended the time [of ceasing]; it has transcended and passed beyond each moment of its arising, having transcended the time [of arising].
For him, that consciousness has not transcended and passed beyond each moment of its arising, nor has it transcended and passed beyond each moment of its ceasing.
That mind of his has transgressed moment by moment, having passed beyond its proper time; or rather, that mind of his which, while not ceasing,
has transgressed moment by moment, having passed beyond its proper time, and which, while not arising, has transgressed moment by moment,
having passed beyond its proper time— that is his mind.
The distinction regarding the mixture of consciousness with the Suttanta:
"In one whose consciousness arises accompanied by lust... [and so on] ...in one whose consciousness arises free from lust;
in one whose consciousness arises accompanied by hatred; in one whose consciousness arises free from hatred; in one whose consciousness arises accompanied by delusion."
The mind of one that arises free from delusion; the mind of one that arises contracted; the mind of one that arises distracted;
the mind of one that arises exalted; the mind of one that arises unexalted;
the mind of one that arises surpassable; the mind of one that arises unsurpassable; the mind of one that arises concentrated.
Consciousness arises. For whom un-concentrated consciousness arises; for whom liberated consciousness arises;
for whom unliberated consciousness arises.
This is the distinction regarding the mixing of consciousness with the Abhidhamma.

In whom a wholesome consciousness arises... [and so on] ...in whom an unwholesome consciousness arises. In whom an indeterminate consciousness arises. In whom a consciousness associated with pleasant feeling arises.
(By this method, [the categories] up to *saraṇa* and *araṇā* should be extracted.
In whom a non-conflict (*araṇa*) consciousness arises and does not cease, in him that non-conflict consciousness will cease, but not...
Or else, for that person whose mind free from conflict (araṇa-citta) will cease but not arise,
his mind free from conflict arises but does not cease.
The Matrix of the Mind-Pairing (Cittayamaka-mātikā) is finished.

The Chapter on Designations in the Indriya-Yamaka:
There are twenty-two faculties— the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty.

The faculty of mind, the faculty of femininity, the faculty of masculinity, the faculty of vital energy, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief,
the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom,
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known.

One who has already known is the faculty of one who has already known; the faculty of one who has already known is one who has already known.

There is no "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown," nor is there the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown"; there is no faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown," nor is there "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown."
There is no "final knowledge" (añña) that is not the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), nor is there a faculty of final knowledge that is not "final knowledge.

This is the Wheel of the Fourfold Investigation based on the Purification of Terms.

Commentary on the Analysis of the Three Categories.
Regarding the phrase "the matrix (mātikā) of the Abhidhamma": in what sense is it called *abhidhamma*? It is in the sense of being a dhamma that exceeds and is distinguished from [ordinary] dhammas.
For here, the prefix *abhi-* indicates the sense of excess and distinction, as in: "My intense painful feelings are increasing (*abhikkamanti*)."
Just as in such passages as “they do not retreat; they are of surpassing beauty,” when among many raised parasols and banners,
that which is of exceeding size and possesses a distinguished color and shape is called an *aticchatta* (extraordinary umbrella),
and that which is of exceeding size and possesses a distinguished color and shape is called an *atiddhaja* (extraordinary banner)— in exactly the same way.
This Dhamma, too, is called "Abhidhamma" in the sense of being a Dhamma that exceeds and distinguishes itself from other Dhammas.
For while the Blessed One, upon reaching the Suttanta, analyzed such categories as the aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties,
and modes of conditionality only partially and not exhaustively, when he reached the Abhidhamma, he analyzed them exhaustively through numerous specific methods.
Thus, it should be understood as "Abhidhamma" in the sense of being a further and more distinguished teaching of the Dhamma.
In what sense is it the *mātikā*? In the sense of being like a mother (*mātṛ*). For it is called *mātikā* because it is like a mother;
just as one says "the lotus-face. Just as a mother gives birth to various kinds of children, protects them, and nourishes them, so too does this [matrix] give birth to various kinds of...
It gives birth to the Dhamma and to its meaning, and it protects and nourishes them so that they do not perish;

therefore, it is called the "Mātikā" (Matrix). For, depending upon the Mātikā, the infinite and immeasurable phenomena and meanings—being expanded out by way of the seven treatises beginning with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*—become as if born from it, protected by it, and nourished by it. Thus, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* treatise...

There are four sections: the analysis of consciousness (*cittavibhatti*), the analysis of matter (*rūpavibhatti*), the collection of summaries (*nikkheparāsi*), and the extraction of meanings (*atthuddhāra*).

Among these, when the analysis of consciousness—which elucidates eighty-nine types of consciousness through various methods—is expanded, it consists of infinite and immeasurable recitation-sections (*bhāṇavāra*);

immediately following that, when the analysis of matter—which elucidates matter by way of its singlefold nature and so forth—is expanded, it likewise consists of infinite and immeasurable recitation-sections.

Immediately following that, when the Nikkhepa-rāsi (the Section on Enumeration) is taught by setting forth the roots, aggregates, bases, and so forth, it consists of infinite and immeasurable recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).

Immediately following that, when the Atthuddhāra (the Section on the Extraction of Meanings), which serves as the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) upon the Buddha’s word contained in the Three Piṭakas, is expanded upon, it likewise consists of infinite and immeasurable recitation sections. Thus is this treatise, the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

Even though it consists of no more than thirteen recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) according to the path of oral transmission, when expanded upon, it becomes infinite and immeasurable in its recitation sections. Likewise, in the *Vibhaṅga* treatise, there are the Analysis of the Aggregates (*khandhavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Bases (*āyatanavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Elements (*dhātuvibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Truths (*saccavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Faculties (*indriyavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Modes of Conditionality (*paccayākāravibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Right Exertions (*sammappadhānavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power (*iddhipādavibhaṅga*),

the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Path Factors (*maggaṅgavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Meditations (*jhānavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Immeasurables (*appamaññāvibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Training Precepts (*sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of the Discriminations (*paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*), the Analysis of Knowledge (*ñāṇavibhaṅga*), the Analysis of Minor Subjects (*khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*), and the Analysis of the Heart of Dhamma (*dhammahadayavibhaṅga*).

The eighteen Vibhaṅgas have been analyzed; when these are expanded through various methods such as the Suttanta-bhājaniya and the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, each one becomes infinite and immeasurable in its recitation-sections (*bhāṇavāra*).

Thus, although this Vibhaṅga treatise consists of only about thirty-five recitation-sections according to the path of oral transmission, when expanded, it becomes infinite and immeasurable in its recitation-sections.

Likewise, the *Dhātukathāpakaraṇa*, which is analyzed in fourteen ways beginning with "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) and "non-inclusion" (*asaṅgaha*), though it amounts to slightly more than six recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) in its textual extent, becomes infinite and immeasurable in recitation sections when expanded upon.

Similarly, the *Puggalapaññattippakaraṇa*, which is analyzed in six ways— namely, the designation of aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*sacca*), faculties (*indriya*), and persons (*puggala*)— though it amounts to slightly more than five recitation sections in its textual extent, when expanded upon...
It consists of an infinite and immeasurable number of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).

Likewise, the *Kathāvatthu* treatise is analyzed according to the method of the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*) as it was established in the oral tradition, comprising one thousand suttas— five hundred suttas in the section on our own doctrine (*sakavāda*) and five hundred suttas in the section on the opposing doctrine (*paravāda*)— and thus its magnitude is equal to that of the *Dīghanikāya*.
When expanded, it consists of infinite and immeasurable recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).

Likewise, the *Yamakappakaraṇa*—the *Mūlayamaka*—is analyzed into ten types: the Yamakas of the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*sacca*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), consciousness (*citta*), phenomena (*dhamma*), and faculties (*indriya*).
When expanded according to the path of recitation, even these one hundred and twenty recitation sections consist of infinite and immeasurable recitation sections.

The *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa*, taking up the twenty-four conditions—beginning with the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), and so forth—is analyzed in twenty-four ways, such as the "triplet-analysis" (*tika-paṭṭhāna*).
Even when each of these is expanded by just a few recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), it results in an infinite and immeasurable number of recitation sections.
Thus, because it gives birth to, protects, and nourishes infinite and immeasurable phenomena (*dhamma*) and their meanings (*attha*):

Among these, the matrix of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* is first; it is twofold: the matrix of triplets (*tika*) and the matrix of couplets (*duka*). Therein, the twenty-two triplets are called the matrix of triplets.

"Phenomena... [and so on] ...the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising"—these forty-two pairs of suttas are known as "spoken by disciples" because they were established by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.
When establishing them, the Elder did not do so by means of his own independently realized knowledge;
rather, he compiled them by harmonizing them with the *Ekuttarika*, the first and second chapters (*ekaka-nipāta* and *duka-nipāta*), and ten suttas from the *Saṅgīti*.

Indeed, the six pairs beginning with "states that are roots" (*hetu-dhammā*) and "states that are not roots" (*nahetu-dhammā*) are called the "Root Cluster" (*hetu-gocchaka*) because they stand together like spokes and like a jar, being mutually connected both in terms of their textual form and their meaning. Following those, the "conditioned" (*sappaccayā*)...

The seven dyads beginning with "states" (*dhammā*) and so forth should be understood as the "Minor Intermediate Dyads" (*cūḷantaraduka*), because they are mutually unrelated, are selected merely by virtue of being dyads, are placed within a separate cluster, and are minor compared to other intermediate dyads.

Following that, there is the cluster known as the "Taints" (*āsava-gocchaka*) by way of the six dyads beginning with the taints. After that, there are the dyads beginning with the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
By way of the six [types of] concealment (*channa*), there is what is called the "Cluster of Fetters" (*saṃyojana-gocchaka*).

Likewise, by way of each of the six—namely, the knots (*gantha*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and pairs (*duka*)—there are what are called the "Clusters of Knots," "Floods," "Yokes," and "Hindrances. By way of the five beginning with the pair of misapprehensions (*parāmāsa*), there is what is called the "Cluster of Misapprehensions.
Following that, there are fourteen pairs beginning with the pair of "having an object" (*sārammaṇa-duka*), which are the "Great Pairs" (*mahantara-duka*).

Next, the six dyads beginning with the clinging dyad are called the "clinging group" (*upādāna-gocchaka*). Following that, the eight dyads beginning with the defilement dyad are called the "defilement group" (*kilesa-gocchaka*).

Subsequently, the eighteen dyads beginning with the dyad of what is to be abandoned by vision are called the "back-portion dyads" (*piṭṭhi-duka*), because they are placed at the conclusion of the Abhidhamma matrix (*mātikā*).
As for the dyads beginning with those pertaining to true knowledge (*vijjā-bhāgiya-duka*)...
The forty-two dyads are called the Suttantika-dukas. Thus, this commentary on the meaning shall now proceed for this [work] which is established by means of fifteen chapters.
Commentary on the Wholesome Triplet (Kusalattika).
Since the Schedule of Triplets is the beginning here, and within that the Triplet of the Wholesome is the beginning, therefore, first, regarding the Triplet of the Wholesome:
By way of meaning, by the division of planes, by each [factor’s] association, and by way of the enumeration of phenomena, through the analysis of their characteristics and so forth.

The exposition should be understood everywhere according to what is appropriate, both in terms of the methods of inclusion (*saṅgaha*)—namely, the void (*suññata*) and so forth—and the distinctions of objects (*visaya*) and other factors.
Therein, first regarding the meaning: in the phrase "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*), the word *kusala* applies to health, blamelessness, skillfulness, happiness, and fruition.

It is seen [in various senses]. For this term is seen in the sense of health in such passages as: “Is it well with you, sir? Are you free from illness? It is seen in the sense of blamelessness in such passages as:
“And what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? That bodily conduct which, O Great King, is irreproachable. It is seen in the sense of skill in such passages as:
“You are skilled in the parts and components of a chariot. [And it is seen in the sense of] wholesome kamma...

In such passages as “because of having been done and accumulated,” it refers to a pleasant result (*sukhavipāka*). Here, however, it applies to health (*ārogya*), to blamelessness (*anavajja*), and to a pleasant result.

For just as the wholesome (*kusala*) is described in the sense of health due to the absence of disease in the physical body (*rūpakāya*), so too should the wholesome be understood in the sense of health among immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) due to the absence of the disease of the defilements (*kilesa*). Furthermore, because of the absence of the blame of the defilements...
It is wholesome in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja*).
Furthermore, this word *dhamma* is seen in the senses of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), cause (*hetu*), quality (*guṇa*), and the absence of a sentient being or a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*).

For it is seen in the sense of the scriptures in such passages as, “He masters the *Dhamma*: the discourses (*sutta*) and the mixed prose and verse (*geyya*)”; and in such passages as, “Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of *dhamma* (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*)”.
In the phrase “hetumhi,” it refers to a cause. In such passages as “For neither merit nor demerit have equal results,” it refers to a quality (*guṇa*).

In such passages as “He dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena,” it refers to the absence of a sentient being and the absence of a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*); and here too, it must be understood precisely as the absence of a sentient being and the absence of a soul.

As for the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) here: they are so called because they “make waver,” “set in motion,” “shake,” and “shatter” those who are corrupt and possessed of evil qualities (*pāpa-dhamma*).
They are wholesome (*kusala*). Alternatively, they are called *kusa* because they lie down in a contemptible manner;

those who cut or sever that *kusa* grass are thus called *kusala*. Or, knowledge that thins out—that is, diminishes—what is contemptible is called *kusa*; what is to be taken up or cultivated by means of that *kusa* is *kusala*.
Alternatively, skillfulness (*kosalla*) is said to be wisdom (*paññā*); they are *kusala* because they have arisen from that skillfulness. This, moreover—

Regarding the two etymological explanations stated immediately before: although they apply strictly (*nippariyāyato*) only to those associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), they should nevertheless be understood to include those dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*) as well, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) because of their similarity to them.

Or, just as a sickle (*kusā*) cuts both parts of the hand that hold it, so too do these [defilements] cut the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*) which consists of both the arisen and the unarisen.

They cut, therefore they are "wholesome" (kusala) because they cut like kusa grass. Furthermore, they are "phenomena" (dhamma) because they bear their own intrinsic nature, or because they are borne by conditions, or because they are maintained according to their intrinsic nature as supports.
"Unwholesome" (akusala) means not wholesome; the meaning is that they are the opposites of the wholesome, just as enemies are the opposites of friends. "Indeterminate" (abyākata) means...

"Indeterminate" (*abyākatā*) means they have not been described as being either wholesome (*kusala*) or unwholesome (*akusala*). Among them, the wholesome are characterized by blamelessness and pleasant fruition; the unwholesome are characterized by blameworthiness and painful fruition; the indeterminate are characterized by having no fruition.
Now, are these terms—such as "wholesome," "dhammas," and so forth—synonymous, or do they have different meanings? What, then, is the case here?
If, first of all, these have the same meaning, then the expression "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*) becomes identical to saying "wholesome, wholesome.

If, on the other hand, they have different meanings, it follows that the triads and dyads would become hexads and tetrads, and there would be a lack of syntactic connection between the terms, as in the case of "wholesome, matter, the eye," and so forth. Furthermore, if these have the same meaning, [it would follow for] the terms "wholesome," "unwholesome," and "indeterminate"...
Because the three phenomena (dhammas) are one in their essential nature (dhammasabhāva), it follows that even the wholesome and so forth are one.

Now, if you say, "There must be a difference between the term 'wholesome' and the term 'unwholesome'," then these do not have the same meaning. In that case, a phenomenon (dhamma) is an existent (bhāva).
