Furthermore, starting from the enumeration of factors, in the first jhāna there are thirty-six factors—excluding the three abstinences among those mentioned for the first wholesome sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness.
Among these, there are the four beginning with desire (chanda), as well as compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā).

And these are the six "inclusion" factors (*cha yevāpanakā*). The remainder—all up to the conclusion of the section on emptiness (*suññatavāra*)—is exactly as described for the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-paṭhama-kusala*).

The only differences are: the absence of the abstinences (*virati*), the presence of five path-factors (*maggaṅga*) in the section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*), and the status of being fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) by way of a different plane (*bhūmantara*); the rest is identical. This is the first jhāna.

Likewise, in the second jhāna as well, the only difference is the absence of applied thought (vitakka) in the enumeration of factors (dhammuddesa), and its status as both a jhāna factor and a path factor in the section on inclusion (saṅgahavāra); the rest is exactly like the first. This is the second.

Likewise, in the third jhāna as well, the only difference is the absence of sustained thought (vicāra) in the enumeration of factors, and its being a three-factored jhāna in the section on inclusion; the rest is exactly like the second. This is the third.

Likewise, in the fourth, the only difference is the absence of rapture (pīti) in the enumeration of factors, and its being a two-factored jhāna in the section on constituents (koṭṭhāsavāra); the rest is exactly like the third. This is the fourth.

Likewise, in the fifth [jhāna], there is simply the absence of compassion, sympathetic joy, and so forth in the description of the factors; in the place of mental pleasure (*somanassa*), there is equanimity (*upekkhā*);

in the section on the constituents, among the jhāna-factors and faculties, there is the presence of equanimity as a jhāna-factor and the presence of the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*)—this is the distinction.
The rest is exactly the same as the fourth. This is the fifth.
In the *Padabhājanīya*, however, the fourfold method is also presented: "With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, the second; with the fading away of rapture, the third;
and with the disappearance of mental pleasure, the fourth. This is stated because for those of sharp wisdom, it is possible to transcend applied and sustained thought all at once.
In that context, since the second jhāna and so forth are entirely identical to the third and so forth in the fivefold method, they are to be understood according to the method explained there.
The entire exposition should be understood right there, as well as its inclusion within that [framework].

This is the method of fourfold classification (*catukkanaya*). However, we shall explain the exposition according to the fivefold method (*pañcakanaya*) by way of the distinctions of object and so forth;

following that, it can also be known by way of the fourfold method. The same applies above for the supramundane (*lokuttara*). Furthermore, these fivefold wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala-dhamma*) are distinguished by way of their kasiṇa objects.
Individually, they are eightfold: the earth-kasiṇa, and the water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, and white kasiṇas;

together with the light-kasiṇa and the space-kasiṇa, they are tenfold. However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*), the light-kasiṇa is not mentioned because it is included within the white-kasiṇa, while the space-kasiṇa is not mentioned because it is impossible to remove [the kasina-object] from it and because it does not belong to the formless jhānas.

For even when that [space] is repeatedly opened up, it remains only as space; therefore, the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) arising therein leads to a distinction of existence and to a pleasant dwelling in this very life, and it also serves as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
However, because it is not formless (*anāruppa*), it does not serve as a basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). As for the remaining nine kasiṇas:

The difference between these is that [the latter] also has cessation as its basis. Furthermore, here the inclusion of breath-meditation (*ānāpāna-jhāna*) within the air-kasina should also be understood.
This concludes the discussion on the kasinas.
Thus, while these are eightfold by way of the kasinas, they are each eightfold by way of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*). For the Blessed One said:
“Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited; having mastered them...
[and so on] ...infinite. Having mastered them... [and so on] ...limited forms, beautiful and ugly...
[and so on] ...infinite forms, beautiful and ugly, as well as perfectly pure blue, yellow, red, and white.”

The eight bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) have been taught; and these are distinguished by the arising of jhāna through the mastery over the *kasiṇas* themselves and through the distinction of having no [internal] object.

For therein, "perceiving no form internally" means that, either due to non-attainment or lack of interest, one is simply devoid of the preliminary perception regarding internal forms by way of the *kasiṇa*. Externally...
"He sees forms" means that he sees the eight external kasiṇa-forms both by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*) and by way of absorption (*appanā*).

"Limited" (*parittāni*) means small in measure; and seeing them while overcoming them is like a person with a full stomach who, having received a ladleful of food, gathers it all together, thinking, "What is there here to be eaten?"—having thus overcome it.
He makes it into a single mouthful; in the same way, one who has knowledge as his supreme guide thinks, "What is there to be attained here in this limited object?
This is no burden for me," and having overcome them, he produces absorption (appanā) simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
Therefore, that jhāna is called an "object of mastery" (abhibhāyatana). "Immeasurable" means great. "Having overcome them"—that is, having mastered them.

Just as one who eats gluttonously might feel satisfied after obtaining a single bowl of food, so too one who excels in knowledge, having obtained an immeasurable [object], brings about absorption (appanā), thinking:
"Let it be this or let it be another; what does it matter here? "Beautiful and ugly colors" means colors that are pure and impure.
For here, the pure ones are blue and so forth, while the impure ones—namely, beautiful and ugly colors—are intended.
These too have been described in the commentaries on the Āgamas as follows: "Whether they be beautiful or ugly, the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) exist by way of the limited and the measureless.

For while the former bases of mastery are described as being accompanied by the absence of attention to color, these [latter ones] are stated to be fourfold because of the presence of a specific distinction consisting solely in that [attention].
However, the four beginning with blue are [distinguished] by way of perfectly pure colors.
Because it is easy to ascend, one who possesses supreme knowledge overcomes [the object] and brings about absorption;

therefore, even though there is no difference in the objective support (*ārammaṇa*), it should be understood that these eight bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) each become eightfold according to the specific way in which the jhāna arises. The Discussion on the Bases of Mastery.
Furthermore, just as they are threefold according to the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), so too they are each threefold according to the liberations (*vimokkha*).
For the Blessed One taught three liberations: "Possessing form, one sees forms; not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally;
being intent upon the beautiful alone. And these are [attained] by way of being intent upon the kasiṇas themselves.
What is this so-called "resolute confidence" (*adhimuccana*)? It is the complete liberation from opposing states and a thorough delight in the objects of meditation.

It is said to be the engagement with the object in a state free from apprehension and without restraint, like a child lying on its father’s or mother’s lap with all its limbs relaxed. This occurs through the distinction of the arising of jhāna and the distinction of the object of cultivation.
Therein, "possessing form" (*rūpī*) means that the fine-material jhāna produced internally with respect to the head-hairs and so forth is called "form";

since he possesses that, he is "possessing form. For even internally, when one applies oneself to the preparatory work by attending to the color-kasinas—blue in the head-hairs and so forth, yellow in the bile and so forth, red in the flesh and so forth, and white in the teeth and so forth—the fine-material jhānas arise. This refers to the kasina.
And having opened [the eyes], the formless jhānas indeed arise. "He sees forms" means that he sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa and so forth with the eye of jhāna;
by this, the attainment of jhāna upon kasiṇas that have both internal and external bases is shown.
"Perceiving no form internally" means one who has not yet produced fine-material-sphere jhāna regarding one's own hair and so forth; by this—

The attainment of jhāna through external acquisition is shown. By the phrase "he is intent upon the beautiful" (*subhantveva adhimutto hoti*), the attainment of jhāna through the mode of being intent upon "the beautiful" in regard to the well-purified kasiṇas of blue and other colors is shown.

Thus, even in the absence of a difference in the objective support (*ārammaṇa*), there is a distinction in the arising of jhāna by way of the mode of intent; therefore, with respect to these three liberations (*vimokkha*), each is threefold.
It should be understood that they exist. This concludes the Discussion on Liberation.
Just as they are classified according to liberation, so too, according to the distinction of the modes of practice (*paṭipadā*), each is fourfold:

practice that is painful with slow direct knowledge (*dandhābhiñña*), practice that is painful with quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiñña*), practice that is pleasant with slow direct knowledge, and practice that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge.
"Quick direct knowledge": herein, the development of jhāna that proceeds from the first mental application until access concentration arises is called the "way" (*paṭipadā*).
For some, this is painful because it is difficult to practice due to the dense manifestation of opposing states such as the hindrances;
for others, it is pleasant because those [hindrances] are absent. From access concentration onwards, until absorption (*appanā*), [it is the way].
Wisdom that has proceeded to such an extent is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*). For some it is sluggish and slow to proceed;
for others it is swift. For one who pursues what is unsuitable, the practice is painful and direct knowledge is sluggish;

for one who pursues what is suitable, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift. There is a mixture of these states depending on whether one pursues the suitable or the unsuitable in earlier and later periods.
And [the paths] should be understood in this way: for one who does not fulfill the preliminary duties, such as the severing of impediments, the practice is painful;
for one who fulfills them, the practice is pleasant. For one who does not master the skill of absorption, direct knowledge is sluggish;

for one who masters it, it is swift. Alternatively, the first [path] arises from the sharpness of the defilements and faculties, the fourth from their opposite, and the second and third from their mixture.

It should be understood that there are two intermediate [paths]. Alternatively, their distinction should be understood by way of the overcoming or non-overcoming of craving and ignorance, or by way of whether or not one has performed the preliminary work in serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

It should also be seen that the distinction between the second and subsequent paths of progress (*paṭipadā*) and direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) exists precisely by way of the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth. Thus, by way of the paths of progress, each...
It should be understood that they are fourfold.

This concludes the discussion on the modes of practice (*paṭipadā*). Just as they are fourfold according to the modes of practice, so too, according to the distinction of objects (*ārammaṇa*), each is fourfold:
limited with a limited object, limited with an immeasurable object, immeasurable with a limited object, and immeasurable with an immeasurable object.
In this context, that which is weak and incapable of becoming a condition for higher jhāna is "limited" (paritta).
Furthermore, that which occurs with a non-expanded object has a limited object; thus, it is "limited-object" (parittārammaṇa).
By contrast, the immeasurable (appamāṇa) has an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa). Through the mixture of these two, the other two [categories] are placed in the middle.
It should be understood thus: it should be known that they are fourfold according to the distinction of their objects (*ārammaṇa*).

This concludes the discussion on objects. Furthermore, just as [they were classified] by way of the path and the objects, so too should their fourfold nature for each [of the kasinas] and their threefold nature according to the inferior triad be understood by applying [the same principles].
The exposition on the analysis of the ten root kasinas is finished.

Just as in the case of the bases of totality (*kasiṇa*), so too in the case of the bases of the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the classification should be understood according to what is appropriate:
for, by way of loving-kindness, compassion, and gladness, the first four jhānas are each threefold—namely, accompanied by loving-kindness, accompanied by compassion, and accompanied by gladness.
However, the fifth jhāna, by way of the divine abiding of equanimity, is of one kind: accompanied by equanimity.

For among the first three [realms], the fifth jhāna does not arise. Why? Because it is dissociated from mental joy (*somanassa*), and because it is the respective escape from ill will, cruelty, and lust which are originated by mental joy. And among the last [three realms], the triple and quadruple jhānas do not arise. Why?
Because they are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*), and because that [equanimity] is the escape from aversion and attraction through its mode of neutrality.

These [types of concentration] should further be understood by applying them, according to the method previously explained, to the classifications of the path, the object, the predominance, and the triads.
In this context, "limited object" (*parittārammaṇatā*) is by way of having few beings as its object, while "immeasurable object" (*appamāṇārammaṇatā*) is by way of having many beings as its object;
and having attained absorption (*appanā*) with respect to a single being, one gradually extends it to beings residing in a single dwelling, a single street, a village, and so forth.

And it should be understood that there is an increase by way of the inclusion of the evil [roots]. In this context, regarding the enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*), there are thirty-five factors associated with compassion (*karuṇā*) and dissociated from sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Among these, exactly five are included as "also-mentioned" (*yevāpanaka*): the four beginning with desire (*chanda*) and compassion itself;

and it should be understood that compassion is fixed (*niyata*). The same applies to those associated with sympathetic joy. The only difference is that they are dissociated from compassion, and sympathetic joy is fixed.

The distinction here is that it "occurs" (*pavattati*). However, in the remaining two divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and in all cases such as the kasiṇas and the foulness meditations (*asubha*), thirty-four states—excluding compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*)—are to be understood;
and therein, only the four beginning with desire (*chanda*) are to be known as the "included" (*yevāpanaka*) factors.
This concludes the discussion on the classification of the roots of the divine abidings.
Furthermore, according to the divisions of the foul (asubha), only the first jhāna is tenfold, being accompanied by the perception of a bloated corpse,

a livid corpse, a festering corpse, a fissured corpse, a gnawed corpse, a scattered corpse, a mangled corpse, a bloody corpse, a worm-infested corpse, and a skeleton. In all these ten kinds of foul objects,
because of their repulsiveness and weakness, the jhāna persists solely through the power of applied thought (vitakka).
Without applied thought (*vitakka*), it is like a boat on a swift-flowing river that cannot proceed by its own power alone; therefore, only the first jhāna arises here.

However, through the perception of the benefits of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) and through the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), rapture and joy (*pīti-somanassa*) arise, just as a scavenger sees a great reward for his wages and experiences joy even amidst a heap of dung, or as one whose suffering from disease has been pacified.

And this should be understood as being like the occurrence of emesis and purgation in one who is ill. Furthermore, that tenfold first jhāna should be understood by applying it individually according to the fourfold method of practice (*paṭipadā*), the objects (*ārammaṇa*), the predominance factors (*adhipati*), and the triads (*tika*).

And herein, because an object of foulness (*asubha*) cannot be expanded, the sign (*nimitta*) that arises at a small location such as a bloated corpse is a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*); [whereas] in a large [location],...

The object should be understood as immeasurable. Among these ten kinds of foulness, however, mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is included as it occurs by way of the thirty-two aspects in general, and by way of the nine cemetery contemplations;

and in the case of the color-kasinas, there is mindfulness directed to the body that arises by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, having the colors such as blue and so forth of the parts beginning with hair as its object.
Included. They are not mentioned separately in the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*); therefore, their classification should also be understood by way of those [categories].
This concludes the discussion on the classification of the foulness-based [meditations].

Thus, although the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala-dhamma*) are divided according to objects and so forth, they are infinite in terms of distinctions such as time and place.

The manner in which the Blessed One taught by bringing [the states] to a single unity, as well as the extension of the method of exposition, should be understood accordingly following what was stated for the wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Hereafter, we shall mention only the specific differences regarding the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara*) and so forth.
Thus should the analysis be understood according to the distinctions of object and other factors.
The wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are concluded.
As for the wholesome states of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), however, they are not distinct in terms of their association; all are associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.

They are also entirely similar to the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere in terms of the description of the factors (*dhammuddesa*) and so forth. Here, the only difference is the state of being immaterial.
The distinction. Regarding "by way of the classification of objects and so forth": here, by way of their objective support (*ārammaṇa*), they are fourfold. Namely:

the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*), the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
Among these, the first occurs with regard to the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa, [perceiving] "space is infinite"; and in that first immaterial-sphere consciousness...
The second [meditative attainment] occurs as "consciousness is infinite"; the third occurs as "there is nothing whatsoever" due to the absence of that first formless-sphere consciousness;
and the fourth occurs as "this is peaceful, this is sublime" with respect to that third.
It should be understood that each subsequent one is more peaceful, more peaceful, and most peaceful than each preceding one.

But surely, it has been stated that among the fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacara*), each successive *jhāna* is more peaceful and so forth due to the transcendence of factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*);
however, how is this explained in the case of the formless attainments (*āruppa*), which are devoid of such transcendence of factors? It is through the transcendence of the object (*ārammaṇa*).

For among these, the first *jhāna* is more peaceful than the fifth fine-material-sphere *jhāna* because of the transcendence of the kasiṇa-form; and even more so than that [first formless *jhāna*] because of the transcendence of the space derived from the removal of the kasiṇa.
The second [jhāna] is superior to that; the third is superior even to that because it transcends consciousness occurring in space;

and the fourth is superior even to that because it completely transcends consciousness occurring in space. Thus, although the factors are equal in number, one should understand that each successive jhāna is more peaceful and so forth due to the progressive refinement of the object through the transcendence of coarser stages—just as among fabrics of equal length and breadth, some are finer than others because the threads are progressively finer.

It is as if [he were looking at it]. But surely, if the third immaterial state is taken as the object of non-existence (*abhāvārammaṇa*) by one who attends to it as peaceful and sublime, how can there be the exhaustion of attachment toward the fourth immaterial state therein, and how can there be its transcendence?

It is because of the lack of desire to attain it, and that [lack of desire] arises from its own peaceful and sublime nature. For just as a king [does not desire] the exceedingly delicate and unpleasant craft of ivory-workers and other such artisans...
Having seen this, even though he is satisfied by their skill, thinking, "These teachers are indeed clever," he does not aspire to that state of mere craftmanship;
rather, having transcended it, he remains in the status of a king. This should be understood as being exactly like that.

Thus, these fourfold [kinds of jhāna] according to the distinction of objects (ārammaṇa) are further divided, according to the previously mentioned method, by the distinctions of the path (paṭipadā), object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), and the triads (hīnattika).
The distinction should be understood individually.

Herein, the first immaterial attainment has a difficult progress because of the suffering involved in exhausting attachment to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere; the second immaterial attainment and those following have a difficult progress because of the suffering involved in exhausting attachment to the first immaterial attainment and so on;
and for one whose attachment has been exhausted, there is sluggishness in the maintenance of that absorption.
The state of sluggish direct knowledge and its opposite should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the four [kasiṇas] rooted in the space remaining after the removal of a limited kasiṇa have limited objects, while their opposites have immeasurable objects.

Herein, those pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres arise only together with their respective predominants, not without predominants; however, those of the sense-sphere may arise even without a predominant.
When they arise, both types of predominance—object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*)—are obtained.

However, for those pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres, only co-nascent predominance applies, not the other. In that context, the states that arise together with desire-predominance (*chandādhipati*) are "governed by desire" (*chandādhipateyya*);
yet, desire itself is only the predominance, not something governed by desire. The others, however, are only "governed by" (predominance), not the predominances themselves.
This is because there is no other desire co-nascent with itself, nor any other predominance factor among the rest.
For in a single arising of consciousness, even when all four—desire and the others—are present, only one co-nascent predominance is obtained according to the conditions.
In the same way, this should be understood accordingly for the predominance of energy and so forth. Thus, the analysis should be understood according to the distinctions of object and so on.
The wholesome states of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*) are concluded.
As for the supramundane (*lokuttara*) wholesome states, they are fourfold according to their association with the paths (*magga*). That is to say:

associated with the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), associated with the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi*), associated with the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi*), and associated with the path of arahantship (*arahatta*). Is it not so?
Since the association with the Path is common to all four paths, and since all eight path-factors arise in every case, how can there be a distinction among them?
It is because of the distinction in the function of the Path, which consists in the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
For the Path is so called because it goes about slaying the underlying tendencies; for the Paths abandon their respective underlying tendencies and emerge from their respective signs.
They are called "cutting off the occurrence" (*pavatta*). "The sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*), and it is these very same aggregates that occur.
That [sign] is twofold: appropriated (*upādinnaka*) and unappropriated (*anupādinnaka*).

Among those, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) cuts off the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), the defilements associated with them, and the [formations] co-nascent with them.
The five unwholesome consciousnesses—those associated with wrong view and that associated with doubt—are eradicated as they arise;
and while being eradicated, one emerges from the remainder of existence, setting aside the seven existences other than those of the states of misery (*apāya*) and the happy destinies (*sugati*).
In this context, that which is worthy of arising prior to the attainment of the first path...
The matter originated by the five types of consciousness associated with wrong view and doubt is the aggregate of form;
those five types of consciousness are the aggregate of consciousness; and the feeling and other mental factors associated with them are the remaining three aggregates.

These are the five aggregates not acquired through clinging (*anupādinnapañcakkhandhā*), which are called the sign not acquired through clinging (*anupādinnanimitta*) and the occurrence not acquired through clinging (*anupādinnappavatta*). From that, the first path emerges and cuts it off.

Name. That which consists of the pentad of kamma-born aggregates arising in the future—excluding the states of misery and the seven [supramundane] existences, as well as those remaining until the non-arising of the first path—is called "clung-to-sign" (*upādinnanimitta*) and "clung-to-occurrence" (*upādinnappavatta*).
From that, the first path emerges and it is said to "cut off" that [sign]. It is from that very point that the first path [cuts off] the underlying tendency (*anusaya*).
It should be understood that while abandoning the signs (*nimitta*), one emerges from them and severs the process of occurrence (*pavatta*).
In the same way, in the other paths as well, emergence and the severing of the occurrence of both acquired and unacquired signs should be understood according to their respective nature.

Furthermore, the once-returning path abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) in its coarse form, the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), and the defilements associated with them.
Simultaneously with that [knowledge], he eradicates the six unwholesome consciousnesses that arise together with it— namely, the four associated with wrong view and the two accompanied by grief—
and while eradicating them, he emerges from the rest of the sense-sphere existence (kāmadhātu), setting aside only one remaining birth. For one who possesses that [knowledge],
even the most intense sensual lust and ill will have become merely attenuated.
And it should be understood that these arise only occasionally.
The path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) eradicates those same six types of consciousness that have arisen by way of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) of subtle sensual lust and ill will;
and while eradicating them, it emerges from the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava). The path of arahantship...
Furthermore, while arising, he eradicates the underlying tendencies of lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, and ignorance; restlessness; all defilements associated with those [tendencies];
the four unwholesome consciousnesses dissociated from views that are co-nascent with them; and the five unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by restlessness.
And while eradicating them, he emerges from both the realms of form and the formless, and from all states of existence. The remainder is as in the first path.

This should be understood according to what has been stated. Thus, the distinction between the four paths should be understood by way of the difference in their functions, which consist in the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

In this way, they are fourfold by way of the distinction of association with the [four] paths; furthermore, each one becomes fivefold by way of the distinction of association with the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*).

How so? First, that which is associated with the first path is associated with initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), zest (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*).
It is fivefold: associated with the first jhāna; associated with the second jhāna (possessing applied thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness);
associated with the third jhāna (possessing rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness); associated with the fourth jhāna (possessing happiness and one-pointedness);
and associated with the fifth jhāna (possessing equanimity and one-pointedness). Thus, including those associated with the second path and so forth, there are twenty types.
And here, the sixteenfold classification should also be applied by way of the fourfold method.
But what is the determining cause for such a distinction in the application of the jhāna factors here? It is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).

For when that [knowledge] has become insight leading to emergence, noble paths accompanied by joy do not arise with five jhāna factors; rather, they arise with four jhāna factors, being accompanied by joy.
Those accompanied by equanimity do not arise as the fourfold jhānas; rather, only those accompanied by equanimity arise as the fivefold jhānas.

Is it not the case that here the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*)—because it is accompanied by both joy and equanimity—is the determining cause for the state of being accompanied by joy and equanimity in both the fourfold and fivefold jhānas?
However, because of the surmounting of factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*), etc., in these [fivefold jhānas]...

There must be something else that determines the arising of the second and subsequent jhānas; for the knowledge of equanimity towards formations does not arise devoid of applied thought and the other factors by which it might be determined. What, then, is that determining cause?

It is either the foundational jhāna or the jhāna that has been taken as the object of comprehension. For among the fine-material and immaterial-sphere attainments, whichever jhāna one enters and remains in, [from that state...]
Some, having comprehended miscellaneous formations (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra*), give rise to paths; all those [paths] are similar to the respective jhānas.

Or rather, whatever jhāna one has, having practiced insight (*vipassanā*) into its associated factors as impermanent and so forth, whichever paths one gives rise to, they too are similar to that respective jhāna, just as a lizard’s color resembles the color of the ground. In this regard:

Furthermore, whether it is the path arisen in a practitioner of dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka), or a path produced by one who has attained meditative absorption (samāpatti-lābhin) without making jhāna the basis and without having practiced insight-contemplation (asammasitvā), or a path produced by making the first jhāna the basis or by contemplating that very jhāna—
all such paths are exactly the same and belong to the first jhāna. For indeed, there is no supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) that does not reach full absorption (appanā).

It exists. Paths produced by taking the second, third, and fourth jhānas as the basis, or by contemplating the phenomena occurring therein, possess four factors, three factors, and two factors respectively.
Furthermore, paths produced by taking the fifth jhāna or the formless-sphere jhānas as the basis, or by contemplating the phenomena occurring therein, [possess one factor].

By way of equanimity and one-pointedness, they consist of only two factors. Furthermore, although for these five types of jhānas the preliminary insight may be accompanied by either joy or equanimity,
the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*) is accompanied by joy for those of the four jhānas,
whereas for those of the fifth jhāna it is accompanied by equanimity.

That very access-concentration (*pādakajjhāna*) or the concentration attained through reflection (*sammasitajjhāna*) should be understood as the cause of entering the certainty of rightness (*niyāmakakāraṇa*). Such is the analysis by way of association.

Furthermore, regarding the enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*) and so forth: first, among the four types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness belonging to the first jhāna, there are thirty-seven factors, excluding compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*), from among the factors already mentioned.
However, here the abstinences (*virati*) are fixed, and in the Discourse (*pāḷi*)...
It should be understood that desire (*chanda*) and the other three [factors] are indicated by form (*rūpa*) and are included among the "others" (*yevāpanaka*).

However, in the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha*), four additional groups should be understood by way of the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) not previously included—namely, the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), and the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). For, among the states associated with the path possessing the first jhāna...

Mindfulness (*sati*) is a foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) in the sense of its establishment; that is fourfold according to the distinction of its objects, while the others are non-foundations of mindfulness.
Thus, all of them are twofold. Likewise, energy (*vīriya*) is right effort (*sammappadhāna*) in the sense of striving;
that is fourfold according to the distinction of its functions, while the others are non-efforts. Likewise, there are four: zeal, energy, consciousness, and non-delusion.

In the sense of being effective (*ijjhanaka*), these factors are called "bases of accomplishment" (*iddhipāda*) by their respective names— "the basis of accomplishment consisting in zeal," "the basis of accomplishment consisting in energy," "the basis of accomplishment consisting in consciousness," and "the basis of accomplishment consisting in investigation"—

while the others are "non-bases of accomplishment. Likewise, when there is mindfulness, these seven factors— namely, non-delusion, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity— are [called "factors of enlightenment"] in the sense of awakening (*bujjhana*).
“The enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity” are so called;
the others are not enlightenment factors—thus are the four groupings.
The remainder, starting from the characteristics and ending with the section on emptiness, is all as in the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness.

It is exactly as stated before; however, in the summary of the path factors (*maggaṅga-saṅgaha*), it is specified in its own form in the word-analysis (*padabhājaniya*) as "there is an eightfold path.

In the summary of the faculties (*indriya-saṅgaha*), under the heading of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) is taken for the first path, and the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) is taken for the other paths;
thus, there is the state of being eight faculties (*aṭṭhindriyatā*). This applies in all cases.
The distinction lies in their supramundane nature (*lokuttaratā*); the rest is exactly the same. There are four paths associated with the first jhāna.

Likewise, regarding those associated with the second jhāna, the only difference is the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*) in the enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*), while in the section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*), there is the state of being a four-factored jhāna and a seven-factored path; the rest is identical to that of the first jhāna. These are the paths associated with the second jhāna.

Likewise, regarding those associated with the third jhāna, the only differences are the absence of sustained thought (*vicāra*) in the enumeration of factors and the state of being a three-factored jhāna in the section on inclusion; the rest is identical to that of the second jhāna. These are the paths associated with the third jhāna.

Likewise, in the case of those belonging to the fourth jhāna, the only differences are the absence of *pīti* (rapture) in the mere enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*), the state of being a two-factored jhāna in the section on constituents (*koṭṭhāsavāra*), and the state of being a six-factored factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
The rest is exactly the same as for the third jhāna. This concludes the paths belonging to the fourth jhāna.

Likewise, in the case of those belonging to the fifth jhāna, the only difference is the substitution of the feeling (*vedanā*) in all instances; the rest is exactly the same as for the fourth jhāna. This concludes the paths belonging to the fifth jhāna. Such is the analysis beginning from the enumeration of factors.
Furthermore, when classified according to their objects and so forth, all supramundane wholesome states have Nibbāna as their object; therefore, there is no distinction among them on that basis.
However, their individual distinctions should be understood according to the previously explained method, based on the distinctions of the path (paṭipadā) and so forth.
And herein, one who, having become weary starting from the discernment of name-and-form, undertakes insight with difficulty—
One who suppresses defilements with difficulty has a painful practice.

However, one whose defilements have been suppressed, while dwelling in the probationary period of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*), reaches the manifestation of the path after a long time; for him, there is sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*).
By this same method, the other three practices and types of direct knowledge are to be understood. And just as [they differ] according to the classification of practice and so forth,
Thus, by way of the divisions of liberation as well, each is twofold: the void liberation (*suññatavimokkha*) and the desireless liberation (*appaṇihitavimokkha*).
In this context, "void" and "desireless" are names for the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*).

For that [path] receives its name through three reasons: from its approach, from its qualities, and from its object. How so? Here, a monk who takes insight meditation (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) as his subject of practice...
From the very beginning, he proceeds by contemplating and investigating while applying the threefold contemplation that "it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
If his insight leading to emergence contemplates the conditioned phenomena of the three planes as non-self, this is called "emptiness" in the sense of seeing the voidness of self.
If he contemplates them as suffering, this is [called emptiness] in the sense of being devoid of the longing of craving.

It is called "the wishless" (*appaṇihita*). Both of them, standing at the point of arrival, give their respective paths the names "the path of emptiness" (*suññatamagga*) and "the wishless path" (*appaṇihitamagga*) according to their sequence. Thus, the acquisition of the name should be understood by way of arrival.

But is it not said in the Suttantas that if the insight leading to emergence contemplates [the object] as impermanent, the path resulting from its influence is the "signless liberation" (*animittavimokkha*)?
Is it because they "occur" that three liberations are taught? True; however, they are taught by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyato*).

But in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyato*), there are only two liberations, because even [the third] itself, being accompanied by a sign (*sanimittā*), is incapable of giving its own path the name "signless.
For all three types of insight (*vipassanā*) involve the removal of the sign of permanence (*niccanimitta*) and the sign of pleasure (*sukhanimitta*).
They obtain the designation "signless" because they proceed by way of the three aggregates which have become signs;
therefore, standing in their own place of arrival, they are unable to give the name "signless" to their own path in its primary sense.
However, because the path itself is empty of lust and so forth, and is devoid of the signs and aspirations of lust and so forth, [it is called signless].

Therefore, it receives the names "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and "the wishless" (*appaṇihita*) precisely because it possesses these qualities. In this way, its acquisition of names by virtue of its qualities should be understood.

Furthermore, because Nibbāna is empty of lust and so forth, as well as of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), and because it is devoid of the signs and wishes associated with lust and so forth, it is called "emptiness," "the signless" (*animitta*), and "the wishless.
Consequently, the path that arises having made that [Nibbāna] its object is likewise so designated.
It receives the names "void," "signless," and "desireless. Thus, the acquisition of names from the perspective of the object should be understood.
Among these, here the Path receives its name only from its arrival [at the goal], not from its qualities, nor from its object;

for the acquisition of names based on both qualities and objects is taught in the Suttantas as a figurative method (pariyāya). For that very reason, here, even though the Paths have both qualities and objects—
Without taking up the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*), it is stated [as such] because of the arrival at the emptiness and wishless liberations (*suññata-appaṇihita-vimokkha*) alone;

and that arrival is twofold: arrival by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and arrival by way of the path (*magga*). In that regard, the path receives the names "emptiness" and so forth from the arrival by way of insight, and it certainly receives them from the arrival by way of the path as well;
however, since the path is intended here, [it is stated] only from the perspective of the arrival by way of insight.
This should be understood. Thus, according to the division of liberations, each is twofold. Such is the analysis according to the distinctions of object and so forth.
The supramundane wholesome states are concluded.
And [this work] called *Mohavicchedanī* is finished.
The commentary on the meaning of the term "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*) from the *Abhidhammamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanā*. The meaning of the term "unwholesome" (*akusala*).
Commentary on the Root of Greed:

Unwholesome states are of one kind according to their plane, being exclusively of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*). However, according to their association and by way of their roots, they are of three kinds:

those rooted in greed (*lobha*), those rooted in hatred (*dosa*), and those rooted in delusion (*moha*). Among these, those rooted in greed are of eight types, accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*).
Associated with views, without volitional effort; likewise, with volitional effort. Accompanied by joy, dissociated from views, without volitional effort; likewise, with volitional effort.
Accompanied by equanimity, associated with views, without volitional effort; likewise, with volitional effort.
Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from views, without volitional effort; likewise, with volitional effort.

In this context, it should be understood that the state of being accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*) arises from causes such as an abundance of greed toward a desirable object, while association with wrong view (*diṭṭhi-sampayutta*) arises from hearing false doctrines, associating with unwholesome friends, and so forth.

For when one—preceded by wrong view in the manner of "there is no danger in sensual pleasures"—enjoys sensual pleasures with a joyful and elated mind, or regards things such as "seeing as auspicious" as essential; at that time, [the consciousness is associated with joy and wrong view].
When the mind is incited by its own natural intensity, then the first unwholesome thought arises;

when it is incited by a mild degree, then the second [arises]. When one, without placing wrong view at the forefront, merely engages in sexual intercourse out of sheer joy and satisfaction, or covets another’s prosperity, or steals another’s property, being incited by natural intensity—[then the third arises].
Then there is the third [type]. When it is aroused by an uplifted mind, then there is the fourth.

However, when—due either to the non-attainment of sensual pleasures or to the absence of other causes for joy—there is an absence of joy across all four alternatives, then the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā). This is the analysis according to association (sampayoga).

According to the enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*), first, regarding the unwholesome states, there are twenty factors: sixteen that are fixed and explicitly mentioned in the Canon, and four that are included by way of being "included" (*yevāpanaka*).

How so? They are: contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), consciousness (*citta*), applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), energy (*vīriya*), one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), life-faculty (*jīvita*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

These sixteen states have come down with their own specific forms; and these four—desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokkha*), attention (*manasikāra*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—are the "inclusionary" (*yevāpanaka*) factors.

However, in the Word-Commentary (*padabhājanīya*), according to the method previously stated, there are five faculties by way of the pentad of contact, the pentad of jhāna-factors, and energy, concentration, mental joy, and vitality; and [five wrong courses] by way of wrong view, intention, effort, concentration, and...
The four path-factors, the four powers by way of energy, concentration, moral shame, and moral dread;
the two roots, namely greed and delusion; the two courses of kamma, namely covetousness and wrong view; the pair that destroys the world, namely moral shamelessness and moral recklessness;
and serenity, exertion, and non-distraction—thus, among these thirty-two states that have been mentioned according to their specific natures, [they are all] contained within the sixteen [factors].

The grouping together and the distinction between those with and without case endings should be understood according to what was stated regarding the first wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
This is the exposition by way of the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*).

As for the analysis by way of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth: it does not feel shame, thus it is *ahirika*; the state of one who is shameless is *ahirikka*; it is not moral dread (*ottappa*).

And lack of moral dread (*anottappa*). Among these, shamelessness (*ahirika*) has the characteristic of not being disgusted by bodily misconduct and so forth, or it has the characteristic of lack of shame;

lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) has the characteristic of not being afraid of those same things, or it has the characteristic of fearlessness. The rest should be understood by way of the opposites of what was stated for shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).
It is called *lobha* (greed) because one is greedy by means of it, or because one is greedy oneself, or because it is merely the state of being greedy.
Its characteristic is the grasping of an object, like the smearing of a monkey. Its function is clinging, like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan.
It is manifested as non-renunciation, like the stain of oil and soot. Its proximate cause is the perception of gratification in things that fetter. By way of its nature as craving...
It should be understood that, like a river with a swift current, as it grows it goes only toward the great ocean, which is the plane of misery (*apāya*).
It is called delusion (*moha*) because beings are deluded by it, or it itself is deluded, or it is merely the state of being deluded.

Its characteristic is darkness of mind, or its characteristic is non-knowing (*aññāṇa*); its function is non-penetration, or its function is the obscuring of the true nature of the object; its manifestation is wrong practice.
It should be understood as having darkness as its manifestation, improper attention as its proximate cause, and being the root of all unwholesome states.
It is wrong view because by means of it they see wrongly, or because it itself sees wrongly, or because it is merely wrong seeing.
Its characteristic is irrational insistence; its function is misapprehension; its manifestation is wrong adherence; [it is opposed] to the Noble Ones...
The states beginning with "the desire not to see" should be understood as the supreme faults (*vajja*).

Restlessness (*uddhacca*) is the state of being agitated. It should be understood as having the characteristic of lack of tranquility, the function of instability, the manifestation of wavering, the proximate cause of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), and its essence is the distraction of the mind.
The remainder here, up to the conclusion of the section on emptiness (*suññatā-vāra*), is as follows:
The entire exposition should be understood according to what has been stated in the section on the wholesome (*kusala*).

The only difference is that, as they appear in the text under the heading of "Inclusion" (*saṅgaha*), there is the state of having five faculties, the state of having four factors of the path, the state of having four kinds of powers, the state of having two roots, and the unwholesome nature in all instances;
the rest is exactly the same. The first unwholesome [course of action] is finished.

And just as in the first [jhāna], so too in the second there is the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*), the possibility of sloth and torpor among the "inclusionary" factors, and their fixed nature—these are the distinctions.
Therein, *thina* is the state of being slothful; *middha* is the state of being torpid;

the meaning is: a lack of exertion, a state of sinking, and a loss of capability. Therein, sloth has the characteristic of non-exertion, the function of dispelling energy, and the manifestation of sinking.
Drowsiness has the characteristic of unfitness for work; its function is to shroud; it is manifested as sluggishness, or it is manifested as nodding and sleep.
Both are rooted in improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) regarding restlessness, lethargy, yawning, and so forth. This is the second [unwholesome root].

In the third [root], the entire exposition follows the same method as that stated for the first unwholesome state; the only difference is the absence of wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) among the "sometimes-occurring" factors (*yevāpanaka*).
The origin of conceit (*māna*), its lack of fixity, and the state of possessing a threefold path in the section on inclusion are the specific distinctions; the rest is exactly as before.

In this context, "he conceives" (*maññati*) is conceit (*māna*). It has the characteristic of puffing up, the function of grasping at excellence, the manifestation of a desire for self-display, and its proximate cause is greed dissociated from wrong view;
it should be regarded as like madness. This is the third [chapter].

And as in the third, so too in the fourth; however, sloth-and-torpor (*thīnamiddha*) and the state of being with effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) are additional here, while the rest is exactly the same. This is the fourth.
In the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth, where there was previously joy (*somanassa*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) arises and joy is absent;

for that very reason, the distinction in the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha*) is the state of four-factored absorption (*caturaṅgajjhānatā*), while everything else is identical to the first, second, third, and fourth consciousnesses.
The section on the roots of greed is finished.

Now, for the commentary on the roots of hatred: those rooted in hatred are twofold—namely, that accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion, being either without volitional effort or with volitional effort.
Thus it is by way of association. However, starting from the enumeration of the factors (*dhammuddesa*), first, in the case of the first unwholesome consciousness, there are twenty-one factors:

having excluded joy (*pīti*), greed (*lobha*), and wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) from those mentioned for the first unwholesome consciousness; having added hatred (*dosa*) from the "sometimes-occurring" (*yevāpanaka*) factors; having added the indeterminate envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and worry (*kukkucca*);
and having substituted grief (*domanassa*) for the place of gladness (*somanassa*). Furthermore, there are seven "sometimes-occurring" factors here. Among these:
It is called *dosa* (hatred) because by it one becomes corrupt, or one is oneself corrupted, or it is merely the state of being corrupt.
Its characteristic is ferocity, like a struck venomous snake; its function is to spread [corruption], like the application of poison; or its function is to burn its own support, like a forest fire.
It is manifested as corruption, like an enemy who has found an opening; its proximate cause is the basis for resentment; it is associated with poison, like putrid urine mixed with poison.
It should be viewed as such. Envy (*issā*) is the state of envying. It has the characteristic of being envious of the success of others;
its function is dissatisfaction with that very [success]; it is manifested as turning away from it; its proximate cause is the success of others;

and it should be viewed as a fetter (*saññojana*). Stinginess (*macchariya*) is the state of being stingy. Its characteristic is the concealment of one’s own successes—whether already obtained or yet to be obtained.

It should be understood as having the nature of being unable to endure sharing those very [virtues] with others; its manifestation is shrinking back, or its manifestation is a state of harshness and rigidity;
its proximate cause is one’s own excellence; and it is the deformity of the mind. What is badly done is *kukata*;

the state of that is *kukkucca* (remorse). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; its function is grieving over what was done and what was left undone; its manifestation is remorse (*vippaṭisāra*).

The section on what has been done and what remains to be done should be regarded as being like slavery. In the section on inclusion, it should be understood that there is fourfold jhāna together with suffering, fivefold faculty together with mental grief, threefold path, and double-rootedness by way of hatred and delusion.
All the remaining analysis is exactly the same as what was stated for the first unwholesome consciousness. And just as it is in the first, so too...

In the second [jhāna] as well, the distinction lies in the presence of effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) and the inclusion of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) among the nine factors; the rest is exactly the same.
The section on the roots of hatred (*dosamūla*) is finished. Now follows the commentary on the roots of delusion (*mohamūla*).
The delusion-rooted [consciousness] is also twofold: that accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt, and likewise that associated with restlessness.

Therein, first, according to the enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*), fourteen factors appear in their own form: the pentad of contact (*phassapañcaka*), applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), energy (*vīriya*), one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), life-faculty (*jīvita*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), delusion (*moha*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*); as well as restlessness (*uddhacca*) and attention (*manasikāra*).
Including the two “and-so-far” factors, there are sixteen states. Here, one-pointedness is merely the steadiness of consciousness;

it does not attain the status of a faculty, path factor, or power. For that very reason, in the section on the summary, excluding concentration, there are four faculties, two path factors, and three powers, together with equanimity. Delusion, however, is the only root cause here. As for the remainder here...
The entire analysis is exactly as previously stated.

In this context, *vicikicchā* (doubt) is so called because it is free from healing (*cikicchā*). It has the characteristic of uncertainty, the function of wavering, and it manifests as indecision or as a state of non-conviction.
Its proximate cause is improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), and its role is to create an obstacle to progress on the path.
They are to be seen. And just as it is with the factors associated with doubt, so it is with those associated with restlessness.
The only difference is the absence of doubt and the presence of resolve; consequently, there is a state of more powerful concentration.

For that very reason, in the section on the summary, there is a state of five faculties together with concentration, a state of the three-limbed path, and a state of four powers. And here, restlessness—
It is described by its own form; the distinction is that the two types of attention—resolute and mental—are included as "mere inclusion" (*yevāpanaka*), while the rest is exactly the same.
Furthermore, these two types of consciousness proceed without being obstructed, whether their objects are diverse or identical.
For the consciousness accompanied by restlessness, having obtained resoluteness, becomes established; having gained a footing, it remains fixed upon a single object.
It should be understood that [the consciousness] proceeds having established itself like a square gem, whereas the other proceeds among various objects like a round gem.
Furthermore, with the exception of that accompanied by restlessness, it should be known that the remaining eleven produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Moreover, these twelve types, according to their classification by way of object and so forth, are first of all sixfold by way of the bases (*vatthu*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*). Among them:

However, the ten [unwholesome courses of action] rooted in greed and delusion are sixfold when they accomplish the function of impulsion (*javana*) at the five sense doors by depending solely on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), or at the mind door by either depending or not depending [on a base].
Likewise, those rooted in hatred proceed only by depending [on a base].
As for those rooted in greed, they consist of taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, frivolous chatter, and covetousness.
By way of the six courses of action (*kamma-patha*), they are sixfold. Furthermore, when associated with views, they become sevenfold by including wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).
However, those rooted in hatred (*dosa-mūla*) are sevenfold by way of killing, taking what is not given, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, and ill will (*byāpāda*).
Moreover, these ten [unwholesome roots] are [further classified] by way of their doors of action (*dvāra-kamma*) and by way of the three predominants (*adhipati*) excluding investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).

And the classification of the wholesome [states] should be understood according to the method already stated. Because they are exclusively inferior, there is no division into an "inferior triad. However, in this context, objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) occurs only in those states rooted in greed, not in the others;
furthermore, in those rooted in delusion, even co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) is absent, as is the division into courses of action (*kammapatha*).
For [delusion] does not exercise any predominant influence while it is active. Nor does hatred [exercise such influence] over its own object.

Furthermore, although a mind of doubt (*vicikicchā-citta*) acts as an obstacle to practice and serves as a cause for misconduct such as killing, it does not constitute a breach of the path of action (*kamma-patha*) because it is finalized only by minds rooted in hatred or greed; rather, it is a cause only in its prior stage.

Therefore, it should be understood that its status as a cause for rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*) is to be abandoned by the first path (*magga*). [This concludes the section] on the classification according to the past and so forth.

Furthermore, the individual infinity of each of the twelve [types of unwholesome consciousness] and the remaining analysis should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on the wholesome (*kusalādhikāra*).
The unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) are concluded.
The meaning of the indeterminate term (*abyākata-padaṭṭhāna*).
Exposition of the Rootless Wholesome Resultants.
As for the indeterminate (abyākata) phenomena, they are fourfold by way of origin: resultants, functionals, materiality, and Nibbāna.

Among these, the indeterminate resultant phenomena are twofold by way of origin, according to wholesome and unwholesome resultants. Among those, the wholesome resultants are [further divided] by plane...

It is fourfold by way of the resultant [consciousness] of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane. Among these, the sense-sphere resultants are twofold:
rootless (*ahetuka*) and with-roots (*sahetuka*). Therein, those devoid of roots such as non-greed are the rootless ones.
They are eightfold according to the divisions of association, basis, object, and so forth. Namely: eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity; likewise ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness.
Body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure, the mind-element accompanied by equanimity, the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy,

and likewise that accompanied by equanimity. For the four consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness [arise] due to the extreme weakness of the impact and friction between derived forms within the four derived forms,
such as the eye-sensitivity, which is like the collision of one drop of oil with another drop of oil.

They are associated exclusively with equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*). However, body-consciousness (*kāya-viññāṇa*)—due to the intensity of the impact and friction caused by the collision of the three primary elements of the tangible object against the body-faculty—is accompanied by pleasure (*sukha-sahagata*), just as a blow from a hammer strikes a ball of cotton placed upon it;

this occurs because resistance arises even within the primary elements that serve as the basis for the sensitive matter. The mind-element (*mano-dhātu*), however, [is accompanied by equanimity] due to its own weakness in grasping [the object].

In the case of what is extremely desirable, they are accompanied by equanimity; however, the mind-consciousness element, when directed toward what is extremely desirable, is accompanied by joy, while when directed toward what is moderately desirable, it is accompanied by equanimity—this is the analysis by way of association.
As for the enumeration of states and so forth, first, in eye-consciousness, the pentad of contact, one-pointedness, and life-faculty appear as distinct entities.
There are eight factors: the seven [mental states] by way of inclusion and attention as the eighth. Regarding their classification, there are five classifications here:

by way of aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), nutriment (āhāra), and faculties (indriya). Among these, the classification by way of elements should be understood as being by way of the eye-consciousness element and the mental-object element;
the classification by way of faculties should be understood as being by way of the mind faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the life faculty. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
And here, although feeling is present, it does not become a factor of jhāna; rather, it is a faculty.

One-pointedness, due to its extreme weakness, does not even attain the status of a faculty, a path-factor, or a power. For jhāna has applied thought as its final limit, while the path and the powers have the root-cause as their final limit.
And as it is in this case, so it is with ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness as well.

However, in the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha*), there is an inclusion of elements (*dhātusaṅgaha*) by way of the ear-consciousness element and so forth, and the distinction is the substitution of feeling (*vedanā*) in body-consciousness.
As it is here, so it is for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as well; however, three additional factors are present:

applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and resolve (*adhimokkha*). In the section on inclusion, there is an inclusion of elements by way of the mind-element and the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*).
The inclusion of the four jhāna factors—initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), equanimity (*upekkhā*), and one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*)—constitutes the distinction.

Although the inclusion of the jhāna factors is not explicitly mentioned here in the text, it must nevertheless be understood because the presence of these factors is necessarily possible in those states accompanied by initial application.
And as it is here, so it is in the two mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). However, due to their being accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), rapture (*pīti*) is predominant here.

In the section on inclusion, the distinctions are: the state of five-factored jhāna, the transformation of feeling, and—in both cases—the inclusion of elements by way of the mind-consciousness element and the mental-object element;
the rest is the same as before.
Furthermore, according to the classification of objects and so forth, the five beginning with eye-consciousness each have, respectively, only one basis, such as the eye and so on.

Depending on the present, upon each respective desirable object such as visible form and so forth, immediately following the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu), the faculties and so forth—having light, space, air, water, and earth as their co-factors—accomplish the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, and ripen within each respective door, such as the eye-door and so on.
Thus, the bases, doors, objects, and functions of these [faculties] are individually fixed. This is the section on the locus (*ṭhāna*).
However, for all these five [elements], there is only one [basis]; therefore, there is no distinction among them.

The mind-element (manodhātu), however, depending solely on the heart-base (hadayavatthu), performs the function of receiving immediately after the fivefold sense-consciousness with respect to all five present objects such as visible forms;
thus, it operates at all five doors. The mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) accompanied by joy, however—

Relying solely upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), it ripens by accomplishing the function of investigation immediately after the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*) regarding the five present objects that are very desirable;

and it also ripens by accomplishing the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) immediately after the impulsion (*javana*) regarding strong sense-sphere objects—whether past, future, or otherwise—across all six doors. Thus, its doors, objects, functions, and positions are not fixed.
From that, there is a distinction; however, when the object is fixed right there, there is no distinction. It is the same with [volition] accompanied by equanimity.
But this [equanimity] alone, even when dissociated from the sense doors, arises at the moment of rebirth-linking for those born blind, deaf, or insane in a happy destination;
it appears through the power of kamma immediately after the final death-consciousness, directed toward kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of the destination.
Taking as its object any of the sixfold sense-sphere objects—whether past, future, or otherwise—it performs the function of rebirth-linking;
thereafter, until the end of its lifespan, it performs the function of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); and finally, it performs the function of death.
Furthermore, by the method already described, it accomplishes the functions of investigation and registration. Thus, it ripens in these five instances. This is [the explanation].
The distinction is this; the rest is the same as before.

And here, when an undesirable object arises through such means as killing or binding, because wholesome states arise by way of patience and reflection, if the sign of the kamma (*kamma-nimitta*) produced thereby becomes the object for the rebirth-linking consciousness and so forth, it is [perceived] as undesirable alone.

It must be so. Thus, since wholesome resultant consciousnesses that have arisen with respect to a desirable object do not arise with respect to undesirable objects, it is understood that their object is exclusively the sign of the destiny determined by karma (*kamma-gati-nimitta*).

Having investigated this, one should accept it in such a way that there is no contradiction. Likewise, for the rebirth-linking consciousness and subsequent consciousnesses produced from wholesome states that have arisen with respect to a desirable object...

It should be understood that there is no contradiction in their having the sign of the kamma as their object. Furthermore, the immediate succession of each of the eight types—according to their divisions into past and so forth—should be grasped by the method explained immediately above.
The wholesome-resultants without root-cause are finished.
Commentary on the Wholesome Resultant with Roots:

However, those associated with roots such as non-greed are "with roots" (*sahetuka*); by way of association, they are of eight types, just like the wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Here, the association with joy, knowledge, and so forth should be understood from the [respective] sources. For that which possesses three roots...
Sensuous-sphere wholesome kamma, having given rebirth-linking with either three roots or two roots, gives sixteen resultants during the course of existence at the six doors.

However, wholesome kamma with two roots, having given rebirth-linking with either two roots or no roots, gives twelve resultants—excluding those with three roots—during the course of existence at the six doors. As for the state of being unprompted or prompted here:

It also arises from a difference in conditions. For that which arises through a strong condition is *asaṅkhārika* (unprompted), while that which arises through a weak condition is the other (*sasaṅkhārika*, prompted).

Some, however, do not accept the arising of results that are *sasaṅkhāra-vipāka* (prompted-results) from an *asaṅkhārika* [kamma], nor the arising of *asaṅkhārika* [results] from a *sasaṅkhārika* [kamma].
But since these [results] occur during the course of existence (*pavatta*) by means of kamma other than that which gives rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), [they arise accordingly].

Unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses] occur; and in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated: "A root-cause-accompanied life-continuum is a condition, by way of proximity-condition, for a root-cause-free life-continuum. Therefore, for a person with a root-cause-free rebirth-linking, even root-cause-accompanied resultants occur during the course of existence in a happy destination (*sugati*).
However, in an unhappy destination (*duggati*) and on the plane of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-bhūmi*), only root-cause-free [resultants] occur.
They proceed. Among these, those accompanied by joy arise when the object is very desirable, and those accompanied by equanimity arise when the object is desirable-neutral;
thus should the distinction of association be understood according to their origin and so forth.

However, from the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*) up to the conclusion of the section on emptiness (*suññatavāra*), the entire exposition is similar to that of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.

Furthermore, among these [mental factors] included in the "only" (yevāpanaka) category, compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) do not exist because they have sentient beings as their object.

For the resultant states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-vipāka) have exclusively limited objects (parittārammaṇa). Moreover, among the worldly (lokiya) factors, the abstinences (virati) do not exist because they are exclusively of a wholesome nature;

for it is said: "The five training precepts (sikkhāpada) are exclusively wholesome. And here, contact (phassa) and the other [mental factors] are effortless and tranquil due to their being resultants, like the reflection of a face in a mirror.

The wholesome states, however, are energetic like a face. Furthermore, in the section on the summary (saṅgahavāra), there is a five-factored path; this is the distinction. The rest is exactly the same.

As for the classification by way of object and so forth, that differentiation mentioned regarding the wholesome states—namely, by way of doors of action, meritorious deeds, and predominance—is not present here, because [these states] do not produce intimation (aviññatti), because they are non-resultant (avipāka-dhamma), and because they do not proceed in that manner. This is the classification according to the inferior triad (hīnattika).
However, there exists [a class of consciousness] that is the result of inferior, medium, and superior wholesome kamma; likewise, it is distinguished by way of doors, objects, and so forth.

For these, depending on the heart-base and being independent of the [sensory] doors, perform the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death among gods and humans for those with two or three root-causes according to the method explained above, as well as the function of registration regarding the six objects at the six doors.
Thus, while they are being accomplished, they ripen in these four stations. In this way, their doors, objects, functions, and stations are not fixed;
therefore, there is a distinction between them. However, the physical basis (vatthu) is fixed right there, so there is no distinction in that regard.
Furthermore, the infinity [of consciousness] here also, by way of the distinctions of past and so forth, is exactly as described in the method already stated.
The wholesome-resultants of the sense-sphere accompanied by roots are finished.
Commentary on the Resultants of the Fine-Material Sphere:
The resultants of the fine-material sphere are also fivefold according to their associated distinctions, just like their own wholesome counterparts. And herein, all of them—
The classification of the analysis is exactly as described for the wholesome [states].

However, regarding their status as fruition (*vipāka*), just as the shadows of elephants and other animals resemble those very animals, so too—due to the occurrence of the wholesome—there is a conjunction with factors such as the jhāna-limbs, as well as distinctions such as the "way" (*paṭipadā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, in this context, there are fruitions of the first jhāna belonging to the three levels of the first jhāna, and likewise for the second jhāna level.
The resultants of the second jhāna and the third jhāna, as well as the resultants of the fourth jhāna belonging to the plane of the third jhāna,
and the resultants of the fifth jhāna belonging to the sixfold plane of the fourth jhāna— namely, the Vehapphala and the five Pure Abodes— perform the functions of rebirth-linking,
the life-continuum, and death, in the manner already described; depending upon the heart-base, they exist entirely dissociated from the sense doors.
The distinction is that they ripen having the designation known as the "sign of the deed" (*kamma-nimitta*) as their object; the rest is exactly the same.
The exposition of the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) resultants is finished.
Exposition of the immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) resultants.
In this way, the resultant states of the immaterial sphere are also fourfold according to the distinction of their objects, just like their own wholesome counterparts.

The entire analysis follows the same method as that stated for the wholesome states. Furthermore, the distinction from the wholesome states here should be understood by the method already explained for the resultant states of the fine-material sphere.
