However, the distinction here is simply that the resultant state of the base of infinite space has as its object a concept that serves as the sign of the kamma.
In the first immaterial plane, there is the resultant consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana-vipāka*) which has a sublime object;

in the second immaterial plane, the resultant consciousness of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-vipāka*) which has a concept as its kamma-sign for its object; and in the fourth immaterial plane, the resultant consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-vipāka*) which has a sublime object.
In these planes, the functions of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death occur without a physical basis (*avatthuka*), according to the method already stated.
"They proceed while being accomplished"—this alone is the distinction.
The exposition of the immaterial-sphere resultant is finished.
Exposition of the supramundane resultant.
Likewise, the supramundane resultants are also fourfold, corresponding to their respective paths and fruits, just like their own wholesome counterparts.
When divided according to the combination of jhāna factors, they become twentyfold—five for each. The analysis here follows the same method as that stated for the wholesome states;
the only difference is in the section on inclusion, where they are categorized as the fruit of the stream-entry path, the fruit of the once-return path, and the fruit of the non-return path.

Among these three, the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) and the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) of the fruit of arahantship are included in the place of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*); thus, there is a state of eight faculties.

It should be understood that the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), such as the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and the path-factors (*maggaṅga*), as well as the divisions of the way of practice (*paṭipadā*) and so forth, occur precisely by way of proceeding along the path.
Furthermore, a distinction of predominance (*adhipati*) is also obtained here. [These are] supramundane wholesome states.
For they are able to exercise predominance because they arise immediately after their own fruits and because they proceed with speed;
however, mundane states, being the opposite, cannot. Therefore the ancients said: "There is no predominance in regard to kamma-result, except for the supramundane.
Furthermore, according to the classification of liberations, these [paths] are threefold by way of proceeding along the path, namely: the void, the signless, and the desireless liberations.
For the paths, having received the two names "void" and "wishless" due to their approach by way of insight, are also called "signless" figuratively because they have a quality as their object;

therefore, standing in the place from which they themselves must be approached, they give all three names directly to their respective immediate fruits. Later, however, for those that have become the attainment of fruition—

They do not arise [simultaneously]. In this regard, the twofold acquisition of the name "path" should be understood according to the method already stated for the path, starting from the point where insight (vipassanā) enters the path.

Furthermore, unlike the paths themselves, these [impulsions] do not last for a single moment of consciousness; rather, in the cognitive process of the path, they occur two or three times, while in the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), they proceed continuously by way of absorption-impulsion (appanājavana) for an entire day—just like the sublime impulsions (mahaggata-javana). This is the distinction.
The supramundane resultants are finished.
As for the unwholesome resultants, they belong only to the sense-sphere; because they lack the roots associated with greed and so forth, they are exclusively rootless (*ahetuka*).
By way of association, these are: eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and likewise ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness. Likewise...
It is of seven kinds: body-consciousness accompanied by pain, the mind-element accompanied by equanimity, and likewise the mind-consciousness-element [accompanied by equanimity].
As for the analysis of this, the method is exactly as stated in all cases regarding wholesome-resultants with similar roots;
the only difference is that these have undesirable objects, body-consciousness is accompanied by pain, and the mind-consciousness-element is accompanied by equanimity.
With the exception of restlessness, unwholesome conditions perform the functions of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death in the four planes of misery;
in the happy destinies, they perform the functions of investigation and registration, as well as occurrence by way of accomplishment. The remainder is exactly the same.
The unwholesome resultants are finished.
The indeterminate states of fruition are concluded.

Now, for the explanation of the rootless functional indeterminate states: these are threefold, according to the spheres of sense-desire, fine-material, and immaterial. Among them, the sense-desire-sphere functional states are rootless.

They are of two kinds: with root-cause (*sahetuka*) and without root-cause (*ahetuka*). Among these, those devoid of the co-nascent root-cause are "without root-cause. These are threefold according to their association and so forth:

the mind-element accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagatā manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagatā manoviññāṇadhātu*), and likewise that accompanied by equanimity.
"Functional" (*kiriya*) means mere performing; the sense is "mere activity. For in all functional consciousnesses, there is the twofold function of adverting (*āvajjana*).

That [consciousness] which does not function as impulsion is like the flower of a fruitless tree. That which functions as impulsion is fruitless—like the flower of a tree whose roots have been cut—because it proceeds from a continuum that is free from underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

However, because it proceeds by accomplishing the respective functions of adverting and impulsion, it is called "functional" (*kiriya*) by way of its mere functional nature. In this context, regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), there is the resultant mind-element...
The entire analysis is to be understood according to the method already stated. However, the distinction is this:

when the five types of physical sensitivity are impinged upon by the five objects—whether desirable or undesirable—at the five doors, then immediately after the arrest of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it performs the function of adverting by taking that same fivefold object as its support and depending upon the heart-base;
thus it proceeds at all five doors. This is the specific difference.
The two mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) are also similar, respectively, to the two wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness elements;
however, energy (*vīriya*) is additional here, and it is through the support of energy that concentration becomes powerful.

For this very reason, in the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha*), there is an inclusion of faculties (*indriya-saṅgaha*) by way of five: energy, concentration, mental joy, and the life-faculty; and here too—

There is no inclusion by strength (*bala-saṅgaha*) here at all. As for the synonyms for strength—“concentration-strength” and “energy-strength”—which are stated in the explanation of concentration and energy within the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*), those are stated figuratively for the purpose of showing that these two are stronger than the factors associated with consciousness that lack other roots.
For this very reason, it is not said in the section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*) that “there are two strengths. Therefore...
It should be understood that, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), there is no power (*bala*) among rootless states.
However, according to the classification by way of object and so forth, those [rootless states] accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*) rely solely upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*):
in the five doors, for the function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana-kicca*); and in the mind-door, for the function of adverting (*āvajjana-kicca*) toward the six types of inferior sense-sphere objects.
And immediately after the mind-consciousness element, it occurs producing the function of impulsion (javana) and giving rise to laughter only in those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
For laughter occurs only through sense-sphere impulsions accompanied by joy;

among these, for those beyond training (asekha), it occurs through the five functional (kiriyā) impulsions, while for those in training (sekha), it occurs through both the wholesome (kusala) and the unwholesome rooted in greed dissociated from wrong view.

Thus, it arises through thirteen consciousnesses: the six [types of sense-sphere resultant consciousness] associated with views among ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), and the eight [types of sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome consciousness].

However, that which is accompanied by equanimity performs the function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) immediately after the resultant mind-consciousness element (*vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu*)—which has the function of investigation—at the five doors, depending solely on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).
At the mind-door, it occurs with respect to all six types of objects, whether they have a physical base (*savatthuka*) or are baseless (*avatthuka*).
Or, immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it proceeds performing the function of adverting.
Indeed, in the three realms of existence, this consciousness never fails to arise for any sentient being with mind in relation to any object whatsoever;
this is its distinction, namely that it is a "great-going" consciousness equal to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). The rest is exactly the same.
The treatment of rootless functional consciousness is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the root-possessing functional consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Those associated with functional roots such as non-greed (*alobha*) are "root-possessing"; by way of association, they are of eight kinds, just like the wholesome [consciousness].
The entire analysis here follows the same method as that stated for the wholesome [states]. The only difference here is that there are no abstinences (*virati*).

Furthermore, while the wholesome states of trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) proceed by accomplishing the function of impulsion (*javana*)—either supported or unsupported by a sense-base through the six doors according to the aforementioned method—these, however, belong to those beyond training (*asekha*); this is the distinction. This concludes the section on sense-sphere functional states (*kāmāvacara-kiriya*).
Commentary on the Functional Consciousness of the Fine-material Sphere:
The functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere is fivefold, just like the wholesome. The analysis therein follows the same method as already stated.

The only difference is that while the wholesome states have concepts as their objects for trainees and worldlings, the fifth jhāna occurring by way of direct knowledge (abhiññā) has the actual thing itself as its object.
Having become universal objects, they proceed at the mind-door, accomplishing the function of impulsion while depending solely upon the heart-base;

this, however, is the specific distinction regarding these "of the Asekhas. This concludes the description of the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere. Now follows the description of the functional consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere.
The functional (kiriyā) consciousnesses of the formless sphere are also fourfold, just like the wholesome ones. The analysis therein follows the same method as previously stated.

For the wholesome [consciousnesses]—whether with a physical basis or without a basis—occur in the manner described below, according to the circumstances, performing the function of impulsion in the mind-door, having either a concept or a sublime state as their object; these, however, are...
However, "of those beyond training" (asekhānaṃ) is the distinction. This concludes the functional [consciousness] of the formless sphere (arūpāvacara-kiriya).
The indeterminate functionals (kriyā-abyākata) are finished.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion (pakiṇṇaka-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

Standing here, having brought together all the states of consciousness and mental factors (citta-cetasika-dhamma) according to their classification by birth and so forth, the miscellaneous discourse (pakiṇṇaka-kathā) should be expounded.
For the aforementioned consciousnesses consist of twenty-one wholesome (kusala), twelve unwholesome (akusala), thirty-six resultant (vipāka), and twenty functional (kiriya);
thus, they total eighty-nine types. As for the supramundane (lokuttara) [consciousness], there is a division according to the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) and the application (yoga).

There are one hundred and forty-one types [of consciousness]. Among them, there are fifty-four belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), fifteen to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), twelve to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), and eight supramundane (*lokuttara*)—making forty in total for these four planes.
Within the sense-sphere types, there are eight wholesome (*kusala*), twenty-three resultant (*vipāka*), eleven functional (*kiriyā*), and eighteen rootless (*ahetuka*). The remainder...

Furthermore, those belonging to the four planes are also associated with roots (*sahetuka*). Regarding them, the enumeration of consciousness types according to their origin has already been stated previously. As for the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, there are twelve:
faith, mindfulness, moral shame (*hirī*), moral dread (*ottappa*), non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and the twelve beginning with bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*);

equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*), non-delusion (*amoha*), the two illimitables (*appamaññā*), and the three abstinences (*virati*). [The unwholesome factors are] delusion (*moha*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and greed (*lobha*).
Wrong view, hatred, doubt, conceit, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, torpor, contact, feeling, perception,
volition, one-pointedness, the life-faculty, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, energy,
desire-to-act, and resolve— these constitute fifty-two [mental factors].

In this context, twelve factors—equanimity (tatramajjhattatā), the two illimitables, the six beginning with conceit (māna), attention (manasikāra), desire-to-act (chanda), and resolve (adhimokkha)—are invariably present (yevāpanaka) in their respective places.
The three abstinences (virati) and restlessness (uddhacca) are present only in certain instances.
Among these, equanimity, attention, desire-to-act, resolve, restlessness, and the abstinences— [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.*
Excluding these, the remaining eight are indefinite according to their respective positions;

however, while the abstinences (*virati*) are indefinite in some instances, these eleven excluded [factors] leave the remaining forty-one states as definitely determinate (*niyata*). Among them, the twenty-five states beginning with faith (*saddhā*) are exclusively wholesome or indeterminate (*abyākata*);
the fourteen beginning with delusion (*moha*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*); and the thirteen beginning with contact (*phassa*) are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
They are of three types. For there are no states that are exclusively either wholesome or indeterminate;
rather, they are wholesome at the time of association with a wholesome consciousness, and indeterminate at the time of association with an indeterminate consciousness.

Delusion and the others, however, are unwholesome by their very nature, while the rest are all unwholesome through association with them. It should be understood that these [factors] possess differentiation solely through the differentiation of the associated consciousnesses.

For among those [mental factors], the nineteen beginning with faith arise in all fifty-nine types of consciousness—namely, in all wholesome states and in all root-cause-accompanied indeterminate states—and thus they each become fifty-ninefold.
Other [factors] should be understood in the same way. Among those [states], non-delusion (*amoha*) occurs in all except for the twelve dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa-vippayutta*);
as for the illimitables (*appamaññā*), however, they occur in the root-cause-accompanied functional and wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
And likewise among the twenty-eight types of consciousness in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), excluding those of the fifth jhāna;

whereas the abstinences (virati) arise only in the sixteen types of consciousness, namely, the wholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and the supramundane (lokuttara). Thus, these twenty-five factors are termed "wholesome-indeterminate" because they arise in both wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses.
However, as for delusion and the other three [root-factors], they occur in all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness.
Greed arises among the eight roots of greed; wrong view arises among those associated with wrong view; conceit arises among those dissociated from wrong view;
hatred, envy, avarice, and worry arise among those associated with resistance; sloth and torpor arise among the five prompted states;
and doubt arises only among that which is associated with doubt. Thus, these fourteen [factors], being unwholesome in themselves, [arise] only among the unwholesome.
And because they arise [only] in unwholesome states, they are called "unwholesome.
Among the others, the seven factors beginning with contact are present in all consciousness;
for there is no consciousness that arises without even one of these. These are indeed universal. However, the factors beginning with applied thought (vitakka) are occasion-specific. For among them—

Initial application (vitakka) arises in fifty-five types of consciousness: namely, in those of the sense sphere excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions, and in the eleven types of consciousness belonging to the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere and the supramundane.
Sustained application (vicāra), however, arises in sixty-six types of consciousness: in those same [fifty-five] and likewise in the types of consciousness belonging to the second jhāna.

Joy (pīti) arises in all types accompanied by mental pleasure (somanassa), excluding those belonging to the fourth jhāna. Energy (vīriya) arises in all types except for the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions, the mind-element, and the three types of investigating consciousness (santīraṇa).
Chanda arises in all states except those that are rootless and those associated with delusion (momūha).

Adhimokkha arises in all states except the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and those associated with doubt. Thus, these thirteen mental factors are called "threefold" because they arise within the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states.

Furthermore, their numerical classification should be understood individually according to the distinctions among the associated consciousnesses; for although consciousness is of a single type from the standpoint of its own characteristic, [it is divided by its association].

Thus, these forty-three types of consciousness arise depending upon their respective bases (*vatthu*) according to the method explained below;

however, the immaterial-sphere resultants (*arūpāvacara-vipāka*) arise without depending on a base at all. The remaining forty-two types arise both with and without a base, since they also arise in the immaterial planes.
For the immaterial beings possess none of the six bases, whereas material beings possess three—the nose, tongue, and body—everywhere.

Furthermore, for those devoid of their respective physical bases (*vatthu*), consciousnesses are restricted to all locations. However, for those in the non-percipient realm (*asaññī*), no consciousnesses whatsoever have a physical base.

For them, only the materiality of the life-nonad (*jīvitanavaka*) functions as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) during the course of existence, and as the death-consciousness (*cuti*) at the time of death.
And just as it is with respect to the mind, so too is it with respect to the mental factors (*cetasika*) associated with it regarding their physical bases.
The classification according to the types of integration (saṅgaha) should be understood. However, this is the distinction:

among those [mental factors], hatred (dosa), envy (issa), avarice (macchariya), and worry (kukkucca) arise only in the sensual world (kāmaloka), supported by the heart-base (hadayavatthu). Compassion (karuṇā) and gladness (muditā), however, arise even in the fine-material world (rūpaloka), but not in the immaterial world (arūpa).
For there, even the preliminary stages (pubbhāga) belonging to the fine-material sphere do not arise; as for all the others, they arise both with and without support.
They arise in all three realms of existence. For therein, the seven factors beginning with contact and the six bases are present; the others, however, consist of the heart-base alone.
The rest is the same as for the [pure] consciousness.
In the summary of functions and doors, however, their consciousness is like that which possesses fourteen functions by way of being independent of the six doors.

The sequence of occurrence should be understood in this way. For when beings are reborn in the three planes by the power of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, then at the time of their death, they generally grasp one or another of the three signs—the kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of the destination—presented through any one of the six doors.
Thereupon, two types of mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity and lacking roots (ahetuka), as well as the eight great resultant [consciousnesses], arise.

The nine types of resultant consciousness pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial realms—making nineteen consciousnesses in total—arise as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in their respective planes according to the method explained below;
these same consciousnesses, by way of being the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and death (cuti), are said to be "door-freed" (dvāravinimutta).
For at the time of death, for beings excluding those in the non-percipient realm, it is the past [kamma] that produces rebirth-linking in another existence.
At the time of performing that action, either the sixfold object consisting of visible forms and so forth—which serves as the instrument for that deed—whether past, future, present, or timeless;
or the sign of the action (*kamma-nimitta*) corresponding to the state of rebirth, such as the sign of a celestial tree, the mother’s womb, or the flames of hell-fire;
or the sign of the destiny (*gati-nimitta*), appearing according to the power of karma through any of the six doors, like the shadow of a mountain on the earth in the evening.

It appears as if clinging to the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*). When that object has thus appeared, for one whose death is imminent—due to the exhaustion of the life-span, the exhaustion of karma, the exhaustion of both, or by an interrupting karma—one of these occurs within the continuum of consciousness proceeding uninterruptedly through the power of karma;

immediately after each respective process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*) or life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), there arises the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). Immediately after that, [the rebirth-linking consciousness arises].
Taking as its object whatever has been grasped among kamma, the signs of kamma, and so forth, the rebirth-linking consciousness—
arising as the first consciousness in another existence within any of the three realms of becoming—
occurs accordingly. And therein, following a death-moment accompanied by two roots or without roots, there are only the ten types of sense-sphere rebirth-linking, and no others.
All [types of rebirth-linking] occur following a death in the sense-sphere with three roots; however, following a death in the fine-material sphere, they exclude rebirth-linking that is rootless.
Following a death in the immaterial sphere, there are rebirth-linkings of the lower immaterial planes—excluding those below—as well as rebirth-linkings of the sense-sphere with three roots.
But for non-percipient beings, starting from their material death and referring to the karma previously grasped in another existence, there are none except those that are rootless.

Only rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) occurs, and not otherwise. However, for worldlings (puthujjana), stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and once-returners (sakadāgāmī), there is no rebirth-linking in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) at the moment of death. For trainees (sekha), there is no rebirth-linking with two roots or without roots, nor with non-perception;
but for those beyond training (asekha), none of the rebirth-linkings occur at all, for they pass from death into nibbāna without residue (nirupadhisesa-nibbāna).
They are said to have attained final nibbāna without clinging. Thus, after the cessation of the rebirth-linking consciousness, that very same consciousness—
functioning as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) with respect to that same object—

proceeds uninterruptedly like the flow of a river for an immeasurable number of aeons, until the end of existence (cuti), during times such as falling asleep without dreaming, provided there is no arising of process-consciousness.
Thus, the sequence of the occurrence of the nineteen types of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and death (*cuti*) should be understood. Now,
while the continuum of the life-continuum is thus proceeding, when a very great visible-object stimulus, accompanied by a similar other condition,
strikes the eye-door due to the ripening of the sense-faculties, then, by the power of that impact, [it occurs] twice.

Therein, there is a vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Immediately after that, having interrupted the life-continuum, the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) arises and ceases, performing the function of adverting toward that visible object.

Likewise, immediately after that, one of the two eye-consciousnesses arises, performing the function of seeing as appropriate; immediately after that, the two resultant mind-elements (vipākamanodhātu) arise.
First, there is a certain function of receiving; immediately after that, one of the three resultant mind-consciousness elements performs the function of investigating;
immediately after that, the functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and rooted in the cause of non-greed performs the function of determining;
and immediately after that, any one among the twenty-nine sense-sphere javanas performs its respective function seven times or six times.
At times such as the moment of death, it performs the function of javana for five times;

immediately thereafter, among the eleven instances of registration (tadārammaṇa), it arises and ceases having performed the function of registration once or twice, as appropriate, within the great resultant investigating consciousnesses.
Immediately after that, the continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) alone proceeds. Thus...
In the eye-door, forty-six types of consciousness arise performing seven functions.

However, when sound-objects and so forth strike the ear-door and other doors in the manner already described, then likewise, forty-six types of consciousness arise for each door individually, just as in the case of the eye-door.
The only difference here is that immediately after the adverting consciousness, in the place where eye-consciousness occurs, [ear-consciousness arises].
The pairs of ear-consciousness and so forth arise performing their respective functions of hearing and so on, in due order.
Thus, when the five objects are very great at the five doors, only fifty-four sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) consciousnesses can occur.

However, some here maintain that "impulsions accompanied by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārika-javana*) do not arise at the five doors because of the impossibility of prior application; these [impulsions] occur only at the mind door."
...they say that [the consciousnesses] arise.

However, in the case of a great [object], those [consciousnesses] excluding the registration (tadārammaṇa) arise. Because the object has already passed away at the very same time as the impulsion (javana), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs at the conclusion of the impulsion.
But in the case of a slight [object], there is no impulsion at all; for here, the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) takes the place of the impulsion.
Having occurred two or three times, it ceases; thereafter, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises.
This sequence, however, is obtained at the time of speaking such words as, "It is as if seen by me," or "It is as if heard by me.

But when the object is extremely slight, because there is no stabilization for the production of determining (voṭṭhabbana), there is merely a vibration of the life-continuum, and not the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) and so forth. For it is by the adverting consciousness that the life-continuum is turned toward the object.
It is impossible that the mind, without reaching the stage of adverting (voṭṭhabbana), should descend into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in the interval immediately after eye-consciousness;

nor do the five-door process consciousnesses arise when the object is not occurring. This is the determination of the occurrence of consciousness according to the different ways objects occur at the five doors.

In the mind-door (manodvāra), however, when the six types of objects have come into the range of perception, following the process already described—after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana)—any one among the fifty-five javana functions consisting of wholesome, unwholesome, fruition, or functional consciousnesses proceeds by taking some sense-sphere object as its support.
From that point onward, there occurs registration (tadārammaṇa) regarding that sense-sphere object. This is the sequence of occurrence in the case of absorption (appanā) javanas.
For those who take serenity and insight as their meditation subjects, having previously developed the preliminary stages within their respective domains, [the thought arises]:

"Now absorption will arise. Then, following the movement of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), within one of the sense-sphere impulsion moments associated with knowledge, there occur four times—namely, the preparatory (*parikamma*), access (*upacāra*), conformity (*anuloma*), and change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*)—or three times, as appropriate.
Or, having arisen and ceased, the fourth or fifth [impulsion] occurs among the sublime (mahaggata) impulsions;

any one that constitutes the first path (kappanā), superknowledge (abhijñā), or the attainment of jhāna (jhānasamāpatti) impels only once, whereas those that constitute the actual jhāna attainment impel even for an infinite number of times.

However, among supramundane (lokuttara) impulsions, the wholesome (kusala) ones impel only once within a single continuum, and immediately thereafter, their respective fruition consciousnesses (phalacitta) impel two times each.
In the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), only the fruition itself flows on even for infinite cycles.

However, in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), by way of successive cessation—from the first jhāna up to the base of nothingness—one enters the attainment through the processes of adverting, preliminary work, and so forth in their proper order.
Then, for one who has emerged from that attainment, immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhu*), when the fourth immaterial-sphere consciousness has flowed twice and ceased:
And the mind does not arise at any time other than that which has been determined;

rather, at the moment of emergence, according to the sequence of adverting and preparatory consciousnesses, either the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arahantship arises exactly once, as appropriate.

In that regard, if it is from a wholesome change-of-lineage consciousness, immediately following it one enters into either a wholesome state or one of the first three fruits; if it is from a functional change-of-lineage consciousness, one enters into a functional state or the fruit of arahantship.
There too, from that accompanied by joy, it enters only into that accompanied by joy; and from that accompanied by equanimity, it enters only into that accompanied by equanimity.

Furthermore, among those of no-more-learning (asekha), only the functional javanas of the fruit of Arhatship occur here; likewise, for those in training (sekha), the remaining supramundane states occur according to their respective levels;

for both those in training and worldlings (puthujjana), only wholesome and unwholesome states occur; and absorption occurs only for those with triple-rooted (tihetuka) consciousness. This is the rule regarding javana.
But beyond the appanā-javana, there is no registration (tadārammaṇa).

For among the javanas that have objects, registration arises only for those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) when the object is very great and clearly manifest, and specifically for those who take rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the sense-sphere.

However, when the object is extremely desirable, the investigating (santīraṇa), functional (kiriyā), and appanā-javanas, as well as the registration, are accompanied by joy; whereas when the object is moderately desirable, [they are accompanied by equanimity].

And with respect to the undesirable, they are accompanied by equanimity. However, when—because the arising of joy immediately after grief is excluded in the *Paṭṭhāna*—in one whose rebirth-linking was associated with joy, the impulsion occurs toward an undesirable object among the "very desirable" and so forth, then neither the registration nor the life-continuum arise.
At that time, even without an adverting consciousness, [the process ceases] due to the cessation [of the flow] by taking another previously familiar limited object as its support.
For one emerging [from jhāna], an investigation consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises in the interval, like the fruit of recluseship;
immediately following that, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs—this is the rule regarding the object (tadārammaṇa-niyama).
However, after the life-continuum, there are process-consciousnesses such as adverting at the six doors. Thus, for as long as the lifespan lasts, it is by this very [process]...
Consciousnesses proceed according to the determination of the mind through kamma.

Immediately after a process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*), or immediately after the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), that last of all nineteen types of life-continuum proceeds, accomplishing the function of death with respect to that very same object.
When that has ceased, the being is said to have "passed away. From that death, once again...

The relinking consciousness, the life-continuum, and the process-thoughts—thus the stream of consciousness proceeds incessantly from one existence to another, like oxen yoked to a machine, as long as it is not liberated from the taints by means of grasping.

And while this stream of consciousness is thus proceeding, [one might think]: "You are the life-continuum; you are the subsequent adverting consciousness... and so on... you are the subsequent [consciousness]."

It is called "having that as its object," yet there is no director or agent who says, "But you are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)," and so forth; rather, this proceeds solely by the determination of consciousness (*cittaniyāma*).

For there are five kinds of determination: the determination of seeds (*bījaniyāma*), the determination of seasons (*utuniyāma*), the determination of kamma (*kammaniyāma*), the determination of phenomena (*dhammaniyāma*), and the determination of consciousness (*cittaniyāma*).

Among these, in the case of the determination of seeds, through the sequence of sprout, leaf, stalk, flower, and fruit, various distinct species of trees, grasses, shrubs, creepers, and so on arise within their respective continua.

The giving of a fruit corresponding to itself by the seed is called the law of the seed (*bījaniyāma*). The simultaneous grasping of the flowers, fruits, and shoots of various trees at their respective times is called the law of the seasons (*utuniyāma*).

And the giving of a result—whether material or immaterial—that corresponds or does not correspond to this or that wholesome or unwholesome kamma, as well as the giving of a result similar to the kamma, is called the law of kamma (*kammaniyāma*).

The thirty-two portents that appear at the time of the Bodhisattas’ conception, their emergence from the mother’s womb, their full enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and so forth, are called the "determination of phenomena" (dhammaniyāma).

The occurrence of consciousness precisely according to the sequence of functions such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and adverting (āvajjana), as previously described, is called the "determination of consciousness" (cittaniyāma).
By means of this determination of consciousness, among those [moments] possessing functions in their respective order—
Among these consciousnesses, the two-fold fivefold sense-cognitions, the mind-element, and the impulsions (javana) have, as far as possible, one function and one door;
the remaining ones, however, have two, three, four, or five functions and doors, and these have been explained previously and are easy to understand.
Thus it is with respect to those having one door and so forth. And just as it is for the consciousnesses, so it is for the mental factors associated with them, according to their functions and doors.

The inclusion [of these factors] should be understood. However, this is the distinction: by way of function, first of all, the seven universal factors perform fourteen functions just as consciousness does.
But the three—applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and resolution (*adhimokkha*)—perform nine functions, excluding the five beginning with seeing;

energy (*vīriya*) performs seven, excluding the [first] two of the five—receiving and investigating; and joy (*pīti*), determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), and adverting (*āvajjana*) likewise [exclude the same].

Excluding [the two types of] investigation (*santīraṇa*), there are six; however, excluding the abstinences (*virati*) and the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), there are twenty—namely, the wholesome and indeterminate [states], as well as desire (*chanda*).
Excluding both investigation and the immeasurables, there are five; further, excluding the immeasurables and their objective support (*tadārammaṇa*), there are four.
As for the abstinences, they perform the function of the impulsion (*javana*) alone. And with respect to the doors, the abstinences belong to the mind-door (*manodvārika*).

Likewise, compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are independent of the doors. For it is only at the mind-door (*manodvāra*) that there occurs the abstention from misconduct and the apprehension of the designation of a "being.

However, the unwholesome states pertain to all six doors; among these, some say that pride (*māna*), envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and remorse (*kukkucca*) belong exclusively to the mind-door.
The remainder belong both to the six doors and are independent of the doors. The rest is exactly the same as for the [wholesome] consciousnesses.
As for the grouping of their objects, that will be made clear in the "Treatise on the Limited Object" (*Parittārammaṇattika*). This concludes the supplementary discussion.
The commentary on the Section on the Arising of Consciousness (*Cittuppādakaṇḍa*) is finished.

However, the section on the indeterminate (*Abyākata*) has not yet been concluded. For among the indeterminate states, there are those that are indeterminate as fruition (*vipākābyākata*) and those that are indeterminate as functional (*kiriyābyākata*).
The indeterminate is divided into the material indeterminate (*rūpābyākata*) and the Nibbāna indeterminate (*nibbānābyākata*), which remain.

Among these, first, the material indeterminate is exclusively of the sense-sphere level (*kāmāvacara*); it is not differentiated [into other planes], nor is there any possibility of its association (*sampayoga*) with mental factors.

For association occurs only between those phenomena that possess an object (*sārammaṇa*), and not between others. As for the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*), this consists of twenty-eight kinds.
Namely: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element;
the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body; visible form, sound, odor, flavor; the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty;
the heart-base; bodily intimation, verbal intimation; space; lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter; and the integration of matter.

“Continuity, aging, impermanence, and edible food. Now, although the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is not mentioned here in the word-commentary (padabhājanīya), it will appear later in the Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi in its own form in such passages as, “That materiality depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element occur,” and so forth;
therefore, it is included here. Some, however, [include] the matter of torpor (middharūpa).

Taking these five—namely, the form of strength (*bala-rūpa*), the form of origin (*sambhava-rūpa*), the form of birth (*jāti-rūpa*), and the form of disease (*roga-rūpa*)—some say, "There are thirty-three forms.
They should be refuted by explaining the non-existence of those [five] and their inclusion within [the other categories].

For among these, *middha* (torpor) is not a form at all, because the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*). It is by means of *middha* alone, in the manner of nodding off, that...
There is the occurrence of materiality; however, nutritive essence (*bala-rūpa*) is included within the air element because it shares its nature with it;

productive materiality (*sambhava-rūpa*) is included within the water element; birth-materiality is included within the [phases of] accumulation and continuity; and disease-materiality is included within decay and impermanence, since it is designated as "disease" among the various modifications of materiality arising from conditions.
Thus, all materiality is indeed of twenty-eight kinds. This is the exposition by way of the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*).
As for the characteristics and so forth here: the earth element has the characteristic of hardness; its function is to act as a foundation; it is manifested as receiving.
The water element has the characteristic of trickling; its function is to consolidate; it is manifested as cohesion. The fire element has the characteristic of heat;
its function is to ripen; it is manifested as the provision of softness. The air element has the characteristic of distension; its function is to cause motion.
They have the manifestation of the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*). All four of these have the remaining three elements as their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

The eye has the characteristic of being a sensitive element capable of striking against visible forms, or the characteristic of being a sensitive element originated by kamma rooted in the desire to see. Its function is to impinge upon visible forms.
It is manifested as the state of being the physical basis for eye-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see.
This, however, is that which is situated in the eye-sockets, bound by a sinew-cord, joined with flesh, and connected to the brain;
wherein there is both white, black, and red, as well as the four great elements;
and which is white due to an abundance of phlegm, black due to an abundance of bile, red due to an abundance of blood, and thick due to an abundance of earth.
It exists; it flows due to the predominance of water, it burns due to the predominance of fire, and it whirls due to the predominance of air.

And that which in the world is called the "eye"—long and wide, variegated with black and white circles, strewn with dark eyelashes, and resembling the petal of a blue lotus—that eye, together with its constituent parts and surrounded by the white circle (the sclera), [is what is meant].
In the center of the black circle, for those standing facing it, the seven layers of the eye-films—
just as oil poured onto seven cotton pads spreads over them— pervade [the eye] and perform their functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and moving,
like a prince being sustained by four nurses whose duties are holding, dressing, bathing, and fanning him.
Assisted by the four elements, maintained by the life-faculty, surrounded by color, odor, taste, and so forth, and supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, it persists—
measured in size as no more than the head of a louse— and performs its function as the appropriate basis and door for eye-consciousness and the rest.
And this has been said by the General of the Dhamma:
“By means of that clarity of the eye with which one perceives forms,
this is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.

[The ear] has the characteristic of a sensitivity of primary elements capable of receiving the impact of sounds, and the characteristic of a sensitivity of primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to hear.
Or the ear has the function of attracting sounds; it is manifested as the basis for ear-consciousness; its proximate cause is the kamma-born elements originating from the desire to hear.

This [ear], however, is located within the hollow of the ear-canal—which is composed of flesh and thin, tawny hair and is shaped like a finger-stall—and is supported by a retinue that maintains it through the assistance provided by the aforementioned elements and so forth, for the sake of ear-consciousness and the rest.
It remains establishing itself as the basis for the door of the object according to its suitability.
The nose has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of matter capable of striking odors, or the characteristic of being a sensitivity of matter originated by kamma rooted in the desire to smell.
Its function is to apprehend odors. It is manifested as the support for nose-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the matter produced by kamma rooted in the desire to smell.

And this [nose-faculty] stands within the nostril-cavity together with its supporting tissues, in a place shaped like a goat’s hoof, acting as the appropriate basis and door for nose-consciousness and the rest, while being supported by the surrounding protective rim.
It is characterized by the sensitivity of the primary elements capable of receiving the impact of flavors;
it is characterized by the sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma, which has the desire to taste as its source.

Or the tongue has the function of attracting flavors; it is manifested as the support for tongue-consciousness; its proximate cause is the kamma-born primary elements originating from the desire to taste.

And this tongue, together with its constituent parts, stands upon the middle of the fleshy tongue in a location shaped like the tip of a lotus petal, maintaining its specific assistance, protection, and support, and thereby fulfilling its role as the appropriate physical basis and door for tongue-consciousness and the rest.

The body has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by tangible objects; or it has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to touch.

Its function is to reach out toward tangible objects. It is manifested as the state of being the basis for body-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to touch.
Furthermore, in this body, throughout all those portions of the earth and water elements that are clung-to (upādinnā), [the body-sensitivity exists].

Like oil permeating a cotton wick, it remains following along with the aforementioned support for the maintenance of assistance and the stabilization of the retinue, establishing itself as the respective basis and door for body-consciousness and the others. However, some say:
"The sensitivity of the elements with a predominance of fire is the eye; those with a predominance of space, air, water, and earth are the ear, nose, tongue, and body. Others...
“They say: ‘The eye has the nature of fire; the ear, nose, tongue, and body have the natures of space, earth, water, and air, respectively.
And they state the reasons for this in due order: ‘Because of their cooperation with fire and the rest, and because their objects—visible form and so on—are the qualities of fire and the rest.

But they should be asked: Who says that the sense-faculties must possess the very same natures as their cooperating factors? Or [who says] that visible forms and the rest [belong] to fire and the rest?”
"qualities. For among the primary elements (bhūta) which are inseparable, it is not possible to say, "this is a quality of this one, and that is a quality of that one.

Furthermore, if they should argue, "Since we observe an excess of visible form and so forth in those constituent parts where fire and the other elements predominate, it must be accepted that 'visible form and the rest are qualities of fire and the others,'" they should be told: "We would accept this, if [the case were] of water-predominance..."
If there were a predominance of earth in fermented liquor, its fragrance would be stronger than the scent of the cotton;

and if there were a predominance of fire in hot water, the color of cold water would be diminished. Since neither of these two cases exists here, one should therefore abandon the postulation of a distinction among these elements that serve as its support.
Just as, despite the lack of distinction among the primary elements within a single aggregate, their visible form, taste, and so forth [are not identical].
It should be understood that the sensitivities of the eye and so forth are likewise mutually dissimilar. But is there no cause for their distinction?
It is not that there is none. What then is it? Karma alone is their specific, uncommon cause, particularly in the case of the primary elements produced by craving as their generator.
For when there is a difference in the primary elements, the sensitivity itself does not arise.
"For clarity belongs to beings who are similar, not to those who are dissimilar," so say the ancients.

Thus, among the mental states distinguished by their specific karma, the eye and ear faculties grasp objects that have not reached them; they cause consciousness regarding objects even though they do not adhere to their own physical bases.
The nose, tongue, and body faculties, however, grasp objects that have reached them, both by way of adhering to their bases and by themselves.
Because consciousness arises only with respect to objects that have come into contact with its own physical basis (*nissaya*).
However, some maintain: "The eye and ear also grasp only objects that have reached them;

for even in the case of forms such as the moon situated at a distance, consciousness arises through the contact of the rays of the eye moving swiftly, and in the case of sounds, through their arrival in succession and striking the ear canal."

For it is precisely because of this that consciousness does not arise regarding forms and sounds separated by walls and the like, or those located within split mountains, caves, and so forth—so they say.
For even in their view, the eye has the capacity to join its rays with distant or near objects such as the moon or trees without discerning a difference in time;
likewise, sounds, whether distant or near, have the capacity to come and strike the ear canal without their difference in distance being known.

It must be approached as that which serves as the cause for the arising of consciousness. Beyond that, it is the approach characterized by the capacity to produce consciousness in those very [objects] while they remain in their own place.
Furthermore, visible forms and sounds obstructed by walls, caves, and so forth, do not come within range due to the absence of the necessary cooperative conditions;

otherwise, one would have to admit that even these [obstructed objects] possess a connection with the sense faculties in such cases. And the prevention of their coming within range is itself the prevention of their arising.

In the same way, it should be understood that due to the absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāripaccaya*), consciousness arises according to the specific manner in which those sense-faculties are conjoined;
for instance, the eye may be considered a non-contact-perceiver because it perceives even the moon and such objects situated at a distance.
However, the ear [is a contact-perceiver] because, for those cutting down a tree or washing a cloth at a distance, it perceives bodily movements and so forth from afar.
How is it that, because it is unable to grasp the sound simultaneously, that [consciousness] which defines it slowly becomes one that does not grasp the object in its entirety?

Even in that case, just as there is no successive transmission of the faint sounds arising from the movement of branches and leaves when a hand is being cut, due to the dullness of the initial sounds of the axe striking the wood and so forth, likewise there is no reaching of the range [of the senses]; however, subsequently, through friction and rubbing...
Just as when a great sound arises from a powerful source, its arrival occurs only for those standing right there,
otherwise there would be no distinction between near and far, as is the case with odors and so forth; therefore, these [faculties] have non-attained objects,
whereas the nose and the others should be understood as having attained objects.
These [objects] are like snakes, crocodiles, birds, dogs, and jackals.

For just as a snake does not delight in a place that has been plastered and smoothed over, but rather leaves it for uneven haunts such as thickets of grass and leaves or anthills, so too the eye leaves behind well-smeared walls and the like, and finds its uneven inclinations among women, men, flowers, creepers, paintings, and so forth. Just as...
And just as the *suṃsumāra* (crocodile) abandons moving on land and has a preference for dwelling in water, so too the ear has a preference for openings such as windows and apertures.
For just as birds such as vultures abandon the ground and trees and have a preference for soaring in the air,
so too the nose, being directed upwards, has a preference for space in order to draw in the air that carries odors.

Just as a dog, having abandoned wandering outside the village, becomes intent on the village, seeking bait with its mind inclined toward the kitchen and so forth, even so the tongue has its inclination toward flavors.
And just as a jackal, having abandoned wandering outside the cemetery, becomes intent on the cemetery, seeking meat, even so the body,
although it obtains pleasant tactile objects such as beds that are not clung-to (*anupādinnam*), still has its inclination toward what is clung-to (*upādinnajjhāsaya*).
It exists. For when beings find no other object of clinging, they even lie down thrusting their knees into their chests and placing their heads upon the palms of their hands.
Furthermore, these conditions—namely, light, gaps, air, water, and earth—are the causes for the arising of consciousness.
Thus, by way of their characteristics, functions, manifestations, proximate causes, supports, objects, inclinations, and conditions, there is a distinction among these five sensitive organs.
The definition should be understood as follows:
visible form has the characteristic of impinging on the eye; its function is to be the objective domain of eye-consciousness; it is manifested as the range of that same consciousness;
and its proximate cause is the four great elements. And just as this is the case for this [visible form], so too is it the proximate cause for all derived material phenomena.

This should be understood; however, we shall explain the distinction. This material form (rūpa) is of many kinds, categorized as blue, yellow, red, white, black, crimson, dark-grey, shadow, glare, light, darkness, and so forth. Some, however, assert that "darkness is merely the absence of light, and for that very reason, visible forms are not seen therein";
this is not tenable. For instance, the shadows cast by blue clouds, gems, and the like are distinct from light.

It becomes a sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*). Thus, the shadows of walls, roofs, ground, mountains, and so forth—which are dense due to their covering of pots, forms, and the like—should be understood as darkness resembling light.
Sound has the characteristic of obstructing the ear; its function is to serve as the objective domain for ear-consciousness;
it is manifested as being the range of that very consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as the sounds of singing, drums, and so forth.
Odor has the characteristic of striking the nose; its function is to be the objective domain of nose-consciousness; it is manifested as the state of being the range of that same consciousness.
It is of many kinds, such as root-odor, heartwood-odor, and so forth. Taste has the characteristic of striking the tongue; its function is to be the objective domain of tongue-consciousness;
it is manifested as the state of being the range of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as root-taste, stalk-taste, pith-taste, and so forth.
The femininity faculty has the characteristic of the female state; its function is to manifest as "female"; it is manifested as the cause for the female sex, signs, marks, postures, and deportment.
The masculinity faculty has the characteristic of the male state; its function is to manifest as "male";
it is manifested as the cause for the male sex, signs, marks, postures, and deportment. These are the causes for both the female and male sex, signs, and so forth.
The state of being a cause does not exist in an ultimate sense (*sarasato*) by virtue of any condition, because their status as conditions is not established in the *Paṭṭhāna*;

rather, it exists only through the arrival of those conditions that produce them. Furthermore, even for the forms corresponding to the specific gender, signs, gestures, appearance, and deportment of women and men, there is a state of being a condition and a state of being a faculty due to their arising in a fixed manner and because the conventional designations of "gender," "signs," and so forth, are centered upon them.

And this has been stated by way of a figurative explanation. For it is precisely for that reason that, although a hermaphrodite female lacks the male faculty (*purisindriya*), the manifestation of male characteristics, signs, and so forth arises solely from past karma;
and likewise, although a hermaphrodite male lacks the female faculty (*itthindriya*), the manifestation of female characteristics, signs, and so forth arises solely from past karma.
For if their respective manifestations were to arise through their corresponding faculties alone, [such would not be the case].
The absence of the second characteristic follows; for those [hermaphrodites] do not possess both states.

If they did, there would be the undesirable consequence of both characteristics being present at all times. For in the case of a female hermaphrodite (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*), only the female faculty (*itthindriya*) exists, not the other.
However, when a mind of lust for a woman arises in him, then the male characteristic...
The female characteristic becomes manifest, while the male characteristic remains concealed; likewise for the other, the other [characteristic] appears.

Since, however, the faculty of these individuals is fixed as one or the other, therefore the female hermaphrodite (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) both conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive.
The male hermaphrodite (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka) causes another to conceive, but does not conceive himself. This is how it is with them.

For those who possess both sexual organs (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), it should be understood that the cause of the organs is precisely the mind of lust acting as an auxiliary to kamma, and not the [previous] state of being.
Likewise, for natural women and men, the conditions such as kamma that produce the two respective states of being are themselves the causes for their respective gender marks and so forth.
And both of these arise during the course of existence (*pavatta*) among the beings of the first aeon; thereafter, they arise only at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for all beings.
However, it changes only during the course of existence (pavatta). Among these, the male characteristic (purisaliṅga) is superior and the female characteristic (itthiliṅga) is inferior;
therefore, the male characteristic disappears through powerful unwholesomeness (akusala), while the female characteristic is established through weak wholesomeness (kusala).
Furthermore, when the female characteristic disappears, it does so through weak unwholesomeness, whereas the other [the male characteristic] appears through powerful wholesomeness.
It is established. Thus, both [the unwholesome and the wholesome] vanish through the unwholesome alone and are established through the wholesome alone within a happy destination (*sugati*).
And like the sensitivity of the body (*kāyappasāda*), it pervades the entire body; yet it does not abide in the specific locations where the sensitivity of the body and so forth reside.

If this is so, are there not body-faculties and mental faculties everywhere? Not so, in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) everywhere; rather, having analyzed [them], [they are found to exist only where appropriate].
It is not possible to define their distinct locations, unlike the case of visible form, taste, and so forth. For in ultimate reality (paramatthato), there is no taste within visible form;
if there were, it would be apprehended by the apprehension of visible form itself.

Thus, the body, the entity, and the faculties do not exist everywhere in ultimate reality, yet they are not entirely non-existent, because they cannot be separated [from one another], as explained below.
Furthermore, their non-mixture is established through the determination of their specific characteristics and so forth as described;
thus, they are distinct even when there is no spatial separation. Not only these, but all material phenomena (*rūpa*) are likewise unmixed.
For example, when a wick is made from five-colored cotton and a lamp is lit, although the flames appear to be joined together as one, each individual thread [of the wick] remains distinct.

Just as the networks [of light rays] are not intermingled with one another, so too the body, the state, the faculties, and so forth—though gathered together in a single location—are not present in separate locations according to their respective positions such as below or above; they likewise remain unmixed.
The life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining conascent material phenomena, the function of making them proceed, and the manifestation of establishing those very same phenomena.

It is the basis for the state of being maintained. It sustains its co-nascent material phenomena only at the moment of their existence, like water sustaining lotuses and the like, and not at the moment of their dissolution because it itself is dissolving;

and it maintains the phenomena produced by their respective conditions, like a nurse maintaining a child, and it proceeds only through its connection with the phenomena that have proceeded from itself.
It should be understood as the "director.

The heart-base has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element; its function is to sustain those very elements, and its manifestation is that of upholding them.
Now, this heart-base is that which is within the body, between the two breasts...
Having removed the outer petals from the middle, it has the shape of a red lotus bud placed face down;
it is smooth on the outside and resembles the interior of a *kosātakī* fruit. It is slightly opened for those of great wisdom, but remains closed like a bud for those of dull wisdom.
Surrounding the heart-flesh, the kidneys, liver, membranes, and phlegm remain situated there.
Within that heart-flesh together with its supporting tissues, there remains about half a *pasata* measure of blood situated in a hollow the size of a *puṇṇāga* seed.
That blood is red in one of lustful temperament, blackish in one of hating temperament,
like meat-washing water in one of deluded temperament, the color of horse-gram soup in one of discursive-thought temperament, and [clear] in one of faithful temperament.
It has the color of a *kaṇikāra* flower; for one whose conduct is governed by wisdom, it becomes clear, serene, undisturbed, bright, and utterly pure.
Like a polished gem of noble birth, it is radiant. Pervading [the body], it is assisted by the primary elements through their functions such as supporting and so forth;

it is maintained by the life-force (*āyu*), surrounded by [the qualities of] color and so on, and supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, as well as by the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
It remains establishing itself as the basis for those [mental states] associated with it.

Bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) has the characteristic of being a modification of the mode of conditionality in the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body by means of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) originated by the consciousness that initiates forward movement and so forth;
its function is to manifest intention; its manifestation is the state of being the cause of bodily vibration.
They have the air element produced by mind as their proximate cause.

Vocal intimation has the characteristic of being a modification of the mode of conditionality in the impact of the earth element—produced by mind and causing the manifestation of vocal differentiation; its function is to reveal intention;

it is manifested as the causal state of the sound of speech; and it has the earth element produced by mind as its proximate cause. Both of these [vocal and bodily intimations] are likewise [of this nature].
They are called "bodily and vocal intimation" because they are themselves cognizable through bodily movements and vocal sounds, and because they communicate intention.

For when someone, standing within the range of sight or hearing, performs a bodily movement such as a hand gesture or raising the head, or produces a sound, the bases of visible form and sound that arise accordingly are what are cognized by the eye and ear; these [bases] themselves are not the intimations.
However, bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) is a modification of the air element arisen from consciousness that serves as a condition for the maintenance and movement of the co-nascent material body;
likewise, verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) is a modification of shape of the earth element arisen from consciousness that serves as a condition for the impact of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*).
These two are not cognizable by the eye or the ear; rather, they are [cognized] by the impulsion consciousnesses of the mind-door.

Just as one recognizes wells and such by means of the signs of palm leaves and the like, so too, by following the bodily movements and vocal sounds as they are perceived, these [expressions] are cognizable even by animals;
and by following those very [movements and sounds], the intention—"He causes this and that to be done, and he speaks"—is also cognizable.
Therefore, because they are themselves cognizable and because they communicate intention, they are called "intimations" (*viññatti*).

In that regard, within the mental-door cognitive process (*manodvārika-javana-vīthi*), among the seven sense-sphere impulsions (*kāmāvacara-javana*) that generate bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), the wind elements produced by the first six impulsions are only able to perform the functions of supporting and maintaining;
they are not, however, able to bring about actual movement such as walking forward. But those produced by the seventh impulsion...

Just as a cart that has been loaded with a burden to be drawn by seven yokes can, having received the support of the air element produced by the six preceding mental impulsions (javana), cause the physical body to move forward, backward, and so forth— just as the ox yoked to the seventh yoke does when receiving the support of the oxen yoked to the other six yokes—
so too, in the case of the seventh impulsion which generates vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti).
It should be understood that even for the earth element that has arisen [simultaneously], there is the state of being a condition for the impact on the clung-to (upādinnaghaṭṭana).

However, in this context, there is no supporting function for that which arises with the first impulsion, nor is there the state of being a condition for movement for that which arises with the seventh impulsion, because those [latter] have the function of the air element;
rather, it is the subsequent earth element, accompanied by the preceding one, that is capable of the impact on the clung-to.
The rest is exactly the same. However, when the air element moves within the body originated by consciousness, the material phenomena originated by that [air] which support it also move;
thus, the whole body performs such actions as advancing and so forth. This should be understood as being like grass or leaves falling into water when the water itself is moving.
The space element has the characteristic of delimiting matter; its function is to manifest the boundaries of matter; it is manifested as the limit of matter.
Lightness of matter has the characteristic of non-obstruction, or it has the characteristic of having gaps and openings;
its proximate cause is delimited matter, by means of which there arises the perception regarding delimited matter that "this is above, below, or across.
It has the characteristic of non-slowness, the function of removing heaviness from material phenomena, and the manifestation of quick transformation.
Softness of matter has the characteristic of non-hardness; its function is the removal of stiffness in matter;
it is manifested as non-opposition to all activities; its proximate cause is softness of matter. Wieldiness of matter has the characteristic of serviceability for bodily activity;
its function is the removal of unwieldiness; it is manifested as a state of non-weakness; its proximate cause is wieldiness of matter.
Moreover, these three do not abandon one another;

they are said to have the function of dispelling heaviness, rigidity, and unwieldiness by way of being the opposites of those qualities, and by way of being the transformation of the light, soft, and wieldy material phenomena born of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment that have arisen.
However, this is not so by way of their own intrinsic nature, because they themselves do not exist as such.
Accumulation has the characteristic of piling up matter; its function is to cause matter to emerge from the past;
it is manifested as the act of conveying [matter] or as the state of fullness; its proximate cause is accumulated matter. Continuity has the characteristic of the persistence of matter;
its function is to link [moments] together; it is manifested as non-interruption; its proximate cause is matter that links [moments] together. Both of these—

This is a synonym for the very same birth-form (*jātirūpa*). For the first arising of the fourfold-originated material phenomena when they are aggregated is called "growth" (*upacaya*), while their successive arising thereafter is called "continuity" (*santati*).
Therefore, in the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*) on those [terms], it is said: "That which is the growth of matter is the continuity of matter.
Nevertheless, they are listed separately because of the difference in their modes of appearance.

The aging of matter has the characteristic of the maturation of matter; its function is to lead [matter] toward its end; it is manifested as the departure from a new state even while its intrinsic nature has not yet departed, like the state of ripeness in paddy;

its proximate cause is matter that is undergoing maturation. And although this [aging] breaks down moment by moment, it is evident among the clung-to (upādinnā) through broken teeth and so forth, and among the unclung-to (anupādinnā) through changes in color and so forth in trees, creepers, and the like.
Because its transformation is easily discernible, it is called "manifest aging" (*pākaṭa-jarā*) and "aging with intervals" (*savīci-jarā*);
because it is difficult to discern and continuous in such things as gems, gold, the moon, and the sun, it is called "unmanifest aging" (*apākaṭa-jarā*) and "aging without intervals" (*avīci-jarā*).

For in such cases, aging would be known through transformation at times such as the destruction of an eon; however, since no transformation is ever perceived in immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*), aging exists therein.
This is what is called "concealed aging. And therein, the transformation of color and so forth are not aging itself, because they are cognizable by the eye.
For aging is not cognizable by the eye; rather, it is cognizable by the mind.
Just as a flood, though unseen, becomes easily understood by seeing the ground and other things swept away by it, so too aging should be grasped by seeing its transformations.

The impermanence of material form has the characteristic of disintegration; its function is to fall away; it is manifested as destruction and vanishing; and its proximate cause is material form in the process of disintegrating.
Furthermore, these factors—birth, aging, and death—are not grasped solely by the four [characteristics] beginning with accumulation (*upacaya*) in the case of material phenomena alone;
they certainly exist for immaterial phenomena as well. And these [factors] are like robbers who enter the forest, seize, bring to ruin, strike down, and kill these beings.
These should be understood as being similar according to their respective order.

Edible food has the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*); its function is to sustain material form; its manifestation is support; its proximate cause is that which is to be taken in morsels. This is the analysis by way of characteristics and so forth.
As for the classification, all this matter is of one kind from the perspective of the aggregates, namely, the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*). Likewise, it is rootless (*ahetuka*).

It is of one kind as "conditioned," "formed," "mundane," "with taints," "subject to fetters," "subject to floods," "subject to yokes," "subject to hindrances," "clung to," "defiled," "without an object," and "not to be abandoned," and so forth.

Furthermore, it is of two kinds by way of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*), and likewise by way of being produced (*nipphanna*) or unproduced (*anipphanna*), and so on. Among these, the four great elements are earth and the rest.
That which is called "derived matter" (bhūtarūpa) is the primary elements; the remainder is called "dependent matter" (upādārūpa).

The eighteenfold matter—consisting of the seventeen beginning with earth and the edible food—is called "produced matter" (nipphannarūpa) because it exists in an ultimate sense; the other is called "unproduced matter" (anipphannarūpa).
The eightfold faculty-matter consists of the five sensitive organs beginning with the eye, the two sexes, and the life-faculty.
The other is non-faculty. These faculties together with the heart-base (hadaya) constitute ninefold clung-to matter; the other is not clung-to.

The five sensitive organs, the four [objects]—visible form, sound, odor, and flavor—and the triad of primary elements excluding the water element, making twelve types in total, are gross matter, proximate matter, and impinging matter; the remainder is subtle matter.
There is visible form that is distant and visible form that is non-obstructive. The sensitive forms and the heart are foundational materiality; the rest is non-foundational materiality.

The sensitive forms and the two types of intimation are door-materiality; the rest is non-door-materiality. The sensitive forms are internal materiality and materiality that grasps its objective field;
the rest is external and materiality that does not grasp its objective field. There are the four primary elements and the material qualities of visible form, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence.
This is called inseparable materiality (*avinibbhoga-rūpa*); the other is separable materiality (*vinibbhoga-rūpa*).
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of the eye and so forth, such as "the eye" and "not the eye. Again, it is threefold by way of the triad of "with visibility" (*sanidassana*) and so on.

Therein, the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) is with visibility and with resistance (*sappaṭigha*); the remaining gross materiality is without visibility but with resistance (*anidassana-sappaṭigha*).
All subtle matter (*sukhumarūpa*) is invisible and non-reacting (*anidassana-appaṭigha*). Likewise, according to the classification of the three types born of kamma and so forth:

therein, nine kinds of matter are called "born of kamma" (*kammaja*), namely the pure octad (*suddhaṭṭhaka*), space, and that which is born of kamma; the two modes of intimation (*viññatti*), the triad of lightness and so forth (*lahutādi*), and sound are called "not born of kamma" (*akammaja*);
and the fourfold characteristic matter (*lakkhaṇarūpa*), such as integration (*upacaya*) and so forth, is called "not born [of anything]" (*aja*). The pure octad...
