Space, the two modes of intimation, the triad of lightness and so forth, and sound are called mind-born (*cittaja*). Whatever remains, being devoid of characteristic-form (*lakkhaṇarūpa*), is called not mind-born (*acittaja*).
Characteristic-form is called unborn (*aja*). The pure octad, space, and the triad of lightness and so forth are called nutriment-born (*āhāraja*).
The rest, excluding the characteristics, are called not nutriment-born (*anāhāraja*). The characteristics are called unborn (*aja*). The pure octad—

Space, the triad of lightness and so forth, and sound are called "born of the primary elements" (*utuja*). The remainder, being devoid of characteristics, is called "not born of the primary elements" (*anutuja*).

Characteristics are called "unborn" (*aja*). For characteristics, by virtue of being the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena that are being born, aging, and dissolving, do not receive the conventional designation of "birth" from anything, lest it follow that even birth itself and the other characteristics would themselves possess birth and so forth. Indeed, it is not the case that "birth is born," nor that "aging..."

Because of its instability, it is appropriate to speak of it as "decaying" (*jīrati*) and "dying" (*mīyati*). However, as for the remaining unconditioned phenomena (*anipphanna*), such as space and intimation (*viññatti*),
although there is no arising from any source because they do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), nevertheless, by depending on the material form (*rūpa*) that occurs in various ways,
there is no contradiction in applying to them the conventional designation of "having a cause" (*sahetuka*), just as there is no contradiction in using the conventional designation of "existing."

It has been stated [thus]. However, as for the fact that even birth (*jāti*) is said in the Pāḷi—such as in the passage, "The visible-object base... [and so on] ...the integration of matter (*upacaya*), the continuity of matter (*santati*), and physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*):

these states are mind-originated"—to have arisen from something, this was stated with reference to its existence at the moment of the arising of matter, because it is seen to possess the characteristic of the functional power of the conditions that produce matter; [this does not apply to] aging and death (*jarā-maraṇa*).

However, it was not stated [in that context] because [the factors] do not exist at the moment of the arising of material form (*rūpa*). But this statement, "Monks, aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen," should be understood as having been said with reference specifically to consciousness, mind-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, which proceed under the heading of aging-and-death.
That material form which is internal, that is derived (*upādā*); that material form which...
It is also threefold according to the method beginning with: "The external; that which is derived (upādā) and that which is not derived.
Furthermore, all of that is fourfold by way of the seen, the heard, the sensed (muta), and the cognized (viññāta). Therein, the sphere of visible form is called the "seen";
sound is called the "heard"; and odors, tastes, and tangibles are called the "sensed" because they must be apprehended only after having been reached [by the sense organs].
[The first] is called "known" (viññāta) because the remainder is to be cognized by the mind. Likewise, it is fourfold according to the classification of derived matter (rūparūpa) and so forth.
Among these, the eighteen kinds are called derived matter; space is called delimiting matter; the two types of intimation and the triad of lightness and so forth are called matter as change;
and the fourfold characteristic matter, beginning with accumulation, is called matter as characteristic. Likewise...
The heart-base is called a "base" (vatthu) but not a "door" (dvāra); the two types of intimation (viññatti) are called "doors" but not "bases";
the five sensitive organs, such as the eye, are called both "bases" and "doors"; and the remainder are called neither "bases" nor "doors. In this manner, it is fourfold.
Furthermore, it is fivefold by way of its single origin and so forth. Indeed, the ninefold clung-to matter (upādinnarūpa) arises solely from kamma, as do the two types of intimation.
It is called "arising from one" because it arises through the mind alone; sound is called "arising from two" because it arises from temperature and the mind;

the triad of lightness and so forth is called "arising from three" because it arises from temperature, mind, and nutriment; the pure octad and space are called "arising from four" because they arise from all four [causes];
and the characteristics are called "non-arising. Thus, there are five kinds.
Furthermore, that [visible form] is sixfold by way of being cognizable by the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

It is sevenfold by way of being cognizable by the seven elements of consciousness. That same [form], when the element cognizable by mind-consciousness is divided into two—namely, primary matter and derived matter—becomes eightfold.
For therein, the water element is called "primary matter" cognizable by mind-consciousness alone; the other [the remaining elements] are subtle matter accompanied by sensitive matter.

This is called derived matter cognizable by mind-consciousness. Furthermore, that same derived matter cognizable by mind-consciousness is divided into two types—by way of faculties and non-faculties—and thus becomes ninefold.
That, in turn, becomes tenfold by way of sensitive matter, object, the water element, the state of being, the heart-base, life, delimitation, change, characteristic, and nutriment.
Furthermore, that same [derived matter] consists of the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and visible-form-base.

The sense base of sound, the sense base of odor, the sense base of flavor, the sense base of tangible objects, and the sense base of mental phenomena—thus, from the perspective of the sense bases (*āyatana*), it is elevenfold;
likewise from the perspective of the elements (*dhātu*). Therein, the triad of primary elements excluding the water element constitutes the sense base of the tangible and the tangible element;
it is called "cognizable by the body" and "cognizable by body-consciousness," and it is subtle matter.

The sense base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) is the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*); that very same [element], when accompanied by sensitivity (*pasāda*), is described as "cognizable by the mind" and "cognizable by mind-consciousness.
The rest is easy to understand.
But why is it stated here that only the primary elements, excluding the water element (*āpodhātu*), possess the quality of tangibility (*phoṭṭhabba*), when the water element also [possesses it]?
Is it to be known as "cold" by way of being touched? No, because even coldness is the fire element (*tejodhātu*). For it is precisely heat that is designated as "cold.
Depending on whether there is hardness or lack of hardness, there is the sparse shade of trees and so forth; or depending on that [shade], there is dense shade and so forth.
Otherwise, what could have this "coldness" as its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)? If you say, "It is the water element (*āpodhātu*)," then [the same applies] to hot water and the like.
Water would not exist [in fire], because of the contradictory characteristics of water and heat as they coexist;
nor does it remain while abandoning its coldness in the presence of heat. For intrinsic natures do not abandon their own nature through any state of coexistence, lest they fall into non-existence;
nor does it have any other nature apart from its quality of coldness, by which a coexistence might be possible. If it were so...

Regarding the statement “water is coldness,” there may be two states because a state possesses a nature characterized by mutual distinctness. Alternatively, if it is argued that coldness is not a [separate] state,

but rather the quality of coldness is the very form (*sarūpa*) of the water element, and that this [quality] disappears when in proximity to heat while only the substance possessing the quality (*guṇin*) remains—
then, in that case, the water element itself would not be tangible, nor would it possess a fixed tangibility.
It might be argued: "That which is the quality of cold-sensation is well-stated by us to be a specific instance of the fire-element (*tejodhātu*).
If it is claimed that this alone is the distinction, then surely coldness and heat are mutually contradictory; how then could they both be the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the fire-element?
This is not a fault, because those two do not coexist within a single aggregate (*kalāpa*), but rather exist in different aggregates.

In the course of its manifestation, just as the qualities of light, darkness, blue, yellow, and so forth do not contradict their status as the sense-base of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*), so too it does not contradict its nature as the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
If coldness is not the intrinsic nature (*sarūpa*) of the water element, what then is its intrinsic nature? It is fluidity (*dravatā*).

If that is so, since fluidity must also be known by touching, would it not follow that it is a tangible object (*phoṭṭhabba*)? No; for while one touches the cold and so forth, one perceives the color with the mind alone.

Because it is to be known [by touch]. For those sleeping in the dark, upon touching a bowl or similar object due to its extreme cold, suspect that "there is water here," or upon touching water, perceive it as a snake or the like;
therefore, the water element alone is not tangible, and it should be understood that only the other three elements are tangible.
But can body-consciousness arise by taking these three primary elements together as its object? It cannot.
Why? Because it arises by taking only one among them as its object, either through the force of attention (*ābhujita*) or through the force of predominance (*ussada*).
For, by the force of attention, having taken a grain of rice from a bowl, one perceives its hardness or softness...
When one investigates— such as when lowering the hand into a vessel of hot water to investigate its heat,
or when opening a window during a hot season to let the wind strike the body— although the other three elements are also present there,
what is actually experienced is, respectively, only those specific earth, fire, and air elements as they are being consumed.
Body-consciousness arises depending [on that]. Thus, it is said to "take an object" by way of being directed toward it.

However, at the time of eating, when one is biting a pebble due to its prominence, or stepping on fire on the road, or even when a strong wind strikes the earlobe—although the other three elements are present in those respective locations—
However, body-consciousness arises in accordance with the respective predominance of the earth,
fire, or air element. Even if the entire body of one submerged in a fire were struck by the flames all at once,
body-consciousness arises only in whichever part of the sensitive body (*kāyappasāda*) is predominant, or wherever there is the friction of contact with the object.
It is strong; therefore, body-consciousness arises first in that very spot and only afterwards in other places.
However, because of the brevity of the moment, it appears as if the entire body were burning all at once due to its rapid rotation and arising.
Indeed, many consciousnesses do not arise in a single moment; rather, they arise by pervading [the body].
Or else, one [consciousness arises]. However, within each inseparable body-decad (*kāyadasaka*), only a single body-consciousness arises by way of predominance;
likewise, in the case of the other bases as well, the arising of only one consciousness at a time in an inseparable location should be understood.
Thus, it is said that one takes the object by way of predominance.
But by what means does the shifting of the mind’s object occur? It occurs either through inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) or through the predominance of the sense-object (*visayādhimatta*).

For instance, in one who wishes to see images of the mind and so forth in various locations, after first seeing them in one place, a spontaneous adverting of the mind (*sarasāvajjana*) arises in order to see the forms in other locations as well.
Thus, shifting occurs through inclination. [Likewise,] a form-object...

Furthermore, even for one who sees something great, or hears the sound of all kinds of musical instruments arising, or when agreeable or disagreeable, intense odors, tastes, and tangibles strike the sense faculties, the mind shifts from one to another; thus, there is a shifting due to the intensity of the objects.
This is the analysis here by way of summary. Furthermore, [the analysis] by way of emptiness, and by way of the past and so forth...
The detailed analysis of each [type of consciousness] according to its infinite subdivisions should be understood as appropriate, following the method already stated in the *Cittavibhaṅga*.
Furthermore, here the miscellaneous discussion concerning their origination and their occurrence within the realms of existence (*bhava*) and the modes of birth (*yoni*) should be understood:

for when material phenomena arise, they do so in two realms and four modes of birth solely by way of groups (*kalāpa*) beginning with the decads, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.
They arise according to possibility. Among them, first, regarding those born of kamma:

in the case of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings in the sense world alone, eight material phenomena—namely, the six bases, one or another of the two sexes, and life—manifest from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards according to possibility. These constitute the "pure octad."
The life-faculty and the life-nonad; that same nonad, together with the eye, becomes the eye-decad;
with the ear, the ear-decad; with the nose, the nose-decad; with the tongue, the tongue-decad; with the body, the body-decad; with the heart-basis, the basis-decad;
and with one or another sex-organ, the sex-decad—thus, arising as nine groups (kalāpa). However, for those who are neuter here...
The sex-decad does not exist [in the form realm], nor do the eye-, ear-, or nose-decads exist for those such as the congenitally blind. Likewise, this applies to egg-born and womb-born beings;
however, in their case, at the moment of rebirth-linking, only the body-decad and the sex-decad arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness.

Thereafter, during the course of existence, the life-nonad, the eye-decad, and so forth arise accordingly. In the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), however, the triad beginning with the nose-decad is absent.
The two sets of ten material phenomena (bhāvadasaka) and the ninefold group of digestive heat (udaraggi-navaka) do not exist;

the remaining [groups] arise from rebirth-linking onwards through the five types of fine-material-sphere wholesome kamma. However, for those possessing knowledge of others' minds, only the ninefold life-group (jīvita-navaka) arises through the wholesome kamma of the fifth jhāna.
Thus, the nine material groups originated by kamma of the sense and fine-material spheres arise, as applicable, in the two realms of existence and the four modes of birth.
From the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) until the seventeenth consciousness preceding the death-consciousness (cuticitta),
the [mental states] arise continuously within the internal continuum throughout the three moments— arising, presence, and dissolution—
of each consciousness; from that point onward, they no longer arise and cease together with the death-consciousness.
However, those born of consciousness (*cittaja*) in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) are produced at the very moment of their own arising by seventy-five types of consciousness—

excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the immaterial-sphere resultants— and exist only within one's own internal continuum from the first life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) until the end of the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*).
These consist of the pure octad (*suddha-aṭṭhaka*), and that same [octad] together with bodily intimation (*kāya-viññatti*) constitutes the bodily-intimation nonad (*kāya-viññatti-navaka*).
There are six groups [of material phenomena] that arise accordingly: the vocal-intimation decad through vocal intimation and sound; the lightness-undecad through the triad of lightness and so forth;
the twelvefold group through bodily intimation and the factors beginning with lightness; and the thirteenfold group through vocal intimation, sound, and the factors beginning with lightness.
Furthermore, among the consciousnesses that produce matter, the sense-sphere javanas accompanied by joy, together with the intimation of posture and laughing, [produce matter].

They all originate all mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*). The remaining sense-sphere javanas, the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the registration consciousnesses (*voṭṭhabbana*), the laughter-impulse (*hasanavajja*), and the absorption javanas (*appanājavana*) likewise [originate it], though they are devoid of postures and so forth;
however, they support the postures as they occur without letting them perish.
But the other nineteen—the fine-material sphere resultants, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and their object-consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa*)—[do not originate it].
They do not produce four groups [of material phenomena], namely: the pure octad, the sound nonad, the lightness-undecad, and the sound-lightness-dodecad.

Furthermore, among those, all rebirth-linking consciousnesses, the death-consciousness of Arahants, those born in the formless realm, and the two types of formless-resultant consciousness and the fivefold sense-consciousness do not originate any material phenomenon.
"In every way they do not arise.
However, those born of nutriment (*āhāraja*) arise only in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), produced by the nutriment known as *ojā* (vital essence) which persists while food is being swallowed;

these exist only within one's own internal continuum (*ajjhattasantāna*) as two groups (*kalāpa*): the pure octad (*suddhaṭṭhaka*) and the elevenfold group beginning with lightness (*lahutādekādasaka*).
Having arisen, they persist for the duration of the life-span, but not on the plane of form (rūpabhūmi).

Those born of temperature (utujā), having arisen within the internal continuum by means of the temperature known as the internal and external fire-element that has reached its state of maintenance, exist for the duration of the life-span as four groups (kalāpa): the pure octad, the sound nonad, the lightness-undecad, and the sound-lightness-undecad, as well as the sound-lightness-dodecad.

Externally, however, in relation to earth, mountains, celestial abodes, Brahmā’s palaces, and so forth, there occur only two groups (kalāpa): the pure octad and the sound nonad consisting of the roar of the ocean and other such sounds.
Furthermore, although the characteristics of space exist within all these groups, they are not counted in the enumeration of the groups because they lack conventional designation (vohāra).
And herein, at the moment of rebirth-linking, those born of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment—

They do not exist, nor do aging and death arise at all places at the very moment of their own arising; thus should the sequence of occurrence for matter produced by the four causes be understood within the realms of existence and the modes of rebirth, as well as during the process of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
Furthermore, it should be understood here both by way of the forty-two components internally and by way of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth.
And external occurrence should be understood in this way: for these twenty components consisting primarily of earth—namely, the internal head-hairs, body-hairs, ...
down to feces and brain-matter; and these twelve components consisting primarily of water—namely, bile, ... down to urine;
and that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed by fever, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted [is digested].
That which undergoes proper digestion—these are the four components predominant in fire (*tejo*): upward-moving, downward-moving, stomach-dwelling, and receptacle-dwelling;
and inhalation and exhalation, which follow every limb—these are the six components predominant in air (*vāyu*). Thus, there are forty-two components in total.
Among them, undigested food, feces, pus, and urine—these four components are born of the season (*utu-jā*).
Thus, among these, each one consists of a single temperature-born octad (*utuja-aṭṭhaka*). Sweat, tears, saliva, and snot—these four are born of both temperature and mind;
in each of them, there are two octads. The fire that digests what is eaten and so forth is born of kamma;

therein, there is only the life-nonad (*jīvita-navaka*). In-breathing and out-breathing, however, are born of mind; therein, there is only the mind-born sound-nonad (*cittaja-sadda-navaka*). Having set aside these ten components...
The remaining thirty-two [elements] are of four kinds.
Therein, in each of the eight portions consisting of fire and air, there are a life-nonad and three octads born of temperature, mind, and nutriment;
furthermore, in the portions consisting of air, there is also a sound-nonad born of temperature and mind. In the remaining twenty-four portions, however...

Except for the locations where the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth are detached from the flesh, there are everywhere two sets of ten-body-elements (kāyabhāvadasaka) and three sets of eight-elements (aṭṭhaka).
However, in the case of the hair and so forth that are detached from the flesh, there is only the eight-element-group of temperature-born (utuja-aṭṭhaka).

These aforementioned groups of ten, nine, and eight elements exist within the parts of the entire body—such as skin, flesh, blood, and so on—which are pervasive, as well as within the non-pervasive parts such as the hair and so forth, where they remain inseparable.
They exist in each single atomic location (*aṇupadesa*), being individually infinite and immeasurable because they have infinite elements as their condition.

For within one's own body, there are infinite great primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—together with their derived matter (*upādārūpa*)—which, having been pulverized into a multitude of atoms, act as mutual conditions for one another;
internally, by way of the forty-two parts, the height, circumference, and shape of the body, and externally, by way of the earth, mountains, and so forth.
And they have arisen according to their respective conditions in this manner. Like magicians and the like, they do not deceive foolish people.

Furthermore, the earth element here, being finely powdered and having become dust, is held together by the water element, maintained by the fire element, supported by the air element, and surrounded by visible form and the other [sensory objects]; thus, it is not scattered within.

It assumes the state of bodies such as those of women, men, deer, birds, devas, and brahmās; and externally, it assumes the state of earth, mountains, trees, deva-worlds, brahma-worlds, the moon, the sun, the stars, jewels, gold, and so forth.

Herein, the water element, which acts as a binding agent within the lymph, is supported by the earth element. The remaining elements—namely, cohesion, expansion, maturation, and envelopment—prevent it from leaking away.
By not leaking, they demonstrate a state of nourishment. The fire element, having reached the state of heat, is supported, gathered, expanded, and enveloped by the other elements.
It brings this body to maturity, and it accomplishes its excellence of color and its state of non-decomposition.
The air element, whose intrinsic nature is distension and motion, performs distension and movement while being supported, gathered, protected, and surrounded by the remaining elements.
It effects the maintenance of the body, palaces, and so forth, as well as the taking of steps such as walking and the like. And when these four [elements] come together, with earth predominating—

They establish the state of hair and so forth, as well as the state of earth and mountains; the state of bile and so forth due to the predominance of water, as well as the state of ocean waters and so forth;
the state of upward-moving winds and so forth due to the predominance of air, as well as the state of the winds that support the earth;

and the state of digestive fire and so forth due to the predominance of fire, as well as the state of the fires of hell and so forth—[all these] by whose provocation there arise disease, old age, and death.

There are also world-destroying aeons and so forth. Thus, because these elements are gathered together in a state of being finely ground and pulverized, each internal constituent consists of infinite and immeasurable clusters; likewise for external forms.
And those [forms] arise and will arise only as they have already arisen, through various conditions and in their respective modes.

If, first, the elements remain in their respective forms and subsequently combine, then because there would be no application [of function] while they remain thus, it can also be understood by another method that here:
[matter] born of kamma is conditioned by kamma and originated by the condition of kamma;

[matter] born of nutriment is conditioned by nutriment and originated by the condition of nutriment; and [matter] born of temperature is conditioned by temperature and originated by the condition of temperature.
"Born of mind," "conditioned by mind," and "originated by temperature conditioned by mind"—thus should the classification according to origination be understood.
In this context, "clung-to matter" is called "born of kamma"; flesh, blood, hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, mucus, and so forth are called "conditioned by kamma";

and such things as the great clouds that bring prosperity, the earth, mountains, and so on, as well as the Wheel-Treasure and the celestial mansions of the gods, are "originated by temperature conditioned by kamma."
The pure octad arisen from nutriment is called "nutriment-born" (*āhāraja*).
Since edible food, by acting as the producer of the nutriment-born, becomes the sustainer of the karma-born, the karma-born matter sustained by it is called the "nutriment-condition.

When one consumes unwholesome food and goes out into the heat, black leprosy and other such ailments arise; this is the temperature-originated [matter] conditioned by nutriment (*āhārapaccaya-utusamutthāna*).
The pure octad arising from kamma-born heat is called "heat-born" (*utu-ja*); when that heat gives rise to another octad, this is called the "condition by heat" (*utūpaccaya*).
When that [second] heat also gives rise to another octad, this is called "arising from heat produced by the condition of heat" (*utūpaccaya-utusamutthāna*).
Thus, in the case of the clung-to (*upādinnaka*), only three continuities (*santati*) are able to connect.
As for that which is not clung to (*anupādinnaka*): a cloud is called "born of temperature" (*utuja*); a downpour of rain is called "conditioned by temperature" (*utupaccaya*).

When it rains, the earth releases its fragrance and seeds sprout; thus, whatever proceeds in a continuous series (*santati*) is called "temperature-originated from the condition of temperature" (*utupaccayautusamuṭṭhāna*).
That which originates from consciousness (*citta*), such as the pure octad (*suddhaṭṭhaka*), is called "consciousness-born" (*cittaja*).
The body supported by mind through the mode of posterior-arising condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) is called "conditioned by mind" (*citta-paccaya*).

That which is externally produced by the mind of supernormal power (*abhiññā-citta*), such as elephants, horses, and so forth, is called "temperature-originated conditioned by mind" (*citta-paccaya-utusamutthāna*). This concludes the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇaka-kathā*).
The indeterminate material phenomena (*rūpa-abyākata*) are finished.
The Exposition of the Indeterminate as Nibbāna:
However, the indeterminate as Nibbāna is exclusively supramundane (*lokuttara*) in terms of plane; in terms of its nature (*dhamma*), it is also one alone, with no division.

But in terms of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, Nibbāna has the characteristic of peace (*santi*), the characteristic of turning away (*nivatti*), or the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
Its proximate cause is the taste of the ultimate (accutirasa); its manifestation is the signless (animittapaccupaṭṭhāna).

However, because it is unconditioned (asaṅkhata), it lacks a footing (padaṭṭhāna) due to the absence of a productive cause; yet, by way of its evil causes, it is appropriate to call it the "footing of the Noble Path" (ariyamaggapadaṭṭhāna), according to such statements as "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, because there is no differentiation within it through inclusion, it does not fall under the aggregates (khandha), but rather under the bases (āyatana) and so forth.

It is included within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu). Furthermore, it should be understood as "emptiness" (suñña) in the sense that it is empty of a self;
as a mere phenomenon (dhammamatta) devoid of self because it maintains its own specific characteristic;

or, due to its unconditioned nature and absolute state, as emptiness of impermanence, emptiness of suffering, emptiness of lust and so forth, and emptiness of signs—thus, the process itself is to be grasped as emptiness.

As for its classification: although it is of one kind by virtue of its intrinsic nature as characterized by peace, it is twofold from the perspective of its causal terminology—as the *nibbāna-element with residue remaining* (*sa-upādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu*) and the *nibbāna-element without residue remaining* (*anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu*). Furthermore, when classified according to the modes conceived through its own inherent power, it is threefold:

the void (*suññatā*), the signless (*animitta*), and the desireless (*appaṇihita*). This is based on the manner in which it is to be negated, taking into account the distinctions among conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*).
It is of infinite modes, such as: "it is not mind, not mental concomitants, not matter, not past, not future, not present, not the path, not the fruit," and so forth.
The section on the indeterminate state of Nibbāna is concluded.
Thus, in this triad of the wholesome, there is no such thing as a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature (asabhāva-dhamma).
Among those things lacking intrinsic nature, although here only the characteristics of delimitation, non-cognizance, and so forth are stated for material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma),

there are nevertheless the counterpart-signs of the kasiṇas and so on, the space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa, the absence of consciousness, the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and the three designations (paññatti) of name, person, and acquisition.

Furthermore, although the characteristics such as impermanence of non-material phenomena have not been explicitly mentioned, they are nevertheless included because they do not exist apart from the phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma).
Therefore, this triad should be understood as a "comprehensive triad" (nippadesattika).

And just as in this case, so too in the subsequent triads and dyads, even in the absence of an explicit mention of "conceptual constructs" (paññatti), their comprehensiveness is established by the inclusion of all ultimate realities (paramattha) without exception.
The opposite case, namely its limited scope, should also be understood. Wherever there is the employment of conventional designation (*sammuti*), we shall explain it there.
The section on Matter and Nibbāna is finished.
Thus ends the *Mohavicchedanī*.
The commentary on the *Kusalattika* (the Triplet of the Wholesome) within the *Abhidhammamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanā* is completed.
Now follows the commentary on the *Vedanāttika* (the Triplet of Feeling), etc.
Now, the explanation of the meaning of the feeling-triad (*vedanāttika*) and the others follows immediately after the wholesome-triad (*kusalattika*). For it was said regarding this wholesome-triad:

“In terms of meaning and classification of planes, In each case according to association, And by way of the summary of phenomena, And the analysis of their characteristics and so forth. Thus [it was stated].
Having set forth the matrix (mātikā) by means of the first [term], the method of exposition is stated as follows: "First, wholesome states (dhammā) are fourfold according to plane:
sense-sphere... up to... supramundane," and so on. This same method applies accordingly to the remaining triads and dyads.
Just as it is here, so too: "First, states associated with pleasant feeling are threefold according to plane..."

By means of such passages as “They are of the sense-sphere, of the fine-material sphere, and supramundane,” the wise are able to discern the method of analysis for all the triplets and dyads in their proper sequence.
Therefore, avoiding that detailed method, and following what has been stated in the *Nikkhepakanda* (The Book of Enumerations) and the *Atthuddhārakanda* (The Book of Expositions),
[I shall treat] the triplets and dyads beginning with the triad of feelings by a method that is neither too brief nor too prolix:

The analysis of the meaning of the terms and their classification according to what is not to be expressed should be understood as appropriate in each respective instance. Therein, regarding the triad of feelings, first,

from the standpoint of the meaning of the words (*padatthato*) in such passages as "for pleasant feeling" (*sukhāya vedanāya*), the word "pleasant" (*sukha*) refers to pleasant feeling, the root of pleasant feeling, the object of pleasant feeling, the cause of pleasant feeling, the condition for pleasant feeling, the basis for pleasant feeling, non-affliction, Nibbāna, and so forth.

It is seen [in various senses]. For this term is seen in the sense of pleasant feeling in such passages as, "With the abandoning of pleasure" (*sukhassa ca pahānā*). It is seen in the sense of the root of pleasure in such passages as, "The arising of Buddhas is pleasant" (*sukho buddhānam uppādo*).

It is seen in the sense of a pleasant object in such passages as, "Because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, pervaded by pleasure, and immersed in pleasure" (*yasmā ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkantaṃ*).

And it is seen in the sense of the cause of pleasure in such passages as, "Monks, this is a designation for pleasure, namely, meritorious deeds" (*sukhassetaṃ, bhikkhave, adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ puññāni*).
“Insofar as it is not easy to reach the heavens by mere description, so pleasant are the heavenly realms;

those who do not see Nandana do not understand happiness,” and so on—in these instances, it refers to the state that is a condition for happiness. “These states are dwellings in happiness in this very life,” and so on—in these instances, it refers to the absence of affliction (*abyābajjha*).
“Nirvana is the supreme happiness,” and so on—in these instances, it refers to Nirvana. But here, however—
This should be understood specifically in relation to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).
The word "feeling" (*vedanā*) occurs in the sense of what is felt (*vedayita*) in such passages as, "Feeling that has been known arises.

The word "suffering" (*dukkha*) is seen in the sense of painful feeling, the basis of suffering, the object of suffering, the condition for suffering, the state of being a condition for suffering, and so forth.
For this term "suffering" (dukkha) is seen in the following senses: in such passages as "with the abandoning of suffering," it refers to painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).

In such passages as "birth is suffering," it refers to the basis of suffering (*dukkhavatthu*). In such passages as "Because, Mahāli, form is suffering, beset by suffering, immersed in suffering," it refers to the object of suffering (*dukkhārammaṇa*).
In such passages as "The accumulation of evil is suffering," it refers to the condition for suffering (*dukkhapaccaya*). "To such an extent, monks... [and so forth].
In such passages as “It is not easy to reach [the end] by mere description, so painful are the hells,” it refers to the state of being a condition for suffering.
Here, however, it should be understood as referring specifically to painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
As for the etymological meaning here: it brings happiness to a being, or it thoroughly consumes and digs away the afflictions of body and mind.
“Pleasant” (*sukhā*) is a designation for bodily and mental pleasure and joy. It “afflicts” (*dukkhayati*), thus it is “painful” (*dukkhā*);
this is a designation for bodily and mental pain and grief. “Neither painful nor pleasant” (*adukkhamasukhā*) is a designation for equanimity (*upekkhā*).
The letter *ma-* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction of words (*padasandhi*). Thus, by means of these three terms, the fivefold feeling is [described].
They are grasped. All [mental factors] are called *vedanā* because they feel and experience the flavor of the object.
As for the term *sampayutta* (associated) used in all three contexts, its meaning is: "they are associated by way of common modes. By what modes?
"There are certain states that are conjoined with, co-nascent with, mixed with, and which arise and cease together with other states."
By these four modes—beginning with simultaneous arising—as stated in the phrase "having one basis and one object," this is an exalted description.
For in the formless realm, association is found even without having a single basis. The rest has already been explained.
This, then, is the analysis according to the meaning of the words.
"Of that same nature" means because it shows the mere nature of that term's referent.

In this context, there are sixty-three types of consciousness associated with pleasant feeling: body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure; eighteen sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by joy; and forty-four fine-material-sphere and supramundane consciousnesses belonging to the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas.
Likewise, body-consciousness accompanied by pain and the two types of consciousness accompanied by mental grief—these three classes of consciousness are said to be associated with painful feeling.
The remaining fifty-five classes of consciousness, which are accompanied by equanimity, are said to be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
And just as there is this association of consciousness with pleasant feeling and so forth, so too...
[This inclusion applies] also to the mental factors associated with that consciousness. And not only here;

in the subsequent triplets and dyads as well, the inclusion of the mental factors associated with the consciousness should be understood by way of the consciousness itself. However, where there is a distinction, we shall explain it there.
Here, among the mental factors, six factors—excluding feeling—are accompanied by zest (*sappītika*).
In this way, they are associated with all five feelings; however, the others are associated with only three, excluding bodily pleasure and pain.

Among those, the eleven factors—consisting of the five [mental factors] excluding joy (*pīti*), as well as delusion (*moha*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), sloth (*thina*), and torpor (*middha*)—are associated with all three feelings as appropriate.
Furthermore, among these, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are excluded from the sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) states.
[The first two] are associated only with pleasure (*sukha*); however, joy (*pīti*) is associated only with pleasure in all instances;

hatred, envy, and stinginess are associated only with pain (*dukkha*); doubt is associated only with equanimity (*upekkhā*); the remaining [twenty-eight] are associated only with the feelings of mental pleasure (*somanassa*) and equanimity;

furthermore, among those, compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*), being sublime (*mahaggata*), are associated only with pleasure—this is the distinction. The rest is the same as in the case of association with consciousness (*citta*).
This is the analysis according to their specific characteristics (*sarūpato*). Regarding the "analysis of what is not to be designated" (*navattabbavibhāgato*):
in this triad, all feelings, all matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena cannot be designated as either "associated with pleasant feeling" or "associated with painful feeling."
Nor should it be said that they are "associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. For a feeling is not associated with another feeling, nor with form and so forth;
therefore, these [categories] are not found within this triad. And this is a triad with specific limitations.
Just as here, so too in the subsequent triads and dyads, the application of what is not to be stated [should be understood]. Whatever has not been stated in a particular context...

It exists; its partial nature (*sappadesatā*) should be understood. Hereafter, however, wherever there are states not included [in the aggregates], we shall show their classification and say merely, "these are not to be stated" (*navattabbā*); by this, its partial nature is also to be known.
But where there are no states not included, we shall call that "complete" (*nippadesa*). By this, the absence of anything not to be stated therein is also [established].
It is to be understood. However, throughout all [sections], we shall explain the meaning of the terms and their specific classifications without first reciting the entire matrix (mātikā).
This concludes the exposition according to the classification of what is not to be stated.
The Triplet on Feeling is finished.
In the triad of results (*vipākattika*), "results" (*vipākā*) refers to the ripenings of wholesome and unwholesome states that are distinguished from one another;

this is a designation for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) that have attained the state of having ripened. Although material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are also produced by kamma just like immaterial phenomena, because they lack an object (*anārammaṇa*), they do not resemble kamma.
Therefore, it is only the immaterial phenomena, which possess an object (*sārammaṇa*), that [are called results] due to their resemblance to kamma.
They are called "results" (*vipāka*) because they resemble the fruit of a seed.
For just as that which emerges from a rice seed is called a "rice fruit," while the sprout and so forth are not, yet those [latter] are said to be "born of rice" and "produced by rice"—
in the same way, only immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) similar to the karma are called "results," whereas material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are "born of karma" (*kammaja*).
“They are called ‘clung-to’ (upādinnā). “States characterized by result” (vipākadhammadhammā) means states whose intrinsic nature is result (vipāka-sabhāva).

Just as beings whose intrinsic nature is birth and aging are called “subject to birth” (jātidhamma) and “subject to aging” (jarādhamma), so too, in the sense of producing result, these are states whose intrinsic nature is result and whose natural tendency is result;
this is the meaning. The third phrase is stated by way of the negation of both those natures; this is the meaning of the term.
Therein, among the four planes, the thirty-six resultant consciousnesses are called "resultants" (*vipāka*).
Likewise, the twenty-one wholesome states and the twelve unwholesome states—these thirty-three—are called "states with the nature of resultants" (*vipākadhammadhamma*).

The twenty functional consciousnesses in the three planes, all matter, and Nibbāna—these are called "neither-resultant-nor-state-with-the-nature-of-resultants" (*nevavipākanavipākadhammadhamma*). Regarding mental factors (*cetasika*):
However, the fourteen unwholesome states are exclusively "states characterized by fruition" (*vipākadhammadhamma*).

The abstinences (*virati*) may be either "fruition" (*vipāka*) or "characterized by fruition. The remainder, however, may be "fruition," "characterized by fruition," or "neither fruition nor characterized by fruition.
Thus, like consciousness, they are of three kinds; this is the distinction. The rest is the same as for consciousness. And this should be understood as the "unrestricted triad" (*nippadesattika*).
The Triplet on Ripening is finished.
"Clung-to" (*upādinnā*) means that which has been taken up by karma endowed with craving and views by way of making it an object; it is grasped as the state of a fruit.
"Favorable to clinging" (*upādāniyā*) means that which is beneficial to the clingings by having entered into the state of being an object through connection with clinging. [Of] clinging...
This is a designation for those things that function as object-conditions (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

"Appropriated and subject to appropriation" (*upādinnupādāniya*) refers to material and immaterial phenomena produced by tainted (*sāsava*) kamma; this is its designation. Following this method, the meaning of the remaining two phrases should also be understood together with their respective negations.
In this context, the thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness and the nine groups of matter born of kamma are called "clung-to and subject to clinging" (*upādinnupādāniya*).

The remaining mundane consciousnesses and the groups of matter not born of kamma are called "not clung-to but subject to clinging" (*anupādinnupādāniya*). Supramundane consciousness and Nibbāna are called "neither clung-to nor subject to clinging" (*anupādinnaanupādāniya*).
Even though the aggregates of clinging belonging to those whose taints are destroyed [are still present], [they do not think] "Our uncle is the Elder," and so forth.
For those who speak, [the wholesome mental states] serve as object-conditions for the clinging of others;

however, the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna—like a red-hot iron ball on a day of intense heat—are not clung to by clinging because they are so full of radiance. The same principle applies to those states that are neither defiled nor subject to defilement (*asaṃkiliṭṭha-asaṃkilesika*).

Among the mental concomitants (*cetasika*), the wholesome ones are exclusively not-clung-to-and-object-of-clinging (*anupādinnupādāniya*); whereas compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) may be either clung-to-and-object-of-clinging or not-clung-to-and-object-of-clinging.
The abstinences (virati) may be neither-clung-to-nor-object-of-clinging, or they may be neither-clung-to-nor-object-of-clinging;
the remaining factors are threefold, just like consciousness. This should be understood as the "triad without limitation. The triad of what is clung-to-and-object-of-clinging (upādinnupādāniya).
It defiles, thus it is "defilement" (saṃkilesa); the meaning is that it afflicts and torments. Those associated with defilement are "defiled" (saṃkiliṭṭha).

The meaning is "accompanied by defilement. They are called *saṃkilesika* (defiled) because they are worthy of defilement by way of occurring with the self as their object, or because they are connected to defilement since they do not transcend the state of being its object;

this is a designation for those things that serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for defilement. They are both defiled (*saṃkiliṭṭha*) and defiled-in-nature (*saṃkilesika*), hence they are "defiled-and-defiled-in-nature" (*saṃkiliṭṭha-saṃkilesika*).
The remaining two lines should be understood according to the method already explained in the first triad.
Therein, the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are called "defiled and subject to defilement" (*saṃkiliṭṭha-saṃkilesika*).

All other mundane consciousnesses as well as all material form are called "undefiled but subject to defilement" (*asaṃkiliṭṭha-saṃkilesika*). Supramundane consciousnesses and Nibbāna are "undefiled and not subject to defilement" (*asaṃkiliṭṭha-asaṃkilesika*).
[This concludes] the section on names. Regarding mental factors (*cetasika*), however, the unwholesome ones are exclusively defiled and subject to defilement;

compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) are exclusively undefiled and not subject to defilement; and the remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors may be defiled and subject to defilement, may be undefiled but subject to defilement, or may be undefiled and not subject to defilement—thus they are threefold. This is the "Unrestricted Triplet. [Next is] the "Defiled and Subject to Defilement Triplet."

They are "with applied thought" (*savitakka*) because they occur together with applied thought (*vitakka*); likewise, they are "with sustained thought" (*savicāra*) because they occur together with sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Thus, being both with applied thought and with sustained thought, they are called "with applied and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāra*). Those devoid of both are "without applied and sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra*).

They are "mere sustained thought" (*vicāramatta*) because sustained thought alone is their measure (*mattā*) or extent (*pamāṇa*) among applied and sustained thoughts; that is, they lack association with applied thought beyond the point of sustained thought.

The meaning is "they do not go. Those which are without applied thought (*avitakka*) and possess only sustained thought (*vicāramatta*) are called "without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*).

In this context, the sense-sphere consciousnesses—excluding the two sets of fivefold sensory consciousnesses—as well as the eleven sublime and supramundane first-jhāna consciousnesses, and all other states associated with them except for applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), are called "with applied thought and with sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāra*). Among those, applied thought...

The eleven types of sublime and supramundane consciousness belonging to the second jhāna, together with the remaining factors associated with them—excluding *vicāra* (sustained thought)—are called "without initial application and with sustained application only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*). Within the second-jhāna states, *vicāra* is included;

the remaining forty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, all their associated mental factors, all material phenomena (*rūpa*), and Nibbāna are called "without initial application and without sustained application" (*avitakka-avicāra*).

Furthermore, wholesome mental factors (cetasika) are exclusively accompanied by both initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra); initial application is accompanied by sustained application but lacks initial application;

sustained application, however, may be without both initial and sustained application in the second jhāna, or it may be so designated when not applicable among minds accompanied by initial application;
all remaining mental factors, however, belong to all three categories. In this triad, it is only sustained application that arises simultaneously with initial application.
It should not be said [that they are the same]. This concludes the triad on applied thought (*vitakka*).

"Accompanied by rapture" (*pītisahagata*) means having attained the state of arising together with rapture; the meaning is "associated with rapture. The same method applies to the other two terms as well.
Here, "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*). For that indeed proceeds without the mode of either pleasure or pain.
It is called *upekkhā* (equanimity) because it looks on (*upekkhati*), owing to its establishment in a neutral mode, and because it proceeds in that manner.

Thus, by taking only two terms from the triad of feelings, this triad is stated in order to show the distinction of happiness free from rapture (*nippītika-sukha*) from happiness accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-sukha*).
In that context, rapture (*pīti*) is fivefold: minor (*khuddikā*), momentary (*khaṇikā*), showering (*okkantikā*), uplifting (*ubbegā*), and pervading (*pharaṇā*). Among these, the minor...
Rapture (*pīti*) is able to cause only a bristling of the hairs on the body. Momentary rapture (*khaṇikā pīti*) is like the flashing of lightning from moment to moment.
Overwhelming rapture (*okkantikā pīti*) descends upon and repeatedly breaks through the body, like a wave upon the shore of the ocean.
Transporting rapture (*ubbegā pīti*) is powerful; it causes the body to rise upward and reach the point of leaping into the air. As for pervading rapture (*pharaṇā*):
But when rapture (pīti) has arisen, the entire body becomes suffused with it—like a water-skin filled by being blown up, or like the interior of a mountain penetrated by a great flood of water.
In this context, the pervasion (pharaṇā) belongs only to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the supramundane (lokuttara); the remaining types belong only to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
Pleasure (sukha), moreover, is twofold: bodily and mental. And although there is no dissociation between them in certain instances...
Joy (*pīti*) is the satisfaction arising from the acquisition of a desirable object; bliss (*sukha*) is the experiencing of the flavor of what has been acquired. Where there is joy, there is bliss;

but where there is bliss, there is not necessarily joy. Joy is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), while bliss is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
Joy is like seeing and hearing about a forest and water to one exhausted by a desert, whereas bliss is like entering the shade of that forest and enjoying the water.
It is like happiness. It should be understood that this was stated because it is manifest at each respective occasion.
In this context, the feelings accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagatā*) and those accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagatā*) have already been mentioned in the triad of feelings;

however, excluding body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure, as well as the sublime and supramundane fourth-jhāna consciousnesses, the remaining [consciousnesses] are accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagatā*).

In that context, joy (*pīti*) is not accompanied by joy; it is indeed accompanied by pleasure (*sukha*). However, pleasure may be said to be accompanied by joy, but it is not accompanied by both joy and pleasure.

In this threefold scheme, two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by mental grief (*domanassa*), body-consciousness accompanied by pain (*dukkha*), matter (*rūpa*), and Nibbāna are not to be classified. Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, joy is indeed accompanied by pleasure.
Doubt is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) alone. Greed, views, and conceit, as well as the twenty-five wholesome and indeterminate states, are threefold [in their association with feeling].
Mental pleasure may be accompanied by joy (*pīti*); in the first, second, and third jhānas it is so, while in the fourth jhāna it is not to be specified.
However, bodily pleasure, pain, mental grief, and all forms of equanimity, hatred, and envy are [associated with the feeling of] equanimity.

Envy (*macchariya*) and worry (*kukkucca*) are indeed not to be designated [as either wholesome or unwholesome]; the remaining seventeen states may be of all three kinds, and they may also be not to be designated.
The rest is easy to understand. This concludes the triad on rapture (*pīti*).
Regarding the phrase "by seeing" (*dassanena*): this refers to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). For that [path] is called "seeing" because it is the first seeing of *nibbāna*.
Although the one who has entered the lineage (gotrabhū) sees [the Truth] earlier,
it is just as when a man who has come to a king’s presence on some business sees the king from afar walking along the road mounted upon the neck of an elephant;
even though he has seen him, when asked, "Have you seen the king?", he says, "I have not seen him," because the purpose for which he had come has not yet been accomplished.
In the same way, because there is nothing further to be done regarding the abandonment of defilements once Nibbāna has been seen, it is not called "seeing.
For that knowledge stands in the position of the preliminary adverting (āvajjana) for the Path. Regarding "development" (bhāvanā): this refers to the remaining three paths.
Indeed, the remaining three paths arise by way of development with respect to the very same phenomena already seen by the first path; they do not concern anything previously unseen.
It does not see; therefore, it is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). The third phrase is stated by way of the negation of both [seeing and cultivation].
In that regard, four types of consciousness-arising associated with views and that accompanied by doubt—these five—are to be abandoned solely by seeing;
that accompanied by restlessness is to be abandoned by cultivation alone; and the remaining six unwholesome types of consciousness-arising...
That which proceeds as a cause for the states of misery (apāya) and that which does not proceed may be abandoned by seeing (dassana), or it may be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā).
However, all mental states (cittuppāda) excluding the unwholesome (akusala), as well as matter (rūpa) and Nibbāna, are neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation.
Among mental concomitants (cetasika), however, wrong view (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), and worry (kukkucca) are exclusively to be abandoned by seeing.
The remaining unwholesome states are of three types: some are to be abandoned by vision, and some are to be abandoned by cultivation;
thus they are thirteenfold. The rest that have been mentioned are to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.

Furthermore, by means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, through the cessation of volitional consciousness, those [states] which would arise in the beginningless cycle of existence—setting aside the seven existences—are [abandoned].
By such methods as "Name and form—herein these cease," the abandoning of even wholesome and indeterminate states is permitted. This was said with reference to this figurative method:
that those [states] which would have arisen because those paths were not cultivated are abandoned because the underlying-tendency (upanissaya-paccaya) defilements have been abandoned.
This is the "Triplet of the Undifferentiated" (nippadesattika). This is the "Triplet of What is to be Abandoned by Seeing" (dassanapahātabbattika).
"Those for whom the cause is to be abandoned by seeing" means those whose causes are to be abandoned by seeing (*dassanena pahātabba-hetukā*). The same method applies to the second phrase as well.

However, regarding the third phrase, one should not take the meaning to be "those for whom the cause is neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation" (*nevadassanena-nabhāvanāya pahātabbo hetu etesan ti*);

rather, the meaning should be taken as "those who possess a cause that is neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation" (*nevadassanena-nabhāvanāya pahātabbo hetu etesaṃ atthīti*). Otherwise, [the classification would be inconsistent].
For otherwise, there would be no inclusion of those things that are rootless (*ahetuka*), since they lack any root that could be abandoned through seeing or cultivation.
Furthermore, even among those things that have roots (*sahetuka*), it would follow that only the factors excluding the roots are abandoned, not the roots themselves;
for it is said that "the root itself is what is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation," and not those other phenomena. And yet, neither of these two [consequences] is intended.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. From this point onward, the entire analysis is similar to that of the immediately preceding triad.

The only difference is that among the mental factors (*cetasika*), delusion associated with doubt and restlessness does not enter into the category of those whose roots are to be abandoned by vision and cultivation, because of the absence of any other co-nascent root;
nor does it enter into the category of those whose roots are to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.

However, it enters [the category] of those with roots to be abandoned by vision. Regarding the roots in the minds rooted in greed and hatred, delusion is "with root" (sahetuka) by means of both greed and hatred, while greed and hatred are "with root" by means of delusion alone;
these are included in the section on "roots to be abandoned by vision. This is the distinction; the rest is exactly the same.
Thus ends the Triplet on Roots to be Abandoned by Vision.

It is called *ācaya* (accumulation) because it is accumulated by the defilements of kamma; this is a designation for the acquired aggregates (*upādinnakkhandha*) comprised of rebirth-linking, death, destiny, and the course of existence.

Because they act as its cause and bring about that accumulation, or because they lead the person in whom they occur toward that aforementioned accumulation, they are called "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmin*). For that very reason, they are designated as "accumulation."

Because it is devoid of accumulation (*caya*), Nibbāna is "devoid of accumulation" (*apeta-caya*); thus, because they proceed by taking that as their object, they are called "leading to non-accumulation" (*apacayagāmin*).
Furthermore, like bricklayers building a wall, they proceed by accumulating the process of existence; thus they are called "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmin*).
Just as a man who destroys each layer as it is built up by that very mason, [they destroy] that same process of existence.
"Those that go by way of diminution" (*apacayagāmino*) means they proceed by way of decreasing. The third term is stated as the negation of both.
In this context, mundane wholesome and unwholesome states are called "those that go by way of accumulation" (*ācayagāmino*); the four paths are called "those that go by way of diminution";
all resultant, functional, and material phenomena, as well as Nibbāna, are called "neither those that go by way of accumulation nor those that go by way of diminution."

Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, the unwholesome ones are exclusively "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmin*). Compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) may be leading to accumulation, or they may be called neither leading to accumulation nor leading to diminution (*apacayagāmin*).
The remaining ones belong to all three categories; this is the "Triplet of the Unrestricted. This is the "Triplet of Leading to Accumulation.

They are called "trainers" (*sekha*) because they are born within the three trainings, or because they belong to the seven types of trainers; for they themselves have not yet completed their training.
They are called *sekkhā* (trainees) because they are training. They are called *asekkhā* (non-trainees) because there is nothing further to be trained in;
or alternatively, they are called *asekkhā* because those who have reached maturity are no longer *sekkhā*. The third category is stated by way of the negation of both.
In this context, the seven *sekkhā* consist of the four supramundane wholesome states and the first three fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
The fruit of arahantship is called "beyond training" (*asekhā*); mundane consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are called "neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training" (*nevasekhā-nāsekhā*).

Among mental factors (*cetasika*), however, the unwholesome ones and the illimitables (*appamaññā*) are exclusively "neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training," while the remainder belong to all three categories.
This is the "Triplet of the Undifferentiated" (*nippadesattika*). This concludes the "Triplet of Trainees" (*sekhattika*).
Because it is broken on all sides, it is called "limited" (*paritta*), as in such expressions as "a limited lump of cow dung.
Indeed, sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*) are "limited" because they possess little power.

[In contrast, these teachings] have attained greatness by virtue of their capacity to suppress the defilements, their possession of great and vast fruits, and their long continuity; or else, they are so called because they are [associated with] great and sublime zeal, energy, mind, and wisdom.
They are "exalted" (*mahaggata*) because they have gone forth and are practiced. "Limited" (*paritta*) refers to states such as lust that act as measures;
however, these [states] have no measure either by way of object or by way of association, and they are the opposites of such measures—thus they are "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).

In this context, the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses and [their associated] form are called "limited," while the twenty-seven fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousnesses are [immeasurable].

The "lofty" (mahaggata) are the supramundane consciousnesses and Nibbāna; these are called "immeasurable" (appamāṇa). Among the mental factors (cetasika), however, the unwholesome ones are exclusively limited (paritta);
the illimitables (appamaññā) are both limited and lofty; the abstinences (virati) are both limited and immeasurable; the remainder belong to all three categories.
This is the "Unrestricted Triad. [End of] the "Limited Triad."

"Those whose object is limited (paritta) are 'limited-object' (parittārammaṇa). This same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Whether they themselves are limited or sublime (mahaggata), those that proceed by taking limited and other such phenomena as their object are called "having that as their object" (tadārammaṇa).
In this regard, twenty-three types—the sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, the functional mind-element, and the rootless impulsion—are exclusively limited-object;

the wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are exclusively sublime-object. Eight... [text continues]

Supramundane consciousnesses have only an immeasurable object. Unwholesome consciousnesses and the eight sense-sphere javanas dissociated from knowledge may have a limited object, may have a sublime object, or may be "inexpressible" (navattabba) because their objects cannot be specified;
they never have an immeasurable object. This also applies to the eight sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge, the direct knowledges (abhiññā), and the mind-door adverting consciousness.

The eleven [types of consciousness] are also of three kinds and are also indeterminate. Among them, the five wholesome types have all objects as their range, with the exception of the path and fruit of Arahantship.
Even there, only for those still in training (sekha) do their respective paths and fruits serve as objects. The six functional types have all objects as their range in every respect.

Furthermore, the six fine-material-sphere consciousnesses—excluding those of direct knowledge—and the consciousnesses of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness [have all objects as their range].

Furthermore, because they are invariably defined by having a cognitive object (ārammaṇa), and because material form (rūpa) and Nibbāna are entirely without a cognitive object, they cannot be described in any way [as being either limited or immeasurable].

Among the mental concomitants (cetasika), however, the unwholesome ones are exactly like the unwholesome consciousnesses. The abstinences (virati) may have a limited object or may have an immeasurable object;
compassion (karuṇā) and gladness (muditā) are strictly immeasurable; the remaining ones belong to all three categories, or may be undeterminable.
The rest is easy to understand. This concludes the triad of limited objects.

"Inferior" means base, unwholesome states. "Intermediate" means those that exist between the inferior and the sublime; these are simply the remaining states of the three planes, namely, the material and immaterial phenomena.
"Sublime" refers, in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being unsurpassed, to supramundane consciousness and Nibbāna.

Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, the unwholesome ones are exclusively inferior; compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) are exclusively middling; the remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors are both middling and sublime;
and the rest are of all three kinds. This is the "Triplet Without Exception. The remainder is easily understood. This concludes the "Inferior Triplet.

[The "Inferior" designation applies] because even when desired in the thought, "May they bring me benefit and happiness," they do not exist accordingly, and because they function in a distorted manner, such as perceiving the foul and so forth as beautiful.

They are "wrongnesses" (*micchattā*) because they are wrong by nature. They are "fixed" (*niyatā*) because, when giving their result, they give that result immediately after the breakup of the aggregates;

thus, being both wrongnesses and fixed, they are "fixed in wrongness" (*micchattaniyatā*). By a meaning contrary to what was stated, they are "rightnesses" (*sammattā*) because they are right by nature;
being both rightnesses and fixed, they are "fixed in rightness" (*sammattaniyatā*). Those which are not fixed in either way are "undetermined" (*aniyatā*).
In its occurrence as an immediate (ānantariya) state, it may be fixed in falsehood; otherwise, in its occurrence, it may be unfixed.
For if one’s view among the rootless, non-doing, or nihilistic views is fixed, not even a hundred Buddhas can awaken them from it.

And because it yields its fruit in the very next existence, it is included among the "immediate" offenses—namely, the killing of a mother, the killing of a father, the killing of an arahant, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
If even one of the five kinds of deeds has been committed with a mind of aversion, then even if one were to construct golden stūpas the size of Mount Sineru,
fill the entire Cakkavāḷa world with them, and serve the Saṅgha headed by a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha with the four requisites for as long as life lasts,
one would still not be able to ward off the immediate ripening of that [unwholesome] karma by means of that wholesome [merit].

However, by its immediate and superior nature, it obstructs the immediate [result]. Therefore, fixed wrong view is both "immediate" (ānantarika) because it obstructs the paths and fruits, and "fixed in falsehood" (micchattaniyata) because it yields its result in hell immediately following [the act] due to its obstruction of the sublime states.
The four paths, however, are called "fixed in rightness" (sammattaniyata); the remaining types of consciousness, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are not so classified.

These are called indeterminate (*aniyata*). Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, these nine—delusion (*moha*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), greed (*lobha*), wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), hatred (*dosa*), sloth (*thina*), and torpor (*middha*)—may be either fixed in the wrongness (*micchattaniyata*) or indeterminate;

the remaining unwholesome factors, compassion (*karuṇā*), and appreciative joy (*muditā*) are exclusively indeterminate. The remaining wholesome and neutral factors may be either fixed in the rightness (*sammattaniyata*) or indeterminate; they are of three types.
Furthermore, they are threefold, and this is the "incomplete triad. This concludes the triad of the wrong course (micchattattika).
Nibbāna is "sought" (maggati), or it "proceeds while slaying the defilements," thus it is the Path (magga).

It is the Noble Path (ariyamagga). Those [states] which have that as their object are "path-objects" (maggārammaṇa). Even the mundane eightfold path is a "cause" (hetu) for these in the sense of being a condition; thus they are "path-caused" (maggahetuka).
States associated with the path (*maggasampayutta-dhammā*). Or, "causes in the path" means *maggahetu*, namely non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth.

Since these are their causes, they are "path-rooted" (*maggahetuka*). Right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is itself both the path and the cause; thus, because the cause is constituted by the path, they are "path-rooted," and these are exclusively supramundane (*lokuttara*).

In the sense of proceeding by way of overcoming, the path is the dominant factor (*adhipati*); since it is either the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*) or co-nascent (*sahajāta*) with them, they are "path-dominant" (*maggādhipatino*), and this applies to both [the mundane and supramundane].

In this context, the wholesome and functional fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, as well as the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), and the mind-door adverting consciousness may have the Path as their object, or they may be "not to be specified" (navattabbā).
For the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of future existences belonging to the Noble Ones (ariya) have the Path as their object at the time of knowing the path-consciousness of others;
however, the knowledge of past lives and the mind-door adverting consciousness have one's own [path] as their object.
Furthermore, at the time when others are taking other objects as their cognitive focus, they are not to be described [as having that knowledge].

However, because the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) necessarily has the minds of others as its object, Noble Ones (ariya) are unable to take as an object the path attained by themselves through that [knowledge].

Moreover, because the knowledge of future possibilities (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) does not have as its object the higher path that will arise for oneself in the future, they are unable [to know it]. For Noble Ones...

Each [type of consciousness] is able to know its own corresponding lower path and fruit, but not the higher ones. However, because those access-mindfulnesses of direct knowledge (*abhiññājavana*) are not conascent with the path, they do not have the path as their cause (*maggahetuka*).
Because they do not proceed by taking the path as an object of esteem (*garu*), they do not have the path as their predominance (*maggādhipati*).
For they do not take any object as a predominance, even the supramundane (*lokuttara*). Why? Because of themselves...
Upon seeing the king, the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) functions like the parents of that king due to its magnanimity;
however, upon seeing the king, it functions like hunchbacked servants and the like due to its own lack of root-cause (ahetuka).

The four path-consciousnesses (magga-citta) are always rooted in the Path (maggahetuka); furthermore, through the predominance of investigation (vīmaṃsā) and energy (vīriya), these very same states may, during their occurrence, be "predominant by the Path" (maggādhipati).

In the case of others whose minds are dominated by desire (*chandacitta*), they may be indeterminate (*navattabba*) during their occurrence. As for the eight sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) impulsion moments associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), they may have the Path as their object (*maggārammaṇa*), they may have the Path as their dominant influence (*maggādhipati*), or they may be indeterminate.

For these [impulsions] have the Path as their object at the time of reviewing the Path realized by oneself or by others; however, at the time of reviewing while esteeming one's own Path, [they have the Path as their dominant influence].

And when they do not arise in such a manner, they cannot be so designated. For even when noble ones review the paths and fruits of others and hold them in high esteem, they do not esteem them as they do their own paths and fruits, nor even as they do those of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Among them, a stream-enterer is able to know the paths and fruits only of stream-enterers, and not those of others; a once-returner...

However, a once-returner knows the paths and fruits up to his own level, but not those of non-returners or arahants; a non-returner knows the paths and fruits up to his own level, but not those of arahants;
whereas an arahant knows the paths and fruits of all. Beautiful mundane consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are simply not to be designated [as belonging to any specific path or fruit].

Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, the abstinences (*virati*) in supramundane wholesome states are identical to the Path; elsewhere, they are not to be designated. Compassion (*karuṇā*),...

Joy (*muditā*) and unwholesome states are not to be so designated; the remainder are of all three kinds and are also not to be so designated. The rest is easily understood. This concludes the triad of objects that are the Path.
Regarding the term "arisen" (*uppanna*): here, "arisen" is of many varieties according to whether it is present, past, future, occasioned, or obtained by plane.
Among these, everything that is conditioned (*saṅkhata*), characterized by arising, aging, and dissolution, is "presently arisen."
The term "past" refers to that which has ceased after experiencing the flavor of its object, being designated as "experienced and departed," including both wholesome and unwholesome [states];

and it refers to the three characteristics of arising and so forth, having ceased after reaching them, being designated as "become and departed"; and it refers to all remaining conditioned phenomena that have arisen and then become departed.
Furthermore, it includes even past karma, as stated in such passages as: "Those karmas previously performed by him... and so forth.

Because it stands having set aside another similar result and made room for its own result, and because that result which has been given such room will certainly arise even though it has not yet arisen, it is called "arisen by making room" (*okāsakatuppanna*).
Furthermore, unwholesome states that have not been eradicated in their respective planes are called "arisen by obtaining the plane" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*).
And herein, those [states] belonging to the three planes that serve as objects for insight...

The five aggregates are called "the plane. When the types of defilements capable of arising within those aggregates have arisen, it is called "having acquired the plane," because that plane has been acquired by those defilements.
Thus, when these [defilements] have arisen, what is intended here is the "arisen-in-occurrence" (vattamānuppanna).
