In this regard, the etymology is as follows: from its origination in the past, until its dissolution, it has gone forth and proceeded.
"Arisen" means present. "Not arisen" means unarisen.
"Bound to arise" (*uppādino*) refers to those that will necessarily arise because they belong to a portion of the causes that have reached completion; by both [terms], only the future is shown.
For this triad is presented by way of filling out two of the three time-periods (*addhā*). For the ripening (*vipāka*) of karma that has obtained an opportunity is called "bound to arise. If...
If all accumulated wholesome and unwholesome karma were to yield its result immediately, there would be no opportunity for it [to ripen later].

That karma, moreover, is of two kinds: that with certain fruition (*dhuvavipāka*) and that with uncertain fruition (*addhuvavipāka*). Among these, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya*), the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), the fourth path (*catutthamagga*), and so forth, are called "with certain fruition.
Furthermore, such karma exists both as that which has reached its moment of fruition (*khaṇappatta*) and as that which has not yet reached it. Of these, that which has reached its moment...
That which has arisen is called "arisen," and that which has not yet reached [the present] is called "unarisen. The fruition (*vipāka*) of these two types is likewise twofold:
that which has reached the moment and that which has not. Therein, that which has reached the moment is called "arisen";

that which has not yet reached it—whether it is to arise in the next moment of consciousness or after the passing of a hundred thousand eons—is called "that which will arise" by virtue of its certainty as a condition. This applies to Metteyya as well.
For a Bodhisatta, the path is called "unarisen" (anuppanna), while the fruit is called "arising" (uppādī).

In that regard, among the four planes, resultant states and kamma-born matter are called "occurrent-arisen" (vattamānuppannā); those destined to arise are called "arising" (uppādino), but they should not be called "unarisen.
Wholesome, unwholesome, and functional states, as well as kamma-born matter, may be either arisen or unarisen.
However, they should not be called "arising" (*uppādino*). Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), the unwholesome ones are exactly like the unwholesome consciousnesses;

the remaining ones are of two kinds [wholesome and indeterminate]. Furthermore, among these, the past and Nibbāna are not to be so designated. The rest is easily understood. This concludes the Triplet on the Arisen (*Uppannattika*).
Having reached their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or the moments of arising and so forth, and having passed beyond them, they have gone or arrived—thus they are "past" (*atīta*).
Because neither of those two has arrived, they are "not yet come" (*anāgata*). Because they have arisen in dependence upon this or that cause, they are "present" (*paccuppanna*);
these are all conditioned phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-dhamma*). Among conditioned phenomena, there is nothing that does not partake in the state of belonging to the three times;
all of them are of three kinds. However, *Nibbāna* here is not to be so classified. This is the triad of the past.
"Those whose object is past" means those for whom the object is past. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.

In that context, the sixfold base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional—are "past-objects" because they proceed by taking a past attainment as their object; [so too are] the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the mind-element.
The remaining eleven sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses and the rootless laughter-consciousness are of three kinds [regarding their objects];

the remaining sense-sphere functional, wholesome, and unwholesome consciousnesses, as well as the supramundane, fine-material-sphere, and fourth-jhāna wholesome and functional consciousnesses, are of three kinds and are also "not to be specified.
Among these, the classification of the occurrence of sense-sphere consciousnesses with respect to the six objects—past and so forth—is as follows:

This has already been explained above. Furthermore, among those [states], the fact that they are "not to be defined" (navattabbatā) applies to wholesome javanas dissociated from knowledge solely by way of having a concept as their object, and not by way of having Nibbāna as their object.

Even among those [wholesome states], the three-rooted javanas and adverting consciousnesses, as well as the path, fruition, and the fine-material and immaterial jhānas—which have Nibbāna as their object in the capacity of being preliminary (purecārika)—are also "not to be defined," both by way of being preliminary and by way of being reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa).

It should be understood as follows: regarding the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), first, in the case of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*), when one transforms the mind by means of the body and makes it dependent on the body, traveling with a visible body, it has the past as its object because it proceeds by taking the past foundational jhāna-consciousness as its basis;
when one resolves, "May forms be thus in the future," it has the future as its object.
Furthermore, when making the body dependent on the mind, at the time of traveling with an invisible body,
and at the time of creating present forms such as the appearance of a youth internally or palaces and gabled houses externally,

the object is present. Thus, it should be understood that the sixfold object of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*)— both internal and external— is threefold in terms of time (past, present, and future).
The object of the divine ear (*dibbasota*) is exclusively the sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*), whether internal—meaning that which has entered the womb—or external, and it must be present.
The object of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) is the past and future mind of others alone, occurring within seven days in the past and within seven days in the future.
However, beyond those seven days, one cannot know that other's mind.
He is not able [to know it]. For this is the domain of the knowledges regarding the past and the future, not of this [knowledge].
However, at the time of knowing a present consciousness, its object is present.
And this "present" is threefold: the present by moment (*khaṇapaccuppanna*), the present by continuity (*santatipaccuppanna*), and the present by duration (*addhāpaccuppanna*).

In this context, that which has reached the stages of arising, presence, and dissolution is called "momentary present" (*khaṇapaccuppanna*). However, the "continuous present" (*santatipaccuppanna*) is twofold, according to the division of material and immaterial phenomena.
Regarding the former: for one who has come from a place of sunlight and entered the womb, it lasts as long as the state of darkness does not disappear;
or for one dwelling inside the womb, it lasts as long as [the darkness remains] while looking toward a place of sunlight during the day until the eyes [are affected].

The state of oscillation that does not subside is called the continuity of form (*rūpa-santati*). Two or three thought-moments of impulsion (*javana*) are called the continuity of the immaterial (*arūpa-santati*).

Both of these should be understood as "present by way of continuity" (*santati-paccuppanna*). That which is delimited by a single existence is called "present by way of duration" (*addhā-paccuppanna*).
However, in this context of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), several moments of impulsion are called "present by way of duration."

In this context, the mind that is present at a single moment (khaṇapaccuppanna) does not become the object of the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), because it ceases simultaneously with the act of adverting (āvajjana).
Indeed, it is not logical for the acts of adverting and the impulsive moments (javana) to have different objects here.

However, the temporal present (addhāpaccuppanna)—which consists of a material continuity (rūpasantati) delimited by several rounds of impulsive moments—becomes its object. This applies to one who possesses supernormal power (iddhimā).

Indeed, when one who desires to know another’s mind adverts [to it], at the very moment of that adverting, [the adverting consciousness] ceases together with that present mind which has been made its object.
Then, taking that very ceased mind as its object, four or five impulsion moments (*javana*) arise;
the last of these is the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*), while the remaining ones are sense-sphere impulsions (*kāmāvacara-javana*). And of those...
Even when there is a single object, only the supernormal power consciousness (iddhicitta) knows another's mind, not the others. Just as in the cognitive process of the eye-door,
only the eye-consciousness sees the visible form and not the others— and among those [consciousnesses], only the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) has a strictly present object,
while the others have it only figuratively by way of the continuity of the time-periods— so too should this [supernormal power] be understood with respect to the past, future, and present.
The mind itself becomes the object, and that too belongs only to another, not to oneself.

However, in the case of the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), when recollecting names, clans, kasiṇas, designations, and so forth, as well as in the recollection of Nibbāna, the object is "indeterminate" (*navattabba*). When recollecting conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), it has only the past as its object.
For in that [knowledge], regarding past states—whether with taints (*sāsava*) or without taints (*anāsava*), internal or external—[the object is the past].
Furthermore, among all phenomena, there is nothing that is without an object; it is co-extensive with the omniscient knowledge of the Buddhas.
For the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*), the internal and external objects are merely past wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) alone.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), it is stated in the Commentaries that "the mind itself is the object, not the mental states associated with it. However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it says: "Wholesome aggregates..."

Since it is stated that “the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of penetration of minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma, and the knowledge of the future are conditions by way of object-condition,” it should be understood that for the knowledge of penetration of minds and the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma,
the four aggregates— whether associated with consciousness or associated with volition— are indeed the objects.
For the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), however, the object is exclusively the present sphere of visible forms (*vaṇṇāyatana*), whether internal or external.
For the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*), the object is likewise exclusively the future—sixfold, internal, and external;

this too, like the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), is similar to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) regarding the future. Thus, among the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), [there is no distinction] regarding the past, future, or present.
Regarding the six internal and external objects that are not to be classified [as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate], their occurrence should be understood according to what is applicable.

The remaining fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses—the wholesome, resultant, and functional types pertaining to the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness—along with the eight supramundane consciousnesses and material phenomena and Nibbāna, are not to be classified. Among the mental concomitants, however, the illimitables...
[They] are not to be spoken of. The rest is easily understood. This is the triad of objects past.
“Internal” (*ajjhatta*) means that which proceeds by taking the self as its reference, as if with the intention: “While proceeding thus, we shall fall into the apprehension ‘this is the self’.
Furthermore, this word *ajjhatta* [is used] in the sense of an internal object (*gocarajjhatta*) and in the sense of one's own [self] (*niyakajjhatta*).

The term *ajjhatta* is seen in four senses: internal-internal (*ajjhattajjhatta*), objective-internal (*visayajjhatta*), one’s own (*niyakajjhatta*), and internal (*ajjhattajjhatta*). In such passages as “Delighting in the internal, composed,” it is seen in the sense of the objective-internal (*gocarajjhatta*). In such passages as “Or he dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena internally,” it is seen in the sense of one’s own (*niyakajjhatta*).
In such passages as “The six internal bases,” it is seen in the sense of internal-internal (*ajjhattajjhatta*). [And] in “Internal emptiness... [it is seen in the sense of internal].
In such passages as “having attained, he dwells,” the meaning is “in the sphere of one’s own [experience]” or “in the place of mastery.
For the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is indeed called the place of mastery for Buddhas. However, here this term refers to what belongs to oneself;

therefore, it should be understood that the individual material and immaterial phenomena occurring within one’s own continuum are “internal” (*ajjhatta*) here. Those existing outside of that are external.
Designations of form and non-form that are bound to the sense faculties or not bound to the sense faculties are called "external";
the third category is stated by way of both of these.
Therein, all mind and mental factors, as well as form bound to the sense faculties, are threefold; [and there is] form not bound to the sense faculties.

And the designations of Nibbāna are indeed external. For in this triad, even those designations not found in the Triad of the Wholesome (Kusalattika) are found here, with the exception of that which has the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) as its object; that alone is here to be called "indeterminate" (navattabba).

For it was by the Blessed One himself, in the Subsequent Triad (Anantarattika), stated that "minds belonging to the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and so forth, which have as their objects the designations of the kasiṇas and so on, have external objects."
And it is said, “the base of nothingness is not to be so stated”; this is the unpredicated triad (*nippadesattika*). The internal triad (*ajjhattattika*):
this triad is stated by way of those [consciousnesses] that occur having made as their object the aforementioned internal and other [bases].

Therein, the sixfold consciousnesses of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have only internal objects; as do the three [consciousnesses] of the base of infinite space.

The fine-material-sphere and supramundane consciousnesses have exclusively external objects. With the exception of determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), the great rootless resultants (*ahetuka-mahāvipāka*) belong to all three types [of object].

Furthermore, the remaining adverting and javanas—excluding those with the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) as their object—and the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) may also belong to all three types.
This occurs in the occurrence of the states of adverting, preparation, and reviewing for that which has the base of nothingness as its object.

It may be "inexpressible" (navattabba). Their status as having internal and other types of objects should be understood according to the method explained previously in the "Treatise on the Immediate" (Anantara-ttika) and below;
however, the three spheres of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and both form (rūpa) and Nibbāna are strictly inexpressible.

Among the mental concomitants (cetasika), the illimitables (appamaññā) and the abstinences (virati) have only external objects, while the remainder are of all three kinds and are also inexpressible. The rest is easily understood.
The triad of internal objects.
"With demonstration" (*sanidassana*) means together with demonstration, which is defined as the state of being visible;

"with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) means together with resistance, which is defined as the state of being impinging; those that are both with demonstration and with resistance are thus "with-demonstration-and-with-resistance" (*sanidassanasappaṭigha*).
It is simply the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). However, the plural designation is used because it includes various distinctions such as blue and so forth.

They are "non-demonstrable" (*anidassana*) because they lack the quality of being demonstrable, which is defined as the state of being visible. And since they are, according to the method already stated, "impinging" (*sappaṭigha*), they are called "non-demonstrable and impinging.
The remaining [categories] are gross forms. The third term is stated by way of the negation of both [qualities], referring to subtle forms, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna.
It should be understood that these are called "non-demonstrable and non-reactive," and this is the triad without limitation.
The triad with demonstration is finished. The commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the triplets is completed.
[Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the pairs of the Abhidhamma.
Regarding the *Dukamātikā*, however, we shall provide the commentary on the meaning of the terms below. First, concerning the "Cluster of Causes" (*Hetugocchaka*):

regarding the phrase "the states that are causes," there are four kinds of causes—namely, the cause as cause (*hetu-hetu*), the causal condition (*paccaya-hetu*), the supreme cause (*uttama-hetu*), and the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*).

Among these, the six states beginning with non-greed (*alobha*) are called "causes as causes"; the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are the "causal conditions" for derived matter (*upādārūpa*) and so forth.

In the arising of fruition, wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as desirable and undesirable objects, are called "pre-eminent causes" (uttamahetu). Ignorance and the rest are called "common causes" (sādhāraṇahetu) for formations and so forth.
However, in this context, "cause-cause" (hetuhetu) is intended. "Causes as phenomena" (hetudhammā) means phenomena designated as causes in the sense of being roots;
"hetudhammā" is also a reading, which has the same meaning. "Not causes" (na hetū) is a statement negating those very things.

In this context, the three wholesome and indeterminate factors—non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*)—and the three unwholesome factors—greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*)—these six phenomena are called "roots" (*hetu*).
With the exception of these, all remaining mental factors (*cetasika*), all states of consciousness (*citta*), and material form (*rūpa*) and Nibbāna are phenomena that are not roots.
This should be understood as the "incomplete dyad. This is the first dyad: the Dyad of Roots.
They are "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*) because they proceed together with a root-cause through association. Likewise, those in which no root-causes exist are "without root-cause" (*ahetuka*).

Among these, seventy-one types of consciousness—excluding the mind-moments without root-cause—are called "with root-cause. Of these, the two rooted in delusion have root-causes through delusion alone;
the eight rooted in greed have root-causes through both greed and delusion; and the two rooted in hatred have root-causes through both hatred and delusion.

The twelve wholesome and indeterminate states dissociated from knowledge are associated with the roots of non-greed and non-hatred; the remaining forty-seven are associated with all three roots, non-greed and the rest.

However, among those rooted in delusion, the following phenomena are rootless: delusion itself, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the mind-element, the three types of investigation, the determining consciousness, the eighteen types of smiling consciousness, and material phenomena and Nibbāna.

Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dosa*), as well as doubt (*vicikicchā*), have delusion (*moha*) alone as their root cause. Wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) and conceit (*māna*) have both greed and delusion as their causes.
Envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and worry (*kukkucca*) have hatred and delusion as their causes. Delusion, moreover, may be associated with greed or with hatred;

thus, among the roots of delusion, it may be either with root-cause or without root-cause. Sloth (*thina*) and torpor (*middha*) may be associated with greed and delusion, or they may be associated with hatred and delusion.
The three [unwholesome roots] are also accompanied by causes; likewise, shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*) are associated with delusion alone.

Non-delusion (*amoha*), however, is associated with only two: greedlessness (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*). Greedlessness may be associated with non-hatred and non-delusion, or with non-hatred alone—thus with two. Non-hatred may be associated with greedlessness and non-delusion, or with greedlessness alone—thus with two.
As for the remaining twenty-two wholesome and indeterminate factors, they may be associated with all three, or with any two.
Those [factors] accompanied by roots are accompanied by roots; desire (chanda), however, may be accompanied by roots through three [roots] as appropriate.

Joy (pīti) may be either accompanied by roots or rootless when excluding the two roots of hatred (dosa). The remaining eleven types are of three kinds: they may be accompanied by roots or rootless through six roots.

Furthermore, among these, feeling (vedanā) that has become mental grief (domanassa) is accompanied by only two roots; mental joy (somanassa) and equanimity (upekkhā) may be accompanied by five roots, excluding hatred, as appropriate.
Those that are rootless (*ahetuka*) are likewise rootless in their states of pleasure and pain; this is "suffering without exception. (The second pair.

"Associated with roots" (*hetusampayutta*) means associated by way of roots through the condition of simultaneous arising and so forth. "Dissociated from roots" (*hetuvippayutta*) means dissociated from roots. This dyad of "associated with roots" is in meaning not different from the dyad of "with roots" (*sahetuka*) mentioned immediately prior. (The dyad of "with roots.")

For indeed, this was stated by the Blessed One either through his skill in teaching or according to the disposition of those persons capable of understanding it, in the form of a pair of factors associated with a cause.
Thus, the reason for the statement of subsequent pairs of factors with identical meanings should be understood. This is the third.
As for the fourth and following pairs, however, they are two pairs formed by joining [the first factor] with the first term of the first, second, and third pairs.
In the first dyad, by joining the last member with the second dyad, one dyad is presented; thus, three dyads have been taught.
Therefore, the meaning of their terms is exactly as previously stated.
And therein, just as in the case of: "states that are both roots and accompanied by roots, and states that are accompanied by roots but are not roots."
This dyad is possible; likewise, the following is also possible: “states that are both causes and rootless, and states that are rootless but not causes.
According to this method, one [dyad] is also obtained through application with the dyad of “associated with a cause.
And just as this is obtained—namely, “states that are neither causes nor accompanied by a cause”—so too is the following obtained: “causes...”
Furthermore, "phenomena are both with-cause and without-cause"—this too [is a dyad].

And just as there are two dyads in the "with-cause" dyad, so too in the "associated-with-cause" dyad, two dyads are obtained: namely, "phenomena that are not causes are both associated with causes and dissociated from causes," and "phenomena that are causes are both associated with causes and dissociated from causes."
It is possible to apply another five dyads to the "Cluster of Causes" (*hetugocchaka*).
However, since these can be understood simply by following what was stated by the Blessed One, it should be known that they are included within the six [dyads] alone.

Among those, first, when two or three causes arise together in a single consciousness, those causes are called both "causes" and "with-cause" (*sahetuka*) because of their mutual dependence. In the case of consciousnesses with cause...
However, with the exception of the root (hetu), all remaining mental states and mental factors (cittacetasika-dhammā) are both "with root" (sahetuka) and yet are not themselves roots (na hetū).

In this dyad, all rootless states (ahetuka-dhammā) are not to be mentioned. Among the mental factors, those that are unwholesome (akusala), wholesome (kusala), and indeterminate (abyākata)—excluding the root—and desire (chanda), are both "with root" and not roots; the remaining three classes [of mental factors] are likewise not to be so described, as is delusion (moha).
But there are those which are both root-cause and possessed of a root-cause, and those which are not so classifiable. This is the fourth.
The "immediate" dyad (*anantara-duka*) is in every respect similar to this dyad. This is the fifth.

Among minds possessed of a root-cause, the mental states and mental factors excluding the root-cause itself are called "not root-causes but possessed of a root-cause"; these include minds without a root-cause, material phenomena, and Nibbāna.
Those which are not causes are called "causeless" (*ahetuka*). However, in this dyad, the six causes are not to be mentioned. The rest is easily understood. [End of] the sixth.
The Group on Causes (*Hetugocchaka*) is finished.
In the seven minor intermediate dyads, those together with the condition that produces them are "with conditions" (*sappaccaya*); these are mind, mental factors, and matter.

Because there is no condition for their arising or for their persistence, and because they do not exist as something that comes into being after having been non-existent, they are "without conditions" (*appaccayā*);
this refers to Nibbāna alone. However, in this teaching, the plural number is used by way of falling within the scope of the ultimate truth (*paramatā*).

The same applies to the categories beginning with "with visibility" (*sanidassana*). This and the six subsequent dyads without remainder (*nippadesa-duka*) should be understood in this way. After that—
Furthermore, wherever we shall not say "these are not to be mentioned," that should be understood as being without exception (*nippadesa*).

This is the dyad of the conditioned-with-conditions (*sappaccaya-duka*). That which is produced by coming together with conditions is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*). That which is not conditioned is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*). And this is in every respect exactly like the dyad of the conditioned-with-conditions. The dyad of both the conditioned-with-conditions and the unconditioned is in every respect identical.

This is the dyad of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-duka*). The sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is called "with visibility" (*sanidassana*). The remaining forms, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna are called "without visibility" (*anidassana*). This is the dyad of visibility (*sanidassana-duka*).

The twelve kinds of material form that are objects of serene confidence are called "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*). The remaining material forms, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna are called "without resistance" (*appaṭigha*).

This is the dyad of "with resistance. They are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*) because they have material form (*rūpa*) as their inseparable property; or, "form" (*rūpa*) has the characteristic of being affected (*ruppana*), and they possess that, thus they are "possessing form"—namely, the primary elements and derived material form. Those that do not possess form are "formless" (*arūpin*): consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna. This is the dyad of "possessing form.

The world (*loka*) is called the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of breaking up and falling away. That which is connected to the world by virtue of being included within it is [called "mundane"].

The mundane consists of the five aggregates of clinging. Because they have crossed over from that world by way of being unincluded therein, the supramundane consists of the noble paths, fruits, and Nibbāna.
Furthermore, whatever is to be said regarding the mental factors herein should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on the Asekhās.
This concludes the dyad of the mundane.
"Perceivable by some" means to be cognized by one or another among the visual consciousnesses and so forth—either by visual consciousness or by auditory consciousness and so on.
"Not perceivable by any" means not to be cognized by that same visual consciousness or by auditory consciousness and so on by any [consciousness].
For it is when there is thus a difference in meaning between the two terms that they constitute a dyad.
In the *Padabhājanīya* as well, one should understand that this is not to be taken as a single dyad consisting merely of the words,
“Those phenomena cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear,” but rather as a single dyad consisting of:
“Those phenomena cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear, or else those phenomena cognizable by the ear are not cognizable by the eye.”

Furthermore, the meaning here is that its visible form is cognizable by the eye, whereas its sound is not cognizable by the eye. In this same way, the analysis of the dyads should be understood for the remaining [bases] as well.
In that context, the sense-sphere of visible form is said to be "cognizable" either by the eye or by eye-consciousness.
All other material and immaterial phenomena are not cognizable by that very eye or by eye-consciousness, nor by anything else.
In the same way, the analysis for the four applications rooted in ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, the five sense objects beginning with visible form are cognizable by one or another of the three types of mind-element (*manodhātu*). All remaining material and immaterial phenomena are not cognizable by any of those three types of mind-element.
Although, in general, there is nothing that cannot be cognized by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*), [the three mind-elements do not cognize all things].
Because they are absent from the text, the dyad based on being cognizable by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) was not mentioned; nevertheless, it must indeed be stated specifically.
For thus, all sixfold sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*) are cognizable by some mind-consciousness, such as the sense-sphere resultant consciousness and so forth;

whereas the designations (*paññatti*) of the fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane realms are not cognizable by that [sense-sphere mind-consciousness] at all. The same applies to the designations of the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms.

Some things, such as unwholesome states, are cognizable by something; supramundane states are not cognizable by that same something. Likewise, Nibbāna is cognizable by something supramundane, while the remaining mundane and supramundane states are not cognizable by that same something.

Following this method, phenomena—classified according to the distinctions of the fine-material and immaterial spheres and so forth—should be applied appropriately to those that are cognizable or incognizable by mental consciousness. Thus, all phenomena [are to be understood].

[Some things] are cognizable by some, while [others] are called not cognizable by some. And it should be understood that within this dyad, designations (*paññatti*) are also found. This concludes the dyad of "cognizable by some.
The Minor Intermediate Dyads are finished.

In the *Āsavagocchaka*, they are called "taints" (*āsavā*) because they flow all around (*āsamantato savanti*). It is said that they flow from the eye... [and so on] ...up to the mind; that is, they proceed.

Alternatively, they are taints because they flow as far as the stage of the lineage-follower (*gotrabhū*) in terms of phenomena (*dhamma*), and as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) in terms of location (*okāsa*).
The meaning is that they proceed having encompassed these phenomena and this location. For this prefix *ā-* has the sense of "encompassing."

They are called *āsava* (taints) also in the sense of being long-fermented, like fermented liquor and the like. And if they are *āsava* in the sense of being long-fermented, then only these [four] deserve to be so called.
Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because, being beginningless, they flow (*savanti*) or pour forth (*pasavanti*) the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Other than those, there are no such things as *āsava*.
In this context, the four taints (āsava) are: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava).
Among these, all greed whatsoever that arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed is called the taint of sensual desire.

However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it is stated: "The lust pertaining to the five strands of sensual pleasure is the taint of sensual desire," and "Lust conjoined with views is not the taint of sensual desire."

It is said: "There is such a thing as lust for views," and, "The desire and lust that arises for Brahmā’s palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, and ornaments is not the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), because lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure has been abandoned right here.
However, in the Canon it is stated: "The taint of sensual desire arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed," and, "Dependent upon the taint of sensual desire..."

Because it is stated, “the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava),” with the exception of the taint of existence (bhavāsava), all remaining greed is understood as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava).
This is because the lust associated with views and the lust for the robes, ornaments, and so forth of the Brahmās do not possess the nature of the taint of existence.
Indeed, only the lust dissociated from views becomes the taint of existence when it proceeds by way of aspiration for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms.

This is because of such statements as, "In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) underlies," and because there is no greed (lobha) that is separate from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence (bhavāsava).
If there were such [separate greed], it would have been stated in the Canon: "Greed may be a taint (āsava), or it may not be a taint.

Likewise, regarding the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), which is associated with greed dissociated from views, it would have been stated: "It may be associated with a taint, or it may be dissociated from a taint."

And it may be said [as follows]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "sensual desire for sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu kāmacchando*) which appears in the *Padabhājanīya* under the exposition of the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the *Aṭṭhasālinī* explains its meaning as "sensual desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

However, one can also apply the meaning of that same phrase as "defilement-sensual-desire (*kilesakāma*) toward object-sensual-pleasures (*vatthukāma*)," because the phenomenon belonging to the three planes [of existence]...
Because of the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), and because of the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) in all those cases.

For this was said by the General of the Dhamma in the *Mahāniddesa*: “What are the objects of sensual desire? Pleasing forms... [and so on] ...all states belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), all states belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and all states belonging to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)...

these are called the objects of sensual desire. “What are the defilements of sensual desire? Desire is sensual desire, lust is sensual desire... [and so on] ...whatever desire for sense-pleasures, lust for sense-pleasures, delight in sense-pleasures...”

“Craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, clinging to sensual pleasures, the flood of sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures, the clinging to sensual pleasures,
and the hindrance of sensual desire… [and so on]… these are called the defilement of sensual pleasure.

Furthermore, here by the General of the Dhamma, through the statement “the flood of sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures,” and so forth, he declares that the defilement of sensual pleasure constitutes the flood of sensual pleasures and the rest.

The status of lust as a *āsava* (taint) and so forth is admitted for lust that has as its object sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) in general, not only for lust directed toward the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no distinction between the floods (*ogha*) and the taints (*āsava*).

For in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanīya*) on the group of clingings (*upādāna*), the phrase "lust for sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu kāmacchando*) is explained with this very meaning: "lust for sensual objects" (*vatthukāmesu kāmacchando*). From that...
In other groups of causes, fetters, and defilements, the complete and total eradication of greed alone is stated, not that of the other groups.

And when examining those [other groups] in accordance with the text, they appear to be merely the "defilement-desire" (kilesa-kāma) aspect of greed. The complete eradication of greed is evident therein.
This should be understood after careful investigation.

Furthermore, the greed that arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views, which functions as the state of desire-and-lust (*chandarāga*) toward existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, and as the state of attachment and craving for sense-pleasures, is called the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*). In the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, however, it is stated: "The taint of existence is lust co-arising with the eternalist view.
But in the Canon, it is said: "The taint of existence [arises] in the four types of consciousness associated with greed and dissociated from views."
Because they are restricted, they cannot be grasped [as a single category]; rather, their underlying intention (*adhippāya*) must be investigated.
All sixty-two varieties of views are called the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). All delusion (*moha*) consisting of eight bases is called the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).

Among these, the taint of views is abandoned by the first path; it is appropriate to say that the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) is abandoned by all four paths, yet [the text] says "by the third."
It has been said. The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) are abandoned by the fourth [path].
Because these taints of sensuality (*kāmāsava*) and existence have the nature of greed (*lobha*), three factors by way of their intrinsic nature become four taints by way of classification.
With the exception of these, all other mundane and supramundane phenomena are not called "taints. This is the first dyad on the taints (*āsava*).
"Those accompanied by taints" (*sāsava*) are all mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhamma*), because they arise together with the taints (*āsava*) taking themselves as their object.

"Those free from taints" (*anāsava*) are exclusively the nine supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*), because when they thus arise, there are no taints for them. As for the mental factors (*cetasika*) herein, they are exactly as described in the mundane dyad.
This is the second dyad, on those accompanied by taints.
The meaning of the four dyads beginning with the third is exactly as previously stated.
The rest here should be understood according to the method explained for the "Root" (hetu) cluster. However, this is the distinction:
just as there, in the first dyad, the concluding dyad—"States that are not roots are both with root and without root"—was stated by joining its second term with the second dyad, so too here...

It was not stated that "states with taints (āsava) are neither with-taints nor without-taints. And it should be understood that this [definition] is included here according to the method explained in various other places.
Just as it is here, so too should it be understood accordingly in the groups of fetters (saññojana) and so forth.

In that regard, the twelve unwholesome (akusala) types of consciousness are called "associated with taints" (āsava-sampayutta). Among the consciousnesses rooted in hatred and delusion, it is delusion (moha) [that constitutes the taint].

Wholesome states, indeterminate states, mental factors, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are called "dissociated from the taints" (*āsava-vippayutta*). Among the mental concomitants (*cetasika*), with the exception of delusion (*moha*), the remaining unwholesome states are exclusively associated with the taints;
however, delusion is of three types and thus belongs to both categories [associated and dissociated]. All others are exclusively dissociated from the taints. This is the third [section].
The four taints are both taints and "with-taint" (*sāsava*); the remaining mundane phenomena are "with-taint" but are not themselves taints.
Regarding "outflows" (āsava): here, however, those that are supramundane (lokuttara) should not be mentioned.

Among the mental factors (cetasika), when "outflows" are spoken of, the remaining unwholesome states (akusala) and both compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) are both associated with outflows (sāsava) and yet are not themselves outflows; the rest are neither. This is the fourth [point].
Furthermore, among those rooted in greed (lobhamūla), there are two or three—namely, greed and delusion (lobha-moha), and the delusion of greed-views (lobha-diṭṭhi-moha)—which arise together as one.

These are both taints (*āsava*) and associated with taints. The twelve unwholesome consciousnesses (*akusalacitta*), excluding the taints themselves, as well as the mental factors associated with them, are associated with taints but are not taints.
However, in this context, those dissociated from taints are not to be mentioned.
Among the mental concomitants (*cetasika*), the unwholesome ones—excluding the taints—are exclusively associated with taints but are not taints; delusion (*moha*), however, may be [either].

That which is both an *āsava* and associated with an *āsava* may be so stated; it may also be said that there are things of three types that are associated with an *āsava* but are not themselves *āsavas*, and these may also be so stated;
those that are wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*) cannot be so stated at all. The rest is easy to understand. This is the fifth [section].

Excluding the supramundane (*lokuttara*), those dissociated from *āsavas* are called "with *āsava*" (*sāsava*). The supramundane, being dissociated from *āsavas*, are called "without *āsava*" (*anāsava*).

In this context, however, those associated with the taints (*āsava*) are simply not to be mentioned. Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*) are dissociated from the taints and are indeed subject to them (*sāsava*);
delusion (*moha*) is both [dissociated and subject to the taints] and is not to be mentioned; the remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors are of both kinds;
the three types [of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate] are neither to be mentioned; and unwholesome factors excluding delusion are simply not to be mentioned. This is the sixth [section].
The Chapter on the Taints (Āsavagocchaka) is finished.

In the Chapter on the Fetters (Saṃyojanagocchaka), those which are found in a person are called "fetters" (saṃyojanā) because they fetter and bind that person to the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). Those other than these are not fetters.

Therein, the fetters are: the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana), the fetter of lust for existence (bhavarāga), the fetter of aversion (paṭigha), the fetter of conceit (māna), the fetter of views (diṭṭhi), the fetter of doubt (vicikicchā), the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa), the fetter of envy (issā), the fetter of avarice (macchariya), and the fetter of ignorance (avijjā).
These ten states are called fetters (*saṃyojana*). Among them, the fetters of sensual desire, existence, views, and ignorance are exactly as described in the section on the taints (*āsava*).
[The remaining ones are: the nine [types of resentment] expressed as: "He has done me harm, he is doing me harm, he will do me harm;
he has done harm to one dear to me, he is doing harm, he will do harm; he has done good to one not dear to me, he is doing good, he will do good."
All hatred that arises toward beings by way of various modes, and toward formations by way of resentment toward what is unattainable, is called the fetter of aversion (*paṭigha-saṃyojana*).
All pride that proceeds by way of the three modes—“I am superior,” “I am equal,” or “I am inferior”—is called the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*).
In this context, for a person who actually is superior, [the thought] “I am superior,” “I am equal,” or “I am inferior”...

And conceit arises in three ways regarding those who are equal and inferior as well. Therein, the conceit of one who is superior regarding one who is superior is conceit that is according to reality (*yāthāva-māna*).

Likewise, the conceit of one who is equal regarding one who is equal, and the conceit of one who is inferior regarding one who is inferior [are also conceits according to reality]. It should be understood that for all three [types of persons], the other two types of conceit each constitute conceit that is not according to reality (*ayāthāva-māna*).

All forms of doubt (*vicikicchā*) that arise by way of wavering with respect to the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, as well as with respect to the past, the future, both, and dependently arisen phenomena, are called the fetter of doubt (*vicikicchā-saṃyojana*).

The fetter of attachment to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa-saṃyojana*) is precisely that view which functions in the mode of grasping [the idea] that purity comes through such things as the cow-vow (*govata*) and the five precepts (*gosīla*).
All remaining views should be understood as the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*).
Envy (*issā*) is the fetter of envy (*issā-saṃyojana*), which functions in the mode of intolerance toward the gains, honors, respect, esteem, salutations, and offerings of others.
It is called *macchariya*. The fivefold stinginess—stinginess regarding dwelling, family, gain, reputation, and the Dhamma—is what is known as the fetter of stinginess (*macchariya-saṃyojana*).

For even while living in the entire monastery, or in a specific cell, courtyard, and so forth, one does not wish for another virtuous and well-behaved bhikkhu to come there; nor, once he has arrived, does one desire his departure.

To desire this is what is called "avarice regarding one's dwelling" (āvāsamacchariya). However, if one does not desire the residence there of those who cause quarrels and the like, it is not considered avarice regarding one's dwelling.
Furthermore, if one does not desire another virtuous person to approach one's own family of supporters or one's own family of relatives, [it is also a form of avarice].
There is stinginess regarding one's family, but there is no such thing for a wicked person who does not desire [to give]. For he acts in order to destroy the confidence [others have] in them.
There is stinginess regarding gains for one who, seeing virtuous people receiving the four requisites at a place where they themselves would receive, thinks, "May they not receive them.
But as for one who squanders what has been given in faith—even when it is going to rot—for another...

There is no such thing as stinginess (*macchariya*) for one who does not give, yet upon seeing another receive it, thinks: "If someone else of virtuous conduct were to receive this, it would come to be of use.
As for "complexion" (*vaṇṇa*), it refers both to the complexion of the body and the complexion of one's virtues. In that regard, "possessed of beauty and pleasing" refers to another’s...

When one’s own physical appearance or the praise of one’s virtues— such as being "virtuous" or "possessing the ascetic practices"— is spoken of in a context where one's own reputation is being discussed,
there arises what is called the twofold stinginess regarding praise (*vaṇṇamacchariya*) for one who cannot bear it.
However, this does not apply to one who, seeing someone else praised for qualities that are actually unwholesome or corrupted, cannot bear it because they wish to censure that evil.
"Dhamma" here refers specifically to the scripture (pariyatti), not to the penetration (paṭivedha) of the Noble Ones, because there is no stinginess regarding that [penetration].
However, for one who does not wish to speak the scripture or the secret texts to others, there is what is called "stinginess regarding the Dhamma.

On the other hand, for one who is greedy for the support of the Dhamma, and who wanders about sometimes as a śramaṇa and sometimes as a Nigaṇṭha or other such ascetics, there is the tradition inherited through lineage.
There is no stinginess with the Dhamma in one who does not withhold it out of concern that,

"If I give this, they will break through the subtle and delicate distinction between phenomena and thereby disrupt our system," nor in one who does not withhold it from a person who is naturally crafty and deceitful out of favor for that individual,
thinking, "Having learned this subtle and delicate Dhamma, he will misrepresent it and go to ruin."
Just as it is for monks, so too should the fivefold stinginess appropriate to householders be understood.
In brief, however, stinginess should be understood as having the characteristic of concealing one’s own excellence, whether among householders or those who have gone forth.
And among these fetters, views, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, envy, and stinginess are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.
It should be stated that "hostility is abandoned by the path of non-returning, and sensual lust by all four paths," yet it is said [in the text] that it is "by the third.

Pride, lust for existence, and ignorance are abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Furthermore, therein, pride regarding what is not as it truly is should be understood as being abandoned by the first path;
this is because these—sensual lust and lust for existence—have the nature of greed, whereas the adherence to views and the adherence to rules and observances [have the nature of delusion].
Because they share the nature of wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), these eight states by their very nature become known as the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Excluding these ten, all remaining mundane and supramundane states are not called fetters. The rest is similar to the pair on taints (*āsava*). This is the first dyad, the fetters.
They are "fetterable" (*saṃyojaniya*) because they are beneficial to the fetters through the increase of the fetters once they have come to serve as their objects.

They are exclusively with-taints (*sāsava*). The same applies here to the phrase "conducive to the hindrances" (*nīvaraṇiya*). They are not conducive to the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—that is, they are not conducive to the fetters and are without-taints (*anāsava*).
The remainder is exactly like the section on the dhammas with-taints. This is the second [set].
The third and subsequent sets are also exactly like the third and subsequent sets in the *Āsava-vagga*; we shall explain only the specific distinction here. In that regard:

Indeed, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are called associated with the fetters (*saṃyojana-sampayutta*); restlessness-accompanied delusion, as well as the remaining consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna, are called dissociated from the fetters (*saṃyojana-vippayutta*). The rest is the same. Third.

The ten fetters are both fetters and objects of the fetters (*saṃyojaniya*). The remaining mundane phenomena are objects of the fetters but are not themselves fetters. The rest is easily understood. Fourth.

Furthermore, among the eleven unwholesome consciousnesses that are free from restlessness, when two, three, or [more] arise together— namely, doubt-delusion, hatred-delusion, hatred-ignorance-delusion, hatred-avarice-delusion, greed-pride-delusion, and greed-view-delusion—
they are called both fetters and associated with fetters. The twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding those [associated with] fetters, are associated with the state of being devoid of fetters.
And they are associated with the fetters, yet are not themselves called fetters. The remainder here—the second dyad—is exactly like the fifth and sixth dyads in the group on the taints (*āsava*).
The only difference is that the word "taint" (*āsava*) is replaced by the word "fetter" (*saṃyojana*). These are the fifth and sixth dyads.
The group on the fetters (*saṃyojanagocchaka*) is finished.

In the *Ganthagocchaka* (Cluster on the Fetter), those things which are found in a person fetter and bind them to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of death and rebirth-linking are called "fetters" (*ganthā*). Those other than these are not fetters.

Therein, covetousness as a body-fetter (*abhijjhākāyagantho*), ill will, adherence to rules and observances, and the dogmatic insistence that "this alone is the truth"—these four states are called fetters.
Among them, it is covetousness itself that fetters the mental body (*nāmakāya*) in the manner already described.
The bodily tie of covetousness. The same applies to the remaining ties as well. Having rejected even the words of the Omniscient One, one adheres in this manner:

"The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Because of such adherence, every view—even one free from the clinging to rules and observances—is called "adherence to the conviction that 'this is the truth'. The rest have already been explained.
And among these, the last two ties— [the tie of adherence to rules and observances and the tie of adherence to the conviction that 'this is the truth']— [are to be abandoned by the path of vision].
They are abandoned by the first path; ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is abandoned by the third, and covetousness (*abhijjhā*) by all four.
These three states, by their very nature, constitute the four fetters (*gantha*). With the exception of these, all other states are not called fetters.
This is the first dyad on fetters.

They are called "to be bound" (*ganthaniyā*) because they are to be bound by the fetters (*gantha*) by way of being their object. Those that are not to be bound are "not-to-be-bound" (*aganthaniyā*). The rest is exactly like the "tainted" (*sāsava*) dyad. This is the second [dyad].
The ten unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding those rooted in delusion; among the consciousnesses dissociated from views, greed;
and among those rooted in hatred, hatred—excluding these, together with their associated states, are called "associated with the fetters. As previously stated, greed and hatred [are included].
Wholesome and indeterminate states of consciousness, as well as material form and Nibbāna, are called dissociated from the ties (*gantha*).
Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, wrong view, conceit, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, and torpor are associated with the ties alone.
Hatred and doubt, as well as wholesome and indeterminate states, are dissociated from the ties alone; the remaining factors belong to both categories. This is the third [section].
The four ties (ganthas) are both ties and objects of tying. The remaining worldly states are objects of tying but are not themselves ties.
Likewise, among the mental factors (cetasikas), those that are unwholesome—excluding the ties—and the illimitables (appamaññās) are objects of tying but are not themselves ties;
the remaining mental factors, however, are neither. Furthermore, supramundane (lokuttara) states are not to be so described here. This is the fourth [section].
Views are both fetters (*gantha*) and associated with fetters (*ganthasampayutta*). Greed is likewise [associated with fetters], yet it should not be called a fetter;

among those things associated with fetters, excluding the fetters themselves, the remainder are associated with fetters but are not fetters. However, in this context, those dissociated from fetters (*ganthavippayutta*) are not to be mentioned.
Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, conceit, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, and torpor are associated with fetters.
And likewise, the fetters themselves, as well as delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and restlessness—these three classes—may be [fetters] and not fetters;
similarly, they may be so-called "not to be spoken of" (navattabbā); the remainder are not to be so spoken of. The rest is easily understood. This is the fifth [section].
Those dissociated from the fetters, excluding the supramundane (lokuttara), are called "subject to fettering" (ganthaniya). However, those that are supramundane and dissociated from the fetters...

"Non-fetterable" (aganthaniya) means: here, those associated with the fetters (gantha-sampayutta) are not to be so called. Among the mental factors (cetasika), however, hatred (dosa), doubt (vicikicchā), compassion (karuṇā), and appreciative joy (muditā) are dissociated from the fetters and are thus fetterable;

delusion (moha), shamelessness (ahirika), lack of moral dread (anottappa), restlessness (uddhacca), and greed (lobha) are likewise not to be so called; the remaining wholesome (kusala) and indeterminate (abyākata) factors are both [fetterable and non-fetterable]; but those of three types [the unwholesome and the indeterminate] are neither to be called one way nor the other.
And the remaining unwholesome [factors] are also not to be so described. This is the sixth [section].
The cluster on the ties (*gantha*) is finished.
The clusters on the floods (*ogha*) and the yokes (*yoga*) are in every respect similar to the cluster on the taints (*āsava*); here, there is only a difference in the wording and the names.
This is the distinction. In this context, those which are found in someone "flood" (oghā) and cause them to sink into the round of existence;

thus they are called floods. Because they must be transcended by making them their object, they are "favourable to the floods" (oghaniyā). The same applies to the term "favourable to the bonds" (yoganiyā).
They are called "bonds" (yogā) because they yoke one to the round of existence. The rest is the same as before.
The groups on the floods, the yokes, and the hindrances are finished.
Regarding the group on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): they are called "hindrances" because they hinder and envelop the mind.
Therein, [the five are] the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
"Obscured by ignorance": these are called the six hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Among them, *thina* (sloth) is the state of density of the mind due to its lack of expansion, like a lump of ghee;
the meaning is "stiffness. *Middha* (torpor) means "it stupefies" (*medhati*); it is the state of unworkability, the meaning being that it causes drowsiness.
And this [hindrance] exists for both trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) prior to sleep, as well as subsequently, as the cause of nodding off.

It arises, but not at the time of falling asleep. For even in those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), sleep occurs through the process of the unperturbed life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to the weakness of the physical body made of kamma; however, that is not caused by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) in their case, but only in others.

Some, however, say that matter itself is "torpor" (*middha*); that is not correct, because [in the formula] "the hindrance of sloth and torpor" [is mentioned alongside] "the hindrance of ignorance" (*avijjānīvaraṇa*).
Because it is stated that it is "both a hindrance and associated with a hindrance," it is indeed immaterial (*arūpa*), due to its association with immaterial phenomena.
Furthermore, it is unwholesome (*akusala*) because of statements regarding its abandonment, such as "due to the abandoning of the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
For only unwholesome states are to be abandoned; therefore, this [hindrance] arises even in the formless realm (*ārūpa*). "Dependent on a state that is a hindrance, a state that is a hindrance..."

In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the statement, "It arises, not by way of the prenascence condition," all of this should be expanded in detail: "In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there are the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and ignorance.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*), the phrase "sleep and drowsiness" is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the result. This refers to "sloth and torpor."
Two [factors] are mentioned as one hindrance in the section on the hindrances; likewise, this pair consisting of restlessness and worry.
Therein, "worry" (*kukkucca*) is the remorse that arises in such ways as, "Alas, I have not done what is good;

I have done what is evil," and so forth. For this very reason, it is stated in its word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*): "It is mental remorse, a gnawing of the mind. "Perceiving the unallowable as allowable," and so forth.
However, it is for the purpose of showing that remorse (*kukkucca*) is the root.

For when a transgression has been committed while perceiving it as such, remorse subsequently arises—as in the case of Sudinna and others—thinking, "I have done wrong. As for the remorse mentioned in the Vinaya, where it says, "Then the Venerable Sāriputta...
being remorseful, did not accept [the food]," that refers to the hindrance of remorse (*nīvaraṇa-kukkucca*).

Indeed, there are no hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in an Arahant; rather, it should be understood that what is called "discipline-worry" (vinayakukkucca)—consisting of the investigation as to whether something is "allowable" or "unallowable"—is merely a semblance of a hindrance. The remaining hindrances have already been explained.
Furthermore, among these, worry and doubt are abandoned by the first path, ill will by the third, and sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and ignorance by the fourth.
Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) should be said to be associated with all four [jhānas], yet it is stated here as being associated with the "third" [jhāna].
These eight states by their very nature constitute the six hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); excluding these, the remaining states are not called hindrances. This is the first dyad on hindrances.

The second dyad is exactly like the dyad on the taints (*sāsava*). Twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are called "associated with hindrances. The remaining consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are not.
They are called dissociated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), the unwholesome ones are associated with the hindrances;
the wholesome and indeterminate ones are dissociated from the hindrances; the remainder are both. This is the third [section].

The six hindrances are both hindrances and objects of hindrance (*nīvaraṇiya*); the remaining mundane states are objects of hindrance but are not themselves hindrances; supramundane states are not to be so described. The rest is exactly like the fourth section in the group on the taints (*āsava*). This is the fourth.
The five hindrances are both hindrances themselves and associated with hindrances. Other mental factors associated with hindrances are associated with hindrances but are not themselves hindrances.
Likewise, among the mental concomitants (cetasika), unwholesome states that are free from hindrances are neither;
those of the three other classes (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate) cannot be so described, and wholesome and indeterminate states cannot be so described at all. Herein:
However, all those dissociated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are not so called. Fifth.

Those dissociated from the hindrances, excluding the supramundane (lokuttara), are called "subject to hindrances" (nīvaraṇiya). Those dissociated from the hindrances that are supramundane are called "not subject to hindrances" (anīvaraṇiya).
Here, however, those associated with the hindrances are not so called. Among the mental factors (cetasika), however, compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā)...

Those dissociated from the hindrances but subject to them are both wholesome and indeterminate; likewise, those of three types [the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate] are both [subject to and dissociated from the hindrances], while the unwholesome are not to be so described at all.
The sixth [section]. The Group on Hindrances is finished.

In the *Parāmāsa-vagga* (Cluster on Grasping), "graspings" (*parāmāsā*) are so called because they grasp after something else by proceeding in the manner of "permanent," etc., having transcended the true nature of phenomena (*dhammā*) as impermanent and so forth.
They are wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). The reason for the use of the plural number in the exposition has already been stated.
All other phenomena are called "not graspings. This is the first dyad on graspings.

They are "clung to" (*parāmaṭṭhā*) because they have been clung to by means of making them an object through the perversions (*parāmāsa*). The rest is exactly like the pair of taints (*āsava*). This is the second [section].

Among the consciousnesses associated with views, those phenomena devoid of view are called "associated with perversions. The remaining consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are called "dissociated from perversions.
However, here view itself is not to be mentioned; among the remaining mental factors, conceit, hatred, envy, avarice, worry, and doubt—
The wholesome and the indeterminate are exclusively dissociated from the perversions (parāmāsa); the remaining [states] are of both kinds. This is the third [section].

View alone is called both a perversion and something perverted; the remaining mundane states are called perverted but not perversions. However, the supramundane states should not be mentioned here. The rest is easily understood. This is the fourth [section].
But in this group, this dyad—“states that are both perversions and associated with perversions”—does not [apply].

It is possible. For one view does not associate with another view. In the latter dyad, those excluding the supramundane are called "not associated with perversions" (parāmāsa-vippayutta) and "pervaded" (parāmaṭṭha).
The supramundane states, being dissociated from perversions, are called "unpervaded" (aparāmaṭṭha).
Here, however, perversion itself and its associated states are not to be mentioned. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The Group on Misapprehension (*parāmāsa-gocchaka*) is finished.

In the Great Pairs (*mahantaraduka*), those that do not arise without taking an object are "with an object" (*sārammaṇa*); these are consciousness and mental factors. Those for which no object exists are "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*); these are material phenomena (*rūpa*) and Nibbāna. This concludes the Pair on Being with an Object.
In the sense of thinking, or by way of being conscious, it is "consciousness" (*citta*). For that [consciousness] is distinguished by way of its basis, door, object, function, and so forth.
It is called "citta" because of its own variety through the distinctions of past and so forth, or because of its capacity for mental creation (*cittakaraṇatā*).
Indeed, in the world there is nothing superior to mental creation; even within that, what is known as "carana" (movement) is called *aticitta* (superior mind).
Or whatever other kind of craft exists in the world, all of that is performed by means of the mind alone. Thus, of that...

The mind that produces that [resultant] mind is likewise a mind. Just as the mind is even more "minded" (cittatara) than the thought because it brings about the complete realization of what was intended,
so too, through the diversity of wholesome and unwholesome kamma among the various destinies— divided into gods, humans, hell-beings, and animals—
there arises within those destinies a diversity such as being footless, two-footed, and so forth, or high and low status.
In each respective state of existence, there is the internal mind—consisting of such things as long, short, stout, or thin; beautiful, ugly, or the like;

gain, loss, and so forth—and the external mind, which consists of the earth, mountains, grass, trees, creepers, and so on, as well as gods, Brahmās, celestial palaces, and wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha), all of which have karma as their condition.
That too was created by the mind alone; therefore, the mind is indeed more "mind-like" (cittatara) according to the principle of what it has conceived.
Because it is impossible for all modes [of consciousness] to exist simultaneously.

Thus, consciousness (*viññāṇa*) should be understood as "mind" (*citta*) in the sense of thinking, in the sense of being variegated, and in the sense of forming mental objects; that very consciousness is what is called "mind.
Mental factors, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are not called "mind. This concludes the dyad on mind.

Mental concomitants (*cetasika*) are those factors associated with the mind by way of non-separation; they are the fifty-two states beginning with contact (*phassa*). Mind, matter, and Nibbāna are called non-mental concomitants (*acetasika*). This is the dyad of mental concomitants.

Those that are exclusively mental concomitants are called "associated with mind" (*cittasampayutta*). Matter and Nibbāna are called "dissociated from mind" (*cittavippayutta*); however, in this context, mind itself is not to be included [in the category of dissociated]. This is the dyad of those associated with mind.
They are "conjoined with mind" (*cittasaṃsaṭṭha*) because they are blended with the mind from the moment of arising until its dissolution, owing to their state of uninterrupted occurrence.
Even when occurring at one time, they are "dissociated from mind" (*cittavisaṃsaṭṭhā*) because they do not attain a state of uninterrupted continuity with the mind.
The remainder is exactly like the "immediate" (*anantara*) dyad. This concludes the "Mind-Dissociated Dyad.
That by which things arise is "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*). Those for whom the mind is the origination are "mind-originated" (*cittasamuṭṭhānā*); these are the mental factors (*cetasika*).

And also the groups of material phenomena born of mind (*cittaja-rūpa-kalāpā*). However, the groups of material phenomena not born of mind and Nibbāna are not called "mind-originated" (*no cittasamuṭṭhānā*). This is the dyad on mind-originated phenomena (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-duka*).

They exist together, thus they are "co-existent" (*sahabhuno*); co-existent with the mind, thus "mind-co-existent" (*cittasahabhuno*), namely the mental factors (*cetasika*) and the intimation of body and speech (*kāya-vacī-viññatti*).

Furthermore, consciousness, as well as material phenomena excluding intimation and Nibbāna, are called "not co-existent with consciousness. This concludes the dyad on "co-existent with consciousness" (*cittasahabhūduka*).

"Following along" means they are "concomitants" (*anuparivattino*); what do they follow along with? They follow along with consciousness; thus, they are "consciousness-concomitants" (*cittānuparivattino*). The rest is exactly like the immediately preceding dyad. This concludes the dyad on "consciousness-concomitants" (*cittānuparivattiduka*).
The three dyads following this are identical to the dyad on mental factors (*cetasikaduka*); the only difference lies merely in the meaning of the terms. Among them:
Those things which are conjoined with the mind and are also originated by the mind are "conjoined-and-originated-by-the-mind" (*cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhāna*).

Those things which are conjoined with the mind, originated by the mind, and are also co-existent with the mind are "conjoined-and-originated-and-co-existent-with-the-mind" (*cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānasahabhū*).

Those things which are conjoined with the mind, originated by the mind, and are also concomitant with the mind are "conjoined-and-originated-and-concomitant-with-the-mind" (*cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānānuparivatti*).
The rest is easy to understand.

Regarding the "Internal Dyad" (Ajjhattika-duka) immediately following that: according to what was stated in the "Internal Triad" (Ajjhatta-ttika), those which are internal are themselves "internal" (ajjhattika).
There are six internal bases (āyatana) consisting of sensitive matter and consciousness. Those existing outside of these are...
External. The six external bases—consisting of the remaining material phenomena, mental factors, nibbāna, and designations (paññatti)—are here also understood to include designations themselves.
This concludes the dyad of internal [bases].

The term *upādā* refers to that which clings only to the primary elements (*bhūta*), but does not cling as the primary elements themselves; it refers exclusively to the twenty-four derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*). The term *no upādā* refers to that which does not cling; it refers to the four great primaries, consciousness, mental factors, and nibbāna. This concludes the dyad of derived [phenomena].

The thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness and kamma-born materiality are called "clung-to" (*upādinnā*). All remaining mundane and supramundane phenomena, as well as Nibbāna, are called "not clung-to" (*anupādinnā*). The rest should be understood according to what has been stated in the "Clung-to and Subject to Clinging" (*upādinnupādāniya*) triad.
This concludes the "Clung-to" dyad. The "Great Intermediate Dyads" are finished.

They are called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because they thoroughly take hold of the groups of clinging; the meaning is that they grasp with a firm grip. It is in the sense of firmness [that this term is used].
For here the prefix *upa-* is used as in such terms as *upāyāsa* (agony). Those other than that are not *upādānas*.
Among them, *kāmupādāna*, *diṭṭhupādāna*, *sīlabbatupādāna*, and *attavādupādāna*—these are what are called *upādānas*.

Therein, *kāmupādāna* is the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) arising toward the objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*), which is called an "appropriation" (*upādāna*) according to the method already stated. The same applies to the remaining ones. Therein, [the first] has twenty bases...
The view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is called the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*). The remaining ones have already been explained above.

Furthermore, the last three types of clinging here are simply views that proceed in such a manner. These are abandoned by the first path (*magga*), while the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is abandoned by all four paths.
By way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), these are two phenomena, but by way of classification, they become known as the four types of clinging. And these—
Excluding these, all remaining phenomena are called "not objects of clinging" (*anupādāna*). This is the first dyad, the *upādāna-duka*.
The *upādāniya-duka* (the dyad of things subject to clinging) is similar to the *saṃyojaniya-duka* (the dyad of things subject to fetters). This is the second.
[It consists of] the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed, and—excluding the greed dissociated from views among those associated with them—the remaining factors.
Those associated with clinging are called "associated with clinging" (*upādāna-sampayutta*).

Those rooted in greed, hatred, and delusion that are dissociated from views, as well as wholesome and indeterminate states of consciousness, and material phenomena and Nibbāna, are called "dissociated from clinging" (*upādāna-vippayutta*). Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, views and conceit are exclusively associated with clinging;
hatred, envy, avarice, remorse, and doubt, as well as those that are wholesome and indeterminate, are exclusively dissociated from clinging. The remainder...
Both are of two kinds. Third.

The four types of clinging (*upādāna*) are called both "clinging" and "objects of clinging. The remaining worldly factors are called only "objects of clinging" and not "clinging. However, supramundane factors are not to be mentioned here. The rest is exactly as previously stated. Fourth.
The fifth and sixth dyads are identical in wording to the fifth and sixth dyads in the *Ganthagocchaka*; the only difference is that in the fifth dyad...
“Among mental factors (*cetasika*), conceit (*māna*) is associated with clinging (*upādāna-sampayutta*) but is not itself clinging;

likewise, delusion (*moha*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), sloth (*thina*), and torpor (*middha*) are of three types and cannot be so described. And this [is stated] in the sixth dyad:

“Among mental factors, hatred (*dosa*), envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), remorse (*kukkucca*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*) are dissociated from clinging (*upādāna-vippayutta*) but are subject to clinging (*upādāniya*); likewise, delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, restlessness, greed (*lobha*), sloth, and torpor...”
And likewise, "they should not be stated"—this much alone is the difference in the wording; as for the meaning, however, the difference is merely in the name.
The rest is easy to understand. The fifth and sixth [sections].
The Group on Grasping (Upādāna-gocchaka) is finished.
The meaning of the terms should be understood according to the method explained in the *Kilesagocchaka* (Cluster of Defilements) and the *Saṃkiliṭṭhattika* (Triplet of Corrupt States).
