Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—these ten states are called defilements (*kilesa*).
These have already been explained; however, here, greed is [treated] as it appears in the clusters on causes, fetters, hindrances, and clinging.
Furthermore, although the defilements removable by the four paths exist without exception, they are established as a single category;
however, in the remaining groups, all that greed is established in two categories each, such as "the taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) and "the taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*).

By this statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, all lust removable by the four paths—excluding the taint of existence and the others—is included within the taints of sensual desire and so forth. [This refers to] the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, existence-taint (*bhavarāga*) is not perceived as being merely the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure;

this should be understood from such scriptural passages as, "In the formless [realms], dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there is the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor," because lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure does not arise in the planes of form and the formless.
And among these defilements, wrong view and doubt are abandoned by the first path.
By the first [truth], ignorance is abandoned; by the second, hatred; by the third, greed and the rest; and by all four together, these ten states are abandoned.
Excluding these ten states, the remainder are not called "defilements" (kilesa). This is the first dyad, the Defilement Dyad (Kilesaduka).
The Corrupt Dyad (Saṃkilesikaduka) is similar to the Tainted Dyad (Sāsavaduka). This is the second.
The "Defiled Dyad" and the "Associated with Defilements Dyad" have the same meaning. These two are identical to the third dyad in the Group on Hindrances (*nīvaraṇagocchaka*).

[Regarding] the third and fourth [dyads]: the ten defilements are both defilements and called "defiled. All remaining mundane phenomena (*lokīya-dhammā*) are defiled but are not themselves defilements.
However, supramundane (*lokuttara*) phenomena are not to be mentioned here. The rest is exactly like the fourth dyad in the Group on Hindrances. Fifth.

The sixth and seventh dyads are likewise identical in meaning to one another. These sixth and seventh dyads, in the *Nīvaraṇagocchaka*, are similar in wording to the fifth and sixth dyads respectively;
however, in terms of meaning, the difference is merely a matter of names.
The rest is easy to understand. [These are] the sixth, seventh, and eighth [dyads].
The Section on Defilements (*kilesagocchaka*) is finished.

Regarding the subsequent dyads (*piṭṭhiduka*), the first four dyads are to be understood according to the method already stated for the triad of "to be abandoned by vision" (*dassanenapahātabba*) and the dyad of "having a cause to be abandoned by vision" (*dassanenapahātabbahetuka*).
However, among those stated in that [first] triad, regarding the factors to be abandoned by vision:
Setting aside the *dhammas* [to be abandoned by vision], the remainder here enter into the second term of the first dyad among those things to be abandoned by vision;
setting aside those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the remainder here enter into the second dyad among those not to be abandoned by cultivation.
And therein, setting aside those with roots to be abandoned by vision mentioned in the second triad, the remainder here [enter] into the third dyad.

Excluding those whose causes are to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka*) and those whose causes are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya-pahātabba-hetuka*), the remainder enter here into the fourth dyad among those whose causes are not to be abandoned by cultivation (*na-bhāvanāya-pahātabba-hetuka*).
As for the word-meaning: "those whose cause is to be abandoned by vision" (*dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka*) means those which possess a cause that is to be abandoned by vision. Thus...

The meaning of "having roots to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanāya pahātabba-hetuka*) should also be understood here. For if that were the case, there would be no inclusion of those states that are rootless (*ahetuka*);
this is the only difference. Indeed, the Blessed One, through his skill in teaching, taught these two triads by dividing them into four dyads.
The rest is exactly the same. The four dyads are concluded.

In the fifty-five types of consciousness accompanied by initial application (*savitakka*), those states of consciousness and mental factors that are devoid of initial application are called "with initial application" (*savitakka*). Initial application itself, as well as the remaining types of consciousness, matter, and Nibbāna, are called "without initial application" (*avitakka*). This is the fifth [pair].
In the sixty-six types of consciousness accompanied by sustained application (*savicāra*), those states devoid of sustained application are called "with sustained application" (*savicāra*).

Sustained application itself, as well as the remaining types of consciousness, matter, and Nibbāna, are called "without sustained application" (*avicāra*). The remainder here, as well as in the preceding dyads and the triad concerning initial application, should be understood according to the method already stated. This is the sixth [pair].
Among these, the pair with zest (*sappītika-duka*) and the pair accompanied by zest (*pītisahagata-duka*) have the same meaning;

and together with the pairs accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*) and accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*), all four pairs follow the same method as explained in the "Zest Triplet" (*pītittika*).
However, the first term of these pairs is included therein [in the Zest Triplet], while the other two terms include all meanings both included and not included in the Zest Triplet.
The meaning is included here in the second members of the dyads in the same manner as explained below; this alone is the distinction, namely that these are the "unrestricted dyads" (*nippadesaduka*).
The seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth [chapters].

In the sections immediately following, regarding the phrase "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*), here [the limit] is defined from below by making the Avīci hell the boundary, and from above...

Including the gods who wield power over the creations of others (paranimmitavasavatti), whatever exists within that interval—belonging to this sphere and included therein—is called "sense-sphere existence" (kāmabhava) in eleven ways according to its spatial extent:
by way of the four lower realms (apāya) as delimited in the Canon, humans, and the six heavenly worlds.
This is expressed by the elision of the latter member of the compound, just as in such cases as "rebirth in the form-sphere" (rūpūpapatti).
The existence in the fine-material realm is "form. They move about and proceed within that sensuality; thus, they are "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara).

This is stated from a majority perspective, as these [beings] also proceed here in the fine-material and immaterial realms, just as in the case of expressions such as "land-dwellers" (thalacara) and so forth.

Alternatively, they are "sense-sphere" because they descend into rebirth-linking within the sensuality known as the sense-sphere existence; this refers to wholesome and unwholesome states. [This includes] the consciousness accompanied by restlessness.
However, it is similar to the indeterminate (abyākata) mind.

It is called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) because the defiled desire (kilesakāma) ranges over it due to its dependence on that [mind], or by way of taking it as its object. Granted, this [desire] also ranges over phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres;

yet, by way of conventional usage (ruḷhi), these alone are called "belonging to the sense-sphere," just as in such cases as "one who cries out is a calf" (vaccho). Furthermore, there is craving for sensual pleasures (kāmataṇhā).

Regarding the terms *rūpataṇhā* (craving for form) and *arūpataṇhā* (craving for the formless), they are called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) because the craving known as *kāmatanha* (sensual craving), as mentioned here, operates within them.
In this way, the status of even the desire and lust for the celestial palaces and ornaments of the Brahmās is established as being sensual craving;

and since the kamma-born forms and so forth belonging to those Brahmās—which are the objects of craving for form—are also objects of sensual craving, their status as belonging to the sense-sphere is likewise established.
Because those [states] do not exist in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, other than those, they are not sense-sphere states.
By this method, the meaning of the terms for the dyads such as "fine-material sphere" and so forth should also be understood accordingly.

In that regard, the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses and all matter are called "sense-sphere. The remaining consciousnesses and Nibbāna are not called "sense-sphere. Regarding the mental concomitants, the explanation is to be found in the dyad on "included" (*pariyāpanna*).
Thus it will become manifest. (Eleventh.
The fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses are called "fine-material-sphere. The remaining consciousnesses, matter, and Nibbāna are not called "fine-material-sphere.
(Twelfth. The twelve immaterial-sphere consciousnesses are called "immaterial-sphere. The remaining consciousnesses, matter, and Nibbāna are not called "immaterial-sphere. (Thirteenth.)
Included within the round of existence consisting of the three planes is what is meant by "included" (*pariyāpanna*); these are exclusively mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhamma*).

In this context, that which is not included is "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*), meaning supramundane (*lokuttara*). Regarding the mental factors (*cetasika*), however, the common analysis for all four dyads—beginning with those of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth—should be understood as follows:
unwholesome mental factors belong exclusively to the sense sphere; the illimitables (*appamaññā*) belong to both the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

The abstinences (*virati*), however, are included within the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and rapture (*pīti*) are included within both the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*);
the remaining factors belong to all four planes. This is the fourteenth [section].
They are "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because, while cutting the root of the round of existence, they take Nibbāna as their object and lead one away from the round. There are four [such factors].
The supramundane path-consciousnesses. Because they do not lead out by this characteristic, they are "non-leaders" (aniyyānika);
these are the remaining consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna. The rest is easy to understand. The fifteenth [section].

Because they are fixed in giving their fruit immediately after death or immediately after their own occurrence, they are "fixed" (niyata): namely, those fixed in the wrong way (micchattaniyata) and those fixed in the right way (sammattaniyata). Because they are not fixed in that manner, they are "unfixed" (aniyata); these are the remaining states. The rest is according to the method already stated. The sixteenth [section].

They are called *uttara* because they rise above (*uttaranti*) and transcend other states. Together with those capable of transcending themselves, they are *sauttara*, meaning merely mundane. Those for which there is nothing superior are *anuttara*, meaning supramundane.

This is the seventeenth [chapter]. They are called *raṇa* because beings cry out (*raṇanti*) by means of them; this is a designation for the unwholesome roots by which beings, being overcome, lament in various ways.
Together with these, by way of association and by way of being abandoned together, [they are so called].
"Having conflict" (*saraṇa*) means "to conflict. In this sense, because they have no conflict, they are called "without conflict" (*araṇā*).

Among these, the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are called "with conflict" (*saraṇa*). Within the phenomena that possess conflict, greed, hatred, and delusion are both conflict itself and "with conflict.
Among those, greed and hatred are "with conflict" by virtue of their association with delusion; likewise, the consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness is "with conflict."
And [the other defilements] associated with them are also [conflict]. However, among those, delusion (*moha*) is conflict by way of association;
furthermore, it is conflict by virtue of being abandoned together with lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), which—through its association with lust for views (*diṭṭhirāga*)—has become conflict.

Among those associated with the roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, however, delusion is associated with greed and hatred, while the others are associated with greed and delusion, as well as with hatred and delusion.
They should be understood as "with conflict" (*saraṇa*). All wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses, as well as material phenomena and Nibbāna, are called "without conflict" (*araṇa*).

Among mental factors, however, the unwholesome are exclusively with conflict, while the wholesome and indeterminate are exclusively without conflict; the three types [of consciousness] are both ways. The eighteenth [section].
The *Piṭṭhiduka* (Back-Pair) is finished.
The commentary on the matrix of dyads in the Abhidhamma is finished.
Commentary on the Matrix of Dyads in the Suttas: Regarding the dyads in the Suttas:
it is called *vijjā* (knowledge) because it feels or knows in various ways; it proceeds as the six direct knowledges (*cha-abhiññā*), consisting of insight-knowledge and the mind-made psychic power.

They are called "belonging to the side of true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgin*) because they function within that portion of true knowledge, within the category of true knowledge, and within the nature of true knowledge.

Alternatively, they are called "belonging to the side of true knowledge" because they themselves are true knowledge, or because they associate with that true knowledge by way of conjunction; thus, they are the states associated with the eightfold true knowledge.

Among these, any one [of the three] is true knowledge itself, while the remaining ones belong to the side of true knowledge. Thus, both true knowledge and the states associated with true knowledge are included.
They should indeed be understood as "sharing in clear knowledge" (*vijjābhāginī*); however, here only those states associated with clear knowledge are intended.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is that which does not cognize; it is delusion (*moha*) of four kinds by way of its obscuring of the Four Noble Truths.

They are called "sharing in ignorance" (*avijjābhāginī*) because they occur within that portion of ignorance, within that division of ignorance, and within the very nature of ignorance. These are themselves ignorance, or [states] associated with that ignorance by way of conjunction.

Those that "partake" are also those belonging to ignorance (*avijjābhāgin*), namely, the states associated with ignorance (*avijjāsampayutta-dhammā*). Thus, both ignorance itself and the states associated with ignorance should be understood as "belonging to ignorance";
however, here only the states associated with ignorance are intended.

In this context, the consciousness of the path of Arahatship, the supramundane states dissociated from wisdom, and the sense-sphere impulsion moments associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*) belong to clear knowledge (*vijjābhāgin*).
Insight associated with the state of being devoid of knowledge is a constituent of clear vision (*vijjābhāginī*) during its active occurrence, but at other times it cannot be so described.
The impulsion consciousnesses of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, associated with the state of being devoid of wisdom,
are constituents of clear vision by way of the supernormal power of mind-made form and the five higher knowledges during their active occurrence, but at other times they cannot be so described.
In that context, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses and ignorance when dissociated from it are indeed associated with the portion of ignorance (*avijjābhāgiya*);

however, in this [classification], ignorance itself, as well as the remaining consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna, are simply not to be so designated. Among the mental factors (*cetasika*), delusion (*moha*) and the illimitables (*appamaññā*) are simply not to be so designated;
the remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors may belong to the portion of true knowledge (*vijjābhāgiya*), may not be so designated, or—being of three types—may belong to both portions.
And they should not be so described. The remainder is easy to understand. First.
Again, because they are incapable of destroying the darkness of the defilements by way of non-overpowering, they are "like lightning" (*vijjūpamā*);
this refers to the knowledge in the first three paths. Because of their capacity to destroy [the darkness] without remainder...
“Vajirūpamā” means those for which the thunderbolt is the simile; this refers to the knowledge on the path of arahantship.

For just as when one has set out on a path in the darkness of a rain-cloud, the thunderbolt dispels the obscuring darkness, and at the moment lightning flashes, the paths in the four directions become visible;
yet when the lightning ceases, the darkness returns and once more obscures the path—so it is for one whose vehicle is insight (vipassanā).
Just as, by dispelling the darkness of the defilements that obscure each respective truth, the four truths become manifest when the three paths arise in their proper sequence;

and when those [paths] have ceased, the remaining darkness of defilements again conceals the Four Truths—therefore, wisdom in the context of the three paths is said to be like lightning. Furthermore, just as a diamond is indestructible...

There is no such thing as a stone that can withstand it; moreover, it completely wears away even diamond, and once a path has been traversed by a diamond, there is no returning the stone to its original state.
Likewise, for the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, there is no defilement that cannot be slain;
it completely exhausts even the defilements of Arahatship, and when those defilements have been exhausted by it, because no further defilements remain...
Furthermore, for that [wisdom], there is no turning back; therefore, in the fourth path, wisdom is said to be like a thunderbolt.

In this context, wisdom alone may be compared to lightning, or it may not be so described. However, all other mental factors, consciousness, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are simply not to be so described. Second.

They are called "fools" (bāla) because they abide among fools; they are fools by way of association with those in whom they abide, or because they perform the functions of a fool—namely, the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness.
However, in this context, moral shamelessness (ahirika) and lack of dread of blame (anottappa) are what are called "fools. They are called "wise" (paṇḍita) because they abide among the wise;

they are wise by way of performing the functions of a wise person—namely, the twenty-one wholesome types of consciousness. However, in this context, moral shame (hirī) and dread of blame (ottappa) are what are called "wise. The remaining types of consciousness, material phenomena, and Nibbāna [are neither].
They are not to be so described. The remainder is easy to understand. Third. "Black" means dark;
they cause the mind to lose its luminosity. "White" means bright; they cause the mind to become luminous. The rest is entirely similar to the "Foolish Couplets. Fourth.
They burn both here and in the future life, thus they are "burning" (*tapanīya*). Those that do not burn are "non-burning" (*atapanīya*). The rest is similar to the "Foolish Couplets. Fifth.
Terms such as “Sirivaḍḍhaka” and “Dhanavaḍḍhaka,” which function by taking a mere verbal expression as their basis, are called designations (*adhivacana*).
“Name” (*nāmadheyya*) refers to the names of various phenomena (*dhammas*). These are fourfold: common names, quality names, fame names, and spontaneous names.
Among these, [the first] was conferred by the great multitude upon those of the First Eon after they had been formally appointed.
Because he was established [in that position], the name "Mahāsammata" (Great Elect) given to the king is what is called a common name (*sāmañña-nāma*).
Such as "a preacher of the Dhamma," "one who wears rag-robes," or "dark-skinned and short"—these names derived from qualities (*guṇato*) are called quality-names (*guṇa-nāma*).

Furthermore, the many hundreds of names for the Tathāgata, such as "the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," are also quality-names. As for the names that kinsmen give to a newborn boy...
Having conceived and formulated it, they give a name such as "this one is named so-and-so"; this is called a conventional name (*kittimanāma*).
However, that which is a prior designation (*purimapaññatti*) is subsumed under a subsequent designation (*aparapaññatti*), as follows:
in the past eon the moon was the moon, and now, and in the future too, it will be the moon. Likewise for "the sun," "the ocean," "the earth," "form," and "feeling."
"Perception, mental formations, consciousness, and Nibbāna"—such expressions as these are called "spontaneous designations" (*opapātika-nāma*).

Furthermore, these are sixfold according to the classification of nominal designations (*nāma-paññatti*): designation of the existent, designation of the non-existent, designation of the non-existent by means of the existent, designation of the existent by means of the non-existent, designation of the existent by means of the existent, and designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

In this context, the seventy-two kinds of name-and-form phenomena (nāmarūpadhammā) as previously described, which are found existing in the ultimate sense (paramatthato), are called "existent" (vijjamāna).
Because they make these [phenomena] known through various modes, the designation (paññatti) for them is called "designation of the existent" (vijjamānapaññatti);
such are words that denote ultimate realities, such as "consciousness," "contact," "earth," "form," and "nibbāna. However, [the designation] based upon the appropriated name-and-form phenomena...
The seven types of persons— distinguished as female, male, deva, human, animal, and so forth— and those distinguished as earth, mountains, trees, carts,
moon, sun, constellations, directions, time, the kasiṇas, and so forth, which are designated based on non-clung-to material phenomena (*anupādinnarūpadhamma*),
are called "non-existent" because they are not found and do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). The designation of these is "designation of the non-existent" (*avijjamānapaññatti*).

Likewise, terms such as “the self is the earth,” which express designations for non-existent things, and terms such as “approaching the color of the mental continuum,” which express designations for existent things, are called designations of the non-existent by means of the existent.

In cases such as “a man’s mind” or “the color of a cloud,” it is called a designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. [Examples include] “lightness of mind” and “the fragrance of the earth.”
This is called a designation of the non-existent by means of the existent. An example such as “a human body is a tree branch” is called a designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

Thus, all six of these types [of designation] are understood through the mental-door consciousnesses that arise immediately after the ear-consciousness process—following the vocal sound accompanied by intimation (*saviññatti-sadda*) produced by the mind desiring to communicate a specific intention—for one who has learned the conventional sign (*saṅketa*), [in the form]: “this belongs to that.”
"Name" (*nāma*) refers to things established by attributing unity to multiple sounds;

they are called "name-designations" (*nāmapaññatti*) because they incline toward the meaning and because they make the meaning known through various modes. The "paths of designation" (*adhivacanapathā*) are the meanings that serve as the tracks for those designations;
all phenomena (*dhammā*), whether conventional or ultimate, have the nature of being expressible by words. Sixth.
From here on, two dyads are exactly like the dyad on designations (*adhivacanaduka*); the only difference lies merely in the meaning of the words.

In that context, "designation" (*nirutti*) refers to the linguistic expression stated with its cause after having analyzed [the term] as "they form (*abhisaṅkharonti*) thus they are formations (*saṅkhārā*").

"Description" (*paññatti*) refers to making known by various such modes, as in "reasoning (*takka*), initial application (*vitakka*), intention (*saṅkappa*"); these are precisely the descriptions consisting of names as previously mentioned.
Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever in meaning among the designations of terms, linguistic expressions, and conceptual descriptions;
however, their individual meanings have been shown through analysis for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between their production and their causes.

Within these three dyads, all phenomena together with conceptual description are found, whereas in the immediately following dyad on name-and-form, they are devoid of conceptual description. Thus, these four dyads [belong] to these dyads of the Sutta Pitaka.
The remaining thirty-eight [factors] should be understood as being with reference to a basis (*sappadesa*). The seventh and eighth [sections].
It is called "name" (*nāma*) in the sense of naming, in the sense of bending (*namana*), and in the sense of inclining (*nāmana*); these are the immaterial aggregates and Nibbāna.
For these, by way of their spontaneously arisen names—such as "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," "consciousness," and "Nibbāna"—always refer to themselves...
They proceed by way of giving names, just like the moon, the sun, and so forth.
For they have no need for the function of naming based on the praise of their common qualities. Thus, "name" (nāma) should be understood in the sense of giving a name.
However, in the sense of bending toward an object (ārammaṇābhimukha-namana), and in the sense of bending toward one another therein, only the four immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) are "name."

Nibbāna, however, should be understood as "name" (nāma) in the sense of bending (namana) toward blameless states within itself by way of being an object-predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipatipaccayatā).
Matter (rūpa) is so called in the sense of being affected (ruppana); this is the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). Ninth:
Ignorance (avijjā) is all delusion that conceals suffering and so forth. Craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is that which proceeds by way of longing for existence.
Greed (*lobha*). Likewise, greed does not occur here; furthermore, the remaining mental factors, consciousness, matter, and Nibbāna are not to be mentioned [in this context].
Hereafter, however, we shall show only the essential nature of the terms without demonstrating such classifications of what is "not to be mentioned" (*navattabba*);
it should be understood that whatever remains unmentioned is "not to be mentioned. This is the tenth [section].
"Becoming" (bhava) is called eternalism. The view that arises by way of eternalism, thinking "the self and the world will exist," is called the view of becoming (bhavadiṭṭhi).
"Dissolution" (vibhava) is called annihilationism. The view that arises by way of annihilationism, thinking "the self and the world will not exist," is called the view of dissolution (vibhavadiṭṭhi).
By both of these, wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is included. The same applies to the following [views] as well.
In the three groups. The eleventh.
Having grasped the five aggregates as "self and the world," the view that proceeds as "self and the world are eternal" is called the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*).
Likewise, the view that proceeds as "it will be annihilated" is called the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*). [The view that it is] "finite" is...
That which occurs as "it is finite" is called the view of finitude. That which occurs as "it is infinite" is called the view of infinitude.
Following the past—that is, occurring by taking the past portion as its object in the manner described in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*—is the eighteenfold view concerning the past (*pubbantānudiṭṭhi*).
Following the future—that is, occurring by taking the future portion as its object in the manner presented in that very same [sutta]—is the view concerning the future (*aparantānudiṭṭhi*).

The "speculation regarding the future" (*aparantānudiṭṭhi*) is of forty-four kinds. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood from the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth [dyads]—the dyad of moral shamelessness (*ahirika*) and the dyad of moral dread (*hiri*)—are indeed easy to understand. The fifteenth and sixteenth [dyads]...
"Difficult speech" (*dubbaca*) refers to a person who speaks unpleasantly toward one who acts in opposition, who is contrary, disagreeable, and disrespectful;
it is a person who shows disrespect when being exhorted and instructed according to the Dhamma. The action of such a person is "difficult-to-speak-to-ness" (*dovacassa*);

the state of that is "difficult-to-speak-to-ness" (*dovacassatā*). It consists of the two types of repulsive consciousness (*paṭighacitta*) that arise by way of disrespect, as well as the mental factors associated with them.
A "bad friend" (*pāpamitta*) is one whose friends are evil persons such as those lacking faith; the state of being that is "bad friendship" (*pāpamittatā*).

This consists of the eight greed-rooted consciousnesses that arise through strong attachment to evil persons and through associating with them by means of body and mind, thereby becoming inclined toward them. This is the seventeenth [unwholesome root].

"Easy to speak to" (*sovacassatā*) and "good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) should be understood by way of the opposites of what has been stated above. In terms of their actual meaning (*attha*), however, they consist of the wholesome and functional sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by roots that arise in such a manner. This is the eighteenth.

Skillfulness regarding the five or seven offenses is "skill in offenses" (*āpatti-kusala-tā*); it is the sense-sphere javana-wisdom that functions by way of knowing the limits of incurring those offenses together with their bases.
Skillfulness regarding emergence from offenses is "skill in emerging from offenses" (*āpatti-vuṭṭhāna-kusala-tā*);
it is [wisdom] that functions by way of knowing the limits of emerging from offenses together with the procedure for emerging.
The "promoter" is simply the wisdom associated with the mind as previously described. This is the nineteenth [factor].

It is called "attainment" (samāpatti) because it is to be attained. Skillfulness regarding those attainments—whether mundane or supramundane, and whether accompanied by applied and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra) and so forth—is "skill in attainment.
This occurs by way of knowing the delimitation of absorption (appanā) together with its preliminary work (parikamma).
Wisdom (*paññā*). Skillfulness in emerging from attainments is skill in emerging from attainments (*samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā*);
it is the wisdom that emerges from those attainments at the very time previously determined, which is indeed the wisdom of sense-sphere impulsions (*kāmāvacara-javana-paññā*). Twenty.
Skillfulness regarding the eighteen elements is skill in the elements (*dhātukusalatā*); it is the wisdom of hearing, retaining, penetrating, and reviewing.

Skillfulness regarding those same elements (*dhātu*) in their attention is "skillfulness in attention" (*manasikārakusalatā*); it is the wisdom (*paññā*) consisting of comprehension, penetration, and reflection upon them.
This same method applies to skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*). For therein, hearing, retention, and reflection belong only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);
penetration is supramundane (*lokuttara*) alone; and comprehension belongs to both the sense-sphere and the supramundane. They are conjoined by depending upon one another.
"Dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda) means that which produces a fruit; it is the collection of conditions specified by ignorance and the rest.
Skillfulness regarding dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā) is the state of skillfulness with respect to that twelvefold dependent origination in its forward order;
it is precisely the mundane javana-wisdom that functions by way of knowing, "With this condition, this comes to be. [These are] the twenty-first and twenty-second [questions].

It is called a *ṭhāna* (basis) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein, owing to its dependence upon that; it is thus a cause. Skillfulness regarding that basis is *ṭhānakusala-tā*. Lack of skillfulness regarding the basis is *aṭṭhānakusala-tā*.

This is the twenty-third [chapter]. Uprightness (*ujubhāva*) is integrity (*ajjava*). Softness (*mudubhāva*) is gentleness (*maddava*). These two refer to the straightness and softness of body and mind. This is the twenty-fourth [chapter].
Patience (*khanti*) is the endurance characterized as forbearance; it refers to the sense-sphere impulsion moments (*javana*) proceeding in such a manner. [Skillfulness] regarding evil... very well.

"Tranquil" (*sorata*) means one who is peaceful; its state is "tranquility" (*soracca*). The mundane and supramundane impulsive moments (*javana*) comprised by the virtue of restraint of body, speech, and mind [are included].
This is the twenty-fifth [factor]. "Gentleness" (*sākhalya*) is the state of being kindly, characterized by pleasant speech and sociability.

"Hospitality" (*patisanthāra*) is the welcoming and covering [of others' needs] with the gifts of Dhamma and material goods, such that no flaw or opening exists for oneself toward others. [This applies] to a guest...

Indeed, by means of going out to meet [the visitor], receiving their bowl and robes, providing a seat, washing and anointing their feet, and so forth; by offering drinking water and asking for permission to depart;
by giving rice-gruel and other foods at the proper time, and drinks and such at the improper time;

and by showing the place for alms-round on the following day, announcing the times for entering and leaving, and so forth—[this is how] those who have gone forth and householders are [to be served] according to the Vinaya.
According to the established method, a hospitable welcome with material gifts should be extended as appropriate. Furthermore, having approached the visitor, one should ask, "Which reciter are you?
and then ask, "Which texts do your teachers and preceptors study?

If the visitor is unable to answer questions on that subject, one should assist them by speaking oneself, giving gifts, preaching the Dhamma, answering questions, providing meditation subjects, or dispelling their remorse and wrong views, and so forth.

The welcome of the Dhamma should be performed by means of disciplinary acts such as the *parivāsa* (probation) and others, as well as by means of ordination (*pabbajjā*) and full admission (*upasampadā*).
This is the summary here; however, this should be understood in detail, together with the illustrative examples showing its benefits, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.

Skillfulness regarding these two kinds of welcome is "skill in welcoming" (*paṭisanthārakusalatā*); the mental adverting and impulsion consciousnesses belonging to the sense-sphere that proceed accordingly are [the factors involved]. This is the twenty-sixth [chapter].

The state of not guarding the doors of the senses is the lack of restraint regarding the sense-faculties—beginning with the mind as the sixth—with respect to objects such as visible forms that have come into their range, characterized by the grasping of signs and so forth.
Not knowing the proper measure in eating is the lack of moderation in food, consisting of unwholesome states of mind occurring in that manner. This is the twenty-seventh [unwholesome root].
In the subsequent pair as well, the sense-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses accompanied by roots should be understood by way of their opposites.

(Twenty-eighth. Lack of mindfulness, characterized as the state of being forgetful, is *muṭṭhassacca*; all unwholesome states; the state of lacking clear comprehension is *asampajañña*; [this is] delusion (*moha*). (Twenty-ninth.
In the subsequent pair, only mindfulness and wisdom belonging to the four planes are mentioned. (Thirtieth.)
In the sense of being unshakable by non-reflection—which is defined as lack of investigation—it is precisely reflection, defined as wise discernment, that constitutes the power;
this is the power of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*), which is simply wisdom pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-paññā*).

The power of development (*bhāvanābala*) consists of the phenomena belonging to all four planes that proceed by way of the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment and so forth. This is the thirty-first [chapter].

It is called *samatha* because it calms (*sameti*) contrary states (*paccanīkadhamma*). It is threefold: tranquility of mind (*cittasamatha*), tranquility of legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*), and tranquility of all conditioned formations (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*).
Among these, one-pointedness within the eight attainments belonging to the preliminary stage is called tranquility of mind;

the sevenfold method beginning with resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) is called tranquility of legal issues; and Nibbāna is called tranquility of all conditioned formations. But here, however—
The concentration intended here is that belonging to the four planes. It is called *vipassanā* because it sees in various ways by way of impermanence and so forth;
it is indeed mundane and supramundane wisdom consisting of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). [This was] the thirty-second.

It is called the "sign of serenity" (*samatha-nimitta*) because serenity itself, having grasped that aspect, becomes the sign for the further exercise of serenity. The same method applies to the sign of exertion (*paggāha-nimitta*). These are simply the concentration and energy belonging to the four planes. [This was] the thirty-third.
In the immediate pair as well, only energy and concentration are mentioned. [This was] the thirty-fourth.

Failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) is the ruin of virtue, termed non-restraint; it refers to unwholesome states occurring in such a manner. Failure in right view (*diṭṭhivipatti*) is simply wrong view. [This was] the thirty-fifth.
Gentleness itself, because it accomplishes virtue and fulfills virtue, is the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*). That which constitutes the fulfillment of view...
The perfection of view is simply knowledge; thus it is "perfection of view. Both virtue and wisdom belong to the four planes. The same applies to the subsequent dyad. [This is] the thirty-sixth.

Purity of virtue is the purity of virtue termed "virtue" which has attained the state of purification. Purity of view is the purity of view termed "seeing" which is capable of leading one to the purification known as Nibbāna. [This is] the thirty-seventh.

Wisdom associated with the path and fruit that accords with the truth of self-agency (*kammassakatā*) is called purification of view (*diṭṭhi-visuddhi*). Effort in accordance with what has been seen is called "effort according to view.
This is the thirty-eighth [chapter]. The causes known as birth, aging, sickness, and death, which produce a sense of spiritual urgency, are called "objects of urgency" (*saṃvejanīya-ṭṭhāna*).

Among these, the agitation consisting of fear arising from birth and so forth through dependent origination is called "urgency" (*saṃvega*); likewise, the wholesome states and so forth that proceed accordingly [are included].
Thus it is. For one who has thus become stirred by spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), striving with wise means is "wise striving for one stirred by urgency";
this is precisely mundane and supramundane energy (*vīriya*).

[This is] the thirty-ninth. Non-contentment is the state of being unsatisfied in the fulfillment of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). As for one who, having given a gift, is not satisfied with that [gift]:
Having offered the sacrifice, he desires the going for refuge; from there, the five precepts and so forth, the going forth, the learning of the Buddha’s words, and serenity and insight.
Not being satisfied even with that, he gradually attains arahantship;
this is non-contentment with wholesome states. Being weary of the cultivation of further wholesome states, he abandons his striving.
"Causes to turn back" means opposition; that which is not opposed is non-opposition (*appaṭivāni*), and the state of that is non-oppositionality (*appaṭivānitā*).

It is the state of not turning back from striving until arahantship is attained, the state of not shrinking back; likewise, it refers to mundane and supramundane wholesome states as they proceed. This is the fortieth [term].
Knowledge (*vijjā*) is so called because of knowing; it consists of the knowledge of past lives, of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).
Liberation (*vimutti*) is so called because of being liberated; it consists of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) and Nibbāna.

For the eight attainments are called "liberation" in the sense of being resolutely intent upon their object and in the sense of being liberated from the defilements suppressed within themselves, while Nibbāna is liberation in the sense of being absolutely liberated from all defilements. (Forty-first.)
Knowledge regarding the four noble paths that bring about the destruction of the defilements is called "knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*).

Knowledge regarding the noble fruits that have arisen at the conclusion of the non-arising of the respective defilements to be abandoned by each path—being non-arisen by way of rebirth-linking—is called "knowledge of non-arising" (*anuppāde ñāṇa*).
The rest is easy to understand everywhere. This is the forty-second [chapter].
The commentary on the meaning of the Suttantika Duka-mātikā is finished.
The commentary on the meaning of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-mātikā within the Mohavicchedanī Abhidhamma-mātikatthavaṇṇanā is finished.

2. The Matrix of the Vibhaṅga (Vibhaṅgamātikā) Now, following the matrix of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, the commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the *Vibhaṅga* has arrived. Regarding that, [it is said]:
"By way of its meaning, by the classification of phenomena, and by the demonstration of the method of analysis..."
There is also a method of commentary that is independent of the canonical text (pāḷi).
This, moreover, is established at the beginning of the eighteen Vibhaṅgas and consists of eighteen types:

the matrices for the Analysis of the Aggregates, the Bases, the Elements, the Truths, the Faculties, the Modes of Conditionality, the Foundations of Mindfulness, the Right Exertions, the Bases of Psychic Power, the Factors of Enlightenment, the Path Factors, the Meditations, the Illimitables, the Training Precepts, the Analytical Knowledges, the Knowledge, the Minor Matters, and the Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix for the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā). Regarding that, first, as to the meaning of the matrix for the analysis of the aggregates which stands at the beginning: in the phrase "the five aggregates" (*pañcakkhandhā*), "five" (*pañca*) is a numerical delimitation;
by this, it shows that there are neither fewer than that nor more. "Aggregates" (*khandhā*) is an indication of the phenomena so delimited.
In this context, the word *khandha* applies to several meanings: as a heap, as a quality, as a designation, and as a conventional term.

Therein, in expressions such as “a great mass of water,” *khandha* refers to a heap. In expressions such as “the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)” and “the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*),” it refers to a quality.
In expressions such as “the Blessed One saw a large log (*dārukkhandha*),” it refers to a designation. [And] “consciousness (*viññāṇa*)...”

In such passages as "the aggregate of consciousness" (*viññāṇakkhandho*), even a single state of mind is called an "aggregate" (*khandha*) by way of conventional usage; however, here it is intended in the sense of a "heap.
For the word *khandha* has the meaning of a heap, and it is also appropriate to say it has the meaning of a "portion" (*koṭṭhāsa*).
In the world, people who have taken a loan and are being pressed for payment say, "We will pay in two installments," or "We will pay in three installments"; therefore, it is called an "aggregate."
"Component" (koṭṭhāsa) is what is meant. Regarding "the aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandha): here, it is called "form" (rūpa) because it is "formed" (ruppati).
It is formed, struck, and oppressed by cold, heat, and so forth; this is the meaning. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"It is formed, monks, therefore it is called 'form. By what is it formed? It is formed by cold, it is formed by heat, it is formed by hunger, and it is formed by thirst," and so on.

That which is both form (*rūpa*) and an aggregate (*khandha*) is the "form aggregate" (*rūpakkhandha*); the meaning is a heap of form, a division of form. This same method applies to the feeling aggregate (*vedanākkhandha*) and the others; this, then, is the method of commentary here according to the meaning.

Regarding the classification of phenomena (*dhamma*), however, all material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*)—divided into the categories of past and so forth as analyzed below in the "Triad of the Wholesome"—are called the form aggregate.
Likewise, feelings and perceptions belonging to the four planes are called the feeling aggregate and the perception aggregate (*saññākkhandha*).
Feeling and perception, however, with the exception of these two, the remaining fifty mental factors beginning with contact are called the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
Among the five aggregates, only Nibbāna is not included; among the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), however, all supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are excluded.

This indeed is the distinction between the aggregates (khandha) and the aggregates of clinging. The aggregates are spoken of without distinction, whereas the aggregates of clinging are [distinguished].

Having distinguished [them] by way of being accompanied by taints (*āsava*) and subject to clinging (*upādāniya*). Here, however, because they are stated without distinction, all remaining phenomena (*dhamma*), with the exception of Nibbāna, are included;
this is the method of commentary according to the classification of phenomena.
"Showing the method of the *Vibhaṅga*" means showing the method of the meaning as it appears in the *Vibhaṅga* text. For in the *Vibhaṅga* text...

The Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga) is analyzed by way of three methods: the Suttanta-analysis, the Abhidhamma-analysis, and the interrogation (Pañhāpucchaka). The same applies to the Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga) and the others.
However, in the Analysis of the Faculties (Indriyavibhaṅga) and the Analysis of the Training Precepts (Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga), there is no Suttanta-analysis;
and in the Analysis of the Modes of Conditionality (Paccayākāravibhaṅga), there is no interrogation. [This is also the case] in the Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga) and so forth.
However, among the three [sections], there are no [further] three methods (*naya*). For among them, the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* is analyzed from one kind up to ten kinds;
the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga* is analyzed from one kind up to sixty-two divisions;
and the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, moreover, is analyzed by means of the ten sections beginning with "The All-Inclusive" (*sabbasaṅgaha*). Therefore, for each of those...

There will be explanations here and there by way of showing the mere headings of the methods (*naya*). In this regard, here is the demonstration of the mere headings of the three methods in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*.
That is to say: first, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is as follows:
"In that context, what is the aggregate of form? Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or..."

“Whatever form there is—whether external or internal, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that, having been gathered together and condensed into one, is called the aggregate of form.
Having thus stated it in brief, it is analyzed in detail; likewise for the aggregates of feeling and the rest. Therein, “one’s own internal” (niyakajjhatta) refers to...
That which is internal materiality is called "internal"; that which is other than this, pertaining to another person, as well as non-conscious matter, is called "external.
The same applies to feeling and the other aggregates. Furthermore, the materiality of the sensitive faculties and their objects is called "gross," while the remainder is called "subtle.
Unpleasant materiality is called "inferior," and pleasant materiality is called "excellent."
Now, is it not the case that what is called "the desirable" and "the undesirable" is not divided into separate categories?

For one thing may be desirable and pleasing to one person, yet that very same thing is undesirable to another. Indeed, garments and such things are not dear to pigs and the like, whereas they are dear to humans and others;
likewise, ornaments and such things are dear to those [humans] but not to pigs and the like. Therefore...
Should the state of being desirable or undesirable be grasped solely by way of personal preference (*ruci*)? No, because desirables and undesirables are analyzed separately.

For that which is born of wholesome karma is called "desirable" only when it is the object of a wholesome result; that which is born of unwholesome karma is called "undesirable" only when it is the object of an unwholesome result.

However, due to a perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), someone might attend to something that is actually desirable—such as the form of the Buddha—as undesirable at the moment of impulsion (*javana*).

One performs [an action], and one regards what is undesirable—such as the fires of hell, weapons, and poison—as desirable. The state of perversion occurs through the impulsion-moments (*javana*) alone, not through the resultant-moments (*vipāka*);
therefore, the desirable and undesirable nature [of results] should be understood as determined by way of their resultants.
However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*:
“For the mire of excrement, though pleasant to touch, is undesirable at the eye-door and nose-door, yet it is desirable at the body-door.
To a Wheel-turning Monarch being struck by the jewel-treasure and impaled on a golden stake,
the jewel-treasure and the golden stake are desirable at the eye-door, but undesirable at the body-door.”
Thus, by way of the door, both the desirability and undesirability of a single object have been explained.

However, these two cannot occur at one and the same moment, because the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) contained within a single group arise from a single common cause.

For when the primary elements arise as undesirable through the influence of unwholesome states, the derived matter and so forth arising from them do not arise as desirable through wholesome states; they arise at different moments.
However, for one who is being struck by desirable things such as jewels and gems, undesirable things arise through the transformation of the temperature-element conditioned by unwholesome states;
and through wholesome conditions, undesirable things such as excrement and mud transform into desirable things—this is our own opinion.
And among these desirable and undesirable things thus analyzed, each respective form should be seen as either inferior or superior according to its specific nature.
Subtle matter, however, is called "distant matter," while gross matter is called "near matter.
Alternatively, depending on this or that particular matter, matter may be regarded as distant or near. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding feeling and the other aggregates, however, unwholesome feeling is gross, while the other is subtle. Wholesome and unwholesome [feelings] are gross, while the indeterminate are subtle.
Subtle. Painful feeling is gross; the other is subtle. Or, pleasant and painful feelings are gross; the other is subtle.

Or, the feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross; that of one who has attained is subtle. That which is with taints (*sāsrava*) is gross; that which is without taints (*anāsrava*) is subtle.
Furthermore, the grossness and subtlety should be understood in relation to this or that specific feeling. Unwholesome feeling...

Feeling should be understood as "distant" according to the method explained above through the distinctions of genus, nature, person, and plane—such as wholesome and indeterminate feelings being distant from one another, and those [indeterminate ones] being distant from that [wholesome feeling].
Feeling should be understood as "near" through the commonality of genus and so forth—such as wholesome feeling being near to wholesome feeling.
Furthermore, feeling should be understood as distant or near in relation to this or that particular feeling. Thus...

In the case of the aggregate of perception and the others as well, their relative grossness, subtlety, and so forth, should be understood according to their respective natures. This is the summary here;
however, the detailed exposition should be taken from the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi* and its commentaries. This is the method of the Suttanta-bhājaniya.

As for the method of the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), [the classification] begins from the "onefold" and so on, up to the "elevenfold," as set forth in the *Rūpakanda*.
They are to be understood according to the method already stated. As for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*), it is of one kind when associated with contact (*phassa*);

of two kinds by way of the dyad of "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*) and "without root-cause"; of three kinds by way of the triad of the wholesome (*kusala*); of four kinds by way of the four planes (*bhūmi*);

of five kinds by way of the distinction of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); of six kinds by way of the six doors (*dvāra*); of seven kinds by way of association with the seven types of consciousness; and of eight kinds among those [seven]...
Having divided the [states] associated with body-consciousness into two types by way of pleasure and pain, making nine;
and having further divided those associated with mind-consciousness into three types by way of the wholesome triad, making ten;

and having then divided within those the states associated with body-consciousness into two and the states associated with mind-consciousness into three—thus, after stating the first section based on the "Rooted-with-cause" dyad:
Furthermore, in the section on the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*), after joining all the triads— excluding the triad of feeling (*vedanāttika*),
the triad of zest (*pītittika*), and the triad of the visible (*sanidassanattika*)— up to ten types, eighteen other sections are stated.

And just as here the application of all the triads is based on the dyad of "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*), so too, for each [of the following], there is an application of all the triads based on the appropriate dyads, beginning with the dyad of "associated with root-cause" (*hetusampayutta*) and ending with the dyad of "having an object" (*sārammaṇa*).
"Should be understood"—this is the method based on pairs (*dukamūlaka*).

Just as the method based on pairs has been explained by way of applying each individual pair to all the triads (*ttika*), so too should the method based on triads (*tikamūlaka*) be understood by way of applying each individual triad to all the pairs as appropriate, and the method of "increasing from both sides" (*ubhatovaḍḍhanaka*) by way of mixing both of these. And just as it is here in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), [so it is elsewhere].

In this way, the method of the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya should be understood as applying the "rooted in pairs" (duka-mūlaka) and other schemes to the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha) and the others as appropriate. However, in the method of the *Pañhāpucchaka* (The Questions and Answers), one asks:
"Of the five aggregates, how many are wholesome (*kusala*), how many unwholesome (*akusala*), how many indeterminate (*abyākata*)?

How many are associated with pleasant feeling (*sukhāya vedanāya sampayutta*)... [and so on] ...how many are with conflict (*saraṇa*), and how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)? The aggregate of form (*rūpa-khandha*) is indeterminate.
The four aggregates may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Form, feeling, and perception are not to be mentioned in the triad of feeling;

the remaining [aggregates] belong to all three types. Form is neither-result-nor-dhamma-of-result; it may be acquired and subject to clinging, or it may be unacquired and subject to clinging, and it is undefiled and non-defiling.
The remaining four aggregates [are treated] by means of the three triads.

They are also threefold. Matter is without initial application and without sustained application (*avitakka-avicāra*). The three aggregates (*khandha*) are threefold; the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is both threefold and not so classifiable.
Matter is not so classifiable. Feeling may be accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*), or it may not be so classifiable;

the [other] three are both threefold and not so classifiable. Matter is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation (*nevadassanena-nabhāvanāya-pahātabba*); it does not have as its cause that which is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.

Neither leading to accumulation nor leading to diminution, neither trainee nor post-trainee, and limited—these are of three kinds; the rest are of all three kinds. In the triad of limited objects, matter is objectless;
the rest are of three kinds and also not so classifiable. Matter is intermediate and indeterminate; the rest are of all three kinds.
In the triad of path-objects, matter is objectless; the rest are either of all three kinds or not so classifiable. Regarding the triads of arisen and past: [matter is]... (as above).
The five [aggregates] are also threefold. In the triad of past objects, matter is without an object; the remaining [four aggregates] are both threefold and not so expressible.
In the triad of internal [objects], all five are threefold. In the triad of internal objects, matter is without an object;
the remaining [four aggregates] are neither threefold nor so expressible. The four aggregates are non-demonstrable and non-reacting; the aggregate of matter is threefold.
The four aggregates are not roots; the aggregate of mental formations may be a root or may not be a root.

Matter is without root and dissociated from roots; the remaining [aggregates] are both ways. Three aggregates may be accompanied by roots but are not themselves roots, or they may be so that they cannot be so described;
the aggregate of mental formations is both ways and cannot be so described; matter cannot be so described at all.
The same applies to the subsequent dyad as well. Matter is neither-root nor rootless; the [other] three aggregates are both;
the aggregate of mental formations is both and is also not so stated. All five are conditioned by causes, are conditioned, and four are non-demonstrable and non-reactive;
matter is both. Matter is material; the rest are immaterial. Matter is mundane; the rest are both. All five are [associated] with something...
They are cognizable, yet not cognizable by anyone. The four [noble] outflows are neither; formations are both; and some are not to be so described.
Form is accompanied by an outflow and dissociated from an outflow; the remaining [aggregates] are both. Form is both accompanied by an outflow and not itself an outflow;
three [aggregates] are likewise both and not to be so described. Formations are both and not to be so described. Form is simply not to be so described.

The three [aggregates] may be associated with the taints (*āsava*) but are not themselves taints; they may also be such that it cannot be said [of them]. Volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are of two kinds and also such that it cannot be said [of them].
Matter (*rūpa*) is dissociated from the taints and yet is subject to the taints; the remaining [aggregates] are of two kinds and also such that it cannot be said [of them].
By this method, the application should be understood for the group of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth as well. For in the dyad of "associated with misapprehension" (*parāmāsa*), only...

Form is dissociated from the outflows; the other three are both [associated and dissociated]; and volitional formations are both [associated and dissociated], though they cannot be said to be so by way of views.
This much is the distinction in the third [section]. Form is without an object; the rest have objects. Consciousness is mind;
the rest are not mind. Three are mental factors; two are not mental factors. Three are associated with consciousness; form is dissociated from consciousness.

Consciousness (viññāṇa) is not to be so stated. The same applies to the pair on "associated with consciousness" (cittasaṃsaṭṭha). Three are "originated by consciousness" (cittasamuṭṭhāna); consciousness is not originated by consciousness.

Matter (rūpa) is of both kinds. The same applies to the two subsequent pairs. Three are "associated with and originated by consciousness"; two are neither associated with nor originated by consciousness.
The same applies to the two subsequent pairs. Consciousness is internal (ajjhattika).

The three external [bases] and form are both [types]. The four [mental aggregates] are not clinging. Form is both [types]. All five may be acquired (upādinnā), may be unacquired (anupādinnā), and are not clinging (no upādānā).

The group of defilements is exactly as previously stated. Form is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation; the remaining [factors] are both [types]. Thus the application should be understood up to the "duad of joy."

Form is not feeling, not pleasant, and not accompanied by pleasure; the remaining [factors] are both [pleasant and accompanied by pleasure]. The same applies to the next pair. Form belongs to the sense-sphere; the remaining [factors] are both [belonging to the sense-sphere and belonging to the fine-material sphere]. In this manner, the application should be understood up to the pair on "with a basis. This is the method of interrogation.

These methods, however, should be known in detail from the Pāḷi and its commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*). And their analysis of meaning is found in the commentary on the matrix (*Mātikā*) of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

It should be understood according to what has been stated. Hereafter, without saying more than is necessary, we shall explain only what has not been mentioned before; thus concludes this method of commentary by way of showing the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga-naya*).
Now, however, herein— By way of order, deficiency, and excess; By way of what is to be seen, and by way of equal divisions;
The method independent of the canonical text (pāḷimuttanaya) should be understood as the desire for proficiency in the Khandhas.

Therein, regarding "order" (kama): among the many kinds of order—such as the order of arising, the order of abandoning, the order of practice, the order of planes, and the order of teaching—it is only the order of teaching that is appropriate for the exposition of the aggregates (khandhā), not the others, because they are impossible [in this context]. Without distinction...
Indeed, desiring to liberate those people to be trained— who had fallen into the grasping for a self within the five aggregates—
by means of seeing the analysis of what was previously perceived as a solid mass, the Blessed One, wishing their welfare, first taught the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*),
which is gross and constitutes the objects of the eye and other senses, so that they might easily grasp it; thereafter, [he taught] that which experiences desirable and undesirable objects.
"One perceives whatever gross feeling one feels"—thus perception (*saññā*) is that which grasps the aspect of the object of feeling;

then there are the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) which construct by way of perception; and then consciousness (*viññāṇa*), which serves as the support and the dominant factor for those [mental states] beginning with feeling.
This, then, is the sequence here.
But why did the Blessed One teach exactly five aggregates, neither fewer nor more? It is because all conditioned phenomena are subsumed under their respective homogeneous classes;
because this is the ultimate extent of the basis for the grasping of "self" and "belonging to self"; and because all other [categories] are included within them.
For when the variously classified conditioned phenomena are grouped according to their commonality, form is subsumed by way of its inclusion within the homogeneous class of form.
There is one aggregate; feeling is one aggregate by way of being included within its own class of feeling. This same method applies to perception and the others as well;
therefore, they are stated as five because of their inclusion within their respective classes of all conditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, this is the ultimate basis for the grasping of "self" and "belonging to self," namely these five beginning with form; therefore, it is also [stated as five] because this is the ultimate extent of the basis for the grasping of "self" and "belonging to self."

Only five are mentioned. Furthermore, those other five aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) beginning with virtue (sīla) that have been taught are also included right here, because they are comprised within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
Therefore, even because of their inclusion therein, only five are mentioned; this is [the explanation] by way of neither deficiency nor excess.

"By way of the equality of what is to be seen and the divisions" means by way of the diversity of what is to be seen and by way of the diversity of similes. Therein, "by way of the diversity of what is to be seen":

To begin with, the five aggregates of clinging should be viewed collectively as an enemy with raised sword, as a burden, as a consumer, and as a murderer characterized by impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Specifically, however, form should be viewed like a lump of foam;
feeling and the others should be viewed respectively like a water bubble, a mirage, the trunk of a plantain tree, and an illusion.
It should be seen thus: Just as a mass of foam cannot withstand being crushed, and even when taken for the purpose of making a bowl or a basin, it does not fulfill that purpose but breaks apart;
in the same way, form also cannot withstand being crushed, and even when perceived by way of beauty and so forth, it does not remain as such, but becomes only the foul and so on.
Or, just as a mass of foam is composed of many joints and is the dwelling place of many aquatic creatures such as snakes;
and how it initially arises only the size of a ripe jujube fruit and grows gradually, yet even when just arisen it breaks up, or after traveling a short distance,
and having reached the ocean it inevitably breaks up— so too, form is perforated and full of holes, composed of many joints.
It is strewn with eighty thousand families of worms; from its very beginning it exists merely as *kalala*, growing gradually thereafter. Even while in the state of *kalala*, it breaks up;
and even in the states of *abbuda* and so forth, having reached the end of its lifespan, it inevitably breaks up. Thus, it should be regarded as being like a mass of foam.
Furthermore, just as a bubble is delightful for only a moment, cannot be grasped, and does not endure for long, so too is feeling (*vedanā*). Just as...

And just as a bubble arises dependent upon four conditions—the surface of the water, a drop of water, the froth of water gathered and formed into a mass, and the wind that seizes it—so too, feeling arises dependent upon four conditions: the physical basis, the object, the froth of defilements, and the impact of contact; thus, it should be regarded as being like a bubble.
Just as a mirage deceives by appearing as a body of water and so forth, so too perception (saññā) deceives by appearing as permanent and so forth;

thus, it should be regarded as similar to a mirage. Just as the trunk of a plantain tree is unfit for grasping and is a mere collection of many layers, so too the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is unfit for grasping, being devoid of any core such as permanence, and is a mere collection of many phenomena such as contact (phassa).
And because it exists [only momentarily], it should be regarded as similar to the trunk of a plantain tree.

Just as an illusion deceives the multitude by making them perceive forms such as gold and silver that are not actually gold or silver, so too consciousness deceives by making one perceive its impermanent nature and so forth as being permanent and so on—as if it were arriving with that very same mind. Thus, it should be regarded as similar to an illusion. And it has been said:
“Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a bubble;
perception is like a mirage, volitional formations are like a plantain tree;
and consciousness is like an illusion—thus has it been taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.”
This is the classification of what is to be seen herein.
Furthermore, according to the classification of similes: the aggregate of clinging to form is like a sickroom; the aggregate of clinging to feeling is like the illness;
the aggregate of clinging to perception is like the origin of the illness; and the aggregate of clinging to volitional formations is like the indulgence in unwholesome things.
The aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging is like a sick person. Furthermore, these [aggregates] are like a prison, the act of imprisoning, the perpetrator of the crime, and the offender;
they are also like a vessel, food, condiments, a server, and an eater. This is the classification of similes here.
Thus should the method of analysis independent of the canonical text be understood.
The commentary on the meaning of the summary matrix for the Analysis of the Aggregates is finished.

Now, regarding the commentary on the meaning of the summary matrix for the Analysis of the Bases (*āyatana-vibhaṅga-mātikā*), first in terms of the meaning: concerning the phrase "the twelve bases," here [it refers to] from the perspective of being a base (*āyatana*) and of the coming (*āyāna*).
They are called *āyatanas* because they extend (*tanana*) and because they lead forward what has come (*āyatassa nayanato*).

For, in the case of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, the mental states and mental factors—by means of their respective functions such as experiencing—extend toward, present themselves before, or exert themselves toward their respective doors and objects;
and these [bases] extend and expand those very phenomena that constitute the "coming" (*āya*). Furthermore, this suffering of saṃsāra is exceedingly long-extended (*āyata*).
They lead [the mind], which is to say they cause it to proceed; therefore, they are called "bases" (*āyatana*).
Furthermore, in both the Teaching and in the world, things are called "bases" in the sense of being a place of residence, a source, a meeting place, a designation for a specific birth, and a cause.
For within the eye and the other [senses], those various states of mind and mental factors—

Phenomena dwell [in them] because their existence is dependent upon them; and they are crowded together within those [bases] which serve as their source, both by way of being the physical locus and by way of being the objective field.
The eye and so forth are indeed their place of birth and their cause. Therefore, the eye and so forth should be understood as "bases" (āyatana) in the sense of being a dwelling place and so on.

Regarding the terms "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth: it is called the "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees; the meaning is that it experiences and discerns visible form (*rūpa*). It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is manifested;
the meaning is that by undergoing a change in color, it makes manifest its state as being present in the heart. It is called the "ear" (*sota*) because it hears.

It is called "sound" (*sadda*) because it resounds; the meaning is that it is articulated. It is called the "nose" (*ghāna*) because it smells. It is called "odor" (*gandha*) because it perfumes itself...
The meaning is that it indicates its object. It is called the tongue (*jivhā*) because it beckons toward life. It is called taste (*rasa*) because beings relish it; the meaning is that they enjoy it.
It is called the body (*kāya*) because it is the source (*āya*) of base, tainted phenomena; it is the locus of their arising. It is called the tangible (*phoṭṭhabba*) because it is touched.
It is called the mind (*mano*) because it cognizes. They are called phenomena (*dhammā*) because they bear their own characteristics. And the eye is [defined] by the meaning as previously stated.

Regarding the term "base" (*āyatana*): the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*)... [and so on] ...and those phenomena (*dhammā*) which are also a base, thus it is the "phenomena-base" (*dhammāyatana*). This, first of all, is the meaning of the words here.
In terms of the classification of phenomena (*dhamma*), however, all consciousness (*viññāṇa*) here is called the mind-base (*manāyatana*).

Mental factors (*cetasika*), subtle matter (*sukhumarūpa*), and Nibbāna are called the phenomena-base (*dhammāyatana*). The remaining bases are easy to understand. And among these bases, those distinguished by divisions such as the past and so forth, as well as those free from time (*kālavinimutta*), [are included].
It should be understood that all mundane and supramundane phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), as well as designations (paññatti), are included herein.

For, according to such statements as, "Birth is included by two aggregates, one base, and one element," the characteristics of material and immaterial phenomena—namely birth, aging, and dissolution—are included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), and the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu); and because of this, the others are also [included].
The manner in which the various designations are included therein as appropriate should be understood; this is the classification of the phenomena (*dhamma*) here.
According to the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga-naya*), first, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, it is stated: "The eye is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change.
Visible forms are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change... [and so on] ... mental objects (*dhammā*) are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change."
Thus, the bases (āyatana) have been explained by way of the sense-faculties and their objects; this is the method of the Suttanta-bhajaniya.
In the Abhidhamma-bhajaniya, however, the sense-faculties and their objects are analyzed according to the method stated in the Rūpa-kanda, beginning with: "Therein, what is the eye-base?
It is that sensitivity derived from the four great elements which is the eye," and so forth.

The mind-base (*manāyatana*), however, is analyzed according to the method explained in the section on the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) from its singlefold division up to its eightfold division.

As for the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), it is introduced as follows: "In this context, what is the mental-object-base? It is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, that form which is non-manifest and non-reactive and is included within the mental-object-base, and the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatā dhātu*). Having thus indicated it, [it is further detailed].

Therein, the analysis of the aggregate of feeling and so forth is explained according to the method stated in the [respective] sections on the aggregate of feeling and the rest, beginning with the words, “What therein is the aggregate of feeling?
Subtle matter and Nibbāna are exactly as explained in the section on matter (*rūpakanda*). This is the method of the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya.

However, not showing the method of the Question-and-Answer (*pañhāpucchaka*) in detail from this point onward, [I shall explain it] by means of the beginning and end of the triplets (*tika*) and couplets (*duka*).
We shall demonstrate [this] by applying the triads and dyads that illuminate specific meanings;
the method of application for the remaining triads and dyads can be understood according to the method explained for the aggregates. How many of the twelve bases are wholesome...
pe ...how many are without conflict (araṇa)? Ten bases are indeterminate; two bases may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate.

In the triad of feeling (*vedanāttika*), ten bases (*āyatana*) are not to be described [as having feeling]; the mind base (*manāyatana*) is to be described in all three ways; and the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) is not to be described in any of the three ways...
[and so on] ...the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) is visible and impinging; nine bases are invisible and impinging; the mind base and the mental-object base are invisible and non-impinging;
eleven bases are not roots (*na hetu*); the mental-object base...
It may be a cause, it may not be a cause... [and so on] ... eleven bases are with conditions; the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) may be with conditions, it may be without conditions...
[and so on] ... ten bases are form; the mind base (manāyatana) is non-form; the base of mental phenomena is both... [and so on] ...
ten bases are without conflict (araṇa); two bases may be with conflict, they may be without conflict—this is the method of interrogation.
Now, however,
