the exposition here should be understood according to the method independent of the canonical text (pāḷimuttanaya), by way of their order, their number, and the distinctions in how they are to be seen.
In this context, "by way of order" refers here as well to the sequence of the teaching.

For among the internal bases (*āyatana*), the eye-base is taught first because it is manifest due to having a visible and impinging object; following that are the ear-base and so forth, which have invisible but impinging objects.
Alternatively, the eye and ear bases are taught first because they are of great benefit, being the causes for the unsurpassed sight and the unsurpassed hearing.
First, the [eye] bases were taught; then the three beginning with the nose base; then, because it is the objective domain for all five, the mind base (*manāyatana*) is placed at the end;
and because they are the objective domains for the eye base and so forth, the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) and the others follow immediately after them.

Furthermore, this sequence should be understood from the perspective of defining the causes for the arising of consciousness. For it has been said: "Dependent upon the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises... [and so on]."
“Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises”—this, first, is the sequence here.
“So far” means to that extent. This is what is meant: for the eye and so forth are also just *dhammas*.
This being so, if one were to say simply “the *dhammāyatana*,” why were twelve bases taught instead? [It is] because of the arising of the groups of consciousness.
These are stated as twelve because their distinction lies in the determination of their respective doors and objects.

For the body of consciousness comprised within the visual-consciousness process, the eye-base alone is the door of its arising, and the form-base alone is its object. Likewise, the other [bases] are the doors and objects for the others.
However, for the sixth [consciousness], the door of its arising is only a portion of the mind-base, which is reckoned as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

And the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) is the uncommon object. Thus, twelve are stated because of the determination of the doors of arising and the objects for the six groups of consciousness;
this, firstly, is the essential nature here.
As for "the distinction of what is to be seen": herein, all these bases (*āyatana*) are [defined] by way of non-coming and non-going.
And they are to be seen thus: for they do not come from anywhere prior to their arising, nor do they go anywhere after their passing away;

rather, having no inherent nature acquired prior to their arising and having their inherent nature dissolved after their passing away, they proceed in dependence on conditions—powerless in the interval between the past and the future—and therefore, because they have no coming...
They should also be regarded as being without exit. Likewise, they are without effort and without activity.
For it does not occur to the eye, visible forms, and so forth, "O, may consciousness indeed arise through our combination!
Nor do they engage in any activity for the sake of producing consciousness, whether by way of being a door, a basis, or an object; rather, this is simply the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
Since eye-consciousness and the rest arise from the assemblage of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, they should therefore be regarded as inactive and devoid of functional effort.
Furthermore, the internal bases should be regarded as like an empty village because they are bereft of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and a self;
the external bases should be regarded as like the thieves who plunder that village. Likewise, the internal bases should be regarded as like six living beings, and the external bases...
"Like their respective spheres"—this is the classification to be understood here. Thus should the exposition be known according to the method set forth in the Pāḷi.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga).
Regarding the *Dhātuvibhaṅga-mātikā*, first as to the meaning: "The eighteen elements" (*aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo*).

Here, it is called an *dhātu* because it heats up (*vidahati*), is held (*dhīyate*), is a disposition (*vidhāna*), is disposed by means of this (*vidhīyate etāya*), or that which is held therein (*ettha vā dhīyati*). For mundane elements are established as causal factors;
they heat up—that is, they produce—the manifold suffering of *saṃsāra*, and they are held by sentient beings.
They are "elements" (dhātus) because they are merely the instruments of suffering; for by these causes, the suffering of saṃsāra is brought about by sentient beings,
and the suffering as it has been ordained is held and placed within them— thus, according to these meanings as applicable,
they are called "elements."

Or, just as the designation "element" (*dhātu*) is applied to the taste, blood, and so forth— which are the constituent parts of the aggregate called the body and which are delimited by mutually distinct characteristics—
so too should the designation "element" be understood for the eye and the other [faculties] within this personal existence (*attabhāva*) termed the five aggregates.
Furthermore, they are called "elements" because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), in the sense of being common to both the mundane and the supramundane.

This is a designation for what is merely soulless (*nijjīva-mattā*); therefore, in the sense already stated, it is "eye" and it is a "constituent" (*dhātu*), thus "eye-constituent" (*cakkhudhātu*). The same applies to the rest. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.

As for the classification of phenomena (*dhamma-bheda*), it should be understood here according to the method explained under the bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, there is the five-door adverting consciousness, the two types of receiving consciousness, and the [five] sense-consciousnesses.

The mind element (manodhātu) is as follows: all consciousness, with the exception of the five types of sensory consciousness and the mind element itself, is called the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu).
The rest is easily understood.

According to the method of analysis (vibhaṅganaya), first, in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, it is stated: “the earth element, water element, fire element, air element, space element, and consciousness element.”
Having listed six elements, the first five are analyzed according to the internal and external division, and the last six according to the division of consciousness.

Furthermore, another set of six elements is listed—namely, the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of joy, the element of grief, the element of equanimity, and the element of ignorance—and these are likewise analyzed accordingly.
Again, another set is listed: the element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-cruelty.

Having enumerated the six elements, it should be understood that in this way, by means of three sets of six, the eighteen elements belonging to the three planes are explained individually according to their intrinsic nature, their characteristics, their sustenance, and their support, object, function, and inseparability; such is the method of the Suttanta-bhājaniya.

In the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, however, having enumerated the eighteen elements according to their intrinsic nature, the elements of the sensitive faculties and their objects are analyzed according to the method stated for the *āyatanas*, while the seven consciousness-elements—
“In this context, what is the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*)? Depending on the eye and forms, consciousness arises... [as before] ...this is called the eye-consciousness element...
up to ...the body-consciousness element. “In this context, what is the mind element (*manodhātu*)? Immediately after the cessation of the eye-consciousness element...
[as before] ...up to ...the body-consciousness element... consciousness arises. Or else, consciousness arises as the first application of attention toward all phenomena... [as before] ...”
This is called the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
"In that regard, what is the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*)? It is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations;

and whatever form is non-manifesting and non-reactive, included within the sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*); and the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatā dhātu*)... [and so forth]... This is [the mental-object element].
This is called the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).

“In this context, what is the element of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)? … [as before] … Immediately after it has arisen and ceased, consciousness arises through the mind-element (*manodhātu*) … [as before] … Depending on the mind and mental phenomena, consciousness arises … [as before] … This is called the element of mind-consciousness.”
"...the mind-consciousness element"—thus it is analyzed.

Therein, regarding the phrase "or else, among all phenomena, the first act of attention," the meaning should be understood as "among all phenomena that are objects of the five types of sensory consciousness.
Also, immediately after [the mind-element] has arisen and ceased, by means of the mind-element...

In this context, however, the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion; therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "by means of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as well as the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), such as investigating (*santīraṇa*), determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "dependent on the mind" (*manañ ca paṭicca*), the meaning is that in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), the impulsion (*javana*) accompanied by the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) arises dependent upon both the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅgamanas*) and the object consisting of phenomena belonging to the four planes of existence. This is the method of the Abhidhamma-Bhājanīya.
In the method of interrogation by questions, however: "Of the eighteen elements, how many are wholesome... [and so on] ...how many are without conflict (araṇā)?
Sixteen elements are indeterminate (abyākata); two elements are of three kinds... [and so on] ...ten elements are neither-resultants-nor-dhammas-of-the-resultant-state;
five elements are resultants; the mind-element may be a resultant, or it may be neither-resultant-nor-dhamma-of-the-resultant-state.
Two elements are of all three kinds. Ten elements are acquired and subject to clinging; the sound element is not acquired but subject to clinging;
five elements may be either acquired and subject to clinging or not acquired but subject to clinging; two elements are of all three kinds...
[and so on] ...ten elements may be either arisen or bound to arise; the sound element may be either arisen or unarisen.
It may be said that they are "arisen," yet the six elements are [not] in all three ways. The mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) is likewise in all three ways... [etc.

...The visible element with resistance (*rūpadhātu*) is with visibility and with resistance; nine elements are without visibility but with resistance; eight elements are without visibility and without resistance.
Seventeen elements are not roots (*na hetū*); the mental-object element is twofold... [etc. ...Sixteen elements are without conflict (*araṇā*); two elements are [with conflict].
"In both ways" refers to this method of posing questions.
Now, however, these [dependent originations] are to be understood: "According to their sequence and repetition, and according to the classification of the conditions."
Herein, the exposition of the elements (dhātu) should be understood as an analysis independent of the canonical text.
Regarding that, first of all, the order of presentation is appropriate here as well. And this [order] is stated by way of the successive determination of cause and fruit.
For the dyad consisting of the eye-element and the form-element is the cause, while the eye-consciousness-element is the fruit.
Thus it is in all cases. This, then, is the sequence here.

Furthermore, those elements (dhātu) which are stated here in the Suttanta-bhājaniya by way of three sets of six, as well as those that appear in various passages of the Suttas and Abhidhamma such as "the light element...
the world with its many elements and manifold elements," and so forth—[all these are included].
Furthermore, many other elements (dhātu) are observed; why, then, are only eighteen mentioned without specifying a limit even for those?
Because they are included within those very eighteen.

Moreover, regarding consciousness (viññāṇa), whose intrinsic nature is cognizing, for those who perceive it as a "living soul" (jīva), its manifoldness through the divisions of eye-consciousness and so forth—

Having demonstrated impermanence by way of the eye’s dependence on conditions such as visible forms, eighteen [bases] were stated for the purpose of uprooting the notion of a "living being" (jīva-saññā) that has long been latent therein.
Furthermore, it is also by way of the inclinations of those to be trained (veneyya).

For those to be trained are of three kinds: those deluded regarding the formless, those deluded regarding form, and those deluded regarding both. For all three of them, respectively, [the bases were taught] neither too concisely nor too diffusely.

The teaching on the aggregates (*khandha*) is suitable for those who wish to discern the classification of the formless; the teaching on the bases (*āyatana*) is suitable for those who wish to discern the classification of form;

and the teaching on the elements (*dhātu*) is suitable for those who wish to discern the classification of both. Thus, eighteen [teachings] were spoken according to the inclinations of those to be trained. And it is said:
“For, by way of summary and detail, in such and such a manner...”
"He proclaims the Dhamma in whatever manner is appropriate for each;
by the power of the True Dhamma, the darkness within the hearts of those beings who are ready to be trained is dispelled and vanishes in an instant."
This much, then, is the essence of the matter here.

As for how they are to be viewed: all these conditioned elements (saṅkhata-dhātu) are to be seen as secluded from the past and the future, as empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and a self-entity, and as existing in dependence upon conditions.
Specifically, however, the eye-element is to be viewed here like the surface of a drum.
The visible-form element is like the stick, and the eye-consciousness element is like the sound.

Likewise, these three should be seen respectively as the surface of a mirror, the face, and the reflection of the face; or as the sesame seeds, the press, and the oil; or as the lower fire-drill, the upper fire-drill, and the fire.

This same method applies to the ear-element and the others as well. However, the mind-element should be understood according to its occurrence in relation to the eye-consciousness element and the rest.

The preceding and following [elements] are to be regarded as like attendants. Within the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), however, feeling (vedanā) is to be regarded as like an arrow-thrusting wound;

perception (saññā) as like an empty fist; mental formations (saṅkhārā) as like a poisonous tree; subtle form (sukhumarūpa) as like a razor-wheel; and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatā dhātu) as like a land of safety.
But the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is to be regarded as like a monkey, like a wild colt—falling wherever it pleases.
It should be regarded as like a stick thrown into the air or like an actor on a stage. This is the manner of viewing it here.

As for the analysis of the conditions: for eye-consciousness-element, the eye is the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), visible form is the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the functional mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*) is the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and the three immaterial aggregates are the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). The same applies to ear-consciousness and the others.

Furthermore, regarding the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), the mind element (*manodhātu*) is its proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*), the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) is its object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), and the associated, support, and conascent conditions are also present;
such is the analysis of conditions. Thus should the exposition independent of the canonical text be understood.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of Elements (*Dhātuvibhaṅga*) is concluded.

**Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix for the Exposition of the Truths** Regarding the meaning of the matrix for the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Exposition of the Truths), first of all: in the phrase "the four noble truths," this word *sacca* is seen in many senses.
For example, in such passages as "one should speak the truth and not be angry," it refers to verbal truth (*vācāsacca*).
In such passages as “The recluses and brahmins who stand firm in truth,” it refers to the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*).
In such passages as “Why do they speak various truths, these proponents who declare themselves skilled? it refers to the truth of views (*diṭṭhisacca*).

In such passages as “For there is only one truth, a second does not exist,” it refers to the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), namely Nibbāna and the Path. In such passages as “Of the four noble truths, how many are wholesome? it refers to—
Regarding the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca*): here too, they apply to the Noble Truths. In what sense are they "truths"? In the sense of being suchness (*tathattha*).

What is this so-called "sense of suchness"? It is that which, when investigated with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), is not deceptive like an illusion, nor misleading like a mirage, nor is it of a nature unfindable like the doctrines of the heterodox teachers (*titthiya*);
rather, it is that which exists as the basis for affliction, its origin, and the path to its cessation.

Because it is a state that is correct, non-perverted, and real, it is the objective domain of noble knowledge. This should be understood as the meaning of "suchness" (tathaṭṭha) being the meaning of "truth" (saccaṭṭha).
And it is said: "Thus, because they are correct, non-erroneous, and real in all four— Regarding suffering and the rest without distinction, The wise have called this the 'meaning of truth'."
They are "Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni) because they are both noble (ariyāni) and truths (saccāni). "Noble" means supreme; the meaning is that they are non-deceptive.

They are truths to be penetrated by the Noble Ones—the Buddhas and others—or they are the truths belonging to the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, because they were produced and proclaimed by him;
or they are truths that produce the state of a Noble One, because he has fully awakened to them.
The "Ariyan states" (ariyabhāva) are the Noble Truths. In such expressions as “Dukkha is the Noble Truth,” however, the syllable *du* is seen to signify what is contemptible (*kucchita*).
For they call a contemptible son a “bad son” (*duputta*). The syllable *kha*, on the other hand, signifies what is empty (*tuccha*).
For empty space is called “*kha*. And this first Truth is contemptible because it is the locus of manifold calamities.
It is "empty" (*tuccha*) because it is devoid of the state of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood imagined by foolish people;

therefore, due to its wretchedness (*kucchita*) and emptiness, it is called "suffering" (*dukkha*). Furthermore, the word *saṃ* indicates conjunction, as in "coming together" (*samāgama*) or "assembled" (*sameta*).
The word *u* indicates arising, as in "arisen" (*uppanna*) or "appeared" (*udita*). As for the word *aya*—
It illuminates the cause. And this second truth is called "the origin of suffering" because, when there is a conjunction with the remaining conditions, it is the cause for the arising of suffering.
As for the third truth, since the prefix *ni-* signifies non-existence and the word *rodha* signifies obstruction, it is therefore non-existence...

In this context, or when this has been attained, it is called "the cessation of suffering" because the cessation of suffering—defined as the prison of saṃsāra—is empty of all destinations (gati) and because it is the opposite of them; or else, because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering.
As for the fourth [noble truth], it is so called because it goes toward that cessation of suffering, or because it causes the being to go there by way of its object.
Because it is directed toward that [cessation], it is the "path leading to the cessation of suffering," and is therefore called "the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

Furthermore, the four meanings of each of the [Four Noble Truths]—suffering and so forth—are analyzed as they truly are, not falsely, and not otherwise; these are what must be fully realized by those who are realizing suffering and the rest. As it has been said:
“The meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of change—these four are the meanings of suffering as suffering;

they are such, not otherwise, and not different. The meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, and the meaning of impediment [are the meanings of the origin]… The meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless [are the meanings of cessation]….”
"The meaning of the path is that of leading out, the meaning of cause, the meaning of seeing, and the meaning of predominance... [and so on] ...it is not otherwise.
Thus, suffering and the other truths are to be understood by way of these fourfold sets of meanings as they have been analyzed. This, then, is the word-meaning here.

As for the classification of phenomena (*dhamma-bheda*), however, all mundane phenomena excluding craving constitute the truth of suffering; or alternatively, all phenomena excluding those subject to defilement constitute the truth of suffering.
Craving, however, is called the truth of origination, while all unwholesome states or mundane wholesome states are called the truth of origination;

Nibbāna is called the truth of cessation; and the eight path-factors associated with supramundane wholesome consciousness are called the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with these path-factors—

Furthermore, it should be understood that the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are not included here. For, according to the statement "whatever is impermanent is suffering," they are indeed included within the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*).

With the exception of those things which, through a certain full understanding (*pariññā*), do not exist as such in the Blessed One’s holy life (*brahmacariya*) and are not called the Noble Truth of Suffering—all mundane and supramundane phenomena (*dhammā*) [are included].
It should be understood as "included. This is the classification of the Dhamma.
Now, according to the method of analysis (*vibhaṅganaya*) here in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, first regarding the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*):
"In this context, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; death is suffering..."
"Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the pleasant is suffering;
not to get what one desires is also suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Having thus recited [the summary], it was analyzed. Therein, suffering is threefold: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and...

"Regarding 'the suffering of formations' (*saṅkhāradukkha*): therein, the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) is twofold—figurative suffering (*pariyāyadukkha*) and non-figurative suffering (*nippariyāyadukkha*).
Therein, bodily and mental feelings of pain and distress are called non-figurative suffering;

however, the remaining five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*), which serve as the basis for the suffering of suffering, are called figurative suffering. [This also includes] feelings of pleasure and joy..."

This is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*). Furthermore, all five aggregates of clinging, or indeed all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*), are called the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*).

By means of these three types of suffering, one should understand, as appropriate, how birth and the other factors constitute the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) within the three realms of existence.
For in the realm of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), birth itself is not inherently suffering; however, in the case of rebirth in the woeful states or among humans, etc., [it is so].

Furthermore, suffering rooted in the burning heat of the hell-fires, suffering rooted in the descent into the womb, and suffering rooted in hunger and thirst—all such physical and mental suffering is, by way of its being the basis for that [suffering], called "suffering" in a figurative sense.
Likewise, aging, death, and so forth are also [suffering]. Specifically, aging is the basis for the root of physical weakness and the root of being humiliated by one's children, wife, and others.

Furthermore, death should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for the suffering of death-bed sensations and for the suffering rooted in the vision of the signs of rebirth in states such as hell;

and grief and the rest should be understood as suffering both because they themselves are suffering and because they are the basis for physical and mental suffering rooted in grief and so forth. Moreover, these possess the nature of the suffering of change and the suffering of formations.
This is already well-established. Thus, the suffering nature of birth and the other factors in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) should be understood through all three types of suffering.

However, since sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, mental grief, and despair do not exist in the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpabhava*), the suffering nature of birth and the other factors there should be understood by way of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*) and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), but not by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*). This is the method regarding the truth of suffering.
As for the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), having first pointed out only that much—namely, "craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence"—it then asks:

"Where, moreover, does this craving arise when it arises? Having thus asked, it explains its arising by way of the objects of the six respective faculties, sense-bases, consciousnesses, contacts, feelings, perceptions, volitions, cravings, applied thoughts, and sustained thoughts, stating: "It is here that this craving arises when it arises. Thus [it describes] the arising.
Having thus announced it, the truth of cessation was analyzed in detail by stating:
"It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishing, its renunciation, its liberation, and the absence of attachment.
Then, having asked again: "But where, when it is ceasing, does that craving cease?"
Having explained the cessation of craving in reverse order by way of the faculties and so forth as stated under the truth of the origin, it is analyzed in detail there.
In that context, the phrases beginning with "the remainderless fading away and cessation" are synonyms for Nibbāna.
For it is by coming to Nibbāna that craving fades away without remainder, ceases, is relinquished, is let go of, is liberated, and does not [arise again].
It clings [to nothing]; therefore it is called "the remainderless fading away and cessation, relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, and non-attachment.
For Nibbāna is indeed one alone; however, its names are many, being applied by way of the opposites of all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).

Is it not the case that there is no separate entity called "Nibbāna," but rather Nibbāna is merely the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*)? And for that very reason, in those [passages]...
If it is argued that in those teachings of the Suttas and Abhidhamma, [the goal] is stated as "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred," and so forth, we say no;

for this would result in the identity of Arahantship and Nibbāna. For even Arahantship—because it arises at the point of the complete exhaustion of lust and the other defilements—is, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), called Arahantship [in that context], as it is said: "Friends, that which is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion: this is called Arahantship."

It is spoken of as the state of the destruction of lust and so forth; likewise, it should be understood that Nibbāna is also spoken of as the state of the destruction of lust and so forth because it is the cause for the destruction of lust and the other defilements.
Otherwise, one would fall into the error of asserting a multiplicity of Nibbānas, since there is a multiplicity in the destruction of the many [defilements] such as lust.
Furthermore, because the destruction of all defilements is a single unity, when views and the rest are destroyed by the first path, there is the destruction of all defilements.
[The path] attains [this state], and its coarseness would be evident even in animals who have attained the destruction of lust through the attainment of Nibbāna;

furthermore, at the moment of the lineage-change (gotrabhū), there is a destruction of lust and so forth, because the lineage-change has Nibbāna as its object, yet it would follow that the Path would not have Nibbāna as its object.
For [the lineage-change] does not take as its starting point the destruction of defilements being destroyed by itself.

The path arises, and its non-existence would follow; for since non-existence—which consists in the destruction of lust and so forth—is empty by nature according to its own side, it too would lack the status of being an entity.
Consequently, it could not have the characteristic of seclusion, and it would possess the quality of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*).
For that which is never perceived cannot possibly be unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), as this would result in everything being devoid of a cause.

Furthermore, even though it is conditioned (*saṅkhata*), it does not possess the nature of *nibbāna* because it is subject to arising, aging, and dissolution, and is thus characterized by suffering (*dukkha*).

Likewise, there is the non-existence of non-existence itself, as well as instability; for even those defilements such as lust that have been exhausted might arise again, since for those very things, non-existence is [merely] the destruction of what was previously present.
Furthermore, when another state arises due to some other cause, there is no diminution whatsoever of lust and the other defilements.

For the arising of one thing does not entail the disappearance of another. If you argue that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the opposite of existence (*bhāva*), and that the other [the defilement] disappears upon the presence of its opposite, we ask:

what is this so-called "disappearance"? If it too is of the nature of an existing entity (*bhāvarūpa*), then it would share the same faults as the former, namely, the lack of stability (*anavaṭṭhāna*).

And there would be no accomplishment of the goal. If it were of a void nature, why should its state of being void, which was accepted from the very beginning, need to be accepted again after traveling so far?
Thus, the void nature of Nibbāna—which consists in the destruction of lust and the other defilements—is disproven;
nor is non-existence itself Nibbāna, because if it were merely the non-existence of past and future faults, there would be no attainment of Nibbāna.
And there is indeed the non-existence of those things currently occurring. This "non-existence" does not mean merely the disappearance of defilements, but rather their state of non-arising.
If it is argued that even Nibbāna accomplishes this absolute cessation, we say no, because it is not the cause thereof. If it is argued that insight (vipassanā) is the cause, we say no;
for without the vision of conditioned phenomena—which produce conceptual constructions such as a "self"—there can be no insight consisting of conceptual constructions such as "non-self."

Because it has not arisen. For if it were to arise, all beings would already be liberated by it, and one would never fail to ask [about it], since there would be no perception of contradictory phenomena. Indeed, conceptualization is not possible without perception;
nor is the very perception of form and so forth that generates the conceptualization "self" the same as that which generates its contradictory conceptualization. And for the Buddhas...
If it is argued that the conceptualization of insight (*vipassanā-vikappa*) regarding form and so forth arises through successive instruction, we say no;

for even in those cases, such a conceptualization does not arise because there is an absence of the perception of contradiction. Indeed, when a particular effect arises from a particular collocation of causes, it is impossible for its opposite to arise from that very same collocation, as that would entail the fallacy of causelessness (*ahetukatva*). Nor is there an absence of the perception of contradiction [in this case].

Because a single person lacks the capacity to produce the various modes of insight (*vipassanā-vikappa*), such individuals can still possess that capacity through a lineage, and instruction in it is likewise possible.
Furthermore, for the Buddhas, the realization of Nibbāna is established by virtue of their immediate teaching of the Three Characteristics;
it is for this very reason that the absolute abandonment of defilements and the efficacy of the instruction in insight are established.
It should be understood that Nibbāna alone is the cause of both [the abandonment of defilements and the knowledge of the three characteristics], and nothing else.
But why is it that by the vision of Nibbāna there is the absolute abandonment of lust and the other defilements, as well as the knowledge of the three characteristics?

For is it not the case that by the vision of something else, the abandonment of those other lusts and the knowledge of the three characteristics would be illogical? No; for by the vision of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata), [this occurs].
This is because either the conditioned nature or the defect [of conditioned things] is made manifest.

For when the ultimate happiness has been seen, the conceit of happiness and the delight in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), as well as in its support and objects, are abandoned—just as a sailor who has seen the further shore abandons his conceit of happiness and his delight in even a portion of the ship.
Furthermore, attachment and other defilements clinging to conditioned phenomena [are abandoned] in the unconditioned phenomenon.
They are unable to remain steady, like flies in a mass of fire or aquatic creatures on dry land.

However, for a mind that has abandoned its defects through the vision of Nibbāna, the perception of the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) in those conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as they truly are becomes possible;

this is like the seeing of forms such as jars by an eye from which the defects of cataracts and darkness have been removed by the application of medicine. And regarding those conditioned phenomena whose defects have been seen...
Furthermore, it should be understood that the arising of passion and the like is not known [in Nibbāna], just as the presence of filth is not known in a cesspool.

But why is it that the realization of Nibbāna is possible for only some beings and not for all? It is because [realization] depends upon the instruction of a succession of Buddhas from time immemorial;
because such instructors are absent everywhere and at all times; and because the attainment of the opportune moment by those who hear is extremely rare.

And because world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) are infinite, it should be understood that only some [beings] realize *nibbāna* by receiving the instruction on the three characteristics at the time of a Buddha’s appearance, not all.

But how, in this context, is the absolute departure from lust and the other [defilements] accomplished by means of *nibbāna*? It is not yet [accomplished], because of those [defilements] of the past and the future...

If it is asked: "Since these [defilements] are now non-existent, whereas they previously existed, and because there is the cessation of their inherent nature (*sarasanirodha*) in those currently occurring, how can there be any room for the aforementioned defects regarding Nibbāna’s status as a cause, given that its nature is void? The answer is:

No, because it possesses the nature of an existent entity (*bhāvarūpa*). For it is precisely the paths that have arisen by way of not generating latent tendencies (*anusaya*) with reference to Nibbāna through the practice of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-paṭipatti*) that constitute the non-arising cessation of the defilements.

Because of its arising, there is the non-arising of those things that would otherwise have arisen in the future; this is like the state of being a seed in a rice stalk that has already emerged, which—due to the presence of fire—is incapable of producing a sprout.
For "non-existence" (abhāva) does not exist as some ultimate reality (*paramattha*) that could be produced by a cause;
rather, it is the state of producing a moment contrary to [the production of] that [effect], which consists in the non-production [of it] through the production of various other moments.

Just as the non-arising of a heap of coals [is spoken of] by way of their non-production, so too, because it is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the Noble Path—which is defined as the non-arising and cessation of the defilements—Nibbāna is described by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) as "the remainderless fading away and cessation," and so forth.
If one asks why it is not stated in its own form, it is because of its extreme subtlety and because it has never been perceived before; and its subtlety is due to the Blessed One’s...
It should be understood from the statement regarding "lack of concern" (*appossukkatā*) and because it is to be seen with the noble eye (*ariya-cakkhu*).
Here, however, an opponent says: "Nibbāna does not exist at all, because it is unobtainable.
It is not unobtainable, because it is established; for it is indeed obtained by the Noble Ones through practice corresponding to it. Furthermore, Nibbāna...

It should not be said that it does not exist, because if it did not exist for all beings due to the presence of contradictory phenomena, it would follow that there is no state beyond existence (apavagga).

And that is not tenable, because just as coldness and so forth necessarily exist as the opposites of heat and so forth, so too Nibbāna must necessarily exist as the opposite of existence (bhava). And it has been said:
"Just as when heat exists, something cool also exists;
so too, while the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna must be sought. And so forth.
Furthermore, because the instruction on insight (vipassanā) is shown to be the cause for the ultimate cessation, Nibbāna certainly exists; without it, [that instruction would be purposeless].

This very point has already been stated by the phrase "because it is impossible for that [to exist]. Since this [Nibbāna] lacks an origin due to the absence of a prior limit (*purimā koṭi*), it is therefore free from aging and death, and is eternal.
If it is argued that atoms (*aṇu*) and other such things also attain the status of being eternal because Nibbāna alone is eternal, we say no.

This is because the definition of a logical reason (*hetulakkhaṇa*) is untenable due to the difference in their substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇatta*). Furthermore, atoms and the like do not possess the quality of being unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

If you ask why this is so: It is not so, because the state of being unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) cannot be established, and because it is impossible for there to be a plurality of unconditioned things.

For if there were such a thing as the "unconditioned," it would have to be only one, since differences in place, time, and intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) are caused by differences in their conditions; otherwise, if things with different intrinsic natures were without a cause, it would lead to an over-extension (*atippasaṅga*).

If it is asked: "How can Nibbāna be causeless, given that it is distinct in nature from conditioned phenomena?"—it is because, by virtue of its unconditioned nature, it is independent of causes, being distinct from the natures of conditioned things. For while the lack of conditioning is common to both, a difference in the nature of existence indicates a difference in cause;
therefore, only one [Nibbāna] can properly be eternal, and that is according to the reasoning already stated.
And according to the word of the Omniscient One, it is Nibbāna alone that exists in the ultimate sense.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “There is, monks, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned. This is the method regarding the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

As for the other [Truth], however, having listed them as “right view... right concentration,” they have been analyzed in detail. The detailed exposition here will be made clear in the Vibhaṅga on the Factors of the Path; such is the method of the Suttanta-bhājaniya.
In the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, however, it is said:
“There are four truths: suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
Therein, craving is the origin of suffering. All remaining phenomena associated with the taints (*sāsava*) … [etc] … are suffering. The abandoning of craving is the cessation of suffering.”

Having said, “The eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,” and having demonstrated the eight path-factors in detail, he explained the four truths in the first section thus: “All remaining states are associated with the way leading to the cessation of suffering. These [truths] are further [explained] by others...
“Craving, and the remaining defilements, are the origin; likewise, craving, the remaining defilements, and the remaining unwholesome states are the origin;
likewise, craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, and the three wholesome roots associated with the outflows are the origin;
likewise, craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, and the three wholesome roots [are the origin].”

These are analyzed by the following sections: "The [states] associated with the taints (sāsavā), and the remaining wholesome states associated with the taints, are the origin (samudaya). The remaining states associated with the taints are suffering (dukkha);
the abandoning of their respective origins is cessation (nirodha); and the Eightfold Path is the way (paṭipadā).
In this context, instead of saying "the Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni), he says "the truths" (saccāni) in order to show the origin, which is defined as conditionality, without limitation.
It has been stated. For among the Noble Truths, craving alone is the origin, not the others. And it is not craving alone that brings about suffering;
the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states also bring about conditions. Therefore, in order to show that these too are the origin, they are called "truths.
Following that, since it is the Eightfold Path alone that is the way, [the factors] associated with it [are included].
However, all phenomena beginning with contact are indeed the path; therefore, in order to demonstrate that method, all [factors] are analyzed even in the section on the comprehensive inclusion.
For here, only the noble treasures are included. The rest is exactly the same.
This is the method of the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.

In the method of the "Questioning" (Pañhāpucchaka), however: Of the four Noble Truths, how many are wholesome (*kusala*)... [and so on] ...how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)? The Truth of Origination (*samudayasacca*) is unwholesome;

the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasacca*) is indeterminate (*abyākata*); the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is of all three kinds. Origination is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*);

cessation is without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*); the Path (*magga*) is of all three kinds; suffering is of all three kinds; and it is also not to be so described. Three truths [are without conflict].
Non-indicative and non-reactive; suffering is threefold. Origination is a cause; cessation is not a cause;
the remaining two are both. Two truths are mundane; the Path and Cessation are supramundane. The truth of origination is with conflict;
two truths are without conflict; suffering is both. This is the method of interrogation by way of questions. Now, however, herein—

The exposition independent of the canonical text (pāḷimutta-vinicchaya) should be understood by way of sequence, deficiency and excess, characteristics and so forth, emptiness, the function of knowledge, and similes.

In that regard, first, as for the sequence: here too, the sequence of the teaching itself is appropriate. This is because [the first aggregate] is gross and because it is common to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is stated first because it is easily understood; after that, the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*) is stated for the purpose of showing its cause;

after that, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) is stated for the purpose of making known that "with the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of existence"; and finally, the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is stated for the purpose of showing the means for attaining that cessation.
Suffering was spoken of first in order to generate a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in those who are attached to the gratification of the pleasure of existence.

Then, for the purpose of making known that "existence does not come without cause, nor does it arise through the creation of a Lord (Issara-nimmāna) and so forth, but rather it arises from this [cause]," there is the Truth of Origination (samudaya-sacca).

Next, for the purpose of generating consolation by showing the escape for those whose minds are agitated because they are overwhelmed by suffering accompanied by its causes, there is Cessation (nirodha).
After that, there is the Path (magga) which brings about that cessation. This is the sequence here.
If one asks why there are exactly four truths, neither more nor less: it is because nothing else is possible beyond them, and because none of them can be omitted.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One explains the process of existence (*pavatti*), he explains it together with its cause; and when he explains cessation (*nivatti*), he explains it together with its means.
Thus, since these are the ultimate limits of the process of existence, its cessation, and the causes of both, only four are stated. This is the sense of "neither more nor less" in this context.
Furthermore, regarding these [truths] by way of their characteristics and so forth: The truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppression;
its function is to torment; it is manifested as occurrence. The truth of the origin has the characteristic of source; its function is to cause non-interruption; it is manifested as an impediment.
The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace; its function is deathlessness; it is manifested as the signless. The truth of the path has the characteristic of outlet...
The truth of the path has the characteristic of abandoning the defilements, and its manifestation is emergence. Furthermore, their characteristics here are, respectively:

the characteristic of occurrence and the cause of occurrence, and the characteristic of cessation and the cause of cessation; likewise, the characteristic of seeing the conditioned and craving, and the characteristic of seeing the unconditioned.
As for emptiness, these truths are empty in successive order because of the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who attains Nibbāna, and a goer. And it is said:
“There is only suffering, but no one who suffers;
there is no agent, but only action exists.
There is extinction, but no person who has attained extinction.”
“The path exists, but no traveler is found.
Alternatively:
“Empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self.”
The state of "mine" is empty of the mere first two [aggregates]; the path is devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self—
thus it is emptiness with respect to them.

Or, there are three voidnesses of cessation: cessation is void of the remaining three [truths], or else, here the cause is void of its fruit—because of the absence of suffering and cessation within the truths of origin and the path, just as "nature" (pakati) is for the proponents of nature (pakativādī). And the fruit is void of its causes, because of the non-association of suffering and origin with cessation and the path;
the fruit of a cause is not conjoined with its cause. This is for those who maintain the doctrine of the association of cause and fruit.
The dissolution of dyads and so forth—this is emptiness in this context.
Regarding "the function of knowledge": here, knowledge of the truths is twofold, namely, knowledge as awakening (*anubodha-ñāṇa*) and knowledge as penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).
Of these, knowledge as awakening is mundane; it occurs with respect to cessation and the path by way of hearsay and the like. Knowledge as penetration is supramundane.
Expelling the defilements that are the opposites of the realization of truth, and taking cessation as its object, it penetrates all four truths by way of its function.
As for that which is mundane: therein, the knowledge of suffering, occurring by way of overcoming the obsessions, turns back the view of a personal entity;
the knowledge of origin, [turns back] the view of annihilation; the knowledge of cessation...
The view of eternalism, the knowledge of the path, and the view of non-action [are respectively] the perversion regarding the fruit—

namely, the perception of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood in those aggregates which are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood— and the perversion regarding the cause— namely,

the occurrence of the conceit that there is a cause where there is none, such as the belief that "the world proceeds from God, primordial matter, time, or inherent nature," when one possesses the knowledge of origination.
The knowledge of cessation (nirodha-ñāṇa) turns back the misconception regarding cessation, which consists in grasping at the formless world and so forth as being liberation;

and the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa) turns back the misconception regarding the means, which occurs by way of grasping at an impure path—such as the pursuit of sensual pleasure or self-mortification—as being the path to purification. This, then, is the function of knowledge here.
By way of analogy, however, the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) should be seen here as like a burden; the truth of origination (samudaya-sacca) as like the taking up of the burden;
the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) as like the laying down of the burden; and the truth of the path (magga-sacca) as like the means for laying down the burden.

Furthermore, this may also be applied respectively by way of the illness, its cause, its pacification, and the medicine; or by way of the near shore, the great flood, the further shore, and the means for reaching it, and so forth.
These [points] are to be understood by way of similes; this is the simile here. Thus should the exposition independent of the canonical text (pāḷimutta) be known.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix (mātikā) for the Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Faculties (Indriyavibhaṅga).

Regarding the analysis of the faculties (*indriya-vibhaṅga*), first as to the meaning: in the phrase "the twenty-two faculties," they are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they possess the characteristic function of a faculty (*indriyattha*).

What, then, is this so-called characteristic function of a faculty? It is the sense of being the mark of a lord (*indaliṅgattha*), the sense of being taught by a lord (*indadesitattha*), the sense of being seen by a lord (*indadiṭṭhattha*), the sense of being granted by a lord (*indasiṭṭhattha*), and the sense of being favored by a lord (*indajuṭṭhattha*). All of these apply here as appropriate. [The section on] wholesome and unwholesome...
Kamma is called "Inda" because it possesses sovereignty over all karmic actions.

For this very reason, the faculties (indriya) produced by kamma indicate their own originating kamma, and since they are bestowed by that [kamma], they are called "faculties" in the sense of being "marks of Inda" (indaliṅga) and in the sense of being "bestowed by Inda" (indasiṭṭha).
However, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is "Inda" because he possesses supreme sovereignty; therefore, all these faculties [belong to him].

They are called *indriyas* in the sense of being taught by the Lord (*indra*) because they were proclaimed by the Blessed One as they truly are and fully awakened to; and in the sense of being seen by the Lord (*indra*).

For that very reason, some are cultivated through the cultivation of the range (*gocarasevanā*) and some through the cultivation of development (*bhāvanāsevanā*), thus they are also *indriyas* in the sense of being mastered by the Lord (*indajuṭṭha*).
Furthermore, these are *indriyas* in the sense of sovereignty (*issariyattha*), which is to say, in the sense of predominance (*ādhipacca*).
Regarding the "eye-faculty" and so forth, the meaning of the terms *cakkhu* (eye) and the others has been explained below. However, as for the last three:

because they arise in one who is practicing with the thought, "In the prior stage, I shall know the Deathless State not yet known, or the Dhamma of the Four Truths," and because the sense of "faculty" (*indriya*) is applicable, it is the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown faculty" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*). It is called a faculty because it is itself knowledge through the act of knowing.

The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*). The faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is the faculty of an arahant whose taints are destroyed and who has completed the task of knowledge regarding the four truths.

In that context, following the faculties of confidence (*pasādindriya*), it exercises sovereignty by ensuring the fixed occurrence of visible forms and so forth during the process of consciousness such as eye-consciousness, and by causing [the mind] to conform to its own intensity or dullness.

This is how it should be understood. Furthermore, the predominance of the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) and the others should be understood in terms of their respective characteristics, such as cognizing.
The remainder is easy to understand. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.
As for the classification of phenomena (*dhamma*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is twofold: material and immaterial. The five beginning with the pleasure-faculty (*sukhindriya*)...
Feeling is a single dhamma by virtue of its nature as feeling; likewise, the four beginning with the faculty of wisdom are single dhammas by virtue of their nature as non-delusion.

The remaining faculties, however, are each single dhammas. Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha), only sixteen dhammas are taught as having the status of the twenty-two faculties.
The other factors here—mental concomitants, matter, and Nibbāna—are not included. This is the classification of dhammas.
However, according to the method of the *Vibhaṅga*, the "Suttanta-bhājaniya" (the section on the analysis of the Suttas) is not included here.
Why? Because these twenty-two faculties do not appear in this specific sequence within the Suttas.
For in the Suttas, two faculties are mentioned in some places, three in others, and five in still others; they do not, however, appear consecutively as twenty-two in this manner.
There is no difference [in name]. There is also no distinction in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*.

However, in the *Pañhāpucchaka* method, regarding the twenty-two faculties: how many are wholesome... pe ...how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)? The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) is wholesome;
the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) is unwholesome; the four faculties—faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*)—are both wholesome and indeterminate.
The faculties of mind, life, mental joy, equanimity, energy, and concentration are each of three kinds; the remaining ten are indeterminate (*abyākata*).
Six faculties may be associated with pleasant feeling, and they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
three are of all three kinds; life is of three kinds and also not to be so designated; and twelve faculties are simply not to be so designated.
Three are results; two are subject to result; the material faculties are seven that are neither results nor subject to result;
the faculty of final knowledge may be a result, or it may be subject to result;

nine faculties belong to all three categories. Nine faculties are both acquired by clinging and objects of clinging; the faculty of mental grief is not acquired by clinging but is an object of clinging; three are neither acquired by clinging nor objects of clinging.

The faculty of mental displeasure (*domanassindriya*) is with initial application and sustained application (*savitakkasavicāra*); the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) is likewise [with initial application and sustained application] and also without initial application and sustained application (*avitakka-avicāra*).

Nine faculties are without initial application and sustained application; eleven are of all three types. Ten are limited (*paritta*): the seven physical faculties (*rūpindriya*) together with the faculties of pleasure, pain, and mental displeasure.
The last three are immeasurable (*appamāṇa*); the remaining nine are of all three types. And therein, the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*)...

It should be understood that [the states] are "exalted" (mahaggata) solely by way of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), while the remaining ones are also [exalted] by way of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara). Five faculties are non-demonstrable and impinging (anidassana-sappaṭigha);
seventeen are exclusively non-demonstrable and non-impinging (anidassana-appaṭigha).

The four beginning with the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) are roots (hetu); the rest are not roots... pe ... The faculty of mental grief (domanassindriya) is with conflict (saraṇa); the faculties of mind, life, joy, equanimity, energy, and concentration are without conflict (araṇa).
In both ways, the remaining fifteen are exclusively without conflict (*araṇa*);

such is the method of the interrogation of questions. Now, regarding these faculties, the exposition outside the canonical text (*pāḷi*) should be understood according to their sequence, for one who desires skill therein.

"Kamato" (by way of order) is also a sequence of teaching. In that regard, because the attainment of the plane of the Noble Ones occurs through the full understanding of internal phenomena, the faculties such as the eye-faculty, which are included within the personal existence (*attabhāva*), are taught first.
That human existence is what, depending upon certain phenomena, comes to be designated as "woman" or "man"; [these are taught first] for the purpose of pointing them out by saying, "This is that."
Then, the femininity faculty and the masculinity faculty. After that, the life faculty, for the purpose of making known that both of these two function in dependence upon the life faculty.
As long as that [life faculty] continues to proceed, there is no cessation of these feelings.
And after that, the pleasure faculty and so forth, for the purpose of making known that whatever feeling there may be, all of it is either pleasure or pain. For the purpose of its cessation...
Then, for the purpose of showing the practice—that these states are to be developed—the faculties beginning with faith are mentioned.

Next, the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" is mentioned for the purpose of showing that this practice is not in vain, by way of demonstrating: "By means of this practice, this state first becomes manifest within oneself.
Because it is the fruit of that very [faculty], and because it must be developed immediately after it, [the faculty of final knowledge] follows next.

The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*). Following this, the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*)—which constitutes the ultimate consolation—is taught at the end for the purpose of making it known that its attainment occurs through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that once this has been attained, there is nothing further to be done.
Thus, the method of exposition independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimutta-vinicchaya-naya*) should be understood according to this sequence.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Faculties (*Indriyavibhaṅga*) is finished.

Now, regarding the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Modes of Conditionality (*Paccayākāravibhaṅga*), first in terms of the meaning: in such expressions as "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*), that which cannot be found (*avindiya*) refers to bodily misconduct and so forth.
*Avijjā* (ignorance) is so called because it finds or acquires; or because it does not find what is to be found, such as bodily good conduct (*kāyasucarita*);
or because it renders the true nature of phenomena unknown; or because it causes beings to run about in *saṃsāra*, which is devoid of an end;

or because it runs toward things that do not exist, or does not run toward things that do exist. It is a *paccaya* (condition) because it brings about a fruit by depending upon it; [this refers to] phenomena.
A phenomenon that assists in arising and in persistence. Ignorance (*avijjā*) is both itself and a condition;

thus it is "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccaya*), and therefore "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*). They construct the conditioned (*saṅkhata*); thus they are "formations" (*saṅkhārā*).

From here on, in such passages as "with formations as condition, consciousness," what has been stated should be understood according to the method already explained. Regarding those not yet mentioned...
It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (*viññāṇa*). It bends, thus it is name (*nāma*); it is affected, thus it is form (*rūpa*).

"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) should be understood by the method of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining one part of a similar group). It extends into the future, and it leads what is extended, thus it is a sense-base (*āyatana*).
"The six sense-bases" (*saḷāyatana*) should be understood by the method of *eka-sesa* (retaining one from a group). It touches, thus...

Contact (*phassa*). It feels (*vedayatīti*), thus it is feeling (*vedanā*). It agitates (*paritassatīti*), thus it is craving (*taṇhā*). It grasps (*upādiyatīti*), thus it is clinging (*upādāna*). It comes into being and it causes to become, thus it is becoming (*bhava*).
Birth is *jāti*. Aging is *jarā*. They die by means of this, thus it is death (*maraṇa*). Sorrowing is sorrow (*soka*). Lamenting is lamentation (*parideva*).
It causes suffering, and it cuts in two ways—by way of arising and by way of persisting—thus it is suffering (*dukkha*). The state of one who is dejected is grief (*domanassa*).
Grief; intense distress and despair. "Arise" means they are produced.
And this application of the word "arise" should be made with every term—not only with sorrow and so forth, but also with such phrases as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
For it is in this way that the determination of conditions and the phenomena produced by conditions is established.

Thus is the demonstration of the method already indicated; by this, he shows that it is through causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, and not through the creation of a Lord (*issaranimmāna*) and so on.
"Of this" refers to what has been stated above. "Entire" means unmixed, or complete.

"Of the mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandha*) means of the aggregate of suffering, not of a sentient being, nor of pleasure, beauty, and so forth. "Origin" (*samudaya*) means arising; "it comes to be" (*hoti*) means it occurs.
This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.

As for the classification of the phenomena (*dhamma*), "ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to non-knowing regarding the four [truths] beginning with suffering according to the Sutta method, or regarding the eight points including the past and so forth according to the Abhidhamma method.
"Volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*), however, are the volitional formations of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable.
There are three [types] of formations—of body, speech, and mind—and together with these three, they are sixfold.

Among these, the thirteen volitions consisting of the eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the five wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are called the "meritorious formation" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). The twelve unwholesome volitions are called the "demeritorious formation" (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*).
The four wholesome volitions of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) are called the "imperturbable formation" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*). Of these...
However, this triad of formations was stated for the purpose of showing the occurrence of only three types of formations by way of the doors:

the eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and the twelve unwholesome volitions constitute the bodily formation when occurring at the body-door and the verbal formation when occurring at the speech-door;
these same [volitions], as well as those occurring at the mind-door, constitute the mental formation when occurring specifically at the mind-door.
Wholesome volition regarding the form and formless realms is called "mental formation" (*cittasaṅkhāra*).

However, in this context, the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) and the volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*)—though they must be excluded from the status of being conditions for rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) later on—must nevertheless be included here because they arise with ignorance as their condition.
Thus, this triad is subsumed within the preceding triad; in meaning, it consists simply of mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions.
"It should be understood that 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]'—this is according to the method of the Suttanta analysis.

However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma analysis, because the twelvefold dependent origination is grasped within each single moment of consciousness—both mundane and supramundane—it should be understood that all volition whatsoever constitutes volitional formations.
In the same way, regarding consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth, [the principle applies] by way of association with every state of consciousness."
And the analysis of the Dhamma should be understood. However, we shall demonstrate it according to the method of the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
With *saṅkhāra* as condition, consciousness consists only of the sixfold eye-consciousness and so forth, and the thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness;
supramundane consciousnesses, however, are not included because they do not apply to the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*). With consciousness as condition, name-and-form...
Furthermore, [the factors are]: the three formless aggregates associated with all mundane consciousness; form, comprising all primary and derived matter;
the six sense bases, consisting of the faculties with the mind as the sixth; contact, such as eye-contact and so forth, including the sixfold resultant contact; likewise feeling;
craving, which is sixfold according to the divisions of craving for forms and so on, being greed; and clinging, beginning with clinging to sensual pleasures.
There are four kinds of views, namely those rooted in greed. Existence (*bhava*), however, is twofold: existence as kamma (*kammabhava*) and existence as rebirth (*upapattibhava*).

Therein, existence as kamma consists of wholesome and unwholesome volition belonging to the three planes, as well as covetousness and other factors associated with it. Existence as rebirth, moreover, consists of all five aggregates produced by kamma. By way of classification, that [existence] is threefold:
existence in the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere; and [it is further classified by] perception...
There are three types of existence: non-perceptual, neither-perceptual-nor-non-perceptual, and those consisting of one, four, and five aggregates;

thus ninefold existence is specified. Birth and the other factors have been explained previously. Among them, by the mention of "birth," consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are included, because they are inseparable from it.
Likewise, by the mention of "aging and death," these very same factors are included, because they constitute its maturation and differentiation. Sorrow and the rest [are also included].
However, they are stated by combining them into a single summary with aging-and-death as the twelfth factor, rather than as separate factors.

If one asks for what purpose, it is for the sake of demonstrating the uninterrupted continuity of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*). For ignorance is established through sorrow and the rest, both because of its dissociation from them and because of its co-arising with them;
indeed, those [sorrow and so forth] arise only in the fool who is struck down by aging-and-death.
And with ignorance thus established by them, there is again "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations";
in this way, through the succession of cause and fruit, the wheel of existence (bhavacakra) is uninterrupted, beginningless, endless, and without final limit.
If this is so, why was ignorance stated first? It was stated first for the purpose of showing its predominance. Of the three...
For among those in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), ignorance is the primary cause, because [the other factors] exist when it exists and cease through its cessation.

Thus, it should be understood that by means of the twelve factors beginning with ignorance, according to the method of the Suttanta-bhājaniya, all mundane phenomena (*lokika-dhamma*) alone are described in terms of the relationship between conditions and the conditionally arisen.
However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara*) are also included; this is the distinction between the categories of phenomena (*dhamma-bheda*) here.

Regarding the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga*), it should be understood that here there is no method of interrogation by question-and-answer; rather, the methods of the Suttanta-analysis (*suttantabhājanīya*) have also been analyzed in detail according to the same method already stated for the classification of phenomena (*dhammabheda*). However, in the Abhidhamma-analysis (*abhidhammabhājanīya*), it is said:

"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, mentality (*nāma*) arises; with mentality as condition, the sixth sense-base arises; with the sixth sense-base as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition..."
Craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth;
with birth as condition, aging and death—thus there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations... [and so on] ...with consciousness as condition, name; with name as condition, contact... [and so on] ...there is origination.”
“With ignorance as condition... [and so on] ...with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the sixth base; with the sixth base as condition, contact...

[and so on] ...there is an origination. “With ignorance as condition... [and so on] ...with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six bases; with the sixth base as condition, contact... [and so on] ...there is an origination. Thus is the tetrad of conditions.
Again, in the same manner stated by the method beginning with “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations have ignorance as their cause,” etc.

The tetrad of causes (*hetucatukka*); again, the tetrad of associated factors (*sampayuttacatukka*) beginning with “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise] associated with ignorance”;
and again, the tetrad of mutual conditions (*aññamaññapaccayacatukka*) beginning with “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise];

with volitional formations as condition, ignorance [also arises]”—thus these four tetrads rooted in ignorance have been stated. Likewise, [the tetrads] beginning with “With volitional formations as condition, ignorance [arises]”...

Having established and set forth as a matrix (mātikā) thirty-two tetrads— four tetrads for each of the eight positions beginning with "rooted in formations" and ending with "rooted in clinging"— one should then apply these thirty-six matrices of tetrads, as they were established,
to each individual consciousness among the unwholesome, wholesome, resultant, and functional states, both mundane and supramundane.
The mode of conditionality has been analyzed in detail according to its appropriate form.

And this is stated in order to show that mode of conditionality in its entirety as occurring within a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*), because this mode of conditionality exists not only in various types of consciousness but also in a single consciousness; nor does it exist only in consciousness pertaining to the round of existence (*vaṭṭacitta*), but also in consciousness pertaining to the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭacitta*) due to the absence of craving (*taṇhā*). Therefore, it was said to demonstrate it without exception as belonging to a single moment of consciousness.

For this very reason, instead of saying here "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), it is stated in the singular as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formation" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro*),
because within a single moment of consciousness there is no plurality of volitions (*cetanā*). Regarding that, as for the first tetrad, in the first section,
by taking "name" in the place of "name-and-form" and the "sixth base" in the place of the "six bases," it is presented in a manner common to all existence, whether material or immaterial.

And it is stated by setting aside material form (*rūpa*) through the inclusion of phenomena (*dhamma*) comprised within a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*), because material form is common to all states of existence and consists of many moments of consciousness.
In the second [formula], at the place of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) only "name" (*nāma*) is taken, and at the place of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) only "contact" (*phassa*) is taken;
this is for the purpose of showing that a specific condition for contact can arise even without the six sense bases.

And the third [classification] is stated by way of taking only the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) in the place of the six bases (*saḷāyatana*), according to the method shown in the Mahānidāna Sutta, with reference to those in the womb whose bases are incomplete and to those belonging to the form existence (*rūpabhava*) and so forth. The fourth is stated thus:
"With name as condition, the six bases; with the six bases as condition, contact," in this way [showing] the six bases even through the other bases.

In particular, having demonstrated the conditionality of contact itself, this was stated with reference to those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) and those belonging to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) who possess complete sense bases. The same applies to the second tetrad and the others.
Furthermore, in all these cases, because sorrow and the rest do not all occur within a single moment of consciousness, and in every instance...
They do not occur in the mind-element or in the existence-element; therefore, they are not included. Birth, aging, and death, however, are here merely the characteristics of formless phenomena.

Although these last for no more than a single moment of consciousness, because they are included within that moment of consciousness, they are taken figuratively as "dependently arisen" for the sake of completing the list of factors.
And here, "existence" (bhava) refers to that which is devoid of conditions such as clinging and the rest.

Regarding the statement "the four formless aggregates; conditioned by craving, there is clinging," here one should understand that only the three types of clinging are intended, excluding sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*).
This is because it is impossible for two phenomena that share the same characteristic to exist simultaneously.

Furthermore, in those wholesome and indeterminate states of consciousness which are devoid of the root of greed (*lobha*) and possess instead the roots of hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*), [clinging arises] conditioned by feeling (*vedanāpaccayā*).
Repulsion, doubt, and restlessness—thus, in place of craving (*taṇhā*), these three, beginning with repulsion, are applied accordingly.
Among them, in the place of clinging (*upādāna*), resolution (*adhimokkha*) is included, excluding doubt and those dissociated from views.
