However, because resolution is also impossible when accompanied by doubt, "existence conditioned by doubt" (*vicikicchā-paccayā bhavo*) is also included. In the place of clinging...
And resolve is also included here. In this context, for mundane wholesome and indeterminate states, ignorance is stated to be a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

However, regarding supramundane states, because one who has not yet abandoned ignorance develops the supramundane path for the sake of abandoning and pacifying ignorance, ignorance is stated to be a condition by way of transcendence (*samatikkamana*), and not by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*).

For that very reason, in their respective sections of exposition, instead of analyzing by asking "What there is ignorance?", it is analyzed by asking "What there is volitional formation conditioned by ignorance?".
However, since functional phenomena (kiriya-dhammas) cannot, by any means, have ignorance as their root,
the method beginning with "consciousness conditioned by volitional formations" and so forth is stated as having volitional formations as its root and so on, rather than having ignorance as its root.
Furthermore, among the mundane wholesome states and so forth, because those phenomena are included within the truth of suffering, the absorption is formulated as:
"Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. Among the supramundane wholesome states and so forth, it is formulated as: "Thus of these phenomena.
This is the distinction between the mundane and supramundane teachings; such is the method in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya.
Now, [the exposition of] the method of conditions is given by way of: emptiness of the factors such as the agent;
by way of the analysis of roots, halves, connections, abbreviations, aspects, and the cycle;
and here, by way of the simile of the elephant and the distinctions of the profound method.
This should be understood according to what is appropriate; it is an exposition independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimutta*).

In this regard, the method of conditions (*paccayanaya*) is twofold: general and specific. Among these, the general method of conditions is that which clarifies the mere fact of something arising through the existence of another.
As for the specific method, it concerns the twenty-four conditions—beginning with the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*)—as they appear in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
It is that which clarifies the mere state of having arisen through specific conditions according to their respective suitability.

And that classification of these twenty-four conditions will be made manifest in the commentary on the meaning of the *Paṭṭhāna-mātikā*. Therein, it should be understood that, in general, formations and the rest exist only when they possess the status of being conditions for ignorance and so forth.
For, regarding one who [does not understand] the four truths, the prior limit, and so on...

And because ignorance has not been abandoned, he—through his lack of knowledge regarding suffering, its origin, and the past and so forth—fails to understand as suffering the "suffering of change" (vipariṇāma-dukkha) consisting of the fruit of merit, which is interspersed with many disadvantages such as birth, aging, sickness, and death within the three realms of existence.

Craving for it under the perception of pleasure, he initiates meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations through the three doors. Likewise, through his lack of knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering], even though they are the causes of suffering...
Not seeing the suffering rooted in craving within the requisites for craving, nor the danger in the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the like which serve as causes for suffering,
one undertakes the three kinds of formations due to the perception of them as causes of happiness and because of being overwhelmed by defilements.
Furthermore, through ignorance regarding cessation and the path, one perceives a particular state of existence— which is not actually cessation— as being cessation.

And even regarding things that are not the path to cessation—such as sacrifice, the immortal state, and so forth—one undertakes the three kinds of formations while perceiving them as the path to cessation.
Through ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently upon specific conditions, one thinks: "Beings arise without cause and without condition;
they do not exist after death," or "The self alone knows or does not know; it [alone...]"
“He conditions volitional formations; he himself arises at rebirth-linking;
atoms, Īśvara, and so forth, fashioning his body through the stages of the *kalala* and so on, provide him with the sense faculties;
he, endowed with the sense faculties, touches, feels, craves, and performs clinging and the rest”—or else, “All beings are transformed by destiny, chance, and nature.”
Or he misappropriates it. Thus blinded by ignorance, he is like a man born blind who has no guide:
at times he travels by the right path, and at times he goes by the wrong path.
“The fool, wandering in saṃsāra, being thus without a guide, at one time performs merit, and at another time even demerit.”— In accordance with what has been stated,
he constructs the threefold formations (*saṅkhāra*). But here, is it ignorance alone that [constructs] the formations?
Is it not the case that from a single cause only a single effect arises, and multiple effects do not arise;
or that from multiple causes only a single effect arises? [The answer is: From multiple causes, multiple effects arise. This is true.

However, in this context, even though there are multiple causes, only ignorance (*avijjā*) is specified as the condition (*paccaya*) for the sake of highlighting its predominance, its manifest nature, and its uniqueness: "With contact as condition... (*phassapaccayā*).

It is like [the expressions] "feeling" or "diseases arising from phlegm," and so forth. For ignorance is the primary cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*); it is manifest, and it is unique because it is the cause even for causes such as craving.

It is not the case that the physical bases, objects, and so forth are the cause, since volitional formations do not exist for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), even though those bases and objects may still be present.
Thus, in this context, it is through ignorance alone that the volitional formations of the round of existence [arise].

The presence [of a phenomenon] should be understood as being dependent on the presence of its cause. Likewise, since consciousness also does not exist in the absence of accumulated kamma, and because it would otherwise follow that the resultant consciousness of all beings would arise everywhere and at all times, the presence of consciousness should be understood as being dependent solely on the presence of volitional formations (saṅkhāra).

And just as it is here, so too in the subsequent stages, the presence of name-and-form and the rest should be understood, in their respective order, through their appropriate experiences and applications, as being dependent on the presence of consciousness and the other factors.
"It should be known"—this is the general method of conditions.

Specifically, however, ignorance is a condition for meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) in two ways: as an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and as a decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

For when [formations] arise by taking ignorance as their object through the process of comprehension (sammasana) and so forth, they are [conditions] for those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
At the time of knowing a deluded mind with a mind possessing direct knowledge (*abhiññā*),
it is a condition for the form-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) formations of merit by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). However,

for one who performs sense-sphere and form-sphere merits after aspiring for the excellence of existence in the sense and form realms due to being deluded by ignorance (*avijjā*) for the sake of transcending that ignorance, it is a condition by way of decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).

It is a condition. However, for unwholesome volitional formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), when greed and so forth arise based on ignorance, it serves as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and others;
for one who commits killing and so forth due to delusion by ignorance, it serves as the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*);

and for the second impulsion (*javana*) and subsequent moments, it serves as the proximity, decisive-support, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions (*anantara-, upanissaya-, āsevana-, natthi-, vigata-paccaya*). Whatever unwholesome [state] there may be...

For that which is performing [kamma], it is a condition in many ways by way of the root, co-nascent, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions; however, for immovable formations (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), it is a condition only by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
In the section on consciousness conditioned by formations, all three types of formations are [conditions] for consciousness, as appropriate, within the three realms of existence.

In the contexts of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*), conditions function in two ways: as kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*) and as decisive-support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).

According to the method of the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, for consciousness that arises simultaneously (*sahajātaviññāṇa*), there are conditions by way of the simultaneous, mutuality, support, association, kamma, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, and so forth.

In the phrase "with consciousness as condition, mind-and-matter" (*viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa*), consciousness—whether it be resultant (*vipākabhūta*) or non-resultant (*avipākabhūta*)—is a condition for mind (*nāma*) alone.

Or, for that which is mixed with material form, it is a condition in nine ways—or eight ways—according to the circumstances, through the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, association, resultant, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance, during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
At rebirth-linking, the resultant consciousness is a condition for the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) in nine ways:
through the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, resultant, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

...is a condition. However, with the exception of the physical basis (vatthurūpa), the remaining types of materiality are conditions for one another by way of those same eight conditions, excluding mutual conditionality.

Furthermore, in the case of the kamma-born materiality within the one-aggregate and five-aggregate existences, the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) is a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) according to the Suttanta method. But in the course of the life-process (*pavatti*), all consciousness whatsoever—

It serves as the appropriate condition for each respective name-and-form (nāmarūpa). In this regard, it should be understood that in the formless realm (arūpabhava), consciousness (viññāṇa) is the condition for name alone;
in the non-percipient realm (asaññibhava), it is the condition for form alone; and in the five-aggregate realm (pañcavokārabhava), it is the condition for both name and form.
For this very reason, the etymological derivation is made such that "name" and "form," or "name-and-form," constitute the term *nāmarūpa*.
In the section on "With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base," "name" refers to both that which is resultant (*vipāka*) and that which is non-resultant.

In the immaterial plane (*arūpabhava*), it is a condition for the sixth base in seven ways, as appropriate, by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, result, presence, and non-disappearance.
However, in the five-aggregate plane (*pañcavokārabhava*), this [name] is a condition for the other five—the eye-base and so forth—[in the same manner].
At rebirth-linking, acting as an associate to the four great elements, it is a condition in six ways: by way of conascence, support, result, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.
Furthermore, in some instances here it acts as a root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*), and in others as a nutriment condition (*āhārapaccaya*);

according to these, the maximum and minimum [of conditions] should be understood for all sections. However, in the course of existence (*pavatta*), the five beginning with the eye—whether resultant or non-resultant—[are treated similarly].

Name is a condition for the sixfold base (saḷāyatana) in four ways: by way of post-nascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, it should first be understood that name alone is a condition for the sixfold base.

As for material form, however, when it serves as the physical basis (vatthu), it is a condition for the sixth base at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

The condition is sixfold. Materiality consisting of the four great elements (mahābhūta) is a condition in four ways—by way of conascence, presence, non-disappearance, and support—for the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. The material life-faculty, however, is threefold by way of faculty, presence, and non-disappearance.
Likewise, nutriment is [threefold] by way of nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance. And that [nutriment] belongs to those who subsist on nutriment-materiality.

Only during the course of existence (*pavatta*), not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Furthermore, those five bases, beginning with the eye-base, act as conditions in six ways—by way of support, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—for the sixth base, the mind-base, which is comprised of the five types of consciousness;
this occurs only during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking. The same applies to the mind-base when it is devoid of the fivefold sensory consciousness.
Basis-materiality is a condition in five ways: as support, pre-existence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.
Thus, it should be understood that materiality alone is a condition for the sixth base and for the sixfold base.

Furthermore, name-and-form—consisting of the three aggregates and basis-materiality—is a condition for the sixth base at the moment of rebirth-linking by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, dissociation, resultant, presence, non-disappearance, and so forth.

"It is a condition according to what is appropriate. Thus, it should be understood that both name and form, as well as name-and-form, are conditions for the sixth base and the sixfold base respectively, according to what is appropriate.
However, in the phrase "with the sixfold base as condition, contact," the sixth base is both resultant and non-resultant; in all cases, it is a condition for the contact associated with it.
Conditionality is ninefold or eightfold by way of co-nascence and so forth.

The five bases, beginning with the eye-base, act as conditions for the five types of contact, beginning with eye-contact, during the course of existence (pavatta) in six ways: by way of support (nissaya), prenascence (purejāta), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).

The five objects, beginning with the visible-form base, act as conditions for those same contacts in three ways: by way of object (ārammaṇa), prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance. [This applies] to mental contact...
Furthermore, those [six bases], the mental object, and likewise by way of mere object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), act as conditions in many ways.
Thus, it should be understood that both the sixth base and the sixfold base (*saḷāyatana*) are conditions for all six kinds of contact (*phassa*).

In the section on feeling conditioned by contact, every kind of contact is a condition for its co-nascent feelings by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance.
It is a condition in eight ways or seven ways, solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) for those things that do not arise simultaneously.

In the section on craving conditioned by feeling, resultant feeling is a condition for craving—whether it has become a latent tendency (*anusaya*) or not—by way of decisive support and by way of arising simultaneously, etc. For it is said:
"The one who suffers longs for pleasure; the one who is happy desires even more."
"But because equanimity is peaceful, it is described simply as 'pleasure';
therefore, on account of craving, all three feelings exist.
Regarding the phrase "with craving as condition, clinging," craving is not co-nascent [with the clingings], but serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for all four types of clinging.

And by way of the immediate [condition] and so forth; however, co-nascent [clinging], excluding clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), is a condition in seven ways—by way of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance—for the other three types of clinging.
In the section on existence conditioned by clinging (*upādānapaccayā bhava*), all four kinds of clinging are also [conditions] for all kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) that is not co-nascent with them.

The rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) is a condition for the present existence solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*); however, the co-nascent kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) is a condition by way of root-cause (*hetu*), co-nascence (*sahajāta*), and so forth.

In the section on birth (*jāti*), "existence" in the phrase "conditioned by existence" refers specifically to kamma-existence; and that [kamma-existence] serves as a condition for birth in two ways: by way of kamma-condition and decisive-support-condition.

In the context of the phrase "with birth as condition, aging-and-death," etc., birth is the condition for aging-and-death and sorrow, etc., merely by virtue of their occurring when it occurs; thus, according to the method of the Suttas, it is a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

This, then, is the method of conditions here. However, because these twelve factors—ignorance and the rest—are empty of an agent and so forth, and because they proceed in an uninterrupted succession from beginningless time, bound together to one another through this relationship of condition and conditioned state without depending on anything else, therefore:

They are devoid of any other agent such as Brahmā, or of causes such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*), atoms (*aṇu*), or time (*kāla*), whether conceived by others as an agent or experiencer, or even of a self (*attā*).
They are not the self, they do not exist in the self, nor do they possess a self;
they are empty of a self, of what belongs to a self, or of permanence, beauty, or bliss—this is emptiness with respect to an agent and so forth.

Regarding the analysis by way of roots, halves, junctions, groups, aspects, and rounds: here, first, by way of roots, it should be understood that two factors—ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*)—are the roots.
By way of time-epochs (*addhā*), however, two factors here—ignorance and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*)—belong to the past epoch;

the eight factors beginning with consciousness and ending with existence belong to the present epoch; and the two factors, namely birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), [belong to the future epoch].
Regarding "the future time," three periods (addhā) should be understood. Furthermore, regarding the "connections" (sandhi), three connections should be understood:

first, a connection between cause and fruit occurring between the formations (saṅkhārā) and rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa); second, a connection between fruit and cause occurring between feeling (vedanā) and craving (taṇhā);
and third, a connection between cause and fruit occurring between existence (bhava) and birth (jāti). In brief:

However, there are four summaries established for the beginning and end of the links of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). They are as follows: ignorance and volitional formations constitute one summary;
consciousness, mentality-and-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute the second; craving, clinging, and becoming constitute the third;
and birth, aging, and death constitute the fourth. Thus, the four summaries should be understood.
As for the classification by way of aspect (ākāra) here:
"In the past, there were five causes; now, there is a pentad of results.
Now, there are five causes; in the future, there will be a pentad of results."
Thus there are twenty aspects.
For here, ignorance and volitional formations are stated by their own nature; through their inclusion, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included because they are inseparable from them.
These five factors are called the causes in the past. The five factors beginning with consciousness, which are stated by their own nature, are now...
The so-called "fivefold fruit" refers, by way of its own nature, to craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*);

through the inclusion of these, ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are also included because they are inseparable from them—these five are now called the "causes. The five factors beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*), which were spoken of under the designations of birth (*jāti*) and so forth, are called the "fivefold fruit" in the future.
Thus, twenty aspects should be understood. Furthermore, regarding the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) here:
Volitional formations and existence constitute the cycle of kamma; ignorance, craving, and clinging constitute the cycle of defilements; and the remaining factors constitute the cycle of resultants.
Thus there are three cycles. As long as the cycle of defilements among these is not cut off by the Noble Path, this wheel of existence continues to turn without interruption.
This is the analysis of the cycles here, according to their roots, halves, connections, summaries, and modes.

Regarding the phrase "like an elephant": first, as for the "elephant" [which wards off], the statement "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" is a warding off of the view that there are no causes or that there are discordant causes;
"with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises" is a warding off of the view of annihilation or the transmigration of a self;

"with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises" is a warding off of the perception of a solid mass, because it shows the differentiation of the bases imagined to be a self; "with name-and-form as condition... [and so forth].
"‘The six sense bases,’ etc., refers to the prevention of such views as: ‘the self sees... [and so on]...
it cognizes, touches, feels, craves, clings, becomes, is born, ages, and dies. This is the prevention of wrong view herein.
By way of simile, however, ignorance is like the blind man; the formative forces (saṅkhāras) are like his stumbling; the fall is like..."
Consciousness is like that; from it, name-and-form appears like the manifestation of an abscess. The six sense bases are like the swelling of that abscess;
contact is like the rubbing of it; feeling is like the pain produced by that;

craving is like the longing for a remedy for the pain; clinging is like the grasping of something unsuitable; becoming is like the application of an unsuitable ointment; and from that, the transformation of the abscess manifests.
Birth is like the eye itself, while aging and death are like its impairment and destruction.

Alternatively, because they obstruct the vision of things as they truly are, these factors beginning with ignorance should be understood through similes such as a cataract on the eye; this is the simile here.

Regarding "the distinction of the profound method": first, the distinction of profundity refers to the profundity of each of these factors—ignorance and the rest—in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*), their meaning (*attha*), their teaching (*desanā*), and their penetration (*paṭivedha*).

These should be understood. For these phenomena, beginning with ignorance, in whatever manner and in whatever state they serve as conditions for their results, such as volitional formations, that status of theirs as conditions is "profound" because it is difficult to comprehend;
this is what is meant here by the profundity of the phenomenon (*dhamma-gambhīratā*). "Phenomenon" (*dhamma*) means cause, according to the statement:
"Knowledge regarding a cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*). [This refers] to the results, such as aging and death.
The sense of being produced and brought about by conditions such as birth is "profound" because it is difficult to comprehend; this is profundity of meaning (*atthagambhīratā*).
"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the fruit, according to the statement: "Knowledge regarding cause and fruit is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Furthermore, the teaching of those causes and fruits in their respective modes, without error, is also profound because it is the domain of the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) alone.

This is the profundity of the teaching (*desanā-gambhīratā*). Furthermore, that intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of these factors—ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth—which consists in their non-perception, accumulation, and so on, is "profound" because it is difficult for those of dull wisdom to fathom;
this is the profundity of penetration (*paṭivedha-gambhīratā*). This, then, is the classification of profundity herein.

As for the classification of methods (*naya-bheda*) herein, there are these: the method of identity (*ekatta-naya*), the method of diversity (*nānatta-naya*), the method of non-agency (*abyāpāra-naya*), and the method of suchness (*evaṃdhammatā-naya*).
It should be understood by way of four methods of meaning (*atthanaya*). For therein, the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;

with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises" refers to the method of identity (*ekattanaya*), which is like a seed attaining the state of a tree through the stages of the sprout and so forth, such that there is no interruption in the continuity (*santāna*).
Seeing this correctly, one understands the non-interruption of the continuity through the connection between cause and fruit.

One abandons the view of annihilationism; yet, seeing incorrectly through the grasping of a unity in the uninterrupted continuity of what proceeds by way of the connection between cause and fruit, one clings to the view of eternalism.
However, the determination of the specific characteristics of ignorance and the other factors is called the method of diversity (*nānattanaya*). Seeing this correctly—
By seeing the arising of ever-new [phenomena], one abandons the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi);
by seeing incorrectly—due to grasping at diversity in what belongs to a single continuum as if it were a different continuum—one adopts the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi).

However, through ignorance (avijjā), there is an absence of such functional activity as "formations (saṅkhārā) must be produced by me" or "consciousness (viññāṇa) [belongs] to us in relation to formations."
This is called the method of non-agency (*abyāpāranaya*). One who sees correctly abandons the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*) through the realization of the absence of an agent;

whereas one who sees incorrectly clings to the view of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*) because of failing to grasp that causal status which is established by the very nature of ignorance and the other factors, even though there is no [personal] agency.
However, the arising of formations and so forth occurs only from causes such as ignorance, just as curds arise from milk and so forth, and not from anything else;

this is called the principle of "suchness of nature" (*evam-dhammatā-naya*). Seeing this correctly, one abandons the view of causelessness (*ahetuka-diṭṭhi*) and the view of non-action (*akiriya-diṭṭhi*) through the understanding of the fruit according to its conditions.
Seeing it incorrectly, however, [one fails to understand] the occurrence of the fruit in accordance with its conditions.
Because one grasps at anything whatsoever from wherever it may come, by way of apprehending what is impossible for anyone, one adopts both the view of causelessness and the doctrine of fatalism;

this is the distinction of method here, which should be understood as the exposition independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimutta-vinicchaya*). The commentary on the meaning of the matrix (*mātikā*) of the Analysis of the Modes of Conditionality (*Paccayākāra-vibhaṅga*) is finished.
Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā).
Regarding the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness: first, "four" is a numerical limit;

by this, it is indicated that there are neither fewer nor more than that. "Foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*): here, there are two kinds of foundations of mindfulness—the domain of mindfulness (*satigocara*) and...

Furthermore, in such passages as, “Monks, I shall teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna),” the objective domain of mindfulness is called “foundation of mindfulness.
Its meaning is: “that in which something is established is a foundation (paṭṭhāna).
What is it that is established? Mindfulness. The foundation of mindfulness is the establishment of mindfulness. Alternatively, “foundation” (paṭṭhāna) means a primary state (padhāna-ṭhāna).

*Satipaṭṭhāna* means the foundation (*paṭṭhāna*) of mindfulness (*sati*). However, in such passages as, “The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,” it refers to mindfulness itself.
Its meaning is: it is a *paṭṭhāna* because it is established (*patiṭṭhāti*);

that is to say, it stands firm, having entered and plunged into [the object], and thus proceeds. Mindfulness itself, in the sense of being a foundation, is *satipaṭṭhāna*. Alternatively, it is so called in the sense of remembering (*saraṇa*).
Mindfulness (*sati*) is called a "foundation" (*paṭṭhāna*) in the sense of being established (*upaṭṭhāna*); this is what is intended here by the term *satipaṭṭhāna*.
If this is so, why is the plural form *satipaṭṭhānā* used? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. For those instances of mindfulness are many due to the diversity of their objects.
"Here" means in this teaching; thus, it refers to one who produces all forty-four kinds of foundations of mindfulness in every way, such as internally and so forth.
It demonstrates that the Teaching alone is the support for a person, and there is no other teaching. For it has been said:
"Right here, monks, is the ascetic... [and so on] ...empty are the doctrines of others of ascetics who are different.
"Bhikkhu" means one who looks for fear in *saṃsāra*. By this, although the Blessed One was seated in the world of the gods, he established mindfulness...
When he descends, having released the host of devas from his presence, there is not even a single bhikkhu sitting there;

nevertheless, whether one is a deva or a human, a householder or one gone forth, it is only one who perceives the terror in *saṃsāra* and practices according to the instructions that is called a "bhikkhu," and no other—thus he shows. As it is said: "Even if he is adorned... and so forth.
*Aj-jhattam* means internal (*niyakajjhattam*). Regarding *kāye*: it comes from the root *āya*, meaning "to come" (*āyanti tato*). What comes? Defiled things such as hair and so forth;
thus, it is the "coming (*āya*) of defiled things (*kucchitānam*)" that is the body (*kāya*). Alternatively, *kāya* also has the sense of a collection of limbs, members, and hair and so forth;
hence it is the "material body" (*rūpakāya*). The meaning is: "in one's own body. *Kāyānupassī* means one whose nature is to contemplate the body. "In the body" (*kāye*).
Having said that, he further uses the second mention of "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) to show:

"In this way, one does not contemplate a single entity separate from the limbs and members of the body, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man separate from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth, nor does one contemplate a single entity separate from the primary elements and the derived matter;
rather, one contemplates them according to their sequence, just as one who contemplates the parts of a chariot, the components of a city, or the divisions of a plantain trunk."
This was stated for the purpose of showing that one should indeed contemplate the collection of material derived elements (upādāya-rūpa), such as the limbs, members, hair, and so forth.
For in this context, no woman, man, or any other phenomenon whatsoever is perceived apart from the aforementioned collection of phenomena;
rather, it is only within that mere collection of phenomena that fools wrongly adhere [to them] as being beautiful and so on in various ways.
They practice; however, it is meant that this yogi, while contemplating the body therein, contemplates it specifically as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.

Alternatively, since one contemplates within this very body all the fourteen aspects of the body mentioned in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta—beginning with inhalation and exhalation—the meaning should also be understood through such expressions as "contemplating the body in the body."

"Viharati" means "to move about. The meaning is that by means of one posture among the four postures, he carries and maintains his physical frame—preventing it from falling—by interrupting any bodily affliction that has arisen through another posture; thus, he causes it to proceed. "In the external body" means in the body of another.
"In the internal and external body" means sometimes in one's own body and sometimes in the body of another. For at times, [one contemplates] even within both the internal and external bodies.

Mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) arises in a single moment; however, what is described here is the time when one who is proficient in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) moves back and forth through it.
"Ardent" (*ātāpī*) means possessing energy (*vīriyavā*) by means of the energy that encompasses the body. For energy is called "ardor" (*ātāpa*) because it scorches the defilements (*kilesa*);
since he possesses this, he is therefore called "ardent. "Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) [means clearly comprehending] by means of that which encompasses the body...
"Endowed with clear comprehension. "Possessing mindfulness" means being endowed with the mindfulness that encompasses the body.

However, since one contemplates by means of wisdom after having encompassed the object by means of mindfulness, and does not fall into despondency midway due to energy, it is therefore for the purpose of showing those factors by whose power this foundation of mindfulness is accomplished that [the following is said]:
“It should be understood that this was said: ‘ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.

Thus, having shown the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body and its associated factor, he now says ‘having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world’ in order to show the factor of abandoning.
Therein, ‘having removed’ means either by removal through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by removal by suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).”

Or having disciplined [the mind]. "The world" (*loka*): that very body which was mentioned here with its internal and other divisions is called "the world" in the sense of breaking up and falling apart.

However, in the *Vibhaṅga*, because covetousness and so forth, which have been abandoned in the material body, are likewise abandoned in feeling and the other aggregates, all five aggregates of clinging are stated to be "the world. In that world, [there is] that which is termed covetousness and dejection...

The connection is: "having removed sensual desire and ill will. It should be understood that by showing the abandoning of these two powerful factors among the hindrances, the abandoning of the remaining hindrances is also stated.
And specifically here, through the removal of covetousness and dejection, there is respectively the removal of attachment and aversion, which are the roots of bodily success and failure.

The abandoning of non-delight in the cultivation of the aspects of foulness regarding one's own body and so forth, as well as the abandoning of the imputation of non-existent virtues and the removal of existent faults, has been stated; by this, the fruit produced through the power of yoga and the practitioner’s capacity for yoga are illuminated.
In the phrases "internally in feelings" and so on, the terms "internal" and the rest should be understood according to the method already explained. Here, however, "feelings" (vedanā) refers to...
The three feelings are mundane, as are the mind and mental objects; their classification will be made clear according to the method of the Vibhaṅga.
However, here only that method must be shown by which one who contemplates feeling and so forth is called "one who contemplates feeling and so forth.
That is to say: among feelings, first, pleasant feeling is to be contemplated as suffering, painful feeling as an arrow, and the other [neutral feeling]...
And they should be contemplated as impermanent. As it is said:
"He who saw pleasure as suffering, and saw suffering as a dart, and saw the peaceful state that is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as impermanent."
All these [feelings] indeed should be contemplated as suffering, according to the statement: "Whatever is felt, that is included in suffering.
Contemplating in this way—whether by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, or by investigating:
"Who feels this feeling? To whom does this feeling belong? For what reason does this feeling exist?"—one realizes: "No..."
One who contemplates that "some being or other experiences [feeling], but feeling does not belong to any being whatsoever;
rather, this feeling arises due to causes such as the physical basis and the object" is indeed called a "contemplator of feelings.

Alternatively, one is a contemplator of feelings by contemplating thus: "Because suffering and so forth are impossible at the very moment of the arising of pleasure and so forth, they are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change."
This is the name [of the practitioner]. In this same manner, following the method of the Pāḷi, the mode of contemplation for the remaining mental states and phenomena should also be understood.

Specifically, it should be understood that one who contemplates by way of impermanence regarding the mind, and by way of non-self regarding phenomena, is called a "contemplator of the mind" (cittānupassī) and a "contemplator of phenomena" (dhammānupassī). The rest is easily understood. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.

However, there is no difference in the nature of the phenomena (*dhamma*) here; it is simply mindfulness that is called "the four foundations of mindfulness" according to its objects, though it is one and the same by way of being a refuge.

According to the method of the *Vibhaṅga*, first of all, in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, the first foundation of mindfulness is explained in detail by way of the cultivation of the parts beginning with head-hair, etc., within the internal, external, and both types of bodies.
Likewise, for each of the internal and so forth, it is explained by way of the carnal and the non-carnal.

The second [knowledge] is by way of the two kinds of feelings—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; the third is by way of the sixteenfold discernment of states of consciousness, distinguished as with lust and without lust, with hate and without hate, with delusion and without delusion, contracted and scattered, exalted and not exalted, surpassable and unsurpassable, concentrated and unconcentrated, and liberated and unliberated;

and the fourth is by way of the jhānas that are the causes for the occurrence or non-occurrence, the arising, the abandoning, the state of having abandoned, the non-arising, and the full development of the five hindrances and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The establishment of mindfulness has been explained in detail. This is the method of the Suttanta-analysis (suttantabhājanīya).

In the Abhidhamma-analysis (abhidhammabhājanīya), however, having first established the matrix (mātikā) thus: "There are four establishments of mindfulness. Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, feelings in feelings... [and so on]... phenomena in phenomena," [it is treated] in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

In the detailed exposition of the eight supramundane consciousnesses according to the method already stated, they are analyzed in detail solely by way of their associated mental factors. In the method of interrogation (*pañhāpucchaka*) as well:
"Of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), how many are wholesome... pe ...how many are without conflict (*araṇā*)? They may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate (*abyākata*)...

pe ...they are exclusively not-clung-to and not-object-of-clinging; they are exclusively neither-defiled-nor-defiling... pe ...they are exclusively non-demonstrable and non-reactive (*anidassana-appaṭigha*).
"Neither with cause nor without cause"... [and so on]... "the unsurpassed state free from conflict (*araṇā*). These are analyzed solely by way of the supramundane.
For in the *Suttanta-bhājaniya*, the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) were taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One as a mixture of mundane and supramundane;

however, in the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* and the *Pañhāpucchaka*, they are exclusively supramundane. And among those, the mundane ones are found only in various states of consciousness. For by means of one consciousness... [text continues].
They take up the body; by another [moment], feeling and so forth. However, all four supramundane [factors] are obtained within a single consciousness at the moment of the Path.

For in a single moment of the Path-consciousness, mindfulness—which has Nibbāna as its object from the perspective of the object—receives all four names in the sense of accomplishing the four functions, because it completely eradicates the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self regarding the body and the other aggregates.
"He obtains"— this is the method of analysis here.
Regarding the sequence of the foundations of mindfulness, and their neither deficiency nor excess,
the method independent of the canonical text should be understood by one desiring skill in that regard.
In this regard, first of all, as to the order: this too is simply the order of the teaching, and that is stated by way of what is evident and what is not evident.
For among these, the meditation subject consisting of the material form is evident; thus, body-contemplation was taught first. After that, the meditation subject consisting of the immaterial.
Even there, feeling—which arises experiencing the object—is evident; thus, next, feeling-contemplation was taught.
Then, as consciousness becomes evident while cognizing the object, there is contemplation of mind;
and when the mind has become evident, even the subtle states dependent upon it become evident, which is why contemplation of phenomena is mentioned at the end. This, then, is the sequence here.
Regarding the phrase "neither less nor more": why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more?

According to the *Visuddhimagga*, for those of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*) and view-temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*), and for those who follow the vehicle of serenity (*samathayānika*) and the vehicle of insight (*vipassanāyānika*), [the practice] proceeds in two ways according to their dullness or sharpness.

For one of dull craving-temperament, the coarse foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) is the path to purification; for one of sharp [craving-temperament], it is the subtle foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*). It is the same for one of view-temperament as well.
For one of dull faculties, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mind that has not reached excessive differentiation is the Path of Purification;

for one of sharp faculties, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental objects that has reached excessive differentiation is the Path of Purification. Furthermore, for one of dull faculties who takes serenity as their vehicle, the first foundation of mindfulness—whose sign is to be attained without difficulty—is the Path of Purification; for one of sharp faculties, it is the second. The same applies to one who takes insight as their vehicle.
The third is for the dull-witted, and the fourth is the Path of Purification for the sharp-witted; thus four are taught according to the inclinations of those to be trained.

Alternatively, they are taught as four because they serve to abandon the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and selfhood; or because they serve to abandon the four floods, yokes, taints, and ties;
or because they serve to bring about the full understanding of the four kinds of nutriment. Thus, they are neither fewer nor more—this is their completeness and lack of excess.

Thus should the method independent of the canonical text (pāḷimuttanaya) be understood. The commentary on the meaning of the matrix (mātikā) for the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga) is concluded.
[Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Right Exertions (Sammappadhānavibhaṅga).
Regarding the summary of the Analysis of the Right Strivings (*sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga*), first in terms of meaning:

"Right strivings" (*sammappadhānā*) means strivings by way of cause, strivings by way of method. Because it is a supreme striving (*dhāna*) due to wise exertion (*yoniso padahana*), it is called "striving" (*padhāna*); the meaning is "the strivings that are energy" (*padhāna-vīriyāni*).
"A monk here" (*idha bhikkhu*) refers to a monk practicing within this teaching. "Of those not yet arisen" (*anuppannānaṃ*) means of those not yet produced. "Evil" (*pāpakānaṃ*)...
"Of the base ones": of those states born of unskillfulness (*akosalla*). "For the non-arising": for the purpose of not producing [them].
"He generates desire": he generates and produces wholesome desire (*kusala-chanda*), which is characterized by the wish to act.
"He exerts effort": he applies exertion and strives. "He arouses energy": he exercises physical and mental energy (*viriya*).
“He exerts the mind” means that he uplifts the mind by means of that very co-nascent energy (*vīriya*).

“He strives” means he performs the effort of striving (*padhānavīriya*). Furthermore, these four phrases should be connected respectively with the energy’s practice, development, frequent cultivation, and persistent application.
“Of those arisen” means of those that have reached a state where they cannot be called “unarisen. “For the abandoning” means for the purpose of relinquishing. “Of those not yet arisen”...

"Of wholesome states" (*kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*) means of those states that have not yet arisen but have originated through skill (*kosalla*). "For the sake of arising" (*uppādāya*) means for the purpose of causing them to arise.

"Of those that have arisen" (*uppannānaṃ*) means of those that have already been produced. "For the sake of stability" (*ṭhitiyā*) means for the purpose of their persistence. "For the sake of non-confusion" (*asammosāya*) means for the purpose of their non-decline.

"For the sake of further increase" (*bhiyyobhāvāya*) means for repeated becoming. "For the sake of abundance" (*vepullāya*) means for the state of vastness. "For the sake of development" (*bhāvanāya*) means for growth. "For the sake of fulfillment" (*pāripūriyā*) means...
For the purpose of fulfillment. The remainder is clear from the words themselves.

As for the meaning here, in such phrases as "of unarisen evil states," the non-arising of defilements should be understood either by way of their not being manifest or by way of their objects not having been experienced.
Otherwise, there would be no unarisen unwholesome states in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

There is no such thing [as a being who has never produced these]. However, among wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), there exist those conducive to emergence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), such as confidence in the Triple Gem, insight (*vipassanā*), and other wholesome factors, even if they have not yet arisen.

If even these had previously arisen, it would follow that all sentient beings would have already attained the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) prior to this. Therefore, these [wholesome states] are the means for establishing their absolute occurrence.

In that regard, for a certain person, regarding the nine tasks consisting of the observances (*vatta*), the bonds (*gantha*), the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), concentration (*samādhi*), and insight (*vipassanā*):
In the case of a certain person who was constantly engaged in effort and exertion, because he had come from the Brahma-world,
the defilements did not manifest due to his lack of habituation to them through the influence of that existence; however, at a later time, having abandoned his duties and the like,
as he lived indolently and became habituated to the defilements through evil friends and so forth, unwise attention arose.
And by relying on the relinquishing of mindfulness, they arise. Thus, first of all, the non-arising of defilements should be understood by way of their non-occurrence.

However, in the case of some, having obtained a pleasant object—such as that pertaining to the divine realms—which was previously unexperienced in that particular existence, defilements arise there by relying on improper attention and the relinquishing of mindfulness; whereas, not having obtained such an object, [they do not arise].
In this way, the non-arising of defilements by way of objects not previously experienced should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "of evil states that have arisen," there are four kinds of "arisen": by way of being present, having been past, having been given space, and having gained a footing;

the analysis of these has already been stated in the *Uppanna-ttika*. Furthermore, there are another four kinds of "arisen": by way of manifestation, by way of grasping the object, by way of not being suppressed, and by way of not being eradicated.
Therein, that which is currently occurring is called "arisen as manifestation" (*samudācāruppanna*). The rest is self-evident.

However, since among these types of arisen states, the fourfold arising—consisting of what is present, what has been, what is past, and what is occasioned—is not subject to abandonment by the Path and so forth, therefore [the text speaks of] the fourfold [abandonment] consisting of what has acquired its plane, what has grasped its object, what has not yet been eradicated, and so on.
It is with reference to what has already arisen that it is said here: "for the abandoning of evil states that have arisen.
But how, at the moment of the Path, is there effort for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and how is there [effort] for the stability of those that have arisen?
It is precisely through the occurrence of the Path itself. For the Path, while occurring, is "unarisen" in the sense that it has never arisen before.
"Arising" (pavatti) is what is called "stability" (ṭhiti); this, then, is the meaning of the terms here.

As for the classification of the phenomena (dhammabhedo), even here it is stated that there are four kinds of energy (vīriya) based on the differentiation of its functions; this is the analysis of the text independent of the commentary.

According to the method of the *Vibhaṅga*, first, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) are presented by way of energy associated with mundane and supramundane wholesome consciousness.
These have been analyzed in detail together with the terms "unwholesome" (akusala) and so forth.

However, in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* questions and inquiries, these are analyzed only by way of association with supramundane wholesome consciousness (*lokuttara-kusala-citta*); those associated with resultant consciousness (*phala-citta*) are not included.

For this very reason, in the questions and inquiries, it is stated: "They are exclusively wholesome; they are exclusively of a nature to produce results; they lead exclusively to diminution; they belong exclusively to those in training (*sekha*)," and so on.
...have been stated. The remaining analysis here, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Vibhaṅga].
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the *Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga* is finished.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the *Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga*.
In the summary of the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*, regarding the phrase "the four bases of psychic power" (*cattāro iddhipādā*):

here, "psychic power" (*iddhi*) means that which succeeds; the sense is that it is accomplished and brought to fruition. "Base of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) is psychic power itself as a base; the sense is a constituent part of psychic power.

Alternatively, it is called "psychic power" because by means of it beings succeed, become successful, and reach excellence. It is called a "base" (*pāda*) because they go forth by means of it; it is a foundation.
The meaning is "the means for attainment. *Iddhipāda* (basis of psychic power) means a foot of psychic power (*iddhi*).

Regarding the phrase "endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving" (*chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*): here, concentration caused by desire, or concentration in which desire predominates, is "concentration through desire" (*chandasamādhi*);

this is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act the dominant influence. Volitional formations that constitute striving are "volitional formations of striving" (*padhānasaṅkhārā*).

This is a designation for the energy of right effort that accomplishes the four functions. "Endowed with" means possessed of that concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) and the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*).

"Base of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) refers to the concentration of desire and the volitional formation of striving—which, in the sense already explained, have attained the status of "psychic power" (*iddhi*)—insofar as they serve as the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the wholesome states of mind associated with access-concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) and so forth.

"The aggregate of the remaining factors of consciousness and mental concomitants that have become like feet. "Develops" means increases; the meaning is that he generates them repeatedly within his own continuity.

In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the others as well. Therein, "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) is wisdom (*paññā*). The rest is easy to understand from the words themselves. As for the meaning here, what has been stated by him?
It is a meditation subject that has reached the pinnacle of the four types of monks.
It has been explained. For just as when four sons of ministers are wandering about having sought positions of authority— one by means of attendance, one by means of bravery,
one by means of excellence of birth, and one by the power of counsel— and thus they each attain their respective positions by pleasing the king through individual causes,
so too, among zeal (*chanda*), energy (*vīriya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), each [of these]...

Having made the foremost factor the leader, they bring about supramundane states. Herein, the three factors—zeal (*chanda*), concentration (*samādhi*), and the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*)—are both supernormal powers (*iddhi*) and bases for power (*iddhipāda*);

however, the remaining four associated aggregates (*khandha*) are only bases for power. Thus, it should be understood that the bases for power are likewise present in those consciousnesses associated with the other dominant influences (*adhipati*).
Furthermore, the preliminary stage of jhāna and vipassanā is the basis of psychic power (iddhipāda). That which is the attainment is the psychic power (iddhi).
For the preliminary preparatory exercises for the first jhāna and so forth are called the basis of psychic power, while the first jhāna and so forth are called the psychic power.
The preliminary vipassanā for the first path and so forth is called the basis of psychic power, while the first path and so forth are called the psychic power. This is also by way of attainment.
It is appropriate to illuminate this. For here, the first jhāna and so forth, as well as the first path and so forth, are called the "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*);
the second jhāna and so forth, as well as the second path and so forth, are called "psychic power" (*iddhi*).
This, then, is the meaning of the terms. As for the classification of these phenomena, it will become clear through the method of the *Vibhaṅga*. For therein, in the Suttanta-bhājaniya:
Having thus explained the analysis of the terms beginning with zeal (*chanda*), at the end it says: "The 'basis of psychic power' (*iddhipāda*) is the aggregate of feeling...
[and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness of one who has become such. 'He develops the basis of psychic power' means he pursues, develops, and cultivates those states;
therefore it is said, 'he develops the basis of psychic power. In this way, all mundane and supramundane states are called the basis of psychic power.
In the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, however, after analyzing the terms beginning with zeal (*chanda*), it concludes by stating that for one who has become thus, "contact... [and so on]...

exertion, non-distraction" are the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*); having thus declared that all supramundane wholesome states are bases of psychic power, it then establishes the matrix (*mātikā*) as:

"the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal, the basis of psychic power consisting of energy, the basis of psychic power consisting of consciousness, and the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation."
“In this context, what is the basis of psychic power consisting in zeal? Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna...

whatever at that time is zeal, the state of being zealous... this is called the basis of psychic power consisting in zeal. By such passages, it is stated that only the zeal, energy, consciousness, and investigation associated with supramundane wholesome consciousness are the bases of psychic power.
Likewise, in the *Pañhāpucchaka* [of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī], they are also exclusively wholesome and are non-demonstrable and non-reactive.
The basis of psychic power consisting of investigation is a cause; the others are not causes... [and so on] ...the basis of psychic power consisting of consciousness is not to be so described;

the others are associated with consciousness... [and so on] ...they are exclusively unsurpassed and are called "without conflict" (*araṇā*). The rest here is exactly as stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta]. However, the method independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttakanaya*) has not been extracted here either.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power (*Iddhipādavibhaṅga-mātikā*) is completed.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Summary of the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga-mātikā). Regarding the summary of the analysis of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgavibhaṅgamātikā*), first in terms of its meaning: "The seven factors of enlightenment" (*satta bojjhaṅgā*).

Here, they are called *bojjhaṅgā* because they are the limbs (*aṅgā*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or of one who is enlightened (*bodhissa*). This is what is meant: by whatever harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggi*), when arising at the moment of the Path, [enlightenment occurs].

The noble disciple awakens by means of the sevenfold harmony of states—mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, and so forth—which serves as the antidote to numerous calamities such as lethargy and restlessness;
he rises from the sleep of the defilements or penetrates the Truths.

These are called *bojjhaṅgas* (factors of enlightenment) because they are factors of that enlightenment (*bodhi*) known as the harmony of states, just like the *jhānaṅgas* (factors of absorption) and *maggaṅgas* (factors of the path). As for...
Because he awakens by means of this aforementioned harmony of the Dhamma, the noble disciple is called "Bodhi" (the Awakened One);
the factors of that Bodhi are the "bojjhaṅgas," just as there are factors of an army or factors of a chariot.
Furthermore, the meaning of "bojjhaṅga" should also be understood according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* method, as in: "They lead to awakening, thus they are bojjhaṅgas. It is praised...
The "beautiful" factor of enlightenment is the "enlightenment-factor"; mindfulness itself is the enlightenment-factor, thus it is the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor. The same applies to the rest.
Therein, "investigation of phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*) means that one investigates, examines, and knows phenomena as impermanent and so forth;

or, it is called "investigation of phenomena" because by means of it sentient beings investigate phenomena—it is wisdom (*paññā*). One "looks on with equanimity" (*upekkhati*) by way of reflective contemplation, through being unoccupied with the diminishing or increasing of phenomena that have reached a state of equilibrium.

"Being neutral" means equanimity (*upekkhā*), which is the state of neutrality therein (*tatramajjhattatā*). For the enlightenment factor of equanimity has the characteristic of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).
The rest is indeed easy to understand. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here. The classification of the phenomena (*dhammabheda*) here is also easy to understand.

However, according to the method of the *Vibhaṅga*, first, in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, it is by way of the mundane and supramundane; and among the remaining [categories], it is by way of the supramundane, the wholesome, and the resultant.
They are analyzed. In the section on the interrogation of questions (*pañhāpucchaka*), however, they may be wholesome (*kusala*) or may be indeterminate (*abyākata*).

The enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) is associated only with pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*); the remaining factors are associated with two [feelings]. …pe… The enlightenment factor of rapture is accompanied by pleasure (*sukha*) alone; the remaining factors are of all three kinds. They are non-demonstrable and non-reactive (*anidassana-appaṭigha*).

The enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) is a root (*hetu*); the remaining factors are not roots. …pe… They belong exclusively to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
"Regarding 'the state of non-conflict' (*araṇāvihāra*): the rest is exactly according to the method explained in the *Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta*. This is the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga*) here.
Now, however—by way of order, by way of number, by way of cause, and by way of the distinction of planes..."
And it is to be understood through discernment; this is the exposition independent of the canonical text.
Therein, first, as to order: this too is simply the sequence of the teaching. For the mindfulness enlightenment factor is mentioned first because it is helpful to all the enlightenment factors.
Then, because one whose mindfulness is established investigates phenomena with wisdom, and one who has investigated phenomena...
One arouses energy; in one who has aroused energy, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, both body and mind become tranquil;
for one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated; with a concentrated mind, one regards that mind with thorough equanimity.
Therefore, the factors beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor are stated in this specific order; such is the sequence here.
But why, then, are exactly seven stated from among those, neither fewer nor more?

Because they are the opposites of lethargy and agitation, and because they constitute all the groups. For here, three factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are the opposites of lethargy. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is lethargic, that is the time for the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga)."

“...the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of energy... [and] the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of rapture. There are three opposites to restlessness. As it is said:
“But at whatever time, monks, the mind is restless, that is the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of tranquility;
that is the time for the development of the enlightenment factors of concentration... [and] equanimity.”
But here, mindfulness alone is to be desired among all the factors of enlightenment, just as salt seasoning is among all sauces. As it is said:

"Monks, I declare that mindfulness is beneficial everywhere. Thus, because they are the opposites of lethargy and restlessness, and because they are beneficial everywhere, only these seven have been mentioned; such is the reason for their number.
Regarding the "Analysis by Way of Causes": first, by way of the analysis of causes for the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*), there are four:
mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and being intent upon that [factor].
Likewise, there are seven factors for the second [enlightenment factor]: questioning thoroughly and making the physical basis pure.
The balancing of the faculties, avoiding persons of weak wisdom, associating with persons possessed of wisdom, reflecting on the conduct of those with deep knowledge, and being intent upon that.
In this context, "cleansing the basis" means making clear the internal and external things that constitute the body and its requisites.

Likewise, there are eleven factors for [the purification of] the third [basis]: the fear of the states of misery, the path leading thereto, the greatness of the inheritance, the greatness of the Teacher, the greatness of birth, and the greatness of one’s fellow-celibates.
These are: reviewing, seeing the benefits, honoring the almsfood, avoiding persons who are lazy, associating with persons who have aroused energy, and being intent upon that.
Therein, "reviewing" refers to the reviewing of the path, thinking: "The path traveled by the Buddhas and others must be traveled by me.
"Seeing the benefits" refers to [seeing] the great fruitfulness of the almsfood given by donors...
“I shall accomplish it”—this is called the taming of oneself and the honoring of alms-food. Likewise, there are eleven qualities:

the recollections of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and deities (seven), as well as avoidance of coarse persons, association with amiable persons, reflection on inspiring discourses, and devotion thereto. Likewise...

Seven factors for the fifth [jhāna]: the practice of refined food, the practice of comfort in season and in postures, two types of equanimous application, avoidance of persons with agitated bodies, association with persons of tranquil bodies, and intentness upon that.
Eleven factors for the sixth: making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, and skill in the sign.
At the appropriate time, there are four: the exerting, restraining, encouraging, and looking on with equanimity of the mind; two:
the avoidance and cultivation of persons who are unconcentrated and concentrated, respectively; and [the remaining] two: the reviewing of the jhānas and liberations, and being intent upon them.

Therein, skill in grasping the signs such as the kasiṇas is called "skill in the sign. Five factors [are required for] the seventh [chapter], which concerns the seven types of persons: those who are fond of worldly activities and those who are neutral.
The avoidance and cultivation [of the two types of objects] are each twofold, as is the inclination toward them. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* (the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga) in the *Sammohavinodanī*. This is the analysis of the cause (*hetu*) herein.

As for the analysis of the plane (*bhūmi*), these are either of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*). Among those of the sense-sphere, they occur in strong insight (*vipassanā*) and so forth.
Thus the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are found [only] in these [supramundane states], and not in others. However, they are found everywhere in the supramundane [states];

they are not found at all in fine-material-sphere or immaterial-sphere consciousnesses because they do not belong to the side of enlightenment (abodhipakkhika). Yet some elders extract the factors of enlightenment even from the jhānas of the kasiṇas, the foulness (asubha), and the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) when these are based on insight (vipassanāpādaka);
and these have not been prohibited by the teachers of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathācariya). Therefore, according to their opinion—
They belong to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and, in no way whatsoever, to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*);

this is the classification of planes (*bhūmi*) here. Regarding the term "seclusion" (*viveka*): here, seclusion means the state of being secluded. This is fivefold, by way of seclusion as a factor (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*).
Seclusion as a factor is insight (*vipassanā*); seclusion as suppression is the eight attainments (*samāpatti*); seclusion as eradication is...
The path is seclusion as subsiding; the fruit is seclusion as [the state of] subsiding; and Nibbāna, which has escaped from all signs, is seclusion as escape.

Among these, they are based on seclusion as partial eradication, seclusion as subsiding, and seclusion as escape. Thus, at the moment of insight, they are based on seclusion as partial eradication by way of function, and based on seclusion as escape by way of aspiration. But at the time of the path—
In terms of function, they are based on the seclusion of eradication; in terms of object, they are based on the seclusion of escape;
and at the moment of fruition, in terms of function, they are based on the seclusion of tranquillization. They are also based on the seclusion of escape in terms of object.

According to the opinion of some elders, at the moment of the fine-material-sphere jhāna that serves as the basis for insight, they are based on the seclusion of suppression; thus, they are also based on five kinds of seclusion.
"They exist"—this is the distinction here. Thus should the exposition independent of the canonical text (pāḷimutta) be understood.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix (mātikā) for the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Factors of the Path (Maggaṅgavibhaṅga).
Regarding the summary of the analysis of the path factors (*maggaṅgavibhaṅgamātikā*), first by way of meaning:

"A Noble One" (*ariya*) is so called because he is far removed (*āraka*) from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, and because he causes the state of a noble one to arise. "Eightfold" (*aṭṭhaṅgika*) means that it possesses eight factors.

"Path" (*magga*) is so called because it is sought after (*maggīyati*) by those seeking Nibbāna, or because it seeks (*maggati*) Nibbāna, or because it proceeds while slaying the defilements. "Seyyathidaṃ" (meaning "as follows") asks: "What is that?"
Now, showing that this very path consists merely of its constituent parts—just like an army with its four divisions—and that there is nothing apart from those parts, he said:
"Right view... right concentration. Therein, "right seeing" is right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), which is wisdom (*paññā*).
"Right intending" or "right thinking" is right intention (*sammā-saṅkappo*), which is applied thought (*vitakka*). The rest is easily understood. Then:
The analysis of the factors (dhammabheda) and the method of classification (vibhaṅganaya) regarding the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are similar to what has been stated [previously].
However, in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, even the five-factored path (pañcaṅgika-magga)—excluding the three abstinences (virati)—is analyzed.

This is done with reference to the predominance of the functions (kicca) of the five factors and the fact that the abstinences are established by implication (avuttasiddha). As for that which excludes the abstinences...
Since the supramundane path is absent [in that state], it too should be understood as being eightfold.
In the *Pañhāpucchaka* (Question-and-Answer Section) as well, right intention is associated only with pleasant feeling; the remaining factors are associated with two feelings.

Right intention is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), accompanied by joy (*pītisahagata*), and accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*) alone, but not accompanied by equanimity; the remaining factors are of all three kinds.
Right view is the cause, while the remaining factors are not causes; this is the distinction. The rest is exactly the same.

Now, however, the analysis independent of the canonical text regarding the path factors should be understood according to their sequence, their functional differences, their differences in plane, and their distinctions.
In this regard, first of all, as for the order [of the factors], this too is simply the order of the teaching.

For the Blessed One taught Right View first because it is of great benefit, since it dispels the darkness of ignorance through the lamp and sword of wisdom for one practicing the path to the attainment of Nibbāna.
Then, following that, there is Right Intention, which—like the hand of a money-changer turning over coins—is the precursor to Right View’s seeing things according to their true nature.
Right intention is so called because it is of great assistance. And this, like right view, is also an assistant to right speech.
As it is said: "Householder, having first reflected and deliberated, one subsequently utters speech. Therefore, right speech follows immediately after that.
Furthermore, because people in the world employ their various occupations by means of speech, having made an agreement through words, therefore—

Immediately after that comes right action (*sammākammanta*). Since it is only for one who has abandoned misconduct of body and speech and is fulfilling both types of good conduct that the eightfold virtue of livelihood (*ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla*) is fulfilled, and not for anyone else, right livelihood (*sammāājīva*) is mentioned immediately after those two.
Thus, even with virtue characterized by purified view, one should not rest content with just this much, but rather "this energy (*vīriya*) must be undertaken."

Immediately after that, right effort (sammāvāyāma) is taught in order to show [this]. Immediately after that, right mindfulness (sammāsati) is taught in order to show that even for one who has initiated energy, mindfulness must be made well-established regarding the body and so forth.

Immediately after that, right concentration (sammāsamādhi) is stated because the mind is able to be concentrated on a single object when mindfulness is well-established. This, then, is the sequence here.
As for their functions, each one has three functions. To illustrate:
right view, first of all, abandons wrong view along with its own opposing defilements; by way of its object, it realizes the truth of cessation;
and by way of non-delusion, it penetrates the remaining truths. In the same way, right intention and the others [function] by way of abandoning wrong intention and so forth.
"According to their respective functions" should be understood as their specific tasks. Specifically, however, in this context, the function is as follows:
right intention directs the co-nascent states; right speech encompasses them; right action originates them;
right livelihood purifies them; right effort exerts them; right mindfulness establishes them; and right concentration concentrates them. This is the function here.

As for the distinction: in the preliminary stage, right view has different moments, different objects, and different names according to the knowledge of the four truths, as expressed by the phrase "knowledge regarding suffering" and so forth.

However, the second [type] consists of the three types of intention—renunciation, non-ill will, and non-cruelty—and also the fourfold abstinences, which consist of the volitions (cetanā) characterized by refraining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct, the three kinds of bodily misconduct, and wrong livelihood.

By way of their functions of refraining, the sixth and seventh [factors]—namely, the four right strivings (sammappadhāna) and the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)—occur at different moments, have different objects, and receive different names. However, at the time of the Path, these factors beginning with right view (sammādiṭṭhi) occur at a single moment and have a single object.

Furthermore, by way of their functions, they receive different names during the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), whereas right concentration (sammāsamādhi) receives its name even during the preliminary stage.
At the moment of the path as well, it is of different moments and different names by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas; however, at the moment of the path, it has a single object.
For one person’s first path is determined by the supporting jhāna and so forth to be either the first jhāna and so on, or any one of the second jhāna and so on;
and his second path and subsequent paths are likewise associated with jhānas similar to or dissimilar from those of the first path.
