It blows at the time of the path as well; it blows at various moments and under various names—this is the distinction here.

The analysis according to plane and according to seclusion should be understood by following what has been stated regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). Thus should the analysis independent of the canonical text be known.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the analysis of the factors of the path (*maggaṅga-vibhaṅga-mātikā*) is finished.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Jhāna Vibhaṅga Matrix Regarding the meaning of the Jhāna Vibhaṅga matrix, first: in such passages as "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," *pātimokkha* refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
For that which protects (*pāti*) one who observes it, and liberates (*mokkheti*) him from the sufferings of the states of misery and so forth—therefore it is called *pātimokkha*.
Therefore, it is called "pātimokkha. It is a "saṃvara" because it is a restraining, or that by which one restrains; thus, the pātimokkha itself as a restraint is "pātimokkhasaṃvara.
This is a designation for the virtue of pātimokkha-restraint—which consists essentially of volition and so forth—that comes into being at the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā).
One who is "restrained by that," meaning whose bodily and vocal applications are closed off, is "pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta."
"Viharati" means he conducts himself or carries on his activity. "Accomplished in conduct and range" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*): here, it is called "conduct" (*ācāra*) because it is to be practiced;
"range" (*gocara*) is where cattle roam, meaning a place for cows to graze. However, by virtue of its similarity to that, the entire sphere of activity should be understood as "range.
Their detailed classification is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Niddesa*.
For in the Niddesa it is said:
"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" means there is proper conduct and there is improper conduct. In this context, what is improper conduct?
Transgression of body, transgression of speech, and transgression of both body and speech—this is called improper conduct; moreover, all...
Immorality is improper conduct; here, someone makes a living by means of giving bamboo, or leaves...

[and so on] ...or by giving flowers, fruits, bath-powder, tooth-sticks, or by flattery, or by bean-soupery, or by servility, or by running errands on foot, or by any other kind of wrong livelihood censured by the Buddhas—this is called improper conduct.
“In this context, what is conduct (*ācāra*)? It is non-transgression by way of body,” and so forth;
thus, conduct is defined by means of the opposite of what was previously stated.
“As for the resort (*gocara*): there is a proper resort and there is an improper resort. In this regard, what is an improper resort? Here, someone has prostitutes as their resort...”
Or she is a widow... [or] a grown virgin, a paṇḍaka, a nun, or one who frequents the homes of laymen;
or she dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and disciples of other sects, through improper association;
or she cultivates and frequents those families that are faithless and lacking confidence... [and so on]... such families as these she serves and frequents.
He attends upon; this is called a non-range.
"In that regard, what is the range? Here, a certain person does not have prostitutes as his range," and so forth—in this way, by the reverse of what was stated, the range is defined.

Furthermore, in this context, bodily conduct and verbal conduct should be understood as the opposites of improper conduct, such as walking in front of elder bhikkhus, sitting down, pacing back and forth, jostling them, or overpowering them;
and likewise, verbal actions lacking respect, such as speaking Dhamma or reviling elder bhikkhus without having first asked their permission.
Moreover, a bhikkhu who is respectful and reverential...

One who is endowed with moral shame and moral dread, well-clad and well-robed, possessing a pleasing deportment such as dignified gait, with eyes cast downward, perfected in the modes of conduct, performing duties with diligence, and dwelling with abundant respect and reverence for the elders—this is called *ācāra* (proper conduct).

Furthermore, *gocara* (range of activity) is threefold: the range of support (*upanissaya-gocara*), the range of protection (*ārakkha-gocara*), and the range of binding (*upanibandha-gocara*). Among these, one who is endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of discourse...

A virtuous friend is called the "supportive resort" (*upanissaya-gocara*). Walking with eyes cast down and so forth, without looking toward the cardinal or intermediate directions while in inhabited areas and the like, is called the "protective resort" (*ārakkha-gocara*).
The four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), however, are called the "anchoring resort" (*upanibandha-gocara*).
Wherever the mind is anchored, this is to be understood as the threefold resort here. By this...
One who is endowed with this conduct and this resort is called "perfected in conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanna*).
Regarding "even in the slightest faults": this refers to defects of even minute proportions. "Seeing fear" means having the habit of seeing fear;
one sees even the most trivial misdeed or mere wrong speech as being like a *pārājika* offense, just as one would see a speck of dust as equal to Mount Sineru.

The meaning is: one who has the habit of seeing [transgressions] as a fault and as a source of fear. "Having undertaken, he trains in the rules of training" means that whatever is to be trained in among the rules of training, he undertakes it well, grasps it firmly, and trains in it.

"Guarded in the sense-faculties" means by means of the restraint of mindfulness, which consists in not grasping the signs and so forth of objects such as forms, with respect to the six faculties beginning with the mind.

"With doors closed": "knowing the right measure in food" means one who knows the proper measure with respect to both receiving and consuming almsfood by means of the knowledge of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) as well as through fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and other such qualities. Furthermore, it should be understood that by the term "almsfood" (*piṇḍapāta*), the inclusion of all four requisites is intended here.
Alternatively, since they are what is to be consumed, they are called "food" (*bhojana*); thus, the inclusion of the four requisites is intended.

It should be understood as follows. Regarding the phrase "the earlier part of the night and the later part of the night": here, the "earlier part of the night" refers to the portion preceding midnight;
by this, one includes both the first watch of the night and the period after the meal. The "later part of the night" refers to the portion following midnight;

by this, one includes both the last watch of the night and the period before the meal. However, the last watch of the night is not included [in the practice], as it is an occasion for a bhikkhu to dispel the fatigue of sleep.

"One devoted to the practice of wakefulness" means one who is intent upon the cultivation of repetition—the practice of the "delight in meditation" known as the development of foulness—and who is diligently engaged in purifying the mind from obstructive states through systematic attention while walking and sitting;
this is the meaning. "Constancy and discernment" refers to that which must be maintained continuously.
The connection is: "He is devoted to energy characterized by constancy and to wisdom characterized by proficiency because it has reached maturity.
By this, he shows that the accomplishment of the practice of wakefulness belongs only to one who is endowed with both energy and wisdom.
Now, showing the nature of that practice of wakefulness, he says: "Of the factors conducive to enlightenment," and so forth.

"Of the states conducive to enlightenment" means of the seventy-three states, such as the four truths, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, which belong to the side of the knowledge of the path characterized by the realization of the four truths.

In its exposition (niddesa), however, only the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are specified, because they alone possess the capacity to function upon a single object among the specific states conducive to enlightenment within mundane development (bhāvanā). By including them, however—
It should be understood that the remaining [terms] are also included therein.
In such passages as "when going forward" (*abhikkante*) and "when returning" (*paṭikkante*), "going forward" refers to moving ahead, and "returning" refers to turning back;
both of these are applicable to the body in its movement toward and away from the front and the rear, whether one is standing, sitting, or lying down. One acts with full awareness (*sampajānakārī*).

One who performs all duties with clear comprehension, or one who acts only with clear comprehension—here, by the inclusion of "clear comprehension," mindfulness is also included because it is never dissociated from it.
For this very reason, its detailed exposition states: "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes forward," and so forth.
Regarding the terms "looking ahead" and so on: "looking ahead" (ālokita) means looking straight forward; "looking around" (vilokita) means looking toward the intermediate directions. Of these two...
Furthermore, it should be understood that by the inclusion of these two, looking down, looking up, and looking behind—which consist of glancing, looking around, and looking back—are also included.
"In contracting and extending" refers to the contracting and extending of the limbs. "In wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the robes" refers to the manner of carrying them.

In this context, "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to the use of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the other robes by way of wearing them as undergarments or upper garments, and the use of the bowl by way of receiving alms-food and so forth.
"Eaten" (*asita*) refers to the consumption of alms-food and the like. "Drunk" (*pīta*) refers to the drinking of rice-gruel and the like.

"Chewed" (*khāyita*) refers to the chewing of flour-based snacks and the like. "Tasted" (*sāyita*) refers to the tasting of honey, molasses, and the like. Regarding "the act of excrement and urine," [this refers to] excrement...
And in the performing of defecation and urination. "Gone" means in walking. "Standing" means in standing. "Seated" means in sitting. "Lying down" means in sleeping. "Awake" means in being awake.
And here, it should be understood that "in approaching" (*abhikkante*) is said with reference to going on alms-round and so forth;
whereas in the monastery, "gone" (*gate*) and so forth are said specifically with reference to postures such as walking meditation (*caṅkama*) and the like. "In speaking" (*bhāsite*).
"In speaking" refers to when one speaks; "in silence" refers to when one does not speak.

However, in all these instances—beginning with "excellent" and so forth—one should understand that there are four kinds of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*): clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of the domain (*gocara-sampajañña*), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*). Among these:
When the desire to go forward and so forth arises in the mind, instead of acting on that impulse, one reflects:

"What purpose would there be for me in going there? This reflection upon the specific purpose of seeing the shrine and so on is called *sātthaka-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of what is purposeful). Furthermore, regarding these purposeful acts such as going and so forth, [one reflects] upon the obstacles to life and the holy life...

Sappāyasampajañña (clear comprehension of what is suitable) is the discernment of the presence or absence of all bodily and mental defilements that obstruct the practice of self-effacement (sallekha),
followed by the adoption of what is conducive [to spiritual progress]. Having thus discerned what is beneficial and suitable,
one should select from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammatthāna) or from insight (vipassanā) whichever meditation subject one personally prefers.
The practice of walking and so forth without relinquishing one’s range of activity is called *gocara-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the range).
Regarding such acts as walking and so forth, blind, foolish worldlings are deluded, thinking, "The self performs the walking and so forth," or "I am doing it.

Without being thus deluded, [one understands] that it is through the combination of causes—such as the mental activity of the desire to walk and the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*)—that [the action occurs].
"This collection of bones known as the body performs such acts as approaching;
other than that, there is no internal self (attā) or sentient being (satta) who approaches or recedes... or remains silent.
To proceed with wisdom by knowing [things] in this way according to their true nature is what is called "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (asammoha-sampajañña). This is the summary here.
The detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the *Sammohavinodanī*.

Now, since forest dwelling is not suitable for one who lacks these aforementioned qualities within him—just as it would be for monkeys and the like—even access concentration does not arise in such a person. For whom...
However, for one who possesses such qualities, dwelling in the forest is appropriate.
For he is able to produce all types of jhāna there; he adorns both the forest-dwelling and the forest-dweller, and he gladdens the entire Dispensation.
Therefore, showing the suitable lodging and the range of association for such a bhikkhu, [the Buddha said]: "He [should dwell] in seclusion..."
“He frequents lodgings,” and so forth, he said. Therein, “secluded” means empty. It is called *senāsana* because one lies down (*seti*) and sits (*āsati*) therein;
it refers to beds and the like, as well as monasteries and the like. For this very reason, in its detailed explanation (*niddesa*), it is stated: “a bed, a bench,” and so forth.
Now, in order to show another classification of it, “the forest” (*arañña*) and so forth was stated. Therein, “forest” (*arañña*) is according to the terminology of the Vinaya.

Setting aside both the village and its precincts, the remainder—referring to a forest-dwelling bhikkhu according to the Suttanta method—is called "the forest" as far as five hundred bow-lengths behind.

However, according to the Abhidhamma method, everything outside the threshold post (*indakhīla*) of the village gate should be understood as "forest. Thus it is said: "Having gone out beyond the threshold post."

For it has been said: *Kandara* means that which is called *kaṃ*, namely water; by that [water] it is *darita*, meaning a mountain region split open by water, which they also call a "slope" (*nitumba*) or a "river-grove" (*nadīkuñja*).
For there, sitting upon sandy beaches like silver plates, in forest thickets with flowing shade resembling jeweled canopies, while water flows like a mass of jewels—
For one who performs the duty of a recluse while being fanned by a cool breeze, the mind becomes one-pointed.
A mountain cave (*giriguhā*) is the space between two mountains, or a single great hollow resembling a cavern.
A forest retreat (*vanapattha*) is a place beyond the village boundary where people do not frequent, where they neither plough nor sow. For this very reason...
In the Niddesa it is said: “‘Forest retreat’ (vanapattha) is a designation for remote lodgings,” and so forth.
“The open air” (abbhokāsa) means that which is uncovered. However, if one so desires, one may dwell there having constructed a robe-tent.
“A heap of straw” (palālapuñja) refers to a pile of straw; for from a large heap of straw they extract the straw and construct a dwelling resembling a mountain cave or a grotto.
This was said with reference to people who, having placed straw on top of huts and such, sit underneath them.
Regarding the phrases "with little sound" and so forth: it is "with little sound" because it is devoid of the sound of speech;

it is "with little noise" because it is free from both the clamor of cities and the cries of wild animals and birds; and "without the wind of people" refers to the absence of the air stirred by wandering folk.

Because it is devoid of the wind of the body, it is "free from the wind of people" (*vijanavāta*); there is also a reading, "free from the talk of people" (*vijanavāda*). The meaning is that it is free from the sound of people's talk within the dwelling.
Because it is suitable for the secret activities of humans, it is "fit for human privacy" (*manussarāhasseyyaka*).
Because the mind settles properly upon the meditation subject after turning away from here and there, it is [the place] of seclusion (*viveka*), which is reckoned as "retreat" (*paṭisallāna*).
"Suitable for seclusion" (*paṭisallānasāruppa*) is used because it is appropriate for one who delights in meditation (*bhāvanārāma*). "He resorts to" (*bhajati*) is the syntactical connection.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "gone to the forest" (*araññagata*), everything remaining after setting aside the forest and the foot of a tree is included under the term "empty place" (*suññāgāra*).
"Having folded his legs crosswise" (*pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā*) means having bound the sitting posture by crossing the thighs all around. "Holding the body erect" (*ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya*)...
Having set the upper body straight and aligned the eighteen vertebrae edge-to-edge—
when one sits thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend; because they do not bend,
painful feelings do not arise moment by moment, whereby the mind becomes one-pointed and the meditation subject attains growth.
"Having established mindfulness at the nose-tip" means having established mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), or having placed it near the mouth.
For this very reason, its description states: "This mindfulness is established, well-established, either at the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth.
And here, the "sign of the mouth" refers to the middle part of the upper lip, where the breath from the nose strikes.

It strikes back. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*: “*Parī-* has the sense of embracing (*pariggaha*); *-mukham-* has the sense of an outlet (*niyyāna*);
*-sati-* has the sense of establishing (*upaṭṭhāna*); therefore it is called ‘mindfulness at the face’ (*parimukhaṃ sati*)”. In brief, the meaning there is:
“having established mindfulness that has the outlet as its embraced object.”
In the passage beginning with "coveting the world" (*abhijjhaṃ loketi*), *abhijjhā* means that which one contemplates or thinks about directly; it is lust (*rāga*).

*Loka* (the world) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. The meaning is: having suppressed sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) toward those [aggregates].

By the very act of suppression, it is "free from covetousness," not in the manner of visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) and so forth—this is the meaning. *Cetasā* means by the mind; thus characterized...
The meaning is "he dwells. "From covetousness" means from greed. "He purifies the mind" means he completely liberates it so that, having been released from it, it does not seize it again;
this is the meaning. It is called *vyāpāda* because by means of it the mind abandons its natural state, like spoiled rice or similar things;
it is corrupted by reaching a state of change, or it corrupts and destroys another.

Ill-will—both of these are synonyms for anger. And because this is taught as being common to all meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), it is not stated here in terms of loving-kindness (mettā) as "compassionate and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings," but rather simply as "one whose mind is free from ill-will.
Sloth is a sickness of the mind; torpor is a sickness of the mental factors. "Perceiving light" means by means of the perception that recognizes light seen both at night and by day.

Furthermore, since mindfulness and clear comprehension are especially required for the dispelling of sloth and torpor by means of that perception of light, he says, "mindful and clearly comprehending.
"Unagitated" means undistracted, with the mind thus internally tranquilized. "Crossed over doubt" means [crossed over] doubt...
He stands having transcended [the five hindrances]. "Without perplexity regarding wholesome states" means he is devoid of doubt—which is termed "perplexity" because it functions as "how is this?
how is this?"—concerning blameless states. Having thus shown the abandoning of the five hindrances, [the text now continues:
since meditative absorption (jhāna) does not arise for one whose hindrances have not been abandoned...

For a mind distracted by various objects due to sensual desire and so forth does not concentrate upon a single object, nor does it proceed toward the transcendence of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*);
therefore, it is said: "Having abandoned these five hindrances," and so on.

In this context, "he" refers to one who, having established himself in the aforementioned qualities of virtue and so forth, has gone to a suitable lodging such as a forest and [engages] with a meditation subject appropriate to his own temperament.

The meaning is: he strives for the attainment of the first jhāna, having abandoned the five hindrances by means of the jhāna that has been produced through constant practice free from lethargy and restlessness.
"Defiling the mind" means making the mind lack radiance. "Weakening wisdom" means because—
When these hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen mundane or supramundane wisdom to arise;
moreover, when mundane eightfold attainment or direct knowledge has already arisen, they cut off its root and cause it to fall.

Therefore, they are called "the weakeners of wisdom. In the passage beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," "sensual pleasures" refers to both sensual objects and the defilements of sensual desire.
“Secluded” (*vivicceva*) means having become secluded, having become apart; the meaning is “having departed.

Furthermore, by the use of the particle *eva* here in the sense of restriction, it shows that the attainment of the first jhāna occurs only through the relinquishing of sensual desires—which are the opposites of jhāna—just as the lighting of a lamp occurs only through the relinquishing of darkness.
This same particle *eva* is also to be supplied to the subsequent phrase: “secluded only from unwholesome states” (*vivicceva akusalehi*).

This should be connected with the word "from phenomena" (*dhammehi*). For it is not possible to enter and dwell in a jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states known as the hindrances other than sensual desire.

Furthermore, in both instances of the word "secluded" (*vivicca*), all forms of seclusion—namely, bodily seclusion and so forth, as well as seclusion by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-viveka*) and so forth—are intended here, with the exception of the seclusion that is the escape by way of substitution of opposites.

For bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka) is mentioned because it expresses seclusion from sense-objects (vatthukāma); whereas mental seclusion (cittaviveka), seclusion from the substrate (upadhiviveka), and seclusions such as suppression (vikkhambhana) are mentioned because they express seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāma) and the remaining unwholesome states.

This should also be understood as including supramundane absorption (lokuttarajjhāna). Thus, by these two terms, in their respective order, the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), the remaining hindrances, and their suppression, etc., [are indicated].
...was said. In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to the floods (ogha) and so forth.

Having thus far shown the factor of abandonment for the first jhāna, the words "with applied thought (savitakka) and sustained thought (savicāra)," etc., are now stated in order to show its associated factors (sampayogaṅga).
Therein, it occurs together with both applied thought and sustained thought.
Like a tree with its flowers and fruits, this jhāna is called "with applied thought (savitakka) and sustained thought (savicāra).

Regarding the term *vivekaja* ("born of seclusion"): here, *viveka* means separation, that is, the disappearance of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Alternatively, *viveka* means that which is separated; thus it refers to the mass of states associated with jhāna that are separated from the hindrances.
Therefore, it is "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*) because it arises from seclusion, or because it is born within that seclusion.

Regarding the phrase "rapture and happiness" (*pītisukha*): here, "rapture" (*pīti*) refers to the pervading rapture that has reached absorption (*appanā*), and "happiness" (*sukha*) is that which is associated with it.
Thus, because this rapture and this happiness belong to this jhāna, or because they exist within it, this jhāna is called "rapture-and-happiness.
Alternatively, "rapture-and-happiness" is both rapture and happiness; it is the rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion (*vivekaja*) that belongs to it, or exists within it.

Regarding "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*): although it should be stated as "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajapītisukha*) according to the single-word compound, it is also appropriate to say "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*) by applying the rule for the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). For just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too is the joy and happiness itself born of seclusion.
It is called the "first jhāna" because it is first in the sequence of counting, and also because it arises first.
First. It is called *jhāna* because of its intense contemplation (*upanijjhāna*) of the object, or because it burns away (*jhapana*) opposing states;
by this method, the meaning should be understood in the subsequent passages such as "the second *jhāna*" and so forth. "Having attained and dwells" means:
having thus reached the first *jhāna*, which is abandoned of five factors, endowed with five factors, excellent in three ways, and perfected in ten characteristics.
The meaning is that it proceeds by means of a mode of conduct (iriyāpatha) corresponding to that. And here,

although one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) is not explicitly mentioned in this passage as "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakkasavicāra), nevertheless, because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga that "Jhāna is applied thought,
sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind," it is indeed a factor (aṅga).

Having thus shown the attainment of the first jhāna, he now describes how one who has attained that first jhāna makes it masterful by means of the five kinds of mastery— namely, adverting, entering, emerging, resolving,

and reviewing— and then, having emerged from it, [perceives] therein both its state of being opposed by the proximate hindrances and its possession of the disturbance of gross initial and sustained application of mind (*vitakka-vicāra*).

Having seen the fault [in applied thought] and having exhausted attachment to it, for one who repeatedly brings that same meditation subject to mind in order to abandon the gross factors such as applied thought and to attain the peaceful factors such as rapture, the second jhāna arises;
and in order to show, by way of referring to the person, the supramundane jhāna that has that as its basis, he said: "With the stilling of applied and sustained thought," and so forth.
In this context, "tranquillity" (*vūpasama*) means "surpassing"; it is said that [the hindrances] are no longer manifest at the moment of the second jhāna.
"Internal" (*ajjhatta*) means born within oneself; the meaning is that it has arisen in one's own continuum (*santāna*). "Tranquillity" (*sampasādana*):

because it is associated with the tranquillity known as faith (*saddhā*), the jhāna itself is called "tranquillity," just as a garment is called "blue" because of its association with the color blue. "Singleness" (*ekodibhāva*): here, by means of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*)...

Because it rises as the one supreme and best, being unclimbed by anything else, it is "ekodi"; this refers to concentration (*samādhi*). One who develops and increases that is said to be "in the state of ekodi" (*ekodibhāva*), which is the second jhāna.
Furthermore, since this ekodi belongs to the mind (*cetaso*) and not to a sentient being (*satta*) or a soul (*jīva*), it is called "the state of ekodi of the mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*).
But surely this faith exists even in the first jhāna, and this concentration is called "one-pointedness";

so why is it stated in this way only here? It is said in reply: because in this jhāna, due to the absence of the agitation caused by applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), faith and concentration are powerful;
therefore, it is stated in this way only here. It is "without applied thought and without sustained thought" because they have been abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā).

In this [state], there is no applied thought (*vitakka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*), unlike the third jhāna and those following it, nor like eye-consciousness and so forth, because they have reached non-existence;
therefore, "with the stilling of applied and sustained thought" should be understood as a statement of the cause.
"Born of concentration" means born from the concentration of the first jhāna, or from the associated concentration, due to the absence of the agitation caused by applied thought and the rest.
This very [second jhāna] is called "born of concentration" for the purpose of praising the mind.

"Attaining and dwelling" means that, having attained the second jhāna— which is characterized by the abandoning of two factors, the possession of three factors, and is endowed with the three kinds of excellence—
one proceeds in the manner already described.
Having thus shown the attainment of the second jhāna, [the text now] explains that immediately thereafter, one who has attained the second jhāna makes it masterful in the manner already described;

then, seeing its fault—both because of the proximity of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*) as adversaries and because of its possession of the gross factor of rapture (*pīti*)—one exhausts attachment to it.
For the sake of abandoning that gross factor and for the sake of attaining the remaining peaceful factors, [one applies oneself].
As one repeatedly brings that same object to mind, the third jhāna arises, as does the supramundane state based upon it;
to show this, he said, “With the fading away of rapture,” and so forth. In this context, *virāga* means the fading away, the transcending;
therefore, it is “from fading away. By the word *ca* (and), he includes the subsiding of applied and sustained thought: “With the fading away of rapture, and...”
"And with the stilling of applied and sustained thought. This was stated for the purpose of illustrating the path by which it is reached and for the purpose of praising it.
Regarding the phrase "he dwells equanimous": here, equanimity (*upekkhā*) is so called because one looks on (*ikkhati*) from a state of arising, having become impartial (*apakkhapati-tā*);

it is the state of mental neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*). Because he is endowed with that [equanimity], which is clear, which has joy as its proximate cause (*pītivirāga-padaṭṭhāna*), and which is firmly established.
One who possesses the third jhāna is called "equanimous" (*upekkhaka*);

however, it is only here that this [equanimity] becomes fully manifest in its function due to the absence of the agitation of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth, and not in the first jhāna and the others.

"Mindful and clearly comprehending" (*sato ca sampajāno*) is stated by way of referring to the person; and this [jhāna] is established precisely through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, being accompanied by that same joy (*pīti*).
It is bliss; yet, when that [bliss] is removed, one does not approach the joy (*pīti*) as a calf [does not approach] its mother cow due to the force of its bond.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this was stated specifically here to show this particular point of meaning: that when this exceedingly sweet bliss exists, practitioners of yoga do not become infatuated with it, whereas they would otherwise do so.
Regarding the phrase "and he experiences bliss with the body," although for one possessing the third jhāna...
There is no active experience of pleasure; nevertheless, because his mental body (nāmakāya) is associated with an exceedingly refined pleasure,
and because his material body (rūpakāya) is touched by the exceedingly refined matter arising from that [pleasure],
through being touched by which he would experience bodily pleasure even after emerging from jhāna— it is in order to show this meaning that [the text says] "and pleasure..."
“He experiences it with the body,” he said. Regarding the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* in the passage beginning with *yaṃ tanti*: *yaṃ* means “because,” that is, because of the jhāna;
*taṃ* refers to that person who possesses the third jhāna, whom the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, describe and praise. How? As one who “dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous.
Thus, [the third jhāna] has abandoned one factor, is endowed with two factors, and is possessed of the threefold excellence, and so forth.
The meaning is that it occurs after having attained the third jhāna.

As for what is stated in the Vibhaṅga, "Jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind," that was said figuratively in order to show the jhāna together with its requisites;
however, by way of the two factors—pleasure and one-pointedness of mind—which have the characteristic of closely contemplating, this [jhāna] consists of only two factors.
It should be understood. As it is said: “There is a two-factored jhāna,” and so forth.

Having thus shown the attainment of the third jhāna, he now—having mastered that third jhāna attained immediately thereafter, having emerged from it, and having seen its fault by the method described therein—exhausts his attachment to it.

By abandoning the gross factor of pleasure and by attaining the remaining peaceful factors known as equanimity and one-pointedness, while attending to that same sign, the fourth jhāna arises, as does its supramundane counterpart (lokuttara).
To show this with reference to the person, he said: “With the abandoning of pleasure” and so forth. Therein, “with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain”:
"By the abandoning of bodily pleasure and pain": the meaning is that this occurs precisely beforehand, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna.
"With the disappearance of mental joy and grief": this is because mental pleasure and pain have already been abandoned previously.
But when does their abandonment take place? It is at the moment of the access concentration (upacāra) of the four jhānas. [These are] pain, grief, pleasure, and joy.
For these [hindrances] are abandoned precisely at the moment of access (upacāra) for each of the first four jhānas in their respective order.
If this is so, why then is it said: "Quite secluded... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna;
herein the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; herein the arisen faculty of mental joy..."?
Is it not the case that cessation is thus stated to occur only in the jhānas, as in the phrase "it ceases without remainder"? This is because what is described is cessation in its most eminent sense.

For the cessation that occurs during the moments of access concentration (*upacāra*) is merely cessation, not cessation in its most eminent sense; however, that [eminent cessation] occurs only during the moments of jhāna.

For this very reason, the qualification "without remainder" is employed here and there; for even though [defilements] have been abandoned here and there [in access], [they are not yet ceased in their most eminent sense].

These feelings are brought together here—namely, the neutral feeling whose characteristic is difficult to discern—in order to distinguish it from suffering and the rest so that it may be grasped as happiness, for the purpose of praising this jhāna, and to show its conditions.
As it is said: "Friend, there are four conditions for the attainment of the neutral liberation of mind."
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure," and so forth.
"Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" means the purity of mindfulness produced by that equanimity which consists in mental neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*).
For its purity arises from being free from defilement. And it is not only mindfulness that is purified here by equanimity; [the concentration is also purified].
Moreover, although all associated states are present, this teaching is given from the perspective of mindfulness. "Having attained,
he dwells" means that having thus reached the fourth jhāna— which is characterized by the abandoning of one factor, the possession of two factors, and is endowed with the three kinds of excellence—
he proceeds by means of a mode of conduct corresponding to that attainment.
Having thus shown the fourfold jhāna of the fine-material sphere and the supramundane, he now shows the immaterial-sphere jhāna.

Regarding that which is first therein: for one who has thus attained the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, in order to transcend the corruptible materiality (karajarūpa) of which the dangers have been seen by way of the taking up of sticks and so forth, as well as afflictions such as eye-disease and the like, [he applies himself] among those [objects] devoid of the space-kasina.
Having produced the fourth jhāna in one of the nine kasiṇas, one who desires to transcend even the kasiṇa-replica form that serves as its object—

because it resembles "corpse-form" (karajarūpa)— should master that jhāna in five ways, just as one fleeing for fear of being pursued by a snake in the forest would transcend the sight of a rope, a palm leaf, or similar objects because they resemble a snake.

Having done so, he emerges from that state; then, seeing the fault in it—namely, its having as its object a counterpart-image of a visible form that must be dispelled, and its being an immediate adversary to joy—he exhausts his attachment.

Considering the base of infinite space as peaceful because it is not something to be transcended among the factors [of jhāna], he attends to it as peaceful, extending as far as the world-system or as much as he desires.
Having either spread out the kasiṇa to that extent or, without attending to the kasiṇa, having removed the kasiṇa by means of the mental attention directed toward the space touched by it as "space,
space" or "infinite space," and then repeatedly attending to that sign of space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa as "space," the base of infinite space arises. To demonstrate that first:
He said, “By completely transcending perceptions of form,” and so forth.
Therein, “completely” (*sabbaso*) means in every way, or the sense is that of all [perceptions] without exception.

“Perceptions of form” (*rūpasaññānaṃ*) refers, by way of the term “perception,” to both the fifteen fine-material-sphere jhānas—by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional—and their respective objects.
For even the fine-material jhāna is called by way of its perception, namely, “perception of form is perception of form” (*rūpe saññā rūpasaññā*);
and since the kasiṇa that is its object is also "form," its perception is called "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*). "Having surmounted" means through fading away and cessation.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it is said: "When perceptions have been surmounted, the object itself has been surmounted; thus for one who has attained [the attainment]..."
By such statements as, "of one who has been reborn [in a higher realm] or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life," it is said that there is indeed a surmounting of perceptions;
for one who is not detached from the object, there is no surmounting of perceptions at all. Therefore, the explanation of the meaning should also be made by way of that surmounting.
"The disappearance of perceptions of resistance" means through the striking against the bases, such as the eye, and the objects, such as visible forms.
The perceptions of the five pairs of consciousness that have arisen are perceptions of resistance; they cease with their subsiding.
Although these perceptions do not exist even for one who has attained the fine-material-sphere jhāna, they do not exist there because they have been abandoned.

For the development of the fine-material sphere does not lead to dispassion toward matter; rather, their occurrence is dependent upon matter. But this development leads to dispassion toward matter; therefore, they [are absent] here.

It is appropriate to say that they are "abandoned. "Non-attention to perceptions of diversity" means the non-attention and non-orientation toward the forty-four types of sense-sphere perceptions (*kāmāvacara-saññā*) that occur with diversity as their object, or those that occur by way of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) as diverse themselves.
And herein, even in the existence produced by this jhāna, there are no perceptions of form or of resistance.
By the phrases "through non-arising," "through surmounting," and "through disappearance," their mere absence is stated.

As for the phrase "through non-attention to perceptions of diversity," it should be understood that this is said because there is the possibility of those twenty-seven perceptions—consisting of the eight wholesome states of the sense-sphere, the nine functional states, and the ten unwholesome states—arising even in the formless realm through mental attention;
therefore, it is stated as "non-attention to them."

Regarding the phrase "boundless space" (*ananto ākāso*): it is "boundless" (*ananta*) because neither its limit of arising nor its limit of passing away is discerned therein. "Space" refers to the space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa;
furthermore, its boundlessness should be understood here by way of attention (*manasikāra*).
For this very reason, it is said in the *Vibhaṅga*: "One places the mind on that space... it pervades it as boundless; therefore it is called 'boundless space. This, moreover, is its—

This is the demonstration of the mode of development. Regarding the term "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*): here, that which has no end is "infinite" (*ananta*); space itself is infinite, thus it is "infinite space" (*ākāsānanta*).

That very infinite space is "infinite-space-ness" (*ākāsānañca*) in the sense of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and it is a "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a source of birth and a meeting place.
That [space] is the object of this jhāna together with its associated states; thus it is the "base of infinite space."
The meaning is that he dwells having attained that in the manner already described.
Having thus shown the attainment of the base of infinite space, [the text now explains] that which follows immediately after:
for one who has mastered that first immaterial attainment, because it has the near-enemy of the fine-material jhānas and because its object is space as a counterpart to form—

Having seen the fault [in that state] and exhausted attachment to it, for the purpose of transcending it, one repeatedly brings to mind the consciousness that has arisen pervading space as "infinite consciousness";
thus, the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) arises. To demonstrate this, it is said:
"Having completely transcended the base of infinite space," and so forth. In this context, by the method previously explained, there is also the jhāna.

The base of infinite space is also the object. For, according to the method previously stated, it is "infinite space" and it is an "āyatana" (base) because it is the object of the first immaterial attainment;
thus, by the aforementioned method, it is called the "base of infinite space.
Therefore, by bringing both together through the non-occurrence and non-attention [to them], it says: "having completely transcended the base of infinite space."
This should be understood as having been said thus:

"Infinite consciousness" means that one attends to that very same consciousness of the first immaterial attainment as it has proceeded pervading space infinitely, thinking "infinite consciousness"; or it is infinite by virtue of the act of attention itself.
For in the *Vibhaṅga* it is also said: "It pervades the infinite. Regarding the term *viññāṇañcāyatana*: according to the method explained here, *ānañca* means simply "infinite";

thus, while it should be called *viññāṇānanta* (infinite consciousness) because it is both consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and that infinity (*ānañca*), it is called *viññāṇañca* by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhito*).
That which has this as its sphere or object (*āyatana*) is the *viññāṇañcāyatana*. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Having thus shown the base of infinite consciousness, he now— having mastered that second immaterial attainment which was subsequently attained—
sees its fault due to its being an adversary to the nearby base of infinite space and due to its having that as its object;
and having exhausted his attachment, for the sake of transcending it, [he perceives] the absence of the consciousness of the first immaterial state as "there is not."
As one repeatedly brings to mind [the thought] “there is nothing,” or “void, void,” or “secluded, secluded,” the base of nothingness arises;

to demonstrate this, he said “entirely,” and so forth. Here too, the surmounting of both the jhāna and its object, the base of infinite consciousness, should be understood in the manner already described. “There is nothing” means “nothing exists.”
The meaning is that one attends to it thus: "There is nothing; it is empty, empty; it is secluded, secluded.

Regarding the term *ākiñcaññāyatana* (the base of nothingness): here, because there is nothing whatsoever (*na assa kiñcanaṃ*) in it, it is "nothing" (*akiñcana*); what is meant is that not even so much as a mere fragment remains.
The state of being nothing is "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*); this refers to the departure from the consciousness of the base of infinite space.
It is called the “base of nothingness” (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) because it has the base of nothingness as its designation and its object. The rest is easy to understand.

Having thus shown the attainment of the base of nothingness, he now—having mastered that third immaterial attainment which was attained immediately thereafter—sees a fault in it due to its being opposed by the nearby base of infinite consciousness, and [abandons] attachment to it.

Having mastered that [base of nothingness] for the sake of transcending it, as one repeatedly brings to mind that very base of nothingness thinking, "It is peaceful, it is peaceful," the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises. To demonstrate this, he said, "In every way," and so forth.
In this context, "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" is so called because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception.
Because the perception of this jhāna together with its associated states is neither perception nor non-perception, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*).
That very same thing is the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) because, being included within the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*), it is a base.

Alternatively, the perception that exists here is "neither-perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of clear perception, due to its subtle state as a mere residue of formations (*saṅkhāra*).
Because it exists, it is not non-perception; thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*).

And because it is that neither-perception-nor-non-perception which is the base (*āyatana*) for associated states in the sense of being their foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

Not only is perception (*saññā*) of this nature here, but contact (*phassa*) is also neither-contact-nor-non-contact, consciousness (*citta*) is also neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness, and the same applies to the remaining associated states.
It should be understood that this teaching is given under the heading of "perception" (saññā).

In this context, "by way of the subtle state of the remaining formations" means by way of the state of formations that have reached an ultimate degree of subtlety. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Here, however, is the explanation of the summarized meaning from the beginning: "In this case, a bhikkhu is restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.

In the Dispensation, he points out the purification of virtue consisting in restraint according to the Pātimokkha among the virtues that serve as the foundation for a person who generates mundane and supramundane jhāna.
By the word “dwells,” he indicates the state of being possessed of a dwelling appropriate thereto.

By the phrase “perfect in conduct and resort,” he indicates the virtue of purity of livelihood and those qualities conducive to it. By the words “even in the slightest,” etc., [he indicates] by means of the aforementioned virtues...

Non-decline, and the undertaking of these [virtues] in their entirety. By the phrase "one who guards the doors of the sense faculties," the virtue of restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara-śīla) is indicated.
By the phrase "moderate in eating," the virtue dependent on the requisites (paccaya-sannissita-śīla) and qualities such as contentment are indicated.

By the passage beginning with "during the first and last watches of the night," the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) that assist one established in the virtues and ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and who delights in cultivation (bhāvanā-rata) are indicated. By the phrase beginning with "of the factors conducive to enlightenment"...
[He shows] the state of being conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiyatā*) through practice.

By the passage beginning with "When he has gone forth" (*so abhikkante*), [he shows] the application of mindfulness for the sake of not losing the qualities already mentioned and for the sake of attaining those yet to be mentioned. By the passage beginning with "He dwells secluded" (*so vivitto*), [he shows] the selection of a dwelling place suitable for meditation.

By the passage beginning with "Having gone to the forest" (*so araññagato*), [he shows] the manner of commencing the cultivation of jhāna. By the passage beginning with "He is free from covetousness" (*so abhijjho*), [he shows] the application to the cultivation of jhāna.
[The text] points out the arising of access concentration for one who has abandoned the five hindrances;

then, by means of the passage beginning with “He, having these five hindrances...,” it indicates the sequence of the arising of fine-material and immaterial jhānas as he exerts himself further and further. This, first, is the meaning of the words here.
As for the analysis of the phenomena (*dhammabheda*), it will become clear in the method of the *Vibhaṅga*. For among the three methods, the sublime and supramundane [states]...

The factors of jhāna—consisting of initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, equanimity, and one-pointedness—which are associated with wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness, have been analyzed by various methods.
However, only the remaining sense-sphere phenomena associated with jhāna are included here.

Although the morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha and so forth are also mentioned herein, they are nevertheless included for the purpose of showing the preliminary practice leading to the jhānas.
They were stated by way of factors associated with jhāna, but it should be understood that they are not included here.

In the *Pañhāpucchaka*, however, they may be either wholesome or indeterminate: three jhānas are associated with pleasant feeling, while the fourth is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; furthermore, equanimity as a feeling should not be mentioned in this context.

They may be results (*vipāka*), or they may be phenomena subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*). The first *jhāna*, excluding initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), possesses both initial and sustained application;

however, in this context, initial application is without initial application and consists of sustained application alone, while sustained application is not so described. The [remaining] three *jhānas* are without initial application and without sustained application.
Two *jhānas*, when devoid of rapture (*pīti*), are accompanied by rapture; three [of the remaining], when devoid of pleasure (*sukha*), are accompanied by pleasure. The fourth...
Excluding equanimity, it is accompanied by equanimity; in the third jhāna there is bliss, and here equanimity is not to be mentioned...
[and so on] ...it may be exalted, it may be immeasurable; three may have an immeasurable object, or they may not be so described; the fourth is not to be described in any of the three ways;
three may have the Path as their root, may have the Path as their dominant factor, or may not be so described.
The fourth [jhāna] is not to be described in any of the three ways... pe ...rapture has external objects; the fourth is not to be described in any of the three ways...
pe ...non-manifest and non-reactive, not roots... pe ...not mind or mental factors, and without conflict. The rest is easily understood.
There is no method here apart from the canonical text (pāḷimuttanaya); henceforth, however, without saying even this much, we shall speak only where it exists.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Jhānas is finished.

Now, regarding the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Illimitables (*Appamaññā*), with respect to the meaning of the phrases beginning "the four illimitables" (*catasso appamaññāyo*), they are so called by way of their pervasiveness and measurelessness.
The "immeasurables" (*appamaññāyo*). For these either pervade immeasurable beings by way of their object, or they pervade even a single being in an exhaustive manner;
thus, they are called "immeasurables" by way of the measure of their pervasion. It is also appropriate to speak of them by way of the seven immeasurables.
"Accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*) means endowed with loving-kindness. "One direction" (*ekaṃ disaṃ*)...
"Among the four directions, beginning with the east, whatever single direction there may be"—this is said by way of pervading the beings included within that direction.
"Having pervaded" means having touched and made it the object. "He dwells" means he causes [the mind] to proceed. Regarding the phrases "likewise the second," and so on:
the meaning is that just as he pervaded one direction, in exactly the same way he subsequently pervaded the second, the third, and the fourth.
Thus, by this same method, "above, below, and across" means that one dwells having pervaded the upper direction, the lower direction,
and the intermediate directions in succession with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*mettā*). Up to this point,
the specific pervasion of loving-kindness by encompassing each individual direction has been shown.
The passage beginning with "sabbadhi," however, is stated for the purpose of showing [compassion] without limitation. In that context, "sabbadhi" means everywhere.
"Sabbattatāya" means by way of selfhood toward all—namely, toward the various classes of friends, enemies, neutrals, and so forth, whether inferior, middling, or superior;
what is meant is that one does not make distinctions among them but regards them as equal to oneself. Alternatively, "sabbattatāya" means by way of every state of mind, even [the slightest].
The meaning is "without distraction externally. "Containing all" means containing all beings; the meaning is "associated with all beings.

"The world" refers to the world of beings (*sattaloka*). Furthermore, the phrase "accompanied by loving-kindness" is stated either to show its connection with the qualifiers such as "vast," etc., or as a conclusion.
In that context, its vastness should be understood by way of pervading. By way of plane...

Furthermore, there is loftiness (*mahaggatatā*). There is immeasurability (*appamāṇatā*) by virtue of proficiency and by virtue of having immeasurable beings as its object. Through the abandoning of the adversary that is ill-will (*byāpāda*), there is freedom from enmity (*averatā*).
Through the abandoning of mental distress (*domanassa*), it should be understood as being without suffering (*niddukkhatā*), conditioned (*saṅkhatatā*), and free from affliction (*abyāpajjatā*).
In this way, the meaning should be understood for the phrases "accompanied by compassion" (*karuṇāsahagata*) and so forth; such, then, is the meaning of the words here.

The distinction between these states is indeed easy to understand. However, according to the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga-naya*), among the three types of fine-material-sphere consciousness—wholesome, resultant, and functional—the four states consisting of non-hatred (*adosa*), compassion (*karuṇā*), gladness (*muditā*), and equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*) are analyzed through various methods as the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) associated with sentient beings.
Furthermore, those associated with these [consciousnesses] that belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are also included here.

They are not included [in the mundane sense]. However, these immeasurables (appamaññā) do not exist at all among the formless-sphere (arūpāvacara) and supramundane (lokuttara) states. In the *Pañhāpucchaka*, moreover, these may be either wholesome (kusala) or indeterminate (abyākata).
Three are associated with pleasant feeling (sukhā vedanā), while the fourth is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhā vedanā).

In the triad of results (vipākattika), they are of all three types; they are accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā) and are without initial application and sustained application (avitakka-avicārā). The remaining ones are of all three types and are exclusively exalted (mahaggatā).
Regarding the dyads of limited object and past object, they are not to be so described;

rather, they have external objects, are non-demonstrable and non-reactive, have loving-kindness as their root, while the rest do not have roots, are not consciousness, are mental factors, belong to the fine-material sphere, and are surpassable. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of the Illimitables is finished.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix for the Analysis of the Training Rules (Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā) Regarding the meaning of the matrix for the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpadavibhaṅgamātikā*): first, in terms of meaning—“training rules” (*sikkhāpadāni*) means words to be trained in, or sections of training.
Furthermore, all wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) are “trainings” (*sikkhā*) because they are to be practiced; in the sense of being their foundation, [the training rules are so called].

A *pada* (foot) refers to any one of the five factors of virtue (*sīlaṅga*). Regarding killing living beings (*pāṇātipāta*) and so forth: "killing" (*pāṇātipāta*) means the excessive striking (*atīva pāto*) of a living being (*pāṇa*), the sense of which is the slaughter of a living being (*pāṇavadha*).
Herein, from the conventional standpoint (*vohārato*), a "living being" (*pāṇa*) is a sentient being; from the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

Now, with respect to that living being, for one who perceives it as a living being, there arises—through the doors of body and speech—an action that originates from an effort (*upakkama*) to sever the life-faculty.
The volition of killing that proceeds through any particular door is *pāṇātipāta*; therefore, it is "from taking life" (*pāṇātipātā*). "Abstention" (*veramaṇī*) means refraining;

that very thing, by the method already stated, is a training precept (*sikkhāpada*), thus it is the "training precept of abstention" (*veramaṇi-sikkhāpada*). "What is not given" (*adinna*) is that which has not been bestowed; it is what is possessed by another.
The taking of what is not given and belongs to another is "taking what is not given" (*adinnādāna*). The seizing from another is theft, robbery.

This has been said. In terms of its meaning, however, taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) is the volition of theft (*theyyacetanā*) that arises from the preparatory effort of one who perceives as such what is possessed by another and takes it away.
"In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means in the case of sense-objects (*vatthukāma*). "Wrong conduct" (*micchācāra*) refers to base behavior driven by defiled sensual desire (*kilesakāma*);
for a man, this concerns women protected by their mother and so forth, and for a woman, it concerns men other than her own designated husband.
And it is said that this refers to transgressing conduct regarding places that should not be approached.

In terms of its meaning, however, sexual misconduct is the volition of sexual intercourse—either initiated by the act of directing the path toward what is not the path regarding objects that should not be approached, or occurring in the form of consent.
"False" (*musā*) means an unreal and untrue matter; "speech" (*vādo*) means [speaking] while knowing its unreality.

It is the making known of things as they truly and accurately are. From the perspective of its characteristic, however, lying is the volition that originates bodily and vocal efforts which destroy the welfare of another, by one who, having recognized a matter as not being so, desires to make it known to others as being so. As for *surā*:
there are five kinds of *surā*—barley-liquor, cake-liquor, rice-liquor, that mixed with fermenting agents, and that prepared from various ingredients. *Meraya*... [is]...
There are five intoxicants (*āsava*): the intoxicant of flowers, the intoxicant of fruits, the intoxicant of molasses, the intoxicant of honey, and that which is composed of various ingredients.

Both of these are "intoxicating drink" (*majja*) in the sense of being intoxicating. The volition by which one drinks that intoxicating drink is a "basis for negligence" (*pamādaṭṭhāna*) because it is a cause of negligence;

therefore, they are called "the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicating drink" (*surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhāna*). The rest is easy to understand. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.
The analysis of the dhammas (dhammabheda), however, will become clear in the method of exposition (vibhaṅganaya). The same applies to what follows.

Among these methods of exposition, there is no Suttantabhājanīya; rather, in the Abhidhammabhājanīya, these five training rules (sikkhāpada) are analyzed in various ways in the first section by way of the abstentions (virati) associated with sense-sphere wholesome consciousness (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta), and likewise in the second section by way of volition (cetanā).

However, in this context, those mental states associated with the volition of abstention (*viraticetanā*) are not themselves training rules (*sikkhāpada*); rather, they are associated with the training rules.
Likewise, in the third method, [the training rules] are analyzed in various ways by way of all the factors such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth.

But in the *Pañhāpucchaka*, because volition and contact and so forth are training rules in a figurative sense (*pariyāya*), [they are excluded from the list of] those that constitute training rules in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*).
They are classified precisely by way of the abstinences (*virati*). For therein, the five training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) are exclusively wholesome;
they may be associated with pleasure, or they may be associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure... [and so on] ...they have only limited objects, only present objects, and only external objects;

they are non-demonstrable and non-reactive; they are not roots, but are accompanied by roots; they are not consciousness, but are mental factors (*cetasika*); they belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and are surpassed by something higher.
“...and the state of non-conflict (araṇā). Herein, as for those training rules stated to have sentient beings as their object:

because they are by nature abstentions, and because they take as their object only those limited phenomena currently present—which are designated as "sentient beings"—they should be understood as being described as having limited objects.
Now, regarding the killing of living beings and so forth from which one must abstain—

The exposition independent of the canonical texts (pāḷimutta-vinicchaya) should be understood according to the following: by way of the nature of the phenomena (dhamma), by way of the paths of action (kamma-patha), by way of the object (ārammaṇa), by way of the root of feeling (vedanā-mūla-kamma), and by way of the factors of the blameworthy (sāvajja-aṅga).
In that regard, first, by way of the nature of the phenomena: all these five, beginning with the destruction of life, have the nature of volition (cetanā) alone. By way of the paths of action...
There are five courses of kamma. As for their objects: killing has the life-faculty as its object; taking what is not given has sentient beings as its object, or else has formations as its object;
likewise for false speech; sexual misconduct has women or men as its object; drinking intoxicants has formations as its object.
As for their feeling-tone: killing is accompanied by painful feeling; taking what is not given is accompanied by three types of feeling; likewise for false speech and sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, in terms of feeling, they are two-fold—pleasant and neutral—and drinking liquor is likewise. From the perspective of their roots, however, the first is rooted in hatred and delusion;
the second may be rooted in greed and delusion, or it may be rooted in hatred and delusion; false speech is likewise [two-fold].

Wrong conduct, however, is rooted only in greed and delusion, as is drinking liquor. As for their nature as kamma, here false speech is verbal kamma, while the remaining ones are exclusively bodily kamma.
Regarding the blameworthy nature [of kamma], first, among the taking of life, it is less blameworthy when the being is a non-human and more blameworthy when the being is human.
Among humans, it is less blameworthy when the body is small and more blameworthy when the body is large. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort.
Even when the effort is equal, it is less blameworthy when the [victim] has few virtues and more blameworthy when they have great virtues. When the virtues of the bodies are equal...
When there is defilement and the effort [of the act] is mild or intense, the offense is minor or major; however, in the case of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), it is even more major.
Regarding taking what is not given, it is minor or major depending on whether the object is inferior or sublime, and whether it is devoid of qualities or belongs to one who possesses them.
Even therein, it is minor or major relative to each specific instance, and it is more major when the object belongs to one whose taints are destroyed.
It should be understood as follows: sexual misconduct consists in the transgression against the objects of those who are immoral or virtuous.

Furthermore, it should be understood that within this category, the offense is minor or major depending on the specific object; it is most blameworthy when there is transgression against one whose taints are exhausted (an arahant).

As for false speech, its degree—whether minor or great—depends on the insignificance or magnitude of the matter it destroys, whether the owner of the subject lacks virtue, and whether they possess such qualities.

Depending on each instance, it is either minor or major in its blameworthiness. Furthermore, that which proceeds with the intention not to give away what belongs to oneself, or with a motive of jest, in such forms as "it does not exist," and so forth, is minor in its blameworthiness;
whereas that which proceeds by means of false testimony and the like, such as saying "I saw it" when one did not see it, is major in its blameworthiness.
However, having spoken a falsehood for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, it is even more major in its blameworthiness. [The same applies to] the drinking of fermented liquor.

Starting from the point where there is at least a drop [of blood], the offense is less blameworthy as one takes [the life] after another; it is more blameworthy when many [drops are involved]; and when the drink is sufficient to produce a bodily reaction, it is even more blameworthy.
As for the factors [of the offense] of taking life: there is the living being, the perception of that being as a living being, the murderous intent, the means employed, and death by that means.
There are five factors. There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishment, by persistence, by means of science, and by means of supernormal power.

For taking what is not given, there are five factors: the fact that it is owned by another, the perception thereof as such, the intention to steal, the preparatory effort, and the carrying away by that effort.
These are indeed the six modes of application beginning with "by one's own hand," which apply respectively to theft, misappropriation, and so forth.

[These] proceed by way of [their respective bases]. For sexual misconduct, there are three factors: an object that is not to be approached, the intention to engage in it, and the act of entering the path as if it were the path.

There is only one mode of action (*payoga*), namely, acting with one's own hand. In this same way, the modes of action for the remaining [offenses] should be understood. For false speech, there are four factors:
an untrue matter, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and another’s comprehension of that meaning.
The factors [for the offense of drinking liquor]: the fact that it is one of the liquors such as *surā*, and the swallowing of it—these are the two factors.

Having thus understood the determination of killing living beings and the other [offenses] from the perspective of their nature (*dhamma*) and so forth, one should now understand the five abstinences, beginning with the abstention from killing living beings, by way of their being paths of wholesome action (*dhammakammapatha*), their objects (*ārammaṇa*), their undertaking (*samādāna*), and their application (*payoga*).
It should be understood by way of its divisions and as an exposition independent of the canonical text.

Regarding that, the exposition by way of the paths of wholesome action is exactly as previously stated. By way of object, however, these have as their objects the various things to be transgressed against, such as the life faculty and so forth.
By way of undertaking, one undertakes them either in the presence of another or by oneself, saying, "I resolve upon the five precepts," either all together or individually.
Or by one undertaking them, these [precepts] become indeed undertaken. However, in terms of application, all of them are applications performed by one's own hand (*sāhatthika*).
As for householders, whatever they transgress, that alone constitutes a breach (*khaṇḍa*), not the others. Householders possess unbound morality;
they guard whatever they are able to keep. But for novices (*sāmaṇera*), in one [instance]...
When [the precept] is transgressed, all [the factors] are broken; thus should the analysis independent of the canonical text (pāḷimutta-vinicchaya) be understood.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix (mātikā) for the analysis of the training rules (sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the analysis of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga).
Regarding the analytical summary (*mātikā*) of the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga* by way of meaning: first, "four analytical insights" (*catasso paṭisambhidā*) refers to four distinct types.

However, since they are defined in the Exegesis (*Niddesa*) by way of knowledge—as in "knowledge regarding the meaning is the analytical insight of meaning" (*atthe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā*)—it should be understood that these are exclusively knowledge and nothing else.

"Analytical insight of meaning" (*atthappaṭisambhidā*) is a classification of knowledge whose object is the meaning; it is so called by virtue of its capacity to discern, reveal, and define the distinctions within that meaning.
"Knowledge that has reached the analysis of the meaning" is the sense. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. And here, "meaning" (*attha*) refers to cause-and-effect.
For that [meaning] is called "meaning" because it is to be sought, to be gone toward, and to be produced by way of its cause.
Furthermore, in terms of its classification, this too is fivefold: whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what was spoken, fruition, and functional [consciousness].
"Dhamma" means condition. For it is called "dhamma" because it brings about, causes to proceed, produces, and leads to the fruit.
In its classification, this too is fivefold: any cause whatsoever that generates a fruit; the Noble Path; what has been spoken;
the wholesome; and the unwholesome.
"Etymology" (niruttī) refers to the word— known as natural etymology— which expresses both the phenomena (dhammas) and their meanings (atthas) as they have been described.

For one who takes these etymologies of phenomena and meanings as an object and reviews them, the knowledge that has become differentiated in various respects therein is called the analytical knowledge of etymology (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
And herein, the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) has sound as its object, not conceptual designation (paññatti) as its object.

For one who has attained the analytical knowledges, upon hearing the sound "contact is feeling" and so forth, knows: "This is a natural linguistic expression"; but upon hearing "contact is a feeler" and so forth, he knows:
"This is not a natural linguistic expression. And a "natural linguistic expression" is the Māgadha language, by which the Fully Enlightened Ones [teach].
They codified the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas into a formal tradition; and while Brahmās in the forest wilderness speak without having heard any speech from others,
and children speak according to their own natural disposition, and the Māgadhī language predominates among humans in the woeful states and in the world of the gods,
subsequently there arose from that the regional languages such as Andhaka, Yonaka, and Damila, as well as the eighteen great languages beginning with Sakkata.

And it is "nibbatta" (produced). For since it does not change even when other languages change, and remains forever in its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it is called "the expression of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvaniruttī*).

Furthermore, regarding that Māgadhī language which is called "Brahma-usage" (*brahmavohāra*) and "Noble usage" (*ariyavohāra*), for the word of the Buddha that has entered into the textual tradition (*tanti*) through that [language], and for those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)...
The very act of coming to the ear is *papañca*. However, as soon as it strikes the ear, the meaning presents itself through hundreds and thousands of methods.
But when it has been committed to a text in another language, that meaning does not immediately enter their minds;

it must be learned with difficulty. And for ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), even after they have mastered the entire word of the Buddha, the attainment of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)—

There is no such thing as a noble disciple who has not attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). One who has attained the analytical knowledges knows sound according to its divisions into nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles;

does he not know it? To the same extent that, upon hearing a sound, he knows "this is a natural linguistic expression" and "this is not a natural linguistic expression," to that same extent he will also know this.

And it should be understood that this is not the function of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). "Ingenuity" (*paṭibhāna*) refers to the all-pervading knowledge whose objects are phenomena, meanings, and so forth;

for one who reviews that knowledge by taking it as an object, the knowledge that has reached differentiation is called the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). Through the attainment of these four analytical knowledges...

It should be understood that by means of five factors—namely, the acquisition of the scriptures (pariyatti), careful listening to the Dhamma, inquiry into the meaning, and prior application—they become clear;
and they reach their differentiation in two stages: the stage of the trainee (sekha) and the stage of the one beyond training (asekha).
This, then, is the word-meaning here.
Furthermore, the analysis of the categories (*dhammabheda*) will become clear here according to the method of the *Vibhaṅga*.

For in all three methods of the *Vibhaṅga*, the analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dhamma*), etymological definitions (*nirutti*), and ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*)—all three—are analyzed in various ways together with the classification of their respective objects by way of the types of knowledge associated with sense-sphere impulsion (*kāmāvacara-javana*).
However, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) pertains to those very knowledges as well as to those associated with the eight supramundane consciousnesses (*lokuttara-citta*).

[This is] together with its classification according to its respective objects.
