For even the supramundane knowledges (*lokuttara-ñāṇa*) are called the "analytical knowledge of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) because they have as their object Nibbāna, which is the "meaning" to be attained by the path.

However, in the section on questions (*pañhāpucchaka*), [the analytical knowledges] may be wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*); the three analytical knowledges may be states that are subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*).
They may be neither-result-nor-dhamma-of-the-result-type; the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*) is of all three types. Three analytical knowledges are limited (*paritta*);

the analytical knowledge of meaning may be limited or it may be immeasurable (*appamāṇa*). The analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*) has a limited object and also has an external object;
the remaining ones are of all three types. The analytical knowledge of language has only a present object; the analytical knowledge of meaning...

They should not be described in either of the three ways; they are non-demonstrable and non-reactive (*anidassana-appaṭigha*); they are roots (*hetu*) and accompanied by roots (*sahetuka*); the three analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are surpassable (*sauttara*);
the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is of both kinds; and so too is the absence of conflict (*araṇā*). The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix (*mātikā*) for the Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (*Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*) is finished.
Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga-mātikā):
Regarding the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of knowledge, first: "In one way" means by a single mode or as a single category.
As for "basis of knowledge" (ñāṇavatthu), it is called "basis of knowledge" because it is both knowledge and a basis for various kinds of attainments.

The five consciousnesses are the five beginning with eye-consciousness. In passages such as "not roots, rootless," the meaning is to be understood everywhere according to the method explained previously under the section on "roots" and so forth.

Furthermore, among the categories of "roots" and so on, the five consciousnesses cannot be called "root phenomena" or "phenomena accompanied by roots"; rather, they are exclusively not roots and are rootless.
Thus it is said. In this way, there is a connection with what will be stated later, at the conclusion of the singlefold classification, namely:
"Wisdom is the manifestation of things as they really are" (*yāthāvakavatthu-vibhāvanā*). By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere according to what is appropriate.
And therein, the term "non-mental factors" (*acetasika*) refers to the consciousnesses themselves, because those associated with the fivefold sensory consciousnesses are not included here.
"Having arisen bases and having arisen objects" refers to the present momentary state;
this excludes the future, for those [consciousnesses] do not arise with respect to the five future bases and objects.

"Having pre-arisen bases and having pre-arisen objects" excludes simultaneous arising, for those [consciousnesses] do not arise dependent upon a simultaneously arisen base and object. "Having internal bases" means...
These arise having made the five types of sensitive matter (pasāda), which are internal-internal by nature, their physical basis (vatthu).
In this context, the fivefold consciousness is itself internal and has an internal basis; mind-consciousness is internal as it is dependent on the heart, but has an external basis;
and the three aggregates associated with the fivefold consciousness are external, yet have an internal basis.
The three aggregates associated with mind-consciousness are external and have external bases; thus should this tetrad be understood.
"With undivided bases and undivided objects" means having bases and objects that have not ceased.

For they do not arise in dependence upon bases and objects that have already ceased. "With diverse bases and diverse objects" means that, respectively, they each have fixed bases and objects such as the eye and visible forms.

They have mutually distinct bases and mutually distinct objects. For visual consciousness does not arise by taking the ear or any other [sense-organ] as its base after abandoning the eye, nor by taking sound or any other [object] as its object after abandoning visible form;
the same applies to the others. By the phrase "they do not experience each other's domain and object,"...
And this demonstrates their very diversity of objects. "They do not arise without attention" means they do not arise in the absence of adverting;
the meaning is that they do not arise when an object has not been adverted to by five-door adverting. "Not without mental engagement" explains the same point here by way of a synonym.
"Not without immediate succession" means [they do not arise] without being immediately contiguous to one another.
They arise. "Neither before nor after" means they do not arise simultaneously even within a single moment.
And it should be understood that not only these, but other consciousnesses as well—whether two or more—do not arise together;
rather, only a single consciousness arises at a time. As it has been said: "One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases," and so forth.
By the phrase "not immediately following one another," it is shown precisely that there is no immediate succession (*anabbokiṇṇatā*).
"Without effort" means they are not of the nature of adverting; standing in the place of adverting, they are incapable of performing the function of adverting.
"It does not discern any phenomenon" refers even to that single [phenomenon] spoken of thus: "Phenomena are preceded by the mind."
No person whatsoever discerns a wholesome or unwholesome state; the meaning is that they do not accomplish it through those consciousnesses.
"Except for the mere falling upon" means setting aside the mere falling upon, the mere coming into the range of objects such as visible forms;
even a more proficient person has no discernment of the wholesome or unwholesome other than the mere discernment of the object that has come into the range of the fivefold sense-consciousness.
The meaning is that it is not able to do so.
"Even immediately after the five consciousnesses" means even after the mind-element (*manodhātu*). Here, the word *api* (even/also) has the sense of inclusion;

by this, it is indicated that it is not only after the mind-element, but also after the five-door consciousnesses that follow it, which conclude with their respective object-impulsions (*tadārammaṇa*).
It should be understood that this meaning—that one does not discern any wholesome or unwholesome state—is what is being shown.

Although impulsive consciousnesses (javana), whether wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise, do arise at the five sense doors, they should nevertheless be regarded as "non-quotable" (abbohārika), like flowers on a withered tree.
The same principle applies to the statements "one does not assume any posture," and so forth. Not...
For indeed, by means of the five-door consciousnesses, one does not assume any posture such as walking and so forth; one does not initiate bodily or verbal action;
nor does one produce intimation (*viññatti*); nor does one undertake wholesome or unwholesome states;
nor does one enter mundane or supramundane concentration (*samādhi*), nor emerge from it; nor does one pass away from one existence, nor arise in another existence.

All this activity occurs solely through the mind-door consciousness (*manodvārika-citta*). Just as these [five sense doors] lack these activities, so too they lack the entry into the path of certainty (*niyāmokkama*) and so forth.
For no one enters into the certainty of falsehood (*micchattaniyāma*) or the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*) by means of five-door impulsions (*pañcadvārika-javana*);
nor do these [impulsions] comprehend a name or clan, or the designations of the meditation objects (*kasiṇa*), etc., or the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), etc.
...or they arise with reference to that. Regarding the phrases "he does not sleep well" and so forth:
he does not descend into sleep nor see any dream by means of any of the five-door consciousnesses.

For when one is sleeping, even if the sense faculties are struck by coarse objects such as the sound of great lamps or musical instruments, the five-door adverting consciousnesses first turn back toward the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

They are not capable [of doing so]; only the adverting consciousness at the mind-door is capable. When that has arisen, the mind-door impulsion (manodvārika-javana) impels and then sinks back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
However, in the second instance, among the five-door adverting consciousnesses, whichever one is appropriate turns back the life-continuum;
thereafter, the various door-process consciousnesses, ending with the registration (tadārammaṇa), proceed in their respective order.
Having occurred, they descend into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). On the third occasion, however, mind-door adverting and impulsion consciousnesses arise;
at that moment, there is the discernment of the five objects such as visible forms, and the being awakens from sleep.
Thus, one awakens by means of the mind-door consciousness itself.
For one sees even a dream by that [mental consciousness] alone, not by the five doors. Furthermore, one seeing such a dream sees it for four reasons:
either from a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*), or from what was previously experienced, or from the influence of a deity, or from a prognostic sign (*pubbanimitta*).
Moreover, they proliferate these in many ways through their combination and conjunction. Among these, that which arises from a disturbance of the elements such as wind and bile—
A dream seen from what was previously experienced is not true.
That which one sees through the influence of a deity may be either true or false; for when deities are angry, they show things even in a distorted manner.
However, that which one sees as a prognostic omen is exclusively true, such as the sixteen great dreams of the Bodhisatta Kosalarāja and others.

Furthermore, it is only trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) who see these four kinds of dreams, not those beyond training (*asekha*), because the latter have abandoned the perversions (*vipallāsa*).
Now, does one see this while asleep or while awake? What follows from this?

If one sees it while asleep, since dreams possess the nature of wholesome states (*kusala*) and so forth, whereas the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) lacks that nature, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma would ensue.

Now, one might argue: "If, upon waking, there were no offense even for a transgression committed in a dream that is not subject to legal formalities (*abbhohārika*), because it is as entirely blameworthy as one that is subject to formalities (*sabbohārika*), then a contradiction with the Vinaya would arise.

Furthermore, since there is no other way by which one could see a dream, it would follow that dreams do not exist at all. This does not follow. Why? Because [the Buddha] was overcome by drowsiness caused by monkeys (*kapimiddha*).
One sees [this] because of the statement: "Great King, one overcome by 'monkey-sleep' (kapimiddha) sees a dream.
Now, that sleep which—like monkey-sleep—is characterized by rapid fluctuations due to being repeatedly interspersed with wholesome and other types of consciousness, is "monkey-sleep.
One who is drowsy by means of that sees a dream; therefore, a dream may be either wholesome or unwholesome, by way of the adverting consciousness and its object.
Even that which is indeterminate, and what is done in a dream, is unable to draw forth rebirth-linking due to the weakness of its wholesome or unwholesome nature;
however, it is to be experienced during the course of existence (pavatta). Regarding the phrase "wisdom as the manifestation of things as they really are" (*yāthāvakavatthu-vibhāvanā paññā*):

herein, that which is not the state of being without root-cause for the five types of consciousness as previously stated—that is, the state of being without root-cause... up to ...the state of not seeing dreams—is the "state as it really is" (*yāthāvaṭṭha*).
It is the wisdom that discerns each respective thing as it truly is; thus, it is the "discernment of things as they really are" (*yāthāva-vatthu-vibhāvanā*).
In this way, by the single method mentioned—that is, by one way, one aspect, or one portion—it constitutes a basis for knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*).
The section on the singlefold is concluded.

Regarding the phrase "atthajāpikā" (meaning-producing) in the *Duka*: among the five meanings explained in the *Atthapaṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*, it is called "meaning-producing" because it produces, generates, or brings about the appropriate meaning.

It is the wisdom associated with wholesome consciousnesses of the four planes, as well as with sense-sphere functional consciousnesses that serve as the preliminary stages (*parikamma*) and so forth for the super-knowledges (*abhiññā*) of those beyond training (*asekha*).
For among these, wisdom associated with the wholesome produces and generates its own respective fruit known as "result" (vipāka) belonging to its own plane;

however, that associated with sense-sphere functional states—when it becomes the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) and so forth for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), or functional states—produces and generates the fruit known as Arahatship.
Therefore, these are called "producers of welfare" (*atthajāpikā*) in the Commentaries.

However, although not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi, the wisdom of functional javanas (kiriyajavana-paññā) in the three planes is called "that which makes the goal exist" (atthajāpikā) because, by way of conditions such as the immediate (anantara), it causes its own immediate functional state to come into being.

Wisdom that has made the goal exist (jāpitatthā paññā) stands having caused the co-nascent resultant state to exist; or, it is itself an existing state (atthabhūtā), having been made to exist, generated, and brought into operation by its own causes.

"Jāpitatthā" means that wisdom associated with the four planes of resultant consciousness (*vipāka*), functional consciousness (*kiriya*), and the attainments of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-samāpatti*) has its purpose fulfilled.

In the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, even the wisdom associated with the remaining types of functional consciousness—which were not mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*)—is described as "having its purpose fulfilled" because it has been brought to completion by its respective causes and constitutes its own end. The rest is easily understood.
The dyads are finished.

Regarding the triads, however, in the case of the "triad of what is born of reflection" (*cintāmayattika*), there are those which—without having seen or heard from another, but by one's own natural capacity (*dhammatā*)—are produced through the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayanubuddhi*) in the form:
"When this exists, that will come to be. These pertain to blameless spheres of action (*kammāyatana*), spheres of craft (*sippāyatana*), and branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*).
Wisdom consisting in the knowledge of the ownership of kamma and the knowledge conforming to the truths is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*).
In this context, "kamma" refers to the sphere of action (*kammāyatana*), which includes both lowly work such as that of a carpenter or a refuse-collector, and noble work such as agriculture or trade.

"Skill" (*sippa*) refers to the sphere of craft (*sippāyatana*), which includes both lowly crafts such as those of a basket-maker or a weaver, and noble crafts such as mathematics, accounting, and writing. [This also includes] protective charms such as the *Nāgamaṇḍala-paritta*.
Only righteous knowledge (*dhammika-vidyā*) is a branch of knowledge (*vidyāṭṭhāna*). Among these, wisdom (*paññā*) arises solely through the power of reflection (*cintābala*).

For bodhisattvas and others, for the benefit of sentient beings, produce—by the power of their knowledge (*ñāṇabala*)—various blameless crafts, skills, and methods of preparation for those tasks, even regarding things previously unseen or unheard;
they also produce protective spells (*paritta*) such as the *Nāgamaṇḍala*, and so forth. Even when performed in this way...

Having first mastered them, those [meditations] performed by practitioners become exactly like the crafts they have learned. Knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*) is the wisdom that understands:
"Wholesome kamma is one's own property among beings; unwholesome kamma is not. Alternatively, it is the wisdom that understands:
"Only wholesome kamma is one's own property among beings, because it leads to their welfare, and nothing else. Conformity-knowledge (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) is...
This is insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). Because it conforms to the ultimate truth of the Noble Truth of the Path, it is called "conforming to the truth" (*saccānulomika*).
Indeed, these two types of knowledge are also merely knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*), produced through the power of reflection without having heard them from another.
Furthermore, this does not arise for just any beings; rather, it arises for those who are renowned and possessed of merit.

It arises only for Great Beings (mahāsatta). Even among those, it should be understood that the knowledge conforming to the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa) arises only for two Bodhisattvas who are in their final existence (pacchimabhavika).

"Wisdom consisting in what is heard" (sutamayā paññā) refers precisely to the wisdom regarding the spheres of action (kammāyatana) and so forth, as previously described, which is produced by means of hearing from another.
However, without having heard from another, [one may know] the spheres of action and so forth, or what is being done by another.
Wisdom acquired by seeing or by learning what has been spoken is called "consisting of hearing" (*sutamaya*).

Both of these—consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) and consisting of hearing—are exclusively of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). However, wisdom consisting of development (*bhāvanāmaya*) is the wisdom of the sublime and supramundane impulsion-moments that arises through the accomplishment of the preliminary stage of development belonging to the sense-sphere, which has proceeded either by way of reflection or by way of hearing.
In the triad beginning with "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*), those consisting of giving are so called because they proceed by way of relinquishing the objects to be given;

those consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*) proceed by way of fulfilling virtue; both of these pertain only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). However, here, those consisting of development (*bhāvanāmaya*) are the wisdom (*paññā*) of the four planes that proceeds by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
In its exposition (*niddesa*), although it says, "the wisdom of one who has attained [meditative absorption]," this refers only to exalted (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) wisdom.
Although it was stated thus, that was said by way of the highest limit.

However, it should be understood that the preliminary-stage developments (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) of the sense-sphere realms, as well as the access-developments (upacāra-bhāvanā) of the recollections, are included within "development" (bhāvanāmaya).

As for the first triad, these are not included in "development" because they were already included in "reflection" (cintāmaya); even there, inclusion should be understood only for those [states] produced by the power of development.

In the triad of higher virtue (*adhisīla*), the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is called "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) because it is a virtue superior to the remaining virtues due to its being the cause for insight (*vipassanā*);
the wisdom associated with that is "wisdom regarding higher virtue" (*adhisīle paññā*).

Furthermore, the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) that establish insight are called "higher mind" (*adhicitta*) because they are superior to other states of consciousness; the wisdom therein is "wisdom regarding higher mind" (*adhicitte paññā*). And here, by way of the term "mind" (*citta*), [the term refers to]...
Concentration has been explained. However, the wisdom of the path and its fruition, together with insight, is called "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*) because it is superior to the others.
And that higher wisdom is spoken of as "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the teaching on the threefold training due to their essential identity. Virtue and the rest are each twofold: "virtue, mind, and wisdom;
higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Among these, the former refers to the five precepts and the ten precepts.

The eight attainments beginning with the "circle-footed" (vaṭṭapādikā) and the wisdom regarding the ownership of kamma pertaining to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-kammassakatapaññā) occur respectively at the time of Bodhisattas,
ascetics and wanderers, and universal monarchs (cakkavattirāja), even when a Tathāgata has not yet appeared;
however, the remaining factors mentioned last become widespread only when a Tathāgata has appeared.

It should be understood as "not arisen. And here, those wholesome states that serve as the necessary conditions for turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*)—whether they arise through honoring the Three Jewels with gifts and so forth, or through going for refuge, hearing the true Dhamma, and so forth—are indeed included within the categories of higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*); thus they should be understood as such.

In the triad on skill in profit (*āyakosalla*), "profit" (*āya*) means growth; it consists in the abandonment of unwholesome states and the like which are disadvantageous, and the arising of wholesome states and the like which are beneficial.

It is twofold. "Decline" (*apāya*) means non-prosperity; that too is twofold, owing to the loss of what is beneficial, such as the wholesome (*kusala*), and the arising of what is harmful, such as the unwholesome (*akusala*).
Skill in these [two] is wisdom, whose intrinsic nature is the wholesome. Skill in decline belongs only to one possessed of wisdom, because it is possible for one with wisdom to understand:

"In this way, through the occurrence of mental attention and so forth, non-prosperity arises and prosperity declines," and thus to apply the appropriate remedy for both. Skill in means (*upāyakosalla*)...

Here, "means" refers to the wisdom that knows the appropriate means for urgent tasks and so forth. Furthermore, all three of these should be understood as wisdom pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
The rest is easily understood.
The triad is finished.
Regarding the tetrads, in the first one, both the knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma and the knowledge in conformity with the truths have already been mentioned.

Here, however, it should be understood that all wholesome wisdom associated with the taints (sāsavā), excluding the knowledge in conformity with the truths, is the knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma.
In the four paths and the four fruits, it is wisdom itself that constitutes the knowledge of one possessing the path and the knowledge of one possessing the fruit.

In the "Tetrad on the Truths," it should be understood that only the wisdom of the Noble Path and its Fruits is included under the four headings beginning with "knowledge of suffering" by virtue of their single penetration of the four truths.
For although sense-sphere knowledge also occurs with the four truths as its object,
it is not included in the text here because what is intended is specifically that which functions through the act of penetration.

In the "Tetrad on the Dhamma," wisdom regarding the path and its fruition is called "knowledge of the Dhamma. For among these, knowledge of the path is called "knowledge of the Dhamma" because it knows the Dhamma of the Four Truths by way of a single penetration.
Knowledge of fruition, however, should be understood as "knowledge of the Dhamma" by way of the truth of cessation.
Furthermore, that which is produced through the power of the path is [so called] because it encompasses the method of penetrating the truths regarding the past and the future.
The reviewing knowledge regarding what has occurred is called "knowledge of conformity" (*anvaya-ñāṇa*). Its mode of occurrence should be understood as knowing by way of the principle that:
"By whatever methods the Noble Ones knew the Dhamma of the Four Truths in the past, they knew this very same Four Truths in exactly this way; and in the future time, they will know them likewise.
Knowledge of discerning the minds of others by way of their being possessed of lust and so forth is [the next stage].

"Knowledge of the conventional" (sammuti-ñāṇa) means knowledge of the conventional. However, with the exception of the knowledge of the penetration of others' minds and the knowledge of the inference of dhammas, it is called "conventional knowledge" because it is recognized as all mundane wisdom and knowledge.
In the tetrad on accumulation, wisdom in wholesome sense-sphere consciousness leads to accumulation and not to diminution; for it accumulates death and rebirth-linking.

Thus, it does not diminish. Path-wisdom, however, leads to diminution and not to accumulation. Skillful wisdom regarding the material and immaterial realms leads both to accumulation and to diminution;
for it diminishes, by way of suppression, both the defilements and the resultant phenomena rooted in them.
The remaining indeterminate wisdom leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
In the tetrad on disenchantment (*nibbidācatukka*), the wisdom of the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere leads to disenchantment but not to penetration (*paṭivedha*).

For that wisdom occurs as a disenchantment with the defilements because it is to be attained through seclusion from sense-desires; yet, because it has not reached the state of being a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), it does not lead to penetration by means of direct knowledge.
The wisdom of the fourth jhāna leads to penetration but not to disenchantment. For that [wisdom], by virtue of its being a basis for direct knowledge...

It leads to penetration even for the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Because of the revulsion toward the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) at the very moment of the first jhāna, it does not lead to dispassion (*nibbidā*).

However, the wisdom of the second and third jhānas should be understood as being based on the first jhāna because they are accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), or as being based on the fourth jhāna because they are without applied thought (*avitakka*). But the path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) leads to both dispassion and...

And for penetration. For here, by way of the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, it should be understood that these [types of wisdom] lead both to disenchantment and to penetration through the attainment of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). The remaining mundane and supramundane wisdoms lead neither to disenchantment nor to penetration. Regarding the tetrad on the partaking of decline: it "partakes of decline," thus it is "declinable" (*hānabhāginī*); the same applies to the others. And here, "penetration" (*nibbedha*)— [The text continues: ...is the piercing of the mass of suffering, the breaking of the mass of suffering, the shattering of the mass of suffering, the demolition of the mass of suffering, the destruction of the mass of suffering, the eradication of the mass of suffering, the abolition of the mass of suffering, the extinction of the mass of suffering, the appeasement of the mass of suffering, the cessation of the mass of suffering, the relinquishment of the mass of suffering, the fading away of the mass of suffering, the cessation of the mass of suffering, the non-arising of the mass of suffering; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of ignorance, the breaking of ignorance, the shattering of ignorance, the demolition of ignorance, the destruction of ignorance, the eradication of ignorance, the abolition of ignorance, the extinction of ignorance, the appeasement of ignorance, the cessation of ignorance, the relinquishment of ignorance, the fading away of ignorance, the cessation of ignorance, the non-arising of ignorance; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the breaking of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the shattering of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the demolition of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the destruction of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the eradication of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the abolition of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the extinction of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the appeasement of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the cessation of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the relinquishment of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the fading away of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the cessation of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the non-arising of the underlying tendency to ignorance; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of defilements, the breaking of the mass of defilements, the shattering of the mass of defilements, the demolition of the mass of defilements, the destruction of the mass of defilements, the eradication of the mass of defilements, the abolition of the mass of defilements, the extinction of the mass of defilements, the appeasement of the mass of defilements, the cessation of the mass of defilements, the relinquishment of the mass of defilements, the fading away of the mass of defilements, the cessation of the mass of defilements, the non-arising of the mass of defilements; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of suffering, the breaking of the mass of suffering, the shattering of the mass of suffering, the demolition of the mass of suffering, the destruction of the mass of suffering, the eradication of the mass of suffering, the abolition of the mass of suffering, the extinction of the mass of suffering, the appeasement of the mass of suffering, the cessation of the mass of suffering, the relinquishment of the mass of suffering, the fading away of the mass of suffering, the cessation of the mass of suffering, the non-arising of the mass of suffering; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of formations, the breaking of the mass of formations, the shattering of the mass of formations, the demolition of the mass of formations, the destruction of the mass of formations, the eradication of the mass of formations, the abolition of the mass of formations, the extinction of the mass of formations, the appeasement of the mass of formations, the cessation of the mass of formations, the relinquishment of the mass of formations, the fading away of the mass of formations, the cessation of the mass of formations, the non-arising of the mass of formations; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of craving, the breaking of the mass of craving, the shattering of the mass of craving, the demolition of the mass of craving, the destruction of the mass of craving, the eradication of the mass of craving, the abolition of the mass of craving, the extinction of the mass of craving, the appeasement of the mass of craving, the cessation of the mass of craving, the relinquishment of the mass of craving, the fading away of the mass of craving, the cessation of the mass of craving, the non-arising of the mass of craving; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of clinging, the breaking of the mass of clinging, the shattering of the mass of clinging, the demolition of the mass of clinging, the destruction of the mass of clinging, the eradication of the mass of clinging, the abolition of the mass of clinging, the extinction of the mass of clinging, the appeasement of the mass of clinging, the cessation of the mass of clinging, the relinquishment of the mass of clinging, the fading away of the mass of clinging, the cessation of the mass of clinging, the non-arising of the mass of clinging; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of becoming, the breaking of the mass of becoming, the shattering of the mass of becoming, the demolition of the mass of becoming, the destruction of the mass of becoming, the eradication of the mass of becoming, the abolition of the mass of becoming, the extinction of the mass of becoming, the appeasement of the mass of becoming, the cessation of the mass of becoming, the relinquishment of the mass of becoming, the fading away of the mass of becoming, the cessation of the mass of becoming, the non-arising of the mass of becoming; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of birth, the breaking of the mass of birth, the shattering of the mass of birth, the demolition of the mass of birth, the destruction of the mass of birth, the eradication of the mass of birth, the abolition of the mass of birth, the extinction of the mass of birth, the appeasement of the mass of birth, the cessation of the mass of birth, the relinquishment of the mass of birth, the fading away of the mass of birth, the cessation of the mass of birth, the non-arising of the mass of birth; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of aging, the breaking of the mass of aging, the shattering of the mass of aging, the demolition of the mass of aging, the destruction of the mass of aging, the eradication of the mass of aging, the abolition of the mass of aging, the extinction of the mass of aging, the appeasement of the mass of aging, the cessation of the mass of aging, the relinquishment of the mass of aging, the fading away of the mass of aging, the cessation of the mass of aging, the non-arising of the mass of aging; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of death, the breaking of the mass of death, the shattering of the mass of death, the demolition of the mass of death, the destruction of the mass of death, the eradication of the mass of death, the abolition of the mass of death, the extinction of the mass of death, the appeasement of the mass of death, the cessation of the mass of death, the relinquishment of the mass of death, the fading away of the mass of death, the cessation of the mass of death, the non-arising of the mass of death; it is the noble path, the penetration of the noble path, the penetration of the noble fruit, the penetration of Nibbāna. It is the piercing of the mass of sorrow, the breaking of the mass of sorrow, the shattering of the mass of sorrow, the demolition of the mass of sorrow, the destruction of the mass of sorrow, the eradication of the mass of sorrow, the abolition of the mass of sorrow, the extinction of the mass of sorrow, the appeasement of the mass of sorrow, the cessation of the mass of sorrow, the relinquishment of the mass of sorrow,

The noble path [is so called] because it brings about that [fruit] by way of being the basis for insight (vipassanā) that produces it. Regarding the term "conducive to penetration" (*nibbedhabhāginī*): in all four instances, it refers specifically to the wholesome wisdom (*paññā*) pertaining to the form and formless realms.
For those [states] are "conducive to decline" (*hānabhāginī*) when, having fallen away from their own intrinsic nature, they become conditions for descending to a lower level;

they are "conducive to distinction" (*visesabhāginī*) when they become conditions for the proximate reflection (*upanijjhāna*). However, due to the strength of attachment to that meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*), one does not attain distinction.

It should be understood that by not recollecting decline, it is "partaking of steadiness" (ṭhitibhāginī) when it remains in its portion of steadiness; and it is "partaking of penetration" (nibbedhabhāginī) precisely when it serves as the basis for the noble path and as the foundation for insight (vipassanā).
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are the analytical knowledges of meaning, phenomena, language, and ingenuity. The four modes of practice (paṭipadā) are...

The "painful way with sluggish direct knowledge" and so forth have already been explained above. Regarding the "four objects," such as "limited, with limited objects" and so on, they follow the same method explained above.
In the tetrads beginning with aging-and-death as well, four applications have been stated by way of path-knowledge alone.
The rest is easy to understand.
The section on the tetrads is finished.
Regarding the pentads, "five-factored right concentration" is that which is endowed with the five factors of knowledge mentioned in the Canon as follows:
pervasion by rapture, pervasion by pleasure, pervasion by the mind, pervasion by light, and the sign for reviewing. Thus it is said.
Concentration (*samādhi*). In this context, wisdom that arises pervading rapture is called "pervasion by rapture" (*pītipharaṇatā*) in two jhānas;
wisdom that arises pervading bliss is called "pervasion by bliss" (*sukhapharaṇatā*) in three jhānas.

Wisdom that arises pervading the minds of others is called "pervasion of mind" (*cetopharaṇatā*), which is the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*). Wisdom that arises in the pervasion of light is the divine eye knowledge (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*).
The pervasion by light is called "illumination. The reviewing knowledge is called the "reviewing sign.
In this context, the pervasion by rapture and the pervasion by pleasure are like the two feet; the pervasion by the mind and the pervasion by light are like the two hands;
the reviewing sign is like the head; and the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge is like the trunk of the body. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
He shows the fivefold right concentration as if it were a man endowed with all his limbs and members.
By this concentration, the five factors should be understood as the five factors of knowledge. Thus:
"Right concentration consisting of five knowledges."
“‘This concentration is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future’— this knowledge arises within oneself.
‘This concentration is noble and spiritual’… [as before] … ‘It is practiced by Great Beings’… [as before] … ‘It is peaceful, sublime, attained through tranquility,
reached through unification, and not constrained by volitional effort’… [as before] … ‘That…”
"Furthermore, the knowledge arises within oneself: 'I enter this concentration mindfully, and I emerge from it mindfully.
Thus, the concentration of the fruit of attainment—consisting of the fruit of Arahantship—is endowed with these five kinds of reviewing knowledge mentioned in the Text.
For it is "pleasant in the present" because it is pleasant at every moment of its absorption; and each preceding moment is [the cause] for the succeeding one.

Because it serves as a condition for the extremely refined bodily consciousness-pleasure at the time of emerging from the fruition attainment—which is itself more sublime than the western concentration-pleasure and has pervaded the entire body through its own arising—a pleasant ripening arises in the future;
by this method also, it is "with a pleasant ripening in the future," which is one factor. Furthermore, because it is remote from the defilements...
It is "nirāmisa" (unworldly) because it is devoid of the bait of sensual pleasures, the bait of worldly gain, and the bait of the world;

it is "not frequented by base men" because it is practiced by Great Beings such as the Buddhas and others; it is "peaceful" because of its stability in its own factors and because it brings peace to all the distress of the defilements;
it is "sublime" in the sense of being unassailable; and it is "attained through subsiding" because the state of the subsiding of the defilements has been reached.

And because it has not yet been attained as a state of singleness— like a weak, tainted concentration that merely suppresses opposing states and wards off defilements through volitional effort and application—
it is not "gone to suppression and warding-off with volitional effort.

[The phrase] "this concentration belongs to the person" refers to this concentration [of the one whose taints are destroyed], by virtue of his attainment of fullness of mindfulness and according to the time-limit he has determined.
Because it possesses the single factor of both entering into attainment while mindful and emerging [therefrom] while mindful— being thus endowed in every aspect with these five factors—
it is called "right concentration consisting of five knowledges.
The group of five is finished.

"Wisdom in the six direct knowledges" refers to the knowledge associated with the six types of direct knowledge (abhiññā) thus described: the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (iddhividha), the knowledge of the divine ear-element (dibbasota), the knowledge of the penetration of others' minds (cetopariya), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati), the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapāta), and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).
Among these, the last is supramundane (lokuttara); the remaining five belong to the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
The section on the Sixes is finished.

Regarding the seventy-seven bases of knowledge in the section on the Sevens: there is one knowledge consisting in the reviewing of “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” and one knowledge consisting in “in the absence of ignorance, volitional formations do not arise”;
thus there are two knowledges concerning the past, and likewise two concerning the future.
Thus, these two together with the reviewing knowledge that "it is subject to destruction" and so forth constitute seven knowledges.

In this same way, for each of the remaining links up to the end of birth— thus, for each of the eleven factors of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time— there are seven [knowledges] by way of the knowledge of positive and negative concomitance and the knowledge of seeing their fall.
By multiplying seven by seven, there are seventy-seven knowledges.
The section on the sevens is finished.
The section on the eights is indeed easy to understand.

"Insight in the nine successive attainments" refers to the eight types of insight associated with the fine-material and immaterial attainments— which are termed "successive attainments" because they must be entered and produced in sequential order by one entering the attainment of cessation— and furthermore,
the insight of one who has emerged after having touched cessation immediately following those attainments, [viewing] cessation as peace.
And including the knowledge of reviewing, there are nine.
The section on the group of nine is finished.
Regarding the "tenfold [section]" and the phrase "of the Tathāgata": it refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One who has come just as the ancient seers such as Vipassī and others have come.
"The powers of a Tathāgata" means the powers belonging exclusively to the Tathāgata and not shared by others;

or alternatively, the meaning is that these powers have come down just as the powers of previous Buddhas came down through the perfection of their accumulated merit (*puññussaya*). In this regard, the power of a Tathāgata is twofold:
physical power and the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). Of these, the physical power is to be understood according to the lineage of elephants.
For this was said by the ancients:
“The Kāḷāvaka, the Gaṅgeyya, the Paṇḍara, the Tambapiṅgala, The Gandha,
the Maṅgala, the Hema, the Uposatha, and the Chaddanta— these are the ten.”
For these are the ten breeds of elephants. Among them, the *kāḷāvaka* is the ordinary breed of elephant;

the bodily strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one *kāḷāvaka* elephant. The strength of those ten is equal to that of one *gaṅgeyya*; the strength of ten of those is equal to that of one *paṇḍara*;
the strength of ten of those is equal to that of one *tamba*; and the strength of ten of those is equal to that of one *piṅgala*.

The strength of ten scent-elephants (*gandhahastin*), the strength of ten *maṅgala* elephants, the strength of ten *hema* elephants, the strength of ten *uposatha* elephants, the strength of ten *bala* elephants, and the strength of ten *Chaddanta* elephants—this is called the Nārāyaṇa-strength of the Tathāgata.
According to the calculation of ordinary elephants, this [Nārāyaṇa-strength] is... [the strength of] elephants.
The strength of ten thousand times ten million men—that is, the strength of ten thousand *koṭis* of men—is the physical power of the Tathāgata.
As for the many thousands of knowledges, such as the ten powers (*dasabala*) and the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), that is called the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*).
Here too, it is specifically the power of knowledge that is intended. For knowledge is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.
"Endowed with these powers" means possessed of these ten powers of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). "The place of the bull" (*āsabhaṭṭhāna*) means the preeminent position.
Furthermore, a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred cattle; a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand cattle. Alternatively, a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred bulls (*vaja*);
a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand bulls; a *nisabha* is the best of all cattle—white, beautiful, and capable of bearing great burdens.
The bull (*nisabha*) is the one who overcomes all dangers and is unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts; it is this that is intended here by the term "bull" (*usabha*).
For this too is a synonym for him. "Belonging to the bull" (*āsabha*) means "of the bull.

"Place" (*ṭhāna*) refers to the immovable position of that bull-like being, who, endowed with the strength of a *nisabha*, presses down upon the earth with his four feet; furthermore, because it is like the place of the bull, it is called "the bull's place" (*āsabhaṃ*).
For just as a bull known as the "leader" (nisabha), endowed with the strength of a bull, stands by pressing the earth with his four feet and remaining in an immovable position,
so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers, having pressed the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence,
stands in an immovable state, unassailable by anyone in the world including the devas.
He claims that very [state], accepts it, does not renounce it, and ascribes it to himself; therefore it is said, "he claims the place of the bull.
"In assemblies" means in the eight kinds of assemblies. "He roars the lion’s roar" means he utters the best roar, the fearless roar, which is like the roar of a lion.
Or he roars a lion’s roar. This meaning is to be illustrated by the Sīhanāda Sutta.

Or, just as a lion is called a "lion" because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hana*), so too the Tathāgata is called a "lion" because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and his slaying of the doctrines of others; he roars that lion’s roar.
In such expressions as *brahmacakka*, the word *brahma* means supreme and pure.
As for this term *cakka*, it is seen in the sense of "accomplishment" in passages such as: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels possessed by which gods and humans [prosper].

It is seen in the sense of a "mark" in passages such as: "Wheels were born on the soles of his feet. And it is seen in the sense of a "chariot part" in the passage: "Like the wheel of one who draws [a cart]."
In the phrase “The four wheels, the nine gates,” it refers to the postures (*iriyāpatha*). In the phrase “Turn the wheel for all living beings,” it refers to giving (*dāna*).

In the phrase “The divine wheel-treasure appeared,” it refers to the wheel-treasure (*ratanacakra*). In the phrase “For the person overcome by desire, the wheel spins upon the head,” it refers to the chest-wheel (*uracakra*).
In the phrase “Even with a wheel whose edge is as sharp as a razor,” it refers to... [the wheel of a chariot].
Regarding "the wheel of weapons": here it refers to the discus of the thunderbolt (*asanimaṇḍala*). Regarding "the wheel set in motion by me": here it refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
But here, it is the Wheel of Dhamma that is set in motion. And the Wheel of Dhamma is twofold:
the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*). Among these, that which is developed through wisdom—

The meaning is that he causes to proceed, arouses, manifests, and expands both of these: the supramundane knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) which brings about the noble fruits for himself, and the sense-sphere knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*) inspired by compassion which brings about the noble fruits for his disciples;
yet both of these are the unique, direct knowledge of the Buddhas alone, not shared with others.
Now, in order to explain in detail those ten knowledges which were initially introduced as "the powers of a Tathāgata," he said:
"What are the ten? Herein, the Tathāgata... and so forth. In this context, "place and non-place" means cause and non-cause.
For a cause is so called because the fruit abides therein; since it arises and proceeds in dependence upon that [cause], it is therefore called its place.
"Place" (ṭhāna) is what is said. "Non-place and non-non-place" means cause and non-cause.
"That by which" means that knowledge by which he understands things as they truly are; the meaning is that this knowledge of place and non-place is called the Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata.
In this way, the application [of the commentary] should be understood everywhere in the subsequent sections as well. But how does the Blessed One [know] here the place...?
"Does he understand, as it truly is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible?
"It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent...
or should regard any phenomenon as a self, or should deprive his mother of life, or his father... or an arahant of life, or with a mind of malice..."
He understands: "It is impossible for one to draw blood from a Tathāgata, to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, to point to another teacher, or to be reborn in an eighth existence;
yet it is possible for an ordinary person (puthujjana) to do all these things.
Likewise, he understands: "It is impossible for two Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, to arise simultaneously in a single world-system..."
He understands: "It is impossible for two Wheel-turning Monarchs to arise simultaneously; such a case does not exist.

Only one arises; such a case exists. Likewise, he understands: "It is impossible that the desirable result of the three kinds of misconduct—bodily misconduct and so forth—and the undesirable result of good conduct should both come to pass; such a case does not exist."
"It is possible that a result contrary to those [causes] might arise for them;

this is a possibility"—thus he understands, as it truly is, that whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, that is a "possibility" (*ṭhāna*), while the opposite is an "impossibility" (*aṭṭhāna*).
Here, however, is the summary of the commentary's analysis: "'One might approach [them] as pleasant'..."
This was stated with reference to the apprehension of [the conditioned] as pleasant by way of the perversion of view (*diṭṭhivipallāsa*), such as "the self is exclusively happy" and so forth;

however, by way of the perversions of perception and mind (*saññācittavipallāsa*), even a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), when overwhelmed by the fever of the defilements, approaches some formation as pleasant—just like one terrified by a rutting elephant might approach a pit of dung out of a desire for purity. This refers to the occasion of approaching [it] as the self.
In order to include the kasiṇas and so forth, as well as Nibbāna, the term "any phenomenon" (kañci dhammaṃ) was used instead of saying "formations" (saṅkhāra).

Regarding the words "mother" and so on, although a noble disciple—even if his head were being cut off—would never, even in another life, commit the taking of life starting from a tiny ant, or any other misconduct such as taking what is not given that serves as a cause for the states of misery; yet...

He is unable [to do so]. However, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya*) alone are cited here for the purpose of demonstrating the great culpability of the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
For the state of being an ordinary person is indeed blameworthy, such that one might even commit deeds of immediate retribution.
And here, it refers specifically to one who is a human being killing a biological mother or father who is also a human being, even if their gender has changed.
For one who deprives [a parent] of life, the deed constitutes an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense.

However, if one deprives of life a mother or father who has become an animal, or if one is oneself an animal and deprives a human being of life, or if one deprives an animal of life, one does not incur an *ānantariya* offense;
yet the deed is grave, and it remains as having come close to an *ānantariya*. The same applies even to an *arahant*, provided they are a human being.

One who kills incurs an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. Even if one strikes someone while he is still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and that person later attains *arahatta*, and then dies from that very same injury, the striker is considered a murderer of an *arahant*. This applies whether the victim was a non-human spirit (*yakkha*) or an *arahant*;

likewise, even if one kills other noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) while they are still human beings, the karma is similar to an *ānantariya* offense. However, as for [the case] when [the victim] was an ordinary person at the time...

If one gives a gift and, having attained Arahatship, consumes it, that gift is considered as given to an ordinary person (*puthujjana*). There is no immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) for one who kills other noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), though the karma is nevertheless heavy. In this context, the "fourfold group beginning with the ewe" should be understood: for instance, if one intends, "I shall kill an ewe," and instead kills one's mother or father lying in the place of the ewe— [The text continues: ...so too, if one intends, "I shall kill my mother," and instead kills a woman who is not one's mother, there is no immediate retribution; however, the offense of killing is still committed. Likewise, if one intends, "I shall kill a woman who is not my mother," and instead kills one's mother, there is no immediate retribution; however, the offense of killing is still committed. Similarly, if one intends, "I shall kill my father," and instead kills a man who is not one's father, there is no immediate retribution; however, the offense of killing is still committed. Likewise, if one intends, "I shall kill a man who is not my father," and instead kills one's father, there is no immediate retribution; however, the offense of killing is still committed. Furthermore, if one intends, "I shall kill an animal," and instead kills a human being, there is no immediate retribution; however, the offense of killing is still committed. Likewise, if one intends, "I shall kill a human being," and instead kills an animal, there is no immediate retribution; however, the offense of killing is still committed. Thus, in these cases, although there is no immediate retribution, the karma remains heavy. This is because the object of the action is grave, even if the intended object was different. It is like the case of a man who, intending to shoot an arrow at a tree trunk, misses it and hits his own son standing nearby; he incurs the offense of killing his son. Or it is like the case of a man who, intending to shoot an arrow at a deer, misses it and hits a man standing nearby; he incurs the offense of killing that man. Therefore, in such instances, although there is no immediate retribution, the karma is nonetheless heavy. This is because the object of the action is grave, even if the intended object was different. One who kills an arahant incurs an immediate offense (ānantariya); however, one who kills a sheep with the intention of [killing] a sheep, or with the intention of [killing] one's mother or others, does not incur an immediate offense.
But if one kills those very persons [the mother, etc. with the intention of [killing] one's mother or others, one certainly incurs it.
This same principle applies to the "fourfold group of thieves" and so forth.

Regarding the shedding of blood: because of the Tathāgata’s indestructible body, even when another person with a malicious mind attempts to wound him, there is no cutting of the skin or the flowing of blood.
However, from the rock hurled by Devadatta, it was as if struck by a pebble that had broken off;
thus, within the body itself at a single spot, there was blood only enough for a tiny fly to drink.
It falls unevenly; for one who acts in such a way, there is an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense.
However, this does not apply to Jīvaka, who—with a gentle mind—removed the malignant blood and restored health; for him, there was only merit.

Furthermore, there is an *ānantariya* offense for one who destroys a *caitya* after the Blessed One has attained *parinibbāna*, for one who cuts down a Bodhi tree, and for one who commits violence against the relics.
There is no offense, though the action is similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense.

However, it is permissible to cut off a branch that obstructs a stupa of the Bodhi tree or a relic image, or to go through a breach in the site of a shrine, or to remove it after cutting it at the root of the Bodhi tree.
Even if birds perched on a branch drop excrement upon the shrine, it is permissible to cut the branch.
For indeed, a bodily relic shrine (*sarīracetiya*) is far more venerable than a shrine of enjoyment (*paribhogacetiya*).
It is not permissible to cut a branch that obstructs a shrine containing relics, whether it be a temple for an image or a Bodhi-tree house;
however, it is permissible to cut a branch that robs it of its vitality or one located at a spot where it is decaying, as this brings merit just like the act of tending to the body.

When a schism in the Saṅgha occurs within a single boundary where the Saṅgha shares common residence and common affiliation, and while the Saṅgha stands as one, someone takes a factional Saṅgha apart and causes a schism in the Saṅgha through five causes, there is a schism in the Saṅgha and it constitutes an act of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma).
For it is said: "Upāli, the Saṅgha is split by five ways. By which five? By formal act (kamma)..."
“By means of a formal act, by means of a recitation, and by means of the taking of voting tickets.

In this context, “by means of a formal act” refers to any one of the four types of formal acts, such as the *apalokana* (motion) and so forth. “By means of a recitation” refers to the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*.

“Speaking” means conversing while illustrating the eighteen grounds for schism—such as “what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma,” and so on—through various arguments. “By means of a proclamation” [refers to the formal announcement].

“Surely you know my state of being learned and so forth; how indeed could one such as I advocate a teaching that is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, a departure from the Teacher’s instruction?
Do I not fear the states of misery?”—having spoken thus into their ears in this manner, he encouraged their minds by means of such proclamations.
“By the taking of voting tickets”: having thus supported their resolve through these formal declarations and proclamations.
Having made it a matter of non-retrogression, he says, "Take this voting ticket," and [proceeds] by means of the taking of the voting tickets (*salākaggāha*).

In this context, the formal act (*kamma*) itself, or the proclamation (*uddesa*), is the criterion; however, the preliminary discussion (*vohāra*), the announcement (*anussāvana*), and the taking of the voting tickets are merely its prior stages.
Even when these have been completed, the Saṅgha remains undivided. But when, through the preliminary discussion and the announcements, four or...

Or, if a monk distributes voting tickets (*salāka*) among those in excess [of the quorum], and having taken a factional assembly (*vagga-saṅgha*), performs a formal act (*kamma*) or a recitation (*uddesa*) separately, then the Saṅgha is said to be "divided.
However, for one whose primary intention is non-division, it is permissible provided there is the perception of unity (*samagga-saññā*).
For one who acts with the perception of unity, there is neither division nor an immediate offense (*ānantariya*); likewise, from that...
For one who acts with an incomplete assembly. For it is said: "Upāli, there are four on one side and four on the other, and a ninth proclaims [the resolution]," and so forth.
Among these five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), the schism in the Saṅgha is verbal action (*vacīkamma*); the remaining ones are bodily actions (*kāyakamma*); indeed, all of them...
These [offenses] arise from both the door of the body and the door of speech.

For instance, the schism of the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda) arises from the door of the body for one who effects a schism by means of hand gestures; and in this case, the schism of the Saṅgha endures for an eon (kappa).
Indeed, one is released from the schism of the Saṅgha only upon the destruction of the eon; however, there is no such fixed rule for the remaining [offenses]. And by whom these five...
When deeds have been performed, it is the schism in the Saṅgha alone that ripens in hell; the remaining deeds fall into such categories as "there was the deed, but there was no ripening of the deed.
In the absence of a schism in the Saṅgha, [the result falls upon] the shedding of blood;
in its absence, the murder of an Arahant; in its absence, the murder of a mother or a father; and even among those, upon one who is more perfect in virtue.
Furthermore, among these, the first four are common to all householders and renunciants;
however, schism in the Saṅgha belongs only to a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu and is not common to others, for even a bhikkhunī does not cause a schism in the Saṅgha, much less the others.
It should be understood that all five of these are associated with painful feeling and have hatred as their root.
Regarding the phrase "he might produce an eighth existence": by what is the noble disciple’s taking of an eighth existence determined?
By insight (vipassanā). For he whose insight is sharp produces only one more existence and, having attained Arahantship, is called a "single-seeder" (ekabījī).
He whose insight is dull attains Arahantship in the second... [or] up to the sixth existence, and is called a "family-to-family" (kolaṅkolo).

However, for one whose [defilements] are very weak, they do not exceed a seventh existence; having attained Arahantship there with certainty, such a person is called "one who has seven births at most.

For even if a thunderbolt or a mountain peak were to fall upon the head of such a person while they have fallen asleep in their seventh existence, they would attain Arahantship at that very moment and pass away into Parinibbāna.
For it is with reference specifically to not exceeding seven more existences at the highest limit that he is called "one who is fixed, destined for full enlightenment.
In such statements as "two Arahants or two Perfectly Enlightened Ones in a single world-system," a "single world-system" refers to the birth-field consisting of ten thousand great chiliocosms;
this is because there is no possibility of the arising of two Buddhas within the scope of their sovereign power.
In this context, the prohibition against the simultaneous arising of two Buddhas is made with respect to the field of birth (*jātikhettam*) alone.

Excluding this particular world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), Buddhas do not arise in other world-systems because of the nature of the causes for Buddhahood—such as the lineage of beginningless Buddhas—and for that very reason, sentient beings do not attain final Nirvana without exception [in all worlds]. For if [Buddhas were to arise] in all world-systems...

If Buddhas were to arise [only occasionally], all beings would have attained final Nibbāna without remainder prior to this; yet that is not the case. Therefore, it should be understood that they arise only in this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), which serves as the dwelling place for those endowed with the supporting conditions for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) through an unbroken succession of beginningless Buddhas. Even here, they are difficult to encounter; and because of their rarity, it is precisely here— [The text continues: ...that one should strive with diligence. For it is said: "Rare is the appearance of a Buddha in the world; rare is the arising of the True Dhamma; rare is the opportunity for human birth; rare is the attainment of the support of the requisites of practice. Therefore, having obtained such a rare opportunity, one should apply oneself with great effort. Furthermore, the Blessed One has declared: "Monks, there are these four things that are difficult to obtain in the world. What four? A Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; the True Dhamma taught by him; the opportunity for human birth; and the arising of faith in the heart. Thus, having obtained these four difficult-to-obtain things, one should not let them pass in vain, but should practice the Dhamma with heedfulness. Moreover, the Blessed One has said: "Monks, there are these four things that are difficult to find in the world. What four? Birth in a noble family; being born in a central region; possessing the faculties of a man; and meeting with a Tathāgata who has appeared in the world. Since these are so difficult to find, one should exert oneself in the practice of the Dhamma. And furthermore, the Blessed One has said: "Monks, there are these four things that are difficult to encounter in the world. What four? A Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; the True Dhamma taught by him; the opportunity for human birth; and the arising of faith in the heart. Having encountered these four difficult-to-encounter things, one should not be negligent, but should practice the Dhamma with diligence. Therefore, it is said: "Rare is the appearance of a Buddha; rare is the arising of the True Dhamma; rare is the opportunity for human birth; rare is the arising of faith in the heart. Having obtained these four rare things, one should strive with vigor. And finally, the Blessed One has said: "Monks, there are these four things that are difficult to obtain in the world. What four? A Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; the True Dhamma taught by him; the opportunity for human birth; and the arising of the desire to hear the Dhamma. Since these are so difficult to obtain, one should not waste this opportunity, but should practice the Dhamma with earnest application. Thus, it is said: "Rare is the appearance of a Buddha; rare is the arising of the True Dhamma; rare is the opportunity for human birth; rare is the arising of the desire to hear the Dhamma. Having obtained these four rare things, one should strive with great effort. Therefore, it is said: "Having obtained this rare opportunity, one should practice the Dhamma with heedfulness. This is what was intended. Thus ends the section on the difficulty of encountering a Buddha. Even for incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*), there may be a period devoid of the arising of a Buddha.

And if Buddhas were easily encountered, it would be possible for even sixty-four Buddhas to arise within a single *asaṅkhyeyya* of the turning away from contraction (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi-asaṅkhyeyya*), because there is an interval between Buddhas during an intermediate eon (*antarakappa*).
Furthermore, in these Fortunate Eons (*bhaddakappa*), only five Buddhas arise. But how is it that even here...
Why is it that Buddhas might arise in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) even more rarely, yet because of the rarity of the cause, Buddhas are rare;

for this reason, do they arise only in this very world-system? Even here, they do not arise in the realms of the gods or the Brahmā-worlds, but arise only in the human world, precisely because it is here that the Jewel of the Saṅgha—the support of the threefold True Dharma in its entirety—manifests.
And because it is impossible to provide benefit in its entirety in other worlds.
For if Buddhas were to arise in the celestial realms and so forth, humans would not even be able to approach them out of fear, let alone perform such acts as listening to the Dhamma or going forth;
for that very reason, our Bodhisatta [arose here] through the perfection of his own physical body, power, and so forth.

Having raised him according to the custom of lying on one's back and so forth, he married him off and provided for his household in order to satisfy the people who were filled with curiosity and wonder at the sight of such a newborn human being. Even after he had gone forth into homelessness,
King Bimbisāra, having entered Rājagaha for alms and seen him sitting on the side of Mount Paṇḍava partaking of his meal, investigated his human nature in various ways.
One is able to approach [the Buddha] in this way, and not otherwise. For Buddhas arise for the purpose of rescuing the world, not for the sake of honor and the like for themselves;
therefore, it should be understood that they arise only among human beings. Even there, only in this Jambudīpa;
even there, only in this Middle Region (majjhimadesa). And it is not only Buddhas who arise there, but also Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka), and Great Disciples (mahāsāvaka).
Furthermore, universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*) and other meritorious beings arise in this very place.

Regarding the phrase "neither before nor after": here, "before" refers to the period prior to taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the mother’s womb; "after" refers to the period following the disappearance of the relics (*dhātu*);
and the interval between these two is called "neither before nor after. Within this interval, no other Buddha [can appear].
The arising [of beings] was prevented; however, when the disappearance of the *dhātu* (element) occurs, the arising of others is not prevented.
Although it is not prevented, it should be understood that they arise only after the intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*) has been exhausted.

For there are five kinds of disappearances: the disappearance of realization (*adhigama-antaradhāna*), the disappearance of practice (*paṭipatti-antaradhāna*), and the disappearance of the scriptures (*pariyatti-antaradhāna*).

The disappearance of the *liṅga* (characteristic marks) is the disappearance of the *dhātu* (elements). In this context, "attainment" (*adhigama*) refers to the paths, fruits, direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
One who is falling away falls away starting from the analytical knowledges.

For indeed, for only a thousand years after the *parinibbāna*, are they able to produce the analytical knowledges; beyond that, the direct knowledges. Even those, being unable to produce them, [disappear].
There are those who have destroyed the taints through dry insight, then non-returners, then once-returners, and stream-enterers.

Even while they are still living, the attainment remains unextinguished; however, with the passing away of the very last stream-enterer, the attainment is said to be extinguished. This is the extinction of attainment.

Then, being unable to realize the paths and fruits, they concluded, "There is now no penetration of the Noble Dhamma for us," and falling into complacency regarding jhāna and insight, they became dominated by indolence.
Merely guarding the fourfold purification of virtue, they did not exhort one another nor remind one another;
they were unconcerned, and from that time on, they suppressed the minor and lesser rules.
Then they incur a grave offense and preserve only the *pārājika* rule itself; even while those [who have committed the grave offense] remain, the practice (*paṭipatti*) remains unimpaired.
However, with the breaking of the virtue (*sīla*) or the death of the very last monk, the practice is said to have disappeared.
This is what is called the "disappearance of the practice."
"Learning" (*pariyatti*) refers to the word of the Buddha together with its commentaries, consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tipiṭaka*).
As time passes, due to unrighteous kings and others of the degenerate age (*kaliyuga*), the prosperity of crops and other necessities declines;

consequently, those who provide requisites become impoverished. The monks, being distressed for lack of requisites, are unable to take on disciples. Thereupon, the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) fall into decline.
They maintain the scriptures (pariyatti) solely by way of the Pāḷi;
subsequently, they become unable to maintain the entire Pāḷi, and first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka declines. Furthermore, its decline begins from the very top.
For first the Mahāpakaraṇa declines, followed by the Yamaka, Kathāvatthu, Puggalapaññatti, and Dhātukathā.
The Vibhaṅga and the Dhammasaṅgaṇī gradually decline; thereafter, starting from the top, the Sutta Piṭaka declines.
First, the Aṅguttara Nikāya declines, beginning from the Ekādasaka-nipāta down to the Ekaka-nipāta;
then, starting from the top, the Saṃyutta Nikāya declines, first the Mahāvagga that declines.
Then the Saḷāyatana-vagga, the Khandhaka-vagga, the Nidāna-vagga, and the Sagātha-vagga [disappear]; thus the Majjhima-nikāya, Dīgha-nikāya, and so forth, vanish starting from their very end.
Then only the Vinaya Piṭaka remains; that too vanishes starting from the Parivāra down to the Mahāvibhaṅga, and finally only the Mātikā remains from the Uposatha-kkhandhaka.
When people still preserve even a four-line stanza among themselves, the scriptures remain unextinguished;
once those have disappeared, the scriptures are said to be extinguished. This is what is called the disappearance of the scriptures.
As time passes on, the deportment regarding the wearing of robes, carrying of bowls, and so forth, no longer remains pleasing, [and] the Nigaṇṭhas and others...
They wander about having placed things like gourd-bowl leaves upon their upper arms, or having suspended them from them, or having fastened them to carrying-frames;
even the dyeing of their robes is not suitable, for they wear them made the color of a dried ox-lip bone;

furthermore, there is neither dye nor the piercing of the waistband, and having cut away the fringes, they wear only a mere scrap of saffron robe like wandering mendicants; then, when that time has come to an end...

When people, having tied a small piece of saffron cloth to their hands or necks, perform agricultural work and so forth to support their families, the people giving alms do so by offering it to these individuals for the sake of the Saṅgha; it was with reference to this that the Blessed One said:
"Ananda, in the future there will indeed be those of the lineage (gotrabhū) who wear saffron robes around their necks but are immoral."
“Ānanda, when those of evil character and immoral conduct give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha, I declare that at that time the offering made to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable.
Then, thinking, “This is a mere nuisance;
what is the use of this to us?,” they cut off that piece of saffron robe and throw it into the forest; at that moment, it is said that the mark [of the monk] has disappeared.
This is called the disappearance of the physical relics (*liṅga-antaradhāna*).

Then, not receiving honor and respect here and there, the relics will go to places where honor and respect are received by the power of the Buddhas' resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-bala*); thereafter, not receiving [such honors] anywhere, all the relics—
They will indeed go to the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa). For not even a relic the size of a mustard seed shall perish in the interval;
rather, they will display the splendor of the Buddha’s body seated cross-legged at the Seat of Enlightenment and the Twin Miracle (Yamakapāṭihāriya).

Then, fire arising from that relic-body causes the body to pass into the state of non-manifestation (apaṇṇattikabhāva); at that time, throughout the ten thousand world-systems (dasasahassacakkavāḷa) —
The deities lament as if on the day of the final *parinibbāna*, perform acts of worship and honor, and then depart. This is called the disappearance of the relics (*dhātu-antaradhāna*).
Of these five kinds of disappearance, the disappearance of the scriptures (*pariyatti-antaradhāna*) alone is the root.

For when the scriptures exist, even the penetration of truth (*paṭivedha*) and so forth are not said to have perished; when they do not exist, they are said to have perished. And just as with a treasure-pot...

Just as a treasure jar does not truly disappear while the letters inscribed upon a stone surface remain for the purpose of knowing its location, but it is considered lost once those letters have perished, so too should this matter be understood. As it has been said:
"As long as the Suttantas endure..."
As long as the Vinaya shines,
so long will they see the light,
just as when the sun has arisen.
“When the Suttantas have disappeared and the Vinaya has been forgotten,
there will be darkness in the world.”
Just as when the sun has set:
"When the Sutta is protected and preserved,
the practice is protected."
“The wise one established in practice does not fall away from security from bondage. Thus,
