among these five disappearances, it should be understood that the last is called "the final disappearance" (carima), occurring after the disappearance of the elements (dhātu).
But why do two Perfectly Enlightened Ones not arise simultaneously, neither before nor after the other?

Because it would be purposeless. For a single Perfectly Enlightened One alone, if he were to become the sufficient condition for all beings throughout the infinite world-systems, would be able—in a single moment—to teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles and perfectly suited to all, thereby training them; how much more so, then, [for those within a single system]?
However, since this does not occur at different times, the arising of multiple Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (*sammāsambuddha*) at one and the same time would be entirely purposeless.

Furthermore, such purposelessness should be understood as resulting from the faults of lack of wonder, lack of reverence, and dispute; and because the great earth would be incapable of supporting two Buddhas, leading to the fault of its being overwhelmed and scattered.
As for Universal Monarchs (*cakkavattin*), however, [this applies] within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Two do not arise together; only one arises. However, it should be understood that in different world-systems (*cakravāḷa*), many may arise simultaneously.
For here, the phrase "in one world-system" should be taken to mean "in one *cakravāḷa*.
Furthermore, the interval between the appearance and the disappearance of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*) should be understood as occurring neither too early nor too late. And its disappearance—
From the passing away of a wheel-turning monarch, or from his renunciation, [the next one] appears on the seventh day;

by virtue of his power, it should be understood that two do not arise together in the same place. The rest is easily understood. The first is the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇabala*).

Regarding the second, "of the undertaking of kamma" (*kammasamādānānaṃ*): this refers to wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed after having undertaken them, or simply, the undertaking itself is the kamma.

"From the standpoint and from the cause" means both from the perspective of conditions (*paccaya*) and from the perspective of the reason termed "cause" (*hetu*). In this context, destiny, the physical basis, time, and effort are the conditions for karmic result (*vipāka*), while karma is the cause.
One understands the relationship between karma and its result as it truly is by way of both these factors. How so?
For the Blessed One has said: "In some cases, many evil karmas are warded off by the excellence of destiny, the physical basis, time, and effort..."

He understands: "They do not ripen; they ripen by way of their failure. For some person, many wholesome kamma-actions, having been obstructed by their failure, do not ripen; they ripen by way of their success.

In this context, "failure of destination" refers to the four states of deprivation (apāya). "Success of destination" refers to the human and divine destinations. "Bases" (upadhi) refers to the individual existence (attabhāva).

Success (*sampatti*) is called accomplishment (*samiddhi*); failure (*vipatti*) is called non-accomplishment (*asamiddhi*). Success of time (*kālasampatti*) refers to a favorable period characterized by a righteous king and wise human beings;
its opposite is called failure of time (*kālavipatti*). Furthermore, the correct application of a particular action is success of application (*payogasampatti*);
incorrect application is called failure of application (*payogavipatti*). For in that regard, for some person, by means of a wholesome action...
For one reborn in a fortunate destination such as the heavenly realms, only wholesome kamma ripens by virtue of that excellence of destination;
however, unwholesome kamma, being obstructed by that excellence of destination, is unable to ripen there.
On the other hand, for one reborn in the miserable destinations such as hell, those unwholesome kammic forces ripen at will by virtue of that failure of destination.
However, wholesome kamma that has been obstructed by such a failure of destiny is unable to ripen there.

On the other hand, for someone endowed with a beautiful and handsome body—even if he is a slave or of low birth—wholesome kamma ripens for him precisely because of that excellence of his physical basis (*upadhi*). For such a person of handsome form, people think: "This man must have performed pure kamma."
Thinking, "This is not suitable," they appoint her to high ministerial positions and the like; they even appoint a beautiful Caṇḍālī woman to the position of chief queen and so forth.
However, because she is shielded by that excellence of physical basis (*upadhi-sampatti*), unwholesome kamma is unable to ripen.
But those same kammic forces ripen at will when one is situated in a deficiency of physical basis (*upadhi-vipatti*). For even though [kamma] has arisen among royal families and the like...

They designate a "bad form" among those who are inferior. However, for certain beings born during a time of prosperity—such as the beings of the first aeon, universal monarchs, Buddhas, or humans with excellent kings—the wholesome deeds alone ripen due to that excellence of the time, not the unwholesome ones.
Yet, when there is a decline of the time, such as among humans with bad kings, those [unwholesome deeds] ripen due to that failure of the time.

They ripen by coming together, yet wholesome deeds do not ripen because they are obstructed by that failure of time. However, for someone who possesses both blameless application— such as restraint of virtue—
and either blameworthy or blameless application according to place and time, as well as the efficacy of the application of weapons, crafts, and so forth,
it is only the wholesome deeds that ripen by virtue of that success of application, not the unwholesome ones.

Furthermore, those [unwholesome kamma-formations] ripen by way of a failure in application that is the opposite of what was previously described, but the wholesome ones do not, because they have been counteracted by that [failure].

For even when people commit unwholesome acts such as killing in battles and the like, they obtain great success—such as the position of a general—only by relying on their proficiency in the application of various weapons and crafts, and certainly not by relying on that unwholesome act itself. Just as...

Even when performing wholesome deeds such as giving or service, people may encounter misfortune and ruin due to the failure of excessive exertion or improper application, but not on account of that wholesome deed itself.

In this way, the Blessed One understands, as it truly is, the distinction between the ripening and non-ripening of wholesome and unwholesome states by means of these four successes and failures. This, then, is the section here.
The second power is explained by way of analysis (*vibhaṅganaya*). Furthermore, another [analysis] of it is as follows:
"There was karma, there was the ripening of that karma; there was karma, but there was no ripening of that karma; there was karma, there is..."
There was action, there was no ripening of action; there was action, there will be ripening of action;
there was action, there will not be ripening of action; there is action, there is no ripening of action;
there is action, there will be ripening of action; there is action, there will not be ripening of action.
“Kamma will arise, its result (vipāka) will arise; kamma will arise, its result will not arise”—by this method stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the exposition should be understood.

In that context, regarding the kamma said to have been accumulated in a past existence, it gave its result right there by way of causes and conditions. It is with reference to this that [it was said].

The first phrase, “there was karma, there was the ripening of karma,” has been stated. However, among the many [types of karma] in the past—such as that to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) and so forth—one [instance of] karma to be experienced in the present life, having obtained the necessary conditions, yields its ripening, while the others remain without ripening.

Furthermore, one [instance of] karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) draws forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), whereas one [instance of] immediate karma (*ānantariya*) [draws forth] rebirth-linking in hell.

[Some] give [result], while the rest are without fruition (*avipāka*). Among the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), by means of one [of them] one is reborn in the Brahma-world, while the rest are without fruition.
It is with reference to this that the second phrase, "there was karma, but there was no fruition of karma," was stated.
It is with reference to that past karma which gives fruition at present that the third [phrase] is stated. That which does not ripen according to the former method—
With reference to this, the fourth [category] is stated. With reference to that which will give its result in the future, the fifth is stated.
With reference to that which does not ripen, the sixth is stated. With reference to that karma which has been accumulated right now and gives its result right now, the seventh is stated.
With reference to that which does not ripen, the eighth is stated. By this method...

The meaning of the remaining terms should also be understood. "This of the Tathāgata" means this knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the various types of kamma and the various types of results of those kamma in the past, future, and present.
This is the second power. Regarding the third: "leading everywhere" means leading to all destinations (gati) and leading to non-destinations (agati). "Way" (paṭipadā) means the path (magga).
"He understands it as it really is" means that even when many people together commit a single unwholesome deed such as killing, he understands:
"The volition of this one will lead to hell; that of this one will lead to the animal realm; that of this one will lead to the sphere of hungry ghosts. Furthermore, he understands:
"In hell and other realms, this [volition] will yield such and such a result in such and such a place; this will bring about rebirth-linking..."
He is unable to draw [the result] forth; rather, for one who has received rebirth-linking through another kamma, there will be a weak ripening of the substrate (*upadhivepakka*).

Or, when many people together perform wholesome deeds such as giving or establish insight (*vipassanā*), the volition (*cetanā*) of this person will lead to the human realm, while that of this other person will lead to the divine realm; even there, the fruition will be exactly thus and so.

"Will it grant [the fruit]? or "Will insight bring this person to the accomplishment of one path, two, three, or four paths—whether accompanied by the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and so forth, or devoid of them?

or "Will it not accomplish any penetration for this person?"—in such infinite ways, one understands without error the practice leading everywhere (sabbatthagāminī-paṭipadā), consisting of wholesome and unwholesome states, which has arisen even with respect to a single object.
"He understands"—this is the third power.
Regarding the fourth [power], "the manifold element" (*anekadhātu*) means the many elements, such as the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*) and so forth, or the desire-element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

"The diverse element" (*nānādhātu*) means an element of various kinds, due to the distinct characteristics of those very same elements. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

"He understands according to reality" means that he understands, without error, the infinite variety of those various elements (*dhātu*) according to the method explained in the *Vibhaṅga* on the aggregates, bases, and elements, and so forth.
And it is not only the Tathāgata who understands the variety of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) consisting of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*);
rather, he also understands the variety of the world of conditioned phenomena not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), which is to be penetrated by Paccekabuddhas and others.
He understands the diversity that is impossible to fathom. Through those [powers], they know the diversity of the world of the clung-to (*upādinnaka*) only in part;
however, they do not know at all the diversity of that which is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), for this is the domain of the Omniscient Buddha alone.
For thus, when this particular element is predominant, there arise these trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, as well as their trunks, stems, vines, bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like.
The diversity of earth, mountains, and so forth is infinite in its divisions due to differences in shape, color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence (*ojā*), as well as differences in place and time;
thus, he is able to know it through infinite modes, and no one else. This is the fourth power.
Regarding the fifth: "of various inclinations" means the state of having various inclinations by way of inferior and other types of inclinations. [He knows this] as it truly is.

"He understands" means that in all three times, those of inferior inclination associate only with those of inferior inclination, and those of sublime inclination [associate] with those of sublime inclination.
Even therein, the faithless associate with the faithless, the immoral with the immoral, and those of wrong view with those of wrong view;
while those endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so forth, associate with those very same [who possess such qualities].

He knows them in their various aspects. For those endowed with faith, virtue, and so forth, do not even serve their own teachers or preceptors if the latter lack these qualities, nor do those [teachers and preceptors] serve others;
rather, each serves only those who are similar to themselves.
This is the fifth power. Regarding the sixth: "of other beings" refers to superior beings; "of other persons" refers to inferior beings other than those.
Or rather, these two terms refer to one and the same thing, stated in two ways according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

"The knowledge of the higher and lower faculties" (*indriyaparopariyatta*) means the superior state and the inferior state, as well as the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith and the rest.

"As it really is" (*yathābhūta*) refers to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of faith and so forth in all beings, by way of their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*), latent dispositions (*anusaya*), temperament (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*).
He knows it in all its aspects. In this context, "abode" (*āsaya*) means a place of dwelling, where the mental continuum of beings constantly resides.

It is twofold: the abode of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāsayo*) and the abode of the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭāsayo*). Therein, all modes of wrong view that proceed by way of eternalism or annihilationism are called the abode of the round.
[This begins] from the discernment of name-and-form together with their conditions; all...

Insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) are called the "inclination toward turning away" (*vivaṭṭāsayo*). For even path-knowledge is indeed an "inclination," according to such statements as:
"Monks, these ten are the abodes of the noble ones (*ariyāvāsa*), which the noble ones have inhabited.

Now, the Blessed One, knowing the inclinations of sentient beings, knows them even at the moment when both types of view-knowledge are not occurring. He knows precisely those who are intent upon defilements such as sensual lust and so forth.

For the Blessed One knows the individual person exactly as they are. He knows one who delights in renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth, whose inclination is toward turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭāsaya*), precisely as he is practicing renunciation and so forth;
and he knows one who delights in sensual desire (*kāma*) and so forth, whose inclination is toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭāsaya*).

This same method applies even to the knowledge of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), temperament (*carita*), and so on. In this context, the underlying tendency is sevenfold, beginning with the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). Temperament (*carita*) refers to the mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitional formations produced through the three doors [of body, speech, and mind].

“Adhimutti” means inclination (ajjhāsaya). Thus, here the two knowledges—knowledge of the underlying tendencies according to disposition (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and knowledge of the degrees of others’ faculties (indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa)—combine into one single power-knowledge. This is the sixth power.
Regarding the seventh: “of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments,” this refers to the four meditations beginning with the first; [the text continues]: “possessing form...”

[This refers to] the eight liberations beginning with “he sees forms,” the three concentrations beginning with “with applied thought and sustained thought,” and the nine successive attainments beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna. “Defilement” (saṃkilesa) means a state conducive to decline.
“Purification” (vodāna) means a state conducive to distinction. “Emergence” (vuṭṭhāna) means the cause by which one emerges from the jhānas and so forth.

That is the cause. Furthermore, that is twofold: purification (*vodāna*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). For the lower, well-mastered jhāna is called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the higher jhāna by way of its own purification;

however, it is also the life-continuum because one emerges from each respective attainment by way of the life-continuum itself. But regarding emergence from cessation, it is only through the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
They emerge. This is called emergence independent of the canonical texts (*pāḷimuttaka-vuṭṭhāna*); the Blessed One understands all of that as it really is in every aspect.

This is the seventh power. Regarding the eighth, "recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*) means the recollection of the aggregates in which one previously dwelt; [he knows them] by way of name, clan, appearance, nutriment, pleasure, pain, and so forth.

He understands, as it truly is, those things existing in various states of existence through their infinite modes. This is the eighth power. Regarding the ninth, "passing away and rebirth" (*cutūpapāta*):

having seen with the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), by way of perceiving the sense-base of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*), beings passing away and being reborn—beings who, according to their karma, are inferior or exalted, beautiful or ugly, and so forth in their infinitely varied distinctions—[he understands them as they truly are]. This is the ninth power.
"He understands in all aspects" refers to the ninth power.

Regarding the tenth, "the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khaya) means the cessation of the taints, which is Nibbāna; he understands that through the penetration of the Four Truths by means of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. This is the tenth power.
"These" refers to those which were previously stated as "the ten powers of a Tathāgata"; these are they—this is the absorption (appanā).

It acts [thus]. Because the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) and so forth—though existing in disciples and others according to their capacity—know only a certain portion of their respective objects and not in all its modes;

whereas the Tathāgata’s powers (*tathāgatabala*), like the Buddha’s omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), proceed unimpeded in a single moment regarding all phenomena within their respective domains, in every respect and in every way; therefore, they are called "the powers of the Tathāgata."

...are so called. If this is indeed a classification of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) alone, why then are they analyzed separately as "the ten powers of knowledge" (*dasabalañāṇāni*)?

It is because they are distinct from one another due to differences in their objects, functions, and planes. For among the ten powers of knowledge, the first knows only what is possible and impossible;
the second knows only the various results of kamma; and the third knows only the limits of kamma.
The fourth is solely the cause of diversity; the fifth is solely the inclination and resolve of beings; the sixth is solely the sharpness or dullness of the faculties;
the seventh is solely their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other states; the eighth is solely the continuity of the aggregates in previous existences;
the ninth is solely the death and rebirth-linking of beings; the tenth is solely the delimitation of the truths; it is nothing else.

The knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), however, knows in a single moment everything that is to be known by these [other knowledges] as well as everything beyond them—divided into the past and so forth—in all its aspects;
yet it does not perform all the functions of those [other knowledges]. For that [omniscient knowledge], having become meditative absorption (*jhāna*), is unable to enter into it;

having become supernormal power (*iddhi*), it is unable to perform transformations; and having become the path (*magga*), it is unable to eradicate the defilements (*kilesa*). As for the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabalañāṇāni*)...

They are able to perform all of those [powers] as appropriate. Among them, in sequence, seven knowledges belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), two thereafter belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and at the end, one is supramundane (lokuttara). However, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) belongs exclusively to the sense-sphere.

Thus, the ten powers of knowledge (dasabalañāṇa) are distinct from the knowledge of omniscience in terms of their objects, functions, and planes. This is the distinction: "The knowledge of omniscience is different. This...

This is the analysis according to the meaning of the words. However, as for the entire analysis starting from the classification of phenomena (*dhammabheda*) and so forth, it should be understood here according to what has been stated beginning from the singlefold section;
for these various methods of analysis, such as the *Suttantabhājanīya* and others, do not exist here in the same way as they do in the subsequent *Vibhaṅgas*.
The commentary on the meaning of the *Mātikā* for the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the meaning of the *Mātikā* for the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, together with its formal arrangement (*nikkhepa*) and its detailed exposition (*pariccheda*).
For in the *Mātikā*, first of all, seventy-one single items beginning with "one intoxicated by birth" are set forth;
then eighteen pairs beginning with "anger and resentment"; thirty-five triads beginning with "the unwholesome roots";
fourteen tetrads beginning with "the taints"; fifteen pentads beginning with "the lower fetters"; and fourteen [groups] beginning with "the roots of dispute."

Having arranged, in their proper order, the six groups of six, the seven groups of seven beginning with the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the eight groups of eight beginning with the bases of defilement (*kilesavatthu*),

the nine groups of nine beginning with the grounds for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), the seven groups of ten beginning with the bases of defilement, and the one hundred and eight modes of craving-conduct (*taṇhāvicarita*) according to the eighteen groups of eighteen,
[the text concludes that] finally, the sixty-two views (*diṭṭhigata*) are shown in detail in the Brahmajāla Sutta.
It should be understood that all these one hundred and sixty-three defilements have been set forth. This, first of all, is the section on their formal presentation (*nikkhepa*).
As for their meaning, however, in such expressions as "pride of birth" (*jātimada*) and so forth, it refers to the state of being born into a high family;

based upon this, by way of self-exaltation and disparagement of others, thinking: "Among the four castes, beginning with the Khattiyas, I am of the highest birth, while these others are not of the highest birth."

Pride that arises in the mode of intoxication is called *jātimada* (pride of birth). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Therein, *gottamada* (pride of clan) is based on a noble lineage such as the Ādicca clan or the Kassapa clan.

*Ārogyamada* (pride of health), *yobbaññamada* (pride of youth), and *jīvitamada* (pride of life)—expressed as "I have lived long and happily, I am living, and I shall live"—as well as *lābhamada* (pride of gain), are stated respectively based on being free from illness, youthfulness, longevity, and abundant profit. [The pride of status is] based on obtaining well-made and excellent requisites.
They ask questions making me the foremost, honoring me with respect such as salutation and prostration, and they follow me in a surrounding circle;
thus, one should understand that honor and the rest occur respectively by depending on precedence, a large retinue, and a pure retinue.
As for wealth (*bhoga*), although it is already included by the mention of "gain" (*lābha*), it is here [treated separately] by way of stored riches.
Gain is to be understood; they also say that it may be described by way of the abundance of enjoyments such as food, drink, clothing, ornaments, garlands, and perfumes.
Pride of beauty (*vaṇṇamada*) is based on the beauty of one’s physical form and the beauty of one’s virtues.

[Pride of] great learning, ready wit, [beauty, the lineage of Buddhas, the lineage of kings, the lineage of provinces, the lineage of villages, the reckoning of days and nights, and the conjunctions of constellations and moments...]
"Long-standing," and so forth, should be understood respectively as being based on seniority (*rattaññutā*), learning (*suta*), and the rest.

Based on being a "born-ascetic" (*jāti-piṇḍapātika*), not being looked down upon (*anavaññāta*), having a graceful deportment (*iriyāpatha-pāsādika*), and possessing great psychic power (*mahiddhika*), one should understand the states of being an alms-food eater (*piṇḍapātika*) and so forth, respectively.
Although fame (*yasa*) is included by the mention of a retinue (*parivāra*), the extent of that retinue's expansion is due to its state of being under one's own control and influence.
Or, based on fame itself, there is the intoxication of glory (*yasamada*). Based on pure virtue, access and absorption concentration,

proficiency in a craft, the perfection of the body’s height, the perfection of its circumference, and the bodily fullness consisting of the lack of deficiency and faultlessness in its major and minor limbs,
the intoxications of virtue and so forth are to be understood.
Having thus shown pride with its basis by this much, he now says "intoxication" (mado) while showing pride in general without a specific basis.
Regarding "negligence" (pamāda) and so forth: negligence is an unwholesome state of consciousness that occurs in the mode of being heedless;
it is defined as the relinquishing of the mind toward the five strands of sensual pleasure, and it serves as the cause for both the practice of good conduct and the practice of misconduct.
Self-satisfaction has the characteristic of self-indulgence. Stiffness (thambha)—defined as a lack of humility even toward one's parents—is like a stomach filled with air;

it has the characteristic of mental inflation. Scheming (sārambha) is an unwholesome state of mind that arises from the impulse to undertake efforts twice as great upon seeing others' success in matters such as their homes or their mastery of knowledge.
[This is] the name. For even a book should not be taken up out of a spirit of contention; it is simply unwholesome. This [desire] has the characteristic of excelling others in doing.
One who has desire for this or that object is *atriccha* (one with excessive desire); the state of such a person is *atricchatā* (excessive desire).
The meaning should be understood in the same way for *mahicchatā* (great desire) and so forth. In that regard, being unsatisfied with whatever one has obtained and [longing for] more and more—
Greed proceeding by way of aspiration is excessive desire (*atricchā*).

By means of this, even what one has obtained oneself appears as if it were base, while what another has obtained appears as if it were excellent, even if it is base. This is characterized by the aspiration for successive gains.
It proceeds both by way of manifesting the excellence of existing qualities and by way of a mode of non-contentment even with very great things that have arisen.
And greed is great desire. That which, when possessed by a person, makes them difficult to satisfy with requisites— like fire with fuel or the ocean with water—
and that which consists in the lack of esteem for the qualities of those who are peaceful, as well as a lack of moderation in receiving and using [requisites], is the characteristic of great desire.

However, *pāpicchatā* (evil desire) is greed that functions both by seeking to manifest qualities— such as faith and virtue, or mundane and supramundane states like the paths and fruits— that one does not possess, and by being dissatisfied even with very great conditions when they have arisen.
Furthermore, this lack of esteem for unpossessed qualities, along with a lack of moderation in receiving and using [offerings], is the characteristic of *pāpicchatā*.
"Siṅga" (the horn) is so called in the sense of piercing; it is a designation for the "horn of defilement" characterized by urbanity.
In its actual meaning, it is simply greed, which functions through the act of making things erotic. "Tintiṇa" means quarreling;
in its actual meaning, it refers to the manner of quarreling among beings in their dwelling place, like dogs, saying, "This is yours," "This is mine."

*Dosova*: *Cāpalya* means restlessness; it is precisely lust (*rāga*) which manifests as the act of adorning, embellishing, and playing with requisites such as the bowl and robes, as well as with one’s own person.
One who is possessed of this appears like a youth even when old. *Asabhāgavutti* means dissimilar conduct or dissimilar activity;
it is that which proceeds as a contrary disposition based on a lack of respect even toward those worthy of honor.
Dosa (hatred) is that by which one, being possessed of it, does not look after one's parents, teachers, preceptors, and so forth even when they are ill;
for the sake of gain and honor, one quarrels with them; and one fails to establish a sense of shame and moral dread toward them, nor does one show reverence toward shrines and the like.
Arati (discontent) is the lack of delight and the state of weariness regarding secluded lodgings, as well as serenity and insight; it functions in such a manner.
An unwholesome arising of consciousness. *Tandi* means laziness. *Vijambhitā* is the quivering of the body in the form of stretching and so forth.
*Bhattasammada* is the unserviceability of the body due to drowsiness from food. *Cetaso ca līnattaṃ* is the contraction of the mind.
As for their meaning, all these are simply modes of illness in the mind by way of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).
Regarding hypocrisy (*kuhana*) and the other [faults]: for one who is motivated by gain, honor, and fame and possesses evil desires, the act of deceiving others by various means is called hypocrisy.
It is threefold, consisting of: (1) the acceptance of requisites, (2) indirect hinting (*sāmantajappana*), and (3) the maintenance of bodily postures (*iriyāpatha*).
Among these, in the case of being invited with robes and so forth, while actually desiring them, one refuses out of evil desire; [this constitutes the first type].

And knowing that those householders were firmly established in faith toward him, he manifested a desire only to favor them when they, thinking, "Oh, this noble one is so modest that he does not wish to accept anything;
how well for us it would be if he would accept even a small thing," offered various excellent robes and other requisites through diverse means.

From the moment of that acceptance onwards, even the act of boasting— which serves as the cause for the offering of loads of carts— is called *kuhana* (hypocrisy), which consists in the utilization of requisites.

Furthermore, for one who possesses evil desires, the act of boasting in various ways through speech that indicates the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), such as saying, "The ascetic who wears such a robe is of great influence," is what is termed *sāmantajappana* (hinting).

“Deceit” (*kuhanā*) means: for one who has evil desires, while actually being composed, the act of impressing others by intentionally assuming and maintaining a posture such as walking and so forth—this is called “deceit,” which consists in the contrivance of deportment.
By the words “addressing” (*ālapanā*) and so on, however, only speech connected with the aforementioned conditions is shown. “Speaking agreeably” (*anuppiyabhāṇitā*) and “flattery” (*cāṭukamyatā*).
Being like bean soup (*muggasūpyatā*) and being like a parasite (*pāribhaṭayatā*) are what is called "flattery" (*ālapanā*). Therein, "flattery" (*ālapanā*) is speaking from the very outset.
"Pleasant speech" (*anuppiyabhāṇitā*) is the repeated speaking of what is pleasing without regard for the truth or the Dhamma. "Fawning" (*cāṭukamyatā*) is lowly conduct;
it is behaving by placing oneself in a subordinate position. "Being like bean soup" (*muggasūpyatā*) is the state of being similar to bean soup.
It is the state of possessing speech that is as little true as an uncooked mung bean.
"Hinting" (*pāribhaṭyatā*) refers to the duties of a parasite, such as carrying children on one's lap and so forth. Thus, this entire variety of activity is called simply "sycophancy" (*lapanā*).
Furthermore, bodily and verbal action that produces the perception of receiving requisites from others is called "signifying" (*nemittikatā*), which—

This is called "indirect talk, hinting, and giving hints. When one oppresses a donor with insults, contempt, blame, and so forth, in such a way that they fear disrepute, that pressure is called "sycophancy" (*nippesikatā*).
For by this means, one scrapes or wipes away another's virtue—just as one might scrape oil from a bamboo scraper—or just as one might grind various perfumes together.
Just as one who seeks fragrance grinds and pulverizes [the scent], this seeking of gain is called "grinding" (*nippesikatā*); therefore, it is termed "grinding.

Furthermore, when one uses the material gain obtained from one family as a means to solicit further gain elsewhere by way of giving, this is called "seeking gain through gain" (*lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā*).
These five, beginning with hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), are unwholesome states of consciousness such as greed that manifest in various ways.

These should be understood. The twelve types of conceit, beginning with "I am superior," are easy to comprehend by following what was stated previously in the *Saṃyojana-gocchaka* (Cluster of Fetters).

Among them, the first three types of conceit are described without reference to a specific person, but rather by way of the bases for conceit such as birth, clan, physical appearance, wealth, craft, learning, and so forth.
However, the nine types of conceit that follow are described in relation to persons who are superior, equal, or inferior.

Having thus explained pride (*māna*) with its objective basis (*savatthuka*) by means of these twelve terms, it is now said, beginning with "pride" (*māno*), in order to show that which is without an objective basis (*avatthuka*).
Following that, regarding "excessive pride" (*atimāna*) and so forth:

pride that arises by way of conceiving in excess, thinking, "There is no one equal to me in terms of birth and so on," is called excessive pride. [Furthermore,] "These people were formerly equal to me, but now I am superior and they are inferior."
Conceit that has arisen as an excessive burden is called *mānātimāna*. Conceit that proceeds by way of disparaging oneself is called *omāna*;
it is similar to the conceit of inferiority (*hīnamāna*) that occurs in the form "I am inferior.

Conceit that arises regarding noble qualities not yet attained, thinking "they have been attained by me," is called *adhimāna* because of its excessive nature; this, however, [occurs] in noble disciples such as stream-enterers.

The thought “I am a once-returner,” and so forth, does not arise for them because they are free from doubt regarding the penetration of noble qualities through the reviewing of the path, fruit, Nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements.
However, it does not arise at all for one who is immoral; nor does it arise for one who possesses virtue but has abandoned the meditation subject (kammatthāna).
It arises, however, only for one whose virtue is purified, who has attained pure serenity (samatha), or who has attained pure insight (vipassanā).

Or it arises in one who has attained both of those. Among them, it should be understood that one who has attained both establishes himself in *arahatta* alone because his defilements have been thoroughly suppressed and his conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*) have been rubbed away; whereas for the others, such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), it persists even in those stages.
Furthermore, the conceit that proceeds toward the five aggregates with the thought "I am" and so forth is called *asmimāna*. However, by means of evil...

Wrong conceit (*micchāmāna*) is the conceit that proceeds by way of wishing for oneself to be superior and so forth, through actions that cause harm to others, such as fields of work, fields of craft, or branches of knowledge.
Regarding the "thoughts of relatives" (*ñātivitakka*) and so forth: it is when, out of worldly affection, one thinks, "My relatives live happily, endowed with prosperity," and so on.

A thought that arises with reference to relatives is called a "thought of relatives" (*ñātivitakka*). However, a thought of renunciation (*nekkhammasita*) such as, "Our relatives have passed away, they have gone to their end; they were faithful and confident," is not what is meant here. The same applies to a "thought of country" (*janapadavitakka*);
its mode of occurrence should be understood as, for example, "Our country has abundant food and is beautiful. For the sake of immortality...

Vitakka means "immortal thought" (*amaravitakka*). In this context, that which proceeds with the thought, "When suffering has been worn away through such practices as squatting and strenuous exertion, the self will be happy and immortal in the future life," is called "thought for the sake of immortality.
Furthermore, that of a theorist who does not settle upon one side, thinking, "It is thus for me, it is not thus for me, it is otherwise for me... [is another type].
That which proceeds because it cannot be grasped—like the immortal fish (amaramaccha) described by the words "Is it mine? and so forth—is called "immortal thought" (amaravitakka).
Combining both types together, they are referred to here as "immortal thought.
Furthermore, that which is associated with a semblance of compassion, such as grieving or rejoicing along with householders, and is joined with worldly affection (gehāsita-pema), is [the other type].

Thought associated with compassion for others is called *vitakka*. Thought associated with gain, honor, and fame is called *vitakka* associated with gain, honor, and renown (*lābhasakkārasiloka*), by virtue of its being engaged with these as its objects;
its mode of occurrence is such that it functions in the form of thinking, "O, may gain and the rest arise for me! and so forth.
It should be understood as follows: "Oh, may others not despise me!"—a thought arisen based on the household life is called a thought associated with non-disparagement (*anavaññatti*).

This concludes the single [category]. Regarding the pairs and so forth, after excluding anger and the rest whose meanings have been explained above, there is a description only of the remaining ones. In that regard:

First, regarding the terms beginning with *upanāha* among the [ten fetters]: in the preliminary stage, anger (*kodha*)—through repeated practice such as thinking "I have been insulted" (*akkocchi maṃ*)—becomes more firmly bound at a later time within a mind of enmity;
this is called *upanāha*. One who possesses this is unable to relinquish the enmity, like a rag smeared with oil and fat; even when being cleansed, his mind does not become pure.
Flattery has the characteristic of binding oneself to one's own interests.
Envy (*makkha*), however, is the anger that proceeds by defiling another’s virtue with faults;
for this first smears one’s own mind—just as a hand holding excrement smears itself with filth—and only afterwards [smears] the other.
“Deceit” (*makkha*) is mentioned; its characteristic is the smearing over of another’s virtues.
“Flattery” (*paḷāsa*) means to praise [another] so as to make one’s own virtues appear equal to theirs; it is greed proceeding in such a manner, and its characteristic is grasping by pairing.
“Guile” (*māyā*) is so called because, like an optical illusion, it conceals a fault that exists even in the three doors [of body, speech, and mind].
It has the characteristic of concealing one's faults. *Sāṭheyya* is the state or the action of one who is crafty (*saṭha*);
it is *kerāṭiya*, and its characteristic is the manifestation of qualities that do not exist.

*Anajjava* and the others are to be understood by way of the unwholesome states that are the opposites of *ajjava* and so forth as explained below. Regarding the phrases "internal fetter" (*ajjhattasaṃyojana*), and so on:
"Internal" refers to existence in the sense-sphere (*kāmabhava*). The five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that function there by way of binding beings are called "internal fetters.

"External" refers to existence in the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpabhava*). The five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that function there by way of binding are called "external fetters.
For it is in the sense-sphere existence that beings have their attachment (*ālaya*).
It is abundant, not in others; therefore, it should be understood as "internal" and the others as "external. This concludes the dyads (*duka*).

Regarding the triads (*tika*), however, the three unwholesome roots beginning with greed are called the "three unwholesome roots. Thoughts associated with sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty are called the "three unwholesome thoughts.
These same three, by way of perception, are the "three unwholesome perceptions. By way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), they are three...
And they are called the unwholesome elements (*akusaladhātu*). The three types of misconduct—bodily, verbal, and mental—are what is meant by "misconduct" (*duccarita*);
these are to be understood in terms of killing living beings and so forth as they occur through the three doors, or alternatively, in terms of all unwholesome states.

According to the method of the discourses (*suttanta*), however, the three taints (*āsava*)—the taint of sensual desire and so forth, excluding the taint of views—are what is meant. These are the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
There are three fetters (saṃyojana).

Craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā), craving for existence (bhavataṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhavataṇhā) are the three types of craving (taṇhā). Among these, lust accompanied by the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) is craving for existence;
lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) is craving for non-existence; and all remaining forms of craving are [craving for sense-pleasures].

Craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). Alternatively, craving for sensual pleasures should be understood as lust associated with the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*); craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) as that associated with the fine-material and immaterial realms;

and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) as that accompanied by the view of annihilationism. Furthermore, there are three other types of craving: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*), and craving for the formless (*arūpataṇhā*).
Again, there are another three: craving for form, craving for the formless, and craving for cessation (*nirodhataṇhā*).

Craving (taṇhā) is as follows: therein, craving for cessation is accompanied by the view of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi). There are three types of seeking (esanā): the seeking of sensual pleasures (kāmesanā), the seeking of existence (bhavesanā), and the seeking of the holy life (brahmacariyesanā). Among these, the seeking of the holy life is the quest for a holy life characterized by the views of eternalism (sassata) and annihilationism (uccheda).
[Furthermore, there are the conceits: "I am superior," "I am equal," and "I am inferior. Thus...
The three modes mentioned above are called "modes" (*vidhā*). Indeed, pride (*māna*) is called a "mode" because it discriminates and conceives itself in terms of superiority and so forth.
The three fears are the fears arisen in dependence upon birth, aging, and death.
These three, described by the passage beginning with "Or referring to the past time," etc., proceed by way of doubt and perplexity regarding the Buddha and the other [refuges].
The three types of ignorance are called the three darknesses (*tama*). In its analysis (*vibhaṅga*), it is stated that ignorance associated with doubt is what is meant by the term "doubt";
this should be understood because that very ignorance possesses the nature of darkness due to its quality of obscuring.
Furthermore, whatever happiness or other states arise for a being, the view that all of this is caused by past actions is one sectarian tenet (*titthāyatana*).
"Through the cause of creation by a Supreme Lord" is the second, and "without cause and without condition" is the third; these are called the three sectarian tenets (*titthāyatana*).

Among them, the proponent of the first view, having rejected everything—such as wholesome and unwholesome actions, the elements, consciousness, and nutriment, as well as destiny, acquisitions, and so forth, and the reliance upon holy men, hearing the true Dhamma, and so on—all of which are conditions and things arisen through conditions, accepts only the ripening of karma (*kammavipāka*). The others...
However, both [of these] reject every cause and instead accept [the world as being] caused by a Supreme Lord (issara-hetuka) or as being without cause (ahetuka).
One should understand the faults corresponding to each of these three positions according to their respective contexts, since there is no purpose [in repeating them here].
We have not, however, elaborated on this here for fear of making the book too prolix.
Furthermore, the three—lust, hatred, and delusion—are called "possessions" (*kiñcana*) in the sense of being obstacles.

For these very same factors are "stains" (*aṅgaṇa*) in the sense of being defilements; they are "impurities" (*mala*) in the sense of causing a state of soiling; and they are "unevennesses" (*visama*) because they are the cause of stumbling and falling.

There are also another three unevennesses, namely the unevennesses of body, speech, and mind, such as the taking of life and so forth. Lust, hatred, and delusion are [also] threefold in the sense of burning.

The fires are called "bitter" (kasāva) in the sense of being harsh and impure. Furthermore, there are three other types of bitterness: the bitterness of bodily actions such as killing living beings, and so forth.

Within the triad of views regarding gratification, the view of eternalism that occurs in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures—thinking, "There is no fault in sensual pleasures"—is called the view of gratification.
However, the twenty-based view of self is so called because it follows after a self.

This is called the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi). Regarding this, there are four views concerning the aggregate of form: one regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
The same applies to the remaining aggregates; thus, it should be understood that twenty bases have been established.

In this context, it should be understood that there are five views of annihilationism (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*) which occur by way of grasping the five aggregates as a self through such modes as "form is the self";

the remaining views, however, are views of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*). Furthermore, the view of non-existence (*natthika-diṭṭhi*), which occurs in the manner of "there is no giving," etc., is called wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*);
the meaning is that it is a base view. In the triad beginning with "displeasure" (*arati*), it refers to the harming of beings with hands, clods of earth, sticks, and so forth.
"Vihesā" means cruelty. "Adhammacariyā" (unrighteous conduct) refers to the practice of unwholesome states occurring through the three doors [of body, speech, and mind].

In the triad beginning with "difficult-to-admonish," there are the perceptions of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty; because they occur toward various objects and because they are of various kinds, they are called "diverse perceptions.

In the triad beginning with "restlessness," "kosajja" (laziness) is the state of one who is indolent, which is simply negligence (*pamāda*). In the triad beginning with "disrespect," it is the occurrence of not heeding instruction.

Anger is what is called disrespect. In the triad of lack of faith (*assaddhiya*), unwholesome states that arise through the mode of not believing in the Three Jewels, kamma, and its fruits are called lack of faith.
Through the fivefold stinginess, the failure to understand the request "Give [me]" is called lack of generosity (*avadaññutā*).

In the triad of restlessness (*uddhacca*), the state of not guarding the doors of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, is called lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*). Transgression of body and speech [is what is meant].

Immorality (*dussīlya*) is as follows: within the triad of the Noble Ones (*ariya*), it is the lack of desire to see or attend upon the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, which is called the unwillingness to see the Noble Ones.

It is the lack of desire to hear or retain the true Dhamma that constitutes the wings of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhika-saddhamma*), which is called the unwillingness to hear the true Dhamma. And it is the act of imputing faults to others, characterized by the search for flaws, which is known as caviling (*upārambha*).
"Upārambhacittatā" means a mind intent on finding fault. In the triad of "muddle-mindedness," *uddhacca* (restlessness) is called "distraction of the mind.

In the triad of "unwise attention," unwise attention—defined as the act of adverting the mind by way of non-strategic attention, such as regarding the impermanent as permanent, or by way of attending to the opposites of the Truths—is called *ayonisomanasikāra*.
The eight factors of the wrong path, beginning with wrong view and wrong intention, constitute the "bad path."
The cultivation of the wrong path is called "following a bad path. Sloth and torpor are called "mental sluggishness.
This concludes the triad. Regarding the tetrads: among the four requisites, such as robes and so forth, the arising of craving with the thought, "Where shall I obtain what is pleasing?
constitutes the four "arising of cravings. Those by which the Noble Ones do not go are "bad ways," namely: lust, hatred, delusion, and fear.
For these are indeed the four "goings on wrong paths" (*agatigamana*): going on paths that should not be gone upon and performing actions that should not be done.
In this context, "bias" (*chanda*) is attachment through partiality. "Fear" (*bhaya*) is hatred proceeding in that same manner.

The four "inversions" (*vipariyāsa*)—such as regarding the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful—are so called because they search for phenomena in a distorted way. Or, they are so called because one sits within them.
There are four inversions (vipariyāsa) starting from entry [into the stream].

These become twelve by being threefold each—according to the inversions of perception (saññā), mind (citta), and view (diṭṭhi). Among them, there are six inversions of perception, mind, and view regarding the impermanent as permanent and the non-self as self;
and two inversions of view regarding suffering as pleasure and the foul as beautiful. Thus, these eight are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga).

It should be understood that the two perversions of perception and mind which take the unattractive to be attractive are abandoned by the path of non-returning, and the two perversions of perception and mind which take suffering to be pleasant are abandoned by the path of arahantship. Furthermore,
the four [perversions] that occur as "the unseen is seen," "the unheard is heard," "the unperceived is perceived," and "the unknown is known" [are likewise to be understood].

These are called ignoble modes of speech. Furthermore, there are four other ignoble modes of speech that occur regarding what has been seen and so forth, namely: saying "it was not seen," "it was not heard," "it was not sensed," and "it was not cognized.
These, together with the former ones, are also called the eight ignoble modes of speech.
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech are called the four types of misconduct.
The four other types of verbal misconduct, such as lying and so forth, are called the four verbal misdeeds (*vacīduccarita*).
The four fears are the fear of birth, aging, sickness, and death. The four [other] fears are the fear of kings, thieves, fire, and water;

furthermore, for one crossing the ocean, there are the four fears arising from waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, and sharks; and the fears of self-reproach, reproach by others, punishment, and an unhappy rebirth.
"Four" refers to these or three other tetrads known as the four fears. In this context, *susukā* means fierce fish.
All of these fears should be understood as states of mind characterized by aversion (*paṭighacitta*).
These four [views] arise in the form: "All pleasure, pain, and so forth, are self-made, made by another, made by both, or arisen fortuitously."
Views. This is the tetrad.
Regarding the pentads, such as the "five lower fetters" (*pañcorambhāgiya*) and so forth: "lower" (*oraṃ*) refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) because it is the lowest state of existence;

since they produce rebirth there, the five—namely, personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), and ill-will (*paṭigha*)—are called "lower" because they belong to that [realm].
The "fetter-bonds pertaining to the lower" (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are as follows: "Above" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the form and formless realms because they exist in a higher state;

those which, according to the method already stated, partake of that [higher state] are the five fetter-bonds pertaining to the upper: lust for the form realm, lust for the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views—these five are called "attachments" (*saṅga*) in the sense of clinging. Those same five are also [called attachments] in the sense of entering into [the world].

In the sense of piercing, there are the five arrows (*salla*). The four kinds of doubt regarding the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, together with resentment toward one’s fellow celibates—these five are called "mental barrenness" (*cetokhila*) because they cause the mind to become stiff, like chaff or a stump.

[The five hindrances are: not being free from lust for sensual pleasures; [not being free from lust] for the body... pe... for forms... pe... having eaten as much as one desires, [seeking] the pleasure of sleep... pe...
One dwells addicted to the pleasure of roaming and the pleasure of torpor;

one leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas—these five states, so occurring, are called "mental bondages" (*cetasovinibandhā*) because they bind the mind and seize it as if making a fist.
Therein, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the internal body, and "form" (*rūpa*) refers to external form. One who perceives...

The five views that occur thus—"the self exists," "the self is non-percipient," "the self is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," "the existing self is annihilated," or "one attains Nibbāna in this very life"—are called the five views (*pañca diṭṭhiyo*).

The five [courses of action] beginning with the destruction of life and ending with the drinking of intoxicants are called enmies (*verā*) in the sense of being causes of enmity. [The five losses are: loss of relatives, loss of wealth, loss through disease, loss through virtue, and loss through views.
There are five misfortunes. In this context, "misfortunes" (byasana) means those unwholesome states arising from destruction and born thereof.
These five—unpopularity among many people, abundance of enmity, abundance of faults, confused death, and going to the states of misery—are the disadvantages of impatience;
the meaning is that they are the defects of non-acceptance. [Furthermore, there are] the fear of livelihood, the fear of ill-repute, and the fear of timidity before an assembly.
The fear of death and the fear of a miserable rebirth—these are called the five fears.

There are five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā), which are theories asserting that by means of five factors—the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure to one's fill, and the four meditative absorptions beginning with the first—one attains for oneself the supreme Nibbāna in this very life. This is the group of five.
Regarding the wheels (*cakka*), however, anger, hypocrisy, envy, deceit, evil desire, and dogmatic adherence—these six are the roots of dispute.
Regarding the six agreeable objects of sense, such as forms and so forth, the desire and lust for them are called the six householder-dharmas of desire and lust.
Regarding the six disagreeable objects of sense, aversion toward them is called the six bases of opposition.
Contradiction itself is the basis for contradiction; thus, it is "the basis for contradiction. Craving toward the six objects of sense is called the "six groups of craving.

Lack of reverence toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, heedfulness, and hospitality is called the "six types of lack of reverence. Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, delight in socializing, and delight in proliferation are the "six factors of decline";
the meaning is that they cause one's spiritual progress to decline. In this context, regarding hearing, seeing, conversing, enjoying [sense objects], and physical contact:

Being engaged and devoted to the five [pleasures] is delighting in social contact. It should be understood that being engaged and devoted to the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views is delighting in proliferation (*papañca*).
Furthermore, there are these other six factors of decline: delight in work, talk, sleep, and society; the four kinds of difficult-to-correctness; and the two—having evil friends.

The applied thoughts (*vicāra*) that arise with respect to the six objects—visible forms and so forth—which serve as the basis for joy and are associated with joy based on attachment, are called "joyous mental explorations" (*somanassūpavicāra*).

These should be understood to include the factors such as initial application (*vitakka*) and those associated with them. This same method applies to the other two [types of mental exploration] as well.
Furthermore, in this context, equanimity (*upekkhā*) should be understood as the feeling of equanimity accompanied by ignorance (*aññāṇa*).

It is also called "equanimity of ignorance. The feelings that arise respectively toward the six types of objects—desirable, undesirable, and neutral—are described by way of three sets of six, beginning with "the six kinds of worldly joy" (*cha gehasitāni somanassāni*), and so forth. [These views include:
"I have a self," or "I have no self," or "I perceive a self by means of a self," or "I perceive a non-self by means of a self..."

Or [the views] that arise as: "I perceive," or "I perceive myself by means of myself," or "This self of mine is the agent, the experiencer, permanent, and eternal"—these are called the six views. Among them, "it exists" is the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

"It does not exist" is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). Having grasped all five aggregates as "self," [one regards] the aggregate of perception as [the self] and the remaining [aggregates]...
The view that "I perceive self by means of self" through the mode of knowing;
the view that, having grasped the aggregate of perception as "self" and the others as "not-self," one perceives not-self by means of self;
and the view that, having grasped the aggregate of perception as "not-self" and the others as "self," one perceives self by means of not-self.
And these are to be understood. This is the group of six.

Regarding the seven, however, sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), aversion (*paṭigha*), conceit (*māna*), views (*diṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), and ignorance (*avijjā*) are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*) because they lie down closely along the continuum of consciousness in the sense of being firmly established and in the sense of not having been abandoned. These very [seven] [keep] beings in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
They are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) by way of fettering; they are to be understood as "obsessions" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) by way of their manifestation through active engagement.
Lack of faith, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, lack of learning, laziness, forgetfulness, and lack of wisdom—these seven are the qualities of the untrue, of unworthy persons;
or rather, because they are non-existent or base qualities, they are called "untrue qualities" (*asaddhamma*). [The same applies to] killing living beings and so forth.

The seven types of misconduct consist of bodily and verbal misconduct. The seven types of conceit are: conceit, over-conceit, conceit beyond measure, inferiority-conceit, superiority-conceit, the conceit "I am," and false conceit.
[The view that] "in the human world, the self born of mother and father is annihilated;
likewise, in the six celestial worlds, the divine self that feeds on solid food [is annihilated]; in the form-world, the self possessing form and mind-made [is annihilated]..."

The seven views of annihilationism are those that proceed thus: “Self; the fourfold formless self in the four formless realms is annihilated and destroyed here and there, and does not exist after death.
Among these, the first three views proceed by grasping the aggregate of form as the self; the remaining ones...
The four immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) should be known. This concludes the section on the sevenfold [group].
Regarding the eightfold groups, however, the eight bases of defilement (kilesavatthu) are: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, and restlessness.
One [thought] is: "Whatever task must be done by me"; likewise, another is: "It has been done by me."

‘The path must be traveled by me,’ ‘It has been traveled,’ ‘I have eaten little,’ ‘I have eaten well,’ ‘An affliction has arisen for me,’ ‘I have recently recovered from illness’—these eight are called the bases of laziness; the meaning is that they are the causes of indolence for one who is lazy.
Regarding gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, and pleasure...
The repelling of the mind by lust and hatred toward suffering, respectively, is called "resistance of the mind" toward the eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhamma*).
The eight ignoble modes of speech (*anariya-vohāra*) are those stated previously in the two tetrads.

The eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*) consist of wrong view, wrong intention, and so forth. When a bhikkhu, being accused of an existing offense, says, "I do not remember," [this is a case of concealment].

There is one [offense] for evading; one for counter-attacking the accuser by saying, "You are a fool," and so forth; likewise, there is one for counter-accusing the accuser by saying, "You yourself have fallen into this same offense";
one for prevaricating with irrelevant matters; one for gesticulating with the arms while speaking in the Saṅgha; one for harassing through silence;
one for departing from the assembly without taking leave of the Saṅgha or the accuser; and one for renouncing the training out of fear of being accused.

These are called the eight faults of a person (*purisadosa*). The eight views of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*) are those occurring as follows: "The self is non-percipient and material," "immaterial," "both material and immaterial," "neither material nor immaterial," "finite," "infinite," "both finite and infinite," and "neither finite nor infinite.

The eight views of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are those occurring as: "The self is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient and material," "immaterial," and so forth. This concludes the group of eight.

In the *Navaka* [Treatise], however, the nine types of resentment that occur in the form: "He has done me harm, he is doing me harm, he will do me harm; he has done harm to one dear to me, he is doing harm, he will do harm;
he has done good to one not dear to me, he is doing good, he will do good"—these very resentments are called the "bases of resentment" (*āghātavatthu*).
Anger, hypocrisy, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, lying, and evil desire.
Wrong view—these are called the nine stains of a person. The ninefold types of conceit, beginning with “I am better than one who is better,” are called conceit.
Dependent on craving comes seeking; dependent on seeking comes gain; dependent on that comes judgment;
dependent on that comes desire and lust; dependent on that comes attachment; likewise, appropriation, stinginess, and guarding.
“From guarding arise many evil states, such as taking up sticks and weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, and so forth.

These are what are called the nine states rooted in craving (*taṇhāmūlaka*). In this context, regarding the four types of deliberation (*vinicchaya*)—namely, by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought—it is the deliberation of thought (*vitakkavinicchaya*) that is intended here.
For, having obtained gain, one thinks: “This is for the sake of the object of form,” and so on.
“This is for the sake of sound-objects and so forth”—thus the analysis is by means of thought (*vitakka*) alone. *Chandarāga* is weak passion;
*ajjhosāna* is strong resolve. *Pariggaha* should be understood as the act of grasping by way of craving and views. “I am,” “I am this,” “This I am,” “I shall be,” “I shall be possessed of form,”...

“I shall be formless,” “I shall be percipient,” “I shall be non-percipient,” or “I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient”—these nine states thus described are called "agitated" in the sense of wavering.

These very same states are "conceived" in the sense of conceiving, "fluctuating" due to their oscillation, and "proliferated" due to their conceptual elaboration; these are [the views] by means of those various...
Because they are conditioned by causes, they are called "conditioned. By all those nine sets, pride alone is described;
for that too proceeds, like a view, through such modes of perception as "I am" and so forth. [This concludes] the set of nines.
In the sets of tens, however, there are greed, hatred, delusion, pride, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread.

These ten defilements are themselves called the bases of defilement (*kilesavatthu*). The nine beginning with “He has done me harm,” together with resentment toward improper objects such as stumps and thorns, are called the ten bases of resentment (*āghātavatthu*).
The ten unwholesome courses of action, beginning with the destruction of life, are called the ten unwholesome paths of action (*akusalakammapatha*).

[The fetters are: the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*), the fetter of aversion (*paṭigha-saṃyojana*), the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikicchā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa-saṃyojana*), the fetter of lust for existence (*bhavarāga-saṃyojana*), the fetter of envy (*issā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of avarice (*macchariya-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avijjā-saṃyojana*).
These are called the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*). There are eight [wrong states] beginning with wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) and wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*);
together with wrong knowledge (*micchā-ñāṇa*) and wrong liberation (*micchā-vimutti*), these are called the ten wrongnesses (*micchatta*).

Among them, "wrong knowledge" is delusion (*moha*) that proceeds both by way of devising means for performing evil deeds and by way of reflecting after having done evil, thinking, "I have done well. "Wrong liberation" is...
The perception of being liberated in one who is actually not liberated.

The nihilistic view that proceeds by way of the ten modes, beginning with "there is no giving, there is no sacrifice," is called the ten-based wrong view (*dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi*). Or [the views]:
"The world is eternal," or likewise "it is non-eternal," "it is finite," "it is infinite," "the soul and the body are the same," or "the soul is one thing and the body another."

The "view of extremes" (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhi*) consists of ten bases that arise as follows: "the body [is the self]," or "the Tathāgata exists after death," or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death... [or] both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist after death.
In this context, "the world" refers to the aggregates and so forth; "finite" (*antavā*) refers here to the limited *kasiṇa*-absorption.
It has been said: "Endless" (*anantavā*) should be understood as "vast. "Tathāgata" refers to a sentient being. [The section on] the tenfold [fetters].
Among the eighteen *taṇhāvicarita* (modes of craving), these are the manifestations and occurrences of craving.

"Based upon the internal" (*ajjhattikassupādāya*) means based upon the five internal aggregates (*khandha*). For here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. Therein, "I am" (*asmīti*)...
There is [the thought]: "I am"; there is [the thought]: "I am this"; there is [the thought]: "I am thus"; there is [the thought]: "I am otherwise.
There is [the thought]: "I shall be thus"; "I shall be this"; "I shall be thus"; "I shall be otherwise. There is [the thought]: "I was thus"; "I was this";
there is [the thought]: "I might be thus"; "I might be this"; "I might be thus"; "I might be otherwise. There is [the thought]: "I will not be thus..."

“‘I might be,’ ‘I might be thus,’ ‘I might be so,’ ‘I might be otherwise’—these are called the eighteen modes of craving’s wandering (taṇhāvicarita) based on the internal [aggregates], as they have been stated.
Therein, ‘I am’ means: when there is the grasping ‘I am’ as a whole with respect to the five internal aggregates.”
This is the meaning. When there is grasping in this way, however, there is a twofold grasping: either without comparison or with comparison.
Therein, "without comparison" means that without comparing or approaching any other mode, one takes the object as its own state and thinks, "I am thus.
Through craving, conceit, and views, one thinks, "Among kṣatriyas and so forth, I am of such a kind."
The meaning is that there is grasping. Furthermore, grasping by comparison (*upanidhāya*) is twofold: by way of similarity (*samatā*) and by way of dissimilarity (*asamatā*).
Therein, grasping by way of similarity is "I am exactly thus"; its meaning is: "Just as this person is a khattiya, or a brahmin and so forth, or possesses form or is formless, and so on, so too am I.
However, "I am otherwise" is grasping by way of dissimilarity; its [meaning] is: "Just as these..."
"Khattiyas and so forth"—the meaning is that one thinks "I am inferior or superior" in a manner other than those [preceding].
These, first of all, are the four modes of craving's movement (taṇhāvicarita) by way of the present; however, the four beginning with "will be" are stated by way of the future.

Their meaning should be understood according to the method explained for the preceding tetrad. Therein, the pair beginning with "I am" (asmīti) is by way of the grasping of eternalism and annihilationism.
It has been stated. For therein, "I am" refers to eternalism; "it perishes" refers to annihilationism;
and the four following [terms], beginning with "might it be," are stated by way of speculative thought involving doubt.

It should be understood that the four [terms] beginning with "may I be" are stated by way of the fabrication of aspiration, occurring in the form "perhaps I might be. This is the first set of eighteen.
In the second [verse], "depending on the external" means depending on the external pentad of aggregates (*khandha*). Therein, by the method stated immediately prior—"By this, 'I am' occurs;
by this, 'I am such' occurs; by this, 'I am exactly thus' occurs;

by this, 'I am otherwise' occurs," and so forth—one should understand that there are eighteen modes of craving’s movement (*taṇhāvicarita*) depending on the external. The phrase "by this" is merely a word.
Herein, this is the distinction from what precedes. Therein, "by this" means by this external form (*rūpa*), or... pe ...by consciousness (*viññāṇa*);
such is the meaning. And therein, external form should be understood by way of such requisites as parasols, swords, fans, food, drink, wealth, and grain.
Feeling and the other [aggregates] should be understood by way of such requisites as male and female slaves, kinsmen, attendants, elephants, horses, and so forth.

In all instances, the application should be understood as follows: "I am this," "I am thus," and so forth, with respect to these external forms and other objects. This concludes the second set of eighteen.

Regarding the others, however, in the passages beginning with "having combined those together into one," it means that by combining both sets of eighteen together, there are thirty-six modes of craving’s movement (*taṇhā-vicari-tāni*).
Thus, for each individual person in the past time, there are two sets of eighteen.

According to this method, there are thirty-six in the past, and likewise thirty-six in the future. However, regarding the present, those same [factors] are obtained for a single being according to what is actually acquired;
yet, from the perspective of all beings, thirty-six are obtained even in the present.
Thus, by combining all that has been stated in this manner, for all beings throughout the three periods of time, there are six groups of eighteen.

The meaning is that there are one hundred and eight modes of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*) by way of these [factors]. In the phrase "there are one hundred and eight modes of craving," the meaning should be understood in exactly the same way.
The modes of craving are finished.

Regarding the phrase "And those which... and so forth: the meaning is that the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) mentioned here were spoken by the Teacher himself when he directly addressed them in the first sutta of the *Dīghanikāya*, titled the *Brahmajāla*.

For in the *Brahmajāla*, there are four eternalist doctrines (*sassatavāda*), four partial-eternalist doctrines (*ekaccasassatika*), four doctrines concerning the finite and infinite universe (*antānantika*), and four doctrines of equivocation regarding death (*amarāvikkhepika*).

There are two views of fortuitous origination, sixteen views of those who maintain that there is consciousness after death, eight views of those who maintain that there is no consciousness after death, eight views of those who maintain that there is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness after death, seven views of annihilationism, and five views of Nibbāna in this very life—these sixty-two types of speculative views have been taught with their origins according to various methods;
their analysis should be understood according to the method explained therein. This, first of all, is [the explanation] following the meaning of the words.
The analysis: as for the remaining analysis here, it is easily understood by following what has been stated regarding the meaning of the terms.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga* is finished.
The commentary on the meaning of the matrix for the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*.
Furthermore, the analysis of the meaning and so forth regarding the matrix of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* has already been stated previously.

However, since the Blessed One has now again, by means of twelve categories of phenomena—beginning with the aggregates (*khandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) which were analyzed below according to various methods—expounded them through ten sections that reveal a thousand unprecedented methods, such as their all-inclusive nature, their arising in the four planes, and their inclusion therein; [the following is explained].

This *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis) is stated solely for the purpose of demonstrating the distinctions by means of the "hearts of the Dhamma" (*dhammahadaya*), which consist of the underlying intentions of all phenomena;
therefore, the detailed exposition here follows the method of analysis (*vibhaṅganaya*).

For in the *Vibhaṅga*, first having set forth a twelve-item matrix (*mātikā*) consisting of questions such as "How many aggregates are there? and so forth, [the text proceeds] according to what was stated below, starting from the general perspective of the four planes.
The section entitled "The Compendium of All" has been analyzed; therein, the seven [factors] beginning with contact should be understood by way of the seven consciousness-elements.
The second section, however, proceeds by way of showing the arising and non-arising of those [factors] in the four planes through four divisions. Regarding that, first, in the first division:
"In the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), how many aggregates... how many consciousnesses? In the sense-sphere element, there are five aggregates, twelve bases..."
