Having set forth the matrix (mātikā) thus: “the eighteen elements, the three truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine roots, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness,” [these] are analyzed.
Therein, because for the most part even the phenomena belonging to the four planes [of existence] pertain to beings of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara),...
They arise, but not exclusively in the sense-sphere plane (*kāmāvacara*). Therefore, by the phrase "the five aggregates" and so forth, those belonging to all four planes are mentioned here.

It is the phenomena arising therein that are intended here, not only those included within that specific plane. The same principle applies to the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) and the others as well.

And herein, regarding the statement "three truths," this refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*), because it cannot be pointed out as being in any particular location due to its being independent of place.

Having excluded that [possibility], it was stated [as follows]: For phenomena (dhammā) that depend upon a cause occupy a location that serves as their own supporting cause, because that which lacks a cause has no support;
or alternatively, phenomena that are occasionally perceived indicate their own conditioned nature (saṅkhata) by virtue of their temporal restriction.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (pasaṅga) of their existence even at other times, or else [their existence] would occur even at this very moment.

Thus, it should be understood that even though non-existence (*abhāva*) is perceived in some place, such a perception does not apply to the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), because it is impossible for either the unconditioned or the conditioned to be non-pervasive across all places.
Therefore, the unconditioned must be understood as being entirely free from spatial and temporal limitations.
Regarding the second section, however—
“Five aggregates, six bases, nine elements, three truths, fourteen faculties, eight roots, three nutriments, four contacts...

[and so on] ...four consciousnesses”—having thus set forth the matrix (mātikā), it is analyzed. However, because the bases such as odors (gandhāyatana) and so forth, though existing, do not perform the function of a base and so on due to the absence of the physical sense organs such as the nose, they are excluded; thus, “six bases, nine... [is stated].
The passage beginning with "the elements" was stated not because those [objects] are absent.

However, some, having said that "in the realm of form (rūpaloka), odors, tastes, physical nutriment, and the function of tangibility regarding the great primary elements do not exist, and for that very reason they are not mentioned in the Pāḷi," then indulge in much proliferation by stating numerous fallacious reasons; this is merely their own opinion and should not be accepted.

Because odors and so forth are inseparable [from their bases], because they are tangible objects, and because they are elemental by nature, one should understand that the nose and the other two [senses], the two [types of] feeling (pleasure and pain), and the faculties of joy and grief exist;

however, this is to be understood as being fourteen faculties and so on, excluding grief-rooted volitional formations, physical nutriment, the contact of the triad beginning with the nose, and the like.
As for the third category:
“In the formless element there are four aggregates, two bases, two elements, three truths, eleven faculties, eight roots, three nutriments, one contact... [and so on] ...one consciousness.

Having thus set forth the matrix (mātikā), it is analyzed. And here, because of the absence of the eye, ear, and “I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown” faculties, the eleven faculties should be understood accordingly.
However, in the fourth section—
“Four aggregates, two bases, two elements, two truths, twelve faculties, six roots, three nutriments, one contact... [and so on] ...

one consciousness”—having thus set forth the matrix (mātikā), it is analyzed. And because there is no such thing as an "unincluded element" (apariyāpanna-dhātu) either by way of location or by way of the arising of beings, therefore, instead of saying "of the unincluded element," it is shown as the supramundane (lokuttara) that has been produced.
“It is said: ‘In the non-included [realms], there are four aggregates,’ and so forth. Thus, the second section should be understood through four divisions.
As for the third section, however, it begins:

‘The aggregate of form is included in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu); the four aggregates may be included in the sense-sphere realm, or they may not be included in the sense-sphere realm,’ and so forth.”
It proceeds by way of seeing the phenomena included within each respective plane, categorized into four sections across the four planes;
since it can be understood according to what has been stated below, it is not elaborated upon here.
In this context, "included in the sense-sphere element" means that, by virtue of being of the sense-sphere realm, it is contained therein; the same method applies to the remaining [planes] as well.

The fourth section, however, proceeds by way of showing, through four divisions, the phenomena that arise and do not arise at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) across the three planes. Therein, first, regarding the first division:
"At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere plane (*kāmadhātu*), the five aggregates manifest for all; for some, eleven bases (*āyatana*) manifest;
for some, ten bases manifest; for some, another ten; and for some, nine."
For some, seven elements; for some, eleven elements... [and so on] ...seven elements. For all, one truth becomes manifest.
For some, fourteen faculties; for some, thirteen; for some, another thirteen; for some, twelve;
for some, ten; for some, nine; for some, another nine; for some, eight; for some, another...
“For some, eight; for some, seven; for some, five; for some, four faculties become manifest;
for some, three roots become manifest; for some, two; for some, they become manifest without a root.
For all, however, the four nutriments, one contact... [and so on] ...and one consciousness become manifest.”

Having laid down the matrix, it is analyzed as follows: therein, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for those of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) who are born spontaneously (*opapātika*), for those in the states of deprivation (*āpāyika*), and for gods and humans with complete sense bases (*paripuṇṇāyatana*), eleven bases (*āyatana*) appear, excluding the sound-base (*saddāyatana*).
These same eleven are also the elements (*dhātu*). For sound absolutely does not arise at the moment of rebirth-linking.
Furthermore, for those born blind, ten [bases] appear; for those born deaf, another ten;
for those born both blind and deaf, nine; and for those born from a womb, seven bases and elements appear by way of visible form, odor, flavor, body-tangible, mind, and mental objects.
For spontaneously born beings with three roots, the six faculties with mind as the sixth appear; in the two genders, one [appears].
There are fourteen faculties: the life-faculty, one of either the joy-faculty or the equanimity-faculty, and the five beginning with faith.
For those with two roots, there are thirteen, excluding the wisdom-faculty; for humans of the first aeon who possess three roots, there are another thirteen, excluding the femininity-faculty;
for those same humans with two roots, there are twelve; and for those born from a womb...
However, among those with three roots (tihetuka), excluding the first fourteen [bases], there are ten;

for those same individuals with two roots (duhetuka), there are nine. Among those born spontaneously (opapātika) who are rootless (ahetuka) and possess complete sense bases, excluding sound and the others from the first fourteen, there are another nine.
For those same individuals who are blind from birth, there are eight; likewise for those who are deaf; and for those who are both blind and deaf, however—
In the case of beings born from a womb, five faculties—the body, mind, life, and equanimity—arise for those who are rootless (*ahetuka*).

For those same beings, if they are neuter, four arise. For in rootless consciousnesses, even though one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) exists, it does not attain the status of the concentration faculty (*samādhindriya*);
however, by way of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), "a single contact" and so forth should be understood.
In the second section, however:
“At the moment of rebirth in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), with the exception of the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) among the devas, the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) become manifest.
There are five bases (āyatana), five elements (dhātu), one truth (sacca), ten faculties (indriya), three roots (hetu), three nutriments (āhāra), and one [path factor].”

“Contact... [and so on] ... one consciousness”—having thus set forth the matrix (mātikā), it is analyzed. Therein, the five bases and elements are to be understood by way of the eye, visible forms, ear, mind, and mental objects.
Here too, the reason for not including odors, tastes, and tangibles has already been stated previously. [The faculties are] the eye, ear, mind, and life-faculties.
One of either joy or equanimity, and the five beginning with faith—these ten faculties are to be understood.
However, in the third section:
"At the moment of rebirth for the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) gods, one aggregate appears—the form aggregate; two..."
“The bases are the visible-form base and the mental-object base; the two elements are the visible-form element and the mental-object element;

one truth is the truth of suffering; one faculty is the material life-faculty; the non-percipient beings are gods who are rootless, without nutriment, without contact… [and so on] …without consciousness.
Thus the Schedule of Terms with Descriptions is set forth. And herein, although matter does not perform for them the function of a base and so forth, it is nevertheless included.
Furthermore, because they are included among those possessing form with consciousness (*saviññāṇakarūpī*), they are also included here;
however, because odors and so forth are not included there, they are also not included here—not because they do not exist.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is extracted here because it is within the range of the eye of the remaining Brahmās who dwell on the same level, whereas for the non-percipient beings (*asaññī*), five sense-spheres and one type of nutriment arise.
In the fourth section, having set forth the matrix headings thus:
“At the moment of rebirth in the formless element (arūpadhātu), there are four aggregates, two bases, two elements, one truth, eight faculties, three roots, three nutriments, one contact...
[and so on] ...one consciousness,” they are analyzed. And herein, the faculties of mind, life, and equanimity, as well as faith and the others—
The five [factors] should be understood as the eight faculties. The remainder is easily understood. Thus the fourth section should be understood by way of four divisions.
As for the fifth section, however, it proceeds by way of analyzing those states according to their different planes, having established the matrix (mātikā) of four dyads as follows:
"states of the sense-sphere, not of the sense-sphere... [and so on]... included. Its meaning is the same as that explained below.

The sixth section, however, having pointed out the conventional gods (*sammutideva*), the gods by birth (*upapattideva*), and the purified gods (*visuddhideva*), is stated by way of showing the karma that causes rebirth and the measure of lifespan within the destinies of humans and gods. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:

beings, having performed sense-sphere wholesome kamma such as giving and virtue, [are reborn] in the human world among families such as those of great wealthy Khattiyas, and also among those reckoned as the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, Tusita, Nimmānarati, and Paranimmita-vasavatti [devas].

And they are reborn in the six deva-worlds. Therein, starting from the middle of Mount Sineru and the surrounding mountains down to the earth, extending horizontally as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains, all those residing on the mountains, in the sky, in the trees, and on the ground—including the Four Great Kings, the moon, and the sun—belong to the realm of the Cātumahārājikas.
Above that, up to the limit of the Cakkavāḷa, are the Tāvatiṃsa and the other [devas].

It should be understood that they are situated one above the other in successive order. There is no world of the devas that does not reach the mountain ranges of the successive world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

However, having developed the first jhāna to a limited degree, beings are reborn among the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārisajja*); having developed it to a middling degree, among the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*);
and having developed it to a superior degree, among the Great Brahmās (*Mahābrahmā*). These three types of persons belong to the plane of the first jhāna.
They dwell on a single level. However, there is a distinction among them according to differences in lifespan and other factors;

the same applies further on. In the fourfold system, having developed the second jhāna, and in the fivefold system, having developed the second and third jhānas—whether limited, middling, or sublime—they are reborn among the Parittābhas, Appamāṇābhas, and Ābhassaradevas respectively. As for the third jhāna, by way of being limited and so forth...
Having developed [the jhānas] in relation to the limited beauty, the immeasurable beauty, and the beautiful-kinha (subhakiṇha) realms;

and having developed the fourth jhāna, due to differences in the object, attention, desire, inclination, and so forth, some are reborn among the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), some in the Vehapphala realm, some in the Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, some in the Akaniṭṭha realm, and some respectively in the four [formless attainments] beginning with the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Among those, indeed, some...

The sectarians, seeing a fault in the mind— thinking, “Based on the mind, lust, hatred, and so forth arise, and from that as their cause, sufferings come into being”— generate a distaste for perception by thinking, “This is Nibbāna in this very life.
Having developed jhāna for rebirth there, they are reborn right there, remaining in that very place either standing, sitting, or lying down, consisting merely of a physical body.
It should be understood that they remain for five hundred kappas.
For those who have attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti), which jhāna ripens? That which is familiar;
among all those that are familiar, whichever one they aspire toward as a plane of rebirth, or in the absence of such an aspiration, whichever one they enter at the time of death.

When even that is absent, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) ripens by way of the highest [kamma]. Furthermore, among the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), such as the Aviha and others, beings other than non-returners (*anāgāmin*) do not arise;
however, non-returners are able to arise everywhere within the Brahma-worlds, excluding the non-percipient realm (*asaññī*).
Moreover, for all Noble Ones (*ariya*), there is rebirth in those higher planes from there, but never rebirth in a lower plane.

For those non-returners born in the plane of the first jhāna, having purified the nine Brahma-worlds and established themselves at the summit among the Vehapphala deities, they attain final nibbāna there; they do not return, because for noble ones there is no rebirth in lower realms.

These three states—the Vehapphala, the Akaniṭṭha, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—are called the "supreme existences. Non-returners born in these three places do not go further upward.

Not below; they attain final nibbāna right there. In the human world, those still in training (sekha) remain in the state of a householder for as long as life lasts, but not those beyond training (asekha).
For they either go forth on the very day they attain arahantship, or they attain final nibbāna.

Among the deities of the earth, even those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) remain for as long as life lasts. Among the six classes of sense-sphere deities, only stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and once-returners (sakadāgāmin) [remain].

They remain; however, it should be understood that for non-returners (anāgāmin), it is appropriate to go to the form-realm existence (rūpabhava) on that very day, while for those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), they attain final Nibbāna.
Thus, among these twenty-seven planes, regarding the beings born in the human, deva, and brahmā worlds included therein:
first, for humans, the measure of lifespan in this current appearance of a Buddha is one hundred years, or slightly more. As for those in the states of misery (āpāyika)...
Furthermore, for the earth-dwelling devas (bhummadevā), there is sometimes no fixed limit to their lifespan; karma alone is the measure.
For they may die after as little as seven days, or they may remain for an entire aeon (kappa).
Now, for the gods of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā), fifty human years constitute one day and night; by that night—
Thirty nights make a month; twelve months of that reckoning make a year;
by that year, the lifespan measure is five hundred celestial years. By human calculation, these amount to ninety million years.
Taking one hundred human years as a single day and night for the Tāvatiṃsa devas, their celestial lifespan thus amounts to one thousand such years.

In this way, having doubled the calculation of the years for the Yāma devas and the others, the measure of their lifespan should be understood as being double and quadruple that of the lower realms respectively.
Among the Brahmās, however, the lifespan of the Brahmapārisajja devas is one-third of a kappa; for the Brahmapurohita devas it is half a kappa;
for the Mahābrahmā devas it is one full kappa; and for the Parittābha devas it is two kappas—in this manner, it is doubled successively at each higher level.
Having done so, one should apply this up to the Subhakiṇha realm. For the lifespan of the Subhakiṇha devas is sixty-four eons;
that of the Asaññasattas and the Vehapphalas is five hundred eons; and that of the Avihā devas is one thousand eons. One should apply this by doubling successively up to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
For the lifespan of the Akaniṭṭha devas is sixteen thousand eons, and for the four formless realms [it is calculated accordingly].
The measure of their lifespan is, respectively, twenty thousand, four thousand, sixty thousand, and eighty-four thousand eons.
Though they have been uplifted by the power of merit and have gone to the realms of desire and form—
even reaching the peak of existence— they return once more to states of misery.
Beings with such long lifespans pass away when their life-span is exhausted;
there is no state of existence that is eternal—thus it was said by the Great Seer.
Therefore, the wise, the prudent, the skillful, and those who contemplate the true goal [should understand this].
"For the sake of liberation from aging and death, they develop the supreme path.
Having developed the pure path that leads to the depths of Nibbāna,
and having fully understood all taints, they attain final Nibbāna, free from taints."
This is the method for the sixth section.
The seventh section, however, proceeds by way of analyzing those aggregates and so forth in terms of their being "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) and so on. For therein it is said:
"The aggregate of form is to be directly known, to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*); it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, and not to be realized."
"The four aggregates are to be directly known and fully understood; they may be abandoned, they may be developed, they may be realized;
or they may not be abandoned, not be developed, and not be realized," and so forth—thus the twelve sections are analyzed in detail.
Therein, by means of the wisdom that discerns characteristics, the aggregates and so on [are analyzed].

All phenomena are to be directly known. All phenomena are to be fully understood through whichever of the three kinds of full understanding—as appropriate—namely, full understanding as the known, full understanding by scrutinization, or full understanding by abandoning.
Even supramundane phenomena are indeed to be fully understood as the known. However, unwholesome states are to be abandoned;
the path is to be developed; and fruition and Nibbāna are to be realized. In this context, the aggregate of form...
It is to be fully understood by way of knowing and scrutinizing. For within the domain of insight (vipassanā), everything is to be fully understood through the full understanding of scrutiny.
In this manner, the state of being "to be directly known" and so forth is to be understood in all instances.
However, the eighth section proceeds by way of elucidating their possession of an object; the ninth [section] concerns what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.

By way of showing the inclusion [of the factors]. The tenth [chapter] proceeds by way of showing the classification through the sets of three and two, beginning with the wholesome triad and ending with the refuge dyad;
these also follow the method explained below. This is the summary here; however, the detailed exposition has already been stated below.
From the beginning onwards, it should be understood throughout in the commentaries on the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi*.
The commentary on the meaning of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga-mātikā* is completed.
The commentary on the meaning of the *Vibhaṅga-mātikā* within the *Mohavicchedanī Abhidhamma-mātikatthavaṇṇanā* is completed.
3. The Matrix of the Discourse on Elements (Dhātukathāmātikā) Now, following the matrix of the Vibhaṅga:
This is the completed commentary on the meaning of the *Dhātukathā* and the other [treatises].
Therefore, because of the matrices (mātikā), and for each of the five [sections] as appropriate—
due to the clarification of the unelucidated meaning, due to the determination of the meaning in brief,
and due to the method of analysis (vibhaṅga)— there is the method of commentary.
In this regard, first there is the commentary on the *mātikā* (matrix) of the *Dhātukathā*. This, moreover, is established in five ways by way of its arrangement:

the matrix of methods (*nayamātikā*), the internal matrix (*abbhantaramātikā*), the matrix of the doors of method (*nayamukhamātikā*), the matrix of characteristics (*lakkhaṇamātikā*), and the external matrix (*bāhiramātikā*). Among these, the passage beginning with "inclusion, non-inclusion...
[and so on]... that which is included by dissociation, that which is not included" consists of fourteen terms.

The "Table of Contents of Methods" (nayamātikā)—also called the "Root Table of Contents"—is so named because it was established to show that the phenomena (dhammā) have been analyzed according to the methods of inclusion and so forth in the *Dhātukathā*, having been set forth by way of more than one hundred and twenty-five terms beginning with "the five aggregates...
[and] attention. This [table] is thus arranged by means of the methods of inclusion and so forth.

Because it is established within the *Dhātukathā* itself by way of its nature as something to be analyzed, it is called the "Internal Matrix" (*abbhantara-mātikā*), which is also referred to as the "Matrix of the *Dhātukathā*" (*dhātukathā-mātikā*).
This [matrix] consists of four phrases: "Inclusion by three, non-inclusion by three; association by four, dissociation by four."
It is called the "matrix of the headings of the methods" (*nayamukhamātikā*) because it was established to show the entrances to these methods,

such as inclusion and non-inclusion, and association and dissociation— wherein, among the categories of aggregates and so forth, as well as the matrices of the wholesome triad and so forth, there is both inclusion and non-inclusion by means of the three terms of aggregate, base, and element; and likewise, there is association and dissociation by means of the four immaterial aggregates.

The phrase “homogeneous and heterogeneous” is called the *lakkhaṇamātikā* (the matrix of characteristics) because it was established to show that, by means of these two terms, there exist the methods of inclusion and non-inclusion as well as the methods of association and dissociation, according to the characteristics of the homogeneous and heterogeneous.
Furthermore, the entire *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* is the matrix for the *Dhātukathā*; this consists of sixty-six triads and two...
And having condensed the two hundred and fifty phrases, the *Dhātukathā* was set forth; because it is placed outside the matrix (*mātikā*), it is called the "External Matrix.
This is the commentary on the meaning of the unelaborated portions of this fivefold matrix.
Regarding the terms beginning with "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*), inclusion first is fourfold by way of genus, birth, action, and enumeration. Among these, "all... [the text continues].

“Let the khattiyas come, friend Visākha; whatever is right speech, whatever is right action, and whatever is right livelihood—these phenomena are included within the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
This is called inclusion by genus. “Let all the people of Kosala come, friend Visākha;
whatever is right effort, whatever is right mindfulness, and whatever is right concentration—these phenomena are included within the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).”
“Included”—this is called inclusion by birth (*sañjāti-saṅgaha*); the meaning is that there is inclusion by virtue of being related by birth in a single place.

“Let all elephant-riders come; and as for right view, friend Visākha, and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-khandha*)”—this is called inclusion by function (*kiriyā-saṅgaha*). “If the eye-base... [etc.]
It goes into the enumeration of the aggregate of form; therefore, indeed, it should be said: "The eye-base is included within the aggregate of form.
This is what is called inclusion by enumeration (*gaṇanasaṅgaha*), and this is what is intended here. By its opposite, non-inclusion (*asaṅgaha*) is to be understood.

From their various permutations, there arise [the categories of] being included and not included, and so forth, by way of simultaneous arising, simultaneous cessation, having a single physical basis, and having a single object.
Association (*sampayoga*) [is to be understood] from its opposite as dissociation (*vippayoga*); from their various permutations, [terms such as] "associated" and "dissociated" arise;
and from the permutation of the combination of both, [terms such as] "included," "associated," and "dissociated" are to be understood.
The rest has already been explained. This, then, is the meaning of the terms not yet explicitly analyzed here.
Commentary on the Terms of Comprehension and Non-comprehension: According to the analysis of the meaning,
since the aggregates of form and so forth from the internal matrix (mātikā), as well as the wholesome states and so forth from the external matrix,

are treated under the headings of the method-matrix such as "comprehension" and "non-comprehension"— by way of the headings of the method-matrix such as "comprehension by three" and "non-comprehension by three"— [the following is explained].

Since these [categories] were established by the Blessed One for the purpose of exposition according to what is appropriate, the determination of the meaning of the aggregates and so forth, including their inclusion and other classifications, occurs in brief exactly according to what is stated in the Canon.
Following this method, the method of analysis (vibhaṅganaya) can be understood;
therefore, we shall not explain it separately.
In that regard, concerning the section on inclusion and non-inclusion, this is the method for the exposition of the aggregates (*khandha*):

first, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is included by one aggregate, eleven bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*). It is not included by four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
In that context, "by eleven" means excluding the mind-base (*manāyatana*). It is also [not included] by the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*).
For some material phenomena (rūpadhammā) are included. By eleven [bases and elements], that is, excluding the seven consciousness-elements (viññāṇadhātu). The remainder is easy to understand.
The three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā) are each included by one aggregate, one base, and one element;
they are not included by four aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements. The same applies to the consciousness-aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha).
However, the only distinction here is that [this aggregate] is comprised by seven consciousness-elements and not comprised by eleven elements.

In that regard, it should be understood that the three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā) are comprised by one base, the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), and by one element, the mental-object element (dhammadhātu).
Furthermore, in the *Pāḷi* text, in the section on the exposition of the aggregates (*khandhapadaniddesa*), it is stated:

In the subsequent explanations of the bases (*āyatana*) and so forth, the method of detailed exposition is also analyzed according to the "two-rooted" system and others, such as: "The aggregate of form and the aggregate of feeling are comprised by two aggregates, eleven bases, and eleven elements.
Since that too is easily understood everywhere by following this "one-rooted" system, we have not elaborated upon it here. This is the method for the exposition of the terms for the aggregates.

Regarding the terms *āyatana* and *dhātu*, their inclusion under three aggregates and their exclusion from three aggregates should be understood by applying the same principles as stated for the terms *khandha*,
as appropriate. However, since the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) is not included among the aggregates within the *dhammāyatana* and *dhammadhātu*,
one should understand the inclusion of the remaining factors within the aggregates, excluding that [unconditioned element].
Among the truths, the truth of suffering is included by all aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).

The truths of origin and the path are included by the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), as well as by the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu). The truth of cessation is not included by any aggregate; it is included only by the base of mental phenomena and the element of mental phenomena.

Among the faculties, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is included by two aggregates: the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and the aggregate of mental formations. The five beginning with the pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya)...
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) [is included]; faith and the others are included in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);

and all these, beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), as well as the female and male faculties (*itthindriya-purisindriya*), are included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*). The remaining faculties are easy to understand.
Regarding dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) consists of the four aggregates excluding consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and eleven bases and elements.
And it is included [in the aggregates]. For here, since both name and form are taken in their process of occurrence (pavatti), it should be understood that the sense-base of sound is also included.
The sixfold sense-base (saḷāyatana) is comprised by two aggregates, by the six bases consisting of the sensitive organs and consciousness, and by twelve elements.
Furthermore, the existence at rebirth (upapattibhava), when it is of the nature of the sensual-sphere existence (kāmabhava), is comprised by five aggregates, excluding the sense-base of sound.

[Existence] is comprised by eleven bases (āyatana) and seventeen elements (dhātu). Fine-material existence (rūpabhava) is comprised by five aggregates (khandha), by five bases excluding sound and the four beginning with odor, as well as the three beginning with the nose and their corresponding consciousnesses, and by eight elements.
Non-percipient existence (asaññībhava) is comprised by one aggregate, namely the aggregate of material form, and by two bases and two elements in terms of material phenomena.
However, the triad beginning with the nose is not included here among the bases and elements because they do not perform the functions of a base and so forth.
Even that which is not included by the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be understood as being included [within the category of the unclung-to].

And because existence (bhava) is exclusively clung-to (upādinna), it should be understood that although the eye-consciousness and so forth—which are resultant states occurring in the course of existence—are included, the sound-base (saddāyatana), being unclung-to, is not included here.
Formless existence consists of four aggregates, two bases, and two elements. Birth, aging, and death are phenomena belonging to the categories of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

By way of their characteristics, [sorrow] is included within two aggregates: the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). Sorrow, pain, and grief are included in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).

Despair is included in the aggregate of mental formations, as well as in the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*). Lamentation is included in the aggregate of form, the base of sound (*saddāyatana*), and the element of sound (*saddadhātu*).

As for the remaining factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādaṅga*) and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) herein, they are indeed easy to understand.
The bases of psychic power (iddhipādā) are comprised within two aggregates, two bases, and two elements.

Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that the basis of psychic power consisting of consciousness (cittiddhipāda) is not comprised within sixteen elements, due to its restriction to the mental-object element (dhammadhātu) and the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu).
The jhānas are comprised within two aggregates—feeling and formations—one base, and one element. The immeasurables (appamaññā)—
It is comprised by one aggregate (khandha), one base (āyatana), and one element (dhātu). The same applies to the five faculties and so forth;
the only difference is that consciousness alone is comprised by the seven consciousness-elements (viññāṇadhātu).
It should be understood that for all these [states], there is likewise non-inclusion by the remaining aggregates, bases, and elements already mentioned.

In this same manner, for the external matrix as well, one should apply the inclusion and non-inclusion by coordinating it as follows: "Wholesome states and unwholesome states are included within four aggregates, two bases, and [eighteen] elements;

whereas indeterminate states—setting aside the unconditioned from the perspective of the aggregates—are included within five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements. Thus should inclusion and non-inclusion be treated.
"It should be known"—this is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Dhātukathā-pāḷi* and its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The analysis of the meaning of the term "inclusion and non-inclusion" is concluded.
Commentary on the Terms "Included" and "Unincluded":
In the section on the terms "included" and "unincluded," it is not possible to provide a definition for all the terms such as the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth.
However, those terms herein that refer to a portion of material form unmixed with the immaterial, and a portion of consciousness unmixed with anything else—

These are explained here. They should be understood by way of ten bases—excluding the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*)—seventeen elements—excluding the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*)—and the seven material faculties (*rūpindriya*), but not by way of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth.
For this very reason, it is said in the Canon:
Ten bases, seventeen elements,
seven faculties, non-percipient existence, one-aggregate existence,
lamentation, the visible, and the impingent.
"Furthermore, that which is non-indicative is again with resistance;

thus the summary verse is stated. For by the aggregate of form, only the aggregate of form is included; likewise, by the aggregates of feeling and so forth, only the aggregates of feeling and so forth are included.
And there are none among those [aggregates] that are not included by some or other bases (āyatana) or elements (dhātu).
Because there is no state of being uncomprised by what is comprised within them, the determination of meaning here occurs solely by way of the bases (āyatana) as previously stated.
This is the characteristic herein: that which, having been comprised by the term "aggregate" (khandha), is not comprised by the terms "base" or "element" (dhātu);
or, having been comprised by the terms "aggregate" or "base," is not comprised by the term "element. Of that...

Non-inclusion by way of aggregates, bases, and elements is now explained. How so? Regarding those phenomena that are included by the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) through inclusion by aggregate (*khandha-saṅgaha*), but are not included by inclusion by base (*āyatana-saṅgaha*) or inclusion by element (*dhātu-saṅgaha*):
by how many aggregates, bases, and elements are those phenomena not included?
Those phenomena are not included by four aggregates, two bases, and eight elements.

They are not included among the elements (*dhātu*). In this same way, the method of application should be understood for the elements consisting of the sense-bases of visible form and so forth—which are the objects of the sensitive faculties—as well as for the material faculties such as the eye-faculty and so on.

Herein, the method is as follows: those material phenomena which are included by the eye-base under the category of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) by means of the classification of aggregates; [these are the elements not included therein].

By way of inclusion within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*): those not included in the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), nor included in the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*)—since this very eye is included separately among both the bases and the elements as the eye-base and the eye-element—all those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) other than the eye-base are included in four [of the five] immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) and in two bases: the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the eye-base.
The eye-element and the seven consciousness-elements are not included among the eight elements.
The same method applies to the visible-object base and the others above.

For in this section, because the eye-base is not un-included—since it is itself included by its own threefold inclusion of aggregates, bases, and elements—it is "included by the aggregate-inclusion" and "not included by the base-inclusion."
Because it is said that [the object] is "not included by way of inclusion in the elements," and because what is distinguished by these three qualifications—

both included and not included— is stated to be "not included" by the aggregates and so forth in such passages as "by how many aggregates," it should be understood that it exists externally together with the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha).
And just as here, only material phenomena (rūpadhamma) characterized by the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) [are meant].

That which is included [by one] is not included [by the other], as is the case with the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*); likewise, this should be understood accordingly for the subsequent sections characterized by the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.

Furthermore, among the remaining factors, those phenomena that are included by the aggregate-inclusion (*khandha-saṅgaha*) and the base-inclusion (*āyatana-saṅgaha*), but not included by the element-inclusion (*dhātu-saṅgaha*) in relation to the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*), are included by four aggregates and eleven bases.

They are not included within twelve elements (*dhātu*). Likewise for the remaining consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*). Among the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), those phenomena that belong to the non-percipient realm (*asaññībhava*)...
[etc] ...those phenomena are not included within four aggregates (*khandha*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and sixteen elements.
Those phenomena among the derived phenomena (*upādādhamma*)... [etc] ...those phenomena are [not included within] four aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements.

These four sections, beginning with "not included among the elements," are identical except for their specific distinctions not previously mentioned. Therein, in the section on eye-consciousness, regarding the phrase "by twelve":

excluding the six consciousness-elements, the remaining twelve elements include the other six consciousness-elements within the aggregates and bases, but they are not included within the elements themselves. By the remaining twelve...
"Not included among the elements" (dhātūhi asaṅgahitā). This same method applies to the remaining consciousness-elements as well.
In the second [case], "by three bases" (tīhāyatanehi) refers to the base of visible forms, the base of mental objects, and the base of the mind.

For in the Brahma-world of non-percipient beings, two bases—the base of visible forms and the base of mental objects—are mentioned in the Canon by way of their existence as rebirth-existence (upapattibhava); however, these are included among the aggregates (khandha).

They are not included within the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). The remaining nine form-bases (rūpāyatana) are said to be uncomprised by those two [bases], namely the mind-base (manāyatana) and the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana).
"By nine elements" means by the seven consciousness-elements (viññāṇadhātu) together with the form-element (rūpadhātu) and the mental-object-element (dhammadhātu).

In the third [verse], "ten" refers to [the bases] excluding the base of visible form and the base of mental objects. "Sixteen" refers to [the bases] excluding the element of visible form and the element of mental objects.
Those called "non-manifesting and impinging" are the nine gross bases; they are included by those [bases] through the inclusion of aggregates, but not included by the inclusion of bases and elements.
As for the two remaining bases—the base of visible form and the base of mental objects—they are included by the remaining bases and elements.
They are called "not included.

In the fourth [verse], "by eleven" refers to the fact that, with the exception of the tangible base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*), they are not included among the bases and so forth due to being derivative phenomena (*upādādhamma*) of the tangible base. The rest is easy to understand. This is the method regarding the terms "included" and "not included.
Explanation of the meaning of the terms "not included" and "included."
Regarding the section on the "unincluded" and the "included," however, only those terms which indicate a portion of the *dhammāyatana* unmixed with consciousness or gross matter are specified here.
These [terms] refer to the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*),
the three truths excluding the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), and the sixteen faculties (*indriya*) excluding the sensitive faculties (*pasāda*) and the mind faculty (*manindriya*).

These should be understood by way of the fourteen modes of conditionality—namely, ignorance, volitional formations, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, kamma, becoming, birth, aging, death, sorrow, pain, grief, and despair—and not by way of the aggregate of form and the other aggregates. For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary:
"Three aggregates, likewise the truths, and sixteen faculties..."
Regarding the modes of conditionality, there are fourteen above and fourteen below.
Thus, there are thirty-two terms in the ten clusters;
furthermore, there are two minor intermediate dyads and eight major intermediate dyads.
Thus the summary verse (uddānagāthā) has been stated. Herein, this is the characteristic:

when something is not included under the category of aggregates (khandha), but is included under the categories of bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), its inclusion under the aggregates and so forth is then stated as distinguished by three specific qualifications.

How so? By the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), those phenomena which are not included in the inclusion of aggregates, but are included in the inclusions of bases and elements—[are thus defined].
By how many aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) are those phenomena (dhamma) comprised?
Excluding the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) from the category of aggregates, those phenomena are comprised by three aggregates, one base, and one element.

Herein is the method: for, according to the inclusion within the aggregates, Nibbāna, subtle matter (sukhumarūpa), perception (saññā), and mental formations (saṅkhāra) are not comprised by the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha).

Being uncomprised [by the other aggregates], they are comprised by way of inclusion within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*). Among these, Nibbāna does not enter into the inclusion of the aggregates;
the remaining [factors] enter into inclusion by way of three aggregates: matter, perception, and formations.

Furthermore, in this context, the bases and elements should be understood everywhere solely by way of the base of mental phenomena and the element of mental phenomena, because the others are impossible here.
And among these, Nibbāna is also included. For this very reason it is said: "Setting aside the unconditioned from the category of aggregates. This is its meaning:
having set aside the unconditioned specifically within the compendium of aggregates, and not within the other compendia.
In this way, the application should be understood for the perception aggregate and the others as well. However, this is the distinction: those phenomena [associated] with the life-faculty... [etc.]

Those states are included within the two aggregates of feeling and perception; the material and immaterial life-faculties, as well as Nibbāna, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness, are not included by way of aggregate-inclusion (*khandha-saṅgaha*).
Among those, however, Nibbāna, feeling, and perception are included by way of base-inclusion (*āyatana-saṅgaha*) and element-inclusion (*dhātu-saṅgaha*).
The rest is easy to understand. This is the method regarding the category of "included by what is not included."
Commentary on the Terms Grouped with Grouped:
Regarding the terms grouped with grouped, however, only those terms which indicate a portion of formations unmixed with anything else,
or a portion of feeling, or subtle matter, or a portion of sound, are pointed out here among the aggregates, bases, and elements.
The phrases standing as if they had grasped even a single portion with their entirety are not tenable.

However, those [phrases] should be understood by way of the two truths of origin and the path, the fifteen faculties, the eleven dependent-origination factors, and so forth. Herein, this is the characteristic:
that which is included among the aggregates and so on by those things already included among the aggregates and so on by themselves is, first of all, [the basis for such a phrase].
The inclusion by means of aggregates and so forth is stated again for the "extracted term.

Herein, this is the method for the first term: those phenomena which are included by the truth of origination through all three types of inclusion—aggregates and so forth—and those phenomena which are included by those [former] phenomena through all three [types of inclusion], aggregates and so forth; those phenomena [are included] by one aggregate and one base.

"Included by one element": for by the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*), the remaining formations (*saṅkhāra*)—excluding craving (*taṇhā*)—are included by the aggregates (*khandha*) and other such groupings;

furthermore, craving itself is included by those same [aggregates, etc.], and that craving, in turn, is included by the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the mental base (*dhammāyatana*), and the mental element (*dhammadhātu*).
This same method applies to the others as well. This is the method regarding the term "included by what is included."

Commentary on the Terms Not Included by Those Not Included: Regarding the terms not included by those [terms] not included, these are the aggregates of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth, which are excluded from the terms that grasp the five aggregates—
such as the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) and the rest— as well as from the terms that grasp subtle matter along with consciousness, such as the non-mental factors (*acetasika*) and the like.

These very [factors] are being pointed out. This is the characteristic here: whatever is not included among the aggregates and so forth by the first term mentioned—namely, the aggregate of form—and whatever is not included by those [other aggregates], it is precisely that which is stated again as not being included among the aggregates and so forth.

In this regard, the construction of the single phrase is as follows: those phenomena which are not included by the aggregate of form, nor included by any of the three types of inclusion beginning with the aggregates.

Those phenomena which are not included among the three categories beginning with the aggregates (khandha) are, by those [same] phenomena, not included in one aggregate, one base (āyatana), and seven elements (dhātu).
For, by way of inclusion in the aggregates, the four aggregates and Nibbāna are not included in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha);

however, by way of the bases and so forth, with the exception of consciousness alone, the phenomena such as feeling (vedanā) and the rest are included in the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and in a portion of the aggregate of form.
"Included" means that consciousness alone is what is called "not included" by the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha) among the three types of inclusion, such as inclusion by aggregates.
Furthermore, the four aggregates together with consciousness—along with Nibbāna—are not included by the aggregates and so forth;
all of these, moreover, are not included by the single aggregate that is consciousness, nor by the single base (āyatana), nor by the seven elements (dhātu).
This is the method regarding the term "not included by what is not included.
Now, for the commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated":
as for those terms [that apply] to the seven consciousness-elements which are mixed with either Nibbāna or material form (*rūpa*).
If [the treatise] were to illuminate even a single immaterial phenomenon (arūpadhamma) that is dissociated [from consciousness],

then the exposition of those bases of phenomena (dhammāyatana), the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), and so forth, would not be possible. However, for those terms such as "form-existence" (rūpabhava), "aggregates of form" (rūpakkhandha), "wholesome," and so on—

which illuminate material-mixed immaterial phenomena dissociated from certain consciousness-elements, or which illuminate exclusively objective referents (ārammaṇa), or the entire aggregate of form— the term "association" (sampayoga) [is not applicable].
Thus, while such a description is not possible [in the case of the material aggregates], it is possible in the case of dissociation.
However, for each of the immaterial aggregates—whether taken individually, in pairs, in groups of three, or as parts thereof—both [conjunction and dissociation] are possible.

For, according to the statement, "There is conjunction with four, dissociation with four; they are similar and dissimilar," there is similarity with the four immaterial aggregates themselves within a single continuum.
Association is obtained only among the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) that arise at the same moment.

However, there is no such thing as association between material phenomena (rūpadhamma) and either material form or Nibbāna, nor between Nibbāna and material form; likewise, there is no association between material form and Nibbāna on one hand and the immaterial aggregates on the other.
For these are of a different nature from them, just as the immaterial aggregates are of a different nature from material form and Nibbāna.
In the same way, there is likewise no association with immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) that belong to a different continuity (bhinnasantānika) or to different moments (nānakkhaṇika).
For these too are indeed dissimilar (visabhāga) because their continuity and moment are of a different nature.

However, this dissimilarity is not included here in a general sense, because association can still occur between them without distinction. But where they are distinguished specifically—as in the case of those associated with eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa), taste-consciousness (rasaviññāṇa), and so forth—[there is no association].

In that context, even here, heterogeneity (*visabhāgatā*) is taken [as a criterion]. However, where those [factors] whose specific distinctions are not determined, there too the characteristic of association (*sampayoga-lakkhaṇa*) is not possible in every respect.
And since that [factor] is exclusively heterogeneous (*ekantena visabhāgo*) to it, it is included here.
In this regard, the method is as follows: Is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-kkhandha*) associated with anything? No. With how many is it dissociated? With four.
It is dissociated from one aggregate, one base, and seven elements; it is dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
This same method applies to the eye-base and so forth when they are without an object.
However, among those with an object, the feeling aggregate is associated with three aggregates, one base, and seven elements; it is associated with one base and one element...
Associated with some. It is dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
it is dissociated from one base and one element, and from some others. This same method applies to the aggregate of perception and the others as well.

In that context, "from one" means from the mind-base (*manāyatana*). "From seven" means from the consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*). "From some" means from those included within the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) and the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*).
[It is] dissociated from feeling, perception, and mental formations. In the second method, "with three" means with the remaining immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha), excluding the self.

"Dissociated from some" means [dissociated] from perception and mental formations within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu). "Dissociated from some" means [dissociated] from material form (rūpa) and Nibbāna.
Thus, in all subsequent cases as well, it should be understood accordingly. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

This, however, is the distinction: "The truths of origin, the path, and so forth are associated with a single mental-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu), whereas resolve (adhimokkha) is associated with both the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mental-consciousness element.
This is the method regarding the terms for association and dissociation.
[End of] the commentary on the meaning of the terms "associated" and "dissociated."

Regarding the terms for "associated" (*sampayutta*) and "dissociated" (*vippayutta*), this is the exposition specifically of those terms among the categories eligible for association that illuminate phenomena associated with the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*) and consciousness unmixed with anything else.
These, moreover, consist of the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*),
the mind base (*manāyatana*), the seven elements of consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*), and [the states] by way of the mind and equanimity.
These [states] are to be understood by way of two faculties; consciousness, contact, and feeling—three links of dependent origination;

the sevenfold contact; three triplets consisting of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant, with initial application and sustained application, and accompanied by equanimity; and the seventh intermediate couplet, etc., because they are possible therein and not because they are impossible in others.
For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary:
Four aggregates and one base,
two faculties, seven terms for elements,
three conditions, and then the group of seven contacts—
Three [jhānas] each, seven great intervals;
one with applied thought and sustained thought,
one associated with equanimity, and yet another alone.

The summary verse has been stated. This is the characteristic here: those phenomena which are associated with the term first mentioned, and those phenomena which are dissociated from them—their dissociation from the aggregates and so forth is now stated.

In this regard, the method is as follows: those phenomena which are associated with the aggregate of feeling, and those phenomena which are dissociated from them, are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements; [they are also dissociated] from one base...

They are dissociated from one element by some [factors]. Regarding those factors that are associated with the eye-consciousness-element, those factors which are dissociated from them are not dissociated from any aggregates or bases, but they are dissociated from one element;
in this way, the application should be understood for all cases.
In that context, "those states" refers to the states of form and Nibbāna; they are dissociated from those associated with feeling.
"By one" means by the mind-base (*manāyatana*). According to the second method, "those states" refers to those states accompanied by joy (*sappītika*).
"By none" means, setting aside the previously mentioned eye-consciousness element, the remaining six consciousness elements, their associated states, form, and Nibbāna.
Because all aggregates (*khandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) are included therein, they are not dissociated from any aggregates or bases.
For it is not itself dissociated from itself, nor is it associated with itself. "One" refers to the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*).
The rest is easily understood. This is the method regarding the terms "associated" and "dissociated."

Commentary on the Terms "Dissociated" and "Associated": Regarding the terms "dissociated" and "associated," there is no phenomenon that is both dissociated and associated; however, this term was cited merely for the sake of completeness in the teaching.
For that very reason, in all sections of the Pāḷi, it is stated simply as "there is not, there is not."
It has been stated: the four aggregates are dissociated from those phenomena that do not have the aggregate of form, etc., as their object, and they have no association with anything else.
Likewise, form and Nibbāna, etc., are dissociated from feeling and the other aggregates, and they have no association with anything at all.
This is the method regarding the terms "dissociated" and "associated."
Commentary on the Terms "Associated" and "Associated-with-the-Associated":

Regarding the terms "associated" and "associated-with-the-associated," this is the exposition specifically for those terms that illuminate only a portion of the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) unmixed with matter;
it is not [the exposition] for those terms that mix matter and the immaterial, nor for those that illuminate the entire aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha).
Because of the absence of association through association. For there is no other thing called "associated" with any of the material aggregates, whether wholesome or otherwise.
This is the characteristic here: when those states first mentioned are again associated with themselves as associated, it is their association with the aggregates and so forth that is spoken of.

In this regard, the method is as follows: those phenomena associated with the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), and those phenomena associated with those [associated] phenomena, are associated with three aggregates, one base (āyatana), and seven elements (dhātu); [they are associated] with one base... and so on...
with some [phenomena]. Those phenomena associated with the truth of origination (samudayasacca), and those phenomena [associated] with those [associated] phenomena...
Those associated states are associated with three aggregates (khandha), one base (āyatana), and one mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu);
they are associated with some [factors] by way of one aggregate, one base, and one element. The rest is easily understood.
This is the method for the section on "associated-with-association."
Commentary on the Terms for Those Dissociated from the Dissociated:
In the section on the terms for those dissociated from the dissociated, however, the same terms as those stated in the section on association are explained.
Herein, this is the defining characteristic: those states which, having been previously mentioned by the term "dissociated," are again dissociated [from others], these...
"Dissociation" is spoken of in terms of the aggregates and so forth.

Herein is the method: those phenomena dissociated from the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*), and those phenomena dissociated from those [other] phenomena—those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base (*āyatana*), and seven elements (*dhātu*); [they are dissociated] from one base... and so on.

"Disjoined by some. Those phenomena that are disjoined from the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), and those phenomena that are disjoined from those [other] phenomena—those phenomena are disjoined from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements; [they are disjoined] from one... [and so on] ... "disjoined by some.
The remainder is easy to understand. This is the method for the section on being disjoined by way of being disjoined.
Commentary on the Terms "Included" (*saṅgahita*), "Associated" (*sampayutta*), and "Dissociated" (*vippayutta*):

Regarding the terms "included," "associated," and "dissociated," those very terms such as the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*) that were indicated under the heading "included-included" are now being indicated here.
This is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) here: those phenomena (*dhammā*) which were first extracted by the term "aggregates" (*khandha*) and so forth...

Those phenomena which are included by all three [truths]—the origin truth (samudaya-sacca) and so forth—are said to be associated with and dissociated from the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). Herein is the method:
those phenomena included by all three types of inclusion—aggregates and so forth—are associated with three aggregates, one base, and seven elements; they are dissociated from one aggregate.
They are associated with one base (āyatana) and one element (dhātu), and with some [factors]. They are dissociated from one aggregate (khandha), ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element, and with some [factors].

Those phenomena which, along with the female faculty (itthindriya), are included by all three—aggregates and so forth—are not associated with any [factors], but [are associated] with four aggregates and one base.
“Dissociated from seven elements, dissociated from one... [and so on]... dissociated from some.
In this context, “from one” means from the mind-base (*manāyatana*). “From one aggregate” means from the mental formations aggregate (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).

“From some” refers to craving within the formations aggregate, and [craving] within the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) and mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*), together with feeling and perception. The remainder is easily understood. This—
The method for the terms "included" (*saṅgahita*),
"associated" (*sampayutta*), and "dissociated" (*vippayutta*).

Now, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the terms "associated-included" and "associated-not-included," the terms such as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) and so forth, which were already indicated under the term "associated-associated," are precisely those [to be considered here].

They are explained. This is the characteristic here: for those phenomena that are associated with the term first mentioned, their inclusion or non-inclusion within the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth is stated.
In this regard, the method is as follows: those phenomena associated with the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) are included in three aggregates and two [bases].
They are included among the eight bases and the [eight] elements, and not included among the rest.
Those phenomena associated with the consciousness aggregate are included among three aggregates, one base, and one element, and are not included among the rest.

In that context, "by three" means by the three beginning with the perception aggregate; they are associated with feeling by those [three]. "By two" means by the mental-object base and the mind-element. The rest is easy to understand. This is the method regarding the section on inclusion and non-inclusion by way of association.
Commentary on the Terms for Factors Associated with and Dissociated from the Unincluded:
Now, as for the terms in the section on factors associated with and dissociated from the unincluded (*asaṅgahita*),

those terms which indicate subtle form, non-consciousness, immateriality with consciousness, or mere immateriality— whether it be coarse form or mere [immateriality]— and subtle form, [these are included here].

This is their exposition. Herein, this is the characteristic: the association and dissociation with the aggregates and so forth is stated for those states that are not included within any of the three categories—aggregates and so forth—that were first mentioned.

In this regard, the method is as follows: those states which are not included among the aggregates and so forth by means of the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*) are [included] by the other three aggregates.
They are associated with one base (āyatana) and one element (dhātu), and are associated with some [factors]. They are dissociated from one aggregate (khandha), ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element, and with some [factors]. This same application applies to the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), the female faculty (itthindriya), and so forth.
Regarding the immaterial realm (arūpabhava), there are no phenomena not included among the aggregates and so forth that are associated; those [phenomena] are [dissociated] from four [aggregates].
They are dissociated from one aggregate, one base, and seven elements; they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
The same method of application applies to the categories beginning with "skilled in the bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*).
In that context, because consciousness alone is not included within the three [aggregates] starting with form, it is associated with those three, namely feeling and the rest.

And dissociation from the others must also be understood. The rest is easily understood. This is the method regarding the terms "associated with what is not included" (*asaṅgahita-sampayutta-vippayutta*).

Now, for the commentary on the meaning of the terms "dissociated from what is included and not included" (*vippayuttena-saṅgahitāsaṅgahita*): as for those terms which refer exclusively to those with objects (*sārammaṇa*) and those without objects (*anārammaṇa*), [the following applies].

Furthermore, terms such as *dukkhasacca* (the truth of suffering), *abyākata* (the indeterminate), *paritta* (limited), *atīta* (past), *ajjhatta* (internal), and so forth, clarify certain mental aggregates (*nāma-khandha*) that are dissociated from some material aggregates due to their differentiation by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), genus (*jāti*), plane (*bhūmi*), time (*kāla*), and continuity (*santāna*).

These terms serve as descriptions for those very [aggregates] when mixed with non-objective phenomena (*anārammaṇa-dhamma*). They likewise function as descriptions for other categories, such as the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*), the six bases (*saḷāyatana*), birth (*jāti*), aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), internal (*ajjhatta*), external (*bahiddhā*), invisible (*anidassana*), non-reacting (*appaṭigha*), rootless (*nahetu*), and so on.

Because it is impossible for them to be dissociated from anything [else]. This is the characteristic here: those phenomena that are dissociated from the term first mentioned are stated as being either included or not included among the aggregates and so forth.

In this regard, the method is as follows: those phenomena dissociated from the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*) are included in four aggregates, two bases, and... [the rest of the sentence continues with the enumeration of the remaining categories].
They are comprised by eight elements (*dhātu*), and they are not comprised by one aggregate (*skandha*) and ten bases (*āyatana*) and elements.
Those phenomena (*dharma*) that are dissociated from the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) are comprised by four aggregates, two bases, and two elements.

In this context, those dissociated from the truth of suffering are the supramundane mind and mental factors; and those phenomena [are comprised] by the four aggregates beginning with the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
By way of the mind-consciousness element and the mental-object element, they are included under two elements. The rest is easily understood.
This is the method regarding the inclusion and non-inclusion by way of dissociation. This concludes here, in brief, the determination of meaning together with the analytical method;
the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Dhātukathā* scripture and its commentary.
The Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Discourse on Elements from the *Mohavicchedanī*, the Commentary on the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrices, is completed. 4.
The Matrix of the Designation of Persons (*Puggalapaññatti*).
Commentary on the Singlefold Schedule:

Now follows the method of commentary for the Schedule of Designations of Persons (*puggalapaññatti*). Therein, regarding the phrase "six designations" (*cha paññattiyo*) from the perspective of the unelucidated meaning:
in the context where it is said, "he declares, teaches, designates, and establishes," *paññatti* refers to demonstration (*sandassanā*) and manifestation (*pakāsanā*).
The term *paññatti* means "well-arranged" (*supaññatta*) in such passages as "the bed and chair are well-arranged," where it refers to placing or setting down;
here, both meanings are applicable. For the phrase "six *paññatti*s" means six ways of arranging, six ways of pointing out, or six ways of making manifest;
it can also be said to mean six ways of placing or setting down. Indeed, those various existing and non-existing things are merely designations (*nāmapaññatti*).
It is also called "pointing out the Dhamma," and it is also called "establishing by way of this or that component.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "the designation of the aggregates" (khandha-paññatti) is a concise demonstration of the essential nature of those designations.
Therein, the making known, pointing out, revealing, establishing, and setting down of the aggregates as "aggregates" is called the "designation of the aggregates"... [and so on]... up to persons.
“Person” (*puggala*) refers to the designation, the pointing out, the making clear, the establishing, and the setting down;
this is what is called "person-designation" (*puggalapaññatti*). These six types of designation alone exist.

Although there are other designations—since conventional and ultimate discourse are infinite—they are mentioned here specifically as characteristics and because they are primary. According to the method independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttakanaya*):
However, six types of designation (paññatti)—namely, the all-inclusive, the non-existent, and so forth—are mentioned in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) as designations of names;

since these have been explained below, they are not discussed here. Among those, only two are applicable here: the "designation of a person" (puggalapaññatti), which is a non-existent designation, and the remaining ones, which are existent designations.
Furthermore, according to the method of the teachers (ācariyanaya) as set forth in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, there are another six designations— namely, designation by way of dependence (*upādāpaññatti*),

designation by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*), designation by way of combination (*samodhānapaññatti*), designation by way of juxtaposition (*upanikkhittapaññatti*), designation by way of suitability (*tajjāpaññatti*), and designation by way of continuity (*santatipaññatti*)—

which are called "designation of meaning" (*atthapaññatti*). Among these, that which is designated with respect to, and in dependence upon, the pentad of aggregates (*khandha*), such as the "being" (*satta*) and so forth, [and that which is designated] with respect to its constituent parts...
Chariots and so forth; east and so forth as derived from the revolution of the moon and so on; the signs of the various elements;

and the counterpart-signs of the kasiṇas and so forth derived from specific meditative development—this kind of thing, which by its nature is not found as a unity either in terms of its actual state or in the ultimate sense among phenomena that possess intrinsic nature, is called "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*). It is so called in the sense of being made known.

This is called a "description" (paññatti), but not in the sense of an act of describing. Whatever description there is of this or that object is merely a "description of what does not exist" (avijjamāna-paññatti).
However, that which depends upon and relates to another—such as "second," "short," "long," "far," "near," and so forth—is [a description based on relation].
Therein, "expecting another" is an approximation; "one with a parasol in hand," etc., is an approximation of what is in the hand;
"one with earrings," etc., is an approximation of association; "a cart of grain," etc., is an approximation of what is loaded upon;

"the Indasāla Cave," etc., is an approximation of what is nearby; "golden-colored," etc., is an approximation of resemblance; "a village of brahmins," etc., is an approximation of abundance; "a jeweled bracelet," etc., is an approximation...
Designations such as "tabbisiṭṭhūpanidhā" (comparison with what is set aside) and so forth, which are of many kinds, are called *upanidhāpaññatti* (comparative designation).

Designations such as "a heap of grain" (*dhaññarāsī*) and so forth are called *samodhānapaññatti* (collective designation). Designations such as "two" or "three," made by setting one thing beside another, are called *upanikkhittapaññatti* (designated-by-contrast).
Designations such as "earth" and so forth, which depend on their respective intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*), are *tajjāpaññatti* (designation according to that [nature]).
...is called a name (*nāma*). Furthermore, that which consists of eighty million and so forth is called a designation of continuity (*santatipaññatti*).

According to the method of the Master [Buddhaghosa] as distinct from that found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), there is also the designation of function (*kiccapaññatti*) such as "preacher of the Dhamma" and so forth;

the designation of shape (*saṇṭhānapaññatti*) such as "thin" or "fat"; the designation of gender (*liṅgapaññatti*) such as "woman" or "man"; and [designations] such as "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) and "from Kosala" (*kosalaka*).

There are six types of designations (paññatti): the designation of planes (*bhūmi-paññatti*), the individual designation such as "three" or "elephant" (*paccatta-paññatti*), and the designation of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata-paññatti*) such as cessation (*nirodha*).

Among these twelve [types of] designations, the "designation of that which is appropriate" (*tajjā-paññatti*), certain "designations of planes," and the "designation of the unconditioned" are comprised within what is termed "existent designation" (*vijjamāna-paññatti*).

Designation by name (*nāma-paññatti*) and the remaining designations of ultimate reality (*paramattha-avasesa*), as well as the designations of non-existent things (*avijjamāna-ādipaññatti*), are explained as "designation of meaning" (*attha-paññatti*).
This, first of all, is the commentary here according to the unelaborated meaning (*anuttānattha*).

Furthermore, the determination of the meaning (*atthanicchaya*) here also proceeds in accordance with the method of the canonical text (*pāḷi-naya*); for it is impossible to state that [determination] without the canonical text.

Furthermore, because the five initial designations (*paññatti*) and the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth that constitute their referents were already explained in full detail below in the *Vibhaṅga* section, they are here indicated only in brief as:
"To what extent is there a designation of aggregates? To the extent of the five aggregates: the aggregate of form," and so on.
These have the same meaning as when they were previously stated. [End of] *Puggalapaññatti*.

However, since it was not stated below, [the following] has been explained in detail by way of the singlefold and other classifications, up to the tenfold, having established the matrix (mātikā) as: "In what respect is there the designation of persons (puggalapaññatti)? The one liberated by occasion (samayavimutta), the one not liberated by occasion (asamayavimutta)," and so forth.

And because that would be difficult to understand if its various divisions were not stated according to what is to be known, therefore, here, following the method of the Pāḷi, [it is explained] specifically regarding the designation of persons (puggalapaññatti).
