In brief, there is a determination of the meaning; and here, rather than enumerating all individuals mentioned in the matrix (mātikā), it is done concisely by way of classifying those individuals who are difficult to understand and hard to discern, starting from the category of the "single" (ekaka) and so forth. How so?
"One liberated by occasion, one not liberated by occasion; one of a nature to fall away, one of a nature not to fall away..."
One capable through volition, one capable through guarding, one restrained by fear, one restrained without fear, one capable of progress, one incapable of progress,
the determined, the undetermined, the one practicing the way, the one established in the fruit, the one with an even head, the one who prolongs existence for a kalpa,

the stream-enterer who has seven births at most, the one who goes from family to family, the one with only one seed remaining, the once-returner, the non-returner, the one who attains nibbāna in the interval, the one who attains nibbāna upon landing, and the one who attains nibbāna without exertion.
"One who attains final nibbāna with exertion, one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm, and the Arahant"—
this is the singlefold matrix. Therein, he who, at the time when it is suitable and appropriate to produce absorption,

having been liberated from opposing states by means of the eight liberations consisting of the form and formless attainments, [is liberated] from his respective defilements by any one of the three paths...
Having emerged after having discarded [the defilements], this one is called "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimutta*).

For, based on such statements as "some taints (*āsava*) are completely exhausted," it should be understood that neither the worldling who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) nor the one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is included here;

rather, only those in training (*sekkha*) established in the fruits who have attained the attainments are included. This also includes the dry-insight practitioner who has exhausted the taints, as well as all noble ones (*ariya*).

With reference to liberation by means of the path, they are called "liberated at all times" (*asamaya-vimutta*). For one who attains the eight external meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), there is both a favorable time—such as when one has found a secluded place—and an unfavorable time—such as when one is occupied with performing duties.
However, for one who is liberated through liberation by the path, there is no such thing as a favorable or unfavorable time; for one whose faith is powerful and whose insight (*vipassanā*)...
Furthermore, it is not the case that for one who has begun [the practice] there is no penetration of the path and its fruits while walking or eating;
therefore, all noble ones (ariya) should be understood as "those liberated at any time" (asamayavimutta) regarding noble liberation (ariyavimokkha).
Even in the previous passage, it was with reference specifically to mundane attainments (lokīyasamāpatti) that those in training (sekha) were called "those liberated by occasion" (samayavimutta).

However, an ordinary person (puthujjana) who has attained mastery and possesses the eight attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti), as well as the two trainees (sekkha)—the stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakadāgāmin)—are called "of a nature subject to disturbance" (kuppadhamma) with reference to the eight attainments.

They are likewise of two kinds as being "of a nature subject to falling away" (parihānadhamma). But the non-returner (anāgāmi) and those beyond are "of a nature not subject to disturbance" (akuppadhamma) with reference to the supramundane states (lokuttaradhamma), because they have mastered their attainment and have completely abandoned the obstacles to concentration.

An ordinary person who possesses mastery and has attained the eight attainments, as well as the noble ones (ariya), are also [called] "of a nature not subject to disturbance" with reference to the supramundane states.
[The term] "nāma" [is used]. "One whose nature is not subject to decline" refers to those very same [arahants].
"Capable of volition" means capable of attaining non-decline by means of the frequent practice of meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) known as volition.

For one who, through mastery cultivated in the fine-material and immaterial jhānas, constantly practices that meditative attainment termed volition, does not fall away from them; whereas one who does not so practice falls away.

This is called "capable through volition" while it is being practiced. As for "capable through guarding," this refers to one who, having understood the factors that are helpful or unhelpful to jhāna, is capable of reaching non-decline even without practicing the guarding;
this is stronger than the former. One who dwells in what has been habitualized, through the perfection of wisdom, having understood the helpful and unhelpful factors, acts accordingly...
It should be understood as "by way of practice.
"Abstaining out of fear" refers to the trainee (*sekha*) and the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) who have desisted from evil due to fear.

Among them, the latter abstains from evil because of the four fears known as the states of woe, the round of existence, the defilements, and censure; the trainee abstains from those [fears] excluding the states of woe.
Because he is liberated from the states of misery (*apāya*). One whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), however, is called "restrained by fearlessness" because his fears have been utterly cut off;
yet, he must refrain from censuring others. "Incapable of entering" means incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*);

[this refers to those who are obstructed] by the obstruction of karma known as the *ānantariya* deeds, by the obstruction of defilements known as fixed wrong view, and by the obstruction of rebirth-linking known as being without roots or with two roots.

Those who possess the obstruction of karmic fruition (*vipākāvaraṇa*), who lack faith in the Buddha and others, who—like those from Uttarakuru and similar regions—lack the desire for the cultivation of the path, and who are devoid of prior supportive conditions (*pubbūpanissaya*):

all these are called "incapable of arrival. Those who are the opposite are called "capable of arrival. For example, those fixed in the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya*) and those with wrong view are incapable of arriving in hell;
the eight noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) are incapable of arriving at [the states of] parinibbāna without clinging (*anupādāparinibbāna*) and so forth.
"Those who are fixed" (niyata) are so called. The remaining persons, because their destiny is not fixed, are called "unfixed" (aniyata).

However, although the inhabitants of Uttarakuru are destined for a happy rebirth, they are not mentioned here as "fixed," because what is intended here is specifically the fixedness in rightness or wrongness (sammatta-micchattaniyāma).

A person possessing the path (maggasamaṅgī) at the moment of the path is called "one practicing for the sake of the fruit" (phalatthāya paṭipannaka); a person possessing the fruit (phalasamaṅgī), even when not actually arising in the fruit, is called "established in the fruit" (phale ṭhita).
But he for whom the exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life occur simultaneously is called one who is "equal at the head" (*samasīsī*).
He is of three kinds: one who is equal at the head regarding posture, one who is equal at the head regarding illness, and one who is equal at the head regarding life.
Among these, he who, having established insight within any one of the four postures and attained Arahantship, [attains final Nibbāna] in that very same posture...
One who attains final nibbāna while in the postures is called "one whose head is level with the postures" (*iriyāpathasamasīsī*).

However, one who, having encountered a certain illness, establishes insight (*vipassanā*) even while in the midst of that illness, attains arahantship, and passes away by means of that very illness, is called "one whose head is level with the illness" (*rogasamasīsī*).
But for one whose ignorance—designated as the "head of defilements"—is severed by the path of arahantship, which is designated as the "head of activity,"...
The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) also reaches its exhaustion simultaneously with the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*); this is called "that which has the same end as the life-faculty.

How is this simultaneous? By way of equality of sequence. For when the reviewing knowledges (*paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa*) arise immediately after the defilements have been destroyed by the Path, he attains final Nibbāna right after that; by this equality of sequence, there is also the exhaustion of both ends.
"Equal" (samaṃ) indeed means this very "one whose life and end are equal" (jīvitasamasīsī) who is intended here.

"One who lasts for an eon" (ṭhitakappī): an eon that remains is a "lasting eon" (ṭhitakappo); one who possesses such [an eon] is "one who lasts for an eon. The meaning is: one capable of making the eon endure while the eon is perishing.
For if the destruction of the eon were to occur at the moment those individuals possess the Path, the eon would not perish at all.
Because they do not realize their respective fruits, even though they are perishing, they establish an eon;

thus they are called "those who establish an eon" (*ṭhitakappino*). Although there is no teaching at the time of the destruction of the eon—for the destruction of an eon occurs only when the ultimate limit has been reached—nevertheless, this reason, though it did not actually happen, was brought forward to illustrate the immediate succession of the fruit following the path.
A *sotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is so called because he is the first possessor of the path—which is termed a "stream"—due to its inclination toward the ocean of Nibbāna;
however, here the one established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*) is intended.

And for the purpose of showing its subdivisions, the phrase "one who has seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparamo*) and so forth is stated. One for whom seven times is the maximum number of rebirths is a *sattakkhattuparamo*; beyond that, there is no eighth [rebirth].

The meaning is that he does not cause existence to continue. For one who, having taken rebirth seven times among gods and humans, makes an end of suffering in his seventh existence, is called "one for whom seven births are at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*).
One who goes from family to family, from existence to existence, is called "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkola*). For he has two destinies, by way of gods and humans, within existence.
Having wandered through the cycle of existence, he makes an end of suffering; this one is called *kolaṅkolo* (one who goes from family to family).

One who has but a single seed of defilement remaining for the linking of karma is an *ekabījī*. For he becomes one whose taints are destroyed within that very same existence. But what determines his specific destiny?

It is the distinction between his insight (*vipassanā*) and his direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Among stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), he who is negligent in insight is one who has "seven births at most."

There is [this distinction]: whoever is diligent to some extent is one who goes from family to family (*kolaṅkolo*). However, whoever is exceedingly diligent in insight (*vipassanā*) is one with a single seed (*ekabījī*).

But those who are exceedingly negligent, whose inclination is toward the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), such as Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, Sakka, and others—they, wandering again and again within the cycle of existence itself, having completed the six celestial realms starting from the beginning, [proceed] even into the Brahma-worlds.
Those who, having been reborn in successive order and remaining in Akaniṭṭha, attain final Nibbāna there, are not included here;

for they repeatedly take up birth in the human realm. However, it is those who take up existence even in the human realm who are intended—namely, the one who has seven births at most (*sattakkhattuparama*), the one who goes from family to family (*kolaṅkola*), and the one who attains Nibbāna upon being born as a human (*ekabījī*).
These, moreover, have arrived by means of faith as their primary faculty (*saddhādhura*).
It should be understood that there are three who have arrived by way of being "dominated by wisdom," making six types of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) in total.
Furthermore, one is a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) because they return to this human realm only once more by way of rebirth-linking; he is the possessor of the fruit of the second path.
By this [definition], among the five types of once-returners, four are excluded and only one is included. For a certain person, regarding the fruit of once-returning...
Having remained [here], one attains final nibbāna in a second existence right here; some, having reached this world, attain final nibbāna in the deva-world;
some, having reached the deva-world, attain final nibbāna in that very place in a second existence;
some, having reached the deva-world, are reborn here and then attain final nibbāna—these four are not included here. However, he who, having reached this world and been reborn in the deva-world...

Having been reborn here once more, he attains final nibbāna; it is this one alone who is included here. It should be understood that the distinction between them is this: for this [non-returner], there are two types of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), whereas for the "single-seeded" (*ekabījī*) there is only one.

He is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) because, by way of rebirth-linking, he does not come back to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*); he is one who possesses the fruit of the third path. Of him...
However, the phrase beginning with "one who attains final nibbāna in the interval" (antarāparinibbāyī) was stated for the purpose of showing the distinctions [among non-returners].

In this context, "one who attains final nibbāna in the interval" refers to a certain non-returner whose nature it is to attain final nibbāna through the extinction of defilements by having generated the path to arahantship precisely within the interval of the middle of his lifespan.
Furthermore, such a person may attain final nibbāna immediately after [the path] has arisen, or they may attain final nibbāna without reaching the middle of their lifespan.
"One who attains final nibbāna upon reaching the midpoint of the lifespan" is of three kinds.

"One who attains final nibbāna after having struck (upahacca)" means one who attains final nibbāna after having struck—that is, having passed—the midpoint of the lifespan, or having struck—that is, having approached—the time of death;

the meaning is that one attains final nibbāna from the point of passing the midpoint of the lifespan until the time of death. "One who attains final nibbāna without exertion" (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī) means by way of non-exertion...
One who attains *parinibbāna* without great suffering and without applying excessive effort is one whose nature is to attain *parinibbāna* without difficulty.
One who attains *parinibbāna* with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*) is one whose nature is to attain *parinibbāna* with exertion, suffering, and great effort.
"One who flows upwards" (*uddhaṃsoto*) means that his stream of craving and the stream of the cycle of existence flow upwards; or it is so called because he must go upwards to obtain [the goal].
One whose stream of the path flows upwards is called an "upstreamer" (*uddhaṃsota*). One who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm is an "Akaniṭṭha-goer" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*).
Furthermore, in order to show the classification of these non-returners (*anāgāmī*), this tetrad beginning with "the upstreamer" and "the Akaniṭṭha-goer" should be understood here.

Among them, one who—starting from the Aviha realm, having been reborn successively in the [four] higher realms in due order, and having remained there for the full duration of his lifespan—passes away...
One who, having been reborn in Akaniṭṭha, attains final nibbāna there is called an "upstreamer bound for Akaniṭṭha.
However, one who attains final nibbāna in the interval without reaching Akaniṭṭha is called an "upstreamer" but not "bound for Akaniṭṭha.
One who, from the human world, goes only as far as Akaniṭṭha and then attains final nibbāna is neither an "upstreamer" nor "bound for Akaniṭṭha. But as for one who...
Having arisen in one of the four lower Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), he attains final nibbāna right there;
this one is called neither an "upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota) nor a "goer to Akaniṭṭha. Thus, these non-returners (anāgāmin) are of forty-eight kinds.

How so? First, in the Aviha heaven, there are three types of those who attain final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin), one who attains final nibbāna upon arrival (upahaccaparinibbāyin), and one who is an upstreamer.
Those five become ten by way of those who attain final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin*) and those who attain final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin*).
Likewise, there are forty in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms. However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm, there is no one who goes upstream (*uddhaṃsota*);
therefore, excluding the two types of those who go upstream—namely, those with exertion and without exertion—there are eight there. Thus, there are forty-eight in total.
An *arahant* is so called because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*) and because his taints (*āsava*) have been exhausted.
He is threefold by way of the three liberations, such as emptiness (*suññatā*), and each of these is further twelvefold by way of the fourfold path.
Just as there are twelve types of *arahants*, there are likewise twelve once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), twenty-four stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and forty-eight non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
It should be understood that they arise individually. Furthermore, all these noble ones (ariya) arise only within this teaching, not outside of it. This concludes the singlefold method (*ekakanaya*).
Regarding the commentary on the meaning of the matrix of pairs and so forth (*dukādi-mātikā*):
among the pairs (*duka*) and so on, there is the pair beginning with, "Two persons: one who is angry and resentful, and one who is slanderous and spiteful," and so forth.
The triad beginning with “three persons: one devoid of hope, one possessing hope, and one whose hope has vanished,” the tetrad beginning with “four persons:
the non-noble person, one more ignoble than the non-noble person, the noble person, and one more noble than the noble person,” and the pentad beginning with “five persons:
there is a certain person who commits an offense and feels remorse, and that liberation of mind...”

One does not understand liberation through wisdom as it really is. There is a certain person who, having committed [an action], feels no remorse... [and so on]... whereby those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder;
there is a certain person who, not having committed [an action], feels remorse... [and so on]... whereby those [evil, unwholesome states] cease without remainder.

Having laid out the detailed matrix (mātikā) in fivefold sets, beginning with, “There is a certain person who does not initiate [an unwholesome state] and does not feel remorse... [and so on]... they cease without remainder,” all those types of persons have been defined.
However, here they are not all recited for fear of over-extending the text; they are to be understood from the canonical text itself.
In this context, "despair" (*nirāsa*) refers to one who is devoid of hope for arahantship and is immoral.
For such a person, having heard that a virtuous companion—who is capable—has attained arahantship, it is like hearing of the consecration of some prince as king when one is a son of a *caṇḍāla*;
at the moment of that attainment, [one thinks], "When, alas, shall I too reach arahantship? Thus, regarding the attainment of arahantship...
Even the aspiration does not arise. "Hope" means one who, aspiring to and longing for Arahantship, is possessed of virtue.

For because he is established in the perfection of virtue through his aspiration for Arahantship, when he hears of someone attaining Arahantship—just as a well-born prince might hear of the coronation of a similar person and rejoice at their attainment of the coronation—he rejoices at that attainment of Arahantship.
an aspiration arises. One who is free from longing (*vigatāsa*) is an *arahant*. For he, by virtue of having attained *arahantship*, is one whose longing for that state has vanished;
this should be understood as being like a noble warrior (*khattiya*) who, upon attaining his consecration, is free from longing for the attainment of that consecration.
In the fourfold classification, however, one who is possessed of unwholesome courses of action such as the destruction of life is called an "untrue man" (*asappurisa*). But he who himself...
Having committed the destruction of life and so forth, and furthermore inciting another to do the same—this one is a "worse-than-unworthy person" (*asappurisena-asappurisatara*);

the meaning is that he is more unworthy even than an unworthy person. By way of the opposites of what was stated, the "worthy person" (*sappurisa*) and the "more worthy than an unworthy person" (*sappurisena-asappurisatara*) are to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "he undertakes [the five] and feels remorse," here the word *ārambha* refers to the transgression of an offense.
Therefore, the meaning is that he both initiates [an action] by way of transgressing an offense and, on account of that, becomes remorseful.
"Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration associated with the fruit [of the path]. "Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the knowledge associated with the fruit.

"He does not understand it as it really is" means that because it has not been attained, he does not understand it according to its true nature. "In which" (*yattha*) means in that which is designated as the fruit of Arhatship.
The connection is as follows: when jhāna has been attained by that person, all evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder, yet he does not fully comprehend them.
Although it is said that they cease at the very moment of the path (magga-khaṇa), they are actually ceased at the moment of the fruit (phala-khaṇa);
however, here it should be understood that they are stated to "cease at the moment of the fruit" by way of the function of the path.

"He commits [an offense] and does not feel remorse" means that he incurs an offense, yet he does not feel remorse because he seeks out a person of similar standing to confess it, or he brings about its resolution. "He does not commit [an offense] but feels remorse" means that he does not incur an offense;
however, due to his lack of proficiency regarding the Vinaya rules, he perceives what is not an offense as an offense even though he has already emerged from it.
He is remorseful because he is unable to dispel that remorse for an offense.
"He does not undertake [the practice] and is not remorseful" means he does not undertake it, he does not commit an offense, and he is not remorseful; yet he does not attain Arahantship.
But what kind of person is this? It is a person who possesses virtue but has abandoned energy. For he thinks: "What to me..."

"Even one who possesses purified virtue does not fulfill the practice if [he thinks], 'I shall attain final Nibbāna at the time of this Buddha's Parinibbāna, or I shall attain final Nibbāna at the time of the future Perfectly Enlightened One Metteyya.
These four types of persons must be established in the destruction of the taints by being exhorted in such ways.
For in this way, they too—like that fifth person who neither begins nor regrets, but exerts energy—[will succeed].
“He attains arahantship; thus they will be exactly equal to him.
Regarding the groups of six and so forth:
“There are six types of persons: there is a certain person who, regarding teachings unheard before, awakens to the truths by himself...”
And therein, some person attains omniscience and mastery over the powers; some person...
awakens, yet does not attain omniscience nor mastery over the powers; some person...
does not awaken, but makes an end of suffering in this very life and attains the perfection of a disciple.
There is a certain person... [as before] ...who makes an end of suffering, yet does not reach the perfection of a disciple. There is a certain person...
[as before] ...who does not attain full awakening, nor does he make an end of suffering in this very life, but he becomes a non-returner who does not come back to this state of being.
There is a certain person... [as before] ...who does not attain full awakening, nor does he [make an end of suffering] in this very life... [and so on].
“By means of the Dhamma, one becomes an ender of suffering; one is a returner, coming back to this state.”—This is the hexad.

“Seven persons: seven persons compared to water—one who remains submerged once submerged, one who emerges and then submerges, one who emerges and stands firm, one who emerges and looks around with insight, one who emerges and crosses over, [and one who, having crossed over, stands on dry land]. — This is the heptad.
The group of seven is given by such passages as: "Having emerged, he has reached a firm footing; having emerged, he has crossed over and gone to the further shore;
the brahmin stands on dry land. The group of eight is: "Eight persons—four who possess the paths and four who possess the fruits.
The group of nine is: "Nine persons—the perfectly enlightened Buddha, the privately enlightened Buddha, and those liberated in both ways..."

Having established the matrix (mātikā) consisting of the group of nine—"one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, and a faith-follower"—and the group of ten—"ten persons:
five for whom the goal is here [in this world], and five for whom the goal is after leaving this world"—the detailed exposition (niddesa) was made in the Pāḷi.
Therein, by the first term in the group of six, the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is indicated.

He [the first] is to be understood as one who, being without a teacher, attained omniscience by fully awakening to the truths in all their aspects through the knowledge of the path to arahantship—the basis for which is the omniscient knowledge produced within himself—and thereby gained mastery over the ten powers of knowledge.
By the second, however, the paccekabuddha is to be understood; by the third, the chief disciple; and by the fourth, the rest.
The Arahants are to be understood by the fifth [phrase], the Non-returners by the sixth, and the Stream-enterers and Once-returners by the seventh;
for they are described as "returning to this state of existence.
In the group of seven, by the first phrase, one who has not yet established faith in the Teaching is excluded, along with those characterized by fixed wrong view, which are entirely dark.
One who possesses [these qualities] is "seized. For such a person is submerged in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) and the lower realms just like a man afraid of water in the ocean;
they do not emerge from further becoming (bhava) again, but wander within existence itself for an infinite time due to the absence of connection with the Teaching (sāsana).
By the second phrase, even one who has gained faith in the Teaching may suffer the decline of that faith and so forth, like Devadatta and others.

The immoral person is "seized" while standing [in the cycle of existence]. For he, like one who has emerged from the ocean for some reason only to sink back down again, may emerge through faith in the Dispensation but will inevitably sink back into the lower realms;

however, this person is to be lifted out of existence by the Buddhas and others after a long lapse of time, or by himself through the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*, even though he has arisen in the Dispensation only once.
This is because faith, by its very nature as liberation, necessarily leads to Nibbāna. For this alone is the distinction between him and the previous person;

otherwise, there would be no purpose in mentioning him separately—this is how it should be understood. By the third [type], one who has developed faith in the Dispensation and is endowed with qualities such as virtue conducive to steadfastness is included.
For he, having emerged [from the ocean] and not yet seeing the shore, remains in the midst of the sea...
Looking toward the arrival of the boat and so forth, he stands as if on high ground without having submerged again;
likewise, having emerged through faith in the Teaching (*sāsana*), yet not yet seeing *nibbāna*, he remains established in heaven and in virtue (*sīla*) while looking toward the Buddha and the rest.
By the fourth [verse], however, the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) is included; for he is like one who, having emerged and stood up, sees the shore and looks about for the means to cross over.
Having emerged by means of supramundane faith as if from the ocean, and having seen the shore of Nibbāna, he looks for the means to cross over.

By the fifth [simile], the once-returner (sakadāgāmī) is included; for just as one who, seeing the shore in the ocean, plunges toward it, so too, having seen the shore of Nibbāna by the first path, he is said to "plunge" toward it by the second path. By the sixth, the non-returner (anāgāmī) is included.
For he, having leaped across and reached the shore, stands as if in water reaching only to his waist;
at the landing-place of the mindfulness-bridge near Arhatship, he stands by means of the third path, characterized by the quality of non-returning. But by the seventh [verse], the Arhat is grasped;
for like a man who has crossed over and stands on the further shore, having crossed the four floods, he stands on the dry land of Nibbāna and is called a "Brahmin whose taints are destroyed."

Regarding "one liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) among the nine types of persons: he is liberated from defilements by means of the liberation of suppression through the form and formless attainments, and by means of the liberation of eradication through the noble path;

or alternatively, he is liberated from the body of form by means of the formless attainments, and from the mental body by means of the path—thus, being liberated in these two respects, he is called "liberated in both ways. He [is one who has attained] the four formless attainments...

There are five types [of those liberated both ways]: four who have attained Arahatship by emerging from one of the [form-sphere] jhānas and contemplating formations, and one Non-returner who has attained Arahatship by emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha*). Among these, only the last is called "liberated both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) in the primary sense;

the others are so called only figuratively. Furthermore, in this context, although the fourth jhāna of the form-sphere is liberated from the mass of defilements, [it is not yet liberated from the body].

It should be understood that what is not liberated from the form-body (rūpakāya) is the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara), whereas the immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) is liberated even from the fear of that [form].

Therefore, it is only by making that [immaterial attainment] the basis and attaining Arahantship that one is "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta), and not by means of the fine-material sphere.

One who is "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta) is liberated from the taints (āsava) by means of the wisdom of the path of Arahantship; for he is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) who, by means of the four fine-material-sphere jhānas...

Including the four who have attained *arahantship* after emerging [from jhāna], there are five types. For even when there is only one of the formless-sphere jhānas (*arūpāvacara-jhāna*), one is indeed called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).

A "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*) is a noble one (*ariya*) who has attained the jhānas of the fine-material and formless spheres. Indeed, he is [one of] the six [types of noble persons], excluding those standing on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
It is sixfold by way of those in training (*sekha*). For it is said in its definition: "some taints (*āsava*) have been completely destroyed.
And for one standing on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), it cannot be said that any taints whatsoever have been completely destroyed;
rather, it can be said that they will be completely destroyed. But for the Arahant, all taints have been completely destroyed, not just some. For he has touched the limit...

One who realizes [cessation] is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī). Alternatively, one is a body-witness because they realize cessation by means of the mental body (nāmakāya) immediately after having touched and attained the jhānas.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by the body," according to the statement, "He realizes the ultimate truth by means of the mental body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom," this refers to the remaining paths and fruits, excluding the fruit of arahantship.
It is a designation (*adhivacana*). Some say that one is a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*) because of the realization of Nibbāna with that very body immediately after the first jhāna.

One who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*) refers to the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*), those who have attained the fine-material jhānas, and the sixfold trainee (*sekha*) as previously described;
this is called "one who has attained vision" because he has reached the end of vision. Vision (*diṭṭhi*) is seeing; it is the first path (*magga*). Immediately after that—
The meaning is "one who has attained cessation. There is also a reading *diṭṭhappatto*, which means "one who has again attained the Nibbāna seen by means of the first path.
*Saddhāvimutto* refers to the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*), the one who has attained the form-sphere jhānas, and the aforementioned sixfold type of trainee (*sekha*).
For this person is "liberated through faith" because they are liberated while possessing faith. But how is there a difference between this person and the one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*)?

Regarding the path of arrival (*āgamanīyapaṭipadā*): one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*) arrives having suppressed defilements with little difficulty through insight (*vipassanā*) in the preliminary stage by means of the perfection of wisdom;
whereas one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*) arrives having suppressed defilements with difficulty due to an abundance of faith.
It is precisely with reference to this distinction that it is said in the *Niddesa*: "Some taints (*āsava*) are completely destroyed..."
It is said: "They exist, but not in the same way as for one who has attained through view.

Regarding the term *dhammānusārī*: one for whom the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is predominant at the moment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is a *dhammānusārī*, because they remember and recollect by means of the Dhamma, which is synonymous with wisdom; this is the name for one standing on the path of stream-entry. At the stage of the fruit (*phala*), [the same applies].

However, when he has attained the fruit, he is called one who has attained through view (*diṭṭhippatto*). As for the "follower by faith" (*saddhānusārī*): one for whom the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is predominant at the moment of the path of stream-entry is a follower by faith because he remembers and recollects by means of faith; this is the name for one standing on the path of stream-entry.
But when the fruit is attained, he is called one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*).
For those producing supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*), there are two tasks (*dhura*), two orientations (*abhinivesa*), and two heads (*sīsa*).
In this context, the "two tasks" are the task of faith (*saddhā-dhura*) and the task of wisdom (*paññā-dhura*).

The "two orientations" are the orientation toward serenity (*samatha-abhinivesa*) and the orientation toward insight (*vipassanā-abhinivesa*). And one who reaches the summit of Arahantship is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*).

"One liberated by wisdom" (*paññā-vimutta*)—these two are called the "heads. For whoever produces supramundane states, they all take these two qualities as their primary burden, fix their resolve upon these two positions, and are liberated through these two positions.
Among them, the bhikkhu who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), having taken wisdom as his primary burden, [proceeds] by way of serenity (*samatha*).

One who is so inclined, taking one of the formless attainments as a basis, establishes insight and reaches Arahantship—this person is called a "follower by Dhamma" (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the stream-entry path. Furthermore, in the six subsequent stages, such a person is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).
Upon attaining the fruit of Arahantship, they are called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutto).
Another, making wisdom itself his burden, becomes intent upon insight; having comprehended either pure formations or any one of the fine-material-sphere jhānas, he attains Arahantship.
This person is called a "Dhammānusārī" (follower by Dhamma) at the moment of the stream-entry path.
Thereafter, however, at six stages he is called a "Diṭṭhippatto" (one who has attained vision), and upon reaching Arahantship, he is called a "Paññāvimutto" (liberated by wisdom).
Furthermore, another who has attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti), making faith his primary vehicle and being intent through concentration,
takes one of the formless attainments as his proximate cause, establishes insight, and reaches Arahantship—
this person is called a "follower by faith" (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the stream-entry path; thereafter, in the six subsequent stages, he is simply called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).
Upon attaining Arahantship, he is indeed called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta). Another person, making faith alone his primary vehicle, becomes intent upon insight;
having comprehended either pure formations or one of the fine-material-sphere jhānas, he reaches Arahantship.
This person is also called a "faith-follower" (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the stream-entry path, and thereafter, in the six stages, he is a "liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutta).

[The one] who has attained Arahantship is called "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*). These seven persons, together with the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) and the Private Buddha (*paccekasambuddha*), are known as the nine supreme recipients of offerings in the world. In this "Decade" (*dasaka*), five [types of persons] reach their final goal here:

the one for whom there are seven more births at most (*sattakkhattuparama*), the one who goes from family to family (*kolaṅkola*), the one who has only one seed remaining (*ekabījī*), and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).
For these five—the one with a sense-sphere rebirth-linking and the Arahant—their final goal (niṭṭhā) is reckoned as Nibbāna without residue right here on this sense-sphere plane;

this is the meaning. For it is only within a sense-sphere existence that these attain Parinibbāna, and not elsewhere. Among the five who have left this world, their final goal is attained [elsewhere]:

the one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), the one who attains Parinibbāna upon arrival (upahaccaparinibbāyī), the one who attains Parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and the one who attains Parinibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī).

"Bound upstream, heading toward the Akaniṭṭha realm"—the meaning of these five is that they reach their final goal only after leaving behind and abandoning their individual existence here in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and remaining in a Brahma-existence. The rest here is self-evident.

This is the determination of the meaning here in brief together with the method of the Pāḷi; however, the detailed exposition should be taken from the *Puggalapaññatti-pāḷi* and its commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the meaning of the *Puggalapaññatti-mātikā* within the *Mohavicchedanī Abhidhammamātikatthavaṇṇanā* is completed. 5.
The *Kathāvatthu-mātikā*.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Person (Puggalakathāvaṇṇanā): Now follows the method of explaining the meaning of the matrix of the topics for discussion. Therein, first, regarding the meaning not yet explained:
"The person is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact" is the question; "Yes, it is so" is the affirmation. Of whom [is this said]?
Furthermore, regarding this question, to whom does it refer when one says "I acknowledge"? It should not be said, "To such-and-such a person.
For the Blessed One did not establish this matrix while engaging in contentious debate with opponents;

rather, based on the teaching on the designation of persons (*puggalapaññatti*) and so forth, he established it for the sake of future monks who would fall into perversion, as well as for opponents, by means of statements such as "In the ultimate sense, there exists what is called a self."
For the purpose of purifying the various bases of views, he established the matrix (mātikā) by way of the method of debate of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa concerning this Puggalavāda,

setting it forth through the very sequence of questions and answers, the attribution of faults, the imposition of refutations, and the exchange of statements and counter-statements between the proponent and the opponent;
therefore, for the sake of easy comprehension of its meaning, [the text is divided into] the questions of the proponent, the questions of the opponent, and the acknowledgments of the proponent.
Having thus shown the distinction with the phrase "the opponent’s admission," we shall provide an explanation of the meaning.
The statement, "A person is apprehended in the sense of a real, ultimate fact," is the question of our own side (the Sakyaputtiyas);
and by this, it is indicated that "those Puggalavādins who hold the view that 'there is a person' should be questioned in this way. But who are they?
Are they the Puggalavādins? Within the Dispensation, there are the Vajjiputtakas and the Sammitiyas, as well as many outsiders who are followers of other sects.
But when did these arise within the Dispensation? Two hundred years after the Parinibbāna.

It is said that after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, having been urged on by him, led the various groups of monks headed by him [to a council] regarding Subhadda, the old man who had gone forth late in life, and others.
Having obtained King Ajātasattu as an ally for the purpose of excluding wicked monks from entry and seating,
and having compiled the body of the Dhamma and Vinaya so that the Dispensation might proceed unshakably, one hundred years thereafter, in Vesālī,
the ten points (vatthu) proclaimed by the Vajjiputtakas were suppressed; those monks were restrained, and [the work was carried out] by those incited by the Elder Yasa.
When the collection of the Dhamma and Vinaya was again performed by the groups of elders, those ten thousand Vajjiputtakas were suppressed;
having obtained support from a certain weak king, they split the Mūlasaṅgaha, inserted words favorable to their own misconduct,
discarded the Buddha’s word, and held a separate collection of the Dhamma and Vinaya apart from the Great Councils.
They gave it the name "the school of the Mahāsaṅghika teachers. However, because the pure dispensation was preserved by the Elders (Theras), it became known as the "Theravāda.
Now, from these two schools, five schools emerged from the Mahāsaṅghikas:
the Ekavyāvahārikas, the Gokulikas, and from those [the latter], the Paññattivādins, the Bahulikas, and the Cetiyavādins. Thus, [there were] five schools from the Mahāsaṅghikas.

Furthermore, together with these, there arose what are known as the six teacher-traditions (*ācariyakula*). Likewise, having split from the Theravāda, there were the Mahīśāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas;
from those [the latter] came the Dhammuttariyas, the Bhaddayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Sammitiyas.
From the Mahīśāsakas came the Dhammaguttikas and the Sabbatthikas; from them the Kassapikas; from them the Saṅkantikas; and from them the Suttavādins.
These eleven doctrines arose. Together with the six preceding ones, seventeen schismatic doctrines appeared in the second century [after the Parinibbāna].

However, the Theravāda alone remained undivided; thus, it should be understood that eighteen schools (nikāyas) came into existence within the Dispensation, which are known as the "eighteen teacher-lineages" (aṭṭhārasācariyakulāni). Of these eighteen...

Having understood that there would be a disturbance of the Dispensation in the future due to the doctrines of various teachers, the Perfectly Enlightened One foresaw that after two hundred years had passed,
when King Asoka Dhammarāja— having gained faith in the Dispensation— was bestowing gain and honor upon the Dispensation alone without looking toward outsiders,
some would assume the guise of the Dispensation for the sake of gain and honor, and [take up] their respective...

Having seated himself within the pure Great Saṅgha of Bhikkhus— after having investigated, by means of his mastery of the various doctrines, those sixty-two holders of speculative views and the seventeen teacher-families mentioned above, and having caused them to be given white robes and expelled—
he sat amidst the assembly and [considered] whatever matters had arisen at that time for the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, as well as those which would arise in the future.
All those [doctrinal points] that were about to arise, having warded them off by means of the mere headings provided by his own Teacher,
he spoke the *Kathāvatthu* treatise— which is adorned with a thousand suttas, crushes the doctrines of others, and possesses the characteristic of long duration—
by way of analyzing those headings; and having included it in the Third Council, he restored the agitated Dispensation.

It should be understood that, after stating this matrix (*mātikā*) of the *Kathāvatthu* by way of demonstrating the method for refuting predictions concerning the future—in order to manifest his own capacity to uphold [the doctrine] within the Saṅgha of monks—the Elder did not state its analytical commentary (*vibhaṅga*), thereby leaving room for others.
In that context, "person" (*puggala*) refers to the self, the living being, or the sentient being. "Is apprehended" (*upalabbhati*) means it is obtained by approaching it through wisdom; it is known.
The meaning [of the phrase] is as follows: Regarding the expression "in the sense of the ultimate reality of what is truly real" (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena*):

here, "what is truly real" (*saccikaṭṭha*) refers to the actual state of being (*bhūtaṭṭha*), which is not to be grasped in an unreal manner like an illusion or a mirage. "Ultimate reality" (*paramattha*) refers to the supreme object (*uttamattha*), which is not to be grasped by means of hearsay and the like.

By both of these criteria, just as phenomena such as form and feeling are perceived through their actual intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), so too is it first stated that "the person (*puggala*) is perceived."

He asks. The opponent admits, saying, "Yes" (*āmantā*). For such an admission appears in some places as "Yes, venerable sir" (*āma bhante*), in others as "Yes" (*āmo*), but here it has come down as "Yes" (*āmantā*). Herein, this is the intended meaning:
for the opponent [admits this] because the Blessed One has elucidated the person (*puggala*) in such passages as, "There is a person practicing for his own welfare," and so forth.
The Blessed One speaks what is not false; therefore, having adopted the position that "it exists only in the sense of being real and ultimate," he asserts "Yes" [to the question].
Then, not giving such a person an opportunity for equivocal speech or deceptive argumentation, the proponent of the true doctrine says: "That which is real and ultimate... and so forth.

In this context, the intended meaning is as follows: This aforementioned classification of phenomena (dhamma), beginning with material form and feeling, is not to be understood by way of conventional truth (sammutisacca) nor by way of hearsay and the like;
rather, it is the "actual reality" (saccikaṭṭha) precisely because of its own ontological existence, and it is the "ultimate sense" (paramattha) because it is directly verifiable for oneself.
A person (puggala) who is designated in that manner [as a "person"] does not exist in that mode of actual reality and ultimate sense.

"It is perceived"—that is, just as the ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*) is perceived again by way of its own specific mode, such as being subject to change (*ruppana*) or experiencing (*anubhavana*), is the person (*puggala*) likewise perceived for you? This is what is meant. "It should not be said so" is the opponent's denial;
for he denies it because he does not accept such a person. For there is no self (*attā*).
Apart from mere delusion, no one whatsoever is seen who is liberated from the aggregates and so forth. Herein, this is the word-division:
“*na hi evaṃ vattabbo*. Some read it as “*na ha evan*,” and the meaning of both is that it should not be stated in this way.

“*Ājānāhi niggahaṃ*” (Understand the refutation) is the statement of the proponent’s own side. Because of your subsequent [position], which contradicts your previous admission of what should be stated...
"It is not to be admitted; moreover, the latter does not connect with the former. Therefore, you have fallen into refutation.
Understand this refutation as a fault and a transgression—this is the meaning:
'Accept it. Having thus caused him to understand the refutation, he now makes it clear by means of its establishment, and by way of applying it both in direct and reverse order:
He said, “If a person,” and so forth. Therein, “if” (*hañci*) means “if,” “provided that”; the sense is: “if a person is apprehended.

This is first called *anuloma-ṭhapana* (conformable establishment), which is characterized by the restatement of the opponent’s position, the establishment of a refutation, and the imposition of the charge of refutation.
Therefore, [the passage] beginning with “By that indeed, O Venerable One” is for the purpose of bringing about a refutation within the conformable position.
This is called *anulomapāpanā* (the method of leading [the opponent] to a conclusion by way of agreement). In this context, "tena" (by that) is a word expressing the reason.

"Vata" is a word of conviction (*okappana*) and a word of restriction (*niyama*). "Re" is a word of address. This is what is meant: "By that, indeed, O you!—'vata re' being an address—O good sir, for that reason one must speak thus"; such is the meaning.
"Yaṃ tattha vadesi" (what you say therein), etc., refers to the refutation within the position of agreement (*anulomapakkhe*).

Because it is superimposed, it is called "superimposing in accordance" (*anulomaropanā*). As for the word "wrong" (*micchā*) at its conclusion, the phrase "this is yours" (*idaṃ te*) should be supplied before it;
thus, the meaning here is "this is wrong for you. The same applies to what follows. This very point has already appeared later in the text (*pāḷi*).
The passage beginning with "If it were not to be so stated," etc., refers to the position that was rejected by the words "it should not be stated thus" (*na hevaṃ vattabbe*).

Because it is established by way of restatement (*anuvadana*), "reverse establishment" (*paṭilomaṭṭhapana*) is the characteristic of bringing about refutation (*niggaha*) and charging [the opponent] in reverse order.
Furthermore, "No ca vata re," and so forth, is called "reverse bringing about" (*paṭilomapāpanā*) because refutation is brought about in the reverse position.
Again, "Yaṃ tattha vadesi," and so forth, is called "reverse charging" (*paṭilomaropanā*) because the refutation is charged in the reverse position.
In this regard, the summary meaning from the beginning is as follows: If a person is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, then indeed, sir, it must be said that he is apprehended.

But as for what you say there—"In the first question, one may say 'he is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact,' but in the second question, one cannot say 'that person [exists] from that [basis]'—[it is not so]."
‘...is apprehended,’ this is wrong for you. Thus, first of all, there are the establishing, the leading astray, and the attribution in accordance with the sequence.
Then, in the second question, it cannot be said that “that person is apprehended from that [basis]”;

nor can it be said in the first question either. As for what you said there—“In the first question, it can indeed be said: ‘He is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact’”—[this is incorrect].
And in the second question, one should not say, "That person is apprehended from that [basis]";

thus, "This is wrong for you"—in this way, there are the setting aside, the leading to, and the attributing in reverse order. Thus, because the leading to and attributing of four types have been stated—two in direct order and two in reverse order for the refutation—it follows that the fivefold set in direct order begins with "it is apprehended," and so forth.

[This concludes] the name. And here, although two refutations (*niggaha*) are made—two because there is one from the positive order (*anuloma*) by means of "bringing down" (*pāpana*) and "attributing" (*āropana*), and one from the reverse order (*paṭiloma*) by means of "bringing down" and "attributing"—this should nevertheless be understood as a single refutation, because this very first refutation is attributed in two ways. This is the first refutation.
Now follows the method of opposition (*paccanīkanaya*). Therein, the question "A person is not apprehended" is posed by the opponent (*paravādin*).
The proponent (*sakavādin*) assents with "Yes," because [the person] is not apprehended in the same way that phenomena such as form and feeling are apprehended.
Again, the other speaks the words beginning with "That which is the true reality (*saccikaṭṭha*)" with reference precisely to the true reality intended by himself.
Alternatively, even when conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) and ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) are taken together, the opponent speaks thus.

The proponent rejects [the question] with "Certainly not," because the person (*puggala*) exists as a designation based upon [aggregates], and because the question was asked by taking the two truths together.
Now, although it was previously stated that [the person] is not to be found by way of ultimate truth—
[The position] was accepted [at first], but later it was rejected either by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) or by way of a mixed [truth].
However, the opponent, relying on a quibble (*chala*) based merely on the commonality of the word "is not apprehended," says:
"That which was first admitted by you has been later rejected. This is like a counter-objection to one's own objection, as if responding to a quarrel.
One performing the counter-action (*paṭikamma*) to the refutation (*niggaha-kamma*) says, “Understand the counter-action.

Now, just as in the *Anuloma-pañcaka* (the Fivefold Sequence of Conformity), where the proponent establishes his position and the opponent’s refutation is made manifest through the application of conformity and reverse order, so too, making the counter-action manifest, he says, “If indeed there is a person,” and so forth. This is according to the method explained below.
It should be understood according to its meaning. For in this context, "setting aside" (*ṭhapanā*) consists merely in setting aside the opponent's position to show, "This is your fault";
it does not constitute the making manifest of either a defeat (*niggaha*) or a counter-argument (*paṭikamma*).

Rather, its manifestation occurs through "leading to the conclusion" (*pāpanā*) and "attributing" (*āropanā*). Therefore, this [section] follows the order of leading to the conclusion and attributing, both in direct and reverse sequence.
One set of four should be understood as the "tetrad of counter-measures" (paṭikammacatukka) because a counter-measure has been performed in four ways by means of this [method].
Having thus performed the counter-measure, he now says, "But if you think," etc.,

demonstrating the faulty nature of the refutation made by the proponent (sakavādin) against him in the "pentad of conformity" (anulomapañcaka), based precisely on that same fallacious argument (chalavāda).
In that context, “*tvaṃ ce pana maññasī*” means “if you think.

The phrase “it should be said (*vattabbe kho*)” is stated with reference to the admission “yes (*āmantā*),” which occurs in response to an objection; whereas the phrase “it should not be said (*no ca vattabbe*)” is stated with reference to the rejection “no indeed (*na heva*”).
Therefore, “*tena tava tatthā*” means “for that reason, you yourself [should say] in that regard: ‘He who...’”
When they thus assert their position, saying, "Yes, it is so," one who asserts it in this way should be refuted by saying,
"It is not so. Then, when one says, "I shall refute him"— meaning, "I shall refute him who is worthy of being refuted in this manner"—
and [the opponent] is well-refuted, he is well-refuted because he has been refuted by means of his own doctrine.
Having thus shown his state of being subject to refutation, [the author] now says "Hañci" (If indeed... and so forth while refuting him.
In this context, *ṭhapanā* (establishing), *pāpanā* (leading to a consequence), and *āropanā* (attributing) are to be understood according to the method explained below.
At the conclusion, however, the phrase "idaṃ te micchā" means "this statement of yours is false. This is the refutation by way of equivocation (*chalavāda*) through four modes.
This is called the tetrad of refutation by way of what has been done. Having thus effected the refutation, he now demonstrates:

"If this refutation made by me according to your opinion is difficult to refute, then that refutation which was made by you against me previously in the 'Five in Accordance' (anulomapañcaka) is also difficult to refute," and says: "Ese..."
He said, “If this [argument] is not well-refuted,” and so forth. Therein, “if this is not well-refuted” means:
either this argument of yours has not been well-refuted by me, or else this refutation made by me against you is not a proper refutation.

“In that very same way, look at it there” means: even regarding the refutation you have made against me below, look at it in exactly that manner. Now, as for the refutation made by our own side (the proponent) below—

Having shown that [the refutation] was indeed made by means of the statement beginning with "It should indeed be said," he then spoke the passage beginning with "But we do not [refute you] by you" while leading that refutation toward the state of being non-refutation.
Therein, regarding the phrases "but we do not [refute you] by you there on that admission as a reason," etc., this is the meaning:
because that refutation made by you against me is a poor refutation, therefore we do not [refute you] by you there in the "conformity pentad."

“‘Yes, sir’—even though we have admitted this by such an affirmation and have thus confessed it, and even when a refutation has been made with ‘It is not so,’ we should still be refuted by saying, ‘Understand the refutation. Yet you have refuted me when I was not to be refuted in that way;
however, by such a refutation, we are poorly refuted. Now, regarding the refutation on account of which we are said to be poorly refuted...”
And he said, "It is so," [meaning] "it is a fire-oblation. To demonstrate that, he said: "If the person... [etc. ...this of yours is wrong.
Thus, because it has been brought to a refutation by means of four applications of the charge through both direct and reverse order, this is called the "tetrad of application" (*upanayana-catukka*).
Now, the section beginning with "it should not be refuted in this way" is called the "tetrad of conclusion" (*niggamana-catukka*). Therein, "not in this way... [etc.]
"Should be refuted": "The way you have refuted me is not how one should be refuted;
for I have established that this kind of refutation is a 'bad refutation' (dunniggaha). Therefore (tena hi)": for that reason.
Since this refutation is a bad refutation, therefore [the statement] "If a person... [etc. ...this is your error" is your refutation.
"Wrong" is the meaning. Therefore, as for the refutation you have made—by whatever reason this is wrong, by that same reason the refutation you performed is ill-done (*dukkaṭa*).
That very counter-argument which was made by me is well-done (*sukata*).
Furthermore, this presentation of the course of discussion by way of the fourfold counter-argument and so forth, which has been performed, is also well-done. That very [point]...

It should be understood that the "conformity-and-opposition" (anulomapaccanīka) method has been demonstrated by means of the fivefold conformity beginning with "the person is apprehended," as well as the fourfold sets of counter-arguments consisting of refutation, subordination, application, and conclusion beginning with "it is not apprehended. Up to this point,
when the proponent's initial position exists, the opponent achieves victory through a sophistical argument based on mere verbal similarity.
Now, in order to demonstrate how the proponent’s victory comes about through the Dhamma alone when the opponent’s position is established,
the pentad of counter-questioning and conforming questioning, beginning with “A person is not apprehended,” is commenced. Therein,
the question in the counter-argument belongs to the opponent, who refers to the categories such as form (rūpa) as being real in the sense of ultimate truth (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha).
The proponent’s admission refers to conventional truth (sammutisacca), whether pure or mixed with ultimate truth (paramattha).

When the opponent asks again, “What is the true reality? it is because the person (*puggala*) cannot be said to exist even by way of convention, or because the question is confused due to being based on a mixture [of truths], that the proponent rejects it, saying, “Certainly not.”
"He rejects what has been admitted" means that, by the mere similarity of words, he [rejects] the opponent's statement beginning with "Understand the refutation.

Thus, based on the second position that "this person is not apprehended," the second refutation occurs; it should be understood in this way that the refutation was leveled by him through a quibble (*chala*).

Now, in order to demonstrate victory for his own doctrine through the admission of the opponent by means of the Dhamma and justice, there is first a question from the proponent (sakavādī) according to the method of conformity (anulomanaya).

Then there is an admission by the opponent (paravādī) based on his own tenet (laddhi). Without granting an opening for that tenet, there is a further inquiry by the proponent from the standpoint of ultimate reality (paramattha).
And because a person (puggala) is not apprehended from the standpoint of ultimate reality, there is a rejection [of the opponent's position].
For the opponent, everything from "State your counter-argument" onwards is merely the statement of the proponent, intended to demonstrate his own victory through righteous and equitable means.

In this regard, the meaning of all the fourfold sets concerning counter-arguments, refutations, lead-ins, and lead-outs should be understood according to the method explained below. Thus, this [is the analysis] of the pentad of counter-objections beginning with "A person is not apprehended."

By means of the fourfold sets consisting of the counter-argument (*paṭikkamma*), refutation (*niggaha*), application (*upanayana*), and conclusion (*niggamana*)—beginning with the phrase “it is apprehended” (*upalabbhati*)—the pentad known as the “reverse-and-direct-order” (*paccanīkānuloma-pañcaka*) is demonstrated.
Thus, these two pentads regarding the first true meaning (*saccikaṭṭha*) have been demonstrated. Regarding this, it is said:
“In the first pentad, the refutation of the opponent’s doctrine is pure.”
But it is impure for him alone; there, victory is achieved through remedial action.
"In the second pentad, the refutation of one's own position is impure;
but it is pure for him alone; there, victory is achieved through remedial action."
“Therefore, in both instances, victory belongs to our own proponent alone;
for victory by means of the Dhamma is true victory—how could there be victory by means of non-Dhamma?
Just as it is here in the true sense, adorned with the two sets of five.”
"Victory and defeat are spoken of only by way of what is dhamma and what is adhamma.
Regarding all subsequent points that are established in truth,
the wise person should analyze both victory and defeat in exactly this same way."
The first section on the meaning of the pure and actual is finished.

Having thus elaborated upon the meaning of the pure and actual, the passage beginning with “A person is apprehended” is now commenced in order to elaborate that same point further by means of other methods, such as the occasion and so forth.
Therein, the question belongs to the proponent of the internal view (Sakavādī), and the affirmation belongs to the opponent (Paravādī).
Furthermore, "in all cases" refers to the inquiry of one's own school (*sakavādin*) concerning the body.

Having seen the fault of viewing the self in form and the fault of falling into the position that "the soul is one thing and the body another," the rejection is made by the opposing school (*paravādin*).
The rest here is to be understood according to the method already stated above for the fivefold set of positive-negative propositions; however, the text is abbreviated. In this regard:
Since it follows that when it is stated, "It is not apprehended anywhere," with reference to the body, one would conclude that it is apprehended outside the body;
therefore, the opponent's rebuttal is a denial of the proponent's position.
By first granting [the premise] and subsequently denying it, the opponent's counter-argument proceeds by way of quibbling (*chala*). The remainder is self-evident.

In the second method, the opponent’s inquiry—"all [beings]"—refers to both the times of previous and subsequent births, as well as the times of being currently living and having attained final Nibbāna.

Having perceived the fault of contradiction in such statements as "that very kṣatriya is that same brāhmaṇa," etc., and the fault of there being no distinction between those currently living and those who have attained final Nibbāna, the proponent offers a refutation. The remainder is exactly as stated in the first method.

In the third method, "in all" refers to the aggregates, bases, and so forth; the question belongs to the proponent (sakavādin), while the denial—due to the fear of faults such as "the self is in form" or "the self is in the eye"—belongs to the opponent (paravādin).

The remainder is exactly like that. Thus, having first analyzed these three modes in the "fivefold positive-negative" set by way of the positive alone in their respective order, one now analyzes them in the "fivefold negative-positive" set by way of the negative alone, beginning with: "The person is not apprehended," and so forth.
It has been undertaken. Therein, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained below.

Up to this point, with respect to each of the four "points of reality" (saccikaṭṭhāna)—namely, the pure [point] and these three—the eightfold method of debate (vādayutti) called "the eight faces" has been demonstrated by way of two types of opposition for each: the positive-negative and the negative-positive.
It should be understood that [the term] "occurs" refers to what is stated by way of each individual *niggaha* (refutation) in each individual mouth. Regarding this, it is said:
"In this manner, within the fourfold questions, distinguished by the two sets of five, this method of debate called 'The Eight-Mouthed' has been elucidated."
“There are eight points of defeat therein; of these, four are according to the Dhamma and four are contrary to the Dhamma.
In all cases, victory belongs to one’s own side, and in all cases, defeat belongs to the opposing side.”
This, then, is the commentary here by way of explaining the meaning that has not yet been fully elucidated.
Furthermore, the determination of the meaning here is likewise provided merely by showing the general method of the exposition composed by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.
For the Elder did not compose an exposition by way of extracting the individual words of this matrix (mātikā) established by the Blessed One; rather—
Having established the method of the eightfold negation of the person as taught by the Blessed One,

and while refuting the theory of a person (*puggalavāda*) through other modes of exposition as well as various other types of false views, the *Niddesa* was composed beginning with the discussion of the person through more than two hundred discourses.

Among these, first, for the purpose of refuting the theory of a person, by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and faculties (*indriya*), [there are] fifty-seven...
In each case among the phenomena, it proceeds by way of correlating the person, such as: "The person is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact;
matter is also apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact... [and so on] ...the person is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact;
feeling is also apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact. Thus it functions by means of the method of correlating the person.

The correlation of the pure [categories]: the correlation by way of simile, which proceeds by means of questioning—namely, that just as the fifty-seven phenomena such as form and feeling are perceived as mutually distinct, so too is a person (puggala) perceived as distinct from form and the other aggregates;
[and the inquiry: "Is form the person? Is the person in form? Is the person apart from form? Is the person in the person?"...
"Form"—thus, by way of the fourfold method, the correlation of the fourfold method as it proceeds through the process of questioning regarding the fifty-seven states has been explained.

In this regard, there are three modes of correlation that have been stated. Among these, since it would follow that a person (puggala) would possess the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of form and so forth, leading to the undesirable consequences of eternalism, annihilationism, and the like, their refutation should be understood according to the appropriate logic. For fear of excessive prolixity, this is not elaborated upon here or further below.

Then there is the discourse on the application of characteristics (*lakkhaṇayuttikathā*), which proceeds by way of questioning: "Just as form and the other [aggregates] possess conditions, or are without conditions, and so forth, so too your 'person' (*puggala*) must be endowed with the characteristic of possessing conditions and so on.
And for the purpose of clarifying the two terms "person" and "is apprehended," there is that which proceeds by way of questioning such as:
"Is that which is a person apprehended? Or is that which is apprehended a person? and so forth.

The purification of statements; the application of designation (*paññattānuyoga*) proceeding by way of purifying the designation of names, such as “one possessing form in the form realm” and so forth;

the application of death and rebirth (*cuti-paṭisandhi*) by way of the transition between states of existence, such as “that same person transmigrates from this world to the next world—neither another, nor not another, nor both another and not another”;
and [the analysis] beginning with “in dependence upon a tree...”

The application of the analysis of derived designations (*upādāpaññatti*) demonstrates the undesirable consequence that [the person] would be impermanent and conditioned, etc., in the doctrine that "the designation 'person' exists in the ultimate sense by depending on the aggregates and so forth, like a shadow and its object.

The application of the analysis of human effort (*purisakāra*) demonstrates the undesirable consequence that the cycle of suffering would not be severed, etc., in the doctrine that "the person is the doer of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
And the application of the analysis of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) refutes various doctrines such as "the person who performs transformations through psychic power is that very person," and so on.

The inquiry concerning relatives is the analysis of the thesis that "there are such things as mother and father, and therefore the person exists. The inquiry concerning birth is [the analysis] beginning with "thus is a kṣatriya," and so forth.

The inquiry concerning practice is [the analysis] beginning with "householder" and "renunciant," and so forth. The inquiry concerning rebirth is [the analysis] beginning with "god" and "human," and so forth.

The inquiry concerning penetration is [the analysis] beginning with "stream-enterer," and so forth. The inquiry concerning the Saṅgha is [the analysis] beginning with "the eight types of persons," and so forth. "Person..."

The application to the true nature of things (*saccikaṭṭhasabhāgānuyoga*) proceeds by way of such passages as "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*); the application to the experiencer (*vedakānuyoga*) by way of such passages as "experiencing a pleasant feeling";

the application to the function (*kiccānuyoga*) by way of such passages as "contemplating the body in the body"; and [the application to the person] when there are suttas based on the existence of a person that establish the individual essence of a person, such as "there is a person practicing for his own welfare."
"All phenomena are non-self; only suffering arises as it arises.
Why do you conceive of a 'being,' O Māra? Is this a mere speculative view of yours?
This is merely a heap of conditioned formations; here no being is to be found."
For it is suffering alone that arises, suffering that stands, and suffering that passes away.
Nothing other than suffering arises; nothing other than suffering ceases.
And because, Ānanda, it is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self... [and so on] ...therefore the world is said to be empty.

“Bhikkhus, when there is a self, the thought ‘this is mine’ occurs with respect to what belongs to the self… But when both self and what belongs to the self are not found to exist truly and ultimately,
even that standpoint of views— ‘This world, this self, shall become after death permanent,
stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same exactly as it is for all eternity’— [does not arise].”
“‘I shall stand firm’—is this not, monks, the entire and complete nature of a fool? And:
“In that regard, Seniya, that teacher who does not designate a self as real and substantial in the present life, nor in the future life... [etc.]...
this, Seniya, is called a teacher who is a perfectly enlightened Buddha,” and so forth; thus it proceeds by way of demonstrating those suttas which reveal the non-existence of a person (puggala).
And the application of the demonstration of the suttas—by this much of the method of discourse, the first discussion on the person (*puggala*) has been analyzed in detail.

In that regard, concerning such statements as "there is a person practicing for his own benefit," the person is not found in the same way that phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are found by way of their individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); rather, it is only when form and the other [aggregates] exist...
“It is by mere worldly convention that one says ‘there is a person. And this was also said by the Blessed One: ‘These, Citta...

[are] worldly conventions, worldly designations. The discourse of the Buddhas is twofold: discourse on conventional designation (*sammuti-kathā*) and discourse on the ultimate truth (*paramattha-kathā*).
Therein, such things as ‘a being,’ ‘a person,’ ‘a village,’ or ‘a mountain’ are called discourse on conventional designation; ‘impermanent,’ ‘suffering,’...”
The discourse on ultimate reality (*paramattha-kathā*) begins with such statements as, "The aggregates and the sense bases are non-self. For the Buddhas,
having awakened in whatever way various beings are capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths, teach them accordingly— whether by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*),
ultimate reality (*paramattha*), or a mixture of both— precisely through the method of discerning name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-pariccheda*).
They proclaim the path to the Deathless.
For it is said: "The Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, has declared two truths:
the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found."
In this regard:
The conventional expression is true as the cause for worldly consensus;
the expression of ultimate meaning is true as the suchness-characteristic of phenomena.
Therefore, the wise person, having avoided adherence to the literal expression and being established in the ultimate meaning, should reject [notions of] a "person" and so forth.
Without overstepping conventional designation, the ultimate meaning has been elucidated.
"Since he [the Buddha] was led by the Leader (Vināyaka), therefore another wise person,
when elucidating the ultimate meaning, should not overstep conventional designation.
This is the method for the discussion on the person (puggala).
Commentary on the Discussion of Falling Away:
Following the discussion on the person (*puggala*), there is the discussion of falling away (*parihānikathā*) which proceeds by way of such statements as, "Does an Arahant fall away from Arahantship?

and so forth; it concerns those beyond training (*asekha*) and those in training (*sekha*)—excluding the stream-enterer—who fall away from the fruit of the highest path, which is known as penetration (*paṭivedha*), just like the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
The discourse on the holy life (*brahmacariya*) proceeds by stating that the dwelling in the holy life occurs only among humans and not among the devas.

The discourse on specific abandonment (*odhisokathā*) proceeds by showing that defilements are abandoned in a particular way through various realizations (*abhisamaya*), such as the vision of suffering, through which defilements are abandoned in part, and likewise through the vision of the origin and so forth. [The one who] attains jhāna...
