The discourse on "abandoning" proceeds thus: an ordinary person (puthujjana) abandons sensual lust and ill will by way of their total eradication;
through the realization of the Four Noble Truths, he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī) right from the very beginning. The discourse on "everything exists" proceeds thus:

all things, such as the aggregates (khandha) and so forth—classified as past and so on—exist in all three periods of time by virtue of the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of the aggregates and so on. [This includes] the past and future aggregates and so forth...

The discourse on "it exists" refers to the discussion concerning past aggregates and so forth. The discourse on "some exist" refers to the discussion that among past phenomena subject to fruition, some have not yet ripened as result, while others have;
thus, only some exist, not all. The discourse on the foundations of mindfulness refers to the discussion that all phenomena are foundations of mindfulness.
[The discourse on] non-existence by way of the past, future, and so forth, or existence by way of intrinsic nature (*sakabhāva*), or non-existence by way of extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*)...
The discourse concerning "it exists" (*hevatthi*) is that which proceeds with the statement "it is not. In this context, *hevatthi* means "it exists" in this manner or by way of this mode.

The discourse concerning "introduction by another" (*parūpahāra*) is that which proceeds with the claim that deities belonging to Māra’s host approach those who are conceited or deceitful—those who profess to have attained *arahantship*—upon seeing their emission of semen.
[It is said: "An *arahant* possesses ignorance regarding the names, clans, and so forth of others."

There are three types of discourse: the discourse on doubt (*kaṅkhākathā*), the discourse on being made known by others (*paravitaraṇākathā*), and the discourse on the communication of another (*paravitaraṇākathā*).

At the moment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), the statement "it is suffering" constitutes the discourse on the breaking of speech (*vacībhedakathā*). When one utters the words "it is suffering," one brings forth knowledge regarding suffering, and that [knowledge] is supramundane (*lokuttara*);
this is the discourse on the bringing forth of suffering (*dukkhāhārakathā*). [This occurs] during meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
The discourse on the stability of consciousness is that which proceeds by way of the mind remaining for a long time.
The discourse on the burning embers is that which proceeds by way of all conditioned phenomena being, in an absolute sense, ablaze like a hell of glowing embers.
The attainment of Arahantship occurs through sixteen divisions, by way of the fourfold arising of each path through the individual vision of the Four Noble Truths.
The discourse on the progressive realization of the truths proceeds; the discourse on conventional expression proceeds with the statement that the terminology of the Buddhas is supramundane;

and the discourse on cessation proceeds with the two types of cessation: the cessation through non-deliberation, which is the cessation of defilements by means of the path without deliberate reflection on the part of pure beings, and the cessation through deliberation, which is the cessation of defilements by means of that same path through deliberate reflection.

The discourse on the powers proceeds thus: "The power of a Tathāgata is shared with his disciples. The discourse on the noble ones proceeds thus: "The nine powers, being devoid of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), are supramundane (*lokuttara*).
The discourse on liberation proceeds thus: "A mind still possessed of lust is liberated from lust by taking Nibbāna as its object.
At the moment of the Path, the mind is first liberated through the suppression [of defilements] by means of jhāna.
The discourse on the process of liberation concerns that which is called "being liberated" through liberation by complete eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*).

The discourse on the eighth person (*aṭṭhamaka*) concerns the fact that for one standing at the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), known as the eighth person, views and doubt are said to be abandoned during the moments of conformity (*anuloma*) and the state of lineage (*gotrabhū*), and are said to be already abandoned at the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*).
At the moment of the path, the eighth person acquires the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the other faculties.
The discourse on the faculties of the eighth person (*aṭṭhamaka*), which maintains that [the faculties] have not yet been acquired;

the discourse on the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), which maintains that the physical eye itself, when fortified by the state of the fourth jhāna, is called the divine eye; likewise, the discourse on the divine ear (*dibbasota*) regarding the physical ear;

and the discourse on the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpagatañāṇa*), which maintains that this very knowledge is the divine eye; [and the discourse on] the gods and brahmās...

The discourse on restraint (*saṃvarakathā*) proceeds from the position that restraint exists even in the absence of the restraint consisting in the complete abstention from killing and so forth, provided there is merely the absence of such non-restraint.

The discourse on the non-percipient beings (*asaññakathā*) proceeds from the position that perception (*saññā*) exists for those in the non-percipient realm at the moments of death and rebirth-linking.

The discourse on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathā*) proceeds from the position that perception does not function in the plane of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The discourse concerning the householder who is an Arahant is that which occurs [with the thought]: "A householder may be an Arahant. The discourse concerning rebirth is that which occurs [with the thought]: "At the moment of rebirth, by means of the rebirth-linking consciousness, non-returners become Arahants in the Pure Abodes.
The discourse concerning the absence of taints is that which occurs [with the thought]: "Even mundane phenomena of an Arahant are free from taints.

[Furthermore, there is] the possession consisting in the state of being endowed [with qualities] at the present moment, and the possession consisting in the acquisition of different planes such as the fine-material sphere.
There are these two kinds of possession (*samannāgama*). Furthermore, setting aside these two, there is another kind of possession here by way of the dhamma of rebirth;
because of that, the discourse on possession proceeds thus: "The Arahant is possessed of the four fruits.
By this same method, the discourse on the possession of equanimity proceeds thus: "The Arahant is possessed of the six kinds of equanimity."

The discourse on the Buddha is that which proceeds from the state of being constantly present with enlightenment (bodhi), which is designated as the knowledge of the path and omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).

The discourse on the marks is that which proceeds from the fact that bodhisattvas are indeed endowed with the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa). The discourse on entering the fixed course (niyāmokkantika) is that which proceeds from the fact that even for bodhisattvas there is a determination regarding the path.
[The discourse on the fruit] begins with: "One who stands at the stage of the fourth path is possessed of three fruits," and so forth.

There is another discourse concerning what has been attained: the discourse on the abandoning of all fetters, which states that, in the direct sense (*nippariyāyato*), Arahantship is the abandoning of all fetters together with those abandoned by the first path and the others.
In the direct sense, the fruit is called liberation; however, the knowledge of insight, the path, and the reviewing knowledge are [liberation] only in the indirect sense (*pariyāyato*).
However, not accepting this, there is the discourse on liberation (*vimuttikathā*), which asserts that any knowledge dissociated from the defilements is liberation;
the discourse on superlative knowledge (*asekhañāṇakathā*), which asserts that the knowledge of those beyond training (*asekha*) has the Buddhas and others as its object;

and the discourse on distorted knowledge (*viparītakathā*), which asserts that the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) such as the earth-kasiṇa are distorted knowledge because they operate upon designated objects (*paññattārammaṇa*) that do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
In this context, the fourfold perversion—such as regarding the impermanent as permanent, and so forth—is to be understood.

The discourse on the "entry into the fixed course" refers to the view that all ordinary worldlings possess the knowledge for entering the fixed course. The discourse on the "analytical knowledges" (paṭisambhidā) refers to the view that all knowledge constitutes analytical knowledge.
The discourse on "conventional knowledge" (sammutiñāṇa) refers to the view that even knowledge whose object is conventional is indeed a real objective referent.

The discourse on the object of consciousness concerns the fact that knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*) has only the mind as its object, and not mental factors such as lust associated with that mind.
The discourse on knowledge of the future concerns the fact that there is knowledge of all future phenomena for everyone.
The discourse on knowledge of the present concerns the fact that knowledge itself occurs within one's own present knowledge. [This is] like the Buddhas.

The discourse on the knowledge of the fruits proceeds thus: even the disciples, having known the fruit to be attained by each person to be trained according to their respective capacity, teach the Dhamma for that purpose.
The discourse on the fixed course proceeds thus:
the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma) is unconditioned (asaṅkhata) in the sense of being constant by its very nature. "The stability of the Dhamma..."
The discourse on dependent origination proceeds from such statements as, "the fixed order of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*), [showing that] dependent origination is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
The discourse on the truths proceeds from such statements as, "the truths are thus, not otherwise," [showing that] the four truths are unconditioned.

The discourse on the formless [attainments] proceeds from the statement, "the four formless [states] are imperturbable" (*āneñja*), [showing that they are] unconditioned. [And so is] the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The discussion on the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) concerns the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The discussion on space (*ākāsa*) concerns "unconditioned space.
The discussion on whether space is visible (*sanidassana*) begins with "the earth element is visible" and concludes with "bodily action is visible.
The claim that "there are no phenomena included by any other phenomena" and thus "form is included in a single way" and so forth is pointless.
The discourse on inclusion concerns that which has occurred. The discourse on association concerns that immaterial phenomena such as feeling and so forth are not associated with one another.

The discourse on mental factors concerns the position that there are no mental factors. The discourse on giving concerns the position that giving is the volitional state itself, and not the object to be given.
[The discourse on merit] concerns the position that there is merit consisting in the enjoyment by the recipients.

Discourse on enjoyment; discourse on what is given from here, [asserting] that the departed (petas) subsist only on robes and so forth given from this world; discourse on the maturation of karma regarding the earth;

discourse on the maturation of aging and death; discourse on the maturation of noble states, [asserting] that the fruit of recluseship consists merely in the abandoning of defilements and not in the phenomena of mind and mental factors; [and discourse on] the conditionality of mutual dependence and so forth.
The discussion on "resultant" and "that which is subject to result.
The discussion on "destinations," which proceeds by stating that there are six destinations including the asura-body.

That intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the period during which a deceased being remains for seven days, or more than seven days, while looking toward the time of union of its future mother and father, and the conjunction of its future parents, within whichever existence it is to inhabit.

The discourse on the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) proceeds with the thought that "it exists. The discourse on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) proceeds with the idea that the fivefold objects of desire, such as visible forms, are themselves the "sensual realm" (*kāmadhātu*), rather than [the distinction between] objective desire (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*).

The discourse on the "five bases of desire" (*pañca-kāmāyatana*) [is similar]. The discourse on the "form realm" (*rūpadhātu*) [proceeds] with the idea that form-phenomena alone are the form realm. The discourse on the "formless realm" (*arūpadhātu*) [proceeds] with the idea that formless-phenomena alone are the formless realm.
Beings in the form realm possess the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) together with the nose and the other [faculties].
The discourse on the bases in the fine-material sphere has proceeded. There is also the discourse on the existence of subtle matter in the immaterial sphere.

There is the discourse on matter as karma by way of bodily and vocal intimation. There is the discourse on the life-faculty, which proceeds with the argument that the life-faculty is exclusively an immaterial dhamma dissociated from consciousness, and that there is no material life-faculty.
There is the discourse on the cause of karma, which proceeds with the argument that one falls away from Arahantship through the act of slandering the Noble Ones.

The discourse on the vision of benefits proceeds thus: "For one who does not see conditioned phenomena as disadvantageous by way of their impermanence and so forth, but sees Nibbāna as beneficial, there is the abandoning of the fetters.
The discourse on having the Deathless as its object proceeds thus:

"There is also a fetter that has Nibbāna as its object. The discourse on whether form has an object. The discourse on whether the underlying tendencies are without an object. The discourse on whether knowledge is without an object.

The two discourses on whether consciousness has a past object or a future object, and thus is without an object; the discourse on whether all consciousness is accompanied by applied thought (*vitakka*);
the discourse on the sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought, and whether that sound is cognizable by the ear;
and the discourse on whether speech proceeds even without consciousness, namely, the discourse on whether speech does not conform to the mind.
The discussion on bodily action proceeding even without consciousness (*citta*) is the discourse on how bodily action occurs independently of the mind.
The discussion on possession of the past and future is the discourse on how practitioners (*yogins*) are endowed with meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) belonging to both the past and the future.

The discussion on the cessation of the continuum is that in which wholesome and unwholesome states of consciousness arise while the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-citta*) has not yet ceased, and that in its absence, there is the cessation of the continuum.
The discussion on the cessation of what has arisen (*sivā*); the discussion on whether the form of intimation (*viññatti-rūpa*) is the path along with vocal expressions;

the discussion on whether there is cultivation of the path even for one possessing the fivefold sensory consciousness (*pañcaviññāṇa-samaṅgissa*); the discussion on whether the fivefold sensory consciousnesses are wholesome or unwholesome;
the discussion on whether the fivefold sensory consciousnesses involve mental effort (*sābhoga*); and [the discussion] on the mundane and supramundane [consciousness] at the moment of the path.

The discussion on how one is endowed with two types of virtue; the discussion on whether virtue is not a mental concomitant (*acetasika*); the discussion on whether virtue does not follow the mind (*cittānuparivatti*);
the discussion on the accumulation of merit caused by undertaking [precepts] which is dissociated from the mind (*cittavippayutta*); the discussion on whether intimation (*viññatti*) is virtue;
and the discussion on misconduct (*dussīlya*) that exists even without intimation, such as the taking of life and so forth.

The latent dispositions (*anusaya*) are indeterminate (*abyākata*), rootless (*ahetuka*), and dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*); thus there are three discourses on the latent dispositions.

Regarding the non-learner (*asekha*), because of the occurrence of a state dissociated from knowledge, it cannot be said that he is "possessed of knowledge"; this is the discourse on the occurrence of knowledge. Knowledge is dissociated from consciousness; this is the discourse on the limit of knowledge.

At the moment of the Path, the knowledge "this is suffering" occurs; this is the discourse on the limit of "this is suffering. Buddhas, by the power of their psychic potency (*iddhi*), [remain] for the duration of their lifespan.

The discourse on the power of psychic potency (*iddhibala*) proceeds with the statement that [the relics] remain even for a great eon (*mahākappa*). The discourse on concentration (*samādhi*) proceeds with the statement that concentration is a continuity of consciousness (*cittasantati*), not a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).

The discourse on the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*) proceeds with the statement that the stability of phenomena is something other than the factors of dependent origination such as ignorance (*avijjā*).
The discourse on impermanence (*aniccatā*) proceeds with the statement that impermanence is something other than material form (*rūpa*) and the rest.

The discourse that proceeds by stating that bodily and verbal action exists even without the restraints of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*). The discourse on karma that proceeds by stating that all karma produces its result (*vipāka*).
The discourse that proceeds by stating that sound is a result (*vipāka*). The discourse that proceeds by stating that the sixfold sense base (*saḷāyatana*) is a result.

The discourse that [asserts] one who is "at most seven times reborn" (*sattakkhattuparama*) even without the Path (*magga*). Likewise, this applies to the discourses on the "family-to-family" (*kolaṃkola*) and the "single-seed" (*ekabījika*). One endowed with right view (*diṭṭhisampanna*)...

The discourse on "taking life"; the discourse on "the miserable destination," which proceeds by stating that for one endowed with right view, the miserable destination—consisting of craving for form and so forth—is abandoned along with rebirth in states of deprivation;
and the discourse on "one bound to seven more existences," which proceeds by stating that for such a person, the miserable destination is not yet abandoned because craving still arises.

The "Discourse on the Duration of an Aeon" (Kappatthakathā) is so called because it explains that after performing an act such as causing a schism in the Saṅgha, one does not merely remain in hell for a lifespan equal to one part out of eighty parts of a great aeon (mahākappa)—which is the measure of time for such an act—but rather suffers in hell for the entire great aeon;

furthermore, even when the aeon itself is perishing, one continues to suffer in other world-systems (cakkavāḷa). [It also states that] a schismatic in the Saṅgha [is reborn in the Avihi hell], where the wholesome states of absorption (appanā-kusala) [are absent].
The discourse on the attainment of wholesome states concerns how one does not even obtain wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

The discourse on the application of immediate retribution concerns how one who instigates an immediate (*ānantariya*) deed, such as matricide, is fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), even in the absence of a command endowed with all its constituent factors.
The discourse on those things that are not fixed concerns how there are certain factors associated with the wholesome among even those things that are not fixed.

The discourse on the fixedness of the destined one (*niyata*). The discourse on being shrouded (*nivuta*) refers to the occurrence of the thought that one abandons the hindrances while the mind is indeed shrouded and concealed by the hindrances.
The discourse on what is present (*sammukhībhūta*) refers to the occurrence of the thought that one abandons only the fetter that has become manifest.

The discourse on one who has attained (*samāpanna*) enjoying [the attainment] refers to the occurrence of the thought that one who has entered meditative absorption enjoys the absorption through attachment to the object of that absorption.

The discourse on the occurrence of attachment to gratification regarding even painful feeling: "There is a feeling of gratification even in painful feeling. The discourse on whether craving for phenomena is indeterminate: "Craving for phenomena is indeterminate. The discourse on whether craving for phenomena is not the origin of suffering: "Craving for phenomena is not the origin of suffering. The discourse on the linking of wholesome and unwholesome states:
"A wholesome state arises immediately after an unwholesome one, or an unwholesome state arises immediately after a wholesome one."
The discourse on the arising of the six sense bases during the course of existence, stating that even for those in the womb, the six sense bases arise at the moment of rebirth-linking as a mere seed;
the discourse on the condition of contiguity, stating that the five types of sensory consciousness arise immediately one after another;

the discourse on the noble limit of form, stating that right speech and right action are intimation; the discourse on whether there is a latent tendency other than sensual lust and so forth; and the discourse on the obsession by defilements being dissociated from the mind.
Just as sensual lust is included within the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), so too are form-lust and formless-lust included within the form and formless planes;

such is the discourse on what is "included" (*pariyāpanna*). The two types of views constitute the discourse on the indeterminate (*abyākatantika*). The discourse on views being "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*).
That which is a cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for certain factors is not, in turn, a co-nascent or other such condition (*sahajāta-ādi-paccaya*) for them.

The discourse on conditionality as it occurs when one thing serves as a condition for another; the discourse on mutual conditionality as it occurs when ignorance is a condition for volitional formations, but volitional formations are not a condition for ignorance;
the discourse on time as it occurs when these [divisions of] time and duration are merely designations established by way of conceptual construction;
likewise the discourses on the moment, the instant, and the minute; and the discourse on the taints of another.

The discourse on the taints (*āsava*) concerning whether they exist or are without taints (*anāsava*). The discourse on aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) concerning whether the supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) possess aging and death or are supramundane.
The discourse on perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita*) concerning whether the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is supramundane.
The second discourse on perception and feeling concerning whether it is mundane (*lokiya*). [And the statement: "One who has entered the attainment of cessation might even pass away."
The third discourse on perception and feeling has been set in motion. The discourse concerning whether the attainment of cessation belongs to the category of non-percipient beings.
The discourse concerning whether there is an accumulation of karma distinct from the kamma itself that is dissociated from consciousness.
[And] that Buddhas and others who have attained power restrain the minds of beings through the power of their supernormal abilities so that passion and other defilements do not arise.

The discourse on the restraint of speech that has occurred. Thus, the discourse on grasping the minds of others for the arising of the wholesome. The discourse on the bestowing of happiness, which occurs with the thought that Buddhas grant happiness to others through their supernormal power (*iddhi*).

The discourse on the attention that grasps thoroughly, which occurs because one who attends to "formations are impermanent" apprehends all formations—divided into past and so forth—as a single object.
The discourse on whether matter has a cause; likewise, the discourse on whether matter is accompanied by a cause; the discourse on whether matter is wholesome or unwholesome;

the discourse on whether matter is a result of kamma—just as matter born of sense-sphere kamma belongs to the sense sphere, so too is the discourse on matter born of fine-material or immaterial-sphere kamma belonging to the fine-material or immaterial spheres;
and the discourse on how lust for the fine-material realm is included within the fine-material element, and lust for the immaterial realm is included within the immaterial element.

The discussion on whether there is an accumulation of merit for an Arahant; the discussion on whether there is no untimely death for an Arahant; the discussion on whether whatever arises, all this is due to karma;
the discussion on the occurrence that suffering is bound to the faculties alone, and not all conditioned phenomena;
the discussion on whether all conditioned phenomena are suffering, with the exception of the Noble Path; [the discussion on] the paths and fruits alone...
What is called the "Saṅgha" does not itself receive offerings; therefore, it should not be said that "the Saṅgha receives offerings.
Likewise, it should not be said that "the Saṅgha purifies offerings. It should not be said that "the Saṅgha eats.
It should not be said that "what is given to the Saṅgha yields great fruit. [The same applies to] the Buddhas...
They do not consume anything at all; therefore, it should not be said that what is given to a Buddha yields great fruit.
The discourse on the purification of the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) proceeds thus: "The gift is purified by the giver, not by the recipient.
Furthermore, Buddhas are reborn only in the Tusita heaven, not in the human world; for in this world, they merely display a manifested form (*nimmitarūpa*).
Discourse on human affairs that has arisen; discourse on the teaching of the Dhamma by a created form, [claiming] "it is not the Buddha" who teaches;
discourse on compassion, [claiming] "compassion is merely passion, and there is no compassion in the Buddhas beyond that";
discourse on fragrances, [claiming] "the excrement and urine of the Buddhas far surpass other types of fragrance"; [and the claim that] "the Buddhas [attain] by a single path..."
The discourse on the single path, which occurs as "they realize the four fruits of recluseship";
the discourse on the transition between jhānas, which occurs as "one passes from the first jhāna to the second jhāna and so forth without preliminary work (parikamma) and the like";
and [the view that] in the fivefold system, the jhāna consisting of vicāra alone without vitakka is not called a separate jhāna, but is called a "jhāna-interval" (jhānantarika).

The discussion on the intermediate jhāna has proceeded. The discussion on whether one who has attained meditative absorption hears sound. The discussion on whether consciousness sees form without the physical eye-faculty.
The discussion on the abandoning of defilements that has proceeded regarding the abandonment of defilements in the three periods of time. Emptiness, which is also designated as Nibbāna...

The discourse on emptiness proceeds by way of [the statement that] "it is included within the aggregate of mental formations" (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). The discourse ending with the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) proceeds by way of [the statement that] "only the unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) [is the fruit].
The discourse on attainment proceeds by way of [the statement that] "the unconditioned is the acquisition of certain phenomena.

The discourse on suchness proceeds by way of [the statement that] "suchness (*tathatā*), which is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of all phenomena, is the unconditioned. Nibbāna, too, [is so called] in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja*).

The Discussion on Wholesome Antitheses (*kusalantika-kathā*). The Discussion on the Absolute Certainty of an Ordinary Person (*puthujjana*), even in the absence of deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) and so forth.
The Discussion on the Faculties (*indriya-kathā*), which proceeds by stating that mundane faith and the rest are not [supramundane] faculties.

The Discussion on the Unintentional, which proceeds by stating that one may incur a deed of immediate retribution even without intending it. "An ordinary person possesses no knowledge" (*natthi puthujjanassa ñāṇaṃ*).

The discourse on knowledge proceeded thus: "It is the kamma of those in hell that strikes them in the form of the hell-wardens; there are no hell-wardens. The discourse on the hell-wardens proceeded thus:
"There are animals among the devas. The discourse on the path proceeded thus: "The three abstinences are dissociated from consciousness;
the path consists of five factors only. The discourse on knowledge proceeded thus: "Knowledge regarding dependent origination is supramundane."
The discourse on the Dispensation (*sāsanakathā*) concerning how the Teaching was made new by means of the three councils (*saṅgītiyo*).

The discourse on non-separation (*avivittakathā*) concerning how an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is not separated at any single moment from the phenomena belonging to the three realms. The discourse on fetters (*saṃyojanakathā*) concerning whether one becomes an Arahant even without abandoning some fetters caused by the obscuration of the knowable (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*).
[And the verse: "May conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) be permanent; may trees be endowed with eternal flowers, fruits, and so forth."

The discourse on supernatural power (*iddhi*) is presented as follows: "May they be secure," and so forth; herein, supernatural power proceeds according to one's intention. The discourse on the Buddhas is presented as follows:
there exists a variety [of characteristics] among the Buddhas other than mere differences in body, lifespan, and radiance.
The discourse on all directions is presented as follows: there are many Buddhas in all world-systems at a single moment. All phenomena (*dhamma*) are determined (*niyata*).
A discourse on the Dhamma was delivered. A discourse on karma was delivered, stating that all karmic actions are fixed in their yielding of results.

A discourse on final Nibbāna was delivered, stating that an Arahant, because he is not omniscient, attains final Nibbāna without having abandoned any fetter regarding the domain of the Omniscient One.
A discourse on wholesome consciousness was delivered, stating that an Arahant attains final Nibbāna with a wholesome state of mind. An Arahant...

The discourse on the imperturbable (*āneñja*) that concludes with "one who is established in the imperturbable attains final Nibbāna" is one such discussion. There are also three other discourses that have been set forth:
the realization of the Dhamma while lying in the womb, the attainment of Arahatship while lying in the womb, and the realization of the Dhamma and the attainment of Arahatship in a dream.
All dreams are of an indeterminate nature (*abyākata*), because of the momentariness of mental states.

The discussion on the absence of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). The discussion on momentariness, which maintains that all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*) last for only a single moment of consciousness.

The discussion on a single intention, which maintains that a monk who has reached a state of single intention by performing acts of worship, etc., with the thought, "I shall enjoy prosperity together with a woman," may engage in sexual intercourse. [Regarding] wicked monks...

The discourse on the appearance of Arahants refers to the occurrence of the claim that non-human beings engage in sexual intercourse under the influence of the appearance of Arahants while they themselves are engaging in sexual intercourse.

The discourse on sovereignty and acting according to one's will refers to the occurrence of the claim that certain beings go to the states of misery by virtue of their own sovereign power and the exercise of their will, rather than by the force of karma.
The discourse on resemblance refers to such statements as "lust is not like lust," and so forth.

The discussion on how the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth are not ultimately established (*aparinipphanna*)—namely, the "Discussion on the Unestablished in the Course of Existence"—consists of more than two hundred topics.
These have been analyzed in various ways according to the differences in the tenets of the schismatic schools, such as the Saṃmitīyas, by way of eight types of formal debates found in the Canon.
Yet all these discussions are merely discussions concerning the person (*puggala*). They [are distinguished] by way of the differences in their respective tenets.
Even when stated in brief, these would constitute an excessively voluminous work; therefore, they have not been expanded upon here.
However, those who desire that method should take it up in detail from the Pāḷi and its commentaries. This concludes the determination of the meaning together with the method of the Pāḷi.
The commentary on the meaning of the *Kathāvatthu* matrix within the *Mohavicchedanī*, the commentary on the meaning of the Abhidhamma matrices, is completed. 6.
The *Yamaka* Matrix.
Commentary on the Root Matrix of the Yamaka:

Now follows the method of commentary for the matrix of the *Yamaka*. This root matrix of the *Yamaka* is tenfold: the matrices of aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*sacca*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), consciousness (*citta*), phenomena (*dhamma*), and faculties (*indriya*).
In what sense is it called "the *Yamaka*"? It is in the sense of a pair (*yugaḷa*). For a pair is indeed called "the Twin Miracle" (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
Regarding the phrase "the twin sāla trees" (*yamakasālā*) and so forth: it is called "twin" (*yamaka*).

Because these ten [chapters] are taught by way of twins (*yāmaka*)—that is, pairs—and because this [work] is a detailed exposition (*niddesa*) that analyzes them, and because it is a compendium (*pakaraṇa*) of them all, it is named the *Yamaka*.
However, here, with reference to the *Niddesa-yamaka*, they are specifically termed the "Yamaka-mātikā. Of these...

Furthermore, among the ten pairs of matrices (*mātikā*), the Root Matrix (*mūlayamaka-mātikā*) is the first. Within that, the pair [of propositions] beginning with, "Whatever states are wholesome, all those have wholesome roots;
or whatever are wholesome roots, all those states are wholesome," is the first.
This is called the "Matrix of Meaning" (*atthayamaka*) because it functions by way of the two meanings designated as "wholesome roots," or because of those very [meanings].
The nature of the *yāmaka* (the "Pairs") should be understood in three ways: either as the *dhamma-yāmaka* by way of the Dhamma of the texts as they occur in direct and reverse order;
or as the *pucchā-yāmaka* by way of questions occurring in direct and reverse order. This same method applies to the others as well.

Now, regarding this Root *Yāmaka* Schedule (*mātikā*) taught by means of these *yāmakas*, [it shall be explained] first by way of the classification of the methods of the *yāmaka*, the questions, and the meaning-sections (*atthavāra*).
The establishment of the text should be understood as follows:

based on the opening phrase "wholesome states" in the wholesome-triad matrix (kusala-ttika-mātikā), there are four methods—the root method, the root-of-roots method, the rooted method, and the root-of-roots method.
Within each of these methods, there are three pairs (yamakas): the root-pair, the single-root-pair, and the mutual-root-pair. Thus, there are three pairs for each method.
There are twelve pairs (yamaka). In each pair, there are two questions according to the direct and reverse orders, making twenty-four questions in total.
For each question, there are two meanings according to the modes of certainty and doubt, making forty-eight meanings in all.
In this context, "whatever is wholesome" refers to the absence of doubt among wholesome states as to whether they are indeed wholesome or not.
In this phrase, the sense of certainty (*sanniṭṭhāna*) is to be understood. Regarding the phrase "all those roots of the wholesome" (*sabbe te kusalamūlā*):
because it was asked by way of doubt—namely, "Are all those wholesome phenomena indeed roots of the wholesome, or are they not?"—the sense of doubt (*saṃsayattha*) is to be understood in this phrase.
And that [doubt] was shown by the Blessed One at a point where there was doubt among those to be trained (*veneyya*), for the purpose of dispelling it.
Thus it was said; however, for the Tathāgata, there is no such thing as a point of doubt.

This same method applies to all subsequent questions as well. And just as these four modes and so forth arise based on the category of the wholesome (*kusala*), so too do they arise based on the unwholesome (*akusala*) category, and likewise based on the indeterminate (*abyākata*) category;
and having combined all three categories—the wholesome and the rest—they are explained together.
Based on the term "likewise" (*tath’eva*), it should be understood that within the four sections of the wholesome triad matrix (*kusalattika-mātikā*),
all sixteen methods (*naya*), forty-eight pairs (*yamaka*), ninety-six questions (*pucchā*), and nine thousand two hundred meanings (*attha*) are stated by way of enumeration (*uddesa*).

Up to this point, there are the Root Section (*mūlavāra*), the Cause Section (*hetuvāra*), the Source Section (*nidānavāra*), the Arising Section (*sambhavavāra*), and the Origin Section (*pabhavavāra*).

There are ten sections in total: the section on origination (samuṭṭhāna), the section on nutriment (āhāra), the section on object (ārammaṇa), the section on condition (paccaya), and the section on origin (samudaya).

In these, the remaining methods (nayas) and so forth should be understood according to the same delimitations as those presented in the section on roots (mūla-vāra). However, the text here is extremely abbreviated;
thus, in all ten sections, there are one hundred and sixty methods, plus eighty-four.
It should be understood that nine hundred and sixty pairs of *yamakas*, nine hundred and twenty questions, and one hundred and eight [sections] have been recited.
Thus, having understood here the determination of the text according to the classification of methods, pairs, questions, and sections of meaning, now—
The method for explaining the concise meaning, accompanied by the system of analysis (*vibhaṅga*), should be understood in this way according to the non-obvious word-meanings alone:
therein, "whatever" is an expression of totality. "Wholesome states" refers to those things that have blameless and pleasant results and lack the nature of a sentient being.
"Are all those wholesome roots? is the question asking whether they are all exclusively wholesome roots.
However, these [answers] are not present in the matrix of questions (*vissajjana-mātikā*).
For in the matrix of pairs (*yamaka-mātikā*), only the question-terms are set forth everywhere, not the answers.

Since the answers are stated only in the exposition (*niddesa*), we shall therefore demonstrate the method of answering everywhere according to the method of exposition alone. Regarding this very [section]: "Whatever wholesome states there are, all..."
This is the opening for the answer by way of analysis to the question, "Are those wholesome roots? [The answer is: "There are only three wholesome roots;
the remaining wholesome states are not wholesome roots. And this is its meaning: not all wholesome states are wholesome roots;
rather, only the three beginning with non-greed (alobha) are wholesome roots. Or, as for those which are wholesome roots...
The three beginning with non-greed (alobha) are stated to be the roots of wholesome states; the question is whether all those wholesome phenomena are themselves these three wholesome factors.
To that, the answer is: "Yes" (āmantā). The meaning is: "I accept that even the state of being wholesome belongs to those three roots.
This, first of all, is the root-yamaka method according to the root-system.

In the *Ekamūlayamaka* (The Pairs on a Single Root), however, all those [factors] should not be understood as "having a single root" (*ekamūlaka*) in the sense of numerical counting—that is, as having the same root by way of being wholesome roots—but rather they should be understood in the sense of identity.
For this is the meaning here: "All those have a single, identical root (*ekaṃ samānaṃ mūlaṃ*) by way of wholesome roots;
thus they are 'single-rooted' (*ekamūlā*). The question "Is that which is the root of contact the very same as the root of feeling and so forth? follows. Then...
The answer in the *Vibhaṅga*, "Yes (āmantā)," is given by way of accepting their state as such. Alternatively, the question is:
"Are all those phenomena which share the same root as the wholesome root (kusalamūla) themselves wholesome?

Now, matter (rūpa) originated by a wholesome consciousness shares the same root as the wholesome root, yet it is not itself wholesome; however, the class of phenomena such as contact (phassa) and so forth [share the same root and are wholesome].

"Both having a single root and being wholesome"—this is the answer. For just as non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] are the "root" for contact and the rest because they serve as the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) by way of establishing their firm foundation, so too are they the root for the materiality originated by them; thus that materiality is said to have the same root as the immaterial states.
However, it is not itself "wholesome," because it lacks the state of having blameless and pleasant fruition (*anavajja-sukha-vipākatā*). This is the method of the "Single-Root Couplet."
In the *Aññamaññamūlayamaka*, however, instead of asking, "Whatever states are wholesome," the question is asked: "Whatever states have a single root with a wholesome root"?

Why? It is for the purpose of showing that this same meaning can be expressed by this phrasing as well, and also for the purpose of including material form originated by the wholesome (*kusala-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa*).
"Mutually rooted" means: do all those [states] stand in the sense of being a mutual cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for one another?
The question is: "Are they root-conditions? The answer is: those two or three roots that arise together are both "single-root" (ekamūla) and "mutual-root" (aññamaññamūla);
the remaining form and non-form phenomena co-arising with the wholesome roots are "single-root" by virtue of the wholesome roots alone, but not "mutual-root.
According to the reverse method, all those—namely, non-greed and the others—are mutual-roots.
"Are they wholesome? is the question. "Yes," is the answer. This is the Root Method (Mūlanaya).

Just as in the Root Method there are sixfold methods of questioning and answering—namely, by way of the Root Yamaka, the Single-Root Yamaka, and the Mutual Root Yamaka—so too should it be understood in the Root-of-Roots Method and the others.
However, this is the distinction here: all of them are the roots of the roots of the wholesome.
All these are roots reckoned as wholesome roots; the meaning is simply "roots that are wholesome roots.
They are "those whose root-root is one" (*ekamūlamūlā*) in the sense of being identical; the meaning is simply "those whose root-root is the same.

They are "those whose root-root is mutual" (*aññamaññamūlamūlā*); "mutual root" means the root of one another, and they are "those whose root is that [mutual root]" in the sense of being its cause-condition.
The meaning is simply that they are mutually root-and-root. The rest is exactly the same. This concludes the Root-and-Root method (*mūlamūlanaya*).

In the Root-method (*mūlakanaya*), however, the question is: "Are all those roots of the wholesome? The answer is: "Yes, they are. [They are called] "roots of the wholesome" because they have a wholesome root in the sense of being a wholesome root by way of the condition of cause (*hetupaccaya*). [The verse continues: "Or else, those which are roots of the wholesome..."
"Are all those states wholesome?"—this is the question. "Setting aside whatever is form, the remainder is wholesome"—this is the answer;
the rest is exactly as before. This is the Root Method (*mūlakanaya*).

In the Root-of-Roots Method (*mūlamūlakanaya*), however, "rooted in wholesome roots" (*kusalamūlamūlaka*) means: those which have as their root that which is designated as a wholesome root are "rooted in wholesome roots. The rest is exactly as before.
This, then, is the method of posing questions and providing answers regarding the wholesome categories. This same method applies to the unwholesome categories and so forth.

However, this is the distinction: among the unwholesome categories, in the *Ekamūlayamaka* (Pairs on Single Roots), for the first question—"Are all unwholesome states those which have the same root as the unwholesome roots?"—the answer in the exposition is: "Unwholesome [states] that are rootless do not have the same root as the unwholesome roots."
It has been stated. Therein, the phrase "unwholesome without root" is said with reference to delusion (*moha*) within the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion.

Regarding the indeterminate (*abyākata*) roots in the *Ekamūlayamaka*, there is the question: "Whatever states are indeterminate, are they all rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root? and the answer:
"With the exception of the indeterminate that is without root, the rest are rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root. Therein—
"Rootless and indeterminate" refers to the eighteen rootless types of consciousness-arising, as well as material form and Nibbāna. Herein,
although material form originating from a rootless indeterminate consciousness also has the same roots as that indeterminate root itself,
it should be understood that this answer was given by treating that [material form] as a marginal case (*abbhohārika*) and by way of what is found together in the exposition (*niddesa*).
In the section on the roots of names (*nāmapadamūla*), there is the question: "Whatever states are names (*nāmadhamma*), are they all rooted in name?
and the answer: "There are nine roots of name; the remaining named states are not roots of name. However, in the method of the single root (*ekamūlanaya*) here, the question is:
"Whatever states are names, are they all rooted in the same root as name? [The answer is: "Excluding name that is rootless (*ahetuka*), the remainder are rooted in the same root as name."

"Single root" is the answer. In this context, "rootless" (ahetuka) should be understood by way of rootless consciousness-arising, doubt, restlessness, and the delusion associated with them, as well as Nibbāna.
The remainder is easy to understand throughout, following the sequence already stated under the section on the wholesome (kusala). This is the method for the section on roots (mūlavāra).
In the nine subsequent sections beginning with the section on causes (hetuvāra), the method of commentary is everywhere the same as in the section on roots.

The distinction here lies merely in the words "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth; and these, by way of being synonyms for the word "root" (*mūla*), have non-greed (*alobha*) and the others as their causes.
For non-greed and the rest are "roots" in the sense of being the foundation for their own fruit, which consists of co-nascent phenomena.
That which "goes toward" (*hinoti*) or proceeds toward the production of that fruit is the "cause" (*hetu*), like one who points [something out] saying, "Come, take this! It is his own...

It is called a *nidāna* because it lays down (*nideti*) the fruit. It is called a *sambhava* because the fruit arises (*sambhavati*) from it. It is called a *pabhava* because the fruit originates (*pabhavati*) from it.
It is called a *samuṭṭhāna* because the fruit arises (*samuṭṭhāti*) therein, or because it is by means of that. It is called an *āhāra* because it brings (*āharati*) that [fruit].

It is called an *ālambana* because it is clung to (*ālambīyati*) as something not to be rejected. It is called a *paccaya* because the fruit goes toward it (*paticca*) depending upon it. It is called a *samudaya* because the fruit emerges (*samudeti*) from it.
The origin. All [these terms]—“root, cause, and source”—are stated by way of synonyms for the causal condition; this verse is called the summary verse (*uddānagāthā*) for all ten sections.
This is the method of commentary on the meaning of the root-yamaka matrix (*mūlayamaka-mātikā*). [Now begins] the commentary on the meaning of the aggregate-yamaka matrix (*khandhayamaka-mātikā*).
The establishment of the text for the *Khandhayamaka-pāḷi* should be understood as follows:
beginning with the phrase "the five aggregates" and extending as far as the phrase "neither aggregates nor formations," this is called the *Khandhayamaka-mātikā*.

It is also called the "Section on Enumeration" (*Uddesavāra*) or the "Section on Questions" (*Pucchāvāra*) within the Section on Designations (*Paṇṇattivāra*). And that is the Section on the Purification of Terms (*Padasodhanavāra*).

It is adorned with four modes of treatment: the Mode of the Wheel for Purifying Terms (*padasodhana-mūla-cakkavāra*), the Mode of Pure Aggregates (*suddha-khandha-vāra*), and the Mode of the Wheel for Pure Aggregates (*suddha-khandha-mūla-cakkavāra*).

Among these, the Mode called the Purification of Terms proceeds by purifying the terms themselves according to the method beginning with, “Material form is the aggregate of material form; the aggregate of material form is material form,” and so forth.
It is twofold, by way of direct order (*anuloma*) and reverse order (*paṭiloma*). Of that—
In the section on the direct order (*anulomavāra*), there are five pairs (*yamaka*) such as: "Form is the aggregate of form; the aggregate of form is form," and so forth.

In the section on the reverse order (*paṭilomavāra*), there are likewise five sections beginning with: "That which is not form is not the aggregate of form; that which is not the aggregate of form is not form," and so forth.
Following that, in the section on the purification of those very terms (*padasodhanavāra*), regarding the aggregates thus purified, [it says]: "Form is the aggregate of form; the aggregates..."
By means of the method beginning with “the aggregate of feeling,” four wheels are bound for each individual aggregate.
Because there exist wheels based on the purification of terms, this is called the “Wheel Section Based on the Purification of Terms.
That too is twofold, by way of forward and reverse order. In its forward section: “Material form is the material-form aggregate; the aggregates...”
There are twenty pairs (yamakas) formed by taking each aggregate as the basis, such as "the feeling aggregate" and so forth, making four for each of the five aggregates.
In the reverse order as well, there are likewise twenty, such as "neither form nor the form aggregate; neither aggregates nor the feeling aggregate," and so forth.
Following that, it proceeds according to the method of the pure aggregates alone, beginning with "form is an aggregate; aggregates are form," and so on.
This is called the Section on Pure Aggregates (*suddhakhandhavāra*). It is also twofold, according to the direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*paṭiloma*) orders.

In its direct order, there are five pairs (*yamaka*), such as "matter is an aggregate; aggregates are matter," and so forth. In its reverse order, there are likewise five pairs, such as "not matter is not an aggregate; not aggregates is not matter," and so forth.

Following that, having bound four wheels based on each individual aggregate by way of such methods as "form is an aggregate" and "feeling is an aggregate" with respect to those same pure aggregates, one proceeds;
this is called the "Section on Wheels Based on Pure Aggregates" because of the existence of wheels based on pure aggregates. That too is twofold, according to the direct and reverse orders.

In its positive section (*anulomavāra*), there are twenty pairs (*yamaka*) consisting of four sets each based on each individual aggregate (*khandha*), such as: "Form is an aggregate; aggregates are feeling," and so forth.
In its negative section (*paṭilomavāra*), there are likewise twenty pairs, such as: "Not form is not an aggregate; not aggregates are not feeling," and so forth.
Thus, here in the four sections of the method (*nayavāra*), there is one hundred pairs and two hundred questions.
It should be understood that four hundred meanings have been indicated by taking two meanings each— based on resolution and doubt— for each single question.
Having thus understood the establishment of this text,
there now follows the method of commentary on the concise meaning together with the analytical system (*vibhaṅga-naya*), according to the sequence of the unexplained word-meanings.
It should be understood in this way. "The five aggregates" is the enumeration of the aggregates to be asked about by way of pairs.
"The aggregate of form... [pe] ...the aggregate of consciousness" is the definition of their names according to their specific divisions.
Following that are the four methodical sections beginning with the section on the purification of terms. Therein, regarding "form is the aggregate of form," whatever is called "form"—

It is called "the aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandha*). This question is for the purpose of clarifying the statement: "Does everything that is called 'form' constitute the aggregate of form? And its answer, according to the method of exposition (*niddesanaya*), is:
"That which is pleasant in form and agreeable in form is 'form,' but it is not the aggregate of form; the aggregate of form is both form and the aggregate of form.
In this context, regarding the terms "pleasant in form," "agreeable in form," and so forth, that which is called "form"—

That which was mentioned is indeed *rūpa*, but it is not the *rūpakkhandha*. However, that which is called the "form aggregate" (*rūpakkhandha*) may appropriately be called both "form" (*rūpa*) and "form aggregate" (*rūpakkhandha*); this is the meaning.
Regarding the statement "The form aggregate is form," the response here is "Yes" (*āmantā*), because the form aggregate must necessarily be called "form. As for "feeling is the feeling aggregate":
Regarding the question, "Is the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha) feeling (vedanā)? the answer is "Yes.

Regarding the question, "Is perception (saññā) the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha)? the answer is: "The perception of conceptual proliferation (papañca-saññā) and so forth, as mentioned in such passages, is perception but not the aggregate of perception;
the aggregate of perception is both perception and the aggregate of perception. And regarding the question, "Is the aggregate of perception perception? the answer is "Yes."

The answer: To the question, "Are formations (saṅkhārā) the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)?", the answer is: "The aggregate of formations mentioned in such passages as 'Impermanent indeed are formations' is the aggregate of formations;
the remaining conditioned phenomena (saṅkhatadhammā) are formations, but not the aggregate of formations.
To the question, "Is the aggregate of formations formations?", the answer is: "Yes. [As for] "consciousness (viññāṇa), is it the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha)?":
Regarding the question, the consciousness aggregate is "consciousness," and the answer to that question is "Yes.
In the reverse order, for the question "Is it not matter? Is it not the matter aggregate? the answer is "Yes";

the meaning is that those phenomena denoted by the term "matter" are not the matter aggregate. For the question "Is it not the matter aggregate? Is it not matter? [the answer refers to] those things devoid of the matter aggregate.
The response is: those phenomena described as "having a pleasant nature" and "having a gratifying nature" are not the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), yet they are form;
however, those phenomena devoid of the aggregate of form that has a pleasant nature and a gratifying nature are neither the aggregate of form nor form.

This is the answer to the questions: "Is it not feeling? Is it not the aggregate of feeling? and "Is it not the aggregate of feeling? Is it not feeling? and "Is it not perception? Is it not the aggregate of perception? and so forth.
And the answer is: “Yes. To the question, “Are they not formations (saṅkhārā) and yet not the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)? the answer is: “Yes.

However, to the question, “Is it not the case that the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) is not perception (saññā)? [the answer is: Wrong-view-perception (diṭṭhisaññā) is not the aggregate of perception, but it is perception;
and apart from that wrong-view-perception and the aggregate of perception, the remainder is neither perception nor the aggregate of perception.
The answer: To the question, "Are they not formations (saṅkhārā) and not the formation aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha)?", the answer is, "Yes.

To the question, "Is that which is not the formation aggregate not a formation?", [the answer is: with the exception of the formation aggregate, the remaining conditioned phenomena (saṅkhatadhammā) are not the formation aggregate but are formations;
however, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatā dhātu) is neither a formation nor the formation aggregate.
The answer: To the question, "Is consciousness not the consciousness aggregate? and to the question, "Is the consciousness aggregate not consciousness?
the answer is, "Yes" (*āmantā*). By this same method, the way of answering should be understood for all subsequent cases;
we shall, however, state only the specific differences.
In the Wheel-Section on the Root of Purifying the Categories (*padasodhanamūlacakkavāra*), however, this is the distinction:
the question is, "Are all aggregates (khandhā) the feeling-aggregate (*vedanākkhandho*)? The answer to that is: "The feeling-aggregate is both an aggregate and the feeling-aggregate;
but the remaining aggregates are aggregates, not the feeling-aggregate. This same method applies to the others as well.
In the reverse order, however, to the question "Are they not aggregates, nor the feeling-aggregate? the answer is "Yes.
Here, those phenomena designated as Nibbāna, which are not even aggregates, are also not the feeling-aggregate;
therefore, the answer is "Yes. The rest is easily understood. This concludes the Wheel of the Root-Analysis of Terms.

In the section on the Pure Aggregates (*suddhakhandhavāra*), however, regarding the question "Is form an aggregate? the answer is "Yes," because forms such as the "lovely form" (*piyarūpa*) and so forth are included within the five aggregates. In expressions such as "The aggregates are form," the meaning should be understood as: "Whatever are the aggregates, all those are the aggregate of form," and so on.
For it is precisely for this reason that in its own exposition (*niddesa*), it says "The aggregates are form," and so forth.
Without picking up the term [“aggregate”] itself, the answer was given by picking up the terms according to their meaning as “the aggregates: the aggregate of form,” and so forth, stating:
“The aggregate of form is both an aggregate and the aggregate of form; the remaining aggregates are aggregates but not the aggregate of form.
For that very reason, it is called the “pure aggregate section. For here, unlike in the “purification of expression,” there is no concern with the literal wording.
The measure is as follows: however the pure aggregates (khandhas) are obtained, in that very way the meaning is the measure.
This same method applies further on in the *Āyatana-yamaka-mātikā* and so forth. In the reverse order, the question "Is it not form, not an aggregate?
asks whether that class of phenomena which is not form is also not an aggregate; the answer to that is: "The aggregates excluding the aggregate of form..."
The answer is: "It is not form; likewise, Nibbāna is neither form nor an aggregate. The remainder is easy to understand. This concludes the section on the Pure Aggregates (*suddhakhandhavāra*).

Regarding the Wheel Section based on the Pure Aggregates (*suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāra*), the meaning should be understood according to the method explained below, starting with "The aggregates: the feeling-aggregate," and so forth. This is the method for the Section on Designations (*paṇṇattivāra*).
However, since in the *Niddesa* [the commentary], after stating the exposition known as the Section on Designations for this matrix (*mātikā*), from that...

Setting aside this sequence of the matrix (mātikā), there are two other great sections—namely, the "Section on Occurrence" and the "Section on Full Understanding"—which, by another method, are stated in the form of questions and answers and are devoid of the formal headings (uddesavāra). Therefore, the method for both of these sections must be shown.
First, regarding the Section on Occurrence, here is a mere indication of its scope, preceded by an establishment of the textual framework (pāḷivavatthāna).
For in this context there are three intermediate sections: the section on arising, the section on cessation, and the section on arising-and-cessation.

Regarding the section on arising, there are six temporal divisions based on the three time periods: the present, the past, the future, the past by means of the present, the future by means of the present, and the future by means of the past. Thus, among these six temporal divisions—
Regarding this first [section] on the present, there are three permutations: by way of person (*puggala*), by way of location (*okāsa*), and by way of person-and-location (*puggalokāsa*).

Therein: "Does the aggregate of feeling arise for that same person for whom the aggregate of form arises? For those beings reborn among the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the aggregate of form arises, but the aggregate of feeling does not arise for them.
For those being reborn in the five-aggregate realm, both the aggregate of form arises and the aggregate of feeling arises.

Or, for whomsoever the aggregate of feeling arises, does the aggregate of form arise for them? For those being reborn in the immaterial realm, the aggregate of feeling arises, but the aggregate of form does not arise for them. [In the case of] the five-aggregate realm...
“For those who are being reborn, the aggregate of feeling arises and the aggregate of form arises. For whom the aggregate of form arises...

[as before] ...for him the aggregate of consciousness arises... [as before] ...or conversely, for whom the aggregate of consciousness arises, for him the aggregate of form arises... [as before] ...[this applies to] the five-aggregate realm... [as before] ...it arises. Thus.

There are four based on the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*); three based on the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) in the manner of “for whom the aggregate of feeling arises, for him the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*) arises,” and so forth; two based on the aggregate of perception; and one based on the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Thus, these ten pairs (*yamaka*) in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*) regarding the present time follow the method of positive concomitance (*anulomanaya*). Among them:

Among the four [questions] rooted in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), only the first was answered in the text; the remaining ones were abbreviated for the sake of brevity in the tradition, as their answers are identical to it.
However, in all instances concerning the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and the others, the answer is uniformly the same: "Yes" (*āmantā*). Regarding feeling and the rest...
Because perception and the other [aggregates] necessarily arise when [the first aggregate] has arisen, all [of them] are condensed therein.

And just as there are ten pairs in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*), so too in the section on bases (*okāsavāra*) one should recite: "Where the aggregate of form arises, does the aggregate of feeling arise there?
In the case of non-percipient beings there... pe... in the fivefold plane there... pe... it arises," and so forth; likewise in the section on persons and bases (*puggalokāsavāra*).
“For whom the aggregate of form arises in a certain place, does the aggregate of feeling arise there for that person?

“For non-percipient beings... [and so on] ...for those in the five-aggregate realm... it arises,” and so forth. In the section concerning the present time, there are thirty pairs (yamakas) in the method of positive order (*anulomanaya*).
Just as there are thirty in the method of positive order, so too in the method of negative order (*paṭilomanaya*): “For whom the aggregate of form does not arise...”
Does the feeling aggregate not arise for that person? For those being reborn in the formless realm, the material aggregate does not arise, but the feeling aggregate does not fail to arise for them.
For all those passing away, neither the material aggregate nor the feeling aggregate arises. Or, for whomsoever the feeling aggregate does not arise...

“Does the aggregate of form not arise for that person? For those being reborn among the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the aggregate of feeling does not arise, yet the aggregate of form does not fail to arise for them.
For all those passing away, neither the aggregate of feeling nor the aggregate of form arises—and so forth—“wherever the aggregate of form does not arise...”
In that context, regarding the question "Does the aggregate of feeling not arise?"—it does arise. Or again, "Where... does it not arise?"—it does arise. And so forth;
and likewise, "For whom, where the aggregate of form does not arise, for him there the aggregate of feeling does not arise...
[and so on]... for all those passing away, both of these do not arise. Thus there are thirty pairs (yamakas). In this way, during the present time...
Sixty pairs [of questions], twice that many inquiries, and twice that many meanings are to be understood.
In this context, "for whom the aggregate of form arises" means for whichever person the aggregate of form arises at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"For him, the aggregate of feeling" means that the aggregate of feeling also arises for that same person at that very same moment.
The meaning is by this same method. In that context, regarding "non-percipient beings" (*asaññasatta*):

for those who are reborn by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) into the non-percipient state of existence, at the moment of their arising, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) arises; however, because they are mindless, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) does not arise.
By this same method, [the meaning should be understood] in the questions and answers beginning with "or for whom the aggregate of feeling," and so forth.
From this point on, the meaning should be understood everywhere else as well.
However, here is the characteristic of fixed necessity regarding arising and cessation:

for throughout this entire *Khandhayamaka*, in whatever instances beings arise, [the analysis concerns] the aggregates during their course of existence until death, or [their occurrence] without limit.
Although arising and cessation are present even in phenomena that undergo rapid change, it is not easy to demonstrate their arising and cessation by isolating them.

Therefore, without referring to arising and cessation during the course of existence (*pavatti*), the section on arising is explained solely by way of the arising of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and the section on cessation is explained solely by way of cessation at the time of death. Thus, regarding arising and cessation here—
Having understood the characteristic of determination (*niyāma*) and having grasped both the arising of rebirth-linking and the cessation of death,
the analysis of the meaning of the questions and answers occurring in those various places should be understood.
In the reverse method, however, "of all those passing away" refers to those possessed of the moment of dissolution of the death-consciousness.
For in those [beings], the aggregate of form does not arise there, and the aggregate of feeling has already arisen at the very moment of the arising of the death-consciousness.
Regarding the question, "Where the aggregate of form does not arise, there the aggregate of feeling does not arise," this answer,
"It arises," was given with reference to the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), as it pertains to the immediately following question.
It should be understood that the answer "it arises" is given with reference to non-percipient existence (*asaññibhava*). The remainder is indeed easy to understand;
this is the method regarding the present time.
And just as there are sixty pairs and so forth in the present time, so too [should they be applied] individually to each of the remaining five divisions of time.
It should be understood. Regarding the questions and answers here, although it is stated in such ways as:
"For whom the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) had arisen, had the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) arisen for him? Yes," and so forth; and also:
"Where the aggregate of form had arisen, had the aggregate of feeling arisen there? It had arisen in the five-aggregate realm (pañcavokāra), but not elsewhere," and so forth.
“Is it the case that for whomsoever the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) had arisen in a certain place, for that person the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) had also arisen there?

“For those of the five-aggregate realm (pañcavokāra), it had arisen there; not elsewhere,” and so forth, according to the method of positive concomitance (anulomanaya) in the past time; and [the negative concomitance]:
“Is it the case that for whomsoever the aggregate of form had not arisen, for that person the aggregate of feeling had not arisen? “There is none,” and so forth.

“Where the aggregate of form had not arisen, had the aggregate of feeling not arisen there? “It had arisen,” and so forth. “In whom, where the aggregate of form had not arisen, had the aggregate of feeling not arisen there for them? “For those non-percipient beings, the aggregate of form had not arisen there, but for them [the aggregate of feeling] had not [necessarily] arisen...
For those of the Suddhāvāsa [heaven], the aggregate of form had not arisen there...”
In that regard, [it is stated] in three sections by way of reverse order, beginning with "Both of those did not arise there," and [also] by way of forward order, beginning with:
"For whom the aggregate of form will arise, for him the aggregate of feeling will arise? Yes. And:
"Where the aggregate of form will arise, there the aggregate of feeling will arise... [and so on] ...in the five-aggregate realm."

By means of such statements as “it will arise,” and by means of the forward method regarding the future time, such as: “For whomsoever the aggregate of form will arise there, for that person the aggregate of feeling will arise there...
[and so on]... For those of the five-aggregate realm, for them it will arise there”; and [by means of the counter-method]:
“For whomsoever the aggregate of form will not arise, for that person the aggregate of feeling will not arise?”
“For those who, having been reborn in the formless realm, will attain final nibbāna, the aggregate of form will not arise, but the other [aggregates] will;
for those in their final existence, neither of these two will arise. And so on, including:
“Wherever the aggregate of form will not arise, there the aggregate of feeling will not arise,” and so on, and: “In whomsoever, wherever the aggregate of form will not arise...”
“Will the aggregate of feeling not arise for him there? [The answer is: “For those non-material beings (arūpa), the aggregate of form will not arise there, but not the other;
for those in their final existence (pacchimabhavika), neither of the two will arise,” and so forth by way of the reverse method; and also by way of the forward method:
“For whom the aggregate of form arises, for him the aggregate of feeling has arisen,” and so forth, as well as: “Where... [the aggregate of form arises]...”
“The aggregate of form arises; therein, has the aggregate of feeling arisen? … [and so on] … “It arises in the five-aggregate realm,” and so forth.
“For whom, wherever the aggregate of form arises, for them has the aggregate of feeling arisen there?
For those being reborn in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) or among the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), the aggregate of form arises there, but [the aggregate of feeling has not arisen].”

“In those [beings], the aggregate of feeling had arisen there; however, in the five-aggregate realm, it had arisen,” and so forth—this is the method of positive concomitance (*anulomanaya*) regarding the past by means of the present. Furthermore: “For whom the aggregate of form does not arise, for him the aggregate of feeling did not arise,” and so forth;
and: “Where the aggregate of form does not arise, there the aggregate of feeling did not arise? It had arisen,” and so forth.
“For whom the aggregate of form does not arise at a certain place, for them has the aggregate of feeling not arisen there?
For those passing away from the five-aggregate realm and for those in the formless realm, the aggregate of form does not arise there;

yet it is not the case that for them the aggregate of feeling had not arisen there. [This is true] for those attaining final nibbāna in the Suddhāvāsa heavens and for those passing away from the realm of non-percipient beings.
In the reverse order, by such statements as, "For them, neither the aggregate of form nor the aggregate of feeling arises there," and in the forward order,
by such statements as, "For whom the aggregate of form arises, will the aggregate of feeling arise for them?
For those final-existence beings who are being reborn in the five-aggregate realm, the aggregate of form arises for them," and so forth, [and] "Where the aggregate of form..."
And by such passages as, "When the aggregate of form arises there, will the aggregate of feeling arise there? In the five-aggregate realm...
it will arise," and "For whom the aggregate of form arises there, will the aggregate of feeling arise there for them?
For those in their final existence in the five-aggregate realm... it will arise," [the relationship] between the present and the future time is shown.
In the forward order (*anulomanaya*): “For whom the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) does not arise, will the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) not arise for them?
[The answer is: “It will not arise for those attaining final nibbāna in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra*) and for those in their final existence in the formless realm (*arūpa*).
And so forth. “Where the aggregate of form does not arise, will the aggregate of feeling not arise there? “It will arise. And so forth.
And in the reverse method: “For whom the aggregate of form does not arise at a certain place, for them the aggregate of feeling will not arise there… [etc.

…for those attaining final nibbāna in the five-aggregate realm, for those in their final existence in the formless realm, and for those passing away from the non-percipient beings—at these places for them… [etc. …it will not arise,” and so forth.

“For whom the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) had arisen, will the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) arise for him?”—“It will arise for those in their final existence,” and so forth; “Where the aggregate of form had arisen, will the aggregate of feeling arise there?
… “In the five-aggregate realm it will arise,” and so forth; “For whom, wherever the aggregate of form had arisen, for him there…”
“Will the aggregate of feeling arise? [The answer is: “For those in the final existence in the five-aggregate realm, for non-percipient beings... it will arise,” and so forth;
thus, by means of the past, there is the method of positive concomitance (*anulomanaya*) regarding the future time.
[And conversely: “For whom the aggregate of form had arisen, will the aggregate of feeling arise for them? “There is none. And so forth; “Where the aggregate of form had not arisen...”
In that regard, [the question] "Will the aggregate of feeling not arise? is answered with "It will arise," and so forth;

and [the question] "For whom, where the aggregate of form has not arisen, for them there will the aggregate of feeling not arise?"... [etc. ...is answered with "For the inhabitants of the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) and for those in their final existence in the formless realm (arūpa), for them there neither has the aggregate of form arisen nor will the aggregate of feeling arise," and so forth.
Furthermore, pure specific meanings are found in the reverse order as well. Nevertheless, for fear of excessive length in the text, we shall not demonstrate them in their entirety;
for by the method already shown, a wise person is able to understand the questions and answers in all instances. This is the method regarding the section on arising (uppādavāra).

And just as in the section on Arising (uppādavāra), there are six sections for each of the six divisions of time— each consisting of six sections according to the individual person (*puggala*) and so forth, by way of direct order, reverse order, and both combined— and since there are ten pairs (*yamaka*) in each section,

making sixty pairs in total, and all these amount to three hundred and sixty pairs, with twice that number of questions and twice that number of meanings, so it is also in the section on Cessation (*nirodhavāra*).

They should also be understood in the sections on arising and cessation. In that regard, [the analysis proceeds] by way of such statements as: “For whom the aggregate of form ceases, does the aggregate of feeling cease for him?... [and so on]... for those passing away from the five-aggregate plane... it ceases,” and:
