“For whom the aggregate of form does not cease, does the aggregate of feeling not cease for him?... [and so on]... for all those being reborn... [and so on].”
In the section on cessation, beginning with the words "it does not cease," it is asked: "Does the aggregate of feeling cease for one in whom the aggregate of form arises?
"No. "Does the aggregate of feeling not cease for one in whom the aggregate of form does not arise? ... [and so on] ...

"For those being reborn in the immaterial realm and for those passing away from the sphere of non-percipient beings, the aggregate of form does not arise, and the aggregate of feeling [does not cease]."

And by the passage beginning with “nor does it cease,” the method of posing questions and providing answers throughout the entire section on arising and cessation should be understood according to the sequence explained below;
this is the method for the section on occurrence (*pavatti*).

However, in the section on full understanding (*pariññā*), among the three sections—the section on persons (*puggala*), etc.—only the section on persons is found, and not the sections on planes (*okāsa*) or on persons and planes.
Because they involve the presentation of similar [cases]. For any person whatsoever who fully understands form and so forth remains exactly the same even when ceased anywhere;
therefore, regarding the six divisions of time, there are two sets each from the perspective of the person in the forward order (*anuloma*).
Calculating ten for each set, there are twenty pairs (*yamaka*) per set, which makes one hundred pairs. The questions are double that number.
And it should be understood that there are twice as many [questions] as that.

In this regard, starting from the three time periods, all questions are to be formulated in both direct and reverse order, beginning with: “He who fully understands the aggregate of form, does he also fully understand the aggregate of feeling?”—“Yes, he does”—and so forth; and also: “He who does not fully understand the aggregate of form, does he also not fully understand the aggregate of feeling?”—“Yes, he does not”—and so forth.

The answer to both [questions] is simply: “Yes, yes. However, regarding the other three mixed periods, for the two other periods as well, in the method of positive sequence (*anulomanaya*), the answers to the questions—“He who fully understands the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) has fully understood the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*)?
and “Or he who... [etc.]?”—are simply: “No, no.”
In the reverse order, however: "Is it the case that whoever does not fully understand the aggregate of form did not fully understand the aggregate of feeling?
An Arahant does not fully understand the aggregate of form, yet he has not failed to fully understand the aggregate of feeling.
With the exception of one who possesses the highest path and an Arahant, all remaining persons neither fully understand the aggregate of form nor have they fully understood the aggregate of feeling."

By the passage beginning with "they did not fully understand," [it is asked]: "Will he who does not fully understand the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) not fully understand the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha)?
Those who will attain the path do not fully understand the aggregate of form, yet they will not fail to fully understand the aggregate of feeling.
[This includes] the Arhats and those worldlings (puthujjana) who will not attain the path; they [do not fully understand] both the aggregate of form and..."

"...they do not fully understand [it], and they will not fully understand the aggregate of feeling," and so forth; and: "Is it the case that whoever did not fully understand the aggregate of form will not fully understand the aggregate of feeling?

Those who will attain the Path did not fully understand the aggregate of form, yet they will not fail to fully understand the aggregate of feeling. [This is true] for one who possesses the Supreme Path (*agga-magga*)."

And the method of answering the questions should be understood through such passages as: "Those worldlings who will not attain the path have not fully understood the aggregate of form, and they will not fully understand the aggregate of feeling," and so forth.
And herein, in the section on the process of existence (*pavatti*), the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are treated by way of death and rebirth-linking.
They are not obtained; they are obtained only by way of the moments of consciousness during the course of existence.
For at the moment of the supramundane path, through the mind having Nibbāna as its object, there is the fulfillment of the function of full understanding regarding the five aggregates.

When one fully understands any one aggregate, one is said to "fully understand" the others as well; thus, in the questions on conformity, the function of full understanding has reached its culmination.
With reference to one who possesses the highest path (*aggamagga-samaṅgī*), the answer "Yes" was stated.
It should be understood that in the reverse questions, "Does he not fully understand? the answer "Yes" was stated with reference to worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others.

However, in this section concerning the past time—"Has he fully understood?"—even though one is established in the highest fruit immediately following the path, because the function of full understanding has already been completed, [the answer is "No"].
“Has fully understood” (parijānittha) indeed means this. One who “fully understands” is said to be one possessing the supreme path (aggamagga-samaṅgī);

**Exposition of the Matrix of the Pairs on Formations** The divisions of the Great Section and so forth in the Matrix of the Pairs on Formations (*saṅkhāra-yamaka-mātikā*) should be understood according to the method already explained above.
However, there is this distinction here: first, regarding the matrix, just as the aggregates and other phenomena were previously enumerated, [it begins with] "form" (*rūpa*).

The section on the purification of terms beginning with “the aggregate of form” (*rūpakkhandha*) has been commenced; however, instead of commencing in that manner, the first three formations (*saṅkhāra*) were analyzed and shown by way of the passage beginning, “In-breathing and out-breathing are the bodily formation. In this context, the formation of the body is the “bodily formation,” namely, in-breathing and out-breathing.
This is because of the statement: “These states are bodily, being bound up with the body,” which refers to the material body (*karajakāya*) acting as the cause.
This formation is called "bodily formation" because it has become the fruit of the body. According to another method: it is called a "formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it is formed (*saṅkharīyati*).
By what is it formed? By the body. For this [breath] is formed by the physical body made of the four great elements, just as air is [formed] in a bellows;
thus, it is a "formation of the body," meaning it is a bodily formation. The meaning is that it is the wind of inhalation and exhalation produced by the body. Having reflected with the mind...

Having reflected, one subsequently breaks forth into speech; therefore, because of the statement, "Initial application and sustained application are the verbal formation" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*), it is called a "formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it forms. What does it form? Speech. It is a verbal formation because it is a formation by means of speech; this is the name for the pair of initial application and sustained application which originates the breaking forth of speech.
"Perception and feeling—these mental states are bound to the mind."
Furthermore, it is called a *saṅkhāra* because it is conditioned by speech itself in the third instance. By what is it conditioned? By the mind.
Thus, it is the "volitional formation of mind" (*cittasaṅkhāra*). This is a designation for all mental factors (*cetasika*) that originate from the mind.
However, because initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) are taken separately due to their status as verbal formations (*vacīsaṅkhāra*), [they are not included here].
“Excluding applied thought and sustained thought” has been stated.

There are twelve pairs (yamaka) consisting of the direct order and the reverse order. However, in the section on pure formations (suddhasaṅkhāra),

Two [formulas] are based on the bodily formation, and one is based on the verbal formation; thus three in the direct order and three in the reverse order—six pairs (yamakas) are stated. For what reason?
Because there is no difference in meaning when taken according to each single term of the "pure" (suddhika) set. However, the distinction is this:
the term "bodily formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra) yields the same meaning through both terms [of the pair]; therefore, it is not [treated as two separate items] according to each single term.

It was stated: "The body is a bodily formation," and so forth; however, that method was also explained in the section on the purification of terms (*padasodhanavāra*) because even without a specific meaning, the expression is logically consistent.

This is because the answers consist of the very terms "body" and so forth being designated by names such as "bodily formation" and so on; for it is not the case that the body and so forth [are themselves the formations].
It is like the name for bodily formations and so forth. In the reverse order, however, the meaning of the question is:

"Is it not the body, nor is it a bodily formation?"—that is to say, that which is not the body is also not a bodily formation. To this [the answer is]: "The bodily formation is not the body, yet it is a bodily formation.
Thus, the bodily formation is not the body, but it is indeed a bodily formation; [it refers to] both the body and the bodily formation.
Excluding the remainder—all that is divided into the conditioned, the unconditioned, and so forth—the answer is: "It is neither body nor bodily formation.
This same method applies to the remaining [questions] as well; and regarding the other positive and negative [formulations]:
"Is body a bodily formation? "No. "Are formations verbal formations? "Verbal formations are both formations and verbal formations; the remainder..."

“Are volitional formations not verbal volitional formations, and are they neither volitional formations nor verbal volitional formations?”—the method of posing and answering questions throughout [this section] should be understood in this manner.
However, in the section on the process of occurrence (*pavatti*), [it asks]:
“When bodily volitional formation arises for someone, does verbal volitional formation arise for that person?”—[the answer being] “No. Without...

At the moment of the arising of inhalation and exhalation through initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) arises for them, but not the other.
However, for those sense-sphere beings (*kāmāvacara-satta*) possessing a mind with both initial and sustained application, both of these arise. Or rather, for whom...

[etc. ...does it arise? For those bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpabhavika*), at the moment of the arising of initial and sustained application, only the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) arises.
...arises, but not the other... [and so on] ...however, for those belonging to the aforementioned sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), both of these arise.
For whom bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) arises, for that person does mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) arise? Yes, it does... [and so on] ...or rather, for whom... [and so on] ...arises...
[and so on] ...at the moment of arising of inhalation and exhalation, both of these arise. For whom verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) arises...
Does mental formation arise for him? Yes... [etc. ... Where bodily formation arises, does verbal formation arise there?
For beings of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) in the second and third jhānas, only bodily formation arises there, not the other;
however, in the first jhāna and so forth, both of these arise. Or, where... [etc. ...

Does it arise? It arises in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), not in the fine-material or immaterial realms (*rūpa-ārūpabhava*). Where the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) arises, does the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) arise there?

Yes. Or conversely... where does it arise? For beings of the sense-sphere realm, in the fourth jhāna, and in the fine-material and immaterial realms, only the mental formation arises there, not the other; [it does not arise] in the other jhānas and so forth.
"But both of those arise," and so forth;
[and] "For one in whom bodily formation does not arise, does verbal formation not arise?

At the moment of the arising of applied thought and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) without inhalation and exhalation, for them only the bodily formation does not arise, not the other, because [it arises] with all consciousness..."

At the moment of dissolution, in the absence of inhalation and exhalation, at the moment of arising of a consciousness without applied thought and sustained thought, and for those who have attained cessation and non-percipient beings—neither of these two arises... [and so on] ...for whom bodily formation does not arise, for him mental formation does not arise...
[and so on] ...at the moment of dissolution of all consciousnesses, and for those who have attained cessation and non-percipient beings.

And by such passages as, “It does not arise,” and so forth; and by such passages as, “Where bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) does not arise, there verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) does not arise… [etc.
…at the moment of the fourth jhāna, or in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), and so forth, it does not arise”;
and by such passages as, “For whom bodily formation had arisen, for him verbal formation had arisen? Yes,” and so forth; and “For whom bodily formation had not arisen…” [and so on].
“Did his mental formation not arise?”—[the answer being] “No,” and so forth;

and likewise: “For whomsoever bodily formation had not arisen in a certain place, for him verbal formation had not arisen there…pe… For those who have attained the fourth jhāna, for the Suddhāvāsa deities while their second moment of consciousness is occurring, and for non-percipient beings—for them, in that state, both bodily formation and verbal formation had not arisen,” and so forth.
“For whom bodily formation will arise, for that person will verbal formation arise?”—“Yes.

Or rather, for whom... [will it arise]? For one whose final consciousness of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) will arise immediately after this consciousness, and for those in their final existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms, only verbal formation will arise, not bodily formation.
Furthermore, by such statements as, "But for others, both of those will arise," and, "For whom bodily formation will not arise, for him vocal formation will not arise...

[etc. ...for those possessing the final consciousness, and for those whose final consciousness will arise immediately after a thought without applied thought or sustained thought, for them both of those will not arise."
The method of application for the section on arising should be understood according to the appropriate manner for all the various time-divisions.

“When bodily formation ceases for someone, does verbal formation cease for that person? … [and so on] … For those who have attained the first jhāna and for sense-sphere beings at the moment of the dissolution of in-breathing and out-breathing, both of these cease. When bodily formation ceases for someone, … [and so on] …
In the section on cessation, [the method is] according to such passages as: "Does his mental formation cease? "Yes.
In the section on arising and cessation, it is according to such passages as: "For whom bodily formation arises, for him does verbal formation cease? "No.

And in the section on full understanding, it is according to such passages as: "He who fully understands bodily formation, does he also fully understand verbal formation? "Yes. In all instances, the method of the text should be understood by following what has been stated above.

In the section on the process of existence (*pavattivāra*), here in the positive order (*anulomanaya*) of the person-section (*puggalavāra*) during the present time, only three pairs (*yamaka*) are found:

two rooted in bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and one rooted in verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*). The same method applies to its negative order (*paṭilomanaya*) as well as to the sections on the bases (*okāsavāra*) and so forth.
Thus, the enumeration of the pairs in all these sections should be understood by way of three pairs for each.
In this *Atthavinicchaya*, however, the following characteristic is given:

for in this *Saṅkhārayamaka*, because of such statements as “at the moment of the arising of in-breaths and out-breaths,” and “at the moment of the arising of applied thought and sustained thought,” the distinction of time—present and so forth—should be understood by way of occurrence (*pavatti*) as well, and not solely by way of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*). [As it says: “In the second jhāna, in the third jhāna...”
Furthermore, from such statements as "therein the bodily formation arises," it should be understood that even *jhāna* is included by way of its basis.
Thus, in this context, the determination of the meaning should be understood according to whatever is applicable. Herein, this is the guide to the method:
the phrase "without applied thought and sustained thought" is stated with reference to the second and third *jhānas*, not with reference to the fourth *jhāna*.

In that context, it is because of the absence of inhalation and exhalation. The phrase "at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness" is stated because the bodily formation is exclusively mind-originated;
for it is only a consciousness that is actually arising which originates matter or non-matter, not one that is dissolving or one that is stable.
The term "one possessing the final consciousness" refers to the very last consciousness, which does not lead to rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*).

[This refers] to those who possess [the path] and whose taints are exhausted. Regarding the phrase "the final consciousness is without initial application and sustained application," the meaning should be understood here with reference to the death-consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) belonging to the second jhāna, and the death-consciousness of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) belonging to the fourth jhāna.
Regarding the statement, "For whom bodily formation ceases, for him mental formation ceases," this is a rule of necessity.

The reply "Yes" was given because the bodily formation ceases at the same moment as the mental formation, not because they share a single momentary unit of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*). For the mental formation arises and ceases even without the bodily formation;
however, the bodily formation, being mind-originated (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), arises together with the specific consciousness by which it is produced.
From that point on, it ceases together with the seventeenth [consciousness]; this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*).

As for what was stated in the Sinhalese commentary (*Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā*) on the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*—namely, "mind-originated matter ceases at the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness"—that contradicts this canonical text (*pāḷi*). "Whose bodily formation..."

In the passage, "When consciousness arises, its verbal formation ceases," the negation "no" is made because bodily formation arises at the moment of consciousness's arising, and yet at that same moment, initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) do not cease.
By this methodological approach, the analysis should be understood for all instances. This is the method for the commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the *saṅkhāra-yamaka*.
Commentary on the Matrix of the Pairs on Latent Dispositions (*Anusaya-yamaka-mātikā*).
Regarding the establishment of the text for the Matrix of the Pairs on Latent Dispositions, it should be understood as follows:

Even in the *Anusaya-yamaka*, unlike in the Matrix of the Pairs on the Aggregates (*Khandha-yamaka*) and others where the teaching was given according to the standard method, the presentation of the text has been composed by another method. How so?
First, two sections—the Section on Delimitation (*pariccheda-vāra*) and the Section on Delimited Enumeration (*paricchinnuddesa-vāra*)—are taught by way of enumeration.
Following that is the Section on the Basis of Origination (*uppattiṭṭhāna-vāra*), which constitutes one minor section.

Then, having applied the [remaining] sections to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*)—namely, the Section on Underlying Tendencies (*anusaya-vāra*), the Section on Those Possessing Underlying Tendencies (*sānusaya-vāra*), the Section on Abandoning (*pajahana-vāra*), the Section on Full Understanding (*pariññā-vāra*), the Section on What is Abandoned (*pahīna-vāra*), the Section on Arising (*uppajjana-vāra*), and the Section on Elements (*dhātu-vāra*)—they are expanded through the method of the "Pairs" (*yamaka*).

The seven great sections (*mahāvāra*) have been demonstrated by way of the *Aṭṭhakaniddesa*; thus, the exposition of the *Anusaya-yamaka* (the "Pairs on Latent Tendencies") has been made in ten sections.

Among those, the two sections beginning with "The Section on Delimitation" (*paricchedavāra*), which were stated by way of enumeration (*uddesa*), should be understood here as the matrix (*mātikā*) for the *Anusaya-yamaka*.
For in that [work], the section on delimitation is so called because the latent tendencies are taught there after being delimited by number, namely, "there are seven latent tendencies."

[This is] the name. Having enumerated the mere names of those [factors] delimited by way of their delimitation—namely, the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), and so forth, up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*)—and having taught them by saying, "These indeed are they," this is called the section on the enumeration of the delimited.

Regarding that, first, from the perspective of the meaning not yet explained: in what sense are they "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*)? In the sense of lying latent (*anusayana*). What is this so-called sense of lying latent?

The meaning of "not abandoned" (*appahīna*). For the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), such as the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), are said to "underlie" within this or that continuum by way of being not abandoned;
therefore, they are called "underlying tendencies. And the meaning of "they underlie" is that they arise upon obtaining their respective appropriate conditions.
Now, it might be argued: "The state of underlying (*anusayana*) is indeed the mode of being unabandoned, and a mode of being unabandoned does not arise."
"Therefore, the underlying tendencies (anusaya) do not arise. To this, the reply is as follows: An underlying tendency is a state that has not been abandoned.
Furthermore, by way of its being unabandoned, an underlying tendency is called a "firmly established defilement" (thāmagata-kilesa).

It is associated with consciousness, possesses an object, and—by virtue of having a condition—is "rooted" (sahetuka); it is exclusively unwholesome, because in the *Kathāvatthu*, the dissociation of underlying tendencies from consciousness has been refuted.
And since that [ignorance] exists in the past, the future, and the present, it is appropriate to say that it "arises.

For instance, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, in the word-commentary on delusion (*moha*), it says: "The underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), the obsession of ignorance (*avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna*)...
at that time, this is delusion. And in this *Yamaka*, in the section on arising, regarding the one for whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*)...
"...when [contact] arises, the underlying tendency to aversion arises," and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that what was said—that "they underlie" means they arise upon obtaining their respective appropriate causes—is well-said.

"Underlying tendency to sensual lust" (*kāmarāgānusaya*) refers to sensual lust itself which, in the sense of being unabandoned, is an underlying tendency; thus it is called the underlying tendency to sensual lust. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

This, then, is the unelaborated meaning here. Furthermore, the determination of the meaning here also occurs by way of showing the method of the exposition (*niddesa*), and that exposition has already been stated below.
There are eight sections, beginning with the "Section on the Source" (*uppatti-ṭṭhāna-vāra*); herein, this is merely an indication of the sequence for establishing the text.
For among these, the first is called the section on the arising-places of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

In that regard, there is no division of sections in the *Yamakayojanavāra* (the Section on the Application of Pairs), but there is in the other seven great sections. Among those, the first—the section on the underlying tendencies—is twofold by way of the direct and reverse orders.
Therein, in the direct order, [it is formulated] as "In whom, where... pe ... the underlying tendency lies," according to the names of the person (*puggala*), the base (*okāsa*), and both of them.
There are three intermediate sections; in each of these, there are pairs of permutations (*yamaka-bheda*) based on those with one root, two roots, three roots, four roots, five roots, and six roots.
Just as it is in the method of direct order (*anuloma-naya*), so too should it be understood in the method of reverse order (*paṭiloma-naya*).

And just as it is here in the section on underlying tendencies (*anusaya-vāra*), so too it is in the sections on "possessing underlying tendencies" (*sānusaya-vāra*), "abandoning" (*pajahana-vāra*), "thorough knowledge" (*pariññā-vāra*), "abandoned" (*pahīna-vāra*), and "arising" (*uppajjana-vāra*).
In all five [sections] as well. However, this is the distinction here regarding the first three sections:

in the section on the bases (*okāsa*), instead of saying "wherever there" (*yattha tattha*), the teaching is given using the ablative case as "whence from there" (*yato tato*). The rest is exactly the same.

Furthermore, this very last section, called the "section on the elements" (*dhātu-vāra*), stands in two ways: as the section of questions (*pucchā-vāra*) and the section of answers (*vissajjana-vāra*). Therein, the section of questions is presented by way of direct and reverse order.

It is twofold. At the conclusion of that, the answer was given according to the sequence of the questions. Thus, first of all, the establishment of the text (pāḷivavatthāna) should be understood here.
Now, this is a mere indication of the beginning of the eight sections, starting from the outset: "Where does the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) lie latent?
In two feelings within the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), there the underlying tendency to sensual lust lies latent. Where does the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya)..."

Does it underlie? The underlying tendency to suffering-vedanā... [etc. ...the underlying tendency to conceit underlies the two types of feeling in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), as well as in the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial realm (arūpadhātu).
The underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt underlie all phenomena included within the personality-sphere (sakkāya).

The underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāga) underlies the fine-material and immaterial realms. The underlying tendency to ignorance underlies all phenomena included within the personality-sphere.
“...it underlies phenomena”—this, first of all, is the method of the text (*pāḷinaya*) for the first section.
Therein, “in two feelings of the sense-sphere element” means in two feelings—namely, pleasant feeling and equanimity—within the plane of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) exists in two ways: by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*).
It underlies and arises; there, having become co-nascent with unwholesome pleasant feeling and equanimity, it also arises taking them as its object.
However, the remaining wholesome, resultant, and functional feelings of the sense sphere arise taking only [other] objects as their objects.
While this [latent tendency] underlies these feelings, it also [underlies] the perception, formations, and consciousness associated with those feelings.

It indeed underlies [them]. However, it is said that this underlying tendency (anusaya) underlies only these two feelings because, in terms of gratification, it is the primary factor for the arising of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) among the remaining associated states; and because, due to its gross nature, it is easily understood by those to be trained (*veneyya*).
The same applies to what follows. Not only does this underlying tendency underlie these two feelings, but it also underlies those states associated with feeling.
It underlies mental phenomena (*dhamma*), and it likewise underlies desirable forms and so forth. This has also been stated in the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*:
"In whatever is lovely and pleasant in the world, there the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) underlies beings. Furthermore, in the *Anusaya-yamaka*, it is said:
"In regard to painful feeling and the form element (*rūpadhātu*), the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie," and so on. By this—
It is meant that it underlies all six objects, including visible forms and so forth, as stated in the remaining passages. However, here one should understand that not all of that has been mentioned;
rather, only a portion has been stated by reason of its preeminence and other such factors.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of suffering": here, there are two types of painful feeling associated with displeasure (*domanassa*) connected with the mind of resistance (*paṭigha-citta*), and those associated with body-consciousness (*kāya-viññāṇa*).

The three feelings—namely, painful feeling (dukkhavedanā) and the others—and the mental states associated with them, as well as the six undesirable objects such as visible forms and so forth, are the bases for the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) by way of co-arising and, as appropriate, by way of being its object.
But are the other two feelings or desirable objects not objects of aversion? They are not non-objects; they are indeed objects for one whose jhāna has degenerated.
Indeed, when grief arises directed toward a lost, desirable object together with its associated mental states, that grief has merely the object as its basis;
it is not a state of underlying tendency (*anusaya*) because the object is desirable. For only that which is undesirable serves as the cause for the repulsion of what is desirable;

however, that which arises toward such [a desirable object] is merely a momentary repulsion (*paṭighamatta*), not an underlying tendency to repulsion (*paṭighānusaya*). [The term *paṭighānusayo*: The underlying tendency to repulsion.

For the latent tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) is a firmly established defilement that has arisen by way of resistance toward an undesirable object; whereas the other [type of anger], even though it arises together with mental displeasure (*domanassa*), does not become a latent tendency of aversion because it does not perform its own function of resistance, and thus it remains outside the conventional designation.
For just as ill will (*byāpāda*), even when arising together with the volition of killing, is not called "mental action" (*manokamma*).

It exists; it becomes beyond conventional designation; thus it should be understood. For that very reason, it is said that the mental distress associated with renunciation (nekkhamma) is to be cultivated.
However, for the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya), all mundane phenomena—excluding painful feeling and mental distress—are the basis for its latent presence. As it is said:
"In regard to painful feeling and in the unincluded [supramundane] states... here the underlying tendency to conceit does not lie latent."

For it has been said: "However, for the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), all phenomena—excluding those that are supramundane—are the basis for their underlying.
Therefore it was said: 'In all phenomena included within the personal existence aggregate (*sakkāya*'). Herein, the meaning is:

'In all phenomena included within the personal existence aggregate' by way of being dependent upon the cycle of saṃsāra. In this same way, the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) is also to be understood. In all cases..."
And the distinction between [the latent tendencies] that are co-nascent and those that have an object should be understood in the same manner as explained below.
As for the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), although it might be said— on account of its arising in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views—
that it underlies two feelings in the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*) by way of being co-nascent, it nevertheless has only the fine-material and immaterial spheres as its object.

It is not only the sense-sphere object that is obtained; however, that [object] is not a place where the underlying tendencies (anusaya) lie latent. Therefore, without making a restriction based on the object, it is said:
"In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, the underlying tendency to lust for existence lies latent there.

By way of that lust, all lust whatsoever should be understood as the underlying tendency to lust for sense-pleasures (kāmarāgānusaya). This is the method regarding the section on the "places of arising."

Furthermore, regarding the other seven great sections: first, "In one for whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) underlies, does the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) underlie?
Yes. Or rather, in one for whom the underlying tendency of aversion underlies, does the underlying tendency of sensual lust underlie?
Yes. In one for whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust underlies, does the underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*) underlie? Yes. Or rather..."

But does the underlying tendency to conceit underlie for him, and does the underlying tendency to sensual lust also underlie for him? For a non-returner, the underlying tendency to conceit underlies, but the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie for him;
for three types of persons, both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlie.
For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies, does the underlying tendency to views also underlie for them? For two types of persons...
The underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies [it], but... [as before] ...the underlying tendency to views also underlies it; or for whomsoever... [as before] ...Yes.

For whomsoever the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies, does the underlying tendency to doubt underlie him? The answer to this question is exactly the same as for the underlying tendency to views.
For whomsoever the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies, does the underlying tendency to lust for existence underlie him? Yes.

Or for whom... pe... "it underlies" (anuseti)... pe... in three types of persons, the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) underlies, and the underlying tendency to lust for sense-pleasures (kāmarāgānusaya) also underlies.

The same method applies to the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya). By this method, the manner of answering the questions rooted in the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya), etc., should be understood. This is the method for those [questions] with a single root.

For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) underlie, does the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) also underlie for them? Yes. For two [of the underlying tendencies], there are [answers] based on two roots...
[and so on]. However, for those based on five roots, the method of answering should be understood according to what was stated regarding the single root.

In that regard, this is the application concerning the final underlying tendencies: "For whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit..."

If, for someone in whom the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence persist, does the underlying tendency to ignorance also persist for them?
Yes. Or conversely, if the underlying tendency to ignorance persists for someone, do the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure...

[and so on] ...and the underlying tendency to lust for existence also persist for them? For a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence [persist].

“...and the underlying tendency to ignorance persists, but not the others; for two types of persons, the underlying tendencies to ignorance, sensual lust, ill will, conceit, and lust for existence persist, but not the underlying tendencies to views and doubt;
however, for the worldling (*puthujjana*), all of them persist. This is the method in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*). In the section on bases (*okāsavāra*), however:
“Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust persists, does the underlying tendency to ill will persist there? No.”

Or, where... [as before] ...does it lie latent? No. Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) lies latent, does the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) lie latent there?
Yes. Or, where the underlying tendency to conceit lies latent, does the underlying tendency to sensual lust lie latent there?

In the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*), the underlying tendency to conceit lies latent, but not the underlying tendency to sensual lust; however, in the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*)...
Both of these underlie two types of feeling. Where does the underlying tendency to sensual lust... [as before] ...underlie? Yes. Or where... [as before] ...does it underlie?
In painful feeling, in the form element, and in the formless element, here the underlying tendency to doubt underlies, but not the underlying tendency to sensual lust;
in the two types of feeling in the sense-sphere realm, both of these underlie. Where... [as before]...
Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) underlies, does the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) also underlie there? No. Or conversely... No.
Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies, does the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) also underlie there? Yes. Or conversely...
it underlies? In painful feeling and in the form and formless realms, the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies there.
The underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie both of those [the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion] in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm.
Where the underlying tendency to aversion underlies, does the underlying tendency to conceit underlie there? No. Or conversely...
No. Where the underlying tendency to aversion underlies, do the underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt underlie there?

“Yes. Or again, where... [as before] ...does the underlying tendency (anusaya) lie latent? The underlying tendency to doubt lies latent in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the form and formless realms; the underlying tendency to aversion does not lie latent there. However, in painful feeling, both of these lie latent. Where the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent, does the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) lie latent there? “No. Where... [as before] ...where does it lie latent? It lies latent in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm and in the form and formless realms; in painful feeling, however, neither of these two lies latent. Where the underlying tendency to attachment to existence lies latent, does the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) lie latent there? “No. Where... [as before] ...where does it lie latent? It lies latent in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm and in the form and formless realms; in painful feeling, however, neither of these two lies latent. Where the underlying tendency to views lies latent, does the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) lie latent there? “No. Where... [as before] ...where does it lie latent? It lies latent in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm and in the form and formless realms; in painful feeling, however, neither of these two lies latent. Where the underlying tendency to conceit lies latent, does the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) lie latent there? “Yes. Where... [as before] ...where does it lie latent? The method should be understood according to what is stated in the section on persons and the world-spheres (*puggalokāsavāra*), beginning with: "Only the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), and not the other, underlies painful feeling; in the undefiled (*apariyāpanna*), neither of those two underlies it;
for a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), only the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies the two feelings in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the form and formless realms;
but for an arahant, neither of those two underlies anything at all. This is the method of the canonical text (*pāḷinaya*).

In that context, regarding the statement, “In one for whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) underlies, the underlying tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) underlies,” the affirmative answer given—“Yes, it does”—appears as if it were wrongly given. Why?

Because sensual lust and aversion do not arise simultaneously in a single moment. For just as [it is said]: “In one for whom the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) arises, the sense-base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) [arises]...”
In passages such as "it arises," the mind-base (manāyatana), the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana), and so forth arise in a single moment;
however, sensual lust (kāmarāga) and aversion (paṭigha) do not do so in that same way, because they arise separately. Therefore, in this context, a negation—"no"—should have been made;
yet, since the reply "Yes" (āmantā) was given instead of that, it is here [to be understood] by way of the present moment, just as in the previous pairs (yamaka).
It should be understood otherwise than by taking it as a conventional expression for the present. How should it be understood? By way of its not having been abandoned.

For this conventional expression "it underlies" (*anuseti*) is stated with reference to the state of being unabandoned, not to the state of being presently arisen at the moment. Therefore, in response to this question:

for one in whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is unabandoned and has not been rendered subject to non-arising, the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) [is likewise unabandoned].
The meaning should be understood as follows: "the underlying tendency to aversion has not been abandoned" means that it has not been brought to the state of non-arising.
And because, regarding those [fetters] of sensual lust and aversion, if one is not abandoned for someone, the other is likewise not abandoned, therefore it is said:
"Yes. This applies to all subsequent answers in the section on arising and so forth of this kind.

The method is the same. "Of three persons" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*). "Of two" refers to the stream-enterer and the once-returner.

Thus, the manner of arising is illustrated. Regarding the first and second questions of the section on the bases (*okāsavāra*), because sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) do not arise in a single moment of consciousness, the negation "no" was made.
And regarding the sections on the pairs of roots (*dukamūla*) and so forth, because sensual lust, aversion, and the rest—
In a single state—meaning in consciousness (citta) or in an object (ārammaṇa)—they do not arise; therefore, the negation "there is not" is made therein.

The intention is that this question has not been asked before. In the section on persons and the world-sphere, "of four" refers to the worldling (puthujjana), the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the once-returner (sakadāgāmī), and the non-returner (anāgāmī).
"Of two" in the reverse order is said with reference to the non-returner and the arahant; such is the method in the section on latent tendencies (anusaya).

In the section on "Those Possessing Latent Tendencies" (*sānusaya-vāra*), however: "Is one who possesses the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) also possessed of the latent tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)?

Yes... [and so on] ...possessed of the latent tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*)? Yes. Or again, is one who possesses the latent tendency of conceit also possessed of the latent tendency of sensual lust?
A non-returner (*anāgāmī*) possesses it only through the latent tendency of conceit, not through the latent tendency of sensual lust; but three types of persons possess both."

By this method, the manner of posing questions and providing answers regarding the remaining sections beginning with the "Duka-mūla" (Pairs on Roots) should be understood; this is the method for the section on persons (*puggalavāra*).
"Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) also possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭigha*)? No...

[and so on] ...is he possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (*māna*)? Yes. Or again, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust?"

"In the section on locations (okāsa-vāra), it is stated: 'In the realms of form and formlessness, one possesses the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya) alone, and not the other; in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one possesses both. And in the section on persons and locations (puggala-okāsa-vāra), it is asked:

'Is one who possesses the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) with respect to a certain object also possessed of the underlying tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) with respect to that same object?

[The answer is] 'No. Thus, in the method of positive concomitance (anuloma-naya), it continues: "He who is free from the underlying tendency of sensual lust is [also] free from the underlying tendency of aversion..."

"Is one free from latent dispositions? "Yes," and so forth; in this way, even by way of reverse order, the method of posing questions and providing answers throughout all sections on latent dispositions (anusaya) should be understood according to what has been stated.

In that context, regarding the phrase "one who possesses latent dispositions due to the latent disposition of sensual lust": from whatever cause one possesses latent dispositions through the arisen latent disposition of sensual lust, is he said to possess latent dispositions also through the latent disposition of aversion arisen from that same cause? Because...
Since these two do not arise from the same state, the negation "no" was made; the remainder is exactly the same.
This is the method regarding the section on latent dispositions (*anusaya*).

However, in the section on abandoning, it says: "He who abandons the latent disposition of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) also abandons the latent disposition of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)? Yes... [and so on]."

Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit abandon that which is associated with it? Yes. Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust?
No... [and so on] ... Does he abandon the underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt? No.
Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust? That which is associated with it.

“He abandons [them]. “Does he who... pe... abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) abandon those associated with them? ... pe...

“From the point where one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, does one from that same point abandon the underlying tendency to aversion? “No... pe... From the point where one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust...”
“He abandons it; does he, from that [state], abandon the underlying tendency to conceit? “Yes.

“Or rather, from what state does he abandon the underlying tendency to conceit, does he from that state abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust? “In the fine-material and immaterial realms, he abandons only the underlying tendency to conceit;
however, in the sense-sphere realm, in two types of feeling, he abandons the underlying tendency to conceit,” and so forth, according to the section on locations.

“He who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust from a certain plane, does he thereby abandon the underlying tendency to aversion? No... [and so on] ...does he abandon the underlying tendency to conceit?

He abandons that which is associated with it... [and so on] ...does he abandon the underlying tendency to doubt? No. Or else, he who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt from a certain plane, does he thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust? The person in the eighth stage (the *aṭṭhamaka*) [abandons it] regarding suffering...”
"In the section on persons and the outflows (*puggalokāsava*), it is stated in the method of direct order (*anulomanaya*) as follows:

'In the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpadhātu*), regarding feeling (*vedanā*), one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) therein, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) therein; however, that same person, in the two feelings of the sense realm (*kāmadhātu*), abandons the underlying tendency to doubt therein and abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust along with its associated factors.'"
And: "Is it the case that whoever does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) does not also abandon the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)?

"Yes. ... [and so on] ... "Does he not abandon the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? "The person in the eighth stage (*aṭṭhamaka*) does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust, but not the other; the one who possesses the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga-samaṅgin*) does not abandon the latter;
and with the exception of these two—the eighth-stage person and the one possessing the path of non-returning—all remaining individuals do not abandon both. And so forth.
And in the reverse order, the method of question and answer should be understood to apply everywhere.
In this context, "he abandons" means he abandons by way of full understanding through abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*) via each respective path.

The phrase "that which belongs to the same category" (*tadekaṭṭha*) is said with reference to the state of belonging to the same category as what is abandoned. For by the first path and so forth, it is not only states such as [wrong] views that are abandoned; [other associated factors are also abandoned].
Furthermore, those [defilements] leading to the states of misery—namely, sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and so forth—are indeed abandoned as well.

For while the types of sensual lust to be abandoned by the first path are indeed abandoned, conceit, ignorance, and so forth, which lead to the states of misery and are to be abandoned by the third path, are abandoned because they are to be abandoned together with that [first path];
thus it was said "no" with reference to the stage of the path of Arahantship. For that [path] abandons only the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

"Because it has been abandoned, one does not abandon it. The phrase "from which one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust" means that from which the arising underlying tendency to sensual lust is abandoned.

The "eighth person" (*aṭṭhamaka*) is one who stands on the path of stream-entry. For, when counted in the order of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya-kamma*), starting from the stage of the fruit of arahantship, he is called the eighth.
In the reverse order, both the one possessing the path of non-returning and the eighth person are included.

"Excluding the remainder" refers to ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), those still in training (*sekha*), and those beyond training (*asekha*). For among them, worldlings do not abandon [defilements] due to the absence of full understanding through abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*);

the others [do not abandon them] because they have already been abandoned by them. In this manner, the analysis should be understood for all instances; such is the method regarding the section on abandoning.

The Section on Full Understanding (*pariññāvāra*), however, is similar to the Section on Abandoning (*pajahana-vāra*) in such passages as: "He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*).
For this too, like the Section on Abandoning, is answered solely by way of the path (*magga*).
In that context, "fully understands" means he fully understands by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*tīhi pariññāhi*). This is the method regarding the Section on Full Understanding.

In the section on persons (*puggalavāra*) concerning what has been abandoned, it is stated: “Is the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) abandoned for one in whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is abandoned?

Yes... Is the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) abandoned? For a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), only the underlying tendency to sensual lust is abandoned; but for an arahant, even the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned. And so forth. Furthermore, regarding the spatial relation:
“Where the underlying tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, is the underlying tendency to aversion abandoned there? It cannot be said [that it is necessarily so].”
"Abandoned or not abandoned? "Or where... [as before] ...it should not be said... [as before] "...is the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) abandoned there?

"Yes. "Or where... [as before] ...is it abandoned? "In the form and formless realms, the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned here, but the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) should not be said [to be abandoned];
in the two feelings of the sense realm (kāmadhātu), both of these are abandoned here," and so forth, according to the section on locations (okāsavāra).

Regarding persons and outflows (*puggalokāsavāra*): thus, in the method of positive concomitance (*anulomanaya*), [it is asked]: "Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) unabandoned in one for whom the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) is unabandoned?
"Yes. "Or conversely... yes... "Or conversely, is the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) unabandoned in one for whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust is unabandoned?
[The answer is: "In the non-returner (*anāgāmī*), only the underlying tendency to conceit is unabandoned; in three types of persons, both are unabandoned."
The method of answering the questions should be understood according to the same principle stated in the reverse order by the passage beginning with “not abandoned.

And here, the meaning should be taken solely from the perspective of those established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*), because for those established on the path (*maggaṭṭha*), there is no state of having abandoned defilements;

for their underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are indeed being abandoned, but they are not yet abandoned. Therefore, only those established in the fruit—such as non-returners (*anāgāmi*) and others—should be taken [as the referents], as in the section on the bases (*okāsavāra*).
However, the statement "it should not be said" is spoken because the locus of origination for both is not common.
For the locus of origination of the underlying tendency to sensual lust is one thing, and that of the underlying tendency to aversion is another.
Furthermore, wherever an underlying tendency arises in one who has not developed the path, it is said to be abandoned right there when the path is developed; therefore, it is "abandoned there."

Or, it cannot be said that [the underlying tendency] is not abandoned; however, in all cases, because of its own absence there, it cannot be said that it is "not abandoned" therein. But with reference to the common locus of both, it was stated: "Yes.
For the underlying tendency to conceit, in the common locus consisting of the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm, is indeed said to be abandoned together with sensual lust.

[The phrase] "it exists" refers to the ordinary person (*puthujjana*) for whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) has not been abandoned, and it should also be understood in reference to those established in the fruits of stream-entry and once-returning;
for it is said, "of three types of persons. The remainder is indeed easy to understand. This is the method regarding the section on what is abandoned (*pahīnavāra*).

In the section on what arises (*uppajjanavāra*), however, the method is similar throughout to the section on underlying tendencies (*anusayavāra*), beginning with: "In whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust arises, in him does the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) arise? This is the method regarding the section on what arises.

In the *Dhātuvāra*, however, it is asked: “For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is being reborn in the sense-sphere realm, how many underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) underlie, how many underlying tendencies do not underlie, and how many combinations (*bhaṅga*) are there?
For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere realm and is being reborn in the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*) … [etc. … how many combinations are there?
For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere realm and is being reborn in the immaterial realm (*arūpadhātu*) … [etc. … for one being reborn in the fine-material realm …” [and so forth].

“For one being reborn in the formless realm... [etc. ...how many permutations (bhaṅga) are there? For one passing away from the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) and being reborn neither in the sense-sphere realm nor in the formless realm...
[etc. ...for one being reborn neither in the sense-sphere realm nor in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
How many permutations are there for one being reborn neither in the sense-sphere realm nor in the form realm? Thus, there are nine [permutations] based on the sense-sphere realm.

There are twenty-seven positive questions (anuloma-pucchā), such as "of one deceased from the form realm" (*rūpadhātuyā cutassa*) and so forth—nine based on the form realm—and nine for the formless realm (*arūpadhātuyā*);
likewise, there are twenty-seven negative questions (*paṭiloma-pucchā*), such as "of one not deceased from the sense realm" (*na kāmadhātuyā cutassa*) and so forth;

and likewise, [questions] such as "of one deceased neither from the sense realm nor from the formless realm, and being reborn in the sense realm" (*na kāmadhātuyā na arūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa*).
"And twenty-seven questions based on groups of six"—thus, in this section on questions, eighty-one questions are to be understood.
Therein, "they follow" means having followed along in the continuum of consciousness; "how many follow? means how many follow?

"How many are to be analyzed as both following and not following at the moment of dissolution?"—this is the meaning. "Not for one being reborn in the sense-sphere realm" means for one who is devoid of the sense-sphere realm.
For one being reborn in both the form and formless realms. "Neither the sense-sphere realm nor the form realm" refers to one being reborn in the formless realm.

"Not from the sense-sphere realm" refers to one passing away from the form and formless realms; thus, in all remaining cases as well, the meaning should be understood by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and by way of the realms (*dhātu*). This is the method for the section on the enumeration.

In the section on exposition (*niddesavāra*), however, it says: "For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is being reborn in the sense-sphere realm, for some seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) underlie;
for some five underlying tendencies underlie; there are no permutations of underlying tendencies.
For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere realm and is being reborn in the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*), for some seven underlying tendencies underlie; for some five..."
The answer for all cases should be understood according to this method: "For some, there are three... [and so on]... there are no three permutations.

However, the distinction here is as follows: for one who has passed away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is being reborn in the sense realm (*kāmadhātu*), exactly seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) underlie;
likewise for one who has passed away from the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*) and is being reborn in the sense realm, and so forth, including those passing away from the formless realm.

However, for one who has passed away there, there is no rebirth in the form realm; if they are reborn below, they are reborn only in the sense realm, and the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya) underlie them.
In this way, the method of answering should be understood for other similar cases as well—this is the distinction;
the rest is exactly as previously stated. This is the method of the text (pāḷinaya) here.
In that context, "of some" is stated with reference to worldlings (*puthujjana*), while "five" is stated with reference to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*).

For in their case, the underlying tendencies of wrong view and doubt have been abandoned; however, because non-returners (*anāgāmī*) do not take rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), the phrase "of some three" was not mentioned in the first section, but was mentioned only in the sections concerning arising in the fine-material and immaterial realms... pe...
For non-returners (*anāgāmin*), because sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) have been abandoned, only those three underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) remain latent.

Here, the method is by way of the arising of the underlying tendencies; however, without taking the actual latency of the underlying tendencies, their persistence at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) must also be understood by way of their state of being unabandoned.
"Seven" refers to [the case of] a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) who has passed away from the form or formless realms and is reborn below.

There is no such thing as rebirth in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth [for those who have attained the formless attainments]; it occurs only for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

Therefore, it is stated with the restriction "only seven," because there is no rebirth in the form-sphere (*rūpadhātu*) for one who has passed away from the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). Why is there none?
Because those who are formless lack the meditative absorption of form (*rūpa-jhāna*). For they have been reborn in the formless realm by completely transcending all perceptions of form.
The rest is easily understood by way of the method; such is the method in the section on the elements (*dhātuvāra*).
This concludes the method for the commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the dyads on underlying tendencies (*anusaya-yamaka-mātikā*).

Now, regarding the commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the dyads on consciousness (*cittayamaka-mātikā*), the establishment of the text (*pāḷi-vavatthāna*) in this matrix should be understood as follows. For in this matrix:

From the very beginning, there are three pure great sections: the Section on Persons (*puggalavāra*), the Section on Phenomena (*dhammavāra*), and the Section on Persons and Phenomena (*puggaladhammavāra*).

Among these, the "Section on Persons" is that which proceeds by way of the person, illustrating the distinctions such as the arising and ceasing of consciousness, as in: "For whom consciousness arises and does not cease.
The [second] proceeds by way of phenomena alone, as in: "That consciousness which arises and does not cease..."
The section called "States" (Dhammavāra) proceeds by explaining the distinctions of the mind's arising, ceasing, and so forth.

The section called "Persons and States" (Puggaladhammavāra) proceeds by explaining the distinctions of the mind's arising, ceasing, and so forth, through both modes [of person and state] together, as in: "For whom this mind arises and does not cease."

Then, by way of the sixteen phrases beginning with "whose mind is with lust" (*sarāga-citta*), there are another forty-eight mixed sections consisting of sixteen sections on persons (*puggala-vāra*), sixteen sections on phenomena (*dhamma-vāra*), and sixteen sections on both persons and phenomena (*puggala-dhamma-vāra*).
These have been abbreviated here after merely showing the basic terms such as "with lust" (*sarāga*) and so forth. Then, "whose wholesome... (*yassa kusalaṃ*)...

By way of the sixty-six hundred and twenty Abhidhamma matrix (mātikā) terms beginning with "citta," there are another sixty-six hundred and twenty sections on persons (puggalavāra) distinguished by terms such as "wholesome" (kusala), sixty-six hundred and twenty sections on phenomena (dhammavāra), and sixty-six hundred and twenty sections on both persons and phenomena (puggaladhammavāra);
thus, there are seven hundred and ninety-eight mixed sections (missakavāra). These too—
Having merely shown the terms beginning with "wholesome" (kusala), [the text] is indeed abbreviated;
furthermore, those terms such as "visible" (sanidassana) and so forth that do not apply to consciousness are included by way of the "vain questions.

Now, among those three sections, first, in the Great Section on the Pure Person (suddhikapuggalamahāvāra), there is the section on the differentiation of the times of arising and cessation (uppādanirodhakālasambhedavāra).

There are fourteen intermediate sections: the section on arising and what has arisen, the section on cessation and what has arisen, the section on arising, the section on cessation, the section on arising and cessation, the section on the ceasing of what is currently arising, the section on the arising of what is currently arising, the section on the cessation of what is currently ceasing, the section on the arising of what has arisen, the section on the past and the future, the section on what has arisen and what is currently arising, the section on what has ceased and what is currently ceasing, and the section on the time that has passed.
Among these, [the first is] the section on arising.
In these three sections— the section on cessation, the section on arising, and the section on both arising and cessation—
there are eighteen pairs (yamakas) formed by taking six pairs each through the forward and reverse order, according to the three temporal divisions of the present-past,
the present-future, and the past-future. In the section on the arisen and the arising, there are two pairs in the forward order and two in the reverse order, according to the past and future times.
There are four pairs (yamaka) in the first three sections indicated at the beginning, three indicated in the middle, and four indicated at the end—thus, ten sections in total.
By taking two pairs each—one in direct order and one in reverse order—there are twenty pairs.
Thus, across all fourteen intermediate sections, there are forty-two pairs, totaling eighty-four.

There are sixty-eight hundred questions. Just as it is in the single Great Chapter on the Pure Person (suddhikapuggalamahāvāra), so it is in the Great Chapter on the Pure Dhamma (suddhikadhammamahāvāra) and in the Great Chapter on the Pure Person and Dhamma (suddhikapuggaladhammamahāvāra). Thus, across these three Great Chapters, there are one hundred and twenty-six sets of the singlefold (ekaka);
from that, the questions should be understood to be double, and the meanings likewise double. Furthermore, these three chapters are [treated] by way of "one who has lust" (sarāga) and so forth.
Having multiplied by sixteen, and then by sixty-six hundred and twenty according to the categories of wholesome states (*kusala*) and so forth,
there arise from this matrix of the *Cittayamaka* many thousands of pairs (*yamaka*), twice as many questions (*puccha*), and twice as many meanings (*attha*), though the text itself is concise.

Having thus understood the determination of the canonical text (*pāḷi-vavatthāna*) herein, one should now proceed, following the meaning of the terms not yet explained, together with the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga-naya*).
The method of explaining the concise meaning (*saṅkhepatthavaṇṇanā*) should be understood as follows:
"For whom the mind arises" means for which person the mind arises by way of being possessed of the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
"Does not cease" means it does not cease because it has not yet reached the moment of cessation (*nirodhakkhaṇa*). "His mind"—what is that?
The question is: "Will the mind of that person cease from that point on? And regarding that [question]:
"At the moment of arising of the final consciousness, their mind arises but does not cease; it will cease but will not arise.
At the moment of arising of the other [types of] consciousness, their mind arises and does not cease, and it will both cease and arise."
And this is the answer. In that context, "their consciousness" refers to those whose taints are destroyed;

at the moment of the arising of their final consciousness—termed the death-consciousness—that very death-consciousness is said to "arise" because it has reached the state of arising, and it is said not to "cease" because it has not yet reached dissolution. But now, having reached dissolution, for them...
The mind will cease; because there is no further rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*), another [mind] will not arise.

"In others" means that, excluding those who possess their final consciousness and those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), for the remaining trainees (*sekha*), non-trainees (*asekha*), and worldlings (*puthujjana*), the mind will indeed cease, but another will either arise in that same existence or in a future one. This is the meaning.

Regarding the second question: “Is it the case that for whomsoever the consciousness will cease and will not arise, for him the consciousness arises and does not cease?”—the answer to this is “Yes,” referring to the consciousness of one who possesses the final consciousness and whose taints are exhausted (an arahant). Regarding the question:
“Is it the case that for whomsoever the consciousness does not arise but ceases, for him the consciousness will not cease and will arise?”... [the answer is “No”].

The answer to the question is simply a negation: "No. For by asking, "Does it not arise and cease?", he asks regarding the final consciousness of an Arahant at the moment of its dissolution, as well as any other consciousness in the process of dissolving.
From that point onward, it can indeed be said that the Arahant's consciousness will no longer cease; however, it cannot be said that it will arise.

Therefore, the negation "no" is employed here; for to the question, "But for whom the mind will not cease and will arise, does that person's mind not arise and cease?", the answer is simply a rejection: "there is none.
For there is no such person for whom the mind will not cease and will arise.

Is consciousness not arisen? At the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, consciousness is not arising, but it is not [therefore] "not arisen";
for those who have attained cessation and for non-percipient beings, consciousness is both not arising and "not arisen. Or, for whom...

[as before] ...is it not arising? Yes. And here, "arisen" is a name applied to that which possesses the factor of arising (*uppāda-samaṅgin*), and "is arising" refers likewise to that which possesses the factor of arising.
Is the consciousness of one in whom it ceases arisen? Yes. Or conversely... [as before] ...does it cease?

At the moment of dissolution, it is so. Is the consciousness of one in whom it does not cease unarisen? [The consciousness] of those who have attained cessation and so forth. Or conversely... [as before] ...Yes.
Does the consciousness that arises in a person have arisen for that person? Yes. Or conversely... [does] it arise?

For all [beings], it is the same at the moment of the arising of consciousness. And here, the meaning stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) by way of the "present moment" (*khaṇapaccuppanna*) is this: because it has reached the state of arising, it has "arisen" (*uppajjittha*); because it is not yet past, it is called "arising" (*uppajjati*). "It has arisen" (*uppajjittha*)... [end of fragment].
However, when the meaning is understood here according to past moments of consciousness, it is evident that this does not conflict with the subsequent text, nor is it otherwise;
therefore, having examined what precedes and follows, the meaning should be grasped without contradicting the scripture.
For one whose consciousness does not arise, has his consciousness not arisen? It has arisen. Or for whom... [and so on].

Does it not arise? There is none. For whom consciousness arises, will that person’s consciousness arise? For all except those possessing the final consciousness and those whose taints are destroyed (the *khiṇāsava*), consciousness will so arise.
Or for whom... [etc. ...does it arise? At the moment of its arising, it is so. For whom consciousness... [etc. ...will it not arise?
For the Asekhas at the moment of the dissolution of their final consciousness, it is so. Or for whom... [etc. ...
Does it not arise? It is so at the moment of dissolution of the final consciousness. For whom consciousness has arisen, will consciousness arise for them?
With the exception of those possessing the final consciousness, it is so for the rest. Or for whom... [etc. ...Yes.
For whom consciousness has not arisen, will consciousness not arise for them? There is no such case. Or for whom... [etc. ...Yes.
But... [as before] ...did it not arise? It did arise.
For whom consciousness ceases, for him did consciousness cease? Yes. Or for whom... [as before] ...does it cease?
At the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa), it is likewise. For whom consciousness... [as before] ...did it not cease? It did cease. Or for whom... [as before] ...?
There is none. For whom the consciousness ceases, will that person’s consciousness cease?

With the exception of one possessing the final consciousness, it is likewise for the rest at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness. Or rather, for whom... [as before] ...for the rest at the moment of dissolution, it is likewise.
For whom the consciousness... [as before] ...will cease. Or rather, for whom... [as before] ...ceases.
If the consciousness of a person has ceased, will the consciousness of that person cease?
With the exception of the final consciousness at the moment of its dissolution, the consciousness of all others is likewise. Or conversely... [as before] ...Yes.
If the consciousness of a person has not ceased, will the consciousness of that person not cease? There is none. Or conversely... [as before] ...has it not ceased? It has ceased.
If the consciousness of a person arises, has that person’s consciousness ceased? Yes. Or conversely... [does] it arise?
For all [beings], at the moment of the arising of consciousness, it is so. If the consciousness of a person does not arise, has that person’s consciousness not ceased?
It has ceased. Or conversely... [is there] none... for whom consciousness arises, will that person’s consciousness cease?
“Yes. Or rather, for whom... [as before] ...does it arise? For all [beings] at the moment of the arising of consciousness, it is so.
For whom consciousness does not arise, will consciousness not cease for them? At the moment of the dissolution of the final consciousness, it is so.
Or rather, for whom... [as before] ...yes. For whom consciousness has arisen, will consciousness cease for them?
[It is] likewise, excluding the final consciousness that is ceasing. Or, for whomsoever... [as before] ...Yes.
For whomsoever consciousness has not arisen, will that person’s consciousness not cease? No. Or, for whomsoever... [as before] ...has it not arisen? It has arisen.
For whomsoever consciousness is arising, is that person’s consciousness not ceasing? Yes. Or, for whomsoever... [as before] ...is it arising?
Is it the case that for all [beings], at the moment of the arising of consciousness, it is likewise? Yes. For whom consciousness does not arise, for him does consciousness cease?
For all [beings], at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, it is likewise. Or conversely... pe ...does it not arise? Yes.
For whom consciousness is in the process of arising, for him is consciousness arisen? Yes. Or conversely... pe ...is it in the process of arising? Yes.
Likewise for all [beings] at the moment of the arising of consciousness. For whom consciousness is not arising, is his consciousness unarisen? [Yes.
Likewise for those who have attained cessation [of perception and feeling], etc. Or, for whom... [affirmative].
For whom consciousness is ceasing, is his consciousness arisen? [Affirmative. Or, for whom... [at the moment of dissolution].

Likewise. Is the consciousness of one whose consciousness is not ceasing also unarisen? [Yes; the consciousness of those who have attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), etc., is likewise. Or, for whomsoever... [affirmative].
