Is the consciousness of one whose consciousness has arisen also arisen? [Affirmative. Or, for whomsoever... [is it] arisen?
The same applies to those possessing consciousness (*cittasamaṅgī*). For whom consciousness has not arisen, for that person has consciousness not arisen in the past?
It has arisen. Or rather... [etc. ...has it not arisen? There is none... [etc. ...For whom consciousness has not arisen, for that person will consciousness arise in the future?
It will arise. Or rather... [etc. ...has it not arisen? It has arisen.
For whomsoever the mind had arisen, but for whom that mind has not [yet] arisen, will that person’s mind arise?
Yes. Or rather, for whomsoever the mind will arise, but for whom that mind has not [yet] arisen, had that person’s mind [already] arisen?
Yes. Herein, the phrase "but for whom that mind has not [yet] arisen" refers to those such as non-percipient beings who are without mind.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). Because there is an absence of the arising of consciousness for those [beings] by necessity, the answer "Yes" (*āmantā*) is given in both instances.
And this section should be understood as having been established by taking all three periods of time into account.
"Is it the case that for whom consciousness has not arisen, and for whom consciousness has not arisen, for him consciousness will not arise?"
There is none. Or, for that whose consciousness will not arise and yet whose consciousness has not arisen, has that consciousness not already arisen?
It had already arisen. Is that which has arisen "arising"?

At the moment of arising, consciousness is so. Is that which is arising "arisen"? Yes. Is that which is not arisen "not arising"? Yes. Is that which is not arising "not arisen"? Consciousness of the past and future is so.

Is that which has ceased the same as that which is ceasing? No. Is that which is ceasing the same as that which has ceased? No. Is it not the case that what has not ceased is not ceasing? At the moment of arising, the future mind is likewise so. It is also likewise that what is not ceasing is not ceased.

Regarding the mind of one for whom the moment of arising has passed and the time has elapsed, and the moment of ceasing has passed and the time has elapsed—is that his mind? [It is], provided it has not passed the moment of dissolution.
Is that which is past mind— having transcended both [the present and future]— or rather, that mind which, while ceasing,
has at every moment transcended and passed beyond its time, and while arising, has at every moment transcended and passed beyond its time,
[called] "mind"? By this method, the manner of answering should be understood throughout the entire section on persons (puggalavāra) as "past mind."
In this context, "the moment of arising" (*uppajjamāna-khaṇa*) means the moment of that which is arising; the meaning is "the moment of origination" (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
"The moment has passed" (*khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ*) means the time has passed; it does not mean that much time has elapsed.

Rather, having passed over that very moment of origination, it comes to be designated as "the time that has passed. "The moment of ceasing" (*nirujjhamāna-khaṇa*) means the moment of that which is ceasing.
The meaning is "at the moment of dissolution. Regarding the phrase "the moment has been transgressed" (*khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ*), which means "the time has passed," he asks:
"Does his mind, having likewise transgressed the moment of cessation (*nirodhakkhaṇaṃ*), also become what is called 'the time that has passed'?

For one whose mind, at the moment of dissolution, having transgressed the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇaṃ*), becomes what is called "the time that has passed," [does it likewise do so] at the moment of cessation?

Having transgressed [the present moment], it is called "past time"; however, since a past consciousness has transgressed both moments at every instant, it is called "past time"—thus the answer is given by way of past consciousness.
By this very method, the meaning should be understood in all subsequent answers, such as those concerning the categories of meaning (*attha*) and phenomena (*dhamma*).
This is the method for the section on the "exceeded time" (atikkantakāla).
That consciousness which arises and does not cease—will that consciousness cease and not arise? Yes.
Or again... [as before] ...Yes. That consciousness which does not arise but ceases—will that consciousness not cease?
Will it arise? No. Or rather, that consciousness which will not cease but will arise—does that consciousness not arise and does it cease? None exists.
That consciousness which arises—is that consciousness arisen? Yes. Or rather... [as before] ...does it arise?
At the moment of arising, consciousness is likewise; thus also in the reverse questions, and in all subsequent ones. “Is that consciousness which does not arise, that consciousness unarisen?
Consciousness of the past and future is likewise. Or again... [etc. ...“Yes. ...[etc. ...“Consciousness at the moment of dissolution,” and so forth.
“Is that consciousness which arises, that consciousness has arisen? No. “Is that consciousness which does not arise...”
“Does that consciousness not arise? [Reply: “At the moment of dissolution, consciousness does not arise, yet it is future. And so forth:
“Is the consciousness that arises the same as the consciousness that will arise? No. Or again... no.

Is the consciousness that does not arise the same as the consciousness that will not arise? Future consciousness does not arise, yet it is not the case that it will not arise; at the moment of dissolution...”
And by such passages as, "The past mind is 'mind'," and, "That mind which has arisen, will that mind arise?
No. Or rather... [etc. ...No; that mind which has not arisen, will that mind not arise? It is the future mind," and so forth;
and by such passages as, "That mind which ceases, has that mind ceased? No," and so forth; and, "That mind which arises..."
“Does that consciousness cease?”—“No,” and so forth; and “Is the consciousness that arises, that consciousness which will cease?”—“Yes,” and so forth;
and “Is the consciousness that has arisen, that consciousness which will cease?”—“No,” and so forth;
and “Is the consciousness that is arising, that consciousness which has arisen?”—“Yes. Or again: “…is it that which is arising?”—“Yes,” and so forth.
And by such passages as, "the consciousness at the moment of arising," and "Is that consciousness which is ceasing 'arisen'?
Yes," and "Is that consciousness which is arisen 'has it arisen'? No. Or rather... no," and "That consciousness which has arisen but is not [currently] arisen—will that consciousness arise? No."
Furthermore, by such passages as: "Or that which... [etc. ...no. That consciousness which has not arisen and has not already arisen—that consciousness will it not arise?"—and by such passages as:
"'The arisen is the arising'... [etc. ...At the moment of arising, it is both arisen and arising.
Is 'the arising' the arisen?'—Yes."—and by such passages as: "'The ceased is the ceasing?'—No," and so forth.

In the section on phenomena (*dhammavāra*), by such passages as: "That consciousness which, while arising, transcends moment after moment and has transcended time; that consciousness which, while ceasing, transcends moment after moment and has transcended time—that is consciousness... [etc. ...past consciousness"; and in the section on persons and phenomena (*puggaladhammavāra*), by such passages as:
"For whomsoever a certain consciousness arises and does not cease, will that consciousness for him cease and not arise? Yes," and so forth;
and in the mixed sections by means of terms such as "with lust" (*sarāga*) and so on, and terms such as "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so on.
In all instances and questions, the method of answering should be understood according to what was stated previously.
This is the method for the commentary on the meaning of the Matrix of the Citta-Yamaka.
Regarding the commentary on the meaning of the Matrix of the Dhamma-Yamaka, however, the determination of the text should be understood by the very same method as that stated for the Khandha-Yamaka.

Because it is stated here, “One who develops a wholesome state abandons an unwholesome state,” this section is called the Section on Development (*bhāvanāvāra*), following the Section on Full Understanding (*pariññāvāra*).
In that regard, since an indeterminate state is neither to be developed nor abandoned, it should be understood that the term for it is not even mentioned.
As for the question and answer here: “Are there wholesome and unwholesome states?”...

The method of answering in the Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra) should be understood through such passages as: “Yes,” and so forth; and “Are unwholesome states ‘states’? Unwholesome states are both states and unwholesome states; the remaining states are states but not unwholesome states,” and so forth. [And:
“When wholesome states arise for someone, do unwholesome states arise for that person? No. Or for whom...”
But... [and so on] ...when wholesome states arise for someone, do indeterminate states arise for that person?
In the five-aggregate realm, at the moment of the arising of wholesome states... [and so on] ...they arise. And:
“Where wholesome states arise, do unwholesome states arise there? Yes... [and so on] ...do indeterminate states arise there?”
“Yes. And furthermore: “Wherever indeterminate states (*avyākata-dhamma*) arise, do wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) arise there?
… [and so on] … “In the fourfold plane (*catuvokāra*) … they arise,” and so forth; and also: “For whom, where, do wholesome states arise … [and so on] …? No,” and so forth; and:
“For whom wholesome states do not arise, for that person do unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) not arise? … [and so on] … “For all [beings] …”

And by such statements as: "In the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, in the moment of the arising of an indeterminate consciousness, in those who have attained cessation, and in non-percipient beings, neither wholesome states nor unwholesome states arise"; and:
"For whomsoever wholesome states do not arise, for him indeterminate states do not arise... [and so on] ...for all those passing away."

And by such passages as: "In the process [of consciousness], at the moment of the dissolution of the mind, and at the moment of the arising of unwholesome states in the formless realm, [they] do not arise";
and: "Where wholesome states do not arise, there do unwholesome states not arise?
Yes... pe ... Where indeterminate states do not arise? They do arise. Or where indeterminate states [arise]..."
In the section on arising (*uppādavāra*), [it is asked]: "When unwholesome states do not arise, do wholesome states not arise there?
[The answer is: "There is none. And so forth. In the section on cessation (*nirodhavāra*): "When wholesome states cease for someone, do unwholesome states cease for that person?

[The answer is: "No," and so forth. In the section on both arising and cessation (*uppādanirodhavāra*): "When wholesome states arise for someone, do unwholesome states cease for that person? [The answer is: "No," and so forth.
“Is it the case that whoever develops a wholesome state has abandoned an unwholesome state? “No.
… [and so on] … “Is it the case that whoever does not develop a wholesome state has not abandoned an unwholesome state?

“With the exception of one possessing the supreme path and an Arahant, all remaining persons”—thus the method of posing and answering questions in the section on development (bhāvanāvāra) should be understood according to what was stated above.
In this *Atthavinicchaya*, however, the following is the characteristic definition:

regarding this "Dhamma-Yamaka" (Pairs of Dhammas), in the section on the Great Chapter of Occurrence (*pavattimahāvāra*), concerning these occurrences and cessations expressed as "arising" and "ceasing," wholesome and unwholesome dhammas are found exclusively within the course of existence (*pavatti*) and not during death or rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*);
neutral (*abyākata*) dhammas, however, are found both in the course of existence and during death and rebirth-linking.
They are found in all three times; thus, in this context, the analysis for each case should be understood according to whatever is found in each respective instance.
Herein, this is the opening of the method: first, because wholesome and unwholesome states do not arise simultaneously, there is the negation "no."
"Done. Regarding "and the indeterminate," this was said with reference to mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).

Regarding "where wholesome states do not arise," this was said with reference to the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*); since there is no place where indeterminate states do not arise, the negation "there is not" was made.
In the section on cessation (*nirodhavāra*), because wholesome and unwholesome states do not cease together, [the answer] is "no."
By this very method, the analysis (*vinicchaya*) is to be understood in all instances.
This is the method for the commentary on the meaning of the *Dhammayamaka-mātikā*.

Regarding the commentary on the meaning of the *Indriyayamaka-mātikā*, however, the establishment of the text and so forth follows the same method as that stated for the *Khandhayamaka-mātikā* and the others.

The entire method of commentary on the meaning should be understood. However, in this context, the mind faculty (manindriya) enters into association with the female faculty (itthindriya) and so forth in exactly the same way as it does with the eye faculty (cakkhundriya) and the others;
therefore, rather than being combined according to the order in which they were listed, it is combined at the end with all of them, beginning with the eye faculty. With the eye faculty...

Furthermore, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*), the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*), and the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*)—along with the supramundane faculties (*lokuttarindriya*)—are not included because they do not exist at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Just as it is here, so it should be understood accordingly in the remaining sets based on the faculties.
However, due to the great number of faculties, there are more pairs (*yamaka*) in this section than even in the "Pairs of Elements" (*dhātuyamaka*); this is the distinction.

The remainder should be understood according to what has been stated below. This concludes the method for the commentary on the meaning of the Matrix of the Pairs of Faculties (*indriya-yamaka-mātikā*).
The commentary on the meaning of the Matrix of Pairs within the *Mohavicchedanī*, the commentary on the meaning of the Abhidhamma matrices, is finished.

7. Commentary on the Meaning of the *Paṭṭhāna* Matrix Now follows the method for commenting on the meaning of the *Paṭṭhāna* matrix. In what sense is it called *paṭṭhāna*? It is in the sense of various kinds of conditions (*paccaya*).
For the prefix *pa-* indicates "various kinds," while the word *ṭhāna* signifies "condition. Alternatively, it is in the sense of analysis (*vibhajana*).

*Paṭṭhāna*. For just as in passages where it is said "laying out, establishing, revealing, analyzing, making plain," the word *paṭṭhapanā* (establishing) is seen to have the same meaning as the word *paṭṭhāna* in the sense of "analysis," so too here, because it analyzes wholesome and other states by way of causes, conditions, and so forth, it is called *paṭṭhāna* in the sense of analysis. Alternatively, in the sense of being established (*paṭṭhita*).

*Paṭṭhāna* means "in the sense of going. For, because it provides the method of detailed exposition regarding wholesome states and so forth—which are differentiated by causes, conditions, and so on—it is called *paṭṭhāna* in the sense of "going" due to its proceeding as an unimpeded movement through all phenomena by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Thus, it is [called *paṭṭhāna*] in the sense of various kinds of conditions, in the sense of analysis, and in the sense of going.
Each one among the twenty-four *paṭṭhānas*, such as the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* and others, is called a *paṭṭhāna*; the collection of these is called the *Paṭṭhāna* treatise (*pakaraṇa*).
This [treatise] is the matrix (*mātikā*) for those *paṭṭhānas*. Alternatively, the matrix itself is the foundation (*paṭṭhāna*);

thus, all of this is the "Matrix of the *Paṭṭhāna*" (*Paṭṭhāna-mātikā*). That which begins with "Root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*)... [and so on] ...non-disappearance-condition (*avigata-paccaya*)"— The final sentence fragment provided in the source text appears to be the opening of the actual matrix itself. The translation reflects the structural analysis of the term *paṭṭhāna* as both individual units and a collective treatise, as well as its identity with the *mātikā*.

Thus, this is called the *Paṭṭhāna-mātikā* (the Schedule of the Conditional Relations), which was established by the Blessed One at the beginning of the treatise according to the divisions of the conditions that serve as its foundation, within the teaching of the *Samanta-paṭṭhāna* comprising twenty-four sections beginning with the "Triplets.

Regarding this, the concise analysis of the meaning—including the explanation of terms not yet commented upon—should be understood as follows: concerning [the terms] such as "root-condition" (*hetu-paccaya*), etc.

It is called the *hetupaccaya* (root-condition) because it is both a cause (*hetu*) and a condition (*paccaya*). Being a cause and being a condition is what is meant by "root-condition"; that is, it is a condition by way of its nature as a root. In this context, "cause" (*hetu*) is a designation for the members of a syllogism, reasons, and roots.

For in common worldly usage, as in the phrase "the reason for the proposition" (*paṭiññāhetu*), the member of a syllogism is called a "cause. However, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), as in the verse beginning "Those phenomena which arise from a cause" (*ye dhammā hetuppabhavā*), it refers to the root.
The word *kāraṇa* (cause) refers to the root, as in such passages as "three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots"; this is what is intended here.
It is called a *paccaya* (condition) because [the effect] goes (*eti*) by depending on that; the meaning is that it functions without abandoning that [cause].
For whatever phenomenon remains or arises without abandoning another phenomenon, that [former] possesses the characteristic of being helpful to the latter.
It is called a condition (*paccaya*). Thus, in the sense of being a root it is a cause (*hetu*), and in the sense of being an assistant it is a condition;

briefly, a phenomenon that is a root and an assistant is a causal condition (*hetupaccaya*). Some say it is "that which establishes the wholesome and so forth as wholesome and so forth" for the wholesome states and so on.

But if that were the case, the status of causal condition would not apply to the material phenomena produced by those [mental states], nor would it apply to rootless consciousnesses in the absence of these [wholesome factors].

The state of being indeterminate (abyākata) is established; and even for those states accompanied by roots (sahetuka), their status as wholesome (kusala) and so forth is dependent upon wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) and the like, not dependent upon associated causes (sampayutta-hetu).
If it were otherwise, there would have to be something else to establish the wholesome status of the roots themselves;

however, rather than grasping the sense of "root" (mūlaṭṭha) of the roots as that which establishes their wholesome status, they are grasped as that which establishes their state of being well-established (suppatiṭṭhita).
When [this condition] is taken up, nothing is contradicted. For phenomena that have obtained causes and conditions become firm and well-established, like trees with well-developed roots;
others, however, are not well-established, like moss from sesame seeds and the like.

Thus, because it assists by way of being a root, and because it accomplishes the state of being well-established, the phenomenon that acts as an assistant should be understood as the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
In the *Niddesa*, it is stated: “Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated by them.
Therein, instead of saying “originated by consciousness,” the phrase “originated by them” (*taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*) is used for the purpose of including those not originated by consciousness as well.
For in the *Pañhāvāra* (the Chapter of Questions), regarding the moment of rebirth-linking, it says: “At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate [states]... [and so forth].
It is stated [in the Paṭṭhāna]: “Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for the associated aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa).
But why is this root a root-condition for matter produced by kamma only at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), and not during the course of existence (pavatti)?
Because at the moment of rebirth-linking, the matter born of kamma exists in dependence upon consciousness, owing to its being the very first descent into a new existence.
Mind-born [matter]. Because it lacks the support of other material continuities, it arises and persists depending solely on the mind, which is its weak substrate.

For that mind, too, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), is itself unstable due to being impelled by the force of karma and because it has not yet established a prior physical basis—just like a man who has merely stepped onto a precipice.

Just as one cannot produce a mental image by performing a craft, [the rebirth-linking consciousnesses] cannot produce material form; rather, they are established depending upon that very *kaṭattā-rūpa*.

For rebirth-linking consciousnesses do not generate material form; instead, it is only *kamma*-born matter that persists in the place occupied by the mind-originated matter of those [consciousnesses].
However, during the course of existence (*pavatti*), because it has obtained support, that matter exists even without being bound to [rebirth-linking] *kamma*.

Regarding the occurrence [of this], the analysis of the root condition (*hetupaccaya*) here—according to its divisions into wholesome and so forth, and according to the divisions of the planes (*bhūmi*)—should be understood by the same method explained below; such is the method regarding the root condition.

Following that, among the subsequent conditions, a phenomenon that assists by way of being an object is the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). In the exposition (*niddesa*), it is stated: "The visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*)..."
The eye-consciousness element [is related] to the visible-object base and its associated states; … the tangible-object base [is related] to the body-consciousness element and its associated states;
… the visible-object base, sound-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-object base [are related] to the mind-element;
… all states [are related] to the mind-consciousness element; … whatever states, having whatever state as their object, arise as consciousness and mental factors.
"States are related to those respective states as object-condition"— since it is defined in this way,
there is no state that does not exist. For just as a weak person stands up and remains standing by leaning on a staff or a rope,
so too do consciousness and mental factors arise by leaning upon any one of the six [objects], such as visible form and the rest.

And because they both exist and persist, it should be understood that all phenomena—whether mundane, supramundane, or otherwise—are, as appropriate, the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for consciousness and mental factors.
This is the method regarding the object-condition.

A phenomenon that assists by way of being predominant is the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*). In the *Niddesa*, it is stated: "The predominance of desire (*chanda-adhipati*) [is a condition] for those states associated with desire..."
It is demonstrated in two ways as follows: “States, and the material phenomena originated by them... [and so on]... with energy, consciousness, and investigation as predominant... [and so on]...

are related to those states by way of predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*). Whatever states, whether mental or mental concomitants, arise by taking whatever state as estimable (*garuṃ katvā*), those states are related to those respective states by way of predominance condition. Thus it is shown in two ways.

In this context, desire and the others are stated by way of being co-nascent dominant factors (*sahajātādhipatibhāva*), while the object is stated by way of being an objective dominant factor (*ārammaṇādhipatibhāva*).
Furthermore, among these, a mundane wholesome state serves as an objective dominant factor for mundane wholesome states and for consciousness accompanied by greed;
it is not so for anything else. However, when it is unwholesome, it is called an "arising of consciousness accompanied by greed."

Because there is an absence of the quality of being "weighty" (*garuka*) in other [types of consciousness], that [resultant matter]—consisting of the worldling resultant form-aggregates with two roots or no roots—is associated only with greed, and not with anything else;
likewise for that which consists of functional [matter]. This is what has come down in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

That [explanation] applies to functional states associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta-kiriya*) that occurred previously as the precursors to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), and so forth, [in relation to] sense-sphere wholesome states (*kāmāvacara-kusala*).
It should be investigated by observing that there is no contradiction between the state of being revered and the state of being non-opposing.
However, it should be understood that supramundane wholesome states are object-predominance conditions only for the impulsions associated with sense-sphere knowledge;
whereas Nibbāna is [the object-predominance condition] for those same supramundane wholesome states as well as for their resultant states. This is the method regarding the predominance condition.
A state that assists by way of immediate succession is the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*);

it is the same as the contiguity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*), the difference being merely one of terminology, as in the case of [the terms] "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*).

As for the opinion of certain teachers that "it is a proximity condition by way of immediate succession of object, and a contiguity condition by way of immediate succession of time," that [does not apply here], because for one emerging from cessation, the wholesome state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
This contradicts such statements as, “The attainment of fruition is a condition for [the consciousness] by way of immediate condition,” and in its own definition:
“The eye-consciousness element and the states associated with it are [conditions] for the mind-element... the body-consciousness element... the mind-element... the mind-consciousness element...
preceding wholesome states are conditions for subsequent wholesome states... [and] for indeterminate states.”
"Of phenomena... [and so on]... preceding unwholesome phenomena are related to succeeding unwholesome phenomena... [and so on]... to indeterminate phenomena...

[and so on]... whatever phenomena, immediately after which, whatever phenomena arise—namely, consciousness and mental factors—those phenomena are related to those phenomena by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya). This is identical to the exposition of the proximity-condition.

Thus the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) has been explained, except for the diversity of names; this is the method regarding the pair of conditions known as the immediate and the immediately preceding.
A phenomenon that is helpful by virtue of its simultaneous arising with that which is arising is the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*); it is stated in the *Niddesa*:
"The four formless aggregates are a mutual co-nascent condition for one another; the four great elements..."
"Mutually... [and so on] ...at the moment of descent, name-and-form is mutually... [and so on] ...mental states and mental factors are conditions for mind-originated matter...

[and so on] ...the primary elements are conditions for derived matter... [and so on] ...material phenomena are, at some times, conditions for immaterial phenomena by way of the conascence condition, and at other times, they are not conditions by way of the conascence condition"—thus it is sixfold.
It has been explained. Therein, by the term "mutually," he illustrates both the state of being a condition and the state of being conditionally arisen for those phenomena at a single moment.
At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*) is called "matter" (*rūpa*).

"Mind and mental factors" refers to the four aggregates during the course of existence (*pavatti*); some say this also includes the four aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking. In that context, "mind-produced" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) also includes the matter produced by past action (*kaṭattārūpa*).
Because they have entered [into the womb]. For their rebirth-linking consciousness and mental factors are indeed related to one another by way of co-nascence condition;

however, those material phenomena, being devoid of a physical base (*vatthu*), do not exercise the function of a condition for the consciousness and mental factors produced by mind during the course of existence (*pavatti*), just as [materiality] does not for those consciousness and mental factors produced by mind.
Therefore, it is not said that they are "mutually" related. The same applies to derived matter (*upādārūpa*) in relation to such primary elements (*bhūta*). For if this were not accepted...

Since it is not stated that the "conascence-dependency" (*sahajāta-nissayatā*) exists for the kamma-produced material phenomena (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the exposition of the conascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) would be incomplete.
However, because the phrase "at some time" (*kiñci kāle*) refers specifically to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) at the moment of descent into the womb, it falls under the third category alone.
Thus, in terms of its actual meaning, this condition is fivefold. This is the method regarding the conascence-condition.
A phenomenon that assists another by way of mutual production and support is the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), like a tripod. This is explained in three ways in the *Niddesa*:
“The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the mutuality condition; the four great elements... [and so on]...
at the moment of descent [into the womb], name-and-form is a condition for one another by way of the mutuality condition. This is it.
The method for the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).

A phenomenon that assists by way of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and by way of being a support (*nissaya*) is the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), such as earth for trees and canvas for paintings;
it is described in the *Niddesa* in six ways, just like the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). The sixth...
In this context, the components are as follows: the eye-base is the support-condition for the eye-consciousness-element;
the ear, nose, tongue, and body-bases are the support-conditions for the body-consciousness-element...

[and so on] ...whatever material form depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed, that material form is the support-condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental states associated with them.
“Condition”: thus it is analyzed by way of showing the pre-arising support (*purejāta-nissaya*); the rest is exactly like that. Therein, “matter” (*rūpa*) refers to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).

Regarding the term “strong-dependence condition” (*upanissaya-paccaya*), this is the word-meaning: it is a support (*nissaya*) because it is not rejected, being dependent upon its own fruit due to its state of being governed by that [object];
and just as there is intense exertion (*āyāsa*) which is “great exertion” (*upāyāsa*), so too there is a support which is “intense support” (*upanissaya*).

“Upanissaya” is a designation for a powerful cause; therefore, a state that assists by way of being a powerful cause should be understood as the *upanissaya* condition. It is threefold: object-*upanissaya*, proximity-*upanissaya*, and natural-*upanissaya*.
Among these, first, the object-*upanissaya* is not differentiated from the object-dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
It is analyzed. In this context, that object which the mind and mental factors arise by treating as important is, by necessity, their strong object among objects;

thus, in the sense of being merely that which is to be treated as important, it is the "object-dominance" (ārammaṇādhipati), and in the sense of being a powerful cause, it is the "object-strong-dependence" (ārammaṇūpanissaya). In this way, their distinction should be understood.
The proximity-object-condition (*anantarūpanissaya*) is also analyzed without making a distinction from the proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*).

Nevertheless, it should be understood that "proximity" (*anantaratā*) refers to the capacity for a succeeding mental state to arise in accordance with its own immediate predecessor, while "proximity-object-condition-ness" (*anantarūpanissayatā*) refers to the power of the preceding consciousness in producing the subsequent mental state. This is just as in the case of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and others.
The mind can arise even without some other state; however, there is no such thing as the arising of a mind without its immediately preceding mind.
Therefore, it is a powerful condition. Thus, in the sense of being a powerful cause, the "immediately preceding" itself is called the "immediately preceding decisive support" (anantarūpanissaya).
In this way, their distinction should be understood.

Inherent decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) is a decisive support that is inherent; "inherent" means a support produced within one's own continuum, or one cultivated through faith, virtue, and so forth, or a support by the very nature of climate, food, and so on—this is the meaning of being unmixed with extrinsic support (*parūpanissaya*).
And that inherent support [is described as]: "Relying on faith, one gives a gift, undertakes virtue, performs the Uposatha duty..."

It is analyzed in many ways according to these factors beginning with faith (*saddhā*), such as: "One performs [meritorious deeds], arouses jhāna; one arouses insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and attainment (*samāpatti*);
relying upon virtue (*sīla*), learning (*suta*), generosity (*cāga*), and wisdom (*paññā*), one gives a gift...
pe... arouses attainment. Thus, the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is threefold. Furthermore, in the *Niddesa*:

“Preceding wholesome states [are related] to succeeding wholesome states … [to some] unwholesome states … [to] indeterminate states … Preceding unwholesome states [are related] to succeeding unwholesome states … [to some] wholesome states … [to] indeterminate states … Preceding indeterminate states …”
“Dhammas... [and so on]... are a condition for indeterminate, wholesome, and unwholesome states by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya);

a person (puggala) is also a condition by way of decisive support condition; and even a lodging (senāsana) is [a condition]”—thus it is defined. In that context, regarding the "preceding" [states], only those immediately past are obtained in the case of the immediate decisive support (anantara-upanissaya).

However, among the object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) and natural strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya), because they function in various ways as prior states, all three groups are found to be wholesome with respect to the wholesome.
But with respect to the unwholesome, those that have just passed away in immediate succession (samanantarātītā) are not found to be wholesome;
therefore he said, "of some. For this [refers to] "a wholesome state being an object-strong-dependence for an unwholesome state."

This was stated with reference to the method found in the *Pañhāvāra* (the Chapter on Questions), such as: "Natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*); object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*): having given a gift... [and so on] ...having revered it, lust arises... natural decisive support:
depending upon faith as a decisive support, one conceives conceit," and so forth.
For in the case of unwholesome states, those that have just passed away (*samanantarātītā*) are not obtained for wholesome states; therefore he said, "for some. However, this...
“An unwholesome state is a natural strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya) for a wholesome state. Depending on lust, one gives a gift...

[and so forth]... having killed a living being, one gives a gift as an antidote to that,” etc.—this was said with reference specifically to the natural strong-dependence as it appears in the section on questions (pañhāvāra).
For just as an unwholesome state is not an immediate strong-dependence (anantarūpanissaya) for a wholesome state, so too it is not an object strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya).
It does not exist. For it is not by making that [unwholesome state] an object of esteem (*garu*) that the wholesome arises.
However, in the case of unwholesome and indeterminate states, the object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) is simply not obtained. This is because those indeterminate states do not esteem it;

rather, they are merely its immediate antecedents (*anantara*). For this very reason, the phrase "for some" (*kesañci*) was not stated here. In the remaining cases, all three [types of strong-dependence] apply.

The decisive support conditions (*upanissaya*) are indeed obtained. The statement, “both the person and the lodging,” refers here specifically to these two by way of the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*);
furthermore, the season, food, and so forth should be included here.

And it should be understood that within this condition, all phenomena belonging to the four planes are included along with certain designations (*paññatti*). This is the method regarding the decisive support condition.
Material phenomena that arise earlier and assist by way of their continued presence are the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).
This is elevenfold, according to the sense-faculties, the objects, and the heart-base. And in the *Niddesa*:

"The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated therewith by way of the prenascence condition... [and so on] ...the body-base is a condition for the body-consciousness element..."
...pe... the visible-form base is [a condition] for the eye-consciousness element ...pe... the tangible-object base is [a condition] for the body-consciousness element ...pe...
the visible-form base, the sound-base, the odor-base, the taste-base, and the tangible-object base are [conditions] for the mind-element ...pe... whatever matter depending upon which ...pe...
that matter is at some times a pre-arising condition for both the mind-element and the mind-consciousness element.

"Sometimes it is not a condition by way of the prenascence condition. Thus, this has been demonstrated in every respect both in the five doors by way of the bases and objects, and in the mind door by way of the base alone.

However, in the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions), because it is stated that "the Arahant contemplates the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self," the object-prenascence condition exists even in the mind door for eighteen [mental states].
Since, by way of material phenomena (rūpa), even the object-prenascence (ārammaṇa-purejāta) is indeed obtained, this is the method regarding the prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya).

A non-material phenomenon (arūpadhamma) that assists prenascent material phenomena by way of providing support is the postnascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), just as the volition of desire for food supports the bodies of young vultures. And in its exposition (Niddesa) it says: "The postnascent mind and mental factors..."
It is said: “States are a condition for this pre-arisen body by way of post-nascence condition.
In that context, “of this body” refers to the body composed of primary elements and derived matter arising from four or three causes.
As for the states, it should be understood that, setting aside rebirth-linking and formless-sphere resultant [states], all remaining immaterial states belonging to the four planes are meant.
This is the method regarding the postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).

A state that assists subsequent states by means of repetition (*āsevana*) through its habituated and powerful nature is the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), such as prior application to books and so forth.
It is threefold by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsion (*javana*). In its exposition (*niddesa*), however, it says: "The preceding wholesome..."
“States are related to subsequent wholesome states... [and so on] ...to unwholesome states...

[and so on] ...to functional-ineffective states by way of the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya),” thus it is demonstrated. In this context, “preceding, preceding” should everywhere be understood as immediately past;
therein too, wholesome states and the like are related even to those of a different class, such as the functional-ineffective, by way of immediate succession.

Due to their inability to cause one to grasp the state— consisting of one's own wholesome and other qualities— that is distinguished by a more proficient and powerful nature through the practice known as *vāsanā*,
they do not function as conditions of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). However, even though they differ in terms of plane and object,
the wholesome and functional states of the sense-sphere with three roots are similar to the sublime and supramundane wholesome states in that they possess feelings identical to their own.

Furthermore, wholesome states of conformity (anuloma-kusala) having formations as their object do indeed serve as the condition of repetition (āsevana-paccaya) for the wholesome state of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-kusala) having Nibbāna as its object.
However, there is no supramundane (lokuttara) condition of repetition, because a resultant state is transformed by karma;
such is the method regarding the condition of repetition.
A phenomenon that assists by way of the state of activity (kiriyabhāva), which is designated as the mental application (cittappayoga), is the kamma-condition (kammapaccaya).
It is twofold: by way of wholesome and unwholesome volition (cetanā) belonging to different moments, and by way of all co-nascent (sahajāta) volition. In the *Niddesa* as well, it is stated:

"Wholesome and unwholesome kamma [is a condition] for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa)... [and so on]... volition [is a condition] for its associated states..."
“Mind-object (dhamma) is a condition for mental states and for the material phenomena originating from them by way of the kamma-condition. Thus it is stated in two ways.
Therein, “kamma” refers exclusively to volitional action (cetanā-kamma). Regarding “and for material phenomena produced by kamma” (*kaṭattā-rūpa*):

it is precisely because of the having been performed (*kaṭattā*), accumulated, and brought to completion of kamma that the kamma-born material phenomena have arisen; for even kamma [only] at a later time, upon the conjunction of the remaining conditions...
When it exists, it produces its own fruit; however, because it has perished, or because it remains [static], it does not produce that [fruit].
Thus, by the phrase "originated by that," the inclusion of *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by past action) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) should be understood.
This is the method regarding the condition of kamma.
A resultant state that, by its quality of being effortless and peaceful, assists in the attainment of an effortless and peaceful state is a resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*).

It acts as a condition for mind-produced matter during the course of existence (*pavatta*), for kamma-produced matter at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and for all associated states everywhere.
As it is said in the section on all questions: "One resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition for three aggregates..."
“...and it is a condition, by way of resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*), for mind-originated matter and for kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking,” and so forth.
However, in its exposition (*Niddesa*), only this much is stated: “The four immaterial resultant aggregates are mutually a condition by way of resultant condition.
This was stated with an omission, referring to the method explained in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*).
This is the method regarding the condition of kamma-result (vipāka-paccaya).
The four nutriments (āhāra), which assist both the material and immaterial by way of providing support, are the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya). In the Niddesa, however, it is said:
"Physical nutriment [is a condition] for this body... the immaterial nutriments [are conditions] for associated states and for those states originated thereby..."

"Form is a condition for forms by way of nutriment-condition"—thus it is defined. In this context, the nutritive essence (ojā) that has entered into the fourfold origination is called edible nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra).
Since it is only when those who consume nutriment have ingested food, and when the temperature-born and karma-born types of nutriment are likewise sustained, that this body persists;
and not otherwise—therefore, [this is stated] for the purpose of showing its dependence upon the physical basis consisting of what is to be chewed and the temperature-element.

It is called "edible food" (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra). Although this is stated without distinction as "of this body," specifically, it acts as a nutriment-condition by being both the producer and the sustainer of the materiality born of nutriment, and by being the sustainer of the remaining materiality produced by the [other] three continuities.
By the phrase "of those produced by that," [it refers to] those produced by karma at the moment of rebirth-linking.

[The nutriment condition] is already included [in the previous section]. For in the Question Section (Pañhāvāra) it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate nutriments are a condition, by way of nutriment-condition, for the associated aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma. This is the method regarding the nutriment condition.
As for the faculty condition: the twenty faculties, excluding the female and male faculties, are the faculty condition in the sense of being supportive through their predominance.

For although the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the male faculty (*purisindriya*) are the seeds for the female and male sexual characteristics, appearance, and so forth, they do not exercise the status of a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) toward those [characteristics] nor toward others.
However, according to the method of the Suttanta, they exercise the status of a natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
Thus, there are exactly twenty-two faculties. Among these, the five beginning with the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*)— [...]*

The faculty condition applies only to non-material phenomena; the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) applies only to kamma-born materiality (*kaṭattā-rūpa*); and the remaining [faculties] apply to both material and non-material phenomena. In the *Niddesa*:
"The eye-faculty is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and for those states associated with it...

[and so on] ...for the body-consciousness element... [and so on] ...the material life-faculty is a condition for kamma-born materiality; the immaterial faculties are conditions for associated states and for those states originated by them."

It is defined thus: "Material phenomena are a condition for material phenomena by way of the faculty-condition. In the phrase "arising from that," the kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) is also included.

For in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate faculties are a condition for their associated aggregates and for kamma-produced matter. This is the method regarding the faculty-condition.

With the exception of the three feelings and one-pointedness found in the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness—which do not function as acts of sustained contemplation—the remaining seven factors of absorption, classified as wholesome and so forth, constitute the condition of absorption (*jhāna-paccaya*).

For, because the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness consist merely of an initial impact, feeling and one-pointedness are not included among the factors of absorption due to the absence of the mode of sustained contemplation therein; however, in the *Niddesa*, it is stated: [...]* *Note: The original text appears to be truncated at this point.*
“Jhāna factors are a condition, by way of jhāna-condition, for the states associated with jhāna and for the material phenomena originated by them”—this is how it is defined.
Here too, by the phrase “originated by them,” kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) is also included. In the sections on the questions (*pañhāvāra*), it is stated:
“At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate jhāna factors [are a condition] for the associated aggregates...”
"...and because of the material phenomena already performed"—thus is stated the method regarding the condition of jhāna.
The twelve path factors, classified as wholesome and so forth, which are helpful in the sense of leading out from this or that [state], are the path condition (*maggapaccaya*).
In the *Niddesa*, however, it says: "The path factors [are the condition] for those states associated with the path and for the material phenomena originated by them..."
"...is indicated as a condition by way of path-condition. Here too, by the phrase "arisen from that," there is the inclusion of *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by kamma).

For in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate path-factors [are a condition] for their associated aggregates and for matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
And herein, the path-factors existing in rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*) are [path-conditions].
They do not exist. This is the method regarding the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*).

Immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) that assist by way of association—characterized as having the same physical basis (*ekavatthuka*), the same object (*ekārammaṇa*), the same arising (*ekuppāda*), and the same cessation (*ekanirodha*)—are the associated condition (*sampayuttapaccaya*).
In the *Niddesa*, however, it says: "The four immaterial aggregates (*khandhā*) are phenomena that [assist] one another..."
"...is related by way of the association condition"—thus has it been defined; this is the method regarding the association condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*).

Material phenomena that assist immaterial phenomena, and immaterial phenomena that assist material phenomena, by not entering into a state of having a common physical basis (*ekavatthu*) and so forth, constitute the dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*).
This is threefold, by way of the conascent (*sahajāta*), the pre-arisen (*purejāta*), and the post-arisen (*pacchājāta*). For it has been said:
“Wholesome aggregates arising together [with them] are related to mind-produced matter... [and so on]...

Wholesome aggregates arisen later are related to this body arisen earlier by way of dissociation condition,” and so forth. However, the “arisen earlier” (purejāta) condition should be understood solely by way of the six bases.
In its exposition (Niddesa), however, it says: “Material phenomena are related to immaterial phenomena... [and so on]... Immaterial phenomena are related to material phenomena.”

“...is a condition by way of dissociation-condition (vippayuttapaccaya)”—thus it is explained in general terms. Therein, the term “material” (rūpin) is stated with reference to the six bases (vatthu);

however, material phenomena such as visible form and so forth, being objects of consciousness (ārammaṇadhamma), are not stated to be dissociation-conditions because there is no possibility of their being associated [with consciousness].
For non-material phenomena arise from within the bases of the eye and so forth as if they were emerging from them.

In that case, there is a suspicion of association (*sampayoga*). For even in the Section on Questions (*Pañhāvāra*), only the six bases (*vatthu*) are mentioned, such as: "The [heart-]base for wholesome aggregates... the eye-base for the eye-consciousness element," and so forth.

Here too, although the immaterial states (*arūpa-dhamma*) are distinct from the material, Nibbāna—though itself immaterial—is not a dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*) for materiality, because there is no suspicion whatsoever of association.
For it is said: “There is association with four [factors] and dissociation with four. This is the method regarding the condition of dissociation (*vippayutta-paccaya*).
A factor that assists by way of providing support for another factor of a similar nature through its state of existence characterized by the present is the presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*).
In the *Niddesa*, this is explained as: “The four formless aggregates [are related] to one another... the four great elements... and so forth.
Mutuality: at the moment of descent, name-and-form is mutually related; mental states and mental factors are related to matter originated by mind;

the great primary elements are related to derived matter; the eye-base is related to the eye-consciousness element and its associated states … pe … the visible-object-base is related to the eye-consciousness element and its associated states … pe … the visible-object-base … pe … the tangible-object-base.

"Mind-element... [and so on] ...is a condition by way of presence-condition for mind-element, mind-consciousness-element, and the states associated with them"—thus it has been explained in many ways by way of both conascence and prenascence;
however, in the *Pañhāvāra* (The Chapter of Questions), it is explained by way of these five: "conascent, prenascent, postnascent, nutriment, and faculty."
The presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*) should also be understood by way of the postnascent kamma-formations, nutriment, material form, and the life-faculty due to their having arrived;
such is the method regarding the presence condition.
Those [mental states] that have ceased immediately prior, which assist by providing a basis for the occurrence of the immaterial phenomena arising immediately after themselves—
Non-material phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) are the non-existence condition (*natthipaccaya*). However, in the *Niddesa*, it is defined in general terms as follows:
"Consciousness and mental factors that have ceased immediately prior are a condition for present consciousness and mental factors by way of the non-existence condition.
Because it is in every respect identical to the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*), the specific distinction here is exactly according to the method explained therein.
"It should be known"—this is the method regarding the absence condition (*natthipaccaya*).

Because the very phenomena that serve as the absence condition are helpful by way of their state of having disappeared (*vigata*), they are called the "disappearance condition" (*vigatapaccaya*); thus, it is similar to the absence condition when stated together with it.

The non-disappearance condition (*avigatapaccaya*) is in every respect identical to the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*); this dyad was taught either for the sake of elegance in exposition or to suit those who are to be trained—this is the method regarding the non-disappearance condition.
The Determination of Miscellaneous Points:
Now, among these twenty-four conditions, for the purpose of clarifying the range of knowledge—
regarding the phenomena, the times, and the single condition that serves as many— *Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya*.
Because many phenomena possess the state of being a single condition for one another—
whether similar or dissimilar, categorized as pairs starting from the "productive" and so forth,
distinguished by all locations and the like, and differentiated by the modes of material and immaterial form.
The miscellaneous determination should be understood from your compendium. Regarding that, as for the phrase "by way of dhamma":
among these conditions, first, the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) is a portion of the mental dhammas within the categories of both mind and matter;
likewise are the co-nascent, predominance, kamma, jhāna, and path-conditions; likewise the repetition and fruition-conditions—even though they are included within the four aggregates.

States subject to ripening (vipākadhammā) are [related] by way of the conditions of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), post-nascence (pacchājāta), association (sampayutta), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata).

It is also appropriate to say that they constitute a portion of the "name" (nāma) aggregate, because Nibbāna is not included therein. The pre-nascence condition (purejātapaccaya) consists only of material phenomena (rūpadhamma);

the remaining conditions consist of both name and form (nāmarūpadhamma) according to their occurrence. Furthermore, among those, the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya), and natural strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya) include conceptual designations (paññatti) as well.
"Comprehended"—this is the analysis by way of dhamma.

By way of time, however, fifteen conditions—namely, root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, prenascence, postnascence, kamma-result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—being themselves present, act as conditions for their own fruits.
The proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions [act as conditions]...
The five [paccayas] exist only as past; however, the kamma-paccaya exists both as present and as past.

The remaining three—ārammaṇa, adhipati, and upanissaya paccayas—exist in all three times, and they also exist as independent of time by way of Nibbāna and concepts (paññatti), acting as conditions for their respective fruits.
This is the analysis according to time.
"One condition for many" means that a single phenomenon (*dhamma*) and a single condition (*paccaya*) function as many conditions. How so? First, regarding the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*):
non-delusion (*amoha*) is a single phenomenon; yet, by way of twenty conditions—excluding the prenascence, nutriment, and jhāna conditions—it becomes a manifold condition.

Without relinquishing its status as a root-condition, it serves as the predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, resultant, faculty, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
Alternatively, there are multiple conditions by way of the other eleven [types of consciousness]. Likewise for non-greed and the others;
however, among those, non-greed and non-hate do not serve as faculty or path conditions. Those three—non-resultant greed, hate, and delusion—do not serve as resultant conditions.
Furthermore, those five, excluding non-delusion, do not serve as predominance conditions; likewise for the remaining ones that are non-resultant.

In the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) serves as a multiple condition for the eye-consciousness element by way of four conditions: object, prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance;
likewise for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the rootless mind-consciousness element (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*).

However, for the root-possessing [mind-consciousness element], it also serves as a condition by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*). This same method applies to sound and the other sense objects as well.
Furthermore, the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) is a multiple condition even by way of being the support for those states dissociated from it;

likewise, while not relinquishing its status as an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), it is also a multiple condition for seven others by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), support (nissaya), decisive support (upanissaya), prenascence (purejāta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).
This is the highest limit in this context. Therein:

However, when non-material phenomena (arūpa-dhammā) or material phenomena (rūpa-dhammā) of the past or future serve as object-conditions (ārammaṇa-paccaya), they receive at most only the status of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and decisive support (upanissaya).

Regarding the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), object-predominance is exactly as described by the aforementioned method. Among the co-nascent predominances (sahajātādhipati), consciousness (citta) becomes a multiple condition by way of nineteen conditions—excluding the root (hetu), prenascent (purejāta), kamma, jhāna, and path (magga) conditions—without relinquishing its status as a predominance condition.
For others, it is by way of ten conditions—conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance;
likewise, energy (*vīriya*) is a condition for all except the nutriment condition, while including the path condition;
desire (*chanda*) is a condition for all except the nutriment and faculty conditions; and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is a condition in the same manner as stated for the root condition.

In the case of the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*), first, among the four aggregates, the feeling aggregate (*vedanā-kkhandha*) functions by way of nineteen conditions, excluding the root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, and path conditions;
the perception aggregate (*saññā-kkhandha*) functions by way of seventeen of those, excluding the faculty and jhāna conditions;
and the formations aggregate (*saṅkhāra-kkhandha*) functions by way of eighteen, excluding the root, prenascence, kamma, faculty, jhāna, and path conditions.

Likewise, volition [is a condition] for those associated with kamma; initial application (vitakka) for those associated with jhāna and the Path, excluding the conditions of root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, and faculty;

sustained application (vicāra) and joy (pīti) for those that are immediate, excluding the Path; and one-pointedness (ekaggatā) by way of twenty conditions, excluding the conditions of root, prenascence, kamma, and nutriment.
Faith and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) are [conditions] for those that are immediate, excluding the conditions of root, prenascence, kamma, nutriment, jhāna, and the Path.
Among the eighteen [mental factors], mindfulness is [a condition] for nineteen when accompanied by the Path;

the triad of moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), and the six pairs beginning with bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*); among the miscellaneous factors (*yevāpanaka*), resolution (*adhimokkha*), attention (*manasikāra*), equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*), and compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) are [conditions] for seventeen, excluding the root-cause (*hetu*), the prenascence (*purejāta*), kamma, nutriment, jhāna, Path, and faculty [factors];

the abstinences (*virati*), however, are [conditions] for eighteen when accompanied by the Path; and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is [a condition] for those same [eighteen] excluding the resultant (*vipāka*).

By way of the seventeen [mental factors], and by way of the nineteen conditions consisting of wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood, together with those same kamma, nutriment, and presence conditions;

and by way of the sixteen [conditions]—namely, lack of shame (*ahirika*), lack of dread (*anottappa*), conceit (*māna*), sloth (*thina*), torpor (*middha*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—which are excluded from the categories of root, prenascence, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path;

and by way of the fifteen [conditions]—namely, doubt (*vicikicchā*), envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and worry (*kukkucca*)—which are further excluded from the category of predominance (*adhipati*).

By way of these, there are many conditions. Furthermore, for those [mental states] that do not relinquish their status as proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*), there are six other [conditions]: the immediately-preceding condition (*samanantara*), the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya*), the kamma-condition (*kamma*), the presence-condition (*atthi*), and the non-disappearance-condition (*avigata*).
The fact that the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) possesses many conditions should be understood through its very nature as a predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*).

Within the co-nascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), the great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) [act as conditions] by way of object, object-predominance, co-nascence, mutuality, support, decisive-support, prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.

The heart-base is [a condition] for those same nine [mental states] by way of dissociation and coexistence. In the case of the dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), the eye-base and so forth are [conditions] for nine factors by way of object, object-predominance, dependence, decisive support, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

In the case of the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), the bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and so forth are [conditions] for five factors by way of object, object-predominance, decisive support, prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.

By way of the concealed (channa): through the nutriment condition, nutritive essence (*ojā*) acts as a condition in many ways by way of six conditions—namely, object, object-predominance, decisive support, nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance.

Without relinquishing their respective status as those specific conditions, they function in all instances as object, predominance, proximity, contiguity, decisive support, and so forth, according to the method already stated.
[This] should be understood. The rest is indeed easy to comprehend;
thus ends the analysis of how a single [condition] acts as multiple conditions. Regarding the phrase "and how multiple phenomena act as a single condition":

among these, with the exception of the kamma-condition, in the remaining twenty-three conditions, many [conditions] act together as individual conditions for many phenomena. As for the kamma-condition...
"But volition is a single dhamma"—this is the determination [of conditions] based on the fact that multiple dhammas function as a single condition.

Regarding "similar and dissimilar": among these, the conditions of proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), proximity-support (*anantarūpanissaya*), repetition (*āsevana*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) are similar;
likewise are the object (*ārammaṇa*), object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), and object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*). However, the prenascence condition (*purejātapaccaya*) here—
The posterior-arisen is dissimilar to the prior-arisen; likewise, the associated is dissimilar to the dissociated, the existent to the non-existent, and the vanished to the non-vanished.
This is the analysis according to similarity and dissimilarity.
Regarding "pairs," here [the classification is based on] similarity of meaning, similarity of sound, opposition in time, and the relation of cause and fruit.
By way of mutual opposition, these reasons should be understood as pairs (*yugala*).

For "immediate" (*anantara*) and "contiguous" (*samanantara*) constitute one pair by similarity of meaning; "support" (*nissaya*) and "decisive support" (*upanissaya*) by similarity of sound; "prenascence" (*purejāta*) and "postnascence" (*pacchājāta*) by opposition of time;
"kamma" and "result" (*vipāka*) by the relation of cause and fruit; and "association" (*sampayutta*) and "dissociation" (*vippayutta*) by mutual opposition.
One pair: likewise, the condition of presence-absence (*atthi-anatthi-paccaya*) and the condition of disappearance-non-disappearance (*vigata-avigata-paccaya*). This is the analysis by way of pairs.

"By way of producers, etc. means by way of producers and supporters. For among these, the conditions of proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), repetition (*asevana*), the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānakkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), and the conditions of absence (*natthi*) and disappearance (*vigata*)—these are producers only, not supporters.

The postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is merely a support, not a producer. The remaining conditions are both producers and supporters; this is the analysis according to their nature as producers and so forth.
"Distinguished by all bases, etc.

means distinguished by the categories of having all bases and not having all bases. For among these, the co-nascent (sahajāta), dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions—
All-pervasive (*sabbaṭṭhānika*). These are required for all conditioned phenomena (*paccayuppanna*); there is not even a single phenomenon that arises without them.

The others are not all-pervasive (*asabbaṭṭhānika*). Among those, the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*), object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), absence (*natthi*), disappearance (*vigata*), natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), prenascence (*purejāta*), repetition (*āsevana*), association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) conditions are not all-pervasive because they function only with respect to immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*). The same applies to the postnascence-condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*).
Because they are the cause of only material phenomena, while the remaining ones are the cause of certain material and immaterial phenomena, they are not "all-bases.
This is the analysis according to the classification of "all-bases" and so forth.

As for the classification by way of the permutations of material and immaterial phenomena: it refers to permutations such as "material is the cause of material," "material is the cause of immaterial," and so on. For among these, not even one...

There is no such thing as a condition that, being material itself, becomes a condition for the material alone; however, there is a condition that is material itself [serving as] a condition for the immaterial alone, and that is the single *purejāta-paccaya* (pre-arising condition). Furthermore, there is no such thing as a condition that, being material itself, becomes a condition for both the material and the immaterial;

yet there is also a condition that, being immaterial itself, serves as a condition for the immaterial alone, and that exists by way of the *anantara*, *samanantara*, *āsevana*, *sampayutta*, *natthi*, and *vigata* [conditions].

It is sixfold. Furthermore, there is a condition that is exclusively non-material (arūpa) for material (rūpa) phenomena; this is the single condition known as postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya).

There is also a condition that, being exclusively non-material, serves as a condition for both material and non-material phenomena; this is fivefold by way of root-cause (hetu), kamma, result (vipāka), jhāna, and path (magga).

Finally, there is a condition that, being a designation (paññatti) of both material and non-material phenomena, serves as a condition for non-material phenomena alone; this is twofold by way of object (ārammaṇa) and decisive support (upanissaya).

Furthermore, both the material and the immaterial exist for the material and the immaterial; this [condition] is ninefold by way of predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.
This is the analysis according to the classification of the material and the immaterial.
Regarding "from existence": among these conditions, first of all, in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), there is indeed no condition that is not obtainable.

All [twenty-four conditions] are obtainable. However, in the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), excluding the prenascence, postnascence, and dissociation conditions, only the remaining twenty-one are obtained.
In the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), there are only seven, by way of conascence, mutuality, support, kamma, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance.
Furthermore, in external matter not bound to faculties, only five are obtainable, excluding kamma and faculty from among those.
This is your analysis. As for inclusion:
all these twenty-four conditions are included within eight conditions—namely, object, conascence, decisive support, prenascence, postnascence, kamma, nutriment, and faculty.
How so? Among them, the conditions of root, mutuality, resultant, jhāna, path, and association—
The six [conditions]—conascence, mutuality, dependence, presence, non-disappearance, and association—are included within the conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

The five conditions—proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance—are included within the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

The dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) is twofold, being divided into conascence and prenascence; therein, the conascent is included in the conascence condition, and the prenascent in the prenascence condition. The predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) is also...
That which has become an object is included under the object-strong-dependence condition; that which has become co-nascent is included under the co-nascence condition.
The dissociation condition is also included under various conditions according to its being co-nascent, prenascent, or postnascent.
The presence and non-disappearance conditions are also included under various conditions according to their being co-nascent, prenascent, postnascent, nutriment, or faculty.
Thus, the inclusion of all conditions within these [eight] conditions should be understood.
For this very reason, in the Tikapaṭṭhāna-pāḷi, under the method of the negative (paccanīya-naya), several questions are answered by means of these eight conditions alone.
Furthermore, there is indeed a mutual inclusion among these eight as well; for among them, the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is predominant.
In the case of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*), that which does not function as a predominance condition (*adhipati*) remains distinct as an object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

As for the kamma condition (*kamma-paccaya*), it is co-nascent with respect to what is co-nascent. However, when it is asynchronous and powerful, it becomes a decisive support for states that are subject to result (*vipāka-dhamma*), and thus it is included within the decisive support condition.
Even when it is powerful, [it acts] toward kamma-born material phenomena (*kammaja-rūpa*); when weak, [it acts] toward...
The immaterial [condition] stands entirely separate, acting as the condition of kamma by way of different moments. The nutriment condition also stands entirely separate:
being immaterial, it exists in the co-nascent; being material, it exists nowhere else. The faculty condition also stands entirely separate:
being immaterial, it exists in the co-nascent; the sensitive faculties exist in the prenascence; and the material life-faculty does not enter into any [of these categories].
Just as [the faculty] remains distinct even while acting as a faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya), so too does mutual inclusion (aññamañña-saṅgaha) indeed exist.
Furthermore, all these twenty-four conditions are included within the four [conditions]: object (ārammaṇa), decisive support (upanissaya), kamma, and presence (atthi).
This is the analysis by way of inclusion. This concludes the concise analysis of the meaning, together with the clarification of the non-obvious terms.
The Determination of Miscellaneous Topics is finished.
Regarding the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga-naya*) here, the establishment of the text should first be understood in brief as follows.

For in the *Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi*, after setting forth the terms for conditions—beginning with "the root-condition" (*hetu-paccaya*) and ending with "the non-disappearance-condition" (*avigata-paccaya*)—as a matrix (*mātikā*), [the text proceeds] with their...

First, the section of the exposition known as the "Analysis of Conditions" (*paccayabhājanīya*) was stated, according to the method beginning with: "Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated by them.
Furthermore, the detailed analysis of the concise meaning of "immediate" (*anantara*) has already been shown in various places. Immediately after that, regarding those twenty-four...

By way of classifying the conditions through various methods based on the twenty-two triplets—such as the wholesome triplet—and the one hundred dyads—such as the root-cause dyad—the compendium of the twenty-four *Paṭṭhānas* is analyzed as the *Anantanaya-samantapaṭṭhāna*. How so?
For the *Paṭṭhāna* is fourfold: the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna* (direct order), the *Paccanīka-paṭṭhāna* (inverse order), the *Anuloma-paccanīka-paṭṭhāna* (direct-inverse order), and...

Regarding the *paccanīkānuloma-paṭṭhāna* (the conditional relations in reverse and direct order): therein, that which proceeds by way of the direct order (*anuloma*) of wholesome and other states, as well as root-cause and other factors— beginning with “Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the root-cause condition” and “Dependent on a state that is a root-cause,
a state that is a root-cause arises by way of the root-cause condition”— is called the *anuloma-paṭṭhāna*.
“Dependent on a non-wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises by way of root condition...
