dependent on a state that is not a root, a state that is not a root arises by way of root condition”—thus, the *paccanīka-paṭṭhāna* (counter-positive establishment) is that which proceeds by way of the opposites of states such as the wholesome and states such as roots. “Dependent on a wholesome state, a non-wholesome...”

The *anuloma-paccanīka-paṭṭhāna* (positive-negative matrix) is that which proceeds as follows: "A state arises by way of root-condition... [and so on] ...dependent on a state that is not a root, a state that is a root arises by way of root-condition.
The *paccanīka-anuloma-paṭṭhāna* (negative-positive matrix) is that which proceeds as follows: "Dependent on a state that is not wholesome, a wholesome state...
[and so on] ...dependent on a state that is not a root, a state that is a root arises by way of root-condition."
Thus, among these four arrangements (*paṭṭhāna*), that which is called the "conformity arrangement" (*anuloma-paṭṭhāna*) is first of six kinds:

the triad arrangement (*tika-paṭṭhāna*), the dyad arrangement (*duka-paṭṭhāna*), the dyad-triad arrangement (*duka-tika-paṭṭhāna*), the triad-dyad arrangement (*tika-duka-paṭṭhāna*), the triad-triad arrangement (*tika-tika-paṭṭhāna*), and the dyad-dyad arrangement (*duka-duka-paṭṭhāna*).
And just as this is so, the three [remaining] arrangements—the opposition arrangement (*paccanīka-paṭṭhāna*) and the others—are each likewise threefold.
The *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa* should be understood as the synthesis of twenty-four *samantapaṭṭhānas*.
For indeed, by the Fully Enlightened One, based on the twenty-two triplets (*tīkā*) in the *anulomapaṭṭhāna*, that which is called the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* was demonstrated;
based on the hundred dyads (*dukas*), that which is called the *Duka-paṭṭhāna*; and then, having combined the triplets within the dyads, that which is called the *Dukatika-paṭṭhāna*.

Then, by inserting the dyads into the triads, there is what is called the "Triad-Diad Conditional Relations" (Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna). By inserting the triads into the triads themselves, there is what is called the "Triad-Triad Conditional Relations" (Tikatika-paṭṭhāna).
And by inserting the dyads into the dyads themselves, the "Dyad-Diad Conditional Relations" (Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna) is demonstrated.

First, here in the Positive Conditional Relations (Anuloma-paṭṭhāna), the method of the Triad Conditional Relations has been demonstrated. Likewise in the Negative Conditional Relations (Paccanīka-paṭṭhāna)...
In the *Anulomapaccanīka-paṭṭhāna* (Positive-Negative Exposition) and the *Paccanīkānuloma-paṭṭhāna* (Negative-Positive Exposition), the twenty-fourfold *Samanta-paṭṭhāna* is taught.

Herein, "positive" (*anuloma*) and "negative" (*paccanīka*) are each twofold: positive and negative with respect to phenomena (*dhamma*), and positive and negative with respect to conditions (*paccaya*).

Among these, [the first type is illustrated by] the passage beginning, "Dependent on a wholesome phenomenon, a wholesome phenomenon [arises]," and so forth, regarding the wholesome and other categories.

The *Dhammānuloma* (Conformity of Dhammas) should be understood by way of the teaching of conformity (*anuloma*) regarding the triads of dhammas, such as the causes (*hetu*), etc., and the dyads of dhammas.

The *Dhammapaccanīka* (Opposition of Dhammas) should be understood by way of the opposition (*paccanīka*) of the triads and dyads of dhammas, beginning with: "Dependent on a non-virtuous dhamma, a non-virtuous dhamma [arises].
Likewise, the twenty-four conditions [should be understood] starting with: "By way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)."
The "conformity of conditions" (paccayānuloma) is to be understood by way of the teaching in direct order (*anulomadesanā*).
The "opposition of conditions" (paccayapaccanīka) is to be understood by way of the opposition of conditions, such as: "Not by way of the root-condition, not by way of the object-condition.

In this regard, the twenty-fourfold *Paṭṭhāna* is to be understood by way of both the conformity of phenomena (*dhammānuloma*) and the opposition of phenomena (*dhammapaccanīka*). [This concludes] the conformity of conditions.

The "negative" (paccayapaccanīka) and the "positive" (anulomika) [conditioning] are found among the twenty-four *paṭṭhānas*—such as the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna*—within each of the triplets (*tīkā*) and dyads (*dukas*).
This will become clear when the method of the text is demonstrated further on.
Since these twenty-four *paṭṭhānas* are explained by way of these triplets and dyads, they are called the "Triplet *Paṭṭhāna*"... and so forth, up to the "Dyad-Dyad *Paṭṭhāna*."

Among those triplets and dyads, each individual triplet and dyad is analyzed in detail by means of seven great sections—each consisting of seven sub-sections—according to the fourfold method of the positive and other modes (anuloma, etc. of these twenty-four conditions, beginning with the root condition (hetupaccaya).

By which seven? The Section on Dependent (paṭicca-vāra), the Section on Co-nascent (sahajāta-vāra), the Section on Conditioned (paccaya-vāra), the Section on Supported (nissaya-vāra), the Section on Conjoined (saṃsaṭṭha-vāra), and the Section on Associated (sampayutta-vāra).

"Pañhāvāra" (The Chapter of Questions) refers to these [sections]. Among them, that which is stated by means of the expression "dependent on" (*paṭicca*), such as "dependent on a wholesome state (*dhamma*), a wholesome state [arises]," is called the "Dependent Chapter" (*paṭiccavāra*).

By means of expressions such as "co-nascent with" (*sahajāta*), "conditioned by" (*paccaya*), "supported by" (*nissāya*), "conjoined with" (*saṃsaṭṭha*), and "associated with" (*sampayutta*)—as in "co-nascent with a wholesome state," "conditioned by a wholesome state," "supported by a wholesome state," "conjoined with a wholesome state," and "associated with a wholesome state"—[the respective chapters are established].

The five sections beginning with "conascent" (*sahajāta*) have been stated. Furthermore, in the two subsequent sections on "associated" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) and "conjoined" (*sampayutta*), both the conditions and the conditionally arisen states are treated solely by way of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
In the remaining four sections and in the seventh section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), they are treated by way of both material and immaterial phenomena.

In the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*) and the section on support (*nissayavāra*), they are treated by way of conascence, post-nascence, and pre-nascence. In the remaining sections, they are treated by way of conascence alone.
This is the distinction: [in the previous sections] the conditions and the conditionally arisen states were explained;

however, in the seventh section, because each respective question has been raised according to the method beginning with "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*), and then all those questions have been unraveled according to the method beginning with "Wholesome roots [are conditions] for the associated aggregates," etc., [the exposition is complete].
Having been made into groups and analyzed, that section is therefore known as the "Section on Questions" (*pañhāvāra*) because it has been thoroughly analyzed according to questions.

Thus, by means of these seven great sections, all the triplets and dyads in the twenty-four *samantapadṭhānas* have been analyzed in detail according to the positive order (*anuloma*) and other modes of the twenty-four conditions. How so? In the *Anulomapaṭṭhāna*:
For indeed, that which is called the *Paṭṭhāna* of Triplets, based on the twenty-two triplets, was explained first of all.

Therein, the "wholesome triplet" (*kusalattika*) is analyzed according to the fourfold method beginning with the positive order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*), by means of these great sections starting with the "Dependent Section" (*paṭiccavāra*).
Among those, this very first one called the "Dependent Section" is twofold: by way of enunciation (*uddesa*) and exposition (*niddesa*).

Therein, the Section on Enumeration (uddesavāra) is called the "Section on Questions" (pucchāvāra) because it proceeds by way of questioning the arising of wholesome and other states—both those associated with wholesome states and those dissociated from unwholesome states—by means of conditions such as the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya).
It is also called the "Section on Designation" (paṇṇattivāra) because it establishes only the questions themselves; for there is no answering therein. This is the Section on Exposition (niddesavāra).

However, in the section on interrogation (*pucchāvāra*), it proceeds by way of only those questions that are applicable, without raising inappropriate questions such as, "Could an unwholesome state arise dependent upon an unwholesome state? and so forth.
But in the others—namely, the [twenty-two] triplets beginning with co-nascence (*sahajāta*), the remaining triplets, and all the other matrices (*paṭṭhāna*)—it is the same.

There is no section on questions (*pucchāvāra*); rather, only the full range of answers (*vissajjana*) as they are applicable has been shown. This, in brief, is the determination of the text (*pāḷivavatthāna*) here.
Now, however, from the very beginning, the method of analysis (*vibhaṅganaya*) should be understood in this way.

For, in the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna*, within the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, regarding the first of the seven great sections (*mahāvāra*) of the "Wholesome Triplet" (*kusalattika*), namely the "Dependent Section" (*paṭiccavāra*), in its "Question Section" (*pucchāvāra*)—

To this extent: “Could a wholesome state arise conditioned by a wholesome state through the condition of root? … [and so on] … an unwholesome state? … [and so on] … an indeterminate state? … wholesome and indeterminate states? … unwholesome and indeterminate states? … wholesome and unwholesome states?
… Could wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states arise conditioned by a wholesome state through the condition of root?”
Seven questions based on the wholesome term have been extracted.

Likewise [those] based on the unwholesome term and the indeterminate term. “Could there be an unwholesome [state] dependent on both wholesome and indeterminate states? … Could there be an unwholesome [state] dependent on both unwholesome and indeterminate states?
… Could there be an unwholesome [state] dependent on both wholesome and unwholesome states? … Could there be a wholesome [state] …” [and so forth].

“Dependent on unwholesome and indeterminate states”—these are the two-rooted [formulations]. There are seven questions for each of the three-rooted [formulations], making forty-nine questions rooted in the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
By this same method, the remaining questions rooted in the other conditions should also be understood, such as:

“Could a wholesome state arise dependent on a wholesome state by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*)... up to ... by way of the non-disappearance-condition (*avigata-paccaya*)? This is the method for the single-rooted [formulations].

And just as it is with the single-rooted [formula], so too is it with the two-rooted [formula], beginning with: "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state may arise by way of root-condition and object-condition...
[and so on] ...by way of root-condition and non-disappearance-condition," and so forth;
and likewise: "By way of root-condition, object-condition, and predominance-condition... [and so on] ...by way of root-condition, object-condition, and proximity-condition... [and so on]."

The methods (naya) are to be understood through the sections beginning with "by way of root-condition, object-condition, and non-disappearance-condition," and so forth, from those based on three roots up to the end of those based on all roots. This is the method based on the root-condition.
And just as it is in the case of the root-based [method], so too: "Dependent upon a wholesome state, might a wholesome state arise..."

The method should also be understood for those sections based on the remaining conditions, beginning with "by way of the object condition" (ārammaṇapaccayā). This concludes the section on the positive order of conditions (paccayānulomavāra).

By this same method, the section on the negative order of conditions (paccayapaccanīkavāra)—which is applicable in all its modes, beginning with "Could it be that, dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of not-root condition" (nahetupaccayā)—is also to be understood. [And likewise: "Could it be that... a wholesome state ... arises by way of root condition" (hetupaccayā).

The positive-negative application of conditions (*anulomapaccanīka-paccayavāra*) is also presented by such passages as, "Not by way of object-condition" (*nārammaṇapaccayā*). Furthermore, the negative-positive application of conditions (*paccanīyānuloma-vāra*)—such as, "Could a wholesome state...
arise without the root-condition but with the object-condition" (*siyā kusalaṃ dhammaṃ... uppajjeyya nahetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā*)—is to be applied everywhere.
This, then, is the method regarding the section on questions (*pucchāvāra*).
As for the Section on Exposition (Niddesavāra), since wholesome and unwholesome states do not arise simultaneously,
it proceeds by way of the exposition of only those questions that receive an answer— having set aside those questions such as "Dependent on a wholesome state,
a wholesome state arises," which do not receive an answer at all. In this regard, it is as follows:
The method: “Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of root condition.
Dependent on one wholesome aggregate, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises; dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise.
Dependent on a wholesome state, an indeterminate state arises by way of root condition. In the wholesome...”

Dependent on aggregates, mind-originated matter arises. Dependent on a wholesome state, both wholesome and indeterminate states arise by way of root condition. Dependent on one wholesome aggregate, three aggregates and mind-originated matter arise;
dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate and mind-originated matter arise; dependent on two aggregates...
“Two aggregates and mind-produced matter”—thus, among the seven questions based on the wholesome category, only three that were obtainable were answered.
Likewise, there are only three for those based on the unwholesome category. However, among those based on the indeterminate category, [it is asked]:
“In dependence upon an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises by way of root condition. [That is,] resultant-indeterminate...”
Dependent on one functional indeterminate (kiriyābyākata) aggregate, there arise three aggregates and mind-produced matter … dependent on two aggregates,
there arise two aggregates and mind-produced matter. At the moment of rebirth-linking, dependent on one resultant indeterminate (vipākābyākata) aggregate,
there arise three aggregates and kamma-produced matter … dependent on two aggregates, there arise two aggregates and kamma-produced matter.

“Dependent on the aggregates (khandhas), there is the base (vatthu); dependent on the base, there are the aggregates. Dependent on one great primary element (mahābhūta), there are three great primary elements...

[and so on] ...dependent on two great primary elements, there are two great primary elements. Dependent on the great primary elements, there is mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa), and derived matter (upādā-rūpa).
Thus, it is only one [formula]. And in the sections beginning with the “Two-rooted” (Dvimūlika), it says: “Dependent on wholesome and indeterminate states, an indeterminate [state arises]...”
“A state arises by way of root-condition (*hetupaccaya*): dependent on wholesome aggregates and great elements, mind-originated matter [arises]”—this is one.
Likewise, “dependent on both unwholesome and indeterminate [states],” and so forth;
thus, among the forty-nine questions based on the root-condition, only nine possible ones were provided with answers. The remaining forty are futile questions.

They were not answered. Thus, in the subsequent sections on the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and so forth, those questions remaining unanswered should be understood as "vain questions" (moghapañhā).

However, it should be understood that all such questions—both those found and those not found in the section on questioning (pucchāvāra)—were nonetheless shown by the Blessed One for the purpose of facilitating understanding.

In this context, "dependent on a wholesome state" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca*) means: having depended upon—that is, having approached—a single wholesome state among the co-nascent aggregates, such as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), etc.;
the meaning is that it has reached [it] by way of a similarity consisting in simultaneous arising.

For here the prefix *pati-* has the sense of "similarity," as in the case of terms like "counter-person" (*paṭipuggala*). "Wholesome state" (*kusalo dhammo*) refers to the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*) and so forth.
A wholesome state that has arisen. "Arises" means that it reaches the stages of arising and so forth from its manifest state, or it acquires its own being.

Regarding "by way of cause-condition": one should understand the meaning as follows—it does not arise depending merely on wholesome states alone, but rather it arises by means of a wholesome root which establishes the status of being a cause-condition.
Having thus given the general answer "it arises" to the question "would it arise," he now states "a single wholesome aggregate," and so forth,

in order to show specifically, by way of the aggregates that are the conditions and the conditioned, which phenomena arise dependent upon which phenomena. For here, one aggregate [arises] for only one...

Or rather, two [factors] do not become conditions for only two, nor do two become conditions for just one; therefore, it should be understood that without singling out those specific modes, all remaining conditionally arisen factors—such as "dependent on one aggregate, three aggregates arise"—are shown by way of their status as conditions. This applies everywhere in the subsequent sections as well. Since the meaning of "dependent" (*paṭicca*) is the same as the meaning of "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*), in order to show that which is co-nascent with the wholesome and also receives the condition of root (*hetupaccaya*), it is said:
"the resultant-indeterminate and the functional-indeterminate. Here, in the context of the condition of root, those things lacking roots (*ahetuka*) should not be included.
Although the basis (*vatthu*) is already included by the mention of "derived matter" (*kaṭattārūpa*) in the phrase "dependent on the aggregates, [there arise] the bases," etc.,...
This was stated for the purpose of showing the arising of the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) dependent upon the [material] basis (vatthu).

However, the passage beginning with "one great primary element" (ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ) is for the purpose of showing the arising of the indeterminate material (rūpābyākata) dependent upon the indeterminate material.

Furthermore, in this context of the root-condition (hetupaccaya), the relationship of condition and conditioned should be understood as being mutual among those mind-born (cittaja) factors that provide support, as well as among those born of kamma (kammaja) at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
This is because there is no arising of mind-produced or temperature-produced matter and so forth without a cause, due to the absence of those causes as conditions.

The statement beginning with "mind-produced [matter] dependent on the great primaries" is stated for the purpose of showing the arising of derived matter and so forth dependent on the great primaries.
By this same method, the meaning of the answers regarding the object-condition and the others should also be understood.
Regarding the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*): "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the object condition.
Dependent on one aggregate... [etc. ...dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise. Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises... [etc.
...dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises by way of the object condition. [This includes] resultant-indeterminate..."

“Dependent on one functional-ineffective (kiriyā-byākata) aggregate … [and so on] … two aggregates; at the moment of rebirth-linking, dependent on one resultant-ineffective (vipāka-byākata) aggregate … [and so on] … two aggregates;
dependent on the [heart-]base, the aggregates”—thus three [answers] were given.

The remaining [answers] were not included because they involve a mixture with material form (rūpa), and because material form does not arise by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). For that very reason, “dependent on the base …” [is stated].

Having stated, "dependent on [the heart-base], the aggregates [arise]," it was not said, "dependent on the aggregates, the bases [arise]. And here, regarding "object condition" (ārammaṇapaccaya), the meaning should be understood as follows:
a wholesome state arising dependent on a co-nascent (sahajāta) wholesome state, by means of another sixfold condition that is an object (ārammaṇa) but not co-nascent with it.
For [an object condition] does not [apply to] what is co-nascent with itself.
Having made it the object, consciousness and mental factors arise.

In the case of the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), the answer is similar to that for the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*). However, in the cases of the proximity and contiguity conditions (*anantara-samanantara*), because of the absence of material form (*rūpa*), it is similar to the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
In the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) as well, it is similar to the root condition. Regarding the arising of the indeterminate (*abyākata*) in dependence upon the indeterminate:

But: "In dependence on one external great primary... [and so on] ...two great primaries. In dependence on the great primaries, derived matter... [and so on] ...one nutriment-produced great primary... [and so on] ...two great primaries...
[and so on] ...one temperature-produced great primary... [and so on] ...two great primaries...
[and so on] ...in dependence on one great primary of non-percipient beings... [and so on] ...two great primaries... [and so on] ...kamma-born matter."

The term “derived matter” (*upādārūpa*) is added here. The same applies to the mutuality condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*). The only difference is that in that case, kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) and derived matter are not included, because they lack the quality of being a mutual condition for one another. Regarding the support condition (*nissayapaccaya*), the answer is similar to that of the conascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*).
However, since the meaning of "conditioned by" (*paṭicca*) here is that of "conascent," the prenascent supports such as the eye and so forth [are not included] here.

"Not taken" means: even in the case of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), because there is an absence of the state of being produced by the decisive support condition for matter, the answer is exactly the same as for the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
However, regarding the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*): "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the prenascence condition.

One wholesome aggregate... [and so on] ...two aggregates. [Dependent on] the physical basis (*vatthu*) by way of the prenascence condition. Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome [state arises]... [and so on]."
“Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate [state arises]... by way of prenascence condition. One resultant-indeterminate or functional-indeterminate aggregate...
up to two aggregates; [dependent on] the physical basis by way of prenascence condition. Thus three questions are answered.
Therein, “dependent on the physical basis by way of prenascence condition” is stated for the purpose of excluding object-prenascence. That—

For this [text] establishes the status of being a pre-arisen condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) for eye-consciousness and the rest alone, but not for the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); thus it is not included here.

Furthermore, the post-arisen condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) is not found among immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) here. Among material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*), it is merely a supporting condition and not a productive one;
therefore, such statements as "dependent on an indeterminate phenomenon (*abyākata-dhamma*), an indeterminate phenomenon arises" cannot be said.
This is not included. Regarding the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), three questions are answered just as in the case of the condition of object (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Regarding the condition of kamma (*kammapaccaya*): "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the condition of kamma.
Dependent on one wholesome aggregate... [etc. ...a neutral state arises... [etc. ...and mind-originated matter... [etc. ...the wholesome..."
And the indeterminate states... [and so on] ... "mind-originated matter. Thus there are three [categories] in the wholesome section, and likewise in the unwholesome section.

In the indeterminate section, however: "dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate [state arises]... [and so on] ... dependent on one aggregate that is resultant-indeterminate or functional-indeterminate... [and so on] ...
dependent on the great elements, mind-originated matter, kamma-born matter, and derived matter."
“For non-percipient beings... pe ... the derived matter consisting of kamma-produced matter”—thus there are three [answers].

“Dependent on wholesome and indeterminate states, an indeterminate [state arises]... pe ... dependent on wholesome aggregates and the great primaries, mind-originated matter [arises]”—by such passages, the answer is similar to that for co-nascence (sahajāta).
For the conditions of absence (natthi) and disappearance (vigata), it is similar to that for object (ārammaṇa).

Thus, having shown the answers to the questions regarding the conditions available for all [twenty-four] conditions, it follows that the root, predominance, jhāna, and path conditions are identical to one another.
The object, proximity, contiguity, strong-dependence, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions are identical to one another.
The conascence, mutuality, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions are identical to one another. In the repetition condition, the resultant state is not obtained.

Having stated that, by way of the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*) and derived materiality (*upādā-rūpa*) are not obtained, and so forth—thus describing the mutual similarity among the conditions—it further states of them:
"Nine under the root condition (*hetu*); three under the object condition (*ārammaṇa*); nine under the predominance condition (*adhipati*);

three under the proximity and contiguity conditions (*anantara-samanantara*); nine under the conascence condition (*sahajāta*); three under the mutuality condition (*aññamañña*); nine under the support condition (*nissaya*); three under the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*); three under the prenascence condition (*purejāta*)."

“In the case of repetition, three; in the case of kamma, nine; in the case of result, one; in the case of nutriment, nine; in the case of faculty, nine; in the case of jhāna, nine; in the case of path, nine;
in the case of association, three; in the case of dissociation, nine; in the case of presence, nine; in the case of absence, three;

in the case of disappearance, three; in the case of non-disappearance, nine. Thus, for each of the conditions beginning with the root-condition, the enumeration of the sections of questions and answers has been stated; this is the method based on a single root.

Just as it is with the single-rooted [formula], so too in the cases of the two-rooted and others, up to the end of the all-rooted, the method should be applied accordingly, starting from "with root condition, object condition," and so forth.
Even in the Pāḷi, without showing the detailed method, the classification of the number of answer-sections is shown by such statements as "With root condition, in the case of the object, three.
This is the method for the positive order of conditions (paccayānuloma).

Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises by way of the root-condition. Rootless...”

Dependent upon one great primary … [and so on] … dependent upon great primaries, mind-produced [matter arises].
"Material form, kamma-produced material form, derived material form... [and so on] ...dependent on one great primary... [and so on] ...derived material form"—these two [answers] have been given.

[dependent on] two aggregates, two aggregates [arise]. Dependent on an unwholesome state... pe ... [dependent on] two aggregates, two aggregates [arise]. Dependent on an unwholesome state... pe ... [dependent on] two aggregates, two aggregates [arise]. Dependent on an unwholesome state... pe ... [dependent on] two aggregates, two aggregates [arise]. Dependent on an unwholesome state... pe ... [dependent on]
The indeterminate... [and so on] ...dependent on unwholesome aggregates, mind-produced matter arises.

Dependent on an unwholesome state, both unwholesome and indeterminate states [arise]... [and so on] ...dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate [state arises]... [and so on] ...dependent on the great elements...
[and so on] ...kamma-produced matter and derived matter. Dependent on both wholesome and indeterminate states, an indeterminate [state arises]... [and so on].
“Dependent on wholesome aggregates and great primaries, mind-originated matter [arises]. Dependent on unwholesome and indeterminate states, an indeterminate [state arises]...
[and so on] ...dependent on unwholesome aggregates and great primaries, mind-originated matter [arises].
Thus nine questions are answered. The conditions of proximity (anantara) and contiguity (samanantara) are not similar to the condition of object (ārammaṇa).

In the case of the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*): dependent on a wholesome state, an indeterminate [state arises]... [and so on] ...dependent on wholesome [states], mind-originated matter [arises].
Dependent on an unwholesome state, an indeterminate [state arises]... [and so on] ...dependent on unwholesome [states], mind-originated matter [arises].
Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate [state arises]... [and so on] ...dependent on resultant-indeterminate or functional-indeterminate aggregates...
Mind-produced matter. At the moment of rebirth-linking, in the case of resultant indeterminate [states]... [and so on] ...kamma-produced matter.
Dependent on the great primaries, there is mind-produced matter, kamma-produced matter, and derived matter. Dependent on external great primaries, there is derived matter.
Dependent on nutriment-produced great primaries, there is derived matter. Dependent on temperature-produced [great primaries],... [and so on] ...derived matter.

Dependent on the great primary elements of non-percipient beings, there is derived matter that is the result of past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). Dependent on wholesome and indeterminate states, there is an indeterminate [state]...
[and so on] ...dependent on wholesome aggregates and the great primary elements, there is mind-originated matter.
Dependent on unwholesome and indeterminate states, there is an indeterminate [state]... [and so on] ...dependent on unwholesome aggregates and the great primary elements...

And "dependent on [the four mental aggregates], mind-originated matter"—thus five [answers] are given. Therein, "dependent on resultant indeterminate aggregates, kamma-produced matter" should be understood as excluding the heart-base.
The non-strong-dependence condition (*naupanissaya-paccaya*) is not similar to the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). Regarding the non-prenascence condition (*napurejāta-paccaya*):
"dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome [state arises]... in the formless realm, dependent on a wholesome [state]... two aggregates."
“Dependent on the wholesome, the indeterminate... [and so on] ...mind-produced matter. Thus there are two [instances] in the wholesome section;

likewise in the unwholesome section as well. “Dependent on the indeterminate, the indeterminate... [and so on] ...in the formless realm, the resultant indeterminate and the functional indeterminate...

[and so on] ...the external... [and so on] ...derived matter. Dependent on both wholesome and indeterminate states, the indeterminate [arises]. [Dependent on] the wholesome aggregates and the great elements...”
And dependent on [the mind], mind-originated matter. Unwholesome and indeterminate... pe... dependent on unwholesome aggregates... pe...
and matter—these are the three [questions] answered sevenfold. The postnascence and repetition conditions are not similar to the predominance condition.
Therein, the occurrence of the repetition condition should be understood by way of the first impulsion (javana) of wholesome, unwholesome, and functional states.

Regarding the kamma-condition (*nakammapaccaya*), three answers are given: "Dependent on the wholesome, there is the wholesome: wholesome volition (*cetanā*). Dependent on the unwholesome, there is the unwholesome: unwholesome volition.
Dependent on the indeterminate, there is the indeterminate: resultant and functional volition. [Also] external, nutriment-produced, and temperature-produced."
Regarding the non-resultant condition (*navipāka-paccaya*): "Dependent on the wholesome, there arises the wholesome and the indeterminate; the wholesome and the indeterminate.
Thus, there are three [answers] for the wholesome category, and likewise for the unwholesome category. "Dependent on the indeterminate...

[omitted] ...external, nutriment-originated, temperature-originated, non-percipient... [omitted] ...derived matter... [omitted] ...dependent on the unwholesome and the indeterminate, there arises the indeterminate. These are the nine answers.

In the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*): “Dependent on the indeterminate, arises the indeterminate: external temperature-born, non-percipient... [etc. ...derived matter. There is only one such instance.

In the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*): “Dependent on the indeterminate, arises the indeterminate: external nutriment-born... [etc. ...temperature-born... [etc. ...dependent on the great elements of non-percipient beings, arises the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*). There is only one such instance. In the jhāna condition (*jhāna-paccaya*):

“Dependent on the indeterminate, arises the indeterminate: associated with the fivefold sense-consciousness... [etc. ...external nutriment, temperature, non-percipient, and derived matter. There is only one such instance.
Regarding the path-condition (*magga-paccaya*): "Dependent on the indeterminate, there arises the indeterminate. [This includes] rootless resultant-indeterminate and functional-indeterminate...
[etc. ...mind-originated... [etc. ...at the moment of rootless rebirth-linking, resultant... [etc. ...and kamma-produced matter... [etc.
...external, nutriment, temperature, non-percipient, and derived matter. Thus, there is only one.
The dissociation condition (navippayuttapaccaya) is not the same as the object condition (ārammaṇapaccaya).
Regarding the dissociation condition: "Dependent on the wholesome, there is the wholesome. In the immaterial plane, only the wholesome. Dependent on the unwholesome... [etc.

...in the immaterial plane, the unwholesome. Dependent on the indeterminate, there is the indeterminate; in the immaterial plane, the resultant-indeterminate and functional-indeterminate. External, non-percipient... [etc. ...and derived matter."

These three questions have been answered. The conditions *non-existence* (*natthi*) and *disappearance* (*vigata*) are not similar to the condition *object* (*ārammaṇa*). However, in this context, all four—namely *conascence* (*sahajāta*), *dependence* (*nissaya*), *non-existence* (*natthi*), and *disappearance* (*avigata*)—are not obtained.

Having thus shown the answering of the questions found in the negative (paccanīka) section, [it continues] from there: "In the case of non-root (*na-hetu*), two. In the case of non-object (*nārammaṇe*)..."
Five. Nine by way of predominance. Five by way of proximity, contiguity, mutuality, and decisive support.
Seven by way of prenascence. Nine by way of postnascence and repetition. Three by way of kamma. Nine by way of resultant. One by way of nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path.
Five by way of association. Three by way of dissociation. Five by way of absence and disappearance.”
The enumeration of the sections of answers has been stated; this is the method based on a single root.

By this same method, the appropriate method should be applied to those based on two roots and so forth. However, in the Pāḷi, the enumeration of the sections of answers is shown by way of the negative conditions (*paccanīya*), beginning with: "With the absence of the root condition, there is one [answer] for the non-object condition," and so on.
This is the method of negative conditions. Following exactly what has been stated by this method: "Dependent on a wholesome state, an indeterminate state arises by way of the root condition."

The method for answering questions should be understood according to the positive-negative method (*anuloma-paccanīya-naya*) by way of such passages as “not by way of object-condition” (*nārammaṇa-paccayā*), and according to the negative-positive method (*paccanīya-anuloma-naya*) by way of such passages as “dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises not by way of root-condition, but by way of object-condition” (*akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca akusalo dhammo uppajjati nahetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā*).

However, in the Pāḷi here, only the enumeration of the sections for the answers is shown. This is the section on the “Dependent” (*paṭicca-vāra*) in the Positive-Negative Wholesome Triplet (*anuloma-paccanīya-kusalattika*).

In the sections on co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth, as well as in the six sections, the method should be applied everywhere according to what was stated in the section on dependence (*paṭicca*).
However, those specific textual variations and specific meanings that are found here and there should be understood in their entirety from the *Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi* and its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) alone.
Here, however, even if all of them were presented by way of summary, it would result in excessive bulk for the book.
"Performing" is not shown. However, in those sections:
"A wholesome state arises conditioned by a co-nascent wholesome state; conditioned by a wholesome state...
supported by a wholesome state... associated with a wholesome state... a wholesome state..."
“A wholesome state arises through the condition of association. Thus, the course of the text should be understood from the beginning in these five sections.

Among them, *paṭicca* (dependent) and *sahajāta* (conascent) have the same meaning; *paccaya* (condition) and *nissaya* (support) have the same meaning; *saṃsaṭṭha* (conjoined) and *sampayutta* (associated) have the same meaning.
Therein, in such passages as “conascent with a wholesome state,” [it means] conascent with that wholesome state by depending upon it.
The meaning should be understood according to the appropriate context starting from the words "having sacrificed" (*hutvā*), etc. However, in the final section of questions (*pañhāvāra*):

"A wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*) is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*). Wholesome roots are a condition for their associated aggregates (*sampayutta-khandha*) by way of the root-condition.
A wholesome [state] is a condition for the indeterminate (*abyākata*)... [and so on] ...for both the wholesome and the indeterminate... [and so on] ...wholesome [roots]."
Regarding the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*): "The roots [are related] to the associated aggregates and to mind-produced matter," and so forth.
Regarding the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*): "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the object condition.
Having given a gift, undertaken virtue, and performed the Uposatha duty, one reviews that. [One reviews] former well-performed deeds... having emerged from jhāna, one reviews the jhāna..."
Trainees review change-of-lineage, purification, and the path. Trainees or worldlings practice insight into the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Through the knowledge of penetration into others' minds, they know the mind of one possessing a wholesome state of consciousness.

Wholesome [consciousness] pertaining to the base of infinite space is a condition, by way of object-condition, for wholesome [consciousness] pertaining to the base of infinite consciousness. Wholesome [consciousness] pertaining to the base of nothingness...

Wholesome aggregates belonging to the wholesome state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are related to the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, and the knowledge of the future, by way of object-condition.
Wholesome [states] are related to unwholesome [states]... [as before] ...having given a gift... having performed [a deed], one relishes it and delights in it; taking that as an object...
Lust arises. Wrong view, doubt, restlessness, and displeasure arise. One relishes former good deeds … [and so on] … displeasure arises.
Having emerged from jhāna, one relishes the jhāna … [and so on] … restlessness arises.
When jhāna has been lost, displeasure arises in one who feels remorse.
The wholesome is a condition for the indeterminate... [etc. ...condition. An Arahant reviews the Path. He reviews past deeds well done... wholesome... [etc. ...he contemplates with insight... [etc.

...the result arises as an object-condition (tadārammaṇa). Wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space is a condition for the resultant or functional consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness...
[etc. ...for the resultant and functional consciousness of the base of nothingness... [etc. ...Wholesome aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of penetration into others' minds... [etc. ...
[An unwholesome state] is a condition for the adverting of knowledge of the future.
An unwholesome [state] is a condition for an unwholesome [state]... [as appropriate]. One relishes lust... agitation arises. An unwholesome [state] is a condition for a wholesome [state]...

[as appropriate]. For a trainee, [the state of] defilements already abandoned... [is a condition] for knowledge of the future. An unwholesome [state] is a condition for the indeterminate... for an Arahant, [the state of] defilements already abandoned... [is a condition].
[The unwholesome] to the defilements... [and so on] ...to adverting.
The indeterminate to the indeterminate: the Arahant reviews the fruit; he contemplates Nibbāna; he contemplates the eye...
[and so on] ...tangible object. He sees a visible form with the divine eye... [and so on] ...the functional state of the base of nothingness... [and so on] ...to the functional.
The visible-object base is a condition for eye-consciousness... [and so on] ...for advertence. The indeterminate is a condition for the wholesome...
for the fruit of the trainee... [and so on] ...for the knowledge of future existences. The indeterminate is a condition for the unwholesome... [as in] "one relishes the eye," and so forth;

thus it is shown as a condition by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). And as a condition by way of the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), [it is shown as]: "The wholesome is a condition for the wholesome by way of the predominance-condition. [It is twofold: predominance as object (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*). As predominance as object: having given a gift... and so forth.
“Wholesome is a condition for wholesome by way of proximity-condition,” and so forth, in detail, regarding the conditions of proximity, contiguity, co-nascence, mutuality, and support;
and regarding the object-condition, according to the method stated as: “Wholesome is a condition for wholesome by way of decisive-support-condition.
[It is] object-decisive-support, proximity-decisive-support, and natural-decisive-support. Object-decisive-support: having given a gift... and so forth.

“Proximity-predominance condition (*anantarūpanissaya*): ‘Preceding wholesome aggregates [are the condition] for succeeding ones,’ etc., according to the method stated under the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
Natural-predominance condition (*pakatūpanissaya*): Relying on faith... one performs the Uposatha rite;
one arouses jhāna, insight, the path, direct knowledge, and attainment. Virtue, learning...”
Generosity, wisdom, and so forth, by way of decisive support... the preliminary work for the first jhāna is a condition for the first jhāna by way of decisive support-condition...
the base of nothingness is [a condition] for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... the knowledge of recollecting past lives is [a condition] for the knowledge of future existences...
the preliminary work for the first path is [a condition] for the first [path]... the third path is [a condition] for the fourth. The path is [a condition] for those in training (*sekha*).

The decisive support for the analytical knowledge of meaning … [and so on] … for skill in [discerning] the possible and the impossible. Wholesome [states] are the decisive support for unwholesome [states] … [and so on] … as object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*).
Natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) … [and so on] … natural decisive support: relying on faith, one arouses conceit;
one adopts wrong view … [and so on] … Faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom are the decisive supports for lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong view. Aspiration … [and so on] …
The wholesome [state] is a condition for the indeterminate... [etc. ...by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇūpanissaya). By way of proximity-predominance (anantarūpanissaya).

By way of natural-predominance (pakatūpanissaya)... [etc. ...natural-predominance: by relying on faith (saddhā), one torments oneself... [etc. ...for bodily pleasure, for pain, and for the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
Wholesome kamma is a condition for its result (vipāka)... [etc. ...the Path is a condition for the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) in an Arahant.
An unwholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state... [etc. ...as natural decisive support: depending on lust (*rāga*), one kills living beings...

[etc. ...one utters frivolous speech... [etc. ...one causes a schism in the Saṅgha. Depending on hatred (*dosa*), delusion (*moha*), conceit (*māna*), wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), or longing (*patthana*)...

[etc. ...one causes a schism in the Saṅgha... [etc. ...the taking of life is a condition for the taking of life... [etc. ...for the formal act of causing a schism in the Saṅgha... [etc. ...is a condition.
The unwholesome [state] is a condition for the wholesome... [and so on]... as natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*): relying on lust (*rāga*), one gives a gift...

[and so on]... one arouses the Path (*magga*)... [and so on]... one arouses meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). Lust... [and so on]... aspiration (*patthanā*). It is the decisive support for faith (*saddhā*), virtue (*sīla*)... [and so on]... wisdom (*paññā*).

Having killed a living being, one gives a gift for the sake of warding off the reaction to that [act], and so forth; thus it is also [illustrated] in the case of the decisive-support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
“An indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of prenascence-condition … [etc. … As object-prenascence: an Arahant contemplates the eye … [etc. … tangible objects;
he contemplates the physical basis … [etc. … he sees forms with the divine eye … [etc. … The visible-form base is a condition for eye-consciousness … [etc.
… As basis-prenascence: the eye-base is a condition for eye-consciousness … [etc. … the physical basis.”
By the passage beginning with "of the indeterminate [states] of maturation" (*vipākābyākatānaṃ*), etc., [it is shown] regarding the pre-nascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*);

by the passage beginning with "the wholesome [state] of the indeterminate... the wholesome aggregates arisen later (*pacchājātā*) [are related] to this body arisen earlier," etc., regarding the post-nascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*);
and by the passage beginning with "the wholesome [state] of the wholesome... the preceding wholesome aggregates," etc., regarding the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*).

Regarding the kamma condition (*kammapaccaya*), [it is stated]: “Conascent wholesome volition (*sahajātā kusalā cetanā*)... [and so on] ...is related to its associated aggregates (*sampayuttakānaṃ khandhānaṃ*) and to mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ*).

Asynchronous [volition] is related to resultant aggregates (*vipākānaṃ khandhānaṃ*) and to kamma-born matter (*kaṭattā rūpānaṃ*),” and so forth. Regarding the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*), [it is stated]:
“An indeterminate [state] is related to an indeterminate [state]... [and so on] ...one aggregate is related to three [aggregates],” and so forth.

In the case of the nutriment condition and others, it is stated as “the wholesome [is a condition] for the wholesome,” and so forth; and in the case of the dissociation condition and others, it is stated as “the wholesome [is a condition] for the indeterminate:
by way of co-nascence, post-nascence, and for the material phenomena produced by consciousness that are co-nascent. By way of post-nascence, for this body... [and so on].
The indeterminate [is a condition] for the wholesome... [and so on]. The pre-nascent physical basis is a condition for the wholesome aggregates by way of the dissociation condition,” and so forth.
And the course of the text should be understood.

In this context, as for what is called a wholesome state (*kusaladhamma*), when it arises, it does so by means of twenty-two conditions, setting aside the postnascence condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*) and the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*). And when acting as a condition for a wholesome state, [it does so] setting aside the prenascence, postnascence, resultant, and dissociation conditions.

There is a condition by way of the remaining twenty conditions. Thus, the wholesome [states] are conditions for the wholesome and so forth, and the unwholesome are conditions for the unwholesome and so forth, each according to its appropriate correspondence.
Therefore, the Chapter on Questions (Pañhāvāra) was stated in order to show the specific classification of the conditions arising from each of those wholesome states and the rest.
In that context, "trainees and change-of-lineage" is said with reference to the stream-enterer; "purification" refers to the once-returner and the non-returner.
For them, the change-of-lineage consciousness is called purification (*vodāna*). "Emerging from the path" means emerging from the cognitive sequence of the path;
for there is no such thing as a reviewing consciousness immediately following the path. This is the method of the triad of the wholesome in the *Anuloma Paṭṭhāna*.
In the triads of feeling and so forth: "Dependent on a state associated with pleasant feeling, [arises] a state associated with pleasant feeling..."
“Dhamma arises by way of root-condition (*hetupaccaya*): dependent on one aggregate associated with pleasant feeling, two aggregates [arise];

dependent on two aggregates, one aggregate [arises]”—following this sequence as stated in the *Kusala-ttika*, there are seven sections beginning with the “Dependent Chapter” (*paṭiccasamuppādavāra*) and ending with the “Questions Chapter” (*pañhavāra*).
In each of these, one should apply the methods (*naya*) such as the positive conditions (*paccayānuloma*), the single-root method (*ekamūla*), and so forth.
Furthermore, this method of enumeration should be understood by applying it according to the terms found in all the triads (*tikkas*).
In that regard, because the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) is not included in the triad of feeling, it is stated: "dependent on one aggregate, two aggregates," and so forth.
In all instances, the specific details should be understood in accordance with the Pāḷi and its commentary. This is the method of the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* in direct and reverse order.
In the *Dukapaṭṭhāna*, however, it is said: "Dependent on a state that is a cause, a state that is a cause arises by way of the cause-condition (*hetupaccaya*).

Dependent on non-greed, there arise non-hatred and non-delusion. Dependent on non-hatred and non-delusion, there arises non-greed and non-hatred. Dependent on greed, there arises delusion. Dependent on delusion, there arises greed.
Dependent on hatred, there arises delusion. Dependent on delusion, there arises hatred. At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), dependent on a state that is a cause..."
“Dependent on a non-root phenomenon, a non-root phenomenon arises... [and so on] ...both root and non-root phenomena.
Thus it is stated in the Root-Duo (*hetuduka*). Also:
“Dependent on a phenomenon with a root, a phenomenon with a root arises by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*). Dependent on one phenomenon with a root...”

“Dependent on an aggregate... [etc. ...dependent on a state with root-cause (sahetuka). Dependent on a state without root-cause (ahetuka)... [etc. ...mind-produced matter. At the moment of rebirth-linking... [etc.
...dependent on both a state with root-cause and a state without root-cause... [etc. ...dependent on an aggregate without root-cause, [arise] aggregates without root-cause.
Dependent on delusion accompanied by doubt or accompanied by restlessness, [arise] the associated aggregates... [etc. ...mind-produced matter; nutriment-produced matter,” and so forth.
Regarding the "Duo with Cause" (sahetuka-duka) and the others— excluding the "Duo Knowable by Some" (kenaci-viññeyya-duka)— among all these duos,

one should understand the method of analysis (vibhaṅga-naya) by applying it appropriately according to the sequence explained in the "Wholesome Triplet" (kusalattika), following the seven great sections beginning with the "Dependent Chapter" (paṭicca-vāra),
each of which contains the four methods (naya) beginning with the "Positive Condition" (paccayānuloma). This applies throughout the entire [work].
Indeed, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, no dyad cognizable by any [consciousness] is found; such is the method of the dyad-presentation (*duka-paṭṭhāna-naya*).

However, in the dyad-triad presentation (*duka-tika-paṭṭhāna*), having joined the wholesome term from the wholesome triad with the root dyad (*hetu-duka*)—beginning with "Dependent on a wholesome state that is a root, a wholesome state that is a root arises by way of root-condition" (*hetuṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca hetu kusalo dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayā*)—and so forth, within the sections beginning with the "Dependent Chapter" (*paṭicca-vāra*).

In seven sections, the conditions obtained by way of the four methods—beginning with the method of conformity (*paccayānuloma*)—are shown through the methods starting with the "single-root" (*ekamūlaka*).
Just as the wholesome section was presented, so too the unwholesome and the indeterminate sections were presented by joining them with the dyads of roots (*hetudukka*) according to the stated method;
thus, it is established as the "Wholesome Root Dyad Triplet. However, the actual text (*pāḷi*) is extremely abbreviated. Just as...

The triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*) is thus presented; likewise, by means of the available phrases beginning with, "Dependent on a state associated with pleasant feeling that is a root-cause, there arises a state associated with pleasant feeling that is a root-cause, by way of root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*), the triads of the feeling-triad (*vedanāttika*) and so forth are also joined with the dyad of roots.
Thus, twenty-one dyads and triads, such as the triad of roots and feelings, have been shown. Just as...
Thus, twenty-two tetrads have been combined with the "root-duality" (sahetuka-duka) by way of the terms that are obtained together with it;
in the same manner, twenty-two tetrads should be combined individually with all [the other categories], beginning with the "root-duality.

However, the Pāḷi here and in all subsequent sections is extremely abbreviated. Having thus taken the twenty-two tetrads and added them to the hundred dualities, the *Dukatika-paṭṭhāna* has been taught.
This is the method of the *Duka-Tika Paṭṭhāna*. In the *Tika-Duka Paṭṭhāna* as well,

by joining the "root" category with the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*)— beginning with the formula, "Dependent on a wholesome state that is a root, a wholesome state that is a root arises by way of root-condition"—
one proceeds according to the fourfold method of the positive and other modes of conditions within the seven great sections, such as the section on dependence (*paṭiccasamuppāda-vāra*).
The available conditions have been shown through all the rounds, beginning with the single root and so forth.

Just as the "root" category was treated, so too the "not-root" category is established by being joined with the wholesome triad (*kusala-ttika*), forming the "wholesome-root triad-duad" (*kusala-hetu tika-duka*).

And just as the root-duad was joined with the wholesome triad, so too [the not-root-duad is joined] by means of such formulations as: "dependent on a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling that is a root," and so forth.
Having applied that [method] to the triads of feeling and so forth as well, the twenty-one triads and dyads beginning with the triad of feeling and the dyad of feeling were shown.

And just as with the dyad of causes, all [the other dyads] beginning with "with cause" (sahetuka) are likewise applied individually according to the basis of the terms found in each of the twenty-two triads.
Thus, having inserted one hundred dyads into the twenty-two triads, the *Paṭṭhāna* of Triads and Dyads was taught.
This is the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* regarding the triads and dyads.

In the *Tikatikapaṭṭhāna* as well, the wholesome triad is [treated] in conjunction with the feeling triad and so forth, beginning with: "Dependent on a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling, a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling arises by way of the root condition (*hetupaccaya*)," and so on.

The conditions have been shown by applying the triplets to one another, as well as the triads of feeling and so forth to the triads of the wholesome and so forth, according to the method already stated.

Thus, by inserting triads into the very triads, the *Paṭṭhāna* of the Triplet-Triads has been taught; this is the method of the Triplet-Triad *Paṭṭhāna*. In the *Duka-Duka Paṭṭhāna* as well, it is said:
"Dependent on a state that is a root and accompanied by a root, a state that is a root and accompanied by a root arises..."

By means of the phrase “conditioned by cause,” etc., the dyads of causes are shown through their association with the dyads of "with-cause" and so forth, and the dyad of "with-cause" is associated with the dyads of "cause" and so forth, according to the methods explained below.
Thus, by inserting dyads into dyads, the *Paṭṭhāna* of dyads within dyads has been taught; this is the method of the dyad-dyad *Paṭṭhāna*.
Such, then, is the case in the Positive *Paṭṭhāna*.
The excellent and most supreme *Paṭṭhāna* consists of the Triplets and Couplets,
the Couplets and Triplets, the Triplets and Triplets,
and the Couplets and Couplets.
"The six methods in the direct order are very profound.

Thus, the six methods should be understood. Furthermore, within each of these six matrices (*paṭṭhāna*) according to conditions, by way of the four methods—direct order of conditions and so forth—in this manner, this *Dhamma-anuloma-paṭṭhāna* is adorned with twenty-four methods.
This should be understood. This is the method of the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna* (Positive Compendium).

In the *Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna* (Negative Compendium), however, it is stated: "Dependent on a state that is not wholesome (*nakusala*), a state that is not wholesome arises by way of the root condition (*hetupaccaya*).
Dependent on one unwholesome or indeterminate (*abyākata*) aggregate (*khandha*)... [and so on] ...dependent on two aggregates, and mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*)" and so forth.
In the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*: “Dependent on a state that is not a cause (*nahetu*), a state that is not a cause arises by way of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*).
Dependent on one aggregate that is not a cause... [and so forth] ...and mind-originated matter,” and so on; and in the *Dukapaṭṭhāna*:

“Dependent on a state that is neither a cause nor wholesome (*nahetu-nakusala*), a state that is neither a cause nor wholesome arises by way of the root-condition. [Dependent on] a state that is neither a cause nor wholesome...”
In the *Duka-Tika Paṭṭhāna*, by way of such passages as, “dependent on one indeterminate aggregate (khandha), three aggregates [arise]”;
and in the *Tika-Duka Paṭṭhāna*, by way of such passages as, “dependent on a state that is neither wholesome nor a root-cause (nahetu), a state that is neither wholesome nor a root-cause arises”;
and [in the *Tika-Tika Paṭṭhāna*], “dependent on a state that is neither wholesome nor associated with pleasant feeling (nasukhāya vedanāya sampayutta), a state that is neither wholesome...”
In the *Tikatikapaṭṭhāna* (the "Three-by-Three" Exposition), by such passages as, "A state associated with feeling arises," and in the *Dukadukapaṭṭhāna* (the "Two-by-Two" Exposition),
by such passages as, "Dependent on a state that is neither-root nor accompanied-by-root, a state that is neither-root nor accompanied-by-root arises by way of root-condition"—

in all [these cases] as stated in the six expositions, namely the six expositions beginning with the *Anulomika-paṭṭhāna* (the Positive Exposition) among the six types of negative expositions (*paccanīyapaṭṭhāna*).

The method of the Pāḷi should be understood in this way. And because this [section] proceeds by way of negating the state of being conditionally arisen for phenomena such as the wholesome and those such as the roots, it is known as the *Dhammapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna* (the Section on the Antithesis of Phenomena).

For therein, "dependent on a phenomenon that is not wholesome" is the negation of the condition for the wholesome; "a phenomenon that is not wholesome arises" is the negation of the state of being conditionally arisen for the wholesome.

Likewise, the meaning here should be understood through such methods as: “Dependent on one unwholesome or indeterminate aggregate... [and so forth]... unwholesome or indeterminate aggregates and mind-produced matter arise.
Thus, in this context of the Negative Conditional Relations (Paccanīya Paṭṭhāna), it is said:
“The excellent Triad and the most sublime Duka—”
The dyads-and-triads and the triads-and-dyads,
as well as the triads-and-triads and the dyads-and-dyads—
these six methods in the section on opposites are profoundly deep.
The six methods (nayā) already mentioned should be understood here as well.

Furthermore, by way of the four methods—namely, the forward order and so forth—applied to each individual condition, this *Dhammapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna* should be understood as being adorned with twenty-four methods.
This is the method of the *Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna*.
In the *Anulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna*, however, it is stated in the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* as: “Dependent on a wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises by way of root-condition;
dependent on wholesome aggregates, mind-originated matter [arises],” and so forth; and in the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* as:
“Dependent on a state that is a root, a state that is not a root arises by way of root-condition,” and so forth.
In the *Duka-Tika Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated: “Dependent on a root wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*), a non-root non-wholesome state (*nahetu nakusala-dhamma*) arises,” and so forth;
in the *Tika-Duka Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated: “Dependent on a root wholesome state, a non-root non-wholesome state arises,” and so forth;

and in the [Tika-Tika], “Dependent on a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling (*sukhāya vedanāya sampayutta*), a non-wholesome state not associated with pleasant feeling [arises],” and so forth.

The method of the Pāli should be understood in its entirety according to the manner explained below, both in the *Tikatikapaṭṭhāna*— beginning with “A concomitant state arises”— and in the *Dukadukapaṭṭhāna*— beginning with “Dependent on a root, root-possessing state, a non-root, non-root-possessing state arises.
This [explanation] does not reject the conditionality of states such as the wholesome and so forth.

Because it proceeds by way of negating the wholesome and other qualities of the conditionally arisen states, it is called the *Dhammānuloma-paccanīya-paṭṭhāna* (the Positive-Negative Exposition of Phenomena).

For therein, the phrase "dependent on a wholesome state" establishes the conditionality of the wholesome, while the phrase "an unwholesome state does not arise" excludes the possibility of that wholesome state being the conditionally arisen result; therefore, [it says] "dependent on wholesome aggregates..."

It should be understood that the answer has been stated by such passages as "matter originated by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ*). Thus, herein in the Positive-Negative Section (*anulomapaccanīyapaṭṭhāna*):
"The excellent Triplets and the supreme Couplets, the Couplets-and-Triples and the Triples-and-Couplets;"
“The *tika-tika* and the *duka-duka*:
these six methods in the positive-negative sequence are very profound.
Thus, the six methods should be understood. Furthermore, here too, by way of conditions, for each one of the four—namely, the positive conditions and so forth—there are...
It should be understood that this *Dhammānuloma-paccanīya-paṭṭhāna* is adorned with twenty-four methods by way of the four methods;
this is the method of the *Anuloma-paccanīya-paṭṭhāna*. In the *Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna*:
"Dependent on a state that is not wholesome, a state that is unwholesome... [etc. ...dependent on a state that is not wholesome..."
In the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*, [it is stated]: “Dependent on [a] determinate state, an indeterminate state arises by way of the root-condition,” and so forth;
in the *Dukapaṭṭhāna*: “Dependent on a state that is not a root, a state that is a root arises,” and so forth; and in the *Dukatika-paṭṭhāna*:
“Dependent on a state that is neither a root nor wholesome, a state that is a root and unwholesome... [and so on] ...a state that is a root and indeterminate arises,” and so forth.

And [it is stated] in the *Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna*: “Dependent on a state that is neither wholesome nor a cause, a state that is unwholesome and a cause... [and so on] ...a state that is indeterminate and a cause arises”;

and [it is stated]: “Dependent on a state that is neither wholesome nor associated with pleasant feeling, a state that is unwholesome and associated with pleasant feeling... [and so on] ...a state that is indeterminate and associated with pleasant feeling...”

The method of the Pāḷi should be understood according to the manner explained below, both in the *Tikatikapaṭṭhāna*— such as, "A state associated [with consciousness] arises"— and in the *Dukadukapaṭṭhāna*— such as,
"Dependent on a state that is neither a root nor accompanied by a root, a state that is a root and accompanied by a root arises. Furthermore,
this [section] refutes the conditionality of wholesome and other such states, and of those...
Because it proceeds by way of not denying the state of being conditionally arisen, it is called the *Dhammapaccanīyānuloma Paṭṭhāna* (the Positive-Counterpositive Exposition of Dhammas).
In that context, "not a wholesome dhamma" is a negation of the status of being a condition for the wholesome;

"an unwholesome dhamma arises" is a specification of the arising of the unwholesome. However, because there is no arising of the wholesome dependent upon the wholesome [in this specific formulation],...
Instead of saying "a wholesome state arises," it is stated as "an unwholesome state arises" according to the available wording.
For there is no such thing as a wholesome state that arises by making another wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate state its co-nascent condition;
therefore, the teaching is given by way of the unwholesome and the indeterminate. It is the same elsewhere.
Thus, herein, in the *Dhammapaccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna*:
“The excellent and most sublime *Tika-paṭṭhāna*,
the *Duka-tika*, and the *Tika-duka*;”
“The threefold and the twofold sets, and the six methods in the positive-negative order—these very deep methods should be understood as having been stated.
Thus, the six methods are to be known. Furthermore, here too, according to the conditions—as in the *Tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth—in each one of them, there are the positive conditions and so on.
It should be understood that this *Dhammapaccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna* is adorned with twenty-four methods by way of four sets of four methods according to a single formulation;

this is the method of the *Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna*. Thus, among the four *paṭṭhānas* beginning with the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna*, for each individual *paṭṭhāna*, [the Blessed One taught] only the triads, dyads, and so forth.
The great treatise, the *Paṭṭhāna*, has been taught adorned with twenty-four methods (*naya*) according to each respective method.

Furthermore, regarding these twenty-four *paṭṭhānas* by way of conditions (*paccaya*), each one is adorned with ninety-six methods—four methods for each of the twenty-four *paṭṭhānas*—by way of the four methods beginning with the forward order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*). This is by way of the phenomena (*dhamma*) alone.
This treatise is stated as the twenty-fourfold *Samantapāṭhāna*; this is the method of analysis (*vibhaṅganaya*) here.
The commentary on the meaning of the *Paṭṭhāna-mātikā* within the *Mohavicchedanī*, the commentary on the meaning of the Abhidhamma matrices, is completed.
The Concluding Statement:
And to this extent,
the commentary on the meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrix has been undertaken.
May all those who have attained the goal— just as this work named *Mohavicchedanī* has reached its conclusion, which is longed for by the modest—
may they all, being at peace, fulfill their noble aspirations.
That which is profound and brings fear, like the ocean to those who are timid—
even for the wise at the time of examining the texts—
of that Abhidhamma, [this is] the first disappearance.
Like inscriptions on stone revealing hidden treasures, this Pāḷi and its commentary are the illuminators of the meaning of the Dhamma;
like a ship upon the ocean,
they are a path for easy crossing— pure and unconfused.
Furthermore, they are unconfused and unmixed by way of their respective schools;
therefore, with mindfulness for the sake of the endurance of the True Dhamma, one should listen respectfully.
One who desires the endurance of the True Dhamma should refrain from self-exaltation and so forth.
By me also, while expounding it with a pure mind,
this commentary on the matrix (mātikā) has been composed according to my ability,
reaching its conclusion in a textual tradition (tanti) measuring thirty-three recitation-sections (bhāṇavāra).
This compendium of all things, with its orderly sequence of words,
may I— having attained supreme enlightenment through whatever merit has been gained—
bring all living beings to their ultimate goal with a mind intent on their welfare.
Of the Coḷa kingdom, which is exceedingly delightful to many people,
which supports the burden of the bearer of the royal lineage,
and which is a sanctuary of welfare through the pure waters of the Kāverī;
In the midst of that lineage, well-nourished by the most excellent royal dynasty,
there was a path marked by the stain of the Coḷas,
yet filled with great families of vast wealth.
It was provided with ramparts, moats, and gate-towers,
with royal highways crowded with people and well-prepared,
and with all kinds of wealth for enjoyment and use.
It was resplendent with various shops filled with beautiful goods;
it was the delight and protector of Coḷa, Ādhipura, and Nandana,
where those who take pleasure in the excellent monasteries of the Sugata dwelt.
Upon their mouths, which were honored by the great image of the Teacher that captivates the hearts of men and are worthy of respect by the virtuous,
there shone the rays of knowledge like the rising sun upon the eastern mountain.
With shrines resembling the peak of Mount Kelāsa,
with excellent palaces, pavilions, and gabled halls,
and with rows of rose-apple, mango, palmyra, and breadfruit trees;
With gate-towers made of pure white plaster,
resembling the coils of the excellent serpent Nandopananda,
and joined by spacious pavilions of white sand;
Dwelling in the excellent monastery called Nāgārjunavana,
which is frequented by the Saṅgha who are well-restrained in virtue and devoted to wholesome deeds,
and where offerings have been brought with joy.
He who by name is honored as the foremost of those who uphold the ascetic virtues (dhuta),
whose wisdom is like the moon risen in the clear sky,
and who is skilled in other teachers' doctrines as well as in the Three Piṭakas—
He who sports like the king of beasts in the forest of the assembly of disputants,
and like the ocean does not overstep the boundary of his virtue,
his self adorned with the essence of qualities such as fewness of desires;
He illuminates the stainless teaching, abandoning everything impure,
while carefully elucidating the Dhamma and Vinaya. Therefore,
[he is one who] has scattered throughout the ocean of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—
Having extracted [the essence] like a collection of jewels from the heart of the meaning,
this *Ratanāvalī* has been composed to sever delusion and to serve as an ornament for the throat of one who understands correctly.
May it shine forth this evening, radiant with excellent praise;
having rightly dispelled the darkness of delusion regarding all phenomena,
may the light of the Conqueror’s teaching continue to shine as long as—
May it endure, bringing benefit to the people.
Thus ends the *Mohavicchedanī* (The Dispeller of Delusion), composed by the Elder Mahākassapa in the Coḷa kingdom.
The commentary on the meaning of the Abhidhamma matrix is completed.
